[h2]Resident Evil 3 Remake: A Classic Vibe Cut Short[/h2]

As a massive, longtime fan of the Resident Evil franchise, stepping back into the chaotic streets of Raccoon City is always a thrill. Resident Evil 3 Remake successfully captures the traditional survival horror content and atmosphere we expect from the series. Despite revisiting an older chapter of the franchise, the gameplay feels incredibly engaging. However, it is not without a few noticeable flaws and missing pieces.

[h3]Pacing, Length, and Story[/h3]
Let’s get the biggest critique out of the way first: the game is incredibly short. 

[list]
[*][b]Playtime:[/b] Compared to other modern Resident Evil titles, RE3 Remake is a sprint. You can comfortably complete a standard playthrough in about 5 to 8 hours.
[*][b]Narrative:[/b] The storyline is just "so-so." It serves its purpose by pushing you from point A to point B while fleeing from danger, but it doesn't offer the deep, sprawling narrative or emotional beats found in other entries. 
[/list]

[h3]Gameplay and Mechanics[/h3]
The mechanics are a mixed bag of great additions and noticeable absences:

[list]
[*][b]The Dodge Mechanic:[/b] The inclusion of a dedicated dodge mechanic is the highlight of the combat system. Mastering the perfect dodge is incredibly satisfying and absolutely vital for survival.
[*][b]No Stealth:[/b] If you are hoping to crouch and sneak past the undead, you are out of luck. There are zero stealth mechanics present here; you either fight, run, or dodge. 
[*][b]No In-Game Merchant:[/b] Unlike the beloved merchant system in RE4 or RE7, there is no in-game shop accessible during the main storyline. You rely entirely on what you can scavenge in the environment. 
[/list]

[h3]Combat, Enemies, and Resource Management[/h3]
While the gunplay is solid, the enemy design and placement can be frustrating.

[list]
[*][b]Buggy Encounters:[/b] In certain areas, zombie placement feels bugged. You will occasionally find enemies glitching or present in zones where they seemingly shouldn't be, which can break the immersion.
[*][b]The "Unkillables":[/b] Special mention goes to the bullet-sponge, seemingly unkillable zombies. Do not waste your ammo on these guys!
[*][b]Hardcore Mode Warning:[/b] If you are playing on Hardcore mode, engaging these sponges is a trap. They will consume all your hard-earned resources and leave you completely dry for upcoming fights. Just use your dodge mechanic, weave past them, and save your gunpowder.
[/list]

[h3]The Final Verdict[/h3]

[b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*]Captures the traditional, classic Resident Evil atmosphere.
[*]The dodge mechanic is a lifesaver and adds a great layer of skill to combat.
[*]Highly engaging moment-to-moment gameplay.
[/list]

[b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*]Far too short (5-8 hours).
[*]Storyline is relatively weak ("so-so").
[*]Buggy enemy placement in certain zones.
[*]Resource-draining, unkillable enemies that discourage actual combat.
[/list]

A complete and utter insult to Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, and one of the single worst Resident Evil games. It genuinely might be worse than RE6.
-Completely gutted of content, including the RPD section (Jill's one, anyway), clock tower section, Grave Digger, choice system, alternate weapons, and Mercenaries (which is hilarious, because RE3 was the original debut of Mercenaries).
-Jill in this game is completely out-of-character for Jill Valentine and all-around unlikeable. Her "cool" moments generally consistent of being moderately rude to Carlos for no reason or just swearing without saying anything clever, because saying the epic f*ck word is really cool and epic.
-Carlos has most of his charm and character stripped away, including his chauvinism and the scene of him suggesting that he and Jill "choose when they die", if you catch my (and his) meaning.
-Nemesis is completely and utterly ruined, completely missing the unique and disturbing "almost human" appeal of Nemesis in the original game. His voice is so garbled and "generic monster-y" that it just sounds like growling rather than him saying "STARS", his new designs are terrible (ESPECIALLY Stage 2), and his gameplay is genuinely awful. He stalks you (THE THING HE'S FAMOUS FOR) for ONE twenty-or-so-minute section, then becomes a disgustingly easy set of scripted boss fights for the rest of the game.
-Brad's death is a massive downgrade of not only his death in Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, but also of Marvin's infection in Resident Evil: Outbreak. The reason he dies is also massively out-of-character for Brad Vickers, whose entire character is that he's extremely cowardly.
-The amount of linear, scripted sections is insane, it genuinely feels like a third-rate Sony game.
-The game CONSTANTLY puts you in unnecessary locked animation states. A perfect example is when Nemesis roars and Jill covers her ears if you're too close. This doesn't stun you and give him opportunity to attack you, thereby discouraging proximity to Nemesis, as his recovery takes just as long as hers, if not longer. It just freezes both of you in place for a few seconds and accomplishes nothing other than wasting the player's time.
-Resource management is nonexistent (at least on Normal difficulty), I had more supplies at "tense" sections of this game than resupply sections in RE5, an ACTION game where you can BUY supplies between levels.
-Difficulty is also nonexistent, 95% of any challenge I encountered came from either unfair game design or my solution being too intelligent and befitting of Resident Evil for the game to handle (e.g. trying to stun and run past the first set of Hunter Gammas).
-The only thing keeping the new version of the dodge from being absurdly broken is the fact that it barely works, and EVEN THEN it's still broken if you're patient enough.
-The writing is borderline bottom-tier, dialogue is stiff and irritating and the plot just feels like a sequence of disconnected setpieces, rather than the gradual unfolding of a Resident Evil conspiracy. Nikolai especially is painful to watch, 70% of his screentime is him being two steps removed from openly saying "I'm an evil bad guy because I'm evil and I like money".
-Various smaller aspects that are too numerous for me to list here, such as Jill's S.T.A.R.S. outfit looking absolutely horrible (they couldn't even get its color right).
TLDR, don't buy unless it's on sale for under ten bucks. This was easily one of the worst gaming experiences I've ever had, and a total disgrace to Resident Evil 3: Nemesis. The only reason to play it is so people can't say "well you haven't played it" when you say it sucks.

Resident Evil 3 Remake is a bit of a mixed bag. While it delivers a highly cinematic. It still falls short in several key areas compared to both the original and Resident Evil 2 Remake.

One of the biggest downsides is the amount of cut content. These removals not only shorten the game but also take away from the overall depth and world building.

The campaign itself is very short. My playthrough lasted around 3.5 hours, which feels underwhelming, especially when compared to the original game or Resident Evil 2 Remake, which offered longer and more replayable campaigns without sacrificing quality.

Another major change is the removal of player choices. The original featured player choice, that allowed players to influence how certain events played out. Their absence here makes the experience feel more linear and less engaging, reducing replay value and player agency.

Nemesis, despite being the face of the game, is also underutilized. Instead of being a constant, dynamic threat, he mostly appears in scripted sequences and boss fights. This takes away from the tension and unpredictability that made him so memorable in the original.

The game also leans more into action than horror. While this isn’t necessarily bad, but i was hoping for more horror elements.

Overall, Resident Evil 3 Remake feels like a solid but disappointing remake. It’s visually impressive. But lacks the depth, content, and tension needed to truly live up to the legacy of the original, especially when compared to Resident Evil 2 Remake.

If you can find it for around €9 or less, it offers decent value, but it’s hard to recommend at a higher price.

Resident Evil 3 Remake is truly an awesome game, even if it also leaves me wishing Capcom had given it more time, more content, and the full director’s cut treatment.

The best thing about this remake is how good it feels to play. The RE Engine makes Raccoon City look incredible, Jill feels great to control, the action is fast, the zombies look disgusting in the best way, and Nemesis still brings that “move now or regret your whole bloodline” energy.

 It is polished, cinematic, and easy to replay when you want a quick survival horror action run.
Jill is also fantastic here. She feels tough, exhausted, angry, and determined, which is exactly how she should feel while Raccoon City is falling apart around her. The pacing keeps things moving, the set pieces are exciting, and when the game is at its best, it really does feel like a high-quality Resident Evil remake.

But I have to be honest: as a fan of the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, this remake is missing some classic pieces that would have made it so much better. The worm boss fight, more city exploration, more of the original route variety, and other memorable sections could have made this game longer, richer, and closer to the remake it deserved to be. You can feel the greatness here, but you can also feel the empty rooms where more game should have been.
That is what makes it bittersweet. 

I really like this remake, but I also wish Capcom would go back and make a proper Director’s Cut with the missing classic content restored. I know that probably is not going to happen, sadly, but this is one of those games where the foundation is so good that you can’t help imagining the bigger version.

Even with those complaints, I still recommend it. The gameplay is fun, the graphics are excellent, Jill is great, and it is a strong action-horror experience. Just know that if you loved the original, you may come away feeling like I did: happy with what we got, but wishing there was more of it.

Resident Evil 3 Remake is a game that gets so much flack from the community for being a complete bastardization of what the original RE3 was, with tons of cut content, mainly by either sizing down some areas, entirely cutting them, or replacing them, but with all of that considered, it's still pretty fun as someone who hasn't played the original.

An easy negative are the areas. Many of them are extremely short-lived, and by the time you truly feel like you've got a grasp on what's going on, you're already done and move on to the next. RE2's RPD is so much better compared to any area you play here; you never truly feel like you're solving or truly changing something within the environment you're in. The streets of Raccoon City could've been great, but you quickly realize that there are maybe three paths to take.
However, the worst thing is how noticeable it is when you enter an area that wasn't in the original. You run away from Nemesis, and all of a sudden, sewer section. It genuinely feels so out of place and shoehorned in. By the end, when I reached NEST 2, I just rolled my eyes; it didn't have the atmosphere of the original NEST, nor did it feel like it expanded the world in any major way. It was just a very obvious "We ran out of time" moment.
So what you're left with are two quite short areas that are original but not mind-blowing.

Another thing that kind of bothered me was the lack of puzzles.
As much as I was annoyed by Resident Evil 2's combat, the puzzles still always delivered and genuinely made me feel smart.
Resident Evil 3 Remake has almost no puzzles. Sure, you can count the railway, but even when they try, they, just like the areas, feel short-lived and not memorable.

So, why do I still enjoy this game? Well, the combat is so much better.
In RE2 I felt like the zombies, the lack of enemy variety, and the bosses were all a hassle. They didn't scare me; they annoyed me to no end.
Resident Evil 3 fixes that with one simple thing: adding a dodge.
This one change makes the combat feel so much more dynamic and fun. Not only can you do a perfect dodge, but Carlos has a full-on counter. Yes, this makes the game a bit more action-oriented, though I wouldn't say by much as you quickly realize the dodge is only useful with a very small group of enemies. The moment you get rushed by bigger groups you realize that the better option is to either run or use your gun.
Enemy variety also has been improved. It's not even just them reusing all the enemies from the Remake, but they actually add a few that spice up the gameplay and need a bit more firepower, or a well-timed dodge.
Bosses benefit from the combat the most, though. Sure, you fight Nemesis like 90% of the time, making it a typical "How many times do we have to teach you this lesson, old man"-situation, but I'm more glad that I'm not running in circles anymore. Bosses have proper attack patterns, and multiple attacks, and it does not feel like I'm playing Dead by Daylight in a confined space. They perfectly fit the more action-oriented combat without fully losing their menacing factor.
Oh yeah, and there are also two characters I should mention, Jill and Carlos. It's quite fun, since Jill feels a bit more survival-horror-like as you get ambushed by everything, and while you have strong weapons you still can quickly run out of ammo. Carlos spices it up, by bringing more confident-feeling sections thanks to his assault rifle and counter attack. It may feel weird for such a short game to have two characters, but they made it work.

Ok, but what about the story? Oh my lord, it's so much more entertaining than Resident Evil 2.
The worldbuilding is a bit more shallow; I mean, it makes sense - they barely flesh out the areas.
Ending-wise, it also kinda sucks, cause it's the same "I wanna burn Umbrella down" shtick we already heard from Leon.
But the dialogue and characters are so much more entertaining. Within the timeline, it starts a few days or so before RE2's story starts, but it ends a few days after RE2, I assume. This makes the story feel more involved, as there are still many characters present who either try to flee or rescue others. Thanks to that, we meet Carlos, who actually works for Umbrella. This immediately makes Jill not really a fan of him, while he tries his best to prove his only intention is to save people. Their dynamic is so much better than what Leon and Ada had, as they play off each other really well without this stilted dialogue. Carlos especially is my favorite; he is so welcoming and kind but doesn't lose track of the situation he's in.

Overall, I absolutely get why people would dislike this game, but for me, the combat and story added and improved enough that this ended up being quite fun. 7/10.

I recently played Resident Evil 3 and decided to finally leave a review after owning it for a while (2023). Once again, the RE Engine delivers impressive results—graphics and performance are excellent. The lighting and depiction of Raccoon City are particularly well done and really stand out.

Compared to RE2, Nemesis felt more like an occasional annoyance than a constant source of fear. Mr. X in RE2 created a stronger sense of tension and horror. I think RE3 could have benefited from making Nemesis encounters more unpredictable or threatening, possibly with more impactful jump scares or higher risk moments.

Another downside for me was the dodge mechanic. It feels clunky and inconsistent at times. Maybe it becomes more useful on higher difficulties like Nightmare, but on a first playthrough it didn’t feel very reliable.

Overall, it’s not a bad game, but I don’t think it justifies full price. Fortunately, it often goes on sale, which makes it a much easier recommendation for what it offers.

What is here is pretty good, it just feels like there is not enough of it. 5.5 hours for a first playthrough, where I feel I explored everything I could is just not acceptable at this price. The fact it was bundled with some forgettable multiplayer mode that nobody asked for suggests the developers were aware of that. Buy it on sale though. It's worth it.

I did have a good time with it despite the incoming rant, Jill is a great protagonist, Carlos is solid too, and the dialogue is engaging throughout. It just does not really feel like survival horror. Ammunition is fairly plentiful, especially when playing as Carlos, and you almost always have the tools needed to deal with whatever the game throws at you.

Nemesis is also a bit of a letdown. He is supposed to be this constant, overwhelming threat, but like Mr. X, he mostly ends up being annoying. The difference here is just how heavily scripted he feels. One of the things I loved in the previous game was the sense of exploration, and there is almost none of that here. Nemesis will simply script his way onto the screen and interrupt whatever you are doing.

It quickly becomes predictable. I move, Nemesis jumps onto a lamppost in front of me. I run away, and he does the exact same thing again. And again. The triggers are so obvious that any sense of tension disappears, leaving it more frustrating than exciting.

I actually did not mind the boss fights. They are a bit bland, but having a proper dodge mechanic makes them more enjoyable than expected.

Overall, this feels like a step back from the Resident Evil 2 remake. The gore seems toned down, the zombies feel less consistent in their behaviour, in a way that is not always satisfying, the exploration is minimal, and the puzzles are extremely basic. It still looks brilliant, but I did notice a few performance stutters during my playthrough.

Disclaimer: I never played the original Resident Evil 3, so I have zero basis for comparison between the old-school version and this remake. Take my thoughts with a grain of salt… or maybe a green herb.
I liked this game — not quite as much as the RE2 Remake, but it was still a solid, action-movie-style romp through zombie-infested Raccoon City. Think less “survival horror puzzle fest” and more “explosive B-movie blockbuster with guns and screaming.”
It’s noticeably shorter than RE2 and has way fewer puzzles. In fact, the game feels like it’s sprinting from set piece to set piece. Speaking of short… Jill’s hairstyle? Absolute perfection. She was cute as heck in this one. Her character modeling gets an easy A++. Capcom clearly spent extra time making sure she looked like she could kick ass and star in a shampoo commercial.
The weapons felt satisfying, and the enemy variety was a big step up from the RE2 Remake — way more creepy crawlies and mutated horrors to keep things fresh. It had fewer genuine scares but way more explosive, over-the-top fun.
The supporting characters from Umbrella were… fine, I guess? They’ll probably vacate my brain by next week, like most disposable henchmen in a zombie outbreak.
Nemesis, on the other hand, was awesome. Cool design, relentless, and ridiculously hard to put down (again… and again… and again). The guy just wouldn’t stay dead. Still, Mr. X from the previous game still haunts my dreams more. Sorry Nemesis — you brought the rockets, but trench-coat guy brought the trauma.
Overall, it was a fun, fast-paced trip through Raccoon City. Short stay, but a total blast while it lasted.
Final score: 7/10. That’s one point lower than my 8/10 for the RE2 Remake, so I guess I’ll leave that extra point in the item box. Maybe Capcom can borrow a first-aid spray to soothe that burn.

Resident Evil 3 has turned into the black sheep of the REmake family and, despite this positive review, I must admit that it took me years to finally go back to and finish it. While it is by no means perfect, it's frequently on sale for under $10 and, at that price, it's a very fun survival horror game that gets a little too much hate.

I say a *little* too much hate because there are some glaring flaws, both compared to other REmake games and the original Resident Evil 3 Nemesis, and most of the criticism is very fair.

Coming off the heels of RE2, RE3 was an undeniable disappointment. It's extremely linear, it's significantly shorter, and and it seems like this was done at the expense of tacking on a multiplayer mode no one asked for or wanted. Compared to the original, they cut massive segments out of the game (the only REmake to have done this), and whittled the Nemesis encounters down to a few scripted events and boss fights. 

Still, there are a lot of positives. It's a fairly competent retelling of Resident Evil 3, with largely minor events changed (and only one ending). The actual gameplay is legitimately better than 2. The standard zombies feel less bullet-spongey, and Jill and Carlos feel a lot less sluggish than Leon and Claire, even without taking the dodge/parry mechanics into consideration. The only negative is that it seems like they toned down some of the dismemberment animations for the zombies from 2. 

When I first played this game in 2020 and paid full price, I felt burned. Expectations were sky-high from the Resident Evil 2 Remake, and it just didn't live up to them. I fully understand all of the criticism this game gets both as a follow up to that, and when compared to the original game. Still, it is by no means a BAD game, and it's absolutely worth buying on sale and playing if you're a Resident Evil fan.

I'm pretty sure most of the hate on this game is coming from the comparisons to the original and just how amazing Nemesis probably was as an antagonist in that game. But coming into this without any prior RE3 knowledge, I absolutely loved this game. For me, thought the pacing and sense of progression worked really well with a shorter run time compared to other modern RE games- though I get why paying full price for a 5 hour game would be kinda disappointing and I know that the team could have delivered more. But the game finds its niche nicely in the modern remake series, with gameplay that is not as methodical as 2 but not as action packed as 4. Everything feels dangerous but it's never so oppressive- you still feel like Jill the "supercop". She's great as a protagonist, and I found her energy and bluntness a lot of fun. I really loved this game and while it's definitely weaker that 2 and 4, the comparisons really didn't lessen the experience for me.

The game also just looks absolutely stunning even on a lower end device like my PC. Ray tracing and lighting are fantastic and add so much to the atmosphere. I played with a few mods for some updated character models, an alternate costume and better camera, which was a nice bit of personalization that I don't think hindered the original game design. An all-around great experience- cannot wait to dive into Requiem!!

A lot of folks complain about how short this remake is, but honestly I don't mind it. Not every game needs to be a 30-40 hour marathon packed with filler just to justify its price. RE3R feels more like a tightly paced experience, something you can finish in a couple of sittings without it overstaying its welcome.

What it lacks in length, it makes up for in intensity. The game constantly throws you onto Nemesis and rarely lets up. The pacing is almost like a high-budget action-horror movie rather than a slow burn. That might not what the fans of the original wanted, but it works on its own terms.

Replayability also helps offset the shorter runtime. Unlockables, higher difficulties, and trying to optimise your runs give you reasons to come back.

That said, I do understand the criticism. Some sections feel extremely trimmed down, and it would’ve been nice to see more content or areas expanded. But what’s here is polished and consistently engaging.

If you go in expecting a compact, action-heavy Resident Evil experience, there’s a lot to enjoy!

I played the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis when I was younger, so I only vaguely remember the story—but I can tell right away that Resident Evil 3 Remake takes a very different approach. Some sequences and locations feel unfamiliar, especially the RPD section. I clearly remember a cutscene with Brad Vickers, and Jill Valentine being able to explore the RPD before Carlos Oliveira, which doesn’t seem to play out the same way here.

On top of that, Raccoon City itself feels scaled down—it’s almost like it’s been reduced to just a couple of streets and a donut shop rather than the sprawling, interconnected urban nightmare I remember from Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.

The game is definitely immersive, but Nemesis didn’t land the same for me. In the original, he felt like a constant, terrifying presence. Here, he comes off more like an annoyance—almost like dealing with Ashley Graham, except this time it’s something actively trying to kill you. The boss fights with him can be frustrating too, especially when he keeps moving around and you’re just waiting for the right moment to land enough shots to take him down.

Gameplay-wise, it’s classic Resident Evil—inventory management is key. You have to choose your loadout carefully and save resources for later. It’s a familiar system, but still satisfying.

Overall, I still had fun with the game, but not nearly as much as with the original. It ends up feeling like a very different experience rather than a true reimagining of what made the original so memorable.

Resident Evil 3 Remake is a survival horror game about former S.T.A.R.S police officer Jill Valentine, who is on the run from Nemesis, who wants to destroy all of the S.T.A.R.S officers. She teams up with mercenary Carlos to find a vaccine and get out of Raccoon City from this zombie apocalypse. My mutuals have told me that out of all the Resident Evil games, this is the shortest to beat. The remake took a lot of stages away from the original, from what I’ve heard. I can’t say if it’s for pacing reasons, the developers didn’t have time, or felt unnecessary for them, since I haven’t played the original game. So while I can’t say for sure whether taking the stages out helped the remake or not for the game itself, it’s definitely better than Zero. The graphics are the same as Resident Evil 2 Remake, where it does look impressive, but it does feel like it’s a bit too similar looking. It’s cool that we get to go outside since it’s usually more inside, and the design of Nemesis looks fantastic. This is quite a beast that I honestly thought I could do the same as everyone else and try to avoid it.

That’s where I went wrong, as Nemesis will go faster than you and will never stop until it neutralizes Jill. It’s honestly a smart enemy to deal with, where I have to change my strategy and figure out how to progress while being chased down by not only dodging and weaving, but also taking down the foot to slow it down. People had issues with the fact that this is more reliant on action than survival horror, but I didn’t mind it just because I thought it handles the action well through its set-pieces, which are fun to watch and play. There was a moment that was straight out of Call of Duty Zombies that gave me a nice piece of nostalgia. It was interesting seeing how Jill was doing, as she clearly is traumatized from the first game, even if it doesn’t go further than I want it to go on a character progression. If anything, Carlos had more of a character arc than Jill did. The bosses were a lot of fun, and I felt the runtime, while shorter than usual, was honestly fine enough that it didn’t drag or feel rushed.

Would it be better as DLC for Resident Evil 2 Remake? Probably, since it does look too similar in some moments, whether it be the graphics or even when Jill goes down the sewers, that gave me flashbacks to the second game, which had my least favorite level in it. The worst part of the game, in my opinion, is Nicholai. Even though he’s not in it much, he still is annoying when he shows up, that’s only there to be an annoyance for the main character and be a stereotype that’s in it for the money. Nothing interesting, just a generic character that’s unmemorable. Regardless, Resident Evil 3 Remake is a lot of fun, which threw me off in the beginning, as I thought it was going to be harder than Zero, but once I got it figured out, it made it easier and more of a smooth experience to go through.

This "remake" hardly makes justice to the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, and while I could complain about the things and ENTIRE AREAS AND PLACES the game is missing, there is no fun in that. Instead, I'll just say this: There is fun to be had with Resident Evil 3 Remake, just that it doesn't last long

The shop is a nice addition, and the fact you can use infinite weapons on Hardcore, Nightmare and Inferno to achieve S-rank is honestly a blessing for people trying to 100% this game. The Unlockables are okay, never really cared for any of the models or concept art myself, but there's people that appreciate those sort of things and that's fine. In all, the game is pretty fun and entertaining the first time you play it. Notice how I say [first time].

However, once you finish a run on either Standard or Assisted, it practically loses all replayability and entertainment. Hardcore -a mode which lives up to its name in most entries of the saga- is, in this case, a slightly harder version of Standard; auto-saving isn't even turned off (which I'm fine with really). Barely anything changes, and it's even worse with Nightmare and Inferno. Nightmare adds a few enemies here and there to basically troll you and catch you off guard and it also changes the location of a few items, but once again that's it. Auto-saving is still turned on and it's not that different from Hardcore really. Inferno is the exact same as Nightmare, just with auto-saving turned off (finally!).

But by far the worst part of it all is how any run in Inferno is piss easy (for the most part) until the final boss. For some god-forsaken reason, they decided to make Nemesis #4 by far the hardest part of the game for that mode. Why is he so hard to beat, you may ask? Well, it all comes down to a concept we are quite familiar with: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. If you get hit even a single time by Nemesis' ♥♥♥♥♥ slap move where he slams the ground, you insta-die. It's not your usual insta-death however; instead, he just combos the same move -which stun-locks and leaves Jill completely helpless- 3 (sometimes 4) times in a row and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ kills you. It is so infuriating and unfair that it genuinely made me dislike the game even more than I did.

There is a point to be made that most of these problems and complaints are invalidated or non-existent if you are only playing the game casually and not trying to 100%. To that I say: ♥♥♥♥ off. If a videogame starts to break at its seams and show many design flaws by simply playing it long enough means that it's not a good game in the first place.

That being said though, that first playthrough is good enough that it makes the game worth a single try. Just don't buy it at full price, it is not worth more than $10 or whatever.

Resident Evil 3 is basically a high-speed panic attack from start to finish. Where RE2 makes you carefully plan every step, this game just grabs you and says, “Run. Now.” And honestly? It works.

Jill Valentine is an absolute powerhouse here—cool under pressure, taking down monsters twice her size, and still finding time to throw out some attitude. Meanwhile, Nemesis exists purely to ruin your day. You think you’re safe? You’re not. You hear that *“STARS…”* and it’s already too late.

The pacing is way more action-focused, which means explosions, chases, and barely any time to breathe. The dodge mechanic feels great when you pull it off, and the game constantly pushes you forward like it’s chasing you… because it literally is.

Carlos also deserves some love—he brings a bit of humor and charm to all the chaos:

* “Now here’s a weird ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ door!”
* “Come on! Not again!”

The downside? It’s definitely shorter than expected, and some parts feel like they could’ve been expanded more. But what’s there is polished, intense, and fun to replay—especially if you’re into speedruns or higher difficulties.

Only downside? Nemesis will live rent-free in your head for a while.

Overall: 8/10. A fast, explosive ride that doesn’t overstay its welcome—just don’t expect it to last as long as you’d like.

Not as good as the original. Not as good as the other remakes. Still a good time.

The game looks excellent and the performances are all amazing. I enjoyed the writing, in particular the various notes, as they really help to flesh out the places you visit and make them feel real and lived in. And this game does have some incredible tie-ins to re2r.

For what it is, the gameplay is good. Somewhere in between re2r and re4r, somewhat oscillating between the two, though less horror than the former and less challenge than the latter. The combat dodge is a wonderful addition for a slightly faster pacing. Plenty of fundamentals are borrowed from re2r, and that isn't a problem at all. The games should feel like two sides of the same event.
Exploration and puzzles are good, though it's hurt somewhat by not having a larger area to explore like the R.P.D. It's more linear, plopping you into a series of smaller puzzle-box areas that get progressively more linear as the tension rises, more like the sewers and especially the lab of re2r. Again, the lack of a larger space to untangle in a metroidvania fashion is unfortunate and does hurt the overall feel. More of an action-packed rush, than a slow nightmare.

And, of course, the main thing. The lack of a free-roaming, pursuer style Nemesis is sorely felt. Especially when both the original and re2r had exactly that. He doesn't exactly feel absent from the game, but not having to personally contest with him so much does put distance between the player and the antagonist. He mostly feels present through some good cutscenes, boss fights, and the one scripted chase where you actually have to manoeuvre around some other lesser enemies instead of just going down the designated corridor. But the sad truth is re3r just isn't built to accomodate a pursuing Nemesis. The areas simply aren't big enough, and the story is too linear. The solution would have been to build with that in mind from the strt. Expand an area like Downtown to somewhere he could actually roam and search, as well as letting us spend more time there. Effectively, the game needed it's own R.P.D. Gaining a few hours of playtime wouldn't hurt it at all either.

I think it says something that Nemesis here left about the same impact on me as Mr. X, when the latter had to share the spotlight with William Birkin (G) and a couple of human antagonists, as well as only really taking centre stage in Leon's scenario. Nemesis only had to share with Nikolai, who exists entirely in cutscenes. (this isn't a criticism of Nikolai as a character, since most of the human antagonists in the remake games are most prominent in, if not entirely confined to, cutscenes. It's where they're most easily characterised with plenty of dialogue and nice clean close-ups, while the non-verbal monster need to be characterised through actions and therefore best form a connection to the player through gameplay.)

All in all, a mixed bag, which is a shame considering how well re2r and re4r turned out. Both of those met the quality of the original classics, so it's unfortunate that re3 didn't get the same. Still a good game in my opinion, just not up to the high watermark. Mostly worthwhile if you're into the story and want to keep up with the remakes' timeline of events.

Despite its short duration, Resident Evil 3 delivers an intense and fast-paced experience that lingers even after completion.

From the very first minute, the game plunges you into the midst of Raccoon City's collapse, never allowing you a moment's respite. Burning buildings, sirens, dark streets… everything is so well-designed that not only progressing but even feeling the environment becomes part of the game. The atmosphere constantly creates pressure, and this feeling never disappears throughout the game.

Jill Valentine carries the story with her strong stance and determination. Her ability to maintain control even amidst the chaos makes her character even more compelling. On the other hand, the sections played as Carlos Oliveira add a different tempo to the game. Carlos's more action-oriented gameplay and perspective save the story from monotony and offer a richer experience.

Nemesis is the game's greatest signature. Not just a powerful enemy, but also a constant source of pressure. The unpredictable timing of his appearance and the challenges he poses in every encounter keep the tension at a constant level. The chase scenes, in particular, are truly adrenaline-pumping.

In terms of gameplay, the game offers a faster-paced and action-oriented structure. While this deviates somewhat from the classic Resident Evil atmosphere, it significantly improves the fluidity. You're constantly on the move, you have to make decisions, and this keeps the game from becoming boring.

On the criticism side, the biggest drawback is definitely its length. Just when you're fully immersed in the game, it can feel like it ends a little too soon. Some players might wish for more detailed exploration of certain sections. However, despite this, the experience it offers is so intense that you don't feel any emptiness while playing.

In short:
Resident Evil 3, despite its debatable length, offers an unforgettable experience with its atmosphere, pace, and character variety. If you're looking for a short but impactful game, it's definitely worth a try.

A short, linear experience, with apparently missing content from the original RE3, the Resident Evil 3 Remake isn't a bad experience for newcomers or those with little experience with the game - still being the weakest of the remakes.

Play as a combination of Jill Valentine from the Racoon Police Special Tactics and Rescue Squad (S.T.A.R.S.) and Carlos Oliveira of the Umbrella Biohazard Countermeasures Service (U.B.C.S.) in their fight against Umbrella's bioweapon - Nemesis - all while trying to escape Racoon City before it is destroyed by the U.S. government. Jill gives you access to her lockpicks, a shotgun, and a grenade launcher with four kinds of rounds (acid, explosive, flame, and mine), while Carlos has access to his machine gun, with plenty of ammunition to spare.

The timeline of this one seems to be taking place just before the events of Resident Evil 2 and continuing through, as we see the cop Leon later encounters getting bit when Carlos reaches the Racoon Police Department later in the game. Much of the game is Jill having repeated encounters, escapes, and mini boss battles with Nemesis. There is a side plot of having to find and recover a vaccine for the T-Virus, but it seems more of an afterthought considering the importance of such an item.

Gameplay is your usual survival horror fare, having inventory management in the form of juggling ammunition, weaponry, medical supplies, and puzzle items between safe rooms, solving item-based puzzles, collecting lore notes, and doing the ol' back and forth to unlock different doors in a particular area. Jill can perform a dodge roll to evade enemy attacks, while Carlos with unleash a counter-punch, knocking enemies on their backs, time slowing for a window of attack.

Damage against enemies feels a bit variable, not always taking the same amount of shots / knife hits to reliably put down a standard zombie; not taking into account the random chance to instantly destroy a zombie's head with a pistol shot. Enemies come in a few different flavours; there being your standard zombie, zombies infected by the Nemesis bioweapon, pale zombies with high regeneration, zombie dogs, lickers, and two versions of a hunter, one being a lizard-like creature, and the second being a two-footed giant mouth that can one-hit Jill with a body consuming chomp. Nemesis will come back again and again, either wielding a new weapon (flamethrower / rocket launcher) or mutating into a new form completely as it attempts to hunt down surviving S.T.A.R.S. members.

I have only played the original Resident Evil 3 once, many a year ago, so I can't comment on what content is missing and to what extent, as I simply don't remember. YMMV in this area depending on how familiar you are with this particular entry in the Resident Evil franchise.

Visually, the game does look fantastic, character models and environments being on point, making a good use of general design, colour, and lighting to great effect to bring the chaos of Raccoon City to life.

While Resident Evil 3 is the weakest of the modern Resident Evil remakes, I still think it would be a fine enough playthrough for newcomers to this title, especially considering it is regularly on sale for a few bucks.

I had never really played a Resident Evil game until recently, so my opinion on these games comes with no first-hand knowledge of the originals. I played RE2 Remake first, and absolutely adored it, so I was very excited to keep going with this game. Because of this, my review is heavily based on a comparison with RE2 Remake. The TLDR for this is that while I enjoyed the experience, I was a little bit disappointed. 

Firstly, I came into this game knowing that it was apparently more action-focused, and it is. Straight out of the gate, you're into a chase sequence with enough explosions and falling to make Nathan Drake wince. At this point, the aptly named Nemesis is probably at his scariest. He's unrelenting, but maybe this was just because it was fresh. The original game was named after him, so Nemesis is an exceptionally important part of the game, but unfortunately as the game goes on you find he's less scary and more of an annoyance at most. One thing I will say, is that the design is impeccable. He really looks awesome. In gameplay terms I understand what they were going for but I don't think it works as well as the previous game. In RE2R, Mr X is slow, but absolutely terrifying. Hearing his footsteps, knowing he is wandering around somewhere, added to the amazing atmosphere, it works so well. Clearly, the devs wanted Nemesis to be an upgrade on Mr X both in terms of lore and in gameplay. He's faster, more agile, can use weapons, and he's more durable, but unfortunately this upgrade actually downgrade's his scariness. Its impossible to make the chases with him stay scary because there is no down time. You're never able to escape, and then hear him wandering around like Mr X. In fact, there isn't really anything outside of a 5 or so minute section of the game where he really pursues you outside of scripted events. I've heard there is some cut content from the original game that had sections like this. Its a shame they took that out, because you really feel it missing. By the end of the game, Nemesis no longer feels scary. Cool yes, scary no.

I do think the move away from the 'puzzle box' style of gameplay that the first two games had was a mistake too. Speaking of which, where are the puzzles? I always got the impression that puzzles were key to Resident Evil, so the lack of them is jarring. Also, combat is just not as tactical or smart. In RE2R getting from one safe room to another felt like a puzzle in itself, even without the presence of Mr X, but in this game enemies are essentially just fodder for your growing arsenal of guns. By the end of the game I had more ammo than I knew what to do with. But that's just a design choice, they went for more of an action horror than a survival horror. Fair enough, but a shame.

So all of the complaints so far are arguable, because it really comes down to taste. If you prefer more of an action focused experience, you may not see these as negatives. However, my main disappointment is that the game just feels like a step down in quality compared to RE2R. It feels rushed, which it probably was. RE2R felt like a love letter to fans of the original game. It is one of the most polished gaming experiences I have ever had. This game though felt off. Animations sometimes looked cheap, the zombie models seem to have been downgraded a bit, the audio feels lower quality, etc. It just doesn't feel like as much effort was put into making it. 

So yeah, overall I still enjoyed the experience, bit it just doesn't live up to its predecessor. If you're already into RE and want to see more of it then you'll enjoy it, but just don't expect quite the same level of experience.

I've been on bit of a RE tear the past few weeks, having never really gotten into any of the games. I started with the RE4 Remake, then RE2 Remake, now this one, with plans to play 7, then 8, then I'll grab 9 whenever it's on sale. 

This game is certainly way shorter than the other two, but it has really good replay value. After you beat it once, it opens up a shop where you can spend achievement points you earn throughout, and you can buy things like unlimited ammo weapons, extra storage space, etc. Also it was fun seeing some of the maps from the RE2 Remake, but it did sorta make me wonder why they cut content from the original, when they had all of these assets already made to save time. Nonetheless, it was fun seeing another side of Raccoon City's downfall.

I believe my first playthrough took around 6 hours, but that was me really taking my time hunting for all the items and figuring things out. Then my second took about 4.5 hours, then just shy of 3 for my third playthrough. I could see myself going for another one at some point, but I think that's all my ADHD can muster at this point in time.

Definitely don't pay full price for this game. I grabbed it when it was on sale for like $4. At that price, I would say it's definitely worth it.

Since Capcom wants the same money for this game as the RE2, which was older and better, I would highly suggest waiting for a sale. Not worth it for the full price.

Some more observations:
The running animation looks weird.
Hitboxes are iffy sometimes, trying to dodge to the side of a monster's attack sometimes gets me hit after the iframes end, even though the monster is almost stationary. The hitbox lingers too long.
The perfect dodge has to be at the last moment before an attack connects. But sometimes grapple attacks put you into a locked animation way before an attack connects. Trial and error dodging, I call it.
Certain attacks are really hard to see off screen (when you have to run from something). Also when aiming the game puts you in extreme tunnel vision which makes it hard to see anything. I had to use FoV mods to make the game playable for me.
The inventory UI, especially the storage box, is cumbersome to use on PC. The scrolling is very slow.
It's cutscene after cutscene. When playing for the second time, this becomes painfully apparent and the skip cutscene combination turns into your best friend. The skip prompt even appeared in my dreams after playing this...
The game is very gamey. First of all it still has the stupid "difficulty adjustment" mechanic where if you do good you get punished with even harder gameplay. So to beat it you have to know the system and take advantage of it.
Second, the game has slightly different enemy positions depending on whether you watched or skipped a cutscene. If you skip a certain cutscene, only on Inferno difficulty, you're making life a lot harder for yourself.
And third, the actions of enemies also depend on whether you are looking at a certain place or not. Nemesis, for example, does not jump to you if you're looking at the ground.
Some might call these deep mechanics or something. I call it ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that has no place in a game. Granted, if you're not doing Inferno runs, these things hardly matter, but that is no excuse.
Also, as everyone knows by now, the story was cut and condensed significantly. My favourite part of the original RE3, the clock tower, was, sadly, also in the cuttings. These changes as a whole were negative in nature and the original story was more interesting and had moments I still remember to this day. Nemesis reveal was a lot better in the original game.
The mercenaries extra gamemode was also cut. A big oof if you ask me.
It works as a game but could have been a lot better with more expert directing.

Final rating: 8/10

There's some things that are pretty good about this, such as the characters, the pacing, and the opening 30 minutes of the game, but wow does this one miss the mark. 

I finished the entire game start to finish in less than 3 hours - and I was taking my time with it. The game is mostly an asset flip from RE2 that has less weapons, worse sound effects, almost identical structure, and feels significantly more arcade-like than before. There's boss battles in these giant open arenas, the game throws a limitless supply of ammo at you, it adds a dodge mechanic that is really only there because Nemesis charges at you with insane speed, and I felt like the game was shuffling me from place to place way too quickly. 

The glory of RE2 was the fact that the gameplay forced you to slow down, learn your surroundings, involve yourself with the puzzles and the strategy, manage your resources, and really take your time. This one has none of that: every level is much smaller than before, there's virtually no puzzles at all, the game gives you so many resources I probably could've beaten the entire game again using only the resources from one save, and there's no incentive to take your time and learn the environments. 

The opening 30 minutes of the game and the final 10 minutes are genuinely great, but the rest of it feels like an arcade asset flip of RE2. There's a section a little after the half-way point in a hospital that was so arcade-like that it actually felt like a deathmatch mode you would find in the Extras menu. The villain also just straight up sucks and the coolest aspects of the story are sidelined as easter eggs. 

There's also no replay value at all - no alternate characters or alternate starting points, so you're playing through a 3-4 hour game that's charging a $40 price. 

It's not a bad game, but compared to RE2 it's basically a glorified DLC.

I went for 100% completion on this game, and honestly… this was the most frustrating Resident Evil experience I’ve had so far.
The biggest issue is the story. It feels incredibly rushed and confusing, like entire sections are missing. The game jumps from moment to moment without proper buildup, so instead of tension, it just feels messy and unfinished. Nemesis, who should be the main highlight, ends up being disappointing. He looks great, but he’s basically just a scripted boss. He shows up, you fight him, then he disappears. There’s none of that constant pressure or fear like you’d expect, it never feels like he’s actually hunting you. The game also has some weird technical issues. Sometimes the graphics just break or look off, and certain animations feel unnatural or poorly timed. It’s not constant, but it happens enough to be noticeable. As a horror game, it barely works. It tries really hard to be scary, but most of the time it just isn’t. The atmosphere doesn’t build properly, and the pacing kills any tension it could have had. On top of that, the game is extremely short and easy to break. Once you learn the routes and mechanics, you can finish it in under 2 hours without much effort. It ends up feeling more like a speedrun arcade game than a survival horror experience. That being said, the core gameplay is still decent, and going for 100% can be fun if you enjoy grinding challenges. I got it on sale, so I don’t regret playing it, but at full price, it definitely wouldn’t feel worth it.
Overall, it’s not a terrible game, but it feels like a rushed and cut-down version of what it could have been.

TL;DR: Worst Resident Evil remake by far. It's incredibly unfaithful to the original, and even if you call it a "reimagining," it's a very poor one.


Full Review (with SPOILERS):
Let’s start with the story. The game is ridiculously short - averaging about 3-4 hours if you’re taking your time and exploring everything. If you rush through it, you can finish in roughly 1-2 hours depending on your weaponry.

But short doesn’t necessarily mean bad, right? Unfortunately, no. The writing is full of corny lines that made me sigh out loud. It’s clear the developers were trying to turn Jill into a copy-paste “girlboss” character. This gets especially cringeworthy during the final fight, when Jill shouts at Nemesis, “Next time, take the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hint!”
I know this sounds picky, but Jill is a major character in the Resident Evil franchise. Her writing deserves to be much stronger. I vastly prefer her design and personality in the original game.

Now for the game’s ultimate antagonist: Nemesis. He was changed significantly from the original - and not for the better.

In the original, Nemesis felt like a capable, calculated bioweapon with a mercenary edge. In the remake, he comes across as a dumb, brutish beast. Despite his incredible abilities and all the cutscene hype, he fails to kill even a single STARS member. If he can chase Jill relentlessly during gameplay, why can’t he finish her off in the cutscenes when she’s injured and on the ground? It makes no sense and completely undermines the idea that he’s a highly effective bioweapon whose sole purpose is to eliminate STARS members.

In the original, Nemesis was introduced by brutally killing Brad - one of the STARS members he was tasked with hunting down. It was a simple but highly effective introduction that immediately showed how dangerous and intimidating he was.
In the remake, Nemesis smashes through the wall of Jill’s apartment, catching her off guard and injuring her. Realistically, she shouldn’t have survived that encounter at all. She had no prior knowledge of his existence, no strong weaponry, and was completely cornered. With Nemesis’ abilities, there’s no way he should have failed - yet he did, despite multiple clear opportunities during that cutscene-heavy sequence.
And how does Brad die in the remake? He gets taken out by some random zombies while trying to hold a door shut. It’s a far weaker and less memorable death compared to the original.

Gameplay-wise, Nemesis is just as disappointing. In the original, you never knew when he would appear. His surprise entrances kept you on edge, and his instant-kill grab made him feel as terrifying as the chainsaw enemies in RE4.
In the remake, most of his appearances are heavily scripted, which removes the constant looming threat that made him (and Mr. X) so memorable. The few non-scripted encounters happen in the city/downtown area - a major location in the original that only lasts about 30-40 minutes in the remake. After that, Nemesis is reduced to boss battles and scripted set pieces.

Speaking of the city, RPD is also handled poorly. In the original, it felt like a natural extension of the explorable city area, which was great. In the remake, you only return to RPD as Carlos - never as Jill. On top of that, RPD somehow looks graphically weaker here than it did in the RE2 remake.

Another gameplay issue is the dodge mechanic. The original RE3 introduced a dodge that you could trigger by pressing the action button (the same one used to shoot) right as an enemy attacked. It was especially useful against zombie dogs and Nemesis himself.
The remake brings it back in the form of a roll, but it does a terrible job teaching you how to use it. There’s no proper tutorial, no safe enemy to practice on - just a brief popup showing the controls. Even after seeing that, most players still have no idea about the timing. If you try it, you’ll likely just get grabbed by a zombie or punched by Nemesis. As a result, many players will assume the mechanic is too difficult or risky and simply never use it.
This is a big problem because on harder difficulties, like Nightmare and Inferno, dodging becomes mandatory in the final Nemesis fight. It ends up feeling more like a Dark Souls boss than a Resident Evil encounter, deviating from the franchise's roots in a ridiculous way.

And one last thing: the DLC problem. Unlike the RE2 remake, if you want the original designs for Jill and Carlos, you have to purchase them. Why? Capcom needs more money, that's why. Their success is simply not enough, now they need to abuse nostalgia even further to wring more money out of their fans. But actually, we need MORE DLC. Now, give the player everything from the points shop in a paid DLC bundle. Infinite ammo rocket launcher? Dodge manual? Defense coins? Everything you need to beat Inferno and get all of your achievements with ease! It really makes the points shop feel less rewarding for people who obtain these items through gameplay.

Look, I don't mind DLC, but when we were able to get Leon and Claire's classic outfits for free in the RE2 remake a year prior, this is just a clear and scummy cash-grab. And DLC that makes the game pay-to-win by definition? Give me a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ break. If you're gonna add DLC, add some story expansions or extra game modes like you did with RE7; stop with the pay-to-win BS and nostalgia-bait.

I could keep going, but this review is already essay-length, so I’ll stop here. Ultimately, this game is no more than a shell of the original it claims to remake. It’s a shame that Capcom no longer seems as passionate about game-making as they once were, and instead leans into soulless nostalgia-bait. Resident Evil 3 deserved better than this.

I've read so many comments on the internet, like:
- Just skip part 3, it doesn't matter anyway
- Part 3 is an action game and nothing like 2 or 4
- There is no story reason to play 3
- Resident Evil 3 is much shorter than RE2

All of these statements are 100% false, and even worse, I bet a bunch of people skipped Resident Evil 3 because of it.

I can confidently say It's the exact same formula as Resident Evil 2, having played both games back to back.
While resource management has been reduced with seemingly more ammo, so has pointless walking and medallion fetching.
The actual gameplay is much more engaging and intense, and dare I say takes actual effort compared to RE2. Zombies are no longer immobile resource hogs but actually pose a threat and I'm sure of it, cause for the first time I'm using healing items.
Mr. X aka Nemesis isn't just an annoyance whenever he appears but actually a dangerous threat.
And graphically? It's even more impressive while also running extremely well.
The Story intertwines with the RE2 and you get a few glimpses of what led to the events of RE2.
Resident Evil 2 took me around 8 hours to beat, and Resident Evil 3 took me around 6. But that doesn’t necessarily mean RE3 is shorter. I had already understood the gameplay formula and gotten better by then. If I had played RE3 first and then RE2, I probably would’ve had the opposite playtime lengths.

To summarize:
- Less walking in a walking simulator (that's a +)
- More challenging enemies
- 6h-10h of playtime
- Beautiful and immersive world, both graphically and design wise
- Interesting gameplay differences between the characters, with Jill’s gameplay leaning more toward RE2, while Carlos’s soldier background is reflected in how he plays.
- No repetitive double playthrough

And I know this is an unpopular opinion, but I think RE3 did everything better than RE2. It’s a clear improvement in every department except maybe atmosphere.
So with that I can confidently give this game a glowing recommendation.
It often goes on sale for like $10, so get it and have a good time.

No, in this action game you don't even need to shoot your gun anymore, just dodge everything and you are fine. What is the game trying to be then ? The game also uses a lot of assets from RE2, while being shorter. So the game feels recycled and the amount of new content is even smaller. 

What I like about RE3.
The characters are pretty good. I'm glad Jill is back, more badass than she was in RE1. And Carlos is interesting too, being introduced as an umbrella soldier who doesnt really know whats actually happening. Their dynamic is relatable, Jill hates his guts, and he loves hers. The way the game portrays Raccoon City in the first hour is really well made. There is panic everywhere, people running around screaming, crying and you're in the middle. The tension the story builds up in the last hour (which sadly is about 1/3 of the game) is great. You are trying to save the city from being blown up, that's cool. Not a typical horror trope, but cool. Nemesis started out really strong, but got weaker the longer the game went on. The rewards for finishing the game are handled different in this one. You have a long list of challenges and you get poinst for finishing them. With these points you can unlock stuff for your future runs, like more inventory space and weapons. I like that change a lot. 

The achievements are pretty boring to be honest. The one that will take the most effort is just playing through the game on the hardest difficulty while earning an S-Rank. But with all the things available to you, it's not hard.

Get it while its on sale because you can expect to finish it in a day or two anyway.

To my surprise, the game feels heavily altered. It’s noticeably shorter, with some locations completely removed, and the iconic Jill vs. Nemesis dynamic has been reduced to just a handful of scripted encounters.

The game itself is fast-paced and leans heavily into cinematic action. I’d recommend picking it up on sale and playing through it once, but definitely not at full price. It’s a short experience, and replaying it, even with New Game Plus, just doesn’t feel satisfying or rewarding.

Despite its high technical quality and impressive visuals, Resident Evil 3 Remake feels like a downgrade from its predecessor. One of the main criticisms lies in the significant reduction of content compared to the original 1999 version. As a result, the game often feels less like a full-fledged release and more like overpriced DLC.
From a technical standpoint, it’s essentially the same engine and mechanics as the Resident Evil 2 Remake, with only minor adjustments in sound design and graphical polish. Even in the early stages, the game’s pronounced linearity is immediately apparent. Unlike the second remake, which featured two parallel campaigns (Leon and Claire) that added replay value, Resident Evil 3 offers a single, straightforward playthrough with little variation — ultimately reducing its overall appeal and longevity.
The entire game can be completed in 6–9 hours (depending on your pace and how much time you spend exploring and collecting items). This entry is best suited for those wanting to experience the full Resident Evil storyline or follow Jill’s personal arc. That said, for most players, watching a YouTube playthrough might offer nearly the same value — without the cost.
Despite the short runtime, the game tries to artificially boost replayability through multiple difficulty modes, unlockable items purchasable with in-game currency (earned by completing story challenges), and an assortment of character skins. Realistically, these additions are targeted at die-hard fans or trophy hunters, in hopes of keeping player engagement alive.

In the end, what do we have? A beautiful protagonist, an unkillable Nemesis, a mediocre plot, and technically — the same game as 2019. I can only recommend buying it to devoted fans of the franchise. For everyone else, it’s probably better to save your money. The game isn’t terrible, but its price tag certainly doesn’t reflect its true value.

I should had not played the Original before the RE3 Remake, cause if you were to play it backwards, you can probably experience remake as a fun short RE entry. Playing the original prior however, you just see just how much ♥♥♥♥ they cut out this game just to STILL end up being shorter then the original. This could be forgiven if the stuff they did keep was peak... but nah, there are some issues I have with this game still

Story
The story of RE3 remake is still largely the same, Jill caught in Raccoon city when the zombie outbreak gets out of control. It does start differently, with Nemesis being shown to be a threat MUCH earlier compared to the original, but its largely the same. it is the smaller bits that I do think its mixed. The game does do a much better job with some of the characters, mainly Jill and Carlos, but still not direct upgrade. For the story, it does start off pretty interesting, but you can tell that they ran out of time after an hour in, cause the story begins to jump so much. Sure, the original also doesn't have the best story out of the RE games, but remake especially does a pretty poor job pacing itself, something that the original didn't struggle with as much. I do wish they focused much more on Jill's struggle that her city is being taken right in front of her eyes just like they teased in the first hour, its an aspect that if they focused way harder on, I would had enjoyed the story more then the original imo. Apart from that, yeah cutting clock tower is just insane and makes the gap that more awkward, as not only is Jill's infection that much more forced in the remake cause they have to justify Carlos not being with her, yet Jill being fine for half a day unconscious before being found. The game also lacks the dread of Nemesis always looming, as without the clock tower they have to transform him WAY earlier, making the best aspect of him, being chased the entire game just gone first hour.

Characters
Mixed bag, Honestly I do think they greatly enhanced some characters. Jill I did find more interesting even with the insane amount of cut content, but I do wish they explored her trauma more, as the atmosphere of having to run out of the burning city was largely removed in this remake, so making this as a remedy would had made up for it. The biggest character upgrade was easily Carlos, as while yeah he was an interesting guy who did everything he could for Jill, I just think he has way more character in this game, even if they did make him mirror chris way more in this game. The rest, yeah I think is just a downgrade. Mikhail went from a soldier who got injured during combat, desperate to keep fighting even if he physically can't, to some mf who sat his ass on a chair till it was time for him to go boom. Again, they cut out the gas station and retrieving stuff for the train, so there goes that. Tyrell did have a bigger impact, mainly because he was barely there in the original, but still nothing crazy. The character I think got the biggest downgrade easily was Nicholai. Face value yeah he is much more in your face, but I did like his original counter part where they introduced his character by having him shoot other members off screen at first, then finally seeing it with your own eyes and piecing that yeah, he is a betrayer. The remake def makes him more out to be a selfish villain that just becomes obvious the moment you meet him. Mixed bag, but they did make the important two improved at least even if the cut content stings way too much for their development.

Gameplay
You would think that this would be a direct upgrade. RE2 remake just perfected that formula, and RE3 had better combat, so the remake should be the best of the three right? Nope, for one reason. They ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up Nemesis. The best part of Nemesis in the original was easily being chased the whole time, and while at first they nailed it, with some bleh scripted sequences of holding W, it was when they forced him to transform so damn early that the chase sequences just leave the game first hour. Its the name of the game and they didn't do even 10% of the quality that Mr X did in RE2 remake, and that mf wasn't even the main focus in the original. Its a shame cause apart from Nemesis, I do think overall the gameplay was improved, somewhat. The lack of puzzles is something I expected from modern RE titles remade. The dodge mechanic is easily 10x better, as the original dodge was just kinda janky asf. The obvious improved gameplay cause remake gameplay just smoother, and zombies being more satisfying to kill. However, there are obvious pitfalls. First, the game barely makes it feel like the entire city was overrun. The original had tons of zombies, screams in the background, gunshots you can't even see, corpses being eaten, all of that is just gone in the remake, and it goes from a desperate retreat to feeling like you are exploring an already abandoned city. The lack of Nemesis encounters as well makes exploring not as scary as before, as you don't feel as pressured as before. Its something that they missed with the remake, is its atmosphere, shame cause if they really had the time to perfect this game, it could had been sooo much better, as you can see the pieces, but its so obvious they were rushed to finish this game so they can move onto RE4 remake.

Music
I enjoyed the music of this game. I do think some songs were just better, especially Nemesis theme was just much more memorable, but overall I do still enjoy the OST of this game. The safe room theme is still hitting, and I did enjoy the credit song. my favorite song was easily the train song, even if you barely visit the location.

Last Positives/Nitpicks
- The change from a semi-open for the city to linear def ruins the atmosphere, as you are no longer exploring a falling city, you are running through an abandoned city, thats how it feels now.
- HDR implementation butt just like RE2 remake, I am so glad RE9 did a much better job, even if its still not the standards cause at least you can use HDR in windowed fullscreen mode.
- Clock Tower.

Conclusion
While yes, it may seem like I despised this game, I do think past the removed content, the game is still enjoyable. I can see myself enjoying it more if I remove the Original from my brain and pretend it doesn't exist, but its a remake, and I expect the remake to at least be LONGER then the original with the same amount of content. The game is still very fun and still worth playing, but it is easily the weakest of the remakes, and a shame they didn't even try to fix the game with DLC to add back the removed content.

Mr. X popped up just often enough to keep you on your toes, but Nemesis is around so often I just stopped being surprised when he appeared. 

But setting aside the obnoxious main monster, the game had a lot of good parts. Carlos was a major saving grace. The man has never seen a hair brush he couldn't ignore. He's got a sense of humor and a Carlos-less world would indeed suck. I'm also a sucker for some RPD exploration, so Carlos gets points in his favor for getting to spend some time at the station. The hospital was a good section too. Overall I liked the locations, it's just that there's not a ton to do at each one since the game is overall shorter. 

I didn't dislike my experience with this one, at least not completely, but I won't be rushing to replay it like I did with some of the others. But I'm still glad to have completed it.

Resident Evil 3 – Steam Review

👍 The Good:
Resident Evil 3 delivers a fast-paced, action-heavy experience that feels smooth and polished. The visuals are fantastic, with detailed character models and environments that really bring Raccoon City to life. Jill Valentine is a strong, likable protagonist, and the voice acting across the board is solid.

The gameplay is fluid and responsive, especially with the dodge mechanic, which adds a nice layer of skill and intensity during combat. The game also does a great job of creating cinematic moments that keep things exciting from start to finish. The boss fights—especially Nemesis encounters—are intense and memorable, even if they’re a bit more scripted than expected.

👎 The Bad:
The biggest downside is the length. The game is very short, and many players can finish it in just a few hours. For a full-priced title, this feels pretty disappointing. On top of that, a lot of content from the original game was cut, which makes this remake feel less complete.

Nemesis, while iconic, feels underutilized compared to how threatening he was in the original. Instead of being a constant, unpredictable threat, he often appears in scripted sequences, which takes away some of the tension. There’s also limited replay value unless you’re into speedrunning or higher difficulty modes.

⚖️ Final Verdict:
Resident Evil 3 is a fun and visually impressive action-horror game, but it lacks depth and content. It’s worth playing—especially on sale—but don’t expect it to have the same staying power as other entries in the series.

While RE3 (2020) is a good game, it is a bad sequel to RE2 (2019) and an absolutely terrible remake of RE3: Nemesis. In short, the game lacks in content and replay value compared to both its immediate successor, other games in the franchise, and the original game it is remaking. It is also lacking in the post-launch support that bolstered both RE2 Remake and Resident Evil 7. Capcom has stated they do not plan to support the game further, and so I do not recommend that you purchase this game until it is priced at what it is worth -- no more than $30, and I would suggest even $20. In fact, for the price they are charging as of this review, $39.59 USD on sale you can get most every other game in the series all of which are much better. Go buy and play pretty much any other game in the series, it is much better bang for you buck and also sends Capcom a message that this kind of treatment of unacceptable.

UPDATE: Recently Capcom has decided that instead of releasing DLC to fix the lack of content in this game, it would be better to release a DLC that allows you to skip the process of playing the game altogether. Now you can pay money to unlock the small amount of unlockables in the game instead of being bothered to even play the small amount of game that is here. I no longer recommend that you purchase this game at all, because doing so might make Capcom think this kind of treatment is acceptable. I will personally be boycotting Capcom from now on in response.
