A short, linear experience, with apparently missing content from the original RE3, the Resident Evil 3 Remake isn't a bad experience for newcomers or those with little experience with the game - still being the weakest of the remakes.

Play as a combination of Jill Valentine from the Racoon Police Special Tactics and Rescue Squad (S.T.A.R.S.) and Carlos Oliveira of the Umbrella Biohazard Countermeasures Service (U.B.C.S.) in their fight against Umbrella's bioweapon - Nemesis - all while trying to escape Racoon City before it is destroyed by the U.S. government. Jill gives you access to her lockpicks, a shotgun, and a grenade launcher with four kinds of rounds (acid, explosive, flame, and mine), while Carlos has access to his machine gun, with plenty of ammunition to spare. 

The timeline of this one seems to be taking place just before the events of Resident Evil 2 and continuing through, as we see the cop Leon later encounters getting bit when Carlos reaches the Racoon Police Department later in the game. Much of the game is Jill having repeated encounters, escapes, and mini boss battles with Nemesis. There is a side plot of having to find and recover a vaccine for the T-Virus, but it seems more of an afterthought considering the importance of such an item.

Gameplay is your usual survival horror fare, having inventory management in the form of juggling ammunition, weaponry, medical supplies, and puzzle items between safe rooms, solving item-based puzzles, collecting lore notes, and doing the ol' back and forth to unlock different doors in a particular area. Jill can perform a dodge roll to evade enemy attacks, while Carlos with unleash a counter-punch, knocking enemies on their backs, time slowing for a window of attack. 

Damage against enemies feels a bit variable, not always taking the same amount of shots / knife hits to reliably put down a standard zombie; not taking into account the random chance to instantly destroy a zombie's head with a pistol shot. Enemies come in a few different flavours; there being your standard zombie, zombies infected by the Nemesis bioweapon, pale zombies with high regeneration, zombie dogs, lickers, and two versions of a hunter, one being a lizard-like creature, and the second being a two-footed giant mouth that can one-hit Jill with a body consuming chomp. Nemesis will come back again and again, either wielding a new weapon (flamethrower / rocket launcher) or mutating into a new form completely as it attempts to hunt down surviving S.T.A.R.S. members. 

I have only played the original Resident Evil 3 once, many a year ago, so I can't comment on what content is missing and to what extent, as I simply don't remember. YMMV in this area depending on how familiar you are with this particular entry in the Resident Evil franchise. 

Visually, the game does look fantastic, character models and environments being on point, making a good use of general design, colour, and lighting to great effect to bring the chaos of Raccoon City to life. 

While Resident Evil 3 is the weakest of the modern Resident Evil remakes, I still think it would be a fine enough playthrough for newcomers to this title, especially considering it is regularly on sale for a few bucks.

Resident Evil 3

A fast, explosive reimagining of survival horror that leans heavily into action. This version trades some of the original’s tension and exploration for a more cinematic, adrenaline-driven experience. It’s intense, stylish… but not without compromises.

Pros:
⚡ Fluid Combat: Movement and gunplay feel sharp and responsive, especially with dodge mechanics adding a layer of skill.
👁️ Nemesis Presence: Nemesis remains a constant threat, creating pressure and memorable encounters.
🎬 High Production Value: Strong visuals, detailed character models, and cinematic cutscenes elevate the experience.
🔥 Pacing: The game moves quickly, with little downtime—perfect for players who prefer momentum over slow buildup.
🎭 Characters: Jill Valentine is more expressive and grounded, adding personality to the narrative.

Cons:
🔁 Short Length: The campaign can feel too brief, especially compared to expectations from a full remake.
📉 Cut Content: Several iconic areas and features from the original are missing, reducing depth.
🎢 Linear Design: Less exploration and backtracking make it feel more like a straight path than a survival sandbox.
😐 Lower Horror Factor: Action focus reduces tension and fear compared to other entries like Resident Evil 2.
🌆 Limited Atmosphere Variety: Raccoon City looks great, but the journey feels less diverse than it could have been.

Verdict:
Do I recommend it? Yes—but with adjusted expectations. If you want a polished, action-heavy Resident Evil experience with strong visuals and tight gameplay, this delivers. However, if you're looking for deep survival horror and long-term immersion, it may feel underwhelming. Think of it as a high-quality expansion rather than a full-scale remake.

Rating: 7.5/10 ⭐

This was the first Resident Evil I ever played as a kid. Not in some perfect setup either—back then we just used good ol’ pen and paper, we exchanged notes in class, scribbling down puzzle solutions, door codes, anything just to survive Raccoon City. Coming back to it now feels like reopening a core memory, just rebuilt in 4K and way more cinematic.

From the jump, Jill Valentine’s escape feels faster, louder, and way more on-rails compared to the 1999 original. The old version had this semi-open structure where you could breathe (and panic) at your own pace. Here, it’s more like the game grabbed your hand and said, “we’re sprinting now.” And honestly? It works… most of the time. I little bit of backstory helps.

But yeah, longtime fans are gonna notice what’s missing. Big locations like the Clock Tower are gone, and the branching choices from the original have been cut entirely. The live-selection system? Deleted. This version is tighter, but also more linear, which might sting if you grew up replaying the OG like it was muscle memory.

That said, what is here is polished as hell. Combat feels sharp, the pacing rarely drags, and the presentation is straight-up blockbuster. Jill, in particular, got one of the best glow-ups in the series. She’s more human, more expressive, and actually reacts like someone trapped in a city that’s absolutely cooked. 

And then there’s Nemesis. In the original, this dude was basically anxiety in a trench coat—random, relentless, and always one step behind you. In the remake, he’s more scripted, showing up in big, cinematic set pieces instead of constantly hunting you down. It makes for some insane moments, but yeah, it loses a bit of that unpredictable dread that made him iconic. He's still the best antagonist in the series for me.

For someone like me, who first experienced this story as a kid, it hits different. Not exactly the same fear, but a different kind of appreciation.

Her bravado in the last battle definitely gives the feeling of "I'm the main character of this game and that's why I'm going to win!" Even RE4 goes out of its way to explain how some of the villains leave Leon alive because they want to use him or else he wouldn't stand a chance.

Shifting Nemesis to being fully scripted, while also making downtown Racoon City small and linear (albeit, absolutely gorgeous to look at) has always felt extremely reductive and far from Resident Evil at its most essential. Nicholai and Tyrell are extremely underrated, with the voice acting serving as a highlight. Carlos is upgraded in meaningful ways over his original version, proving to be fun-loving but also genuinely, Leon-esque funny. The weapon variety is exquisite, and the dodge mechanic feels both necessary and smooth, including extremely rewarding the more you experience the gameplay and attempt to truly master it. After about 20 hours with Resident Evil 3, I feel pretty confident calling it an 8/10 experience—flawed, but still a really fun and polished ride.

First off, the presentation is top-tier. The RE Engine continues to carry hard here, with incredibly detailed environments, realistic lighting, and character models that bring Raccoon City to life in a gritty, cinematic way. Jill Valentine looks and feels like a total badass, and the overall atmosphere—especially early on in the city streets—is intense and immersive.

Gameplay is where things really shine. Movement feels smooth and responsive, and the dodge mechanic adds a layer of skill that rewards timing and awareness. Combat is tight, with satisfying gunplay and just enough resource management to keep that survival horror tension alive. The pacing is faster than traditional Resident Evil titles, leaning more into action, but it still manages to deliver some genuinely stressful moments.

Nemesis is a highlight, even if a bit underutilized. When he’s actively hunting you, the game hits its peak—those encounters feel chaotic and dangerous in the best way. However, compared to what fans might expect, his presence feels more scripted than dynamic, which takes away some of the unpredictability.

The biggest drawback is the length and missing content. Even stretching it out to 20 hours with higher difficulties, challenges, and unlockables, the core campaign is noticeably short. Sections that fans of the original game loved are either trimmed down or completely absent, which makes the experience feel a bit rushed. It’s clear this could’ve been something even greater with more content and exploration.

That said, replayability helps soften the blow. Unlockable weapons, higher difficulties, and ranking systems give you reasons to jump back in and improve your runs.

Overall, Resident Evil 3 Remake is a sleek, action-heavy survival horror game that delivers great moment-to-moment gameplay and strong visuals, but falls short of its full potential due to its length and cut content. Still, it’s absolutely worth playing—just don’t expect it to stick around as long as some of the other entries in the series.

If the Resident Evil 3 remake had been advertised as a $40/$50 expansion for the RE2 remake, it would have been received WAAAAY better. It's a fun action/horror game with solid level design and gorgeous graphics, and because the entire foundation was basically lifted from another fantastic game, it's a quality production through and through.

...but Resident Evil 3 wasn't touted as an expansion or DLC. When it was revealed, it was said to be a full-on remake just like the game that came before it - and then Capcom announced that the Live Selection feature was going to get cut...and then they announced that several levels and environments got cut. Then the extra endings got cut, and the unlockable modes got cut - you get the idea. When so much of what made the original such a classic get stripped away, what are you left with?

I stand by the idea that the Resident Evil 3 remake is a game worth playing. It's fun, it's polished, it's pretty - but as a remake, it's just a shell. Given that the team only had a year or so to make the game, it's commendable what they were able to do, but so much of what made the 1998 original is gone with nothing to replace it. What we got was solid, but it's hard not to lament what could have been.

Comes across as the bad timeline version for what the original RE3 could have turned out to be: an asset flip of its predecessor with half-assed ideas and sense of identity.

Capcom's push to make these remakes a more gritty take on the original is not necessarily bad, as it lent itself well to the more transformative gameplay of RE2R, as well as to more properly differentiate RE4R from its original, but it's a total misfire here. RE3R tone is underwhelming at best, wanting to come across as the HBO Max take (derogatory) of RE3 while gutting it of its most memorable moments and places. This wouldn't be much of an issue if it replaced such segments with something new or interesting, but it does not, and the entire game feels like they are cutting corners. I don't mind them tackling Jill as a more traumatized (Joker #damaged) survivor of the Mansion incident, nor shedding more light into Umbrella's experiments and its control over Racoon City, still, after all was said and done, I felt that RE3 OG left more of an impact on its protagonist and setting (given its simplicity and striking direction) over this more expensive and flanderized reimagining.

Mr. X lent itself as a unique obstacle in RE2R, and it would have been a no-brainer to tweak such AI work into Nemesis so it could dynamically chase you around the map; yet aside from the initial segment in the city, Nemesis is restricted to a railroad obstacle and is the only Boss enemy of the game. There are instances in its presentation where it feels like a return to the more extravagant set pieces of RE5-6, while not committing to such entries' more abrasive cinematography or style.

I was genuinely struck by the fact that this only has ONE puzzle in its entirety, which can mostly be resolved by pushing down keys at random until it solves itself. Again, linear RE has worked in the past, given the satisfying feel to its combat, the progressing sense of escalation in its set pieces, as well as gradually expanding the player's arsenal to grant them more expression in combat. But, well, RE3R is neither that type of game, where the omission of a Mercenaries mode (which is particularly insulting given RE3 is where that mode originated) wouldn't even have turned out in a compelling time given the blandness of its shooting.

While the original first two games get a lot of the focus in media discussions, Resident Evil 3: Nemesis was always MY Resident Evil. I had the privilege to live within a block of my school and I would often be able to go home for lunch. I would spend fifteen minutes or so eating half cold corn dogs while playing Resident Evil 3, specifically the Gamecube port. To me, it was always the essential experience and how I remembered Resident Evil. To me, Nemesis was the scariest thing ever.

Resident Evil 3 REmake has a dubious reputation, many critique it for what it left out, for what it added and what it exaggerated while minimizing other aspects. I was one of those people who pre-ordered it and played it rather thoroughly over a few playthroughs. Admittingly, there is not a lot of content here compared to RE2, but truthfully, RE2 and by an extension, RE2, is very much so the same game with some character specific subversions. 

RE2 REmake was interesting in that Claire's route was far superior, (Sherri's section is honestly one of the best horror sections ever) but Leon's character completely carried the game and he had significantly more Mr. X action. RE3 is much like the original, which funny enough, as its often not remembered, was also dubiously received due to its avert shift to more action. Code Veronica X was going to be the original RE3, being the first game to ditch the pre-rendered cutscenes in favour of fully rendered graphics and yet, NEMESIS, which was going to be the branded spin off, ended up becoming the third in the original zombie trilogy. As a result, it was a bit rushed and fairly different from the other two main titles. 

But it also, largely, showed the direction Resident Evil was soon to go in. RE3 remake may not be what people expected or wanted out of it, but I honestly think it does a great job being a sequel to RE2 REmake, more than it does being a remake. In other words, its more appropriate to see RE2 as a reboot and this a sequel to that reboot, rather than a full fledged remake of Nemesis. 

The puzzles are extremely easy, I know this because I can often do them on just one try and gather most of the things needed in a single passing, compared to how much I tend to biblically get lost in the Raccoon City Police Department. So much so, that when we take a brief detour there in this game, I immediately started bumbling around familiar hallways with slight frustration. Despite having 60 some hours in RE2 and S ranking it several times over, I still find myself backtracking unnecessarily due to forgetting a specific item placement. 

If you hated the survival horror aspects of RE2 but loved everything else, RE3 was made for you in particular, specifically. As a result, you will likely hate the hospital section as Carlos, as it has all the worst parts of RE2 in that regard. But the atmosphere is peak. 

I always preferred 3 for its intensely urban environments, suffocating streets. If anything, the remake almost loses the scale of disaster the original had besides the spectacle of an intro sequence it had. There are a lot of things to like, the only crime RE3 commits is that sometimes it is not the most entertaining in its more difficult sections. On the higher difficulties, the checkpoints are very punishing in the most tedious way. 

A lot of things are retained, the hideous transliteration of "Nicholai" and Mikhail Victor still being mostly nonsensical pseudo-Russian. 

UBCS is just as interesting as the USS goons of RE2 and sadly, the most unremarkable of their cast get all the focus through T and Carlos. Sometimes I wish the remake would be bold enough to make Nicholai the  occasional companion, in a fragile alliance with Jill, before ultimately betraying her. Carlos is still mostly a sort-of-kind-of character that is certainly one of the most of all time. 

Overall, virtually no side content to engage in, but the game itself is far more linear in an enjoyable way, has a bit more variety and is a great game to revisit for a single play session that can be completed in one sitting. Ultimately, it certainly is overhated and if the length truly bothers you, pick it up super cheap alongside RE2. But really, if you are really invested in the new REboot-verse and newer games, it may not be the best of the bunch, but its still worthy of having. 

it is hard to critique the story of a Resident Evil game, because well, its Resident Evil. But if you have very little idea of what is going on, this isn't the best to start with. Definitely hop onto RE2 remake and then play 3 soon after, as it really helps complete a picture of the Raccoon City outbreak from beginning to end. But still, both games are going to rely a lot on your knowledge of the events of the first game and to be honest, its likely you have subconsciously absorbed enough of it culturally that you should be fine.

A shorter and more action oriented companion piece to the RE2 remake. The game is decent enough and admittedly kept me entertained throughout my playthrough. Nemesis and all his forms are amazing, but the scripted chase scenes heavily deflate any horror and tension a stalker type enemy should create. The game is also very short, with my first thorough playthrough lasting about 4.5 hours. 

That said the short play time lends itself to the game's replay value. RE3 offers a much more varied selection of post game items/weapons that allow you to tweak and create unique playthroughs. Along with the dodge mechanic there's plenty of room for skill expression and fun playthrough limitations. There's also additional difficulties beyond hardcore which change up enemy and item placement. The final nemesis fight in these modes becomes a literal dark souls boss, where timing your dodges is essential for completing the fight.

Ultimately I don't think the game is what people coming from either the RE2 Remake or OG RE3 were expecting, however it's still an enjoyable game on its own right. Worth picking up in a bundle with RE2R.

The main characters feel lifelike and complement each other well. Jill Valentine is composed, decisive and always in control of the situation, even in the most tense moments. Carlos Oliveira initially seems more light-hearted and easy-going, but gradually reveals himself to be a reliable and responsible partner. Together, they create the feeling of a team you can trust in the face of constant danger.

Overall, the remake is short but packed with emotion. It’s the kind of game you can breeze through in an evening, yet it leaves you with a flood of emotions and the urge to play through it again – already knowing what awaits you.

Resident Evil 3 Remake is a fast-paced survival horror game developed and published by Capcom, released on 3 April 2020. It reimagines the classic Resident Evil 3 with modern visuals, smoother gameplay, and a more cinematic style.

You play as Jill Valentine, a S.T.A.R.S. officer trying to escape Raccoon City during a deadly outbreak. The story moves quickly, focusing on action and survival as you’re relentlessly pursued by the terrifying Nemesis.

Gameplay is more action-oriented compared to *Resident Evil 2 Remake*. The addition of a dodge mechanic makes combat feel fluid and skill-based, allowing you to avoid enemy attacks and counter effectively. Gunplay is satisfying, and encounters are more frequent, keeping the pace intense.

Nemesis is a major highlight, acting as a constant threat throughout the game. However, his appearances feel more scripted rather than dynamic, which slightly reduces the unpredictability and tension.

Visually, the game looks excellent. The environments are detailed, character models are realistic, and lighting effects enhance the overall atmosphere. Sound design also plays a big role in building tension, especially during chase sequences.

One of the biggest drawbacks is the game’s length. It’s relatively short and cuts several locations and features from the original, which disappointed many fans. The focus on action also means fewer puzzles and less exploration.

The game also includes **Resident Evil Resistance**, a 4v1 online mode, though it feels more like a bonus rather than a fully developed feature.

A Disgrace to a Masterpiece
If you were expecting a faithful recreation of the 1999 classic, prepare to be stabbed in the back. After the triumph of the RE2 Remake, Capcom had the blueprint for success. Instead, they handed us a glorified DLC masquerading as a full-priced game. This isn't Resident Evil 3; it’s a hollowed-out carcass wearing Jill Valentine’s face.
Where is the Rest of the Game?
The most insulting part of this "remake" is what’s missing. Capcom didn't just trim the fat; they amputated the heart of the game.
The Clock Tower? Reduced to a boss arena background.
The Park and Graveyard? Deleted.
The Puzzles? Non-existent.
Live Selection? Gone. The choices that made the original infinitely replayable were stripped away for a linear, "hold forward to win" cinematic experience.
Nemesis: From Stalker to Scripted Joke
The original Nemesis was a persistent, terrifying threat that could hunt you through doors and catch you off guard. In this version, he’s a scripted puppy.
"Nemesis has been reduced to a series of predictable QTEs and cinematic chase sequences. The tension is dead."
Once he mutates into a generic four-legged beast ten minutes into the game, the iconic "Stalker" vibe is replaced by a boring boss fight you’ve seen a thousand times before.
Identity Crisis
Even the characters feel wrong. While the graphics are "next-gen," the personalities have been swapped for generic action-movie tropes. The atmospheric, dread-filled vibe of Raccoon City has been replaced by explosions and scripted set-pieces that belong in a bad Michael Bay flick.
Final Verdict: Buy the Original
Do not waste your money on this "reimagining" if you actually care about survival horror. If you want to see what a true masterpiece looks like, go to GOG and buy the original 1999 version. It’s older, but it has ten times the soul, double the content, and a Nemesis that will actually make you sweat.
Shame on Capcom. This wasn't a remake, it was a robbery.

I don't really know why I decided to replay the game on Hardcore difficulty. It would've been a really streamlined and cinematic experience with how (over)tightly structured or rushed (however you wanna look at it) the game is, but I guess I was craving more challenge, and it got a bit too much to handle at times. Zombies are tougher to stagger (except when using SG) and thus tougher to kill, so the ammo is pretty generous, but your HP is pretty low. Health items are stingy, and sometimes I used to get pranked by the game's RNG by getting two red herbs and zero green ones, hence being forced to progress without getting hit even once since it's impossible to heal and you're cooked from just one attack. You'd die instantly 9/10 times if zombies caught you off guard and took a bite out of you from behind.
Carlos' fight at the hospital would've been so much more fun if not for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ scaling in Hardcore, where you immediately die from a Hunter's attack after its head has been exposed. Took me a number of tries to get through that. All of these frustrating things that I mentioned make me never wanna try any RE game on a higher difficulty than Standard (at least without perks like infinite ammo), but I still wanna give RE4 a shot on higher difficulty someday though.
Surviving the Nemesis chase sequences in those extremely simple map layout of Raccoon City was pretty intense since I had no healables and was forced to perfect those perfect evades. It was pretty fun to dodge his attacks, look for openings to stun him and other enemies by shooting those generators, evade his laser rockets, and avoid getting bit by zombies all at the same time, albeit it was tedious to die after getting hit just once. I bet this would've been a cakewalk on Standard since he's not even close to being as aggressive or quick, and of course, stuff like health and healing, but I remember having fun when I played it for the first time.
Using mag ammo weapons in the remakes feels so underwhelming after requieming through RE9. Jill and her corny one-liners like "♥♥♥♥♥ can't even swim" is what got me into playing this game and then the rest of the franchise. The boss fights on Hardcore got a bit too much to handle, but I remember them being really fun on Standard, like having to shoot mine rounds to stun Nemesis and pin him down, and you could actually use the same strategy for the 3rd stage Nemesis fight instead of shooting those electric things.
Maybe I don't treat RE3 as harshly as others because I played it before RE2, and now after playing both multiple times, it's pretty obvious which one's the better game, but I still feel there's fun to be had with RE3. The boss fights here feel much better than RE2 because of the evade mechanic and the arenas, but RE3 fumbled hard due to the absence of any meaningful unscripted long-term stalker enemies and the lack of puzzles to some extent. Imagine Mr. Nemesis chasing you around a more complex Raccoon City map unscripted with that dodge mechanic.
I haven't played the OG myself but have seen how much of it has been removed and changed for the worse in the remake, and it's sad to see the lost potential since it could've been the best out of the three had it been reprised faithfully like the other two games instead of being rushed.
The color tone here looks nicely saturated compared to the unsaturated tone in RE2. The optimisation is peak—I was able to run this at 720p on my GT 740M laptop back when I first played it. Real "Tony Stark was able to build this in a cave with a box of scraps" type ♥♥♥♥.
Playing it now, the game was crashing consistently despite the VRAM usage being way less than what I had, and apparently it was because of some Ray Tracing DX12 update. Switching back to DX11 removed the constant crashes. The ray tracing makes no difference, yet it destroys the experience for no reason. I guess devs love to shoot themselves in the foot with these unwanted updates.
Narratively, this feels trash just like RE4- extremely forgettable, and Jill's character could've used more depth. It really does feel like a game that's rushed to the core with a lot of incomplete pieces, but then again, it's still a good game if you're not introduced to the OG. Hopefully there's a director's cut or something that tries to bridge the gaps.

I played the original games when they first came out (back when you bought a physical box at a store), but I never finished RE3 because I found the constant stalking by Nemesis to make the rest of the game unenjoyable.  This remake is a much more forgiving version of the original game, with no ribbon requirement for saving and less Nemesis stalking (at least on standard difficulty).  While I found that to be a welcome change, I can understand that this might be a minus for those who enjoyed the design of the original game.

Also, this remake is more like RE4 than 1 and 2.  Originally there was a paradigm shift between 3 and 4 from survival horror to action shooter horror.  The remake pushes 3 much more into the latter, with a more mobile protagonist and lots more ammo available.


-- THE GOOD --

- Cutscene cinematography and character models are very good
- Excellent use of light and shadow
- Music and ambient sound effects are used well to create tension
- So refreshing to play a game where normal walking is the default movement speed
- User interface is designed well for PC
- When inventory is full and you pick up an item that can be combined, you can combine it directly from pick-up rather than needing to have an empty slot first
- A kind scattering of strategic autosaves


-- THE BAD --

- Dialogue in cutscenes and text in documents seem to be written by teenage boys trying to sound edgy
- Silly hair for men, a trademark of the RE games
- Terrible lip syncing
- Character models with enough pouches to make Rob Liefeld shake his head in dismay
- The combination of the usual RE sluggish movement and some quick-time dodging situations doesn't mesh well
- One enemy type regenerates, but the visual effect is so subtle that unless you already knew this you'd think none of your weapons could damage it at all
- One pointless and unintuitive QTE


-- THE UGLY --

- One instance of terrible player training. After you defeat a particular boss the first time, you get a useful pickup if you search around the body.  This would lead the rational player to believe it's important to search the body if in the same situation in the future.  However, the second time you defeat this boss if you go to the body before searching the entire room, you trigger a cutscene that ends up with you shut off from the previous map and unable to collect the many pickups there.

I haven't even owned the game until now, and for good reason. Before I begin, let it go on record that my negative review doesn't mean that I don't find this game enjoyable in its own special way ; I do. But already being familiar with a superior experience, I'm not going to recommend it before you play the original.

Another element crucial to my negative review is that I am biased :

Jill Valentine is an icon of my childhood ; much like Claire, I spent my arduous early teenage years looking up to her and merely wishing I could be as badass. These characters mean the world to me, and it breaks my heart in a million pieces to see their blatant mistreatment.
In conclusion, my "hatred" for this game is born from burning frustration as to the wasted potential. 
Do you hate Jill, Capcom? I mean, we haven't even seen her in the game's chronological universe since 2009. The least you could do is put as much effort as you put into RE2R into her game.
---------------------
Let me start with the cons :
Resident Evil 3 "remake" is but a shell of what RE3:Nemesis stood for. I can't give this game a positive review in good conscience, as Capcom have proven themselves capable of honouring source materials (RE2R, RE4R) yet chose to settle with mediocrity. Play the 1999 masterpiece, and tell me if this "remake" does it justice.

Jill Valentine is one of the few characters that have ultimately shaped me into who I am today. Put some respect on her name, and associate her modern rendition with a remake that fully embodies the un-dethronable, legendary female gaming protagonist. (Also, her implicit sexualisation in this game sickens me, but I won't go on a rant.)

If you're an OG or played the classics, you'll agree that the Nemesis has been humiliated to a degree that makes me personally giggle. The original B.O.W was relentless, fatal and efficient in its hunt ; an unstoppable killing machine that legitimately frightened us. 

He was credible.

The remake Nemesis? 
A shelf stopped him. He could've killed Jill in the game's intro. Perhaps Capcom decided to tweak his character into one that plays with its food? I much prefer the merciless monstrosity with a thirst for elimination. (Also, why didn't he kill Brad before Jill's eyes like in the OG? That would reinforce the potency of her trauma due to the events.)

Let us not forget the OG's decision-making feature, the non-linear exploration of the city, the crazy RNG that made it so incredibly re-playable, the MANY costumes that set Jill as a fashion example, her going into the RPD, THE CLOCK TOWER!! and much more.

This partly a joke, but I miss Carlos' iconic line : "I know, you wanna ask me out! All the foxy ladies love my accent, it drives them crazy!"
-----------------------------
The pros, baby!

For once, a character was done justice! Carlos was improved in every best way, making him a much more likeable character that feels convincing. Did you know that his face model is Algerian? A great guy.

Much like RE3:Nemesis, this game has an amazing soundtrack that I listen to practically on a daily basis. Kudos to Capcom's sound design and artists that never falter in their excellence!

Jill's modernised outfit might be one of the greatest sights I've laid my eyes upon. That practical, signature-blue button-up inspires my own fashion sense (like all RE characters do, to be truthful.)
I do feel like her classic outfit was slightly botched, but that's nothing we haven't seen before. (Claire's classic outfit was a downgrade as well.)

I hate to say this, god I do. But this game is fun.
My rational conscience begs me to up my standards and not fall into the trap of settling for something that doesn't live up to its full potential...

 But I'm a slave to Resident Evil. It literally doesn't matter how atrocious the game is, if it has RE in the title, boy am I playing the ♥♥♥♥ out of it.
--------------

In conclusion, I think the original is superior ; but I am aware that not everyone is cut out to play retro games with tank controls.

Resident Evil 3 Remake won me over hard. My first impression was honestly pretty rough because the dodge timing felt insanely tight, a few sections absolutely beat the hell out of me, and this game will punish you fast if you waste ammo or stop paying attention to resources. But once I slowed down, explored more carefully, and started playing around what the game actually wanted from me, my opinion improved massively. The visuals are excellent, the atmosphere is filthy in the best way, Nemesis rules, and the whole thing has a really strong forward momentum that makes it easy to keep playing. I also loved how it ties Raccoon City together if you’ve played RE2 Remake, because that added a lot to the experience for me. I still prefer RE7/8/9 overall because first person feels more tense and immersive to me, and there are definitely a couple of encounters here that crossed over from exciting into irritating, but I still came away thinking this was a very good game. It’s shorter, meaner, more action-heavy, and occasionally frustrating, but it looks great, keeps the pressure on, and absolutely does enough right for me to recommend it.

The remake was especially dissapointing given the fact that it feels very rushed. I didn't feel very scared at all for a action horror game. It seemed like they tried to use the original formula of the game but added so much into the game that it feels rushed and forced. Guns feel unreliable for how little the game gives. at times feels like i rather avoid shooting entirely. 

Not to mention the dodge mechanic was very terrible and it wasn't polished. i didn't understand why it needed this mechanic as it made the more heavy sessions where you have to run but instead you ran into another zombie and get killed. 

The story itself was not the best either. puzzles and exploration where limited. And this felt more that it was meant for Carlos more than Jill. Carlos's sessions are more fun than Jill's given that the horror is present with him. Despite how trained he is, the horror element did not fade away with Carlos. I liked his gameplay more than Jill's, but at the time he did need polishing as well. 

The game had potential, but given how rushed it is... im not surprised it was at 3 dollar discount.

That doesn’t mean RE3 is bad though. The graphics and presentation are great thanks to the RE Engine, and Raccoon City looks fantastic. Jill is a great protagonist, Nemesis is intimidating (at least early on), and the overall polish of the game is very solid.

The problem is that it feels cut down compared to what it could have been. A lot of sections feel more linear than expected, and the game ends right when it feels like it’s getting started.

So overall:
Good game? Yes.
Better than RE2 Remake? Not even close.

If you enjoyed Resident Evil 2 Remake, this is still worth playing — just don’t expect it to reach the same level.

I’ve been a fan of the Resident Evil series for years, so I went into Resident Evil 3 (2020) expecting a good remake of a classic. What I got instead feels like a rushed and stripped-down product that barely resembles the original in terms of depth and content.

The most glaring issue is how much content is simply missing. Entire sections, locations, and mechanics that defined the original game are either heavily simplified or completely removed. What was once a tense and atmospheric survival horror experience now feels like a short, linear action game with very little replay value.

The pacing is another major problem. Everything happens too quickly, leaving no room for exploration or proper buildup. Even Nemesis, who should be a constant source of fear and pressure, ends up feeling underwhelming and predictable.

And then there’s the value. For a full-priced release, this is honestly unacceptable. It feels like, in honor of Capcom’s anniversary, they decided to hand fans a “gift from the trash bin” — one of the weakest entries in the modern remake lineup.

To make matters worse, there’s additional DLC featuring a single costume and hairstyle that nobody asked for. Instead of adding meaningful content, it only highlights how barebones the base game really is.

As for the developers : NeoBards, M-Two, and K2 — they should be ashamed of this result. A project based on such a legendary game deserved far more care, effort, and respect.

In the end, Resident Evil 3 is not just a missed opportunity — it’s a disappointing remake that fails to capture what made the original special. For longtime fans, it feels less like a tribute and more like a letdown.

Resident Evil 3 Remake: The 2026 Retrospective
"The High-Octane Action Sprint"

The Story: Lean and Relentless
Resident Evil 3 Remake is a masterclass in cinematic pacing. It trades the slow-burn atmospheric dread of the RPD for a non-stop, neon-soaked race through a city in its final hours. Playing as Jill Valentine, you aren't just surviving; you’re being hunted by a weaponized stalker, the Nemesis, whose presence turns the game into a tense game of cat-and-mouse.

While some long-time fans miss the slower exploration of the original 1999 title, the Remake succeeds by modernizing the relationship between Jill and Carlos Oliveira. Their banter and teamwork make the stakes feel personal, even if the 4-hour runtime feels more like a summer blockbuster than a long-haul survival epic.

Gameplay: Precision and Power
The addition of the Perfect Dodge (and Carlos’s Punch) completely changes the rhythm of combat compared to other entries. It rewards high-risk play, allowing you to slow down time and counter-attack with massive damage. It’s an "action-first" approach that makes Jill feel like the elite STARS operative she actually is.

Final Thought: RE3 Remake isn't a replacement for the classic; it’s a high-speed reimagining. It’s the perfect "Saturday night" game—intense, beautiful, and incredibly satisfying to replay once you unlock the infinite weapons.

Unfortunately I'd say that the reputation for being the weakest post RE Engine Resident Evil is pretty well deserved. The game never really does anything that makes itself stand out. It's not scary like RE7, but not because the game is action-oriented. Rather, it just does a very poor job at being scary in any way. Unless you're spending 30 bullets per zombie, you will never even come CLOSE to being out of ammo on any of your guns. This is mixed with the same canned animations that were already boring by the first 20 minutes of the last game. The game as a result feels totally weightless. There's not enough anxiety for the game to be scary, but nothing unique enough to make any action set-pieces stand out either.

The game's story is also a step down from the other modern RE games. Jill and Carlos are certainly not bad or unlikable protagonists, but they pale into comparison to other leads. I enjoyed them being on screen, but I really can't tell you anything that unique about them. They're both just morally acceptable soldier guys. I will take Leon/Claire or Grace/Leon over Jill/Carlos any day of the week. Even Ethan Winters From RE7/RE8 has more personality in subtle dialogue cues than Jill or especially Carlos.

With all of this being said, the game's problems are (mostly) only highlighted when it's put to scale with the other modern Resident Evils. In a vacuum,  the game still looks great and plays very well. Combat, aiming and movement are all top notch. The fact I didn't want to actively root against the protagonist's places the game higher than 80% of other game protagonists. Examining items and finding secrets are still very satisfying mechanics. These things don't really fix the game's design issues, but they certainly makes it playable and at times, very enjoyable. While the game is too short to leave any real lasting impression, that also means it's short enough that the major issues don't have time to really sink in.

At full price, I cannot recommend this game. However, I also think that 4$ for a game that plays this well is a steal. I would say that if you are really interested in playing this game or the whole series, go ahead. If not, I would say skip it. There is really nothing in this game that isn't done better in both RE2 Remake and RE9. I'd give it a light 6/10.

I have been playing this on my Steam Deck and I've almost beaten it on Hardcore. Here is my take on the game so far. I'll update it if anything changes:

First of all, the game runs amazing on the Steam Deck and looks amazing. It was very clearly well optimized just like the rest of the RE series. 

The game is somewhat hard on Hardcore, but to be frank, it isn't all that hard. I did have to reset quite a bit but I've already almost beaten the game in just 6 hours. I've got maybe 2 hours to go. I have a crap ton of grenades for the nade launcher, bullets for the handgun, and about 7 full heals right now. Again, 7 full heals. 

For Carlos I had 6 and that was right after a huge fight (No spoilers). And for him I had 250 bullets on the SMG and about 50 for the handgun. No nades though. Again, this was after a tough fight. I used 4 nades and 3 full heals and STILL had plenty firepower left over.

Now this was after a few restarts here and there and some practice but keep in mind the timer doesn't reset when you restart and I'm just finishing the hospital after 6 hours so I'm doing pretty good I think for my first playthrough. 

What keeps going through my mind is this: the game is a zombie version of Dark Souls with guns. As I play this game it makes me really wanna go back to playing Dark Souls. Like really badly. I may do just that once I'm done, I'm not sure. 

Resident Evil just frankly scares the ♥♥♥♥ out of me every time I play a new game. Zombies come up from behind occasionally, even when I'm on hard. Sometimes im randomly surrounded and unprepared or sometimes I just miss that one zombie who came out of nowhere and I got to restart. Hardcore is pretty damn unforgiving. 2 hits and you're dead for the most part. Rarely 3 and more often just 1. So i try to stay topped off. You would think "Well if 2 hits kills you then don't make full heals" right? Very wrong. Often times you'll find yourself with 3 ticks of damage which makes a full heal required. I often rather not heal than die in caution state than to heal and live with no heals for boss fight anyway. It's very easy to restart and only certain areas does it take a while to get back to your restore point.

As for the game mechanics, the evade mechanic for Jill was very well done and I probably spent most of my time practicing that. Huge window to dodge, easy to grasp the timing, and extremely effective in using counter attacks such as with the shotgun or grenade launcher since time slows for a very long time. (3-5 seconds.)

Carlos on the other hand is a bit... Clunkier. His "evade" is a shrug and a punch, it cannot be done in danger state (I think.) and it's extremely unreliable. Even with perfect timing it simply doesn't work, against bigger enemies they immediately get back up and unless you are running away, all it does is piss them off. Against groups of zombies it stun locks you for so long that you simply die. So due to all these reasons, I quickly realized that it was better for me to simply not use it unless it was literally my only option. When I began doing that, Carlos became much easier to manage. 

Carlos' story is also the toughest part. You have an SMG that tickles enemies and that is IT. Thankfully, I don't use nades unless I have no other option because I actually ran out and that was from using them absolutely perfectly in my opinion. There were multiple areas I had to just run by because I didn't have the firepower to deal with the enemies. 

As for Jill, by the hospital she's just planely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ laughable on Hardcore. I have I don't know like 15 nades. 12 mines minimum. Don't get me started on my gunpowder and high quality gunpowder count. Pretty sure I have 7 of each. Im literally playing Resident evil 3 fallout 3 edition. (Now THAT sounds like a best seller.) 

The story has been absolutely phenomenal as well, the gameplay as stated I loved. It is quite challenging and don't let me make hardcore sound like a breeze. It isn't. I just have a lot of experience in games in general so i always max difficulty because otherwise I wouldn't really enjoy myself. It would be like playing a game on "story" mode for most people. 

If you got this far in my review then i will make it plain as day for you: Absolutely buy this. At full price. (If you got the money.) It is worth it. You will love it. 

Every resident evil game has been amazing. Yes, even the 'action' oriented ones. I'm not a fan either, a fan indicates bias. I simply play anything i deem "fun" or "challenging".

So far I've beaten old 3, old 4, 5, 6, 7, halfway through 0, beaten new 2 multiple times, and I'm about to beat new 3. They all have been given a 7/10 or above except for RE0 remake. I hate that game with a passion, it's clunky and it's directional storytelling is absolutely garbage. 

If I had to recommend a game to start with, I'd say start with Biohazard or Village. Those games are more built around newer players because to be frank I found Biohazard to be laughably easy. Let me take you back to release weekend - April 4th of 2020 to be exact. COVID has everybody at home and in lockdown. I see this game releases. "Hm, I really enjoyed RE7 and RE2R, I'm probably going to enjoy this game too." I think to myself. So I buy it and gather my buddies on Discord to play it. 

A good 8 hours later we're still in the call, watching the last cutscene of this game. The sun rises, I look out ouf my window to see the sun irl rising as well. A truly magical moment.

I had played through this game in one sitting. I was captivated. That is what I think of when I hear Resident Evil 3 Remake. Not how short it is, not how much content has been cut, none of that. But all of the criticisms you've heard elsewhere sadly still apply.

Out of all the new Resident Evil games to come out in the past few years (meaning 7, 2R, 3R, 8, 4R and 9) this is by far the worst. First things first, the content of this game is laughable compared to the others. You can realistically finish this game in 6 hours for your first playthrough. I took my sweet ass time and finished it in around 8 hours, as I said. I had lots of fun though, even if it was a short game. Let's break it down.

The story in this game is servicable. Nothing very good, nothing very bad, just servicable. We follow Jill Valentine, a returning character from Resident Evil 1, during the 1998 T-Virus outbreak in Raccoon City. The very same outbreak happening in Resident Evil 2. As someone who hasn't played RE1, I understood all story beats perfectly and there is no need to have played RE1 or even 2 for that matter. The pacing is fine, although on repeat playthroughs it can be a bit jarring. Lots of setpieces and scripted events that make the game feel tightly packed but it doesn't overstay it's welcome. There are sections where you play as a different character, but these add to the gameplay rather than take away from them (looking at you MJ stealth sections *cough cough*)

Speaking of gameplay, is it any good? 
I think yes, and no. The game uses the same over the shoulder camera of RE2R and has almost identical gunplay. I just started a new playthrough of RE2R and I'm pretty sure there is almost nothing different about how the guns handle whatsoever. One big criticism I have of the gunplay in RE3R is that it feels very light. Coming off of RE9, the guns in this game feel like airsoft guns most of the time. Shots don't stagger enemies at all and there seems to be no tactical advantage in where you shoot the zombies (other than the head.) Damage models have been toned down from its predecessor for whatever reason, making the zombies feel less like actual non-living breathing beings and more like video game enemies. Sad. The sound design doesn't help, being very flat and boring. No punch to the guns (not even the shotgun or magnum, they just sound and feel flat) and the only sound that I liked was that of Nemesis.

Nemesis is the main antagonist of this game. He's a tyrant sent by Umbrella to kill the last remaining S.T.A.R.S. members in Raccoon City. (This ties into the first game.) Where Nemesis succeeds is in it's visual and sound design and in providing a recurring threat throughout the game, that I was always excited to fight one more time. Sadly, every encounter with Nemesis is scripted so, unlike Mr. X in RE2R, Nemesis won't stalk and hunt you through Raccoon City. This is also mostly because of the limiting level-design and overall linearity of the game, compared to its earlier entries and original. The bossfights themselves were pretty good. Nemesis takes on different forms each time you fight him which makes said fights stand out from one another easily.

The graphics are gorgeous, even before the visual overhaul update that added ray-tracing and more to the graphics options. The character models look great, voice performances (including Neil Newbon btw) are good across the board and I enjoyed playing as and rooting for Jill and Carlos. They have some nice chemistry and dialogue in the few scenes they get.

In closing: To anyone who's interested in a Resident Evil title, pick this up when it's on discount. It's a fun game, albeit a bit short, but it's a good experience all the same. Being the worst of the modern RE games doesn't mean it's bad. It's just not as good as the others. If you want to see if the gameplay is to your liking, you can download the Demo for free and give it a shot. I had lots of fun 100% completing this game and even if you don't want to go for all achievements, you can have many hours of fun with this game.

Cut Content and Locations: Major, memorable locations from the original game were removed, including the Clock Tower, the Graveyard, and the Dead Factory.
Linear Structure: The game is highly scripted and linear, lacking the open city exploration and backtracking present in the original RE3 and the Resident Evil 2 remake.
Nemesis Weakness: Nemesis, designed to be a persistent stalker, is mostly limited to scripted set-pieces rather than roaming freely, making him feel less intimidating.
Short Length and Value: The campaign is exceptionally short, with many players finishing it in under 4 hours on their first playthrough, lacking the replay value or modes (like Mercenaries) that the 1999 game offered.
Asset Reuse: The game reuses many assets from the RE2 remake, making it feel less like a unique, ambitious project, even though it was released soon after.
Action over Horror: The focus shifted heavily from survival horror toward arcade-style action and quick-time events, reducing the tension.

It’s a visually impressive, well-acted game with some solid gameplay mechanics, but it doesn’t quite live up to the legacy of the original or even its immediate predecessor, Resident Evil 2. As a long-time fan of the series, I can’t help but feel a little let down by its brevity and the lack of content that made the original so memorable. It’s a solid entry, but it’s not the comeback I was hoping for.

Still, if you’re a Resident Evil fan who enjoys action-packed gameplay with a bit of nostalgia, it’s worth playing. Just be prepared for a short journey through Raccoon City.

Extremely fun action-horror reimagining of Resident Evil 3: Nemesis. While this game differs greatly from the vision and style of the original, it exceeds and surpasses the original in many ways. The combat is fantastic and feels really good, the dialogue and interactions between characters are great and the world of Raccoon City looks incredible. 

There are some notes that this remake does not capture from the original. Much of the atmosphere and vibe of the original has not been preserved. Entire segments such as the park are absolutely missing from this remake and it's a shame as I really would've liked to have fought the tunnel worm. The game also felt quite easy and did not necessarily keep you starved of ammo, but these are all minor complaints that have no real impact on the quality of this game. One thing I will praise about this remake is keeping the story relatively intact. I also appreciate how they expanded on Carlos and Jill's characters through their dialogue and interactions. 

If you've never played Resident Evil 3 and want to experience it, I'd recommend playing either this game or the original. I think this game can stand toe to toe with the original (though you SHOULD play both since they are very different experiences) but ultimately it's up to you. If you like action and gameplay, RE3 Remake is the way to go. If you're more of a fan of atmosphere and survival horror, the original is for you.

Coming straight from RE2, RE3 feels like a deliberate shift in tone. Where RE2 traps you in a sprawling, resource-starved nightmare, RE3 moves fast and plays more like an action thriller. You're less a survivor piecing together a terrifying world and more a hardened fighter pushing through it. That's not a criticism it's just a different game.

And as that different game, it's genuinely fun. The visuals are a step up, the story is well-told, and the way it weaves into the broader Resident Evil universe is its strongest quality. The callbacks and connective tissue to RE2's events give it real weight for anyone coming in as a fan of the series.

The caveat worth knowing upfront is the length. RE2 gave me 24 hours across both Leon A and Claire B. RE3 gave me 8. It's a weekend game, not a marathon, and if you go in expecting that, it's a great one. But if you're measuring value by playtime per dollar, it falls short.

My one genuine frustration was the Nemesis encounters. The more aggressive, relentless design wore on me in a way the RE2 Tyrant never did. Less dread, more annoyance.

Still, RE3 is worth your time, especially if you're already invested in the story. Just temper your expectations coming off RE2.

I completed Resident Evil 2 both Claire and Leon Campaign on 1st try in hardest difficulty with regular weapons, but i couldn't do the same with Resident Evil 3 Inferno difficulty as it was so tough that i practically gave up and cheezed through with Infinite Shop items.

The ideal Resident Evil experince is playing the game on Hard difficulties. Anything else is a waste of time.

RE 3 story campaign may be short but its a fantastic followup of RE 2 and interestingly takes place a little ahead of the events in RE 2, even at same location like the RPD Police station HQ. With RE3 the Queen of Resident Evil Jill Valentine returns and this time she is wearning strapless Tube Tops while constantly flashing those sweaty clean shaven arm pits in so many cut scenes which is bound to make men go crazy. I found the campaign as short and sweet with a pleasant side kick Carlos who you can play as a character.

But when it comes to Gameplay, RE 3 is many times far more tougher than RE2. The Regular Zombies have longer tether and therefore the lunge distance is significantly higher, the ammo at higher difficulties is harder to find so you have to conserve strategize and fight very tactically like many times you need to stun zombies to get away than kill them. [h1]Solid Game, Flawed Remake[/h1]
Resident Evil 3 is an immediate follow up to the remake of Resident Evil 2. After proving they could pull off an old school survival horror game with RE7, and then running a victory lap with RE2 being as polished and financially successful as it was, it makes sense to remake the third game in the series. Unfortunately, while this is still a polished game, it seriously pales in comparison to the original PlayStation title and is the first Resident Evil Remake to be noticeably lacking compared to its source material.

RE3 follows the story of Jill Valentine, one of the two playable characters from the original Resident Evil, as she tackles with the trauma of surviving the zombie outbreak inside the Spencer Mansion. Umbrella has done goofed in the events of Resident Evil 2, which this game runs parallel to in the story, and has created a zombie apocalypse in Raccoon City. While Leon and Claire deal with the mad scientist Birkin, Jill is surviving the zombie hordes in the city itself. But it's not just zombies she has to worry about, as Umbrella has dispatched a nightmarish creature to hunt her down and eliminate her from being a witness to their corruption, The Nemesis. Jill must team up with unlikely allies to stop Nemesis and escape Raccoon City before it is wiped off the map.

The presentation of the remake is incredible. Running on the RE Engine, the game manages to look and run phenomenally on most machines and has great support for mods as well. Jill herself is very true to the design of the character from prior games, and her voice actress delivers a top notch performance. In addition to Jill, Carlos is a terrific supporting role with an equally great performance and role in the story. There's also a little more insight into the events that led to the destruction of the police department before Leon arrived which was a welcome surprise.

The gameplay is excellent as one would expect by a modern Resident Evil game. You have the same excellent level design, finding keycards and tools to remove obstructions in the environment, and limited resources. However, being a returning protagonist from the first game, Jill Valentine is no rookie like Leon and Claire were. She has a very capable dodge move which is a mechanic inspired by the counterattack system that you had in the original game on the PlayStation. This allows you to dodge attacks and pull of sick headshots that can kill enemies instantly. Combine this with multiple difficulties which mix up enemies and the placement of items, as well as a ton of fun New Game Plus unlocks, and you have a complete Resident Evil package... kinda.

The biggest problems with this game are its omission of content from the original. You have entire sections from the PlayStation version, such as the iconic clocktower dungeon, that are gone here. You no longer have the split second decision moments from the original either which encouraged replays, just a straight shot linear campaign. You have no mercenaries mode that acted as a fun extra in the original which you used to unlock infinite ammo weapons. Instead, they bundled this game with a gimmicky Dead by Daylight knockoff multiplayer game called Resident Evil Resistance which nobody plays anymore. But the worst, the absolute WORST thing they did to this remake was what happened to Nemesis. 

Nemesis just isn't dangerous in this game. He wasn't a totally random anomaly in the original, and you could use exploits to avoid him, but he was this constant pursuer that NEVER stopped chasing Jill. Every brief respite you had was ruined by this thing showing up and murdering people or destroying your escape ride out of the city and he didn't mess around at all. Here, he is largely just a scripted set piece you run away from or shoot at once in a while. His redesign is pretty cool looking, but he gets mutilated into a xenomorph ripoff about halfway through the game which is very disappointing. All in all, he deserved better than this game. And Jill deserved to finish him off with a magnum shot to the head with her iconic line "You want STARS? I'll give you stars!" Now she has the lamest catchphrase before dispatching the final boss. Lame.

Overall though, this is still a great game. But unlike RE1, 2, and 4 remakes which could be argued have better qualities over their original versions, this is a clear downgrade over the PS1 classic. Check that out first before playing this game.

Visually, Resident Evil 3 looks fantastic. Just like Resident Evil 2, the RE Engine brings Raccoon City to life with incredible detail, and from a technical standpoint the game looks great.
Unfortunately, that’s where most of my praise ends.
The original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis is one of my favorite games in the entire franchise, alongside Resident Evil 4. I played it countless times growing up, even speedrunning it and unlocking the infinite ammo rewards through the Mercenaries mode on the GameCube version. Because of that, I was extremely excited when this remake was announced after how good the RE2 remake turned out.
Sadly, this remake feels like a massive missed opportunity.
One of the biggest problems is how quickly everything happens. In the original game there was a sense of buildup before encountering Nemesis. In the remake, he appears almost immediately and starts chasing Jill without much tension or setup.
Another disappointment is how Nemesis is handled overall. In the original game he felt unpredictable and constantly threatening, appearing at unexpected moments. In the remake, most of his encounters feel heavily scripted. Once you’ve played through the game once, it becomes very obvious when he’s going to appear, which removes a lot of the tension.
The game also removes several iconic locations from the original, including the park and the clock tower. Instead of expanding on these areas, the remake cuts them entirely, which makes the overall experience feel much smaller. The city exploration that made the original so memorable is significantly reduced, and the story moves very quickly from the streets to the sewers, the hospital, and then the final underground lab.
The puzzle design is also extremely simplified compared to the original games. Most puzzles feel more like minor interruptions than actual challenges, which further contributes to the game feeling rushed.
Another change I personally didn’t like was how Jill Valentine is written here. While she’s clearly portrayed as a capable and experienced survivor of the mansion incident, her personality often comes across as unnecessarily aggressive toward other characters, particularly Carlos Oliveira and the U.B.C.S. In the original game she was skeptical of them, but she wasn’t nearly as hostile.
The game does have some positives. The visuals are excellent, the gameplay mechanics are smooth, and it’s interesting to briefly explore the RPD again from Carlos’s perspective. But overall, the experience feels rushed and significantly smaller than the original game.
Out of all the modern Resident Evil remakes, this is the only one where I would honestly recommend playing the original instead.
The game isn’t terrible, it’s short, polished, and still somewhat enjoyable, but it never lives up to the potential it had.

Resident Evil 3 leans much more into cinematic storytelling than traditional survival horror gameplay. The pacing is fast, and the game moves quickly from one big moment to the next. In some ways, this actually works in its favor. The story felt a bit more entertaining than Resident Evil 2 to me, mostly because the characters and cutscenes keep things moving and make it feel like a playable action-horror movie. The visuals look fantastic, though there are occasional minor stutters.

Combat is also helped by the solid weapon variety. The game gives you a good mix of weapons to work with, a strength that has been consistent throughout the franchise, and switching between them keeps fights from feeling repetitive.

That said, the biggest downside is how short the campaign is. The game honestly feels like it ends right when things are really starting to pick up. It also lacks the same level of challenge and tension that made RE2 so memorable. Many encounters feel easier, even on Inferno difficulty, which takes away some of the survival horror pressure.

Replay value is also limited since there isn’t much extra content once you finish the story. It’s also noticeably less scary overall, leaning more toward action than horror.

Rating: 7.5/10 – Cinematic horror that entertains throughout, but held back by its short length and lack of challenge.

We have idiotic wooden boxes as well with bright yellow on them that you can slash like in Resident Evil 4 (which was made to be a shooter-style game, there it makes a bit of sense but here this is just out of place).
[*]This game has SO much content cut, why did they even bother? This could very well be a short 2h DLC to Resident Evil 2. And yes, even if you play this game normally you are done in about 2h, even less when you “rush”. Clocktower, gone. Worm-Boss and park/graveyard, gone. Decisions to make it more interesting, gone. Costumes, gone. They left in maybe 30% of the original content and hell, the original was already short!
[*]Jill gets sidelined in her own game. Half the game we play as Carlos. HE goes back to the RPD for some senseless sidemission to detain a suddenly very important scientist no one ever heard of before. HE gets to face Brad when it doesn’t even have any impact whatsoever on him and he just brushes said encounter off in a second but it would have been very traumatic for Jill. Brad? He gets thrown to the side and pitifully deleted in an absolute emotionless slop cutscene with no buildup whatsoever. But the biggest disrespect is yet to come…
[*]Nemesis. He is an absolute JOKE in this game. Since you only have like three streets as areas in the city, he can’t suddenly show up or roam around like Mr. X in Re2 keeping you on our toes and surprise you (I mean even if he did, we don’t do any exploration so whatever I guess?) but it gets even worse: Every single encounter with him is scripted. He will only show up after you picked up certain items so you feel safe all around, when he shows up it is always the same three or four times and places - there is absolutely no randomness here. Oh and since we have dodge-mechanics now why even be afraid? You can just bully him with dodge and strike at him, even on harder difficulties. Or… you know, you could just throw a single grenade or two. On top of that the encounters feel so cheesy and overdramatic, it’s like a stupid action-movie. Removing Jill from the RPD altogether destroyed so many great moments as well, like how Nemesis suddenly jumped through one of the hallway windows. Personally I also found his extremely fast mutations progressing way too quickly…
[*]Jill… holding a solargun double the size and probs three times the weight of herself with no issues… really? The gun is so powerful, the ground made of concrete and steel underneath Jill’s boots broke apart and there is a kilometer long hole drilled into the laboratory but here she is being absolutely fine firing it. Listen, this is Resident Evil with the traditional rocketlauncher ending sequence of almost every game but this moment was stupid, even for Resident Evil standards.
[*]Instead of adding the missing 70% of content of the original game… we get a section with Carlos just being in a small room shooting hundreds of zombies coming in like it’s an online multiplayer raid-mode… and the zombie-corpses explode to make room for the next ones… really? (RE4 could make it work, this one again is so cheesy… why?)
[*]But hey, at least we get a very detailed hentai-scene of Jill getting parasiteworms put into her mouth by an insect and another very detailed scene of her puking the parasite worms out. Totally worth all the effort of animating that specific thing so preciously instead of adding the missing content back into the game.
[*]Hey, it’s not all doom and gloom though, at least we get a long unskippable moment of Carlos listening to a tape of our scientist/doctor and how he berates, insults and degrades a nurse with typical below-the-belt humour. Totally worth hearing him saying she should polish his shoes and wipe her patients’ asses instead of adding the missing content to the game. Carlos didn’t enjoy having to listen to that stuff either, he cracked me up!
[*]Instead of actually making this Remake great (and it could have been so great!) we got an unnecessary extra multiplayer game added to this as a “bundle” called RE Resistance - I played it a few times and as someone having 4000h in Dead by Daylight… no, it’s a disaster and an awful attempt at 4v1. And I have a sad suspicion that the Remake is partially so bad and sloppy because a lot of time was put into this rather than the remake itself.

Also, I just have to say that the physical design doesn't look like her original self at all. The only good thing they did with this remake was Carlos. They fixed his character just to absolutely ruin Jill's (one of the most loved characters of the franchise). Then, the developers still had the audacity to shove this version of Jill in Death Island, making her cold, reckless, and mean as if they completely forgot about the tone of her email that she sent to Barry in Revelations 2. I’ve loved Resident Evil for a long time, and I was so excited for this. Unfortunately, this remake completely misses the soul of the game it’s based on. Its simply a quick cash grab for Capcom to fund RE4R.

The original RE3 had a very specific atmosphere. It felt like you arrived thirty minutes late to the end of the world. The last stand had already happened. The barricades had failed. The cops were all dead. What you were running through wasn’t a city under siege, it was a necropolis. Burning streets, abandoned defenses, dead cops and UBCS. You weren’t saving anyone here. You were trying to escape what was left of it. That tone is almost completely gone here.

One of the most baffling omissions is the opening sequence from the original game. The original intro showed the RPD attempting one last effort. Barricades, swat, firing lines trying to hold back a tidal wave of infected civilians. It ends with a perfect shot: a dead officer lying on the ground, seen through the reflection of a riot helmet visor, slowly rising back up as a zombie. The UBCS rope in, "lets do this!" is said with bravado, then you get a montage of them getting slaughtered. The implication is clear. Organized resistance is already dead. The city is lost. This was replaced by live action news reels and Umbrella commercials. That original scene perfectly established the tone of RE3. Which is not recreated here at all.

Instead, the remake opens like an action movie. Explosions, a QTE scripted chase, Nemesis smashing through Jills apartment (then is stopped by a wood door with a bookcase in front of it) The pacing never slows down long enough to let the dread settle in. The original game gave you time, to think and plan, but also kept the threat of Nemesis there, pushing you to hurry. This type of strategic planning and thinking of the original is gone, replaced by action set pieces and what comes down to a series of corridors to shoot through.

Nemesis himself is a casualty. In the original he was unpredictable and oppressive. He could appear in places you didn’t expect and forced you to constantly weigh the decision to fight or run. Here he’s reduced to 4 boss fights and 2 "chase sequences" with only one that feels slightly dynamic. The sense that something is actively hunting you through the city is entirely gone. 

Just as disappointing is how much of the character dynamic between Jill and Nemesis has been stripped away. In the original game, their encounters felt personal. Nemesis wasn’t just another monster he was the game, he was so popular that when you thought of RE as a series Nemesis was what you thought of as a BOW. Specifically sent to eliminate the remaining STARS members he kills zero STARS members in this one making him more of a joke than threat. The final confrontation carried weight because Jill had endured the entire nightmare and finally faced him down. With the iconic “You want S.T.A.R.S.? I’ll give you STARS.” perfectly capturing the frustration both she and the player had been through. Further Nemesis was more of a character in the original. Its first interactions with Jill are all business, but as time goes on, as she evades or defeats him constantly, it becomes well, personal. The highlight of this is the clocktower scene, rescue is coming from a helicopter. Nemesis does not wait for Jill to board, or it to land, he shoots it as she sees it come in. Why? Because he wanted her to know there is no escape, when she turns in the original cutscene, he just looks right at her. At the end, Nemesis is a snarling, wounded, insane animal, with only one desire, kill Jill. In this one he has none of that.

Jill herself also feels very different from her original portrayal. In the original game she came across as a trained professional pushed to her limits, determined, resourceful, trying to stay alive in a situation that had spiraled beyond control, she was an exhausted stoic. In the remake she’s much more modern hollywoods idea of a strong female character, she's acidic, filled with barbs and quips, cursing constantly, it just feels like its trying to hard to make her a "bad@$$" when the original game fulfilled that with a very quiet and composed Jill.

The remake also cuts a staggering amount of content from the original game. Entire locations that defined RE3 are simply gone. The Clock Tower, one of the most memorable sections of the original, has been reduced to a brief boss battle. The Dead Factory, which served as the original game’s final area and tied directly into Umbrella’s role in the disaster, has been removed entirely. Several branching paths, choices, and encounters that gave the original replay value are also missing. There are many more.

Another thing the original did extremely well was how it handled survivors. The people you meet aren’t organizing a resistance or forming heroic plans. They’re broken and trying to escape or you arrived just after they took what they felt was their only option. Some refuse to go with you. Many die moments after meeting you. Even when others manage to save civilians, you often arrive too late to make a difference. Such as the clock tower survivors. That bleak tone is what made the original so memorable. The remake, on the other hand, feels like it’s trying to be a fast paced action game instead of a slow burn survival horror experience. It’s polished and it plays well mechanically, but it’s also shockingly short and missing huge sections, moments, and the "soul" of the original. 

The result is a game that’s technically competent but hollow, that relies on nostalgia baiting for older players, and the lack of knowledge of new fans. It recreates the surface elements the characters, the locations, Nemesis, but loses the atmosphere and tone that made the original one of the most unique entries in the series.

For newcomers it might be a decent action horror game (but you're frankly doing yourself a diservice if you never played the original)
For fans of the original, it feels like, ironically enough, a zombie. Its not the "person" you knew, its a shell, puppeteered by malevolent forces, it looks superficially like them, but its just a corpse, shuffling forward, moaning for your money and time.

Resident Evil 3 is a great experience that ends too soon.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Graphics and Performance[/h2]

The game looks incredible and runs well. Personally, I did not like the reused assets from the previous remake and the reused locations.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Story and Characters[/h2]

Carlos is my man, but due to the short game time (5–8 hours) there is not much development or anything particularly interesting. The story is very simple and predictable. To be precise, you are once again in Raccoon City, but this time from the perspective of Jill and Carlos. I really liked Nemesis and how he was more aggressive and powerful compared to Resident Evil 2. The chase sequences were cool, but it would have been better to have more of them.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

The gameplay is similar to the Resident Evil 2 remake. You have basic third-person movement and you can shoot. To make it feel fresher, they added a dodge mechanic for Jill and a parry mechanic for Carlos. The guns felt great and each one felt unique and different.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Sound and Music[/h2]

The ambient sound of this game is really great. You hear every step and every little noise that your opponents make. The music is on the more generic side. Nothing memorable, but still serviceable.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

I really enjoyed the experience. They took the good things from the previous remake and added a few new features.

However, due to its very short playtime, recycled locations, and minimal replayability, I cannot recommend the game at full price to anyone.

[b]Recommendation:[/b] Wait for a sale and then definitely buy it.
