[h1]Bummers Scoob! This guy really is after our buns! It's like he’s our Nemesis or something![/h1] 
[b]It’s an okay game, but it fails to capture how intimidating and unpredictable the Nemesis truly was. On top of that, it’s a significantly shorter experience with less content than RE2 Remake.[/b] 

The disease from the Arklay mountains reached Raccoon City and infected most of its population. Meanwhile, the remaining members of the S.T.A.R.S. unit are hunted by a new, deadly, and unrelenting bioweapon. 



The setup is simple – Jill tries to escape the city while being hunted by the new stalker monster. For a survival horror scenario it’s perfectly fine. On top of that we have Carlos, who, although is part of Umbrella, has his heart in the right place and just wants to help people. And that’s pretty much it for the main plot, as you are constantly being attacked by the undying menace that is the Nemesis. 

The introduction of Nemesis is rather intimidating, especially when you compare him to the guy from the RE2 Remake. He doesn’t just slowly walk behind you but runs up and tries to sucker punch you into oblivion. You think you ran far enough to lose him? Boom, he jumps down from a building next to you and trips you with his ?tentacle?. Unfortunately, this initial intimidation wears off really quickly. 

The actual “Nemesis-stalking-you" part of the game is maybe 20% of the whole thing somewhere at the beginning. After that the guy mutates and either “attacks” you in scripted sections/cutscenes or is just a boss fight. The guy called Nemesis, actually stalks you less than Mr. X in the previous game, at least in the gameplay sense. While he appears constantly throughout the game, he is not an actual AI threat hunting you down and hindering whatever you need to do, but just a story element really. 

I do like the atmosphere of the city – burning streets with animated corpses roaming all around them. Zombie dogs looking for scraps, people running for their lives. Feels like an actual crisis city. 



In a typical RE fashion, you run around areas infested with zombies and other wacky mutants. You either avoid them or try to clear them out somewhat efficiently. You solve puzzles and look for key items to progress further. 

In the game you play either as Jill or Carlos – instead of choosing characters at the beginning, this time there is just one campaign that just alternates between perspectives. The RESIDENT HELPERS have different loadouts and evasive maneuvers. 

The game is a step up in action – not only I feel you get more ammunition in general, but your move set also gives you more options. Jill’s spacebar lets you dodge in the four cardinal directions, and if you do it at the right time, you perform a perfect dodge letting you roll out of harms way and even slow mo aim for a critical hit. Carlos punches s.hit instead of rolling, being able to put something to the ground if done right. The perfect dodge window felt very weird for me, especially when fighting the mutated Nemesis. Idk whether it’s me timing it wrong or the weird, wide punch hitbox of the guy. It’s a matter of getting used to, and the counterattacks are very satisfying and useful, but it just felt really unreliable at the beginning, with me constantly screaming “I PRESSED IT GO.DD.AMNIT”. 

I already talked about the Nemesis – compared to the original, his role is rather small. He is everywhere while simultaneously contributing very little to the whole fear factor. You don’t feel this anxiety when entering new areas, that he might be off-screen about to fire a rocket at you or run up to you to beat you up. The first part of the game tries to emulate that and maybe if it stuck to it a little bit longer, it would’ve been fine. Instead, the guy is very underwhelming. In the OG he was also a lot less predictable; he could give you a break for a few areas, and then jump on you randomly, making each playthrough a little different. Here, his appearances are scripted to always trigger, making it easier to plan and just avoid him most of the time. 

There is not a lot of puzzles – there is the train tracks one, vaccine mixing and I struggle to remember much else apart for looking for safe codes. These mostly contain weapon upgrades. 

Boss fights are ok, even though some stages felt weird to get the dodging right. I’d say they are nothing extraordinary though, making the Nemesis into just another mutant to take down. Zombie behavior is a little different, being able to only fake death once and lunging at you a lot more from the ground, making knifing harder. 

The game feels rushed – not only are there discussions of tons of cut content from the game, but it is short and sometimes even not balanced. In the hospital for example, Carlos faces Hunters, for which he is completely not prepared for. [b]That is not to say that anyone would be prepared for a 7 foot tall heavy-armored reptile,[/b] but his loadout feels very underwhelming. You pretty much need to use grenades for them, because there is no other reasonable option. For the record, Jill’s shotgun takes these things down in 1-2 shots. Apart from that, there is recycled content – Carlos gets 2 whole sections in the game and one of them is just R.P.D. from the previous installment. 

Compared to RE2R, the game just has a lot less content. RE2 had 2 campaigns with 2 scenarios each – they weren’t crazy different, but it was still something. It also had several other gamemodes. Here, the game does not only feel short, but for replayability’s sake they just added two more difficulties and that’s it. Oh, and instead of unlocking infinite guns and other unlockables through performing specific feats, you get points for these feats with which you can choose rewards. Not a bad system to be honest. 



Graphically the game looks very nice; the only nitpicks are zombies that go into 10 frames per second mode when you get far enough from them. I also really like the aesthetic of the destroyed city. Next – say what you will about the Nemesis here, but they nailed this design – he appears as this mysterious bioweapon covered in tape, to then mutate and strip that tape off him throughout multiple stages of the game. Very cool visual design choice. 

RE2 remake valued the quiet ambiance disturbed by your own footsteps. This game has much more soundtrack playing, and while it’s not bad, I wish they maybe just left the ambiance of the destroyed city in chaos. General ambiance and sound design is really good. Voice acting is nice, apart from a few lines delivered into the wrong context and Jill saying her quips... well, that’s not the VA problem, but it still hurt me internally, I’d take the Jill Sandwich over this any day. 



Overall, it’s an okay albeit short game, that is definitely the weakest remake installment of the series. It feels like there is a lot missing here, and it does not do justice to neither Nemesis nor RE3 as a whole. But it’s RE alright, you will have some fun with it.

[h1]The third entry in the series, and easily the shortest. [/h1] 

For what it is, though, this remake does a solid job. Yes, a few things are missing that only exist in the original game, but the fast-paced action and strong replayability make it surprisingly enjoyable, even on absurd difficulties like Inferno.

I would have loved a structure where you could fully commit to either Jill or Carlos. Instead, the game blends their paths together, forcing you to play both. I was hoping for something closer to [i]Resident Evil 2[/i], where choosing Claire or Leon led to distinct A and B routes. Because of that, and since much of the gameplay mirrors [i]RE2[/i] with a different slice of Raccoon City, this remake sometimes feels more like an oversized DLC than a full standalone title. That’s likely why it’s divisive among fans. Personally, I didn’t mind. I had a good time with it, and it made me appreciate how Capcom handled the remake overall, especially the visuals and the streamlined story.

[i]Confession time:[/i] I’ve finished this game three times. Once on [b]PS4[/b], then again on [b]PC[/b] through a [i]Humble Bundle[/i], where I played it together with my ex, who loved the franchise just as much and even earned all the achievements herself. And now, once more on [b]PS5[/b]. Each run was a blast, and because the game is so short, it became easier and faster every time. Knowing all the codes, shortcuts, and little tricks turned even Inferno mode from pure chaos into something surprisingly manageable.

In terms of changes, Jill received a strong upgrade in both appearance and writing, but Carlos easily got the biggest glow-up. Between this game and his portrayal in [i]Dead by Daylight[/i], it’s no surprise he suddenly gained a massive fanbase. And honestly, it’s well deserved. The simplified story also helps the pacing. The original could drag at times, though this remake arguably overcorrects by making it a bit too short. You can’t please everyone.

Visually, it’s a feast. The music takes a backseat here, overshadowed by constant combat, monster sounds, and the ever-present threat of Nemesis, but that works in favor of the tension. Speaking of Nemesis, they absolutely leaned into his role as a relentless stalker. His design and mechanics are intense, and I genuinely panicked during my early encounters. After the twentieth time though, he starts feeling more like a troublesome child than a nightmare, which is oddly funny. Outside of Nemesis and a few new enemy types, the game plays almost identically to [i]RE2[/i]. That makes sense, given that both stories unfold at the same time. In the end, while I genuinely enjoyed my time with it, I’m recommending the game. 

Still, as a fast, replayable, adrenaline-fueled experience, it absolutely does its job.

Then the game becomes It Follows.

A large, disrespectful thing with big guns, zero boundaries, and a The Crow cosplay begins following you. He does not explain himself. He just shows up; like a DM you ignored that escalated into urban collapse.

You’re briefly rescued by a soldier who clearly eats salad, goes to the gym, and moisturizes. His hair looks like it bathes in aloe vera. You trust him immediately.

What follows is a speedrun of Raccoon City tourism: Train guys. Downtown chaos. Subway switches. Power plant. Museum police station. And finally, an underground lab decorated in white walls and brownish-red “don’t ask” stains.

Meanwhile, your stalker keeps evolving like a Pokémon powered by resentment and steroids. By the end I wasn’t sure if I was playing Resident Evil, Alien, or a very angry trench coat.

I recommend you to break up with him. Go no-contact. Block Nemesis on all platforms.

Resident Evil 3 Remake is a good game that exists under the massive shadow of its predecessor. As someone who hasn’t played the original, I approached this remake without nostalgia, and overall I found it to be a very enjoyable experience. The story is solid, the pacing is fast, and the character designs are excellent. Visually, the game looks very similar to RE2 Remake, but with slightly more detail that helps elevate the presentation. One of the biggest improvements is the dodge mechanic, which feels absolutely necessary and adds a layer of skill and satisfaction that was missing in the previous game.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay closely follows the RE2 Remake formula, which works very well here. Inventory management is familiar, shooting feels responsive, and enemy encounters are tense without becoming tedious. Puzzles exist, but they are clearly not the main focus and are mostly straightforward and forgettable. The third-person perspective fits the game perfectly, and the addition of the perfect dodge mechanic completely changes how encounters play out. Successfully dodging attacks, especially on higher difficulties, feels incredibly rewarding and never gets old.
The weapon variety is solid, and progression feels natural as you unlock new tools to deal with increasingly dangerous enemies. The game also switches between protagonists at certain points, which I found to be well executed and helpful in keeping the experience from becoming repetitive.

[h1]Difficulty & Inferno[/h1]
The difficulty curve is well designed up to Nightmare. On these difficulties, the game is challenging but fair. Planning routes, managing resources, and learning enemy behavior all feel meaningful. When you die, it usually feels like a mistake you made, which makes overcoming sections satisfying.
Inferno difficulty, however, is where the balance completely falls apart. Even with bonus weapons and defense coins, success often depends more on RNG than skill. Random one-shot attacks, unavoidable grabs, and enemies appearing from off-screen make many deaths feel unfair. Defense coins help against standard damage but do nothing against sudden instant-kill situations. The final boss fight is particularly frustrating, often resulting in stun-locks where a single mistake can mean instant death with no chance to recover.

[h1]Nemesis & Design[/h1]
Nemesis is intimidating, but his encounters feel more scripted than expected. While he looks fantastic and creates tension, he lacks the unpredictability that could have made him truly terrifying. That said, the game’s visual and technical quality is excellent. Environments are detailed, character models are incredibly well done, and facial animations look amazing on higher settings. Performance was flawless throughout my playthrough, even with most settings near max.
The biggest downside is the game’s length. It feels significantly shorter than RE2 Remake, which makes the experience feel more compact and slightly rushed in places. Still, shorter doesn’t necessarily mean worse, and the game remains engaging from start to finish.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
Resident Evil 3 Remake is often criticized because it followed one of the best remakes ever made. While it doesn’t reach the same heights as RE2 Remake, it is far from a bad game. It delivers a fun and intense experience, a decent story, fantastic visuals, and one of the most enjoyable combat mechanics in the series thanks to the dodge system. Inferno difficulty holds it back, but aside from that, it’s a game well worth playing.

[h1]Rating: 7.5/10[/h1]

Consider this review coming from a fan of the franchise , This game certainly has polished visuals and tight gameplay but it feels like a dlc or a single chapter of a game. 

For fans coming off the heels of the expansive Resident Evil 2 Remake or looking forward to the epic scale of Resident Evil 4, this entry is a massive disappointment in terms of value and variety.

The most glaring issue is the length. While Resident Evil 4 is a sprawling odyssey that takes players through villages, castles, and islands over 15+ hours, Resident Evil 3 can easily be cleared in under 5 hours on a first playthrough.

Because so many locations from the original 1999 game (like the Clock Tower and the Park) were cut, the game lacks a sense of journey. It feels like one long, linear chase sequence rather than a fully realized survival horror experience. By the time you feel like the story is ramping up, the credits are already rolling.

The mini-bosses and enemy variety in this game feel uninspired and "empty." In other Resident Evil titles, mutations feel like grotesque, biological nightmares.

Nemesis is supposed to be the ultimate upgrade to Mr. X. In reality, he becomes an annoyance.

Wont recommend playing this if you are a true fan of the franchise , rather hurt your eyes a bit and enjoy the og version.

As an OG Resident Evil fan, this game provides a relatively conflicting experience. It's a competent survival horror game, but a hollow adaptation of the original.

I came to this one late, already well aware of the complaints regarding this game and after finally playing it myself, I have to agree with the criticisms. 

Jill is excellent, the gunplay is tight, and it looks great. No issues there. But the missing pieces of content hurt this game, especially when it comes to Nemesis. After RE2 Remake nailed the persistent threat with Mr. X, I expected the same organic terror here. Instead, Nemesis is largely confined to scripted chases and boss arenas. The relentless pressure that defined him in the original just isn't there.

Even the gore system took a hit. RE2 Remake let you blow chunks off zombies in gruesome detail. Here, that visceral feedback is dialed back noticeably. You can tell this game was rushed out the door, even if Capcom did a respectable job with it. 

Newcomers to the franchise won't feel this same disappointment. Their main gripe will likely be the shorter campaign and minimal replayability for the price point.

That said, grab it on sale. The core experience is enjoyable, and Jill Valentine deserves more time in the spotlight. (Any chance to see her back in action is worth it IMO)

Resident Evil 3 feels much more like an addition to Resident Evil 2 than a fully fledged sequel for a number of reasons. For one, it takes place at the same time as its predecessor, and even shares some locations. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, I actually thought it did a good job of fleshing out the story of Resident Evil 2, but at only around 6 hours long, and being limited to one campaign. it doesn't do quite enough to feel like a fully fleshed out sequel that meaningfully pushes the story forward as the next mainline game. Now, enough of looking at it as a sequel, how is it as a game? Well luckily it's very very good. The same great combat that RE 2 remake created is expanded upon with the addition of a dodge, and it's a very welcome change. Dodging is always something that's been done by players, just by running side to side. so having a dedicated button for it, and being able to pull off perfect dodges is a welcome change. The main villain here is Nemesis, and he's a mixed bag. Some of the chase sequences can be frustrating due to his fast attacks, and the fact that he's usually out of sight behind you so dodging can be difficult, but these sections have checkpoints so they're not too bad. The boss fights themselves are pretty good, but feel far too similar to the fights in RE 2, not only in the way you fight Nemesis, but in the way he grows as a threat. Jill and Carlos are great protagonists, and there's an all right set of side characters. None of them stand out as amazing, but they do a fine job fulfilling their role in the game and its plot. While I wouldn't say it's worth the full price, mainly due to how short the game is, it goes on sale for $10 and it is 100% worth that price. I thoroughly enjoyed my time with it, and definitely think it's worth the time to play it. TLDR: IMO it's a lesser, shorter RE 2. Still a good title though. There's a little replayability, but nowhere near as much as RE 2, especially since RE 2 had you playing the campaign multiple times to see -all- of the campaign. RE 3 initially received a lot more flak than it deserved, and, while it isn't the best, it's definetely not as bad as a lot of people used to say. 

Story: Play as Jill Sandwich, lockpick master, tanking all sorts of punishement like it's nothing, trying to escape Raccoon city before its inevitable downfall. A very linear story progression, packed with a lot of action. 
Nemesis still plays a big part in the game, but he is too gimmicky to be considered an ever looming threat. You will meet all the characters you've met in the OG, but they might come and go with slight variations. There will not be multiple endings, nor is there any choices like in the OG, which made me vewy, vewy, sad.

Gameplay: Plays very much like RE2, development being overlapped with RE 2 and all. The only real difference between RE 2 and RE 3 is a dodge/counter mechanic (depending on which character you're currently playing as), and that the knife doesn't break (meaning you get to stab them zombies on the ground, you ammo hoarder, you).
I felt like some boss fights were too gimmicky, but the ammo wasn't scarce enough for me to regret it if I didn't get the gimmick right away.
I didn't care much for the instant death Hunters but they've been an annoying staple for the RE franchise forever, so, this was sadly expected.
The guns feel nice, with upgrades spread throughout the game for the keen observer. 
Lots of backtracking, but it's done in an intelligent manner; it never overwhelms, is always rewarding, and always changes just enough to keep you on your toes.
Once you've beaten the game, a ''shop'' unlocks, allowing you to spend hard earned points for various things: inventory space, health regen and a couple of guns with infinite ammo, just to name a few.
Back to Nemesis, arguably the most important/iconic element of RE 3, doesn't seem to, uh, ''work'' properly when met randomly. His attacks can sometimes chain endlessly until you're dead, through no fault of the player. Like... he seems fairer on boss fights, which seems counter intuitive.
The city, which a player might eagerly anticipate to explore, is quickly replaced by the next ever shrinking area, and it just keeps going like that until the game is finished. It might have been just me, but I was hoping for a Nemesis to chase me through a huge town... Seems like I'll need to go back to RE 2 to have a proper stalker.

Graphics: Superb, as expected with any RE engine game.

Audio: Everything is good, from the subtle tense ambiance to the quips of the characters. It's still RE like, meaning it's sometimes a bit goofy, but it serves its purpose. 

I have to say the third entry of the OG RE franchise birthed a monster that could chase you down, through a big town, giving P.T.S.D. to any and all who've ever heard: ''STAAAAARRSSSS''. In RE 2, they brought something similar back, with Mr. X chasing you, and he was well rounded at that... While in this entry, I felt like Nemesis wasn't present enough, was a bit cheesy when met randomly... maybe I can't exactly put my finger on the why, but his precense pales in comparison to Mr. X, making the title solely rely on everything BUT what the OG title had originally put a main focus on. So, yes, while it's still a good game, it isn't ''great''. IMO, RE 2 is, at least ''overall'' plain better.

I preface this by saying I am not a longtime fan of the series. I knew about the Resident Evil universe a little but didn’t play the games for whatever reason. Something recently changed, and I decided to give the franchise a try. I watched RE 0 and RE 1 walkthroughs to familiarize myself with what was happening and started my journey with RE 2 Remake. And oh boy, it was a blast! I 100%’d everything possible in the game and continued to RE 3 Remake, expecting a similar level of experience.

On the surface, RE 3 Remake is indeed very similar to RE 2 Remake. You immediately feel familiar with the gameplay, crafting, inventory, etc. However, the more you play, the more you notice that the game allows much less freedom and generally feels on rails often times. There are still sections with wider areas, puzzles, and things to explore, but nothing matches the RPD.

Next, the biggest focus of the game - the Nemesis. He is surely an upgrade of Mr. X! Faster, scarier, deadlier! He looks absolutely amazing, too! His first appearance is insanely good, but the scripted behaviour feels cheap very quickly. Like, he breaks through a wall but is then stopped by a certain door. Breaks through the ceiling but can’t get through some rubble. The mysteriousness of Mr. X lets you entertain the possibility of safe rooms he doesn’t enter. But the Nemesis, sent to destroy you, but unstoppable only in specific areas takes a lot from the immersion. There’s no more searching around to find you or anything - he appears out of nowhere and disappears just as easily once “the chase” is done. It’s also tiring how every time the Nemesis catches you, instead of just snapping you in half, it tries to make it cinematic and loses his chance.

Another complaint about the Nemesis [spoiler]is its mutation stages. I just don’t get it! Why does it evolve and grow so quickly after defeat? The G-stages in RE 2 were understandable since that virus seems far less controlled, given the atrocities it produces. But the Nemesis is a human-like, engineered killing machine. It’s cool seeing him use different weapons, but the mutations in the later parts of the game felt out of touch. Like they just copy-pasted G-stages formula from RE 2 without thinking.[/spoiler]

There are no different scenarios anymore. No bonus missions, either. Apparently, the only thing you unlock after playing the game is harder difficulties, and it’s also very confusing after RE 2. Hardcore isn’t so hardcore anymore, then there’s Nightmare for whatever reason, and then Inferno. You unlock the next hardest difficulty by beating the hardest one available to you, but it feels like an artificial increase of “content” - there’s no reason Hardcore couldn’t be the hardest difficulty, as it is in the previous game.

Seeing locations from the previous game, like the RPD and Kendo shop, was a really nice touch. The music, voice acting, and sound are all still great. The game is gorgeous. The story and writing, in general, are alright. But in the pursuit of the cinematic presentation they hurt the immersion - it just feels too videogamey at times. Overall, the game is good, but it could have been so much better. It is definitely worth playing, but it is not as great as RE 2 Remake.

Like I mentioned in my RE2 review, I’m not the biggest fan of horror, so this game being way less scary was actually a positive for me. Don’t get me wrong, it is still tense and scarier than most games, so it still somewhat benefits from a scary atmosphere, but it definitely puts a bigger emphasis on action rather than survival horror.

Halfway through the game, I was sure I liked it more than RE2. I prefer the reduced focus on ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ your pants, for example. While RE2 has Mr. X, this one has Nemesis, and he is used far differently. He’s more of a setpiece, and you are never required to navigate an environment while avoiding this big scary monster, which was the scariest part of RE2 for me. Instead, Nemesis is just badass and overpowered, and you’re meant to run from him in these tiny action set pieces that I enjoyed a lot.

But as the game got closer to the end, I realized I couldn't say it was better than the previous one. I noticed Jill was far stronger than Leon ever was, which made me feel less inclined to explore. It also didn't help that the levels themselves, apart from the first level in Raccoon City, are far inferior to anything in RE2. Since exploring was my favorite part of that game, the less incentive to explore mixed with the objectively worse levels made it so I just could not put it above RE2.

Many people also dislike it because it is very short, but I’m always of the opinion that the length of the game should never be taken into consideration when talking about quality. If we attach length to quality, we get slop games like AC Valhalla. But I’ll make a special exception for this game, since it not only came out at full price but it also had whole levels that were ripped out of RE2. In a 4 hour game, any level regardless of length is already too much. Since I got the game on discount and the price is lower now, this is less egregious.

Overall, I really enjoyed this game. Saying it’s a bit worse than RE2 is still a compliment, since RE2 is a masterpiece of survival horror.

## 🎮 **Resident Evil 3 Remake 

### 🔥 **First Impressions & Overall Experience**

**Resident Evil 3 Remake** is a modern, high-fidelity reimagining of the classic survival-horror title from the late ’90s. Built on the same engine that powered the acclaimed *Resident Evil 2 Remake*, this version delivers sharp visuals, moody lighting, and beautifully detailed environments that make Raccoon City feel alive (and terrifying). 
The game leans heavily into **fast-paced action** while still retaining key survival horror elements like resource management and tense combat encounters. 

---

## 🎯 **Gameplay & Mechanics**

✔️ **Tight, responsive combat:** Weapons feel satisfying and enemies react well, making each gunfight engaging. 
✔️ **Dodge mechanic adds depth:** The new dodge/roll system gives fights a dynamic rhythm, rewarding timing and positioning.
✔️ **Inventory and survival feel:** Like previous remakes, you manage limited space, forcing strategic choices on ammo and items. 

⚠️ **Shift toward action:** Compared with the original *Resident Evil 3* and *RE2 Remake*, this remake leans more into combat than puzzle-solving and slower tension-building exploration. Players who love survival horror pacing might miss that deeper strategic layer. 

---

## 📖 **Story & Characters**

The core narrative follows Jill Valentine trying to escape a zombie-overrun Raccoon City while hunted by the relentless Nemesis. The remake expands characterization with strong performances from the cast—especially Jill and Carlos—which adds emotional weight and personality to the journey. 

However, some iconic parts of the original game were cut or reimagined, which has divided long-time fans. 

---

## 👹 **Nemesis – The Star of the Show**

Nemesis remains the centerpiece antagonist, but **his role is more scripted** compared to the original’s near-constant pursuit. Some players find this less frightening and more like boss encounters than a stalking terror, while others enjoy the intensity of set-piece battles. ([NME][5])

---

## ⏱️ **Length & Replayability**

A common critique is the **short campaign**—most first playthroughs are around ~4–6 hours. ([Gamepressure.com][3]) Critics and players alike note this makes the game feel brief for a full-priced release. ([Metacritic][6])
There isn’t a traditional New Game+ or branching storyline, but unlockables, challenge modes, and the online *Resistance* multiplayer add some extended value.

---

## 📊 **Critic & Player Reception**

* **Critics overall:** Generally favorable reviews with solid scores (around high-70s / 80s). 
* **Player reaction:** Mixed—many love the visuals and gameplay, others criticize the shortened content and changes from the original. 

This split reflects how *RE3 Remake* is best enjoyed **on its own terms**, rather than as a *Resident Evil 2 Remake* successor. 

---

## 🧠 **Pros & Cons (Quick Summary)**

### 👍 **What It Does Well**

* ⭐ Gorgeous visuals and atmospheric presentation.
* 🎮 Fun, action-oriented combat with satisfying mechanics.
* 👩‍🚀 Strong characterization (Jill, Carlos) and voice acting. 
* 🔁 Unlockables and modes encourage replay beyond the first run. 
### 👎 **Where It Falls Short**

* ⏳ Short main campaign and low replay variety. 
* 🔪 Removes or streamlines some classic content and puzzles. 
* 🤖 Nemesis’ threat sometimes feels less persistent than expected. 

---

## 🎯 **Final Recommendation**

It’s much shorter than the first remake; we play as Jill and Carlos, but it’s not like the first remake where you finish the game and then go back to solve the same puzzles in the same locations. That would have been the logical approach, but it would have unnecessarily dragged on just for two cutscenes and a 5-minute true ending. I think we switched between Jill and Carlos once, which added some variety. The weapons and such are pretty good—you don’t need a lot of variety, but if you want, you can customize them using in-game currency from RES. 

The story is good; it was nice to see some locations and characters from RE2. The biggest difference from RE2 is that while RE2 was a tension-action game, I think this one is purely an action game. Mr. X’s presence relies more on a cold-blooded approach—he chases you on foot, and thinking about what he’d do if he got right up close is terrifying. They’ve also added a tracking mechanic to Nemesis throughout the game, but he chases you more like an action boss—running, screaming, and the weirdest part is that he uses everything from RPGs to various space-age weapons. Consequently, the game leans heavily toward the action side of the spectrum. In that regard, the game has turned out to be similar to a Call of Duty zombie-themed game.

The virus, Raccoon City, and so on add some lore to the story. In my opinion, the game falls short of the first one—it lacks some of the great tension elements, story depth, and puzzle complexity found in the first game, but they’ve made up for these shortcomings by focusing on different aspects. The action is intense; you can’t easily tear yourself away from the game. The innovations and the story pull you in from a different angle. Plus, unlike the first game where you’d run around taking damage if you ran out of ammo, a dodge mechanic has been added—even if you can’t use the knife for counters, you can dodge almost every attack. In short, if it were a bit longer, it could have rivaled RE2. It’s a notch below RE2 in terms of score, but it’s still good—10/7.

Pros:
Beautiful. 
Gameplay is fun.
You can now dodge. 
There are multiple difficulties which don't just increase HP/damage but also the speed (testing your reflexes) of enemies. 
The item shop is quite useful as it makes achievement chasing infinitely easier. 

Cons:
The game is short. You can beat RE2 and RE3 in about the same time if you are chasing S rating. But, this game has very, very little side content. Case in point - in RE2 you can of course go straight to each objective (provided you are experienced and you know every single key item) and you can beat Normal/Hardcore in about 1h45m. In RE3 you can beat the game in about 1h30m-1h45m while doing a bit of exploration for ammo. But RE2 has 2 characters and 2 different runs you can choose so 4 permutations. Each character also has unique areas they can visit and their own plotlines. Also just the area of the map, if you want to explore it, is much bigger.

In RE3, almost all of the map is the main route. You can visit 2 shops and 1 roof if you want want to "max out" but I'm confident you can 100% this game in under 2h. And these extra areas are cleared in like 5 mins, combined. Imagine in RE2, you cut down the RPD and the sewers in half, remove one of the main characters, remove one of the runs and that was the game, this is exactly what they did with RE3. The main storyline is good but why would you replay it other than going for all achievements? You never experience new storylines or characters.

The game is good, you can absolutely have fun but it just doesn't have the depth of content of other Resident Evil games like Village or RE2. Pick it up during a sale if you miss Racoon City and RPD (yes, you do go there again and it's fun). But don't pay full price for such a cut down product. RE2 and RE3 released a year apart and to me it seems obvious they didn't give enough time for the team to add depth but what we did get is of good quality.

On one hand, RE3 (original) was always a more action oriented game in the series, on the other it had genuinely terrifying moments with Nemesis upon its debut in 1999. The original had cutscene esque moments where the player would need to quickly make a decision. These decisions could influence the games outcome, items, and difficulty. there was also a level of randomness to it. By all means RE3 launched to pretty critical success and was praised for creating a villain so iconic, that even non resident evil fans know about Nemesis.

Now on to the Remake, I'll be up front and state that I did not complete the game, I gave up when, Spoilers, Nemesis turns into a Penis headed dog and the game becomes Capcom's most successful I.P. That's Monster Hunter for those of you following along. 

The game I love is here but it's a shell that's been hollowed out. choices are cut pretty much completely, Brad dies to zombies..., entire sections are removed, and Nemesis somehow seems to have lost his personality or Identity. The standard brought on by RE2 Remake is here, moving while aiming, over the shoulder camera angles, fast moving enemies, and ammo... lots and lots of ammo.

Why doesn't Nemesis feel the same you may be asking, simple Resident Evil 2 Remake. Nemesis is no longer distinct from his counterpart Mr. X they move similarly, they behave similarly, they appear similarly. Nemesis ends up feeling like a reskin of Mr. X more often than he feels unique even when they give him a bad ass flamethrower on a rooftop. 

Speaking of Reskins, the entirety of Resident Evil 3 feels like a reskin, or at least DLC for RE2. I understand that it uses the same RE Engine, but the game reuses assets from 2 constantly, and with how short the game is and how much Capcom cut from the Original; one has to wonder, is this really worth $40? I would venture to say no.

It pains me to say it, but do yourself a favor and just play the excellent 1999 Resident Evil 3, this version just isn't it.

[i]Resident Evil 3 Remake[/i] is a masterful reimagining of the classic survival horror title, delivering relentless tension, polished gameplay, and a modernized aesthetic that makes every encounter with the monstrous Nemesis unforgettable. While it preserves the essence of the original, the remake enhances pacing, combat, and environmental design to create a gripping, cinematic horror experience from start to finish.

You step into the shoes of Jill Valentine, a resourceful S.T.A.R.S. operative caught in the outbreak of Raccoon City. The narrative is immediate and high-stakes — survival is a constant struggle, and the relentless Nemesis stalks you throughout, creating fear and urgency in every scene. Jill is portrayed with depth and determination, and the story effectively blends personal stakes with the chaos and destruction of a city collapsing under a viral outbreak.

The environments are striking and immersive. From the crumbling streets of Raccoon City to abandoned labs and makeshift safe havens, every area is meticulously crafted with modern lighting, textures, and environmental effects. The city feels alive, oppressive, and dangerous, with tight alleys, claustrophobic interiors, and open areas that offer both exploration and strategic combat opportunities. Environmental storytelling is rich, with details that hint at the city’s downfall, amplifying tension without needing constant exposition.

Combat in [i]Resident Evil 3 Remake[/i] is refined and satisfying. Weapon handling feels tight and responsive, while encounters with zombies, mutated monstrosities, and the terrifying Nemesis are challenging, rewarding, and adrenaline-fueled. Resource management remains key — limited ammo, scarce healing items, and improvised tactics make every decision matter. The Nemesis encounters are particularly memorable, blending cinematic set pieces with unpredictable chases that keep players constantly on edge.

The remake also improves exploration, puzzles, and progression. Inventory management is intuitive, and the addition of dynamic enemy placements and environmental hazards keeps players alert. Optional objectives and collectibles encourage careful exploration without breaking tension, rewarding players who engage deeply with the world.

A must-play for fans of survival horror, fast-paced action, and tense cinematic experiences — [i]Resident Evil 3 Remake[/i] is a terrifying, thrilling, and beautifully crafted journey through the collapse of Raccoon City, delivering unforgettable encounters and relentless suspense at every turn.

Worst remake, worst RE game.

Resident Evil 1 and 2 were knockout punches. While survival horror was a genre prior, the Resident Evil games took it outside of Japan, with those games seeing immense success in the US and elsewhere. A threequel was in order. Resident Evil 3: Nemesis released in 1999, and was the end of the Raccoon City trilogy. The remake you’re looking at came out 21 years later. Both this game and its remake are something of a black sheep in the RE series. Is it bad? That’s why I’ve written this. 
Skip to the end for a quicker review.

Story
The game opens with you playing in the first person. Jill Valentine walks around her apartment, but when she starts to wash up, she becomes overcome by an infection. She wakes up from this nightmare in her Raccoon City apartment, during the middle of one of the worst virus outbreaks in history. She was sent there as a member of S.T.A.R.S (an organization about combatting things like this) in the events of the first game to help with it. Then, all of a sudden, a massive creature known as Nemesis breaks through her wall and chases her throughout uptown Raccoon City. A mercenary working for Umbrella eventually saves her by fending off Nemesis. His name is Carlos, and he’s the other protagonist of the game. You can see him on the box art. He gets you to the subway, where refugees are flooding in the hope that it will get them out of the city. Jill’s goal now is to get the subway up and running and help these people.
I find this opening premise very interesting. The story is a lot more action-y and quick than that of RE2, but it's captivating. I really like Jill and especially Carlos in this game. They’re sympathetic, smart, and they make lots of decisions I feel like I would in their situation. That’s not something I can say about Ethan Winters.

Gameplay
If you’ve played the RE2 or 4 remakes, it’s the same here. It takes the third person camera angle that the series is famous for. Resource management is paramount, as there isn’t lots of inventory space, and there isn’t lots of ammo. Fighting every enemy is a struggle. Of course, the game has the normal Resident Evil tropes of finding key items to solve in puzzles, but on a much smaller scale than in RE2. Like lots of later RE games, it’s more action focused than 2 was. Areas are much wider, and there’s lots of more over-the-top setpieces, such as burning buildings. A big part of this game is Nemesis. He is probably the best stalker enemy in the series. You can’t kill him, and he chases you, and he kills you. He is the only boss in the game, but every incarnation of him is much, MUCH different. This game still has lots of enemies, and when you’re wedged between them, you can get stun-locked. Maybe this is a skill problem, but I’m not too fond of this. As for the actual combat, the gunplay feels super good, and you can dodge enemy attacks with a new dodge mechanic that you have to time well. If you time it super well, time slows down, and you can lay the pound down on your opponents. Now, this is probably the least scary RE game I’ve played so far (for reference, I’ve played 2, 7, and Village). The camera angle just isn’t conducive to scariness for me. Paired with the larger scope and bigger setpieces, and the game just doesn’t frighten me. Of course, this is up to debate, because it still has the Resident Evil atmosphere, and I’m sure it can be scary to some others, it’s just my own personal taste.

Presentation
These remakes set out to make these old games look pretty, and this one succeeds. You can tell that by this point, they had mastered the RE engine. Every setting looks photorealistic. They didn’t really cut any corners here. There’s just not a lot to say here.
As for sound effects, again, very good. The voice acting is as well, except one character sounds like his lines were recorded in a different studio than every other character’s. He sounds muffled and quiet. Odd.

Content
According to Howlongtobeat.com, Resident Evil 3 is 6 hours long. You may understand why you get it with 2 now. The original version of the game is actually longer, and this is a complaint that the community has; this remake cuts vital parts of the game out, for whatever reason. As someone who never played the original, this doesn’t affect my enjoyment of the game whatsoever, but it leads to the middling reception this remake received. It also reuses some areas from RE2. You return to the police station from RE2. This wasn’t cool. This wasn’t fanservice. It was just uninspired.
The game only has one campaign, where it swaps characters when the story calls for it. I see some people complaining about this, but this is fine to me. It leads to a more cohesive story. It does lead to a shorter runtime however, and less replay value. 
In the way of extra modes, there isn’t too much. There’s a new game +, but I’ve never been someone who plays those. This isn’t really a problem here, because it already comes with Resident Evil 2, which has a bunch of side content, and 2 campaigns, and a weird multiplayer spinoff called RE Resistance which you shouldn’t play. There was a weird time where they tried to make multiplayer RE games, and none of them are good.
Positives:
-Outstanding story and characters
-Breathtaking visuals and atmosphere
-Nemesis

Negatives:
-Very short, reuses areas, and cuts ones that were in the original
-Enemy stun-locking
-No side modes

Resident Evil 3’s reputation is certainly deserved. It’s an imperfect game. It’s short, and this remake makes it shorter by cutting areas out. However, at the end of the day, it’s still a Resident Evil game. All of these games have good qualities, and I like to think RE3’s goods outweigh it’s bads. Of course, there are many better games in the series, but if you enjoyed RE2, then I would fully recommend 3. 3’s more of 2. 
You’re not buying this game alone. The only way to get it is with 2 and Resistance, which is $40 normally, but $10-$15 on sale. That’s a bargain.

Resident Evil 3 delivers an action-packed, pulse-pounding experience from start to finish. As Jill Valentine, you’re thrown into the chaos of Raccoon City as it falls apart, and the constant tension is masterfully crafted. The revamped visuals are stunning, with atmospheric environments that make every corner feel dangerous and every shadow a potential threat.

[h3]The Positives[/h3] 
• Impressive [b]graphics[/b], even if they don’t surpass RE2’s presentation 
• Punchy and relentless [b]action-horror atmosphere[/b] 
• Smooth and refined [b]combat[/b] that builds on RE2’s foundation 
• Strong visual design and concept of [b]Nemesis[/b] 


[h3]The Negatives[/h3] 
• Heavy reuse of [b]assets[/b] from RE2 
• Reduced [b]exploration[/b] and fewer meaningful [b]puzzles[/b] 
• Overuse of [b]cutscenes[/b] and occasional, unnecessary QTEs 
• [b]Nemesis encounters[/b] are heavily scripted rather than dynamic 
• Very short campaign with almost no [b]replay value[/b] 
• Large amount of [b]cut[/b] or [b]altered content[/b] from the original 


[h1]Verdict[/h1]
[u][b]A good game wearing the wrong name[/b][/u]. Resident Evil 3 is an enjoyable and polished action-horror experience in isolation but as a remake it fundamentally misses the mark. Its short length, heavy asset reuse and extensive cuts strip away much of what defined the original while a heavily scripted Nemesis undermines the game’s core threat. Fun moment to moment, yet compromised in identity, it’s hard to recommend this as a faithful or worthwhile reimagining of a classic.

As someone who played the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis countless times as a kid on his mom’s work PC, and as someone who has replayed this game many times to get different perspectives, I was disappointed with the outcome of this remake. It didn’t hold up nearly as well as Resident Evil 2 (2019), and it definitely didn’t live up to the expectations set by the original. That said, two things the remake absolutely improved on were the character redesigns. Jill’s updated look was a major upgrade — she finally looked like an actual police officer trying to survive a city-wide outbreak rather than someone dressed for a night out, with the miniskirt, tube top, tall boots, and sweater tied around her waist. Carlos’ redesign was also a massive improvement; instead of looking like a guy from a boy band, he actually looked serious, rugged, and like a believable “macho man” UBCS soldier.

The game starts off with a bang — a major change from the original. You get to see how everything unfolds in Jill’s apartment, and you quickly learn how much of a threat Nemesis is from the moment he appears. It gets your blood pumping with excitement. But after finishing the prologue and meeting Carlos and his team in the train station, you start to think, “Wait, we’re already trying to get the train started? But the game just started?” That’s when I began to worry, because it felt like we skipped the part where you truly get to explore Raccoon City. This disappointment was amplified by the fact that the developers had implied before release that players would be able to navigate more of Raccoon City than ever before. Instead, you barely get to explore the city at all — maybe a quarter of it — before being rushed out entirely. For a game that was supposed to focus on exploring the city itself, not just the RPD or the sewers, this limited navigation felt like a massive letdown.

From there, the game goes downhill, at least for me. Jill doesn’t visit the RPD like she did in the original — instead, Carlos does. And while the RE2–RE3 connection in the RPD was cool to witness, it barely had any real narrative impact. Nemesis also didn’t feel nearly as threatening as he did in the original. His early appearances in the Raccoon City section, especially being scripted during the sequence where you're trying to restore power to the train, felt cheap. After one or two replays, it wasn’t scary at all. The fact that he can’t chase you through the sewers or other major areas — something the developers implied he would do before release — was another huge disappointment.

Iconic locations like Jack’s Bar and the Stagla Gas Station were barely shown and not explorable. The Raccoon Park was entirely removed, along with the Gravedigger boss fight that came with it. The Dead Factory/Waste Disposal Plant was completely redesigned into NEST 2 — and that entire section felt extremely short. But the biggest issue for me was the Clock Tower section. One of my favorite parts of the original — a mini-mansion filled with enemies and puzzles — was reduced to a simple exterior courtyard that served as a boss arena for “Doggy Nemesis.” Changing Nemesis into a giant dog instead of giving him his classic tentacle transformation felt like an unnecessary downgrade.

The final boss fight with Nemesis was, in my opinion, extremely easy — just like the original — except on Inferno mode, which was an actual nightmare. The destruction of Raccoon City also lacked the emotional weight that the original ending carried. Overall, almost everything felt like a letdown and didn’t land with the impact I expected.

And then there’s Resistance. I understand what Capcom was trying to do — experimenting with a new multiplayer concept and expanding the Resident Evil universe in a different direction — but it ultimately didn’t work. Resident Evil has always been intended as a single-player survival horror experience, not an online competitive game. The inclusion of Resistance felt out of place, especially when fans would’ve much preferred Mercenaries Mode, which would’ve actually increased replayability.

Overall, Resident Evil 3 is a fun game, but not a good remake. It’s disrespectful to the original, and the lack of content makes it less enjoyable and less replayable. My final score is 6/10.

In theory, I should like Resident Evil 3 (the remake) more than its predecessor… but honestly, I don’t really know. But it has fewer weapons, fewer enemies (number-wise), less “game depth,” fewer puzzles, etc. The last one should’ve been an advantage compared to RE2, because in that game [i]I was too dumb to solve half the puzzles by myself[/i]. But here, it feels like the puzzle-heavy character that defines Resident Evil is just kind of missing.

And honestly, I find it weird that the Tyrant from RE2 felt way more terrifying than the supposedly much more powerful Nemesis.
One thing I found especially cool was that the story connects directly to RE2 and that you get to play in a small area from the predecessor.

But one thing that almost made me [i]not[/i] recommend RE3 was the [spoiler]second Nemesis boss fight at the plaza. God, I can’t even tell you how bad the game design is there. TLDR; this game is a massively watered down mediocre rush project with an identity crisis, made for Fast-Paced Adrenaline Junkies, while trying to appeal to traditional horror fans.

RE3 holds your hand as tightly as a parent who cannot stomach the thought of letting go of their teenage child's hand. There's so little for you to actually think about it's more like you're playing an arcade auto-walk shooter. Clues for 'puzzles' are always right next to the 'puzzle', & the items you need are basically within 2 minutes of travel at all times. The game also has a horrible habit of SPOILING a boss fight that's 30 seconds away & an extreme reliance on the dodge mechanic during said boss fights.

The game starts with a nightmare sequence & drops lore files referencing the events of Spencer Mansion where Jill faced the infected for the first time. This is only ever referenced again in the 2nd nightmare cutscene at the Hospital but that's basically it. Jill never talks about it, & we never see any manifestation of her PTSD outside the 2 dreams.

The title enemy for this game is Nemesis, but despite being the major focus of the game's advertising, he appears in only a select few areas & successfully serves as an imposing threat while you're confined to those areas, but when he's a boss fight, this balance shifts & his attacks are slow & easy to evade.

The map design comes up next as...really pathetic. The downtown section is the best part but even that has very little in the way of detour & exploration. ALMOST anything that is locked down behind a key-item like the bolt cutters will be completely fine for you to ignore, because the game will demand you go back to that area for one reason or another. The only thing i regretfully missed was the handgun sight.

Next up is combat & this plays into the map design somewhat. Enemies spawn in really big groups & oh-look, a convenient red barrel in the middle of the whole lot...It doesn't feel cool when it's staring you in the face.

There was also something wrong with the aiming in this game, i've had this with a few games in my time, where there's just SOMETHING that feels wrong about how the camera moves, i turned off reticle deceleration & Aim assist but yet there still feels like something is miss-matched with the way the game interprets my input.

Next is the sound issues, i've tried BOTH the RTX supported Version AND NON-RTX. BOTH versions had audio desync in cutscenes AND inconsistent Volumes throughout the WHOLE game. Enemies often sounded like they were 2 rooms away. & the camera is so close that you'll occasionally be grabbed from behind by a silent zombie.

This is where i feel conflicted about the RE direction. In RE4, 5, 6, 7 & 8. Killing EVERYTHING in your way was standard. in the Titles before OG-4, it was mostly optional & discouraged, especially for 1-time visits.

In RE-2: REMAKE, the game-pace was a return to the slow of older Titles. Enemies were slow & tanky, but shooting their leg often gave enough time to slip past unharmed for a significant ammo save & the map design supported going AROUND most areas if one was completely swarmed.

In RE-3: REMAKE, we return to the faster paced action of the modern titles & the idea of going AROUND enemies is replaced with a dodge button & key factors of the OG are scrapped, namely more than half the map, along with the randomized encounters you could see & depending on where you travelled first also mattered, even extending to the nemesis encounters being randomised.

The Resident Evil 3 RE:make is an unfortunate reimagining of what is my favorite game in the entire Resident Evil franchise from 1999.

I had high hopes with this project, when compared to the incredibly faithful remake of RE1 Remake and the positively reimagined RE2 and RE4 Remake which wasn't as faithful, but still had an incredible amount of heart and took creative liberties primarily instead of shortcuts.

First of all, this game is incredibly short. Which isn't usually an issue for me, as Resident Evil games are relatively short, and in fact-- RE3 original is also shorter in comparison to the series as a whole. What begets problems is that in the REMAKE of an already short game there are completely missing segments in this game from the original. The extensive streets and alleyways of Raccoon City from the original has been truncated to like 2-3 slightly bigger main streets, that are relatively linear due to car wreckages blocking effectively everything. The entire clocktower and park locations remain almost non-existent in R3make, other than a boss encounter in front of the said clocktower. You would think they would add content to existing locations, but no, we get a mind-numbing sewers section, and a decent underground facility section as a replacement. But they are no replacement for the already missing sections. Worst of all, the 1999 original included a Mercenaries gamemode that is non-existent in the R3make.

The original game had cause and effect depending on what routes/choices you would take, and you could see different outcomes, and had several endings. In the R3make, that doesn't exist at all. I am content with the player only being able to receiving a singular ending in the R3make, as it can establish a canon, that is fine with me. I am not a fan of them removing what was a core gameplay mechanic of several opportunities where you could effectively take certain risks or make evasion whenever the player would encounter the game's main baddie, Nemesis.

Speaking of Nemesis... R3make's treatment of him genuinely makes me so upset. This guy is supposed to be incredibly stressful and scary to encounter, but this game throws that all away. The redesign of Nemesis is okay, and I do like the mask he starts out with, it is pretty cool. But overall Mr. X from RE2 Remake ends up being much scarier than R3make Nemesis, which 100% should not be the case from a gameplay standpoint, nor a canon standpoint. He mutates way too fast for my liking, and I only end up liking his first "boss fight" where he wields a flamethrower, as well as his final boss fight. however the other boss fights just kinda frustrate me. This guy looks so awesome and menacing in the cutscenes, but as a gameplay mechanic, he is easily taken out other than his boss fights as his mechanics or severely abusable, and his chase sequences are considerably shorter. Also this guy doesn't kill a single STARS member in the R3make, which is so unfortunate, because his whole thing is like hunting down STARS, and screaming it everywhere.

Jill is a relatively big sin too. Her physical redesign is whatever, not my preference, but it is palatable, she ends up looking a bit bland than how she did in the original. The game starts off in a first-person sequence that sort of demonstrates the trauma she is going through after the events of Resident Evil 1's Spencer Mansion, which is something I thought was really cool. But other than that, and one other tiny instance, that specific subplot is dropped and left ignored unfortunately. She's suddenly mischaracterized to be pretty sarcastic and a bit of a jerk, kinda like my ex-wife. Rather than being more light-hearted and nice like her original appearance. Which I was maybe hoping was due to the trauma she was facing or something, but no, she ended up making a comment to Mikhail within the first segment that genuinely upset me as a player, because I genuinely did not feel like this character was Jill.

Nikolai also was kinda made out to be more transparently evil from the get-go in the R3make, which isn't a huge problem, but not my cup of tea. I preferred his original appearance, but this one is okay I suppose. Mikhail is still a great character here, so no problems there. Tyrell gets a much better role here and I am a fan of that.

The best part about this game is probably Carlos, he has been reimagined into a much more likeable character, both in design and writing. And Carlos has some really strong moments here in this game, which funny enough are my favorite moments of this game. The RPD segment, while now exclusively Carlos' segment, is a ton of fun as well as his segment in the hospital, including fighting off the large hoards of zombies. Those sections were made a ton of fun the R3make, but aside from that and maybe the endgame facility location with Jill, everything else in this game is pretty bland. Just like my ex-wife's personality.

The cons outweigh the pros here in my opinion, and this game was released with the same price tag as RE2 Remake. When it is apparent that the content and replay value here is significantly less. When comparing it to RE3 (1999), it fails as a remake. And when looking at it standalone, it is a very underwhelming experience. I wouldn't recommend this game for anything more than like $15 USD. And at that point, I would heavily recommend the original, unless you didn't have the means to play it. It's a big disappointment with a pretty coat of paint over it, which is the perfect way to describe my ex-wife.

But with even how much I dislike my ex-wife, even I probably wouldn't recommend this remake to her either. So what does that tell you?

The Resident Evil 3 Remake on PC is a visually stunning reimagining of the 1999 PlayStation classic. CAPCOM’s RE Engine once again delivers breathtaking detail, from the atmospheric streets of Raccoon City to the terrifying presence of Nemesis. The gameplay feels fluid and modern, with tight gunplay, responsive controls, and cinematic presentation that makes every encounter feel intense. Jill Valentine is brought to life with strong voice acting and character modeling, and the game runs exceptionally well on PC hardware, offering smooth performance and crisp visuals that elevate the horror experience.

That said, while the remake succeeds technically, it falls short in capturing the charm and depth of the original Resident Evil 3. Much of the branching storylines, exploration, and memorable content from the PlayStation version were cut, leaving the remake feeling more streamlined—and at times rushed—compared to the Resident Evil 2 Remake. Nemesis, once a relentless and unpredictable force, is now relegated to scripted sequences, which diminishes the tension that made the original so iconic. This could have easily been a watermark title for CAPCOM, standing shoulder to shoulder with the RE2 remake, but the lack of care in preserving the original’s spirit makes it feel more like a missed opportunity than a definitive reimagining

[h1]A Short but Good Remake[/h1]

[i]Jill Valentine is one of the last remaining people in Raccoon City to witness the atrocities Umbrella performed. To stop her, Umbrella unleashes their ultimate secret weapon: Nemesis! Also includes Resident Evil Resistance, a new 1 vs 4 online multiplayer game set in the Resident Evil universe.[/i]

[h2]Story[/h2]
Jill Valentine, a former S.T.A.R.S. member, fights to escape Raccoon City as the T-Virus outbreak turns it into a zombie-infested nightmare. She is relentlessly hunted by Nemesis, a bioweapon designed by Umbrella Corporation to eliminate surviving S.T.A.R.S. members. With Carlos Oliveira’s help, Jill uncovers Umbrella’s secret experiments and strives to stop both the corporation and Nemesis.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Resident Evil 3 (2020) is a third-person survival horror remake of the 1999 game. This remake reimagines the gameplay and story for modern audiences. The tank controls and the fixed camera angles are replaced with a dynamic, over-the-shoulder view that zooms in while aiming.

The game focuses on exploring and managing your supplies carefully. You’ll move through connected areas, searching for important items like ammo, healing herbs, and puzzle pieces that help you move forward. You can inspect items in detail to find hidden clues, combine things like mixing herbs for stronger healing or gunpowder for ammo. Once an item has served its purpose, it can be safely discarded to free up space.

Jill’s loadout includes a handgun, shotgun, grenade launcher, and the powerful Lightning Hawk magnum. Carlos uses a handgun, assault rifle, and grenades. These unique weapon sets make each character feel distinct and keep the gameplay fresh and varied. Some weapons can be upgraded with special parts, enhancing attributes.

For up-close fights, you can use backup weapons like combat knives and regular or stun grenades, helping you escape grabs or deal extra damage when needed.

New to the game, Jill can perform quick dodges to evade attacks at the last second, adding a layer of timing and precision. Carlos relies on heavy melee counters that stun enemies, opening a brief window to strike or escape. These unique mechanics keep combat fast, tense, and exciting—and perfect dodges or counters even slow down time, letting you line up precise shots.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
Zombies are the most common threat you’ll face. They’re slow but unpredictable, staggering in erratic patterns that make them difficult to hit. If they manage to grab you, they’ll try to sink their teeth in—and don’t assume they’re down for good just because they’ve fallen. Unless you destroy the head, there’s always a chance they’ll get back up.

Hunters are deadly foes—fast, agile, and able to leap great distances to strike or dodge attacks. Their razor-sharp claws and relentless aggression can tear through you easily if unprepared. Their armored hide must be shattered before you can hit the weak flesh beneath, making precision and heavy firepower essential to bring them down.

The game features several boss battles, each one testing your reflexes and aim. Nemesis is the game’s main villain—a terrifying, unstoppable creature that chases you through key parts of the game, turning every encounter into a tense, high-pressure battle that forces you to stay sharp and think fast. Defeating him only leads to more dangerous, mutated forms, keeping the intensity high and ensuring no place ever feels completely safe.

These are just a few examples of the enemies you face.

[h2]Environment & Scares[/h2]
The game world may seem straightforward, but areas cleverly loop back on each other, keeping exploration engaging. Some familiar locations from Resident Evil 2 appear, set before Leon and Claire arrive, though the interconnected design isn’t quite as strong as in that remake.

The horror shines in the level design—tight hallways, cramped rooms, and low lighting create a constant sense of being trapped. Dark, shadowy areas lit only by your flashlight heighten tension, while Nemesis, a relentless and massive enemy, keeps you on edge with footsteps that echo through halls and shake the streets, forcing split-second decisions in moments of panic.

Exploring the environment is made easier by an excellent map system. Rooms that still have items to find show up in red, and once you’ve collected everything, they turn blue to show they’re cleared. When your inventory is full, uncollected items are automatically marked on the map for later retrieval. Doors are clearly labeled—red for locked, blue for unlocked. It’s an incredibly smart system that helps you keep track of what’s left to do and where to go next. Simply put, the map is one of the game’s best features.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
One of the most unforgettable aspects of the game is Nemesis—both his appearance and presence. Dressed entirely in black with an exposed, deformed face showing muscles, tendons, and teeth, and missing lips and nose, he exudes an unnerving, unnatural menace. Nemesis moves fast and decisively, his footsteps echoing through halls or shaking the streets, signaling his approach long before he appears. Every encounter feels personal, nerve-wracking, and genuinely terrifying. Later, he mutates into increasingly larger, more intimidating, and grotesque forms, each transformation making him an even more terrifying and formidable threat.

The game’s visuals go far beyond just creating atmosphere. Enemy damage looks and feels realistic—bullets rip through flesh, and you can even blow off limbs, which changes how enemies move and attack. This attention to detail makes every shot feel powerful and satisfying.

[h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2]
Nemesis chases through the streets can feel scripted, making the encounters less tense and unpredictable. Unlike RE 2’s Tyrant, which reacts dynamically to your actions, Nemesis often feels less intelligent and relentless, leaving some moments predictable and less thrilling.

The game feels shorter than expected and lacks the immersive survival horror of the RE 2 Remake. Removed “extra scenarios” and no additional modes or DLC limit replay value, making revisits less appealing. The inclusion of Resident Evil Resistance may explain the trimmed single-player campaign, but many players would likely have preferred a longer, more engaging solo experience.

Sometimes, I ran into stunlocks, especially when facing Nemesis’s final form. One hit could quickly be followed by several more, leaving no chance to react or escape. These moments felt unfair and frustrating, breaking the immersion and turning what should have been exciting encounters into annoying, unavoidable deaths.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
Resident Evil 3 Remake is a brilliant reimagining of a classic and easily one of the best games in the series. The story and characters are engaging, playing as both Jill and Carlos is fun and contributing with their own weapons to bring some variety. 

Combat is satisfying and impactful—every weapon feels different, responsive, and powerful. Ammo is limited, so every shot matters, making battles tense and exciting. Nemesis stands out as the game’s most terrifying and memorable enemy, always keeping you on edge. The crafting system is simple but rewarding, letting you combine items and plan strategies without slowing down the action.

Exploration is a real highlight. Smart level design and a user-friendly map make collecting items, solving puzzles, and navigating interconnected areas both satisfying and immersive. The game world feels alive, and discovering its secrets is genuinely fun.

In short, Resident Evil 3 Remake balances horror, action, and strategy, delivering a thrilling, tense, and unforgettable experience from beginning to end—even if Nemesis feels overly scripted and the game is short with limited replay value due to the lack of extra content.

⭐ You think you’re buying an action-horror game. You think you’re here for zombies, explosions, and that big trench coat disaster Nemesis yelling “STARS!” every five minutes. But then Jill Valentine walks onto the screen, Carlos Oliveira starts talking, and suddenly you realize this isn’t a game — it’s a spiritual awakening wrapped in gunfire and romantic tension.

Let’s start with Jill. Jill doesn’t just fight — she moves like she’s personally offended by the concept of fear. She’s sweaty, dirty, angry, exhausted, and somehow the most breathtaking person I’ve ever seen rendered in 4K. Every snarl, every glare, every heavy breath after dodging death for the fiftieth time — it’s art. She’s the blueprint of survival: battered but unbroken, sharp-tongued, and entirely too hot for someone who’s been through literal bioweapon hell.

There’s this moment when she tells Nemesis, “You want S.T.A.R.S.? I’ll give you S.T.A.R.S.” and I swear the earth tilted. The confidence, the rage, the absolute dominance in that delivery — my soul just packed its bags and left my body. Jill Valentine could dropkick me through a flaming police station and I’d call it character development.

And then… Carlos.

Listen, I didn’t know I had a thing for reckless mercenaries with ridiculous hair until this man showed up. He’s got that deep, easy voice that feels like it’s leaning in a little too close. The kind of guy who’s half flirting, half saving your life, and somehow doing both flawlessly. The way he calls Jill “supercop”? It’s not just a nickname — it’s a religious experience.

Carlos walks through fire, punches zombies, gets covered in blood, and still manages to look like he just stepped out of a romance novel titled Apocalypse, But Make It Sexy. His smile alone could heal the T-virus. He flirts like it’s an act of survival. He’s equal parts chaos and comfort — reckless in battle, gentle with Jill. And when he looks at her, you know he’d burn the city down to keep her breathing.

Together? It’s not chemistry anymore. It’s combustion. The kind of connection that makes the air feel heavier. Jill’s trying to stay focused, all mission and muscle memory, and Carlos keeps pushing with that stupid, perfect grin like he knows she’s seconds away from giving in. Every snappy exchange, every glance they share in the middle of carnage, feels like it’s one heartbeat away from turning into something that would make the ESRB reconsider the rating.

That hospital scene — you know the one — Carlos carrying Jill, whispering to her like she’s something holy? I ascended. He’s bleeding, exhausted, but all he cares about is her. The tenderness in his voice, the way his hands shake as he injects the vaccine, it’s more romantic than any confession I’ve ever heard. Jill’s unconscious, but somehow she feels it — you can feel it.

And when she wakes up? The world’s still burning, but she’s there, ready to fight again. Jill Valentine, too strong to die. Carlos Oliveira, too loyal to leave. Two people who shouldn’t have time for each other, finding something like love in the middle of apocalypse ash.

By the end, I wasn’t thinking about Nemesis or Umbrella or the outbreak. I was thinking about how unfair it is that fictional people can have that much pull over me. Jill’s power. Carlos’s devotion. The way their story ends but doesn’t feel over.

Resident Evil 3 isn’t horror. It’s suffering — the kind where you’re begging for just one more scene, one more smirk, one more moment between them.

10/10. Jill could knock me out with one punch. Carlos could resuscitate me with one wink. And I’d do it all again, over and over, until Raccoon City burns itself out of my heart. ⭐

Resident Evil 3 (RE3) 2020 is a short, fairly action-packed game, though calling it a DLC to Resident Evil 2 (RE2) 2019 is more appropriate. The gameplay is almost the same between these games, though the atmosphere and environment in which the games take place differ greatly. In RE3 however, the gameplay is much smoother, and everything happens faster, which makes sense since you control S.T.A.R.S member Jill Valentine instead of a rookie cop or a college student. The best part of the game is first hour or so, while you're still in downtown Raccoon City and Nemesis periodically shows up to chase you which, to be fair, is quite nerve-wracking. After this, it kind of becomes meh. Has some decent replay value to it, though not in terms of different events happening in-game, rather more challenges to complete.

Overall, a solid 8/10 as a DLC, but maybe a 6/10 as a full-priced game. Buy it on sale and have fun.

Resident Evil 3 remaster is a very good game sandwiched between two legendary games (RE2 and RE4 remasters). In my opinion this probably skews a lot of perspectives on RE3. If you experience and view this game on its own merit, it is a very good and competently made remaster. Other reviewers are unhappy about segments from the original RE3 being cut in this remaster, but the truth is that even when these games were originally released, RE3 was considered the lesser between 2, 3 and 4. 

On maximum graphical settings at 4K resolution with 120 frames per second on a 65" TV with noise cancelling headphones on Hardcore difficulty, Resident Evil 3 remaster was an exciting, immersive and often scary experience. The zombies are directly pulled from the RE2 remaster and they are way scarier than any of the villagers or cultists from RE4. Actually, even though I think RE4 is an amazing game, it never really scared me except for a couple of moments. RE3 on the other hand gave me several good scares.

However, it does feel like Resident Evil 3 needed something more. Resident Evil 2 has puzzles. Resident Evil 4 has looting, economy and shop. In my opinion, Resident Evil 3 could have been amazing if they gave it its own unique focus on exploration. If there were larger areas and more secrets to explore, it could have enhanced the gameplay significantly. They sort of hinted at the idea a couple of times when you backtrack with your lockpick to unlock a bunch of stuff you couldn't access before. Those segments had a fun feeling to it and made me wish there was more exploration and secrets to unlock. Besides a few areas where you backtrack with the lockpick, RE3 remaster mostly feels like you're on rails/following the set path.

The Resident Evil 3 remaster is often on sale for $9.99 and that is an absolute steal for a game of this caliber. Yes it's a little on the short side (10 to 12 hours of gameplay) but there are plenty of thrills, chills and action sequences to enjoy in that time. For me both RE2 and RE4 remasters are a 10 out of 10, some of my favorite games ever, and this RE3 remaster is somewhere between an 8 to 8.5. Avoid paying the full price of $39.99 for it but absolutely buy it when on sale at $9.99.

As much as I did say I love Nemeisis’s design, I do NOT like him in this game. The thing about the original RE3 is that Nemesis was unscripted, unpredictable. So when he did show up, it felt ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ terrifying and tense and made the whole game fun. In RE3 Remake, Nemesis is reduced to a scripted character who only shows up when the game tells him to. I mentioned that I did say that the first section in the city is the best part in the entire game, and that’s because of Nemesis. He shows up, and it’s actually scary to see him walk under doors, jump ahead of you, grab you with his tentacle, etc. But after that, you ONLY see him during chase sequences and boss fights (which I will talk about later). RE7 had that Texas Chainsaw/Evil Dead feel to it, RE2 had that unsettling yet tone in the police station, The original Resident Evil had that creepy and tight corners of the mansion, not knowing what is going to pop up, Village… Village had a big booby vampire, LMAO. And in the original, it's scary because of the unpredictable sequences Nemesis showed up, which is what made it feel scary. But in this game? Prepare to walk in empty areas with the occasional zombie shoot sections, and let’s reuse assets without doing our own twist on it. Even in the underground section and hospital, I wasn’t even scared in the slightest. That atmosphere that the RE2 Remake ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nailed is just gone.

The original is 5 - 6 hours long, which might seem like a dumb complaint, but the game had pacing, character development, and cool sections. Carlos… why does he look like a TikTok e-boy, and then charging $5 to change his original look is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ retarded.
