A Rant on the Resident Evil 3 Remake

I usually try to stay positive with my gaming experiences, and try to judge things on their own merits. But this....... this was not a great time. I'm a HUGE HUGE HUGE fan of the series, and have been playing them since I was WAY WAY WAY too young to be looking at them. I've played every game in the franchise, watched all the movies, and own a decent amount of merch. This entry was just..... so disappointing on both the grounds of a Remake and as a standalone title.

I have only 2 playthroughs on this and that felt like it was 2 too many. My FIRST completely BLIND playthrough of it was only 3 hours long. I took my time with it and looked around every nook and cranny I saw. I very recently did another playthrough that only lasted 2hrs 58m. Again, taking my time with it, exploring as much as I could. I don't know how it managed to feel like both a slog and rushed at the same time, but it did. I tried my best to come back to it with a fresh mindset, but the second I started it up, the dread of playing it again sank in.

On its own, it just feels like a very rushed mess. The game is incredibly short, the characters AND story fall a bit flat, and the actual difficulty is a roller coaster. The average zombie falls over relatively quickly, and you get PLENTY of ammo to just kill every single thing in your way. 

The dodge mechanic was getting on my nerves personally. It may be a skill issue on my part, but it happened enough to frustrate me. I had too many instances where I would tap the button, and Jill/Carlos would not perform the dodge/shoulder check. I would also get caught by grabs at VERY inconsistent times. Unless I am GROSSLY misunderstanding it, the mechanic read like "dodge at the last moment" kinda deal. But that window seemed to change rapidly. Again, maybe just a skill issue on my end, it just felt very inconsistent.

Now as for comparing this entry to the others, both the original and RE2R, it still falls VERY flat. Having played the OG RE3, I could feel how much got cut. At least a third of the game is just..... missing. Credit where credit is due, it has a PHENOMENAL opening, and REALLY sets Nemesis up for some greatness! Greatness they do not deliver on. In RE2R, you get Mr. X thrown at you, and his presence is felt for the REST of the game. He endlessly pursues you, and once you are FINALLY rid of him, you still wonder if he will come back (spoiler: he does). Nemesis in RE3R feels like the Mr. X we have at home. He only actively pursues you for ONE segment. Outside of that, EVERY moment with him is scripted. The one time he actually is a constant threat to your exploration, it's PHENOMENAL! He feels like he did in the original! But once you leave the streets of Raccoon City, he only shows up for short little boss segments that feel WAY too easy. 

The horror...... just wasn't there. There are a couple moments that made me jump, or one in particular that actually gave me the creeps (the power station). Otherwise, it just didn't feel like a survival horror game. It's way more of an action game than RE2R, but you can still have the action and feel horrifying. The OG and RE4 (2005) are perfect examples of this. There is a particular enemy that gets introduce in the late game that I believe was meant to be spooky and illicit a fear response. However, it is just....... dropped in front of you. I audibly laughed when that happened, and could not take them seriously. Afterwards they being to feel more like a bother to deal with than an actual threat. They felt more annoying and frustrating every time they popped up. In fact, there is a room with not one, not two, not 3, but FOUR of these guys. When I realized that, I just paused and let out a deep sigh. The special infected that Nemesis can make on the streets of RC are pretty creepy and gross looking I guess.

There are some positives, just not enough to completely nullify what's wrong. For starters, the graphics are STUNNING! Jill and Carlos never looked so good! There is so so so so much detail EVERYWHERE! They really outdid themselves with the RE Engine on this one. The gameplay has never felt smoother for an RE (until the 4 Remake, but pretend like that isn't out yet). Gameplay-wise, this title is VERY similar to RE2R, but WAY more action heavy. If you are more of a fan of Third Person-Shooters, this game is a pretty solid one. It's honestly a shame it was such a rushed project.

I REALLY wish I could recommend this one, but I just can't. The graphics are great and for me, the game ran like butter. But being an RE fan and having played the original just makes this one look so sloppy. It genuinely amazes me how much of the original is just...... gone. Especially after recently replaying the OG RE2 and the Remake, and seeing the true essence of the original be made for modern audiences. This fell so flat for me on so so many levels. It's a decently fun third person shooter, but if I wanted a Resident Evil TPS, I think I would just rather play RE6 if I'm being honest. Hell, I'm one of the weirdos who actually likes Operation Raccoon City, so I would rather just play that instead. RE3R just felt like a bore the first time, and a chore the second time. I just left both times feeling so very let down by a series I adore.

TL;DR: Cannot recommend as either a fan or a newcomer. Just genuinely play the OG.

I'm going to start by saying outright that I liked this game and would recommend it, but there's a lot of not great stuff in it which I'm going to discuss first.

After the Resident Evil 2 remake was a big win, it was not unreasonable to expect that Resident Evil 3 would also get a remake. What's more after the positive reception of Mr. X a smarter, more dangerous version in Nemesis was an obvious next step. Finally, modern hardware could provide us a true city-wide-nonlinear-cat-and-mouse-other-hyphenated-words-game that Capcom had struggled against the PS1's limited resources to create.

Unfortunately, that isn't exactly what we got. Resident Evil 3 Remake is far shorter and more linear than 2, and swaps out the constant threat of Mr. X for scripted encounters with Nemesis. What's more, there is only 1 campaign unlike Resident Evil 1 and 2. This was true on the PS1 as well, but canceled out by the original game having lots of a little choices that had minor but noticeable effects on the plot, but is not true here.

Finally, for reasons known only to Capcom this game is less stable than most of the other RE:Engine games, and you may need to do some tweaking it get it to behave properly. It's probably not going to be fixed or improved at this point, but mods exist to improve it. 

Having said all that, Resident Evil 3 Remake isn't a bad game, it's just not really a great remake of 3. Considered more as an expansion pack campaign for Remake 2 it's quite enjoyable. Ironic, given the original Resi 3 was meant to be an expansion pack for 2 that bloomed into it's own game, that the remake should feel more like an extra DLC campaign. The game goes on sale fairly often so probably wait for a discount before picking it.

Resident Evil 3 Remake is a, well, “Remake” of the original RE 3: Nemesis. It follows Jill Valentine during the downfall of Racoon City as she seeks escape from both the city and the Nemesis Tyrant.

Positives:

+++ Visuals. REngine continues to look great without demanding a huge level of hardware
++ Graphics options with helpful preview window and VRAM meter
++ Audio design and sfx is spot on
+ The intro with Nemesis is a quick shock and gets things going but doesn’t overstay itself
++ Voice acting. It’s good throughout.
+ Unlockable art gallery and models from gameplay
+ Dodge mechanic. Works well (expect when it doesn’t)
+ The map provides indicators if there are items in an area to be found
+ The game lets you know when key items are no longer needed
+ Map layout is pretty good with a mix of area types and looping
+ Distribution of items and gear. The gear you need is often where it would be most useful
+ The final fight isn’t too bad of a fight and more of a victory lap moment
++ Points shop with unlockable gear for future playthroughs
+ Kill counts and Charlie Dolls persist across playthroughs making it easy to accumulate these rewards

Negatives:

- First time start up issue: Game starts at incorrect resolution making for an awkward process to get to the settings
- Same weird consolitis menu issues as other newer RE games
- Inventory size is a bit too small to start out with
- Nemesis’s speed and reach is a bit too much in the street encounters
- Nikolai and his weird habit of just “appearing” suddenly in scenes with no logical reason for him being there is… weird. I chalk this up to some bad story writing.
- The dodge system is nice, but it does rely on tells from enemies. This gets negated when the enemy is often behind Jill (in many of the Nemesis encounters) so you can’t see those tells to know when to dodge
- Cutscene incompetence? Jill repeatedly assuming Nemesis is dead when it obviously isn’t. She really should know better when it comes to tyrants.
- Game disables all windows controls when in focus, notably system volume control
- The 3rd Nemesis fight is a bit overtuned to the point of borderline frustration. It’s practically the real final fight of the game as the one following is remarkably simple.
- Nikolai’s Voice over volume is weirdly low compared the other voice actors

So, that’s about it. No really. This is a remarkably short game compared to other Resident Evil games. It’s not uncommon for a first playthrough be under the 10 hour mark. I don’t note this as a positive or negative as game length is very subjective to different players. I think the length was fine, but that’s just me. I wouldn’t had minded it being a bit longer though.

Overall, it’s much of the same as Resident Evil 2 Remake in both visuals and playstyle. It’s not quite as fleshed out in terms of polish, puzzles and variety as RE2R though so those expecting it to be as good as that will probably be disappointed.

I think the game itself is all right. I don’t love it as much as other RE games, but I don’t dislike it either.

I give it a recommend, but consider nabbing it on sale.

I was aware a lot of people shat on this game a lot on realease, specially comparing it to the original, I've yet to played the original RE3 so my distaste for this game is purely based on it's merit.

The positive's here for me are I really liked Carlos's segments (barring the end of his hospital segment), I liked his punch parry attack and I liked the way they handled Brad and Marvin here and I liked the first chase sequence with Nemesis.

That's about it, Jill is my favorite character of RE1 and from that game I was left with the feeling that she's a super capable badass who has no problem blowing the heads of a thousand zombies, but I think she's the type of person to start blushing the moment they say more than 3 swear words in a conversation due to how polite they are. That's ... not how she's characterized here. No shade to her VA here, but I don't thinks the writers did her character justice here, I don't even necessarilly think that what we got here is bad, it just doesn't feel like Jill to me.

The titular monster was a real let down too, I used to see his face on the corner of shelf in videogame stores as a kid and was he was chilling, hell I've even had nightmares about Mister X after playing RE2 remake. So I was looking forward to see what this guy who's supposed to stalked you throughout the entire game has to offer and the answer is, no a whole lot. 

I can excuse the first chase with him being more cinematic and quick-time-eventy since it was a cool setpiece. But when he first shows up bursting through the wall and start stalking you, you truly feel the sense that he's in the wrong game. You spent most of the time rolling out of his way both in regular gameplay and in his bossfight that you may be deluded in to thinking your in a souls game. Also the strech of the game he "stalks" you in is a lot more different then Mister Xs, you felt his presence as a constant remider through the NCPD and when you lost him and had a little brething room it make him feel all the more smart when he would out of nowhere catch up with you. Here Nemi just waits for you to get out of the safe room indefinitevely, no going away and finding you in a cool way, just camping you and forcing you to make a run for it. Also it's comically easy to bring him down and while it's "encouraged" since he always drops something when you do but after the first few times, it's hardly worth the ammo you spend bringing him down. And after you get to the sewers fairly early on that's it, now you're only getting him in boss fights, and even then only for one of those boss fights you get him in his iconic desing after that you just fight him in his blob form which fell really lame as that was Birkin's gimmick in RE2.

I also sorely missed the defense item mechanic from the first to remakes, sure you get the dodge with Jill and the parry with Carlos, and I get that it's something inspired by the original, but I don't see a reason why you couldn't have both. As it stands while Nemesis attacks are fairly predictable and you can learn his patterns quickly, regular zombies are a lot harder to read and force you into a QTE unless you want to get one shot at full health, they could have at least given us the damage and had as inmediatly keep going like in RE2 when you're out of items.

While the first 2 remakes felt like a love letter and evolution on everything that came before them, this game seems to have been rushed out the door before it was ready by money hungry execs and it's a damn shame. If you skip this one you're truly not missing much.

I will admit beforehand that the original RE3 has a special place in my heart as it had been my comfort game while grieving over a childhood pet--- and also counter with "RE2 is special to me too". 

RE2R was not at all a disappointment at release, and even upon seeing some of its faults I still believe it is a great experience alongside the original game. RE3R though...

THE PROS:
- Some of the early Raccoon city segments are actually pretty decent. The original design of the city can be visible at some points. 
- The gameplay taken from RE2R is solid, with intimidating zombies that take a lot to put down and smooth movement.

THE CONS:
- Jill doesn't feel like 'Jill' to me. Her redesign doesn't look bad but does lose a lot of what made her classic look so iconic.  
- The game doesn't feel like RE3 past the opening. They abridge and replace so much with sequences that feel more like an action movie than a dynamic survival horror experience. I didn't really feel as if it adequately portrayed the apocalyptic, depressing and overwhelmed raccoon city.
- Many of the assets are ripped from RE2 remake. I understand their need to make the games overlap in visual identity, but I feel that distinction is important. Something that really gave RE3 original its memorable identity was how ghostly the zombies felt, with their hollow and pained moans rather than generic voracious screeches and grunts (that is a complaint with RE2R as much as RE3R). 
- The sequences towards the end with the big cannon thing felt way less convincing.  The original trilogy certainly had sci-fi elements but they always felt fairly convincing; her being able to lug around something like 5 times her size does not at all feel convincing. 
- Nemesis is a JOKE. He is a setpiece.  They supposedly had the tech and time to do more with him, but they chose not to? 
- There is NO non-linearity.  The original game had quite a bit which gave it significant replay value. I rarely ever think about returning to RE3Remake.

I remembered being excited for this game when I was first getting into Resident Evil in late 2019. In fact, this was also the third game I got into when I finally started getting into the games. Even though I loved this game back when I was 16, does this still hold up even with me getting into the franchise more? Well, yes and no.

Positives: The game is still a fun time just like RE7 and RE2. Seeing Jill in another RE title even in a remake is always great. I hope this won't be the last time we see her in a game, even in this decade. There were still some creepy moments like the hospital section where you play as Carlos to save Jill's life. And lastly, the main man himself. Nemesis. Good God almighty was he threatening as hell. Sure, it would've been more scarier if he wasn't always scripted, but he never hold back any punches.

Now onto my negatives: The obvious main problem with this game is that it is TOO short. If this were to be a worthy remake to the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, I'd expect it to be exactly that while introducing new elements that makes the experience more unique and fresh. Just like the new enemy types we actually did get to see in this game. I also don't like how most parts are completely cut out for no apparent reason and I'm sure that was the case because of the other game they were working on at the time. (Resident Evil: Resistance) I don't get why they decide to do that to begin with. Yes, I'm also aware enemies were also cut for the RE2 remake like the spiders and crows, but that's still not excusable if you ask me.

In conclusion; Resident Evil 3 (2020) is a good game, however it is NOT a good remake. The remake portion is cut in half with some poor creative choices and came out as one of the most controversial RE games to be released. Now, even with my issues with this game, I still had fun with it. But I wish it had much more. As far as I know some people might say this is one of the worst games in the franchise and I can understand why. Mostly with it failing as a remake. However, it didn't piss me off like Resident Evil 6 did where it wasn't a RE game at all. At least this one still had the basic formula. But even then, that's all I really have to say regarding this game. Good game, but a bad remake. If you're wanting to experience the original RE3, there's GOG.

A decent enough Resident Evil game by itself, but ultimately a disappointing remake. As Jill says at the end of the game; "All this death wasn't caused by a monster-making virus, it was greed. Human greed.", and for this game, the same rings true. What killed any hopes for this game paying tribute to its original, was Capcom's need to ride sales hype and push out a new game and make a quick buck.

I've despised this game for years, refusing to touch it with a ten foot pole, but for the sake of fairness, I'd finally resolved myself to give it a fair chance, even if it might not change my mind. Having experienced it myself, I did somewhat enjoy it, but my overall opinion remains the same. 
Resident Evil 3 (2020), is a survival horror action-adventure game, and the remake of Resident Evil 3: Nemesis (1999), aiming to modernize the final entry in the original RE trilogy, and set up a new Remake continuity to follow. You're placed during the events of the Raccoon City T-Virus outbreak, set parallel to the story of Resident Evil 2, as S.T.A.R.S member Jill Valentine attempts to flee the city, all the while pursued by a relentless force bent solely to wipe out her squad. RE3R was developed shortly after the release of RE2R, to take advantage of the massive buzz that game generated, only it was handed off to Capcom's B-team, instead of their more experienced A-team. Ontop of this, they were only given a year of development time to produce the title, resulting in many cut corners. As Capcom's final sin, they also decided to package RE3 with RE: Verse, a sort of Left 4 Dead 2-style PvP game to increase the price. The original is contested in the community, but has a large enough cult following, and contributed multiple lasting and memorable gameplay systems that justify its existence; dodging, ammo crafting, the live selection system, Nemesis' and the stalker enemy type, randomized items, and the iconic Mercenaries mode. 3R butchers most of these elements.

RE3R is a fairly linear game, building in some ways off of its predecessor, degenerating in others, much like the shambling horrors you'll be contending with. Ammo crafting and resource management make a return, but you're given a handy dodge button that lets you slip past enemies easier if timed properly (similar to Revelations 2, though now you enter bullet time and auto-aim when perfect dodging). Unfortunately, the enemies and some aspects of the game are far less polished, zombie variety is cut down, and the gore is reduced. The map this time around is far more on-rails, not giving you many hubs to slowly unwind. In the original, you had a sprawling set of alleys and establishments to go through to solve puzzles and obtain key items, here Raccoon City is comprised of two main streets, and the other areas such as the Sewers and NEST 2 are similarly short, only having maybe two or three major areas. Jill doesn't even get to see the RPD one last time, her workplace, instead it is handed off to Carlos. The only remotely interesting location this time around is the newly-expanded Spencer Memorial Hospital, which I admit is an improvement over what it was in the original. The new enemy types are fun, at least, with the Hunter Gammas and Betas, more engaging than the G-Adults from RE2, requiring a bit more tactical approach. Now, we cannot talk about gameplay without addressing the parasite-infested elephant in the room-- Nemesis. In the 1999 game he is scripted, yes, however the frequency of his encounters, as well as the branching path system changing up when he'll apear next, made him less predictable, and a far bigger threat. In RE3R, he is given only a handful of limited, fully-scripted sequences, relegated largely to boss encounters, making him lose a lot of the impact he once had. His second and final forms in particular being excessive, giving him a bland beast form and a final blob form (Birkin G5 called, he wants his fit back), rather than the tentacle-armed form and the smaller, but more challenging final mutation from the original. Several parts of the original were cut, such as areas (the Raccoon City Clock Tower, the park, the "dead factory" with the aftermath of the skirmish between UBCS and the T-103's), a boss (Gravedigger, a massive earthworm) and mechanics (live choice system and Nemesis' encounters), as well as no post-game content like Mercenaries. The greatly reduced development time likely contributed to this. It's overall content starved compared to the original. It's almost as if even the game isn't proud of itself, as it quickly tries to rush you through every major area and story beat to get to the end as quickly as possible, with none of the new additions lingering long enough to be appreciated, almost like an amusement park ride.

The RE games were never super big on story quality, but they were fun enough to overlook. 3R for the most part does an alright job, but has several brutal stumbles along the way, mostly with Jill. Every character in this game has a bad case of sailor mouth, and it doesn't come off as very believable. Jill and Carlos, in particular, sometimes swear like teenagers in a COD lobby, defusing any tension there could've been with how corny their one-liners would sometimes be (and not in a fun way like the past games). It's made worse as this is inconsistent, sometimes giving them genuinely sincere moments, only to be derailed by hilariously uncharacteristic zingers (the car scene). Jill's almost unrecognizeable here compared to any of her other appearances, as you'd think S.T.A.R.S.' resident B&E agent and former military bomb disposal specialist would be more level-headed, especially after being hardened from the events of RE1, but I guess the writers had a different idea. Last time I checked, neither RE2R, nor any of the games after this, ever had these problems, not even RE8, which had some very bad writing at some points. The only character who acted like this in the past was Moira, who is a 20-something with no military background, and gradually improves as a character over the course of the game. It's just a shame to see. Resident Evil scarcely uses swearing, and when they do, it's done sparingly and in times when the situation calls for it, so this is just an unwelcome tonal whiplash, especially when it doesn't complement the story in any meaningful way, as well as the fact that most of the characters (namely Carlos and Jill) spend their time calling Nemesis playground level insults and dismissing him, completely washing away any intimidation factor or tension he might've provided. Buildup is also completely ripped out of the game by having Nemesis bust through Jill's apartment wall only five minutes into the game, as opposed to having you slowly learn that something is chasing you down, not helped by you seemingly being able to stop him with a shelf in the apartment escape setpiece (the creature who just went through a solid brick wall a minute ago). Nearly no horror game disrespects their main antagonist in this way, it's pretty much the number one rule. Carlos and Brad especially are out of tune, Brad being nonchalant in the apocalypse and Carlos being obnoxiously flirty and nice. For a game and its' fans claiming realism, these characters sure feel like caricatures.

All in all, the game itself isn't bad by its lonesome, but compared to the original it's a shameless cashgrab not given enough time to bake in the oven before being haphazardly packaged with a game no one asked for, just to pad its pricetag. It is one of the worst remakes of an existing game I've ever seen, as it cannot be viewed separately if its' goal was to adapt an existing piece of media. Thankfully, you can at least give the original PS1 1999 game a try, even if just on easy mode, on GOG or Steam, and it's cheap too. I doubt RE3 will be revisited for a few decades, so this is the modern version we're stuck with. Buy on sale if you must.

Coming off the RE2 remake, I was excited to see what RE3 had to offer in terms of gameplay, theme, and feel. While I was not disappointed, this game is a different experience that's a lot farther than the original in terms of a remake. I almost want to considerate this separate because of how different the experience largely is compared to the original. So let's do some quick bullet points of the stuff I did and did not like, and I'll give a flat rating at the end. 

Likes
>Nemesis' original design is burned into brain because of how iconic the look is, the remastered version of him isn't only an improvement but speaks to nemesis' relentless nature as a bioweapon. A new iconic look never hurts and this game delivered.
>Nemesis' presence while entirely scripted, it provided the illusion that it wasn't, considering that there are plenty of unique ways to get him off your tail in the downtown sections of the game, almost every encounter I needed to do something different each time. 
>Nemesis' new forms are a pleasure to look at.
>Weapon variety this time around was really nice, and the carlos sections with a more strapped up soldier were always fun to raise hell in. 
>While 2 made me feel dread walking through the spaces, 3 was more fast paced and I'd argue more intense then it's precursor, this was a feeling I welcomed in the game about a relentless pursuer and I genuinely felt like I was always seconds away from getting my teeth knocked out by the hulk that is the tyrant. 

Dislikes
>While the original was a lot more linear then 2, not this linear like it is in the remake, the game essentially cuts out a chunk of exploration during the middle portions of the game and the latter portions of the lab and hospital, not to mention that you actively had to be seeking out side objectives to fully explore the space. 
>I know everyone says this but the amount of *cutscenes* with nemesis got annoying after hour 2 of the game. This was especially frustrating since you fight the same form basically twice in the same song and dance routine then a final boss fight. I felt like there was no build up to the climax considering it went from curing Jill to entering the bunker to immediately slaying Nemesis. 
>This might just be a skill issue, but the dodge/punch mechanic to me is really floaty and unnecessary. I understand it exists to help compensate for the heightened aggression of enemies and the new enemy types, but the mechanic is really only used to dodge the tyrant and fight hunter betas, I just wish this system was a little more flushed out and was more accessible then 1 screw up and you take a hit. If they wanted to incorporate into gameplay like with the hunters, I think they should've made it more consistent to lean on. 
>Cmon man, you had to cut out the clock tower?
>While I knew going into this game that RE3 was more action focused, I thought it would keep a lot of the original horror elements established in the 2 remake. This game isn't only tonally different, it almost plays completely different from even the previous title. I wasn't hesitating at enemies or deciding where to spend ammo as often, considering that enemies just respawned and the game gave me enough to compensate for that. Once I got to the hospital the horror was almost completely lost for me and the only reason why I got anxious was because as stated above, I didn't think the punch/dodge mechanic was consistent enough to reasonably take on hunters, outside of that I felt like I was going through the motions of an action shooter by that point. 

Closing thoughts

RE3make while nowhere close to the original, as a standalone title, I can't get that mad at it as I'll admit, I found a lot of the game entertaining, I thought Jill was strong as an action protagonist and Carlos being around for the whole game was a nice change of pace. Nemesis while nowhere close to his original design mechanically, is still worthy of iconic status in the horror universe through his design and mutations. I praised early sections of the game for his inclusion and I just wish they stuck with it through the entirety of the game. But all in all, as a standalone, it's really good and has a lot to say and show. But when you contextualize from the original and the remake before it, it's a downgrade in every aspect. Menus aren't as clean, enemy behavior is as unique, things are unpolished in some areas compared to two, and because of that it's obvious this game was rushed, so if you're a die hard fan who praises the originals like no tomorrow. I'd skip this one. 

But if you're a casual fan who enjoys just seeing bioweapons duke it out with our heros and are interested in the universe, I can't really not recommend it in good faith. It's a solid title and it was an attempt on a tight dealine and for that I can't be too mad. 

7.5/10 Might go for the platinum if it's easy. If it's a chore, I'll probably skip.

Resident Evil 3 Remake — Reviewed by Albert Wesker (Disappointed, and Rightfully So)

Ah… Resident Evil 3 Remake.
Capcom’s attempt to resurrect yet another chapter of Raccoon City’s tragic downfall. I approached it with mild curiosity — perhaps they’d finally learned from their mistakes. Perhaps they’d deliver something... evolved.

Instead, what I witnessed was a dissection — a once-proud experiment, stripped of its vital organs and left twitching on the table.

Let’s begin with the obvious: it’s short.
Painfully short. The original Nemesis Incident was a sprawling, chaotic masterpiece of survival and pursuit — a city consumed by infection and fear. Here? It’s as if someone pressed fast-forward on Armageddon.
One moment you’re admiring the ruins of Raccoon City, the next you’re in an underground lab wondering how the entire outbreak concluded in the time it takes to make a pot of tea.

And Nemesis… oh, Nemesis.
In 1999, he was the pinnacle of Umbrella’s bio-weaponry — relentless, unpredictable, a walking embodiment of terror.
In the remake? A glorified QTE with a designer coat. He lumbers in for a scripted chase, grunts a few times, then politely waits for his next cutscene.
They neutered him — declawed the monster and called it innovation.

Then there’s Jill Valentine.
Once a paragon of elite tactical precision. Here, she spends half her time exchanging forced banter and the other half diving out of explosions like she’s auditioning for an action movie. A waste of her potential — though I suppose mediocrity is what happens when you remove Umbrella’s guiding hand.

The city itself feels empty — a stage set, not a living, dying organism. Gone are the branching paths, the choices, the sense of chaos.
It’s not survival horror; it’s horror tourism.
"Here’s your linear route, Mr. Player. Please enjoy your conveniently timed explosions and cinematic camera angles. Don’t worry about exploration — we’ve already done the thinking for you."

Even Carlos, the soldier with a conscience, is reduced to comic relief with a haircut. Tragic, really. He had potential.

The irony is delicious — Umbrella was infamous for cutting corners, and now Capcom has done the same. How poetic.

Visually, of course, it’s stunning. Every failure is rendered beautifully. But a polished failure remains a failure.

My verdict:
An experiment that could have been sublime — but was rushed from incubation before it ever reached perfection.
Stripped of depth. Stripped of dread. Stripped of soul.

5 out of 10.
A disappointing replication... from a company that clearly still hasn’t learned the lesson of hubris.
If Umbrella had produced something this underwhelming, I’d have personally ordered it terminated.

The expectations coming from the RE2R led me to be really excited to see how opening up Raccoon City would expand upon the rock solid gameplay loop. The RE Engine still delivers on its wonderful fidelity but the team made some baffling choices in changing the tracks for action rather than horror.  This is a very underbaked sequel and a massive overcorrection from such a wonderful predecessor.  This a meek regression from such a confident blueprint and I came away very mixed. 

(+)  The game is stunning and wonderfully charismatic in the way everything is animated. The zombies are still mesmerising in the way they move and collide with the environment. There’s a lot more variety in the weapons and there are a few new additions to the enemy variety which was a nice surprise. It was hard to snap out of the mentality taken through from rolling credits on RE2R but I did enjoy the Carlos sections and their focus on action.  The game was at its best when wide open spaces were matched with its exploration loop and there were a couple of inspired locations very on brand with the RE franchise.  There were a lot more customisation items to find and click into your arsenal so the exploration loop was a little meatier.  Much like its siblings, this game runs amazingly well and is optimised beautifully. 

(-)  From the first enemy I felt that this was a step down from RE2R, for some bizarre reason we’ve lost all the impact of the combat. Zombies are stiff and more resilient to gunfire meaning you can’t pop and run through areas. The gore has been tragically scaled back, only the flesh from the skull comes away and even knife slashes don’t rip frabic which gave the game a very cheap and undercooked feeling.  The game wants you to stand and fight which melted all the tension as I was always healthy and well stocked. I HATED how the game relied on quick time events, cutscenes and radio calls in its presentation. It really fuelled the hanging feeling of this being sloppy seconds because a lot of the shine and mystique of RE2R is gone.  The games pace was constantly being interrupted from phone calls and cutscenes where it would have been much less effort to keep everything in gameplay. I hated the clunky dodge roll, the game never explained how it worked and I must have done it correctly less than five times, the intention of shaking the gameplay up for the better was there but much like most of the game the execution was shockingly poor.  I never played the original but this was a little skimpy even with some unimpressive objectives acting as desperate padding. Nemesis himself was relegated to the boss fight sub-bench and made much less waves than Mr X with him ironically being the less memorable of the two.

Overall, the game was a major step down from its sibling and I came away very disappointed in the mediocre execution of what was supposed to be a knockout continuation from the revolutionary RE2R.  There is barely enough meat in its bones to give it a recommend and it was only the last two areas that pulled this above the recommendation line. I was out in under five hours and that was for a fresh first playthrough.  It worked perfectly with my X1X controller and I had no technical problems with it.  I would, very tentatively, recommend it at a sale price and only as a way through a series playthrough like I’m on at the moment.

A lot of content from the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis is missing, which makes the experience feel stripped down. The game is also much more linear, with less exploration and fewer meaningful choices. Nemesis himself is disappointing—he looks cool, but instead of being a constant threat, he feels scripted and less intense than he should be.

Overall, it’s not a bad game—it’s just underwhelming. It feels more like a DLC-sized experience sold as a full-priced title. I’d recommend picking it up on sale rather than paying full price.

This is a game that fits into the category of 'Not bad, not amazing'. The reason for this is that whilst the game is fun and has many positive qualities, it stands in the shadow of both the previous remaster and, even more so, the original game of which this is based on. Many consider this game to be a poor remaster due to extensive cut content from the original and too heavy of an emphasis on action over survival horror.

Personally, I can't comment on the cut content due to not having played the original as of the time of writing, though that will certainty be changing in the near future, but I can comment on the obvious change of pace from RE2R. There certainty is more action though I didn't think it ruined the experience by any means. Enemies still felt deadly and I still had to watch my ammo count, it was the scripted events I found disappointing. 

I can easily say I preferred the times Nemesis was stalking me freely around the map as I went about by business rather than the several interactable cutscenes we get of him throughout the game. It really was simple case of press W to survive on many occasions and I specifically remember watching a few cutscenes with Nemesis and thinking 'Damn, it would be cool and absolutely heart pounding if I was in control right now'. 

For those having played Resident Evil 2 Remastered you can expect the same experience here consisting of exploration and puzzle solving combined with keeping an eye out of useful items and inventory management to deal with the undead hordes, though the game is overall easier in all these aspects. Puzzles were a complete cakewalk and the mostly liner levels made it obvious where to go. If all else failed the notes scattered about the map effectively spelled out what to do. This game really did feel like it held my hand a lot and took away some of the enjoyment of figuring things out that the previous remaster gave me. 

One important thing to note also is that the game has no additional content beyond the RE:Reverse game coming packaged with this. Once you beat the campaign that's it, no mercenaries or new game plus. Given how short the main game is, roughly 5 hours on my first playthrough, I'd recommend it only if you can get it on a sale. Those 5 hours were a blast, gameplay was fun, the actual level design and set pieces were immersive and detailed... but 5 hours isn't a lot specially for a title that does little to provide replayability beyond a love for the story. The shop feature, where in you complete challenges to buy unlockables, is the only thing really that provides something in this avenue. A nice addition, but beyond some player boosting upgrades and infinite ammo weapons and one outfit for Jill, it provides no new content.

**FULL SPOILERS** 

I would recommend just playing RE2 remake and avoid this game altogether. As has been observed before, this game feels like a glorified DLC for RE2 and if you were to play them back-to-back, this critique would ring true. RE2 remake was a tight, suspenseful and challenging horror survival game with great atmosphere, combat mechanics, a good variety of enemies and environments and decent characters who you cared about. For me there is always a distinct sense of anxiety hanging over you as you carefully creep around the dimly lit environments, just waiting for a zombie or Mr. X to jump out at you. RE3 remake on the other hand was a massive letdown. Going into it, it would have been good to just have the atmosphere, puzzle solving and combat mechanics of RE2 mixed in with a different story, characters, enemy types, environments and weapons. It seemed like it would be an easy

1. STORY 

As far as I know the story is the same as in the original game and again is a pretty standard RE offering. You play as Jill Valentine and after getting attacked by Nemesis at her apartment, she flees into downtown Raccoon City which is overrun by zombies. She eventually meets Carlos, a U.B.C.S soldier who becomes her ally and Nicolai, another soldier who is eventually revealed to be the main human villain. Whilst trying to avoid being killed by Nemesis, the main plot involves Jill and Carlos trying to secure the T-Virus vaccine.  About half the game takes place in downtown Raccoon City before Jill and Carlos go to Spencer Memorial Hospital, beneath which is an Umbrella facility housing the vaccine. All the while Nicolai is lurking about and at the end it is revealed that he wanted to record Jil fighting Nemesis so he could sell the recordings for profit. There are the usual boss battles against Nemesis throughout the game and towards the end a race against the clock for our protagonists wherein they must escape Raccoon City before it is nuked. In the end, Jill defeats Nemesis with a railgun, Nicolai is wounded and left to die while Jill and Carlos escape in a helicopter, with Jill vowing to do whatever it takes to take down Umbrella. 

It’s all very standard action movie stuff. As for the characters, there’s not much to like. Jill is a standard female action hero who has plenty of one-liners but not much personality. No character arc, just a badass with an attitude. The main villain Nicolai is super generic. Nothing more than a mercenary who is willing to let millions die so that he can get paid. Nothing we haven’t seen in a thousand times before. The only character who I even remotely liked was Carlos. His earnest and down-to-earth personality made you root for him, and he had some good banter with Jill.  

I had to roll my eyes at the sequence wherein Brad Vickers (people who have played the original game will know who that is) shows up and attempts to get to safety with Jill. Not two minutes after meeting him he gets grabbed and eaten by a pack of zombies and the game shows it as being this highly dramatic moment of loss as Jill loses a close friend. The problem being that we the audience have no sense of who this guy is as a character. He is just a blank slate that shows up one minute and is gone the next. I never played the original RE3 and maybe he actually had some screentime and characterisation in that game but in the remake, he gets nothing. When you introduce a character into a story and you want their death to be impactful on the audience, you must put in the work of giving them some characteristics like motivations, goals and flaws. Anyway, RIP Brad, I guess. 

2. COMBAT 

This game is obviously going for more of an action movie vibe as opposed to survival horror which is fine but the execution I feel is very lacking. The game makes it all too easy to progress through any given level. On regular difficulty, zombies die with approximately 3 to 4 shots to the head, which is super easy given that the game gives you a plethora of ammo even early in the game. There are also numerous explosive barrels scattered about in some of the more open areas which, when timed right, will kill 4 to 5 zombies at once, eliminating any kind of danger or tension in these zombie encounters.  

This is far from the experience of RE2 remake, which has zero explosive barrels in it (as far as I can remember). In that game, it was always a case of here’s a zombie, ok, do I kill it or try to go around it? Do I have enough bullets to take it down? If I’m going into a new, unknown area should I save my ammo and health items for then? The player soon learns the value of their limited resources in RE2 and learns when and where to engage or avoid enemies. It pushes you to be careful about spending ammunition, so you might not want to kill all zombies that you encounter but at the same time if you leave enough alive, there’s a good chance one will get you eventually. The player must factor all this in and then decide how they want to proceed.  

Back to RE3, it seems to me that the levels are so small (again, very rushed in development) you’re finding ammo for your starter weapon on every street corner. I played this game on Hardcore difficulty, and I was never worried at all about running out of ammo, for any of the weapons. The same goes for gunpowder and herbs as well, both being very plentiful.  The normal zombie types are very easy to kill; again, you don’t have to worry about ammo because you always have heaps and the wide open, well-lit environments make it easy to spot a zombie at a safe distance and then take them down, no problem. No real tension, just a shooting gallery, especially once you play as Carlos who has the fully automatic M4 rifle, with which you can just mow down everything in your path.  

3. NEMESIS 

When compared to Mr. X from RE2R, Nemesis is a good example of why sometimes less is more. Like the original game, his sole mission is to kill Jill Valentine. Throughout the early sections of the game, he crashes through walls, jumps from buildings and at one point can walk through fire unscathed. This game reiterates the old cliche of the protagonist getting knocked down and then the villain slowly walking towards them and then something or someone distracts the villain so that the protagonist survives. This happens with Nemesis and Jill a lot, in a few subpar cutscenes where the game really tries to make Nemesis look cool and menacing but for me at least it just comes off as hollow.  You don’t dread Nemesis the way you dread Mr. X, what with his blank, unemotional demeanour and the way he just keeps coming after you like the T-800. Nothing beats creeping around RPD while hearing Mr. X’s footsteps echoing all around you.  

The boss fights are pretty mediocre when compared to the RE series' best. The first one is a basic run-and-gun wherein you fight Nemesis on a rooftop until you get knocked off said roof onto a fire escape below. The only thing that sets this fight apart from the usual shooting and avoiding getting hit is that you can shoot a fuel barrel on Nemesis’s back to deal him a good chunk of damage. The next two are strangely similar wherein you fight Nemesis in his second form in a cylindrical shaped environment (a plaza with a fountain and then a massive lab containment chamber) and these two fights play out pretty much the same. There’s the usual shooting and chasing and then Nemesis takes to the walls of the area and runs around in circles before jumping down on top you to deal some damage. The only real difference is that in the second fight you can shoot some poles that electrocute Nemesis and slow him down. The final fight is probably the best one wherein the player must dodge the fully mutated and tentacled mass of Nemesis and attempt to restore power to a railgun which the player can then use to kill him once and for all. For me it was still pretty underwhelming but so is the entire game. 

All up, 2/10; play RE2 remake instead.

Resident Evil 3 is a very good action survival horror game, although more emphasis on action rather than the horror aspect of the franchise, and signifies the turn of the series to suspense action kind horror which Resident Evil 4 would end up perfecting down the line.

Jill Valentine is probably the most badass character the franchise has to offer so far. Far from Ada Wong's mysterious femme fatale persona or Claire Redfield's compassionate activism, Jill Valentine is efficient, resilient, and an all around consummate professional that is very much a soldier at heart. It was really cool seeing her chuck an experimental prototype railgun into Nemesis' mouth and drop crazy lines like “You want S.T.A.R.S.? I’ll give you S.T.A.R.S.!” or "Next time, take the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hint!" She is sassy, confrontational, and has a sarcastic grit kind of humor. She is reckless too, but her experienced background and ultra confident way of settling things makes her recklessness look purposeful, intentional, and gives off the "just another day in the office" type of vibe which I hella respect.

Carlos Oliveira IS SUCH AN UNDERRATED CHARACTER, CAPCOM WHY DIDN'T YOU BRING HIM BACK FOR THE OTHER GAMES?! He is witty, courageous, loyal, and HE IS SO HEAD OVER HEELS FOR JILL THAT I'M HERE FOR IT. I like how everyone around him knows what's up too and teases him about it, but he is all too aware that Jill is way too big for him to handle so he just tries his best to spot for her as a dependable and reliable partner. What sealed the deal for me was that he was willing to brave through and punch his way through a zombie infested hospital, with other bioweapons lurking about, just to get Jill a vaccine for her infection. Like CAPCOM, what are we doing here?

Nikolai Zinoviev is a purely self-interested character that only cares about turning the disaster of the Raccoon City Incident into a profitable opportunity. His sole goal is to gather bioweapon combat data by having them fight with experienced and trained platoons sent to evacuate civilians. He is not above betraying his comrades at their expense by locking off their escape routes to have them brutally massacred if it means getting data he could sell. He is cold-hearted and adaptable to the rapidly deteriorating state of the city.

All in all, I WISH THIS GAME WAS LONGER. If I am being honest and fair, this game was too short and had too much cut content from the original. Although, this game has a lot of the things I felt like have been missing from Resident Evil 2 - which was MORE ENEMIES. In RE2, enemies were few in between several hallways and rooms, BUT the areas to combat them were extremely narrow and claustrophobic, not to mention ammo was way more scarce in RE2. In RE3, space was much more generous and literal hordes were blocking you from getting to your objective and they were hella spongy so you had to get creative with your methods in reaching the objective. The dodge was, in my opinion, way too powerful. In the end, dodging was just another means of the player to fight back but the timing to execute it is too generous. Combine that with the open spaces and you find yourself lacking in the horror department, leading to a discounted sense of agency. I get that the agency was supposed to come from Nemesis chasing and hunting you down around the city with literal zombies skulking about, but the execution leaves much to be desired as Nemesis only appears to hunt you around for the first 1/3 of the game. This was such a wasted opportunity too because, unlike Mr. X from RE2 with his menacing ass footsteps making you cower in a corner listening as his footsteps becomes increasingly distant with his "in the edit" walk, NEMESIS RUNS AND JUMPS AND WIELDS A FREAKING FLAMETHROWER AND A ROCKET LAUNCHER which could have been 10x more panic inducing if only his appearances wasn't as limited. Overall, don't let such details discourage you from a having a good experience. I say, experience the nightmare first and formulate your own conclusions.

Never seen a game miss the mark more than this.

To get a better understanding of why this game was so controversial, I decided to play the OG version from 1999 and it was a pretty fun experience. Nemesis was such an immediate threat CONSTANTLY throughout the majority of the game. The setpieces in the original were very fun to navigate, and there was plenty of fun puzzles and choices to make throughout the game to make multiple playthroughs of the game fun and fresh. Though the game was short it was very sweet.

The remake however decides to throw all of this out the window for something completely different that just falls through hard. The story has almost no time to settle because the game drops Nemesis immediately through scripted cutscenes giving him no buildup at all. The city portion of the game is SIGNIFICANTLY cut down in size, zones and puzzles are just gone entirely and the maps are much worse designed. The maps are much too linear.

Nemesis is himself is also a major downgrade. He goes from a terrifying seemingly unstoppable terror in the OG. To a minor nuisance that goes down much too easily. His boss fights are also somehow worse. The two Dog Nemesis fights are very tedious and lack any sort of feedback on whether or not you are progressing the fight properly. The final boss is just a lame wall boss where you shoot some weakpoints to allow you to charge up an instant kill. Any ammo or powerful guns you have been collecting throughout the game are absolutely worthless here. 

The few strong points the game has are just raw gameplay. Parrying is much more responsive here than in the OG. Shooting guns and finding specific weaknesses feels good. The cast is enjoyable and Jill has some fun banter to listen to.

Clearly they wanted to try something different for this remake but the terrible execution of Nemesis, and its tedious boss fights, lame set pieces, and significant cut of already short content, leave a lot to be desired. I do not recommend anyone play this over the OG 1999 version. However if you have already played the OG and are looking for something with more responsive fast paced gameplay, this might be worth a buy on sale.

Resident Evil 3 (2020) is a prime example of how a remake can honor a classic while bringing fresh ideas to the table. While it’s true that the game is on the shorter side compared to other entries in the Resident Evil series, what it lacks in length, it more than makes up for in heart-pounding action and adrenaline-pumping moments. This reimagining of the 1999 survival horror title shifts the spotlight on fun, fast-paced gameplay, and a more streamlined experience while keeping true to the series’ horror roots.

A Thrilling Reboot with a Fun, Focused Approach

At its core, Resident Evil 3 remains an exploration-driven survival horror game. However, the developers have streamlined the experience, making it feel more action-packed and less drawn out. Jill Valentine is back, this time fighting to survive against the relentless Nemesis, a hulking monstrosity with a singular goal: to hunt her down. The game’s focus on tight, intense encounters rather than sprawling exploration makes for a fun, quick ride.

The star of this show, without a doubt, is the Nemesis himself. While not as omnipresent as his original version, the new Nemesis is still an imposing threat—he’ll burst through walls, chase you down, and keep you on your toes throughout the game. The tension and fear of being stalked by him, combined with well-timed jump scares, makes each encounter memorable.

A Short, Sweet, and Action-Packed Adventure

One of the most talked-about aspects of Resident Evil 3 is its brevity. The game can be completed in around 6 to 8 hours, which may leave some feeling like it’s over too soon. However, the game isn’t designed to be a sprawling epic like Resident Evil 2 or Resident Evil 4. Instead, it’s a tight, concise experience that keeps the action intense from start to finish. Every moment feels important, and there’s little filler in between. The design decision to cut out some of the more laborious aspects from the original game (such as excessive backtracking or too many environmental puzzles) ultimately leads to a more fast-paced and thrilling experience.

Additionally, the game offers replayability through different difficulty levels, unlockable items, providing players with incentives to return for multiple playthroughs.

Unique Take on the Franchise

The game may not have the same level of survival horror dread as Resident Evil 2 (2019), but it brings something fresh and distinct to the table. The mix of action, resource management, and quick-thinking combat sets it apart. The game’s focus on action doesn’t necessarily diminish the horror; rather, it keeps the player constantly on edge, never knowing when the next Nemesis encounter will happen.


Graphics and Sound Design

On a technical level, Resident Evil 3 shines. The game runs beautifully on modern hardware, with stunning visuals that breathe new life into Raccoon City. The environments are well-designed, capturing the eerie atmosphere of a city on the brink of collapse. The lighting and textures are top-notch, and the sound design is exceptional, with ominous, unsettling music and creepy ambient noises that heighten the sense of dread.

Final Verdict

In conclusion, Resident Evil 3 (2020) may not be the longest or most groundbreaking entry in the franchise, but it offers a fast-paced, fun, and thoroughly enjoyable take on the series. The game’s shorter length means that while it doesn’t overstay its welcome, it also leaves you craving more. Its unique mix of horror and action, paired with stunning visuals and memorable moments, make it an excellent addition to the Resident Evil franchise. Whether you're a fan of the original or a newcomer, it’s a wild ride that’s well worth taking.

I must admit, I like this game. It looks nice and it has it's moments but that doesn't excuse it's shortcomings. First of all, due to all the content they cut from the game, it's way too short! I had 1 full run, didn't rush, and yet it took only about 10 hours. This is not worth the 40€ price tag. I also strongly disapprove that you can only buy this game as a part of a bundle with another game I didn't even want.
Secondly, having already said that I like this game, I would've like it a lot better (and spent more time with it) if it had been a more faithful reproduction of the original game. I never played the original, but I was very disappointed when I heard that an entire area (and arguably the game's most iconic area), the Clock Tower, was cut from the game completely. it's very clear to me that this game was approached from a desire to quickly capitalise on the success of the RE2 Remake. It feels like glorified DLC for it's predecessor instead of the independent game RE3 deserves to be and because of that, it falls far short of the standards that were established by Resident Evil 7.
This really was a missed opportunity which is why I would encourage Capcom to take the assets they made for this game and use them to rebuild it to much better match the original, while keeping it in the style of RE7 that we fans love and expect. What I want to see are adjustments in matters of scale, story, gameplay elements and tone. That last point refers particularly to Jill Valentine. She's a core character of the series and from what I've heard, this remake does not accurately reproduce her character at all. Speaking of which, I do like the way Carlos looks but I would appreciate a more faithful reproduction of Jill's appearance. I've seen what she look like in the original and the way she looks now is objectively fine but she just doesn't look like Jill anymore and no, the "Classic Costume" isn't enough to change that. I do like the changes made to Nemesis' initial appearance but the way he behaves and how he transforms throughout the game is nothing like the original. Nemesis is supposed to be his own unique character, but in this remake he just feels like a copy of G from RE2. Correcting this would probably be the single most important adjustment. However, I did like that he drops rare loot if you can hit him right, but it definitely needs to be more difficult/complicated than a grenade to the face.
If Capcom can manage to properly re-remake this game, I would even be willing to pay for an optional upgrade. I would be comfortable with something akin to what was offered for Death Stranding (Kojima Productions offered owners of the original version of the game an upgrade to the Drictors Cut version (which also happens to cost 40€) for only 10€).

The original Resident Evil 3 was one of the worst RE games ever made. Somehow, Capcom managed to make the remake even worse! From cheap enemy AI that constantly stun locks and cc's you, to overly suggestive hentai themes, to the game's short length, RE3 remake is a shallow experience. Thought Nemesis was annoying in the original? Well, now he has tentacles.

The mechanics and gameplay are just so damn sluggish. Zombies and attack animations will home onto you, regardless of which way you're moving. This is more evident on the game's higher unlockable difficulties where dodging is crucial for survival.  The final boss on Nightmare difficulty is so broken and so egregiously cheap that I'd rather fight every Souls and Nioh boss in succession than do this! He will literally alter the speed of his attacks so that at the exact moment you get hit he is able to kill you while you are staggered. This means that you cannot use dodge! You also can't heal since the game doesn't let you bring up your inventory if you're currently being hit by an attack. They may as well have made it one-hit kills. You also need some insane reflexes to constantly avoid the near-constant attacks. It's honestly the worst boss experience I have ever had.

Anyway, everything about RE3 remake lacks polish and feels tacky. Honestly, did Capcom not do any quality control with this game? The campaign is really short and can be easily beaten in under 6 hours. It kind of feels like an expansion pack for RE2 rather than a stand-alone title. It's like like Capcom decided to just make the enemies as cheap as possible to make the game last longer. There are plenty of unlockables, but, unless you are a completionist or just like killing zombies most players are probably going to be content with a single playthrough. If the game was at least scary I could overcome many of its flaws, but it's not even remotely scary. RE3 Remake is, in my opinion, by far the worst game in the franchise, where the only thing good about it is that it makes all of the other games in the series look way better by comparison.

Resident Evil 3 Remake is a bittersweet experience. On the one hand, it looks incredible and runs flawlessly, but on the other, it feels too short and lacks the tension that made the original such an iconic game.

First off, the length: I finished it in about two or three hours. For a full-price remake, that’s really disappointing. 

Then there’s Nemesis. In the original, Nemesis was terrifying, unpredictable, and a constant threat that kept you on edge. Here, he’s much more scripted, predictable, and, honestly, boring. Most of his appearances are tied to cutscenes or brief encounters, which completely eliminates the fear factor. This was one of the biggest disappointments for me.

On the plus side, the controls are very accessible and easy to understand. Personally, I struggled to master the dodging mechanics, but overall, movement and aiming feel fluid and responsive. It’s easy for newcomers to learn and play.

The graphics are fantastic: the environments, lighting, and character models are very well done. Raccoon City looks beautiful (and terrifying) with the modern RE Engine, and the atmosphere is perfect. The sound design is also solid, though the soundtrack isn’t as memorable as it could have been.

Another issue is replayability. Once you beat it, there isn’t much incentive to go back unless you’re a completionist. Compared to Resident Evil 2 Remake, this one feels much more linear and limited, with fewer puzzles and exploration opportunities.

If you only care about graphics and want a short, action-heavy Resident Evil experience, you might enjoy it. But if you loved the original for its suspense, Nemesis encounters, and survival horror pacing, this remake may leave you disappointed.

After over 130 hours with Resident Evil 2, I must admit I expected more from Resident Evil 3, since it was developed either concurrently or even later than its predecessor. Compared to Resident Evil 2, it feels like a downgrade: you can’t realistically dismember zombie corpses anymore, there are no blue herbs and thus no shields, the game world is substantially more linear, the story sometimes seems thoughtless, and with a bit more care it could have been much better.

I also have to criticize the exaggerated amount of action, which becomes laughable over time. In Resident Evil 3 it feels completely normal that our main character survives a rocket launcher explosion at point-blank range, etc. In the end, the time was fairly well spent, but I won’t touch this game again after 30 hours and all the achievements. Even though I would have preferred to rate the game witout comparing it to the predecessor, I can’t accept that CAPCOM released a significantly worse game than its predecessor just to boost the fiscal year and treat a major part of the Resident Evil franchise so carelessly.

I can still recommend it to all Resident Evil fans who want to play it anyway. Yes, there are phases where it’s fun, but to newcomers I’d rather recommend Resident Evil 2 or even Part 1 (Remake). If someone absolutely wants to play both titles, I’d suggest starting with Part 3, since – as described above – the third part does not even come close to the second (except for the graphics).

Boss fights are my favorite part, they are challenging but manageable. My biggest annoyance is the noisy footsteps again in this game; it really breaks immersion since rubber shoes shouldn’t be this loud. It seems that the shoes are made of rock or wood and every time you take a step the sound is so annoying. Do you know what will make a perfect mechanic for games like this? A custom crafted shoes that reduce noise and maybe introduce some mechanic that normal shoes attract more zombies than shoes that make less noise. Overall, the game is fun and captures the survival horror genre well. I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys this type of game.

While some players may find the game a bit short, there’s no denying that this is a strong, modernized version of a classic, made with care and style.

As a disclaimer, I did not grow up with the original RE3, so my opinion may not have as much value as someone who has played both. Still, despite all the hate that this game got for cutting content, I personally love this game. Sure, it doesn't have as much content as RE2 Remake (which I agree is definitely better as a Resident Evil game), but you've got a memorable cast, awesome gameplay, cool boss fights (which, granted, I'd say can be better appreciated on higher difficulties), and amazing dedication to both atmosphere (especially with all of the locations they let you go through) and the storytelling. If I had any nitpicks for RE3 Remake, it'd be that Nemesis could have been implemented in more unexpected ways like how I've seen in demonstrations for the original game's version of events. Those "make your choice" segments would have been cool to see in this title, too. Even so, this game is a fun time as is, and after having done 4 playthroughs, I would say that it's very good. Resident Evil 3 Remake delivers sharp, detailed environments and polished character models, but it omits so much of the original’s content that the experience feels hollow. Raccoon City has been reduced to a few narrow streets rather than the expansive urban area fans remember, and Nemesis only appears in scripted scenes—he no longer stalks you through loading screens or ambushes you at random, and his new “tape‑wrapped” look feels arbitrary. Puzzles are trimmed to straightforward on‑screen clues instead of requiring note‑taking and exploration, and the rewarding Mercenaries mode is gone alongside half of the enemy types, including the familiar crow encounters. Timed choices and alternate endings have been removed, crafting is limited to basic ammo with no enhanced rounds, and Jill and Carlos each have only two outfits where there used to be eight. On the plus side, the 1990s‑style lighting and textures capture a grimy, rain‑soaked atmosphere, voice performances are solid, Carlos’s redesign is a clear improvement, the save‑room theme is exceptional, and the hospital segment feels fully realized, with ambient details more consistent than in the original. Despite these strengths, the extensive cuts and simplifications leave the remake as a streamlined action game rather than a true survival horror experience, so veterans of the 1999 classic may find themselves missing the depth and unpredictability that made the original so enduring. If you have the ability I would recommend a play-though of the original as well.

This is a completely different game from the original. All locations have different layouts, puzzles are non-existent and Nemesis himself does not stalk you, but rather chases you during the opening segment of the game, which is, by far the best part of it. And yet, most encounters with him will be during cutscenes or sequences where Jill has to traverse a corridor whilst running from his attacks, being unable to interact with him at all. Those few moments on the RC streets where you have to face him in your first run are actually very fun. It's sad how underutilized that mechanic turned out to be.

There's also an inordinate ammount of Gears of War style radio walk-n'-talk moments that cannot be skipped, most of which occur after cutscenes, bloating the game's duration without purpose. Combat, however, is fun, though monster AI suffers from glaring faults, such as being tethered to some places, allowing you to walk back, say, to a room's door to snipe some zombies a few steps away, or even walking to an open adjacent room and doing the same with impunity. This was also an issue in RE2R. AI in both games was wholly inconsistent, with some enemies chasing you through multiple rooms and opening doors, while others did not. There's a mod to alleviate this issue (Nowhere Safe), which I recommend using.

As you might be aware, the game is incomplete. There's no Mercenaries mode, no decision quick time events and some areas and enemies are missing. Yet, in spite of all this, I had my fill of fun. The game ran very well on my potato (locked 60 with near imperceptible graphics impact), and some of the reimagined enemies (like the hunter line and even Nemesis phase 1) where fun to fight. Now, you might say, "well, this isn't what I asked for", and I hear you. Thankfully, you can still play RE3 with a whole cast of modern conveniences, such as upscaled backgrounds and FMVs (see Seamless HD Project and REscale), high framerates (thanks to Lossless Scaling, with no downsides outside of some input lag) and gamepad support, on GOG and through Dolphin, so it's not a real loss. Yet I can't help but wonder how great this game could've been if Capcom cared to update it to include all of this missing content, different as it couid have been.

The content that is included in this remake is not bad if you buy it for 75% off or more, but I can't ever justify giving Resident Evil 3 a recommendation simply because of how much content was cut from the original which sadly means that Resident Evil 3 ends up feeling more like a DLC for the Resident Evil 2 remake rather than its standalone own game.

It is very obvious that Capcom wanted to cash in on the success and hype of the Resident Evil 2 remake so they rushed this game out as quickly as possible and therefore ended up having to cut out vast swathes of content from the original game to meet the tight deadline. Apart from the plethora of locations that have been either entirely cut or redesigned into background props like the clock tower, the park and the city hall, to me the worst change has to be to Nemesis himself. Compared to the menacing, unstoppable, looming threat that Nemesis was in the original, in the remake Nemesis is relegated to a few, short linear sections at the start of the game where he is given barely any time to actually chase you around like a stalker enemy should. Even in these sections, Nemeis is pathetically easy to defeat with a few bullets or a single grenade and the game actually rewards you with weapon upgrades and ammo for downing him several times over, essentially turning what should be the ultimate enemy the player should dread to encounter and seek to avoid into a lousy punching bag. Even smaller pieces of content that also ended up being cut from the original could have been added via post-launch updates like extra character costumes or the mercenaries game mode, but instead Capcom chose to do nothing and actually chose to paywall the only two available character costumes in the entire game which were unlocked simply by beating the game in the original.

Overall, while this is not a bad game and if you pick it up chances are you'll have a great time with it, this is undoubtedly the worst of the recent resurgence of Resident Evil games and remakes since Resident Evil 7. What could have saved this game was a 'director's cut' re-release with most of the cut content added back in, but by this point it is very clear that Capcom has moved past this game a long time ago.

Resident Evil 3 takes a more action oriented approach compared to its predecessor, much like the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis did within the classic trilogy. However, even among those older titles, Nemesis was arguably the weakest entry, and unfortunately, this modern remake doesn't manage to elevate its source material in a meaningful way. In fact, it not only falls short as a remake but also struggles to uphold the identity of a Resident Evil game.

Like the Resident Evil 2 Remake, it's not a one to one recreation. It is more like a reimagining with considerable creative liberties, not all of which work in its favor. While some of the original's core ideas are still present, they have been altered in ways that make the game feel more like a cinematic action thriller than a survival horror game. There's a clear emphasis on cutscenes, dialogue, and scripted moments, which gives the game a more "movie like" quality but at the expense of player agency and atmospheric tension.

Visually, there's little to complain about. The RE Engine continues to impress, with highly detailed environments, excellent character models, and realistic facial animations. Zombies, although largely recycled from Resident Evil 2, still look convincing. From a technical standpoint, the game is well produced. But gameplaywise it moves the game further away from its survival horror roots.

Nemesis, the big bad thing you already see on the covers, should have been a standout feature. In the original, his encounters were tense, unpredictable, and often dynamic. Here, he is reduced to a mostly scripted presence. His initial appearance in the city streets is arguably the highlight of the game one of the few moments that captures the chaotic energy of the original. But subsequent encounters are heavily controlled and lack tension. His mutations are less grotesque and feel disconnected from the biological horror that once made him terrifying. Instead of evolving in response to the player's actions, his transformations now follow a fixed, cinematic path, turning him into a quadruped like creature that's visually odd rather than intimidating. It's strange, with the Tyrant from Resident Evil 2, they've already introduced an enemy into the series who has somehow evolved from the original. But here, it really seems to be the case that Nemesis is even better in the original than he is in the remake.

Also Carlos, a side character from the original, plays a much larger role in the remake. His expanded sections include new locations and extended gameplay time sometimes even replacing segments originally played with Jill. While his improved presence could have added depth, these sections often feel more like a generic third person shooter. Armed with an assault rifle and abundant ammunition, Carlos storms through waves of zombies, holding out against dozens of them in a sequence that feels more like a scripted shooter scenario than a survival horror game. It was similar in the original, but here they could go on a different road, instead of making everything more over the top.

Equally disappointing is the removal or truncation of key areas from the original. The clock tower and parts of the factory are missing entirely, and some of the game's characters are introduced so briefly that they leave no lasting impression. The Mercenaries mode has also been cut, and puzzles once a staple of the series have been either removed or simplified to such a degree that they no longer offer any meaningful challenge. You get Resident Evil Resistence instead, a stand alone multiplayer game nobody asked for.

Unfortunately, combat often feels unsatisfying. Zombies are unusually durable, absorbing bullets unpredictably. The game doesn't encourage careful aiming or offer consistent feedback for well placed shots. Critical hits seem to occur at random rather than as a reward for skill. Boss fights are similarly unengaging, typically resolved by unloading the most powerful weapons until the enemy collapses. There's little strategy involved, and these encounters rarely evolve beyond their visual spectacle. The new dodge roll require also less precise timing and makes them far more forgiving and with full control over aiming and movement, there's little reason to flee one of the core survival instincts that the older games used to evoke. While this makes the game more accessible, it also reduces the sense of vulnerability that once defined the series
