[h2]TLDR:[/h2] While Resident Evil 3 Remake (3R) maintains the excellent gameplay and presentation upgrades introduced by the remake of the second RE game (2R), it is also far too brief and derivative to be considered anything other than "competent."

[h2]GAMEPLAY OVERVIEW:[/h2] 3R picks up the story of Jill Valentine after the events of the first game. Jill is now trying to escape from a virus-infested Raccoon City. Along the way, she meets Carlos Oliveira, a security operative of the Umbrella Corporation. Together, the two work against the clock while being stalked by Nemesis, a juggernaut bioweapon created by Umbrella.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3535467740
Nemesis arriving early in the game.

This remake retains the shift from the fixed-camera perspective of the original RE2/3 to the over-the-shoulder perspective of 2R, making it easy to navigate the streets and buildings of the infected city. The player starts as Jill, transitions to Carlos for several segments mid-game, then back to Jill. The two characters have slightly different move sets and available weapons.

For each character, zombies and other foes litter the way forward. Just as in the remake of the second game, these walking corpses are quite durable, soaking up multiple headshots from starter weapons. They are also surprisingly fast, shambling toward the player with deceptive leisure, only to lunge and cover the final stretch between themselves and the player in the blink of an eye, so stay alert. Old enemies from previous games make appearances, along with some new ones. The action is gloriously gruesome, with exploding heads and sprays of blood. Player deaths are equally horrific. 3R definitely earns its "Mature" rating, so keep the young ones away.

Puzzles were a hallmark of the early RE games and while there are a handful in 3R, I found this game's riddles laughably easy. This game definitely shifts away from that aspect to a more action-oriented experience. There are some new environmental wrinkles added, such as mobile power carts, which spray an arc of electricity when shot, stunning all enemies in range for a few seconds. The player can use these to slip past large groups without using ammo, though save for the end of several prolonged bouts of combat, I never felt a lack of bullets or healing items while playing on Standard. Resource management is usually an staple in survival horror but I never felt the pinch in 3R. Supply status wasn't much of an issue as long as I picked my fights and ran when I could.

One new feature in 3R is the dodge mechanic. It's a little tricky to get the timing down but once you've done so, it's a very effective method of avoiding damage—and honestly, it's essential for the boss fights, so I recommend a player practice early until they are comfortable with it.

With the exception of one fight against waves of zombies, the boss fights in 3R are against Nemesis in some form or the other. Unlike the original RE3, where Nemesis could appear and attack the player at random, in this version, encounters with Nemesis are fixed occurrences at specific points of the journey. Players can opt to fight him but since Nemesis is a bullet sponge who can't be permanently disabled before the game's end, running is usually the better option. There are several mandatory fights against the hulking menace but those encounters are marked by hallmarks of the genre—wide-open arena-like spaces littered with ammo and healing items—so the player should see these encounters coming. After mastering the dodge timing, I found these fights more tedious than anything.

My real issue with 3R is its incredibly short length. I died a lot, explored every nook and cranny I could find, repeated several segments to get the exact outcome I wanted, and still finished in under eight hours. Replay value is minimal; unlike 2R, there is only one real route here and any subsequent playthroughs will proceed along the exact same path. 

The story and gameplay are adequate but there just isn't enough of either on offer. 3R's controls and interface are much like 2R and (aside from the dodge) doesn't innovate much new ... which would be fine, if 3R had retained the bulk of the story and events from its original version, and clocked in at a 25-hour-plus playthrough. But since it doesn't, it's hard for me to do more than give it a slim thumbs up. RE fans will likely enjoy 3R for what it is—and just as likely be left dissatisfied and hungry for more. I did, and was.

[h2]STORY / WORLDBUILDING:[/h2] This story takes place around the same time as the events of 2R, though the two tales don't intersect. More of Umbrella's experiments and dastardly deeds are uncovered as the player progresses, and the narrative is consistent with the lore of previous games. On the other hand, the 3R setting is a bit light. This remake uses multiple locations and tile sets from 2R. At the risk of repeating myself, this probably wouldn't matter if 3R was a longer game but as it stands, such reuse feels like a lazy corner-cutting shortcut. The fact that 3R slashed so much interesting story and so many locations from the original RE3, like the Clock Tower, Raccoon City Park, and Factory, and the boss fight with the Gravedigger, for example. This reduction in length and content only exacerbates the impression that this game could have easily been a DLC to 2R.

[h2]TECHNICAL ASPECTS:[/h2] Like 2R, 3R is a visual and aural feast. Environments are rendered in fine detail and character animations were fluid on my ten-year old rig. The sound design is excellent. In the early areas, ambient noise alerts the player to nearby threats, by both volume and direction, and fills the background with the sounds of a city falling apart. This is in marked contrast to later scenes, where the silence itself becomes almost oppressive and adds to the tension. Voice acting and dialogue for the main characters is generally pretty good, and far better than the original. In terms of presentation, the game excels.

I didn't have any errors or glitches and the game felt perfectly stable. Steam achievements are generally accessible, though maxing out requires finding all collectibles and speed running the hardest difficulty.

[h2]FINAL SCORE: 6.5/10[/h2]

I left feeling pretty underwhelmed, especially after playing the remake of 2. It's not that it's a bad game, it's just not up to the standard set only a year prior in terms of execution and content. 

That said, I'd still recommend it purely as a standalone game, because it's still fun. With the huge caveat that I picked it up on sale, in a bundle, so I'm not approaching it as a full-priced game.

An awful lot of 3 is just absent. Whole areas are gone, and what isn't cut is abridged beyond recognition. Nemesis perhaps got it the worst, after the first few encounters being relegated to scripted cinematic moments and the occasional boss fight. What wasn't cut, but instead remixed, I like a lot. I just really would've liked to see the whole game get that treatment, instead of huge chunks just being cut out.

I don't strictly understand some of the changes either, like the removal of sub-weapons, defence items, and how aiming for the legs just doesn't seem effective now. Though Jill's dodge is actually usable now, which is a massive plus, and I like that a perfectly timed dodge opens a window for counter-attack. 

It's a bit too focused on being "cinematic" for my tastes, with tons of scripted explosions and destruction, etc. As a result, it doesn't feel like a game I want to replay any time soon. There's not really any room to do things different, and given there are no alternate scenarios or bonus modes.. this really feels noticeably shorter and lighter than the previous game.

Where 2R has Claire & Leon, A & B, plus 4th Survivor, plus Ghost Survivors, 3R just has one scenario. It would be balanced out if Jill's scenario was longer, and richer, but it's the same length as one of Claire or Leon's.

On the positive side, it's at least still fun to play, and visually gorgeous. I wasn't particularly precious about Jill, so the changes to her character here didn't bother me. I liked the dynamic between her and Carlos. She felt independent, headstrong, jaded after the Mansion incident and the struggle for accountability afterwards. 

It's definitely worth a play, and if you haven't played the original RE3 you'll probably enjoy it more as you have no knowledge of what's missing.

An absolute embarrassment of a remake, especially following the stellar RE2 (barring a mangled B route) and a stain on Jill Valentine's name. On its own its a very linear campaign over in less than 2 hours, if you play smart you could finish it and still get a refund, but as a remake it soils the name of Resident Evil 3. It rips out the identity and soul of Resident Evil 3, no exploration, no chases. no puzzles. no narrative choices, no different paths. As a result you end up with the shortest resident evil game, the speed run achievement is under 2 hours and you can optimize it down to 40 minutes.

First off, this is hilariously such a misogynistic game, most of the flaws Brad and Carlos had in the original gets transferred to Jill. Brad the coward (who never even sets foot in the Spencer Mansion) becomes this weird man of action that just brushes off the Nemesis threat while Jill is acting dazed like a deer in the headlights. Carlos meanwhile also becomes a man of action, inversing their meeting in the original and now he saves Jill. Finally, there's literally sexual assault in this game, no joke, Jill is forced to throat a bug, completely unavoidable, its so unavoidable that the "no-heal" run allows for 1 instance of healing just so you can clear the parasites the bug shoots down Jill's throat. This specific bug isn't even in the original game and it only exists in that one section. Finally, when Jill finally gets her hero moment for the first time in the whole game she gets sucker punched again by Nikolai and Carlos has to save her AGAIN 

As for the titular Nemesis, again he has multiple chances to kill Jill but just doesn't, seriously he has her head in his hands multiple times and he just stands around. First off, his design makes him look like a mindless killing machine, whereas in the original he has a bit more personality, emotionless sure, but alot you can tell he's alot more deliberate with his actions. His fit is chopped too, he's literally in a garbage bag instead of the trench coat he had in the original. Sure, in the original game Jill has the opportunity to beat him in various ways but due to that it shows how resourceful Jill is, here you can still get him to one knee for those weapon upgrades (one grenade ftw) but in the narrative he gets stopped mostly by explosives or heavy duty equipment, most of the time by Carlos, Jill is the only character that has difficulty dealing with him. In gameplay there's only ONE instance where he actively hunts you that isn't down a single corridor or boss fight,  which is compounded by the fact that Mr X in the RE2 remake functions exactly how you'd expect Nemesis to work but instead remake Nemesis works almost exactly like OG Mr. X, that is, only a threat in very scripted encounters. 

The most obvious failings of this travesty is the absurd amount of cut content. First is the clock tower, the most memorable location in the original game, that has 3 separate Nemesis encounters, including him aura farming twice. 

Raccoon City was originally two maps (Uptown and Downtown) brimming with atmosphere and content, and is now cut down to two streets, there's nothing to do here, nothing to see. By removing the city and the clock tower, half the damn game is missing. They even had the audacity to replace Jill's iconic Samurai Edge with a dinky glock you pickup from  dead officer. 

Significant aspects of gameplay unique to RE3:N is gone as well, Live Selection, multiple routes, multiple endings, epilogue slides, survivor encounters, and especially the nemesis encounters. The Nemesis is present  in most of the game and shows up in different ways depending on the order of your actions and VERY difficult to take down. Here, he's a loser that's easy to kill and only shows up early in RC and in 4 scripted encounters where he chases you down a designated path in which you deal with it in the same way. And his actual boss battles are extremely easy as well, and 2 of them require you to have a specific weapon and ammo type otherwise you're soft locked. 

That's already disappointing and there's even more. No extra costumes, no Park, no City Hall, no Press office, no Dead Factory, no Grave Digger, No Barry, Carlos in RPD instead of Jill, and they cut Mercenaries in favor of RE:sistance, which lasted less than a year before EOS and its still bundled to the game. The damn S.T.A.R.S uniform doesn't even look right, dinky little shoulder pads and a cotton shirt instead of the durable, ribbed, clearly heavy weight compression shirt she had on in REmake (and even OG1 a little bit)

To be fair, Capcom seems to have course corrected since 2020, but this game is still an embarrassment to the franchise and Jill Valentine deserves another shot considering RE3 was the last time she was ever a playable protagonist in a numbered, mainline game. Although considering how Jill was portrayed in Death Island, I'm still worried at how they might continue with the character.

Resident Evil 3 is another amazing remaster from Capcom. Racoon City looks incredibly detailed with plently of realistically looking abandoned spaces, lovely in-game advertising and devastating environmental storytelling. A very enjoyable experience again with a thrilling atmosphere and some of the best background I've ever heard in any game. It takes place at roughly the same time as RE 2, this time from the perspective of S.T.A.R.S. Officer Jill Valentine and the U.B.C.S. mercenary Carlos Oliveira, who called her to help save the remaining residents of a devastated Racoon City from the chaos caused by the outbreak of the T-Virus.

Once again working with the RE Engine, CapCom has done an incredible job with the small details: From the in-universe advertising, to the detritus left by citizens who had to escape in a hurry, to RE 2-related Easter eggs and just generally very compelling in-game notes and journalists giving background context to people's tragic last moments before their eventual death thus revealing a code for a safe lots of times. 
Some spaces feel abandoned, while others feel up-until-recently very inhabited full of details and supplies, which makes you want to explore every inch in this game. The broader environments are not left out though. Smashed cars are piled up outside of flickering neon signs, ablaze stores and broad industrial spaces are just eerily empty. The atmosphere around you just everything in its power to make you feel small, weak and vulnerable.

Just like in other game of this series, every single part of Resident Evil 3 feels deliberately put together. Every single room contains useful items or secrets and all enemies have a purpose and is not just randomly thrown in, which is something very notable. What I love about this series is that not every accessible building is next to another one and not accessible from just the front door. No, some areas are can only be discovered when you start solving issues in other houses which then lead you into the other houses, whilst trying to search for a clue in order to solve a problem in the other house. For instance when a fire obstructs one route, it can only be extinguised with the help of a tool hidden in a nearby building also housing a weapon that can't be accessed without another tool that's located past the areas obstructed by the fire, so you are basically "forced" to return to that specfic area in order to take the weapon with the tool, which was in accessible before due to the fire blocking the way to it. 

Item micromanagement is part of RE 3 again meaning items are rare and very limited, so you need to be very cautious about not wasting to many of them. You might not be able to pick up certain items, so you need to either combine items or run back towards a storage chest to put them in there in order to make space for the items you just found, so you can finally pick them up. This also forces you to thoroughly explore every inch of the game possible, as I said before. As long as you do all of that and don't skip scavenging in certain areas or waste a unnecessarily amount of ammo in certain situations you will be fine.

Awareness is key to progress through this game, as you can easily be caught off guard by a number of deadly nasties. There's plently of enemy design here to keep things fresh and exciting ,with the spider-like Drain Deimos poisoning Jill with parasites, Pale Heads who can only be take out with extremely accurate blows to the head with your most lethal weaponry and additionaly things trying to eat your brains serving as just few examples. 

Jill is way more nimble on her feet than Leon or Claire for RE 2, which gives RE 3 a more frantic- action-oriented feel than its predecessor. She's able to sidestep incoming attacks and when the timing is right you earn a sligh slow-motion effect helping you to escape. Just like in RE 2 the protagonist unlocks various weapons ranging from pistols, to shotguns, to grenade launches to simple hand grenades and flash bangs. Every gun was fun as hell to use, also thanks to upgrades to some of those weapons found by exploring every inch of the in-game world.

The player also gets to enjoy and play Carlos and his perspective. He's a little less nimble and agile than Jill with a very powerful assault rifle that can clear any room in the blink of an eye, at the cost of very limited and precious ammunition. His mission in the hospital to locate the vaccine and use it on Jill was very challening, atmosphering and enjoyable. Even though this game is mostly about Jill, the chapter of Carlos is very fun as well.

The central antagonist, Nemesis, is very powerful and moves like a giant and you need to be very careful about him crushing you to death. You need to time your doge perfectly in order to survive. The downside is that he only shows up in certain, pre-programmed boss fights, unlike Mr. X in Resident Evil 2, who roaming around the police station all the time, meaning you could never ever feel safe, no matter where you were at.

There is no New Game PLus after the Resident Evil 3 campaign, which I personally like,  as they were simply short versions of the campaign themselves, so they were totally unnecessary. However, by completing certain in-game challenges a shop is unlocked where you can cash in your points on useful items, which can be used in future playthroughs. These items, such as coins, make your attacks more powerful and devastating.

Just like with Resident Evil 2 before, CapCom has done a stellar job with remaking Resident Evil 3 making it feel more polished and modern, which may spur the younger people on to give this series a shot.

Let's set this straight, this games is very good. Most negative reviews of this game are sprung from the fact that unlike the RE2 or RE4 remakes, this game cuts out and modifies content from the original. Despite that, it stands on its own two feet quite well. This may not have been the faithful remake everyone wanted, but it is still an excellent game. (This is review after completion)

If you have played any of the other remakes you have a pretty good idea of what to expect from the gameplay. This game puts you over the shoulder of Jill Valentine and occasionally Carlos (idk his last name). You will use a variety of weapons to a wide range of enemies including: zombies, mutated creatures, infected dogs, parasites, tyrants, and more. It is much more an action game than the RE2 remake as most of the game you have a wealth of ammo and healing items (played on normal). The gunplay feels similar to other TPS games, nothing super special. 

In terms of story it follow JV and a couple of side characters after the Spencer Mansion incident. After that incident she returned to Racoon City where all hell broke loose. As she tries to escape Racoon City she is hunted down by a Tyrant who is relentlessly pursuing her. FYI It takes place right before the events of RE2 until right after RE2. I thought it was a fun parallel to the events seen in RE2 that was satisfying to watch unfold from beginning to end. It felt well paced and a decent length despite being a pretty short game.

In terms of scares, it is less scary than RE2R, and more scary than RE3R. It had a few moments that made me jump a little, but overall its definitely not nightmare fuel. The more action oriented gameplay definitely makes you feel more "in control". 

The elephant in the room is obviously the cut and modified content. Although I think it is also important to note this isn't a FF7R situation where the game modifications are off the rails. It is still recognizablely RE3. It should also ne mentioned that if you never played the original you probably won't notice anything. I do personally believe this is the better way for new players to experience the game as (imo) the modernization of the game outweighs its cons. 

The sound design was decent, not something that will have you seeking out the music, but it gets the job done. It relies mostly on ambient music to enhance the feeling of the game. This strategy works, but it also means there is not a single track from this game i can actually recall. At least the soundtrack wasn't Crazy Bus (if you know you know). On the flip side the  VA did a phenomenal job. The acting was great and didn't feel stiff or forced.

My biggest complaint with this title was the boss fights.  There are 3 (major) boss fights and I didn't find any of them particularly great. The first one was OK, the second one was WAAAAAAYY too long and repetitive, and the third fight was basically the second one again. 
The stalker segment (where you are actively hunted) was also not great because of its length. The segment was laughably short. If you played RE2R you would know that in that game the stalker segment is about 1.5-2 hours. Here it was about 30 minutes. Granted those 30 minutes are far more intense than the previous game (the Tyrant is on steroids with better moves, ai, and a more intimidating design).

Finally we are at the graphics. Just like the other 2 remakes this game is a visual masterpiece, especially when you have the hardware to make the game looks its best. All the models, animations, and textures look great. The game looks so good that the transitions from cutscene to gameplay are pretty seamless. Despite this it actualy performs very well for an RT title. (Reviewed using an RTX 3080 and Ryzen 7 5800x with 32gb of 3200mhz ddr4 at 1440p near max + RT high). 

A side note on the price is that despite my high opinions of the game it is NOT worth the $40 USD price tag. A game that can be easily beat it 7-8 hours is not worth that much imo. If you are going to pick it up I recommend waiting for a sale where it can normally be purchased for $10 or bought in a bundle with the other remakes for ~$40 (yes the whole trilogy for the normal price of just one.).

In conclusion/ TLDR if you want to get into RE3 without dealing with the issues of the original, this is a great option despite its cut content. I just don't recommend paying $40 for an 8 hour long game. I give it an 8/10.

The Nemesis-T Type is handled the worse BY FAR (and that's saying something because Jill is reallll bad) acting like a complete joke and total downgrade. He is not scary, nor threatening, nor overpowering, nor competent, nor well-designed. Every single cool or scary moment (killing Brad, destroying the chopper, the clocktower jumpscare, etc.) is stripped from him, and what's left is an incredibly stupid adversary unworthy of the title "Nemesis", let alone "threat". It's no RE2 remake. I was teetering between boredom, annoyance, and occasionally enjoying myself the whole game.

- Jill is an A-hole now; not classy yet tough like before. Most of her writing reminds me of when you take a peek at your girlfriend's crappy book... where putting a swear word every other sentence counts as writing. I appreciated Jill's input maybe literally once the entire game, and was otherwise rolling my eyes at the divorced mom tough girl writing.

- Combat is fine enough although the character is covering up WAY too much of the screen. Changing FOV can help I guess. One way combat is not fine is how much you're forced to endlessly use the dodge button. Most boss fights are waiting until you press dodge, unloading, and then repeating. Many things cannot be reasonably avoided without dodge. It just gets very old and I wish they innovated combat more deeply if they were changing it so much.

- Some memorable locations are simply not in the game. There is even a pamphlet found in the game about the clocktower, but you never visit it.

- No more examining scenery for random interesting information, like was done so well in earlier RE and Silent Hill games. So much character is deleted from the game due to this.

- Insulting amount of braindead quick time events where you lazily tap a button or hold forward, as if anything is happening. These are a complete cancer to gaming. When it was used more tastefully for unimportant sequences in shenmue, it was fun. It's now a cancer in gaming only the most braindead people could feel a high from. I know I'm just watching a scripted scene, and pretending my input means anything is like handing an unplugged controller to an adult and saying it works.

- More streamlined than the original.

- Overpriced for sure. It's short.

- No branching paths (quick decision choice moments). They were minor in original, but having nothing at all is a bit sad. No different endings.

- The amount of stupid scripted explosions and lame hollywood action sequences is way too much. They reminded me of RE6 and why it sucked. Tone it down. Overusing things leads to a less visceral response to it.

The remake of Resident Evil 3 is often seen as the "lesser child" of the franchise, and while I do agree that it's not the best, I do wholeheartedly believe it's worth the time and money to play it. It's not by any means a bad game, it just isn't what it could've been. I personally don't think it's as bad as a lot of things online will lead you to believe, and I personally think that this game is the best way for anyone to get into Survival horror. 

Resident Evil 3 Remake was my first venture into survival horror, and I genuinely believe it's a good jumping off point for people who like traditional shooter games like myself. For my example, I'll use Resident Evil 2 Remake. I don't think I would enjoy Resident Evil 2 at all if I didn't play Resident Evil 3. Like I've said, I come from traditional shooters, some online, some offline. When I play a game with guns, I expect to be able to dispatch of all my enemies. I learned hard and fast in RE2R that you can't just attack everything, and for a few days I genuinely despised RE2R, I didn't understand the spirit of survival horror. RE3R gave me the tools to dispatch of my enemies, but it also gave me a threat that seemed overwhelming. Without RE3R, I never would've liked Survival Horror in the first place.

[b]Forward[/b]: I have finished every Resident Evil game in the main series. Resident Evil 3 is weaker than RE2 Remake and RE4 Remake, but it still holds up as a staple in interconnected storytelling within the series.

[b]Graphics: 93[/b]
The RE Engine continues to impress with cinematic lighting, fluid animations, and grotesque creature detail. Raccoon City looks both grimy and alive—when you’re not sprinting for your life.

[b]Control: 88[/b]
Tight third-person aiming and movement carry over from RE2. Dodging adds a fun layer but can be inconsistent. Inventory and weapon switching are quick and responsive.

[b]Audio Quality: 85[/b]
The environmental sound design adds to the tension. Gunfire, footsteps, and Nemesis's snarls all hit hard. The soundtrack isn't as memorable as RE2, but it does its job.

[b]Stability: 95[/b]
No crashes or major bugs. A technically solid experience throughout my playthrough.

[b]Load Times: 92[/b]
Fast loading across the board, even when backtracking or reloading after death.

[b]Level Design: 78[/b]
The game's biggest shortcoming. It's far more linear than RE2, with fewer puzzles and minimal backtracking. Carlos’s segments break things up but don’t elevate the design.

[b]AI Competence: 80[/b]
Enemies are aggressive, especially on higher difficulties. Nemesis is a threat, but scripted encounters make him feel less dynamic than Mr. X in RE2.

[b]Writing + Replayability: 84[/b]
Jill’s story fits well into the RE timeline and her character shines, but the short campaign and lack of impactful choices limit replayability.

[b]User Interface: 86[/b]
Clean and efficient. Inventory management, map tracking, and item descriptions are all intuitive.

[b]Game Balance: 89[/b]
Challenging but fair on standard and hardcore difficulties. Ammo and healing are tight but manageable. Certain boss fights feel more style than substance.

[b]Grade: 87.0[/b]

I recently finished Resident Evil 3 Remake (2023) on my PC through online streaming, and overall, I would still happily recommend it, especially to fans of the Resident Evil series or gamers who love action-packed survival horror experiences. Visually, the game looks absolutely stunning—the graphics are crisp, detailed, and full of atmosphere, which made exploring Raccoon City feel thrilling and immersive. The developers did a great job in bringing the classic game into modern times, with smooth controls and impressive sound design that keeps you on edge in the best possible way.

Playing as Jill Valentine and teaming up with Carlos was truly exciting. The character models and animations were excellent, and the intense moments against Nemesis kept my adrenaline pumping. The action sequences were solid, and the combat felt satisfying, making it fun to keep going even during tough battles. It’s clear that a lot of care and technical polish went into the remake.

However, while I really enjoyed my time with the game, I felt a bit nabitin (bitin) or “bit short-changed” because the storyline was quite short. I was hoping for more depth and longer gameplay, especially in exploring Raccoon City’s downtown areas. There were places and moments that I wished the game spent more time on, perhaps showing more about the city’s downfall or expanding the story arcs of Jill and Carlos. It felt like the potential for storytelling was so big, but the game ended sooner than I expected.

Still, despite the short length, I’d say Resident Evil 3 Remake is a solid and fun experience for both newcomers and loyal fans. It delivers high-quality visuals, intense gameplay, and the nostalgia of a classic game reimagined. Just be ready for a shorter ride compared to some other titles in the franchise.

I’d definitely recommend it—but if you’re hoping for a longer, story-rich journey, you might wish it lasted a bit more. Overall, it’s a great game worth trying if you’re into horror and action!

It begins with fire. Not the kind that warms — the kind that devours.

The city screams in sirens and smoke. Ash sticks to your skin. Streets you once knew twist into something unrecognizable, swallowed by panic and rot. The world feels like it’s ending — not with silence, but with teeth.

People run, but not fast enough. Doors slam, barricades fall, voices fade. Infection spreads like a whisper passed from hand to hand, and suddenly everything familiar turns hostile.

But the worst part isn’t the chaos.
It’s the rhythm.
The sound that doesn’t stop.
The footsteps.

Measured. Heavy. Inevitable.

You run until your lungs burn, and still — it’s behind you. Not hunting for food. Not for revenge. Just… to end you.

Walls collapse. Creatures claw through the dark. Streets become labyrinths of debris and blood. You keep moving, not because you’re brave, but because stopping means becoming part of the rubble.

Weapons buy you seconds, not safety. Choices feel like coin flips made in fire. And through it all, that sound returns: those steps, like a countdown you can’t reset.

But something awakens inside you. A refusal. A flicker of fight buried beneath the fear. You slam a door. You fire a shot. You scream not because you’re afraid — but because you’re still alive.

And maybe, just maybe, survival isn’t about escaping what chases you.

Maybe it’s about proving that no matter how monstrous the world becomes — there’s still someone in the rubble who refuses to break.

Resident Evil 3, the 2020 remake of the 1999 PlayStation classic, is a visually stunning, high-octane survival horror experience that delivers intense action, striking visuals, and a gripping—if somewhat streamlined—narrative. Developed by Capcom using the RE Engine (the same engine behind Resident Evil 2 Remake and Resident Evil 7), this reimagining of Jill Valentine’s desperate escape from a zombie-infested Raccoon City is more than just a graphical facelift. It reinterprets the original story through a modern lens, focusing heavily on cinematic flair, tighter gameplay mechanics, and fluid character control. However, its ambition to provide a faster, more action-driven experience sometimes comes at the cost of depth, player agency, and atmospheric pacing that fans of the series have come to cherish.

The game begins with an intense and moody cinematic that sets the tone—Jill Valentine is once again at the center, hunted relentlessly by the bioweapon Nemesis, an even more advanced and terrifying stalker than Mr. X from Resident Evil 2 Remake. The first-person intro sequence transitions into third-person gameplay seamlessly, immediately immersing players in a city falling apart. Jill is rendered with painstaking detail, her facial expressions, physical movements, and voice acting (courtesy of Nicole Tompkins) bringing a grounded sense of vulnerability and strength. Unlike RE2 Remake, which leaned more into puzzle-solving and exploration, RE3 adopts a more linear approach. This isn’t inherently negative, as the game’s pacing is relentless in a way that underscores Jill’s desperation, but it does mean there’s less freedom for players to soak in the world at their own pace.

Combat is one of the game’s strongest aspects. It feels responsive and refined, building upon the systems introduced in RE2 Remake while offering new mechanics like a well-timed dodge that can give players an edge in tight encounters. Gunplay is crisp and satisfying, especially when it comes to blasting off zombie heads or staggering mutated creatures. The enemy variety, while not overly expansive, keeps encounters fresh, especially when Nemesis appears—smashing through walls, wielding flamethrowers, or sprinting after the player in a relentless pursuit. These set-piece moments are thrilling and cinematic, though some fans argue that Nemesis is underutilized in later parts of the game, reduced more to boss fights rather than a persistent threat, unlike the unpredictable AI-driven Mr. X from the previous game.

Narratively, Resident Evil 3 refines the original’s plot but also truncates it in key areas. Entire locations such as the Clock Tower and Park are either heavily abbreviated or removed altogether, which disappointed longtime fans hoping for a fuller remake. The trade-off, however, is a more cohesive and focused story. Supporting characters, particularly Carlos Oliveira, receive more attention and development this time around. Carlos’s segments are expanded and surprisingly enjoyable, offering a fresh perspective and some of the game’s most thrilling action sequences. His personality is more fleshed out than in the original, and his banter with Jill gives the game emotional texture.

Graphically, Resident Evil 3 is among the best-looking games of its generation. Raccoon City is brought to life with richly detailed environments, dynamic lighting, and grotesque enemy models that elevate the horror atmosphere. Sound design is equally immersive—squelching gore, distant screams, and Nemesis’s guttural roars all contribute to a constant sense of dread. The soundtrack is more subtle compared to the bombastic score of the original, leaning on ambient cues and horror-driven compositions that serve the new tone well, though some players missed the iconic themes of the 1999 game.

That said, the most common criticism levied against Resident Evil 3 is its brevity. A first playthrough typically takes 5–6 hours, and while there are incentives for replayability—unlockables, higher difficulty modes, and a grading system—some may feel shortchanged, especially when comparing it to the more expansive and exploratory RE2 Remake. Capcom also released Resident Evil Resistance, an asymmetrical multiplayer component, bundled with the game. While a novel concept, it felt disconnected from the main experience and received mixed reviews, with many seeing it as a filler addition rather than a compelling companion piece.

Ultimately, Resident Evil 3 is a bold and visually spectacular remake that prioritizes pace, action, and cinematic tension over exploration and length. While it may not reach the same critical heights or offer the same depth as its predecessor, it succeeds in modernizing a classic for a new generation. It’s a thrilling, polished experience that captures the chaos of Raccoon City’s downfall and the heroism of Jill Valentine with flair, even if it leaves some longtime fans wishing for more substance and less streamlining. For newcomers and action-horror enthusiasts, it’s an exhilarating ride. For veterans, it’s a beautiful but somewhat bittersweet revisit.

[i]Resident Evil 3 (Remake) [/i]is a slick, punchy, and high-octane reimagining of a PS1 classic that shines when it remembers it’s supposed to be a survival horror game. Unfortunately, it too often forgets that, swerving hard into action territory and dragging itself down with repetitive boss fights and a villain who’s more frustrating than frightening.

Still, there’s a lot to love here. The opening segment is incredible, the gunplay is tight and responsive, and Jill Valentine remains one of the most compelling protagonists in the franchise. If you go in expecting a fast-paced, zombie-blasting theme park ride rather than a tense horror crawl, you’ll likely come away satisfied. Just … maybe not scared.

🔫 Pros:
[*] Strong voice acting and character animation. Jill’s performance carries the entire game. She's snarky, competent, and resilient in a way that feels grounded even amid the chaos. Carlos also gets more screentime and comes off more likable than in the original. The facial animations and lip-syncing are excellent.

[*] Excellent gunplay and satisfying arsenal. Weapons feel punchy and impactful. Every shot has weight, especially with the shotgun and grenade launcher. The dodge mechanic, while timing-based, adds a fluidity to combat that encourages skill over brute force. Blasting zombies feels good.

[*] Leans into survival horror in the early game. The first third of the game—in the city streets, dodging Nemesis in dark alleys—is the highlight. Resource management is tight, enemies are threatening, and the pace is just slow enough to build tension. For a brief while, it really feels like RE2 Remake’s moody sibling.

[*] Visually stunning. Raccoon City has never looked better. Neon signs, rain-slicked pavement, and ruined storefronts give the setting a cinematic polish. The RE Engine continues to impress with lighting, texture work, and atmospheric detail.
[/list]

😠[b] Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Too action-heavy for its own good. While the remake starts strong with moody lighting and a desperate dash through a ruined Raccoon City, it quickly shifts into a bombastic action game. Explosions, set pieces, and waves of enemies dominate the second half. Ammo becomes too plentiful, resources are rarely scarce, and there’s little incentive to sneak past or carefully manage threats. The worst example of this was the "Defend Jill" mission. Just boring.

[*] Nemesis isn’t scary—just annoying. Nemesis had the potential to be a terrifying, dynamic stalker like Mr. X, but instead, he’s reduced to scripted encounters and repetitive boss battles. His attacks are cheap: tentacle grabs from off-screen, leap attacks that break your flow, and set pieces where he teleports around to stop you. You don’t outsmart him or dread his presence—you just get repeatedly stunned and hope you can heal fast enough. He becomes a chore, not a threat.

[*] Too many boss and mini-boss fights. Now, to be honest, I don't care for any boss battles in any game. I find them run of the mill and irritating. But Nemesis mutates into multiple forms throughout the game, and each time you fight him, it feels more like a routine than a climax. The arenas are often circular, the mechanics are shallow (dodge, shoot weak point, repeat), and the fights drag on. It gets to a point where you groan when the music swells, knowing you’re in for another 5-minute slog. It’s exhausting rather than exhilarating, and the lack of variation between encounters makes it worse.

[*] Forgettable story and bland villain. The core plot—Jill escaping Raccoon City while uncovering Umbrella’s schemes—is functional but unremarkable. Nicholai, the primary antagonist, is cartoonishly evil and lacks depth or charisma. There’s no mystery, no clever twists, just explosions and shallow betrayals. Even if you don’t expect high art from Resident Evil, this story feels like it’s on autopilot. It’s hard to care about what’s happening when the characters themselves don’t seem that invested either.

[*] Short runtime with linear, limited replayability. The game clocks in at about 5–6 hours on a first playthrough. While the remake does include unlockables, higher difficulties, and time trial incentives, its linear design limits replay value. Most players will see everything meaningful in one run, and aside from Challenge Mode unlocks, there's little reason to return. 

[*] Loss of survival horror tone. One of the biggest missed opportunities is tone. The first third of the game are genuinely atmospheric and intense—dodging through fire-lit alleys, hearing distant screams, and scavenging bullets in fear. But as the game progresses, the horror dissipates. You’re rarely afraid. Enemies stop being threatening and instead become obstacles between you and the next explosion. There are barely any classic RE-style puzzles, no real exploration, and no sense of creeping dread. Just more set pieces, and more bullets.
[/list]

After the fantastic Resident Evil 2 Remake and having spent years with RE3 Nemesis (PS1), I expected something on par. Sadly, RE3 Remake is the weakest of the new remakes.

Technically — flawless: great graphics, smooth performance, zero bugs.
Looks and runs great.

But content-wise? A huge disappointment:
	•	Playtime: 2–3 hours tops. The original had way more content — branching paths, choices, replay value.
	•	Clock Tower — cut (just a boss fight now).
	•	Park and Dead Factory — gone.
	•	Grave Digger boss — gone.
	•	Mercenaries mode — gone.
	•	Live Selection system — removed.
	•	Multiple endings — removed.

Nemesis in the OG game used to hunt you dynamically — here he’s just a scripted sequence most of the time. No more tension or fear factor.

Difficulty balance is bad —
On anything below Inferno, final boss is laughably easy.
But on Inferno, the final boss becomes the hardest boss I’ve ever fought in ANY game — and I’ve beaten Elden Ring and I’m a long-time Isaac player.
Absolutely brutal — skill and precision required in every frame of that fight.

Overall: Great visuals, but a stripped-down experience compared to RE3 OG.
If you haven’t played the original, you might enjoy it for a couple of hours.
But for veterans — prepare for disappointment… and one of the hardest boss fights you’ll ever see (on Inferno).

I came into Resident Evil 3 Remake starved of some fresh Resident Evil content after just replaying a handful of the other titles. I never played this game when it came out as it never really got the right amount of attention on release so I never really deemed it worthy of giving a shot. Fast forward to now where I have fully embraced my 'survival horror supremist identity' and with the recent buzz of Resident Evil 9 Requiem and added the fact I've  been non-stop playing the other entries in the series, I wanted to finally give Resident Evil 3 a shot. So I got myself a $9.99 discounted copy of the game and jumped in. I'm definitely am someone who was utterly blown away by the Resident Evil 2 remake for its modern yet classic dreadful atmospheric terrifyify take on survival horror.  This game in all aspects  felt noticeably scaled back. While still enjoyable in parts, the game quickly gave the feeling of a cheaper, more streamlined version of its predecessor and after doing some research, it made sense: it was developed by Capcom’s “B team.” That doesn’t make it bad, but it does explain why so much of the depth, tension, and atmosphere that made RE2 Remake so special feels absent here. Nemesis who is this game's more aggressive version of Mr.X from RE2 comes off as overly scripted and less menacing than Mr. X. The game overall never reached a point of being more than serviceable. The game was doing its job just good enough never reaching a peak or hitting a stride. As a fully priced follow up to Resident Evil 2, Resident Evil 3 is a step down in every way and is more in line with a kind of experience you could expect from an 10-20 dollar indie game on steam. Some people have said that this game could have served better as a big DLC/expansion to Resident Evil 3 and I agree. That said, the RE Engine continues to be nothing short of phenomenal. The game as a whole and especially the character models look fantastic and the game runs like a dream for the fidelity it outputs. Its smooth, responsive, and incredibly well-optimized. Whether you're exploring ruined city streets or dodging a surprise attack, the controls are tight and fluid in a way that makes every encounter satisfying on a mechanical level. I also have to give credit where it’s due: the chemistry between Jill and Carlos is genuinely enjoyable. Their banter and dynamic brought some much-needed levity and heart to a game that otherwise felt a bit thin. And while the campaign is on the shorter side, I didn’t mind it moves at a fast pace and doesn’t overstay its welcome. Overall, Resident Evil 3 Remake isn’t a bad game it’s just incredibly hard not to see it as a missed opportunity. It feels more like a filler episode in the franchise than a major installment, especially following the excellence of RE2 Remake and especially considering the fact RE4 Remake came after. There’s still fun to be had here, but it’s clear this one didn’t get the same level of care or attention. The reception this game got could be a blessing in disguise as it lit the fire under capcom to really swing for the fences with their next remake and it delivered as I think Resident Evil 4 Remake is one of the best video games of all time.

Playing through the remakes as my first experience with the series I find RE3 to be a decent game, but not so much an RE game. I was really enthralled with the first game and the fact that its difficulty was based on puzzles and resource management. RE2 took a step into action based gameplay but retained the air of mystery and puzzle systems of the first game. RE3 tries to continue that trend with a few hiccups along the way. 

Perhaps due to a constantly changing setting the game has few puzzles compared to the first 2. Leaning more into the action gameplay there is more of an emphasis on combat, but rarely is this combat difficult. On the standard difficulty the game gives you enough resources to kill every zombie you see and then some. The most difficult aspect then becomes using the finicky dodge system during chase sequences that have respawned those zombies. 

Finally the story has little to no depth to it. Even with memos and notes littering the game in the same way the first two did, it didn't feel like any of them were worth reading save the ones that hinted at enemy weaknesses. The (main?) antagonist is uninspiring and makes decisions that make little sense even in retrospect, and the story isn't even always consistent between 2 and 3.

I can't say how the remake stacks up against the original, and I do believe it is actually an alright game, but in the end it was not a good as I had hoped it to be.

While RE3 (2020) is a good game, it is a bad sequel to RE2 (2019) and an absolutely terrible remake of RE3: Nemesis. In short, the game lacks in content and replay value compared to both its immediate successor, other games in the franchise, and the original game it is remaking. It is also lacking in the post-launch support that bolstered both RE2 Remake and Resident Evil 7. Capcom has stated they do not plan to support the game further, and so I do not recommend that you purchase this game until it is priced at what it is worth -- no more than $30, and I would suggest even $20. In fact, for the price they are charging as of this review, $39.59 USD on sale you can get most every other game in the series all of which are much better. Go buy and play pretty much any other game in the series, it is much better bang for you buck and also sends Capcom a message that this kind of treatment of unacceptable.

UPDATE: Recently Capcom has decided that instead of releasing DLC to fix the lack of content in this game, it would be better to release a DLC that allows you to skip the process of playing the game altogether. Now you can pay money to unlock the small amount of unlockables in the game instead of being bothered to even play the small amount of game that is here. I no longer recommend that you purchase this game at all, because doing so might make Capcom think this kind of treatment is acceptable. I will personally be boycotting Capcom from now on in response.

Where Resident evil 2 remake felt like a bigger, better, more ambitious version of the original, resident evil 3 remake feels smaller, more stripped out, less interesting, less ambitious and far less impactful. 

With that being said, this is still a very good game. A very good game that is tragically bogged down by its short length, it’s re-used assets and locations from the previous game, and by a failure to innovate or bring anything new to the franchise. It’s because of this, compounded by it’s hefty price tag, that despite how good it is in its short run time, it still manages to dissapoint.

Starting with the good, this game has incredibly gorgeous visuals and the detail in the environments and characters are truly jaw-dropping. The facial features of the characters were especially impressive as every gesture, emotion and muscle is captured so well and it really elevates the characters and the story. The combat is very snappy and the feedback you feel when you shoot or dodge is very satisfying. There’s a healthy variety of enemies that keep you on your toes from fear, and the combat sequences are impressive.
 
More importantly than anything though, RE3 has that classic resident evil horror atmosphere that we all know and have come to love. Eerie, somber and gory level design that are still filled with so much detail and color. Environments filled with small claustrophobic dark hallways and corridors that make you feel trapped in closed spaces with horrific undead. Skin crawling horror music that plays as you push forward knowing you will have to earn every room you enter. It is incredible horror and it’s what made Resident Evil a one of a kind franchise. This is all present in RE3 and it is an incredible thing to experience as always.

All of this, ofcourse, is overshadowed by its very short run time of 5 hours. it’s re-used locations from the previous game that wear out their novelty very quickly. its disappointing rework of the nemesis villain that feels forgettable and fails to leave an impression on you like the original. This failure to innovate, when mixed with a hefty price tag, results in a game that feels lazy and incomplete for a full standalone title. For this level of scale and content, this game should’ve been a DLC/expansion to RE2, not a fully priced title.

At full price, I just cannot recommend this game. It just does not offer anything new or fresh enough to justify its price tag, especially compared to it’s predecessor RE2. 

But it’s still Resident evil man, and holy hell do I love Resident evil. Like yes it's got all these flaws but it's still Resident evil. It's still got all the hallmarks that makes this franchise so beloved and so good. 

And that’s why, even though it was disappointing compared to the other games, I still recommend Resident Evil 3.

Resident Evil 2 Remake: A Mixed Bag of Nostalgia and Modern Hiccups

The Resident Evil 2 Remake is an ambitious reimagining that delivers both heart-stopping intensity and modern polish, but it isn’t without its quirks. For longtime fans and newcomers alike, the game offers a thrilling journey into Raccoon City’s dark corridors—if you’re willing to overlook a few missteps along the way.

Gameplay and Mechanics
On one hand, the gameplay nails the balance between tension and action. The over-the-shoulder perspective brings clarity to intense firefights and sneaky escapes, and the revamped controls feel responsive when you need them most. However, the inventory system sometimes feels clunky, and occasional pacing issues—where tension fizzles out in less engaging moments—can disrupt the immersive experience. These imperfections frustrate what could otherwise be a seamless survival horror encounter.

Graphics and Atmosphere
Graphically, the remake is a visual triumph. Meticulously detailed environments, atmospheric lighting, and realistic textures pull you into the eerie, rain-soaked streets and oppressive interiors of a city teetering on the brink of disaster. Yet, some areas of the game reveal technical hiccups or repetitive design choices that detract from the overall sense of dread. While many moments shine with cinematic brilliance, the occasional graphical inconsistency reminds you that this project, though impressive, isn’t perfect.

Audio and Narrative
The sound design is mostly stellar—each creak, distant echo, and ambient score accentuates the horror that lurks around every corner. The dual campaigns following Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield offer fresh perspectives, injecting new layers into the narrative. Unfortunately, the added dialogue and branching story elements sometimes feel padded or superfluous, detracting from the tightly woven mystery of the original. The narrative’s ambition occasionally overreaches, leaving some players wishing for a more focused plot that honors the game’s roots without unnecessary embellishment.

Conclusion
In summary, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a fascinating experiment that successfully marries classic survival horror with modern technology, even if it stumbles in places. It captures the spirit of Raccoon City through excellent visuals and innovative gameplay, yet its pacing, occasional technical glitches, and overextended narrative elements leave a bittersweet taste. This mixed bag of highs and lows makes the game an intriguing but imperfect reimagining—a must-play for fans and a cautionary reminder that even brilliant remakes can stumble under their own ambition.

Exploring the balance between nostalgia and innovation in horror remakes can lead to deeper insights on what truly resonates with players. How do you think modern updates can best honor classic horror, and which areas call for a more delicate touch?

Review Title: Nemesis Made Me Realize I’m Into Furry Femboy Foxes


When I first booted up Resident Evil 3 Remake, I expected zombies, explosions, and Jill Valentine’s iconic skort. What I did not expect was a soul-shaking journey through tight alleyways, ruined cityscapes, and the darker corners of Nexus Mods. The game hits the ground running and never lets up—Nemesis smashes through walls like a 9-foot-tall metaphor for repressed feelings, and boy did I feel something stir every time he growled “S.T.A.R.S.” in my general direction.

The combat is punchy, Jill’s dodge roll is slick, and Carlos’s hair has more volume than my will to resist downloading increasingly unholy character skins. Around hour 12, after installing a mod that turned Jill into a neon-pink fox girl with thigh highs and an attitude, I started asking myself questions. Deep questions. Why does this mod have custom idle animations? Why is Carlos now a smug, purple-furred femboy named "Kyrren" with visible abs and lore? Why am I… into this?

By the time I reached the hospital section, my game was less Resident Evil and more Anthro Escape: Foxy Apocalypse. Zombies were reskinned into shirtless werewolves. Nemesis was now a buff otter in leather straps with glowing red eyes and a collar that said “BITE ME.” I wasn’t scared anymore—I was confused, aroused, and fully invested. The horror had shifted from external threats to internal awakenings. Jill wasn’t just fighting for survival—I was, too.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 3 Remake is a criminally underrated experience. Sure, it’s shorter than RE2, and yes, some content got cut. But what it lacks in length, it makes up for in... revelation. Between dodging infected and dodging the implications of my mod folder, I’ve emerged a changed man. A man with a fursona. A man who no longer fears Nemesis, but instead wonders if he’s free Saturday night. 10/10. Life-changing. Do NOT install the “Foxboy Carlos Romance Expansion v2.1.” Or do. I’m not your dad.

This isn’t my first trip through Raccoon City. I’ve completed Resident Evil 3 Remake more times than I can count — on PS4, PS5, and even earned the Platinum trophy. So playing it again on PC wasn’t about discovery; it was about seeing how the game holds up after all this time, and once again facing the chaos of one of Resident Evil’s most intense entries.

And honestly? It still delivers — though not without its flaws.

From the start, the game wastes no time pulling you into the action. Jill Valentine, one of the series’ most iconic characters, is thrust into survival mode as Nemesis crashes through her apartment like a wrecking ball in a trench coat. What follows is a high-speed descent into a city overrun by infection, where danger is around every corner, and safety is never guaranteed.

Nemesis remains the heart of the experience.
He isn’t just a boss — he’s a constant threat, appearing when you least expect it and breaking the rules of space and physics while he’s at it. His presence is overwhelming, relentless, and often terrifying. Whether he's smashing through walls or launching missiles mid-chase, he gives the game a distinct identity that sets it apart from Resident Evil 2 Remake’s more methodical approach to tension.

Combat is fast, responsive, and satisfying.
Gunplay feels tight, especially when lining up clean headshots on shambling zombies. Jill’s dodge mechanic adds a layer of skill and urgency, though it can be inconsistent in tight encounters. The inventory system — a long-standing Resident Evil tradition — continues to challenge players with limited space, forcing tough choices about what to carry and what to leave behind. It’s frustrating at times, but by design.

Visually, the game still impresses.
Even years after release, the RE Engine shines. The lighting and environmental design create a city that feels genuinely apocalyptic — dark, claustrophobic, and crumbling. The sound design is equally strong, with ambient noise and enemy cues creating constant tension. Nemesis’ various forms are grotesque and memorable, escalating in intensity until his final, monstrous evolution.

However, the game’s biggest issue remains its length and structure. It’s a short experience — often around 5–6 hours on a first playthrough — and many sections feel streamlined to a fault. Several areas from the original game are missing entirely, and the narrative moves at a breakneck pace, rarely giving you time to absorb what’s happening. As a result, Jill’s journey sometimes feels more like a guided sprint than a fully fleshed-out survival story.

The voice acting is solid, though not always emotionally engaging, and some moments lack the weight they should carry — likely a result of the game’s quick pacing and limited downtime between set pieces.

Final Thoughts:
Resident Evil 3 Remake is a visually stunning, action-driven reimagining of a classic. It doesn’t quite reach the same heights as RE2 Remake in terms of depth or atmosphere, and it trims a bit too much from the original game. Still, it’s a thrilling experience, and one that I continue to enjoy revisiting.

I don't normally write reviews for games, but I purchased this on sale and am maintaining a randomizer for it via Archipelago so I felt implied to at least toss out my thoughts on it.

The Good:

Graphics & Atmosphere: Visually, the game is top-tier. Raccoon City is dripping with detail, and the horror elements, while less frequent, are polished and immersive.

Combat: Shooting feels responsive and satisfying. Jill is more nimble, and dodging plays a bigger role than ever before.

Pacing: The game keeps moving at a brisk pace, which some players appreciate — there's almost no downtime between setpieces.

The Not-So-Good:

Length & Depth: The remake significantly trims content from the original game. Several areas — like the Clock Tower and Park — are either heavily reduced or missing altogether. Exploration and puzzle-solving take a backseat.

Nemesis: While intimidating early on, he becomes less of a persistent threat and more of a scripted boss encounter. Compared to Mr. X in RE2 Remake, his impact feels underwhelming.

Replayability: There are unlockables and higher difficulties, but with such a short runtime (~5–6 hours casually), some players may feel shortchanged — especially at full price.

Verdict:
Resident Evil 3 Remake isn’t a bad game by any stretch — it’s polished, entertaining, and has moments of brilliance. But if you're expecting a one-to-one remake with the depth and branching paths of the original, you may walk away wanting more. It feels more like a solid side entry or companion to RE2 Remake, or rather it's a re-imagining of what RE3 could've been if they had the technology back in the day.

Recommended: On Sale. At a discount, it’s well worth a playthrough for fans of the series or newcomers who enjoyed RE2 Remake. Just go in knowing it’s more of an action-horror thrill ride than a deep survival experience. Also don't forget Archipelago Randomizer!

Unlockable items, speedrun incentives, higher difficulty tiers, and in-game shop rewards keep the experience feeling fresh and rewarding.
What many skip past is the multiplayer companion mode, Resident Evil Resistance, which deserves far more credit. It introduces an asymmetric 4v1 setup where one player becomes a sadistic mastermind while others band together as survivors trying to escape. It’s chaotic, unpredictable, and surprisingly strategic – a real gem for fans wanting to extend their RE3 experience beyond the main story.
Whether you're a newcomer or a diehard fan, Resident Evil 3 Remake offers a high-octane, replayable survival horror adventure backed by one of the most creative multiplayer twists the franchise has explored. Resident Evil 3: Nemesis sometimes feels like the black sheep of the original PlayStation trilogy. It's been very well received in past and contemporary times and was a massive sales success. Still, despite being a great game, I can't help but feel like many of its elements feel strange compared to its immediate predecessors. The path choice system, the copious amounts of RNG, and its development history as a spin-off title add to this feeling. Naturally, the idea of remaking RE3:N, while not entirely necessary, is enticing. How do you adapt its quirks into a modern context while improving upon its admittedly minor flaws? Apparently, according to Capcom, the answer was: you don't. The Resident Evil 3 remake isn't even close to being as bad as some fans make it out to be, but it is a very disappointing game nonetheless. I've never played a game that simultaneously felt so polished and yet so incomplete. While it does manage to improve upon the original game in some ways, by and large, it serves as a massive step back from both the original RE3 and its immediate predecessor, the Resident Evil 2 remake.

From the onset, it's clear that RE3make is different in tone from RE2make, with a breakneck pace that seldom offers the player any respite. There's little room for RE2make's lonely hall wandering or silent tension when the game grabs you by the neck from the first moment of real gameplay and drags you along for seven odd hours. This lends itself to an entirely different tone and while I don't necessarily dislike it, I do think the game could have benefitted from more moments of silent tension, which feel almost absent. On a game design level, RE3make is for the most part fairly faithful to RE3:N, preserving the more action-oriented style of gameplay while remaining directly tied to core survival horror design philosophies. This isn't a downright action horror game, though it does border on it at points. Changes from RE2make such as the knife being invincible, the dodge mechanic, and the lack of ink ribbons on first-time playthroughs make RE3make a fairly unchallenging game even on hardcore difficulty compared to the brutality of RE2make's hardcore mode. Despite this, it's a very polished and fun gameplay experience that while somewhat breezy is still one I enjoyed playing through. The dodge mechanic is one of the few things this game does much better than RE3:N, being infamously finicky in that game and much smoother to execute in this one. It's satisfying to accomplish and it encourages the player to stay away from enemies rather than engaging them directly. The Hunter Betas, in particular, are designed heavily around this system, and either dodging their attacks as Jill or countering them with a punch from Carlos is satisfying even with the threat they represent. I just wish the game was more punishing towards the player - you're given tons of dangerous weapons very early on that can almost trivialize many encounters. The Hunter Gammas are cool, but when they die in two hits to flame rounds the game keeps handing to me, their threat level is greatly reduced. The lack of ink ribbons or any kind of save limiting feature means that there's no consequence other than time to just saving as much as you want, and no strategy. It's still a very polished and enjoyable time, but it lacks the gameplay sophistication that RE2make has.

The elephant in the room here is how RE3make handles accuracy to the source material. You've probably heard a thousand times that this is a severely cut-down remake and you'd be entirely correct. The biggest disappointment here is how Nemesis T-Type, the tyrant that at least narratively stalks you throughout the whole game, is handled. Nemesis in RE3:N is infamously a case of carefully crafted smoke and mirrors. Most encounters with him are mandatory, and outside of a few areas that he "patrols" for the player being based around RNG, he is less dynamic and random than most people remember. However, the reason why Nemesis struck fear into the hearts of players more than RE2's Mr. X was that the mixture of genuine randomness and scripted encounters was done in a manner that felt convincing. It genuinely felt like Nemesis was hunting Jill down and would not stop at any cost like you were getting to play your own Terminator film. This is not the case at all in RE3make, where Nemesis feels more scripted than ever. While I remember having a few random encounters with Nemesis while playing the Raccoon City demo that was released a month before the game's release, in the finished game I never encountered him outside of what felt like explicitly scripted moments. Perhaps I was just genuinely unlucky, but there appear to be very few spots where encountering Nemesis is a chance and not a guarantee. The boss battles with him, especially the rooftop flamethrower fight, are great, making great use of the game's mechanics alongside making him, if for a moment, feel intimidating and threatening. Almost every encounter with him that isn't a boss fight, however, feels like a playable cinematic cutscene from a Naughty Dog game or something. That's a fine thing to have occasionally, but when it consists of the majority of his encounters, this supposed ultimate bioweapon feels far weaker than RE2make's terrifying Mr. X, the exact opposite of what happened with the PSX games. The game also cuts many memorable and iconic locations from the original, such as the cemetery, clock tower, and dead factory (with the grave digger cut too, unfortunately) without replacing them with anything similarly memorable. NEST 2 is cool and all, but come on, it's no dead factory. Remakes will always inevitably cut things, after all, it's a brand new game and not just the original prettied up, but how RE3make flagrantly throws out core aspects of the game it's based on it almost feels disrespectful even if that's not intentional. Most of its setpieces are perfectly fine if not outright good, but none of them reach the same iconic heights as the original.

Resident Evil 3 remake is a solid game in many departments. It plays great, with fun gameplay mechanics and boss fights that offer a tense, exhilarating experience. The game features many writing upgrades over the original, great graphics with a lot of technical quality, and just generally is a polished, bug-free, and well-made game. Unfortunately, the game doesn't even come close to living up to the lofty expectations of the classic 1999 survival horror game and it suffers from many deep flaws. Nemesis has been kneecapped, feeling less dynamic than the original '90s PSX game, many memorable and iconic locations are cut from the game without any sort of equivalent replacement, a serious lack of difficulty even on hardcore mode, a version of Jill that is less interesting and developed, impressive graphical features of the prior game have been heavily downgraded, and the score is not as oppressive as the original or as atmospheric as it's immediate predecessor. It's still an alright game despite this, I had my fun with it and I can see myself revisiting it at some point, but I struggle to recommend this past RE fans like myself.

Decided to revisit the RE series which I played through for the first time only a few years ago since there's rumors we'll be seeing RE9 soon. This game isn't bad, but it really isn't that good. I haven't played the original, so I can't really talk about it is a remake. But as a game, it has problems. The dodge which is a core feature feels like it doesn't work half the time. Whenever an enemy attacks, I end up just stumbling in this weirdly done animation that feels like ♥♥♥♥. The guns feel nowhere near as good as they do in RE2 or RE4 remake, The shotgun doesn't even give you that satisfying crunch of zombies' heads. There's a fundamental flaw with these RE Engine games and that's the FOV. The camera is literally inside of my ass at all times, which wasn't that big of a problem with RE2 Remake, because of the cramped environments, but it is a problem in this one and RE4 Remake with their more open design. The first phase of the final boss is not a fight against the Nemesis, it's a fight against the ♥♥♥♥ camera. I think there's a mod out there to fix it, but that should come standard.

As for the story, it's fine. But I really don't like Jill's characterization here. She feels so tonally distant from the professional agent she is in all the other games to the point that I'm willing to call her a "girlboss" in this one. And the excessive swearing. Swearing doesn't make strong characters, it just makes me roll my eyes. Totally a different character,

Game's really short too. Doesn't even have bonus modes like RE2's extra challenge missions. Isn't the original RE3 the one that introduced Mercenaries? They coul;dn't even do that? Especially considering how much more action than horror there is in this.

I wouldn't necessarily say it's a bad game, it's just that we ALL know it could have been so much better. Get it on sale. But like a REALLY good sale. Oh, and go find an FOV mod.

Unfortunately this game just isn't good, I played this before I played the original RE3 and thought this game was okay and kind of just treated it as a DLC to RE2R but upon playing the original RE3 and replaying this it is safe to say that this is the worst remake I have ever played. Starting off Nemesis has been completely sidelined in his own game, he went from one of the best stalker enemies in all of gaming to a completely watered down after thought and the best evidence for this is that they removed his name from the title in a remake of HIS OWN GAME. Before I say this next point I want to say that cutting content isn't this like horrible sin people make it out to be, in my opinion its okay as long as its replaced with content that's equal in quality but in this games case its absolutely horrible. This game cuts SO much content and doesn't add ANYTHING to compensate, not to mention that the areas that DO remain have been significantly shortened and extremely watered down. Next is the characters, every single character has absolutely no depth whatsoever, they completely misrepresent Jill and make her something she isn't; Jill is supposed to be strong on the surface but have a softer more caring side, shes supposed to take no ones ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but also be understanding and supportive of those around her and in the remake they remove all of her caring traits and make her this obnoxious and kind of mean protagonist. Carlos has just been turned into oblivious tough guy which sucks because I LOVED him in the original where he was strong for Jill until he finally broke and panicked in the clock tower before Jill (literally) knocked some sense into him. My theory is they didn't even want to remake this game after RE2R and just wanted to go right to RE4R cause they knew it would be a best seller but knew people would get mad if they skipped it so instead they pumped out a product completely devoid of the love and care they've given to the other 2 games. Unironically this game needs a remake more then the OG ever did and its sad to say that I really hope someday they will release an RE3R directors cut or something of the sort just to give it the love it so desperately needs. To end this review I want to say that if you like this game thats fine but I hope you recognize that everything I said is not my opinion, it is instead a factual and objective look at what this game fails to do as a remake of an underappreciated masterpiece. 4/10.

TLDR; Don't play this game, you can get the OG RE3 on the GOG launcher for $10 and get a significantly better game for significantly less money

Resident Evil 3 : Fast, Furious, and… a Little Trimmed

Resident Evil 3 (2020) is a remake of the classic game Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, and like the Resident Evil 2 remake, it offers a refreshed look at a familiar story, but with some compromises. The game delivers a more action-oriented gameplay experience than its predecessor, immersing you in the chaotic streets of Raccoon City, consumed by the zombie apocalypse.

What's Good:

•  Thrilling Action: RE3 (2020) focuses on dynamic action. Battles against zombies and mutants have become more intense and spectacular. Dodging, counter-attacking, and using the environment play an important role in survival.
•  Superb Graphics and Sound: The game looks stunning, thanks to the RE Engine. The environment of Raccoon City is recreated with incredible detail, and the zombies and monsters look disgustingly realistic. The sound design creates a tense and terrifying atmosphere.
•  Great Performance by Jill Valentine: Jill is portrayed as a strong and determined heroine who is interesting to watch. Her interaction with other characters, especially Carlos Oliveira, looks believable and convincing.
•  Nemesis – A Nightmare Come to Life: Nemesis remains the scariest pursuer in the series. He constantly hunts you, adapts to your actions, and uses various weapons to destroy you. Every encounter with him is a test of your skills and nerves.

What's Not So Good:

•  Short Length: This is perhaps the biggest drawback of the game. A playthrough only takes 5-7 hours, which is significantly less than the original game and the Resident Evil 2 remake.
•  Cut Content: The remake is missing some locations and bosses from the original game. This is disappointing, especially for those familiar with the original.
•  Fewer Puzzles: RE3 (2020) emphasizes action, resulting in fewer puzzles that are simpler than in Resident Evil 2.
•  More Linear Level Design: Unlike the more open structure of RE2, RE3 (2020) offers a more linear and predictable level design.
•  Resistance Multiplayer Adds No Value: The Resistance mode, although trying to bring something new, feels rushed and doesn't offer enough depth to keep players engaged.

In Conclusion:

Resident Evil 3 (2020) is a thrilling and visually impressive remake that offers excellent action and a creepy atmosphere. However, its short length and abundance of cut content make it less significant than the Resident Evil 2 remake. If you are looking for a dynamic and adrenaline-pumping horror experience, then you will enjoy RE3 (2020). But if you were expecting a deeper and more prolonged game, you may be disappointed.

Recommendations:

•  Worth buying if you are a Resident Evil fan and love action.
•  Wait for a sale if you are concerned about the short length.
•  Don't expect a repeat of the Resident Evil 2 Remake triumph.

This is an underwhelming and unworthy remake of a great classic game. It's missing an enormous amount of content: entire sections are missing from the original (like the clock tower), there are no alternate paths through the game, and there's no Mercenaries mode. The original had a lot of replay value since you couldn't see everything in one playthrough, you unlocked items by playing Mercenaries with different characters, and you unlocked different character endings by doing speedruns.

In the remake, aside from an in-game "store" that opens after you finish the game the first time (you earn "money" based on certain achievements in the campaign to buy costumes and items), there's no real reason to replay the game because you've already seen it all. I wanted to replay RE2's remake because it was fun (if slightly disappointing compared to the original) and because I wanted to play as the other character and see their (mostly identical, unfortunately) path through the game. There's nothing like that here.

And perhaps the greatest sin of the remake: Nemesis is no longer intimidating. At most, he's annoying, and there's really nothing separating him from a standard RE boss character like Birkin or Mr. X. The story TELLS you he's relentless, but you don't FEEL it.
