My Take
Let’s get this out of the way: I loved how Jill Valentine carried this game. She’s an absolute badass, and her redesigned outfit (no tube top, finally!) made her feel like a believable survivor . The game felt like a Hollywood action flick—explosions, chases, and set pieces that kept me glued even on my potato PC (yes, 13fps struggles are real). The short runtime? Honestly, it worked for me. I binged it in two sittings, obsessed with finishing despite technical hiccups. But I get why die-hard fans might feel shortchanged.  

Pros to Play
Jill Valentine & Carlos Redesigns
Jill’s modern look is practical and badass, ditching the original’s questionable fashion choices. Carlos also gets a glow-up, blending charisma with combat grit. Their dynamic adds heart to the chaos .

Nemesis: Terrifying but Underutilized
   The first encounter with Nemesis is chef’s kiss—he sprints, leaps, and wields a flamethrower like a nightmare come to life. While his later appearances feel scripted, those initial moments are pure adrenaline .  

Cinematic Action & Set Pieces
   If you’re here for spectacle, this delivers. The subway escape, rooftop battles, and a Raiders of the Lost Ark-style boulder chase had me grinning. It’s more Michael Bay than classic survival horror, but I’m not mad .  

Dodge Mechanics & Combat Flow
   The dodge system (especially the slow-mo “perfect dodge”) feels slick. Pair that with the infinite knife for zombie kneecapping, and combat stays tense yet empowering .  

Replayability & Speedrunning
   Short? Yes. But that makes it perfect for replaying. I knocked out a 4-hour run easily, and the ranking system (based on time/saves) hooks you into optimizing routes .  
Cons to Consider
1. Too Short, Too Linear
   Clocking in at ~6 hours, the campaign lacks the depth of RE2 Remake. Locations like the Clock Tower and Park from the original are missing, replaced with linear corridors .  

2. Nemesis: Wasted Potential
   After the first act, he’s reduced to scripted boss fights. Fans expected Mr. X-level persistence; instead, he’s more of a jump-scare cameo .  

3. Survival Horror? More Like Action-Horror
   Limited puzzles, no window-boarding mechanics, and fewer backtracking opportunities. The focus on action might alienate fans craving slow-burn tension .  

4. Performance Issues
   My Sub-Geforce GT rig wheezed through this, but even optimized setups note inconsistent physics (zombies feel less “weighty” than RE2) and jarring dodge animations .  

5. Resistance Multiplayer: Forgettable
   The tacked-on 4v1 mode is unbalanced and lacks staying power. Stick to the campaign .

Final Verdict
I recommend it! If you treat it as a cinematic spin-off rather than a faithful remake, RE3 shines. Jill’s charisma, Nemesis’ early scares, and the rollercoaster pacing make it a blast—especially on sale. Just don’t expect RE2 Remake’s depth.  
For: Action lovers, Jill stans, speedrunners.  
Avoid if: You crave classic survival horror or hate short games.
Play it like I did: Embrace the chaos, ignore the purists, and enjoy Jill’s shotgun-wielding glory. And maybe upgrade your GPU first.

[h1]THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS![/h1]

This review will primarily compare the game to its contemporaries (the remakes of Resident Evil 2 and 4), as well as the games that inspired it (the original Resident Evil entries of 1 and its remake, 2, and 3).

I grew up playing the originals. This game feels like a pale imitation of the original whereas REmake 1, 2, and 4 all shine brightly. REmake 2 is imperfect, but I can forgive that it lacks the fully fledged zapping system of the original and kinda half-asses the zapping system because it captures the spirit of the game and brings Claire, Leon, Ada, and Sherry to life with wonderful results to show for it. Ada is much more likable and humanized despite her deception and betrayal of Leon. Leon feels both more competent and also more naive and gullible. Claire feels a lot more realistic. Sherry is better written and likable.

In that same vein, we must evaluate the cast of Resident Evil 3. Carlos is different from his original incarnation. He has a heart of gold and is a noble soldier who wants to help people. Original Carlos is an everyman caught in the middle, he's a little sleazy and flirty, but still likable. Mikhail is a stronger character than before and feels like a grizzled veteran and NCO (think of a Sergeant) whereas Nicholai feels like a very self-interested, slimy Lieutenant (and this contrast is unfortunately somewhat common in the military in real life, too). Tyrell is a loyal friend and a good guy. These are good.

Jill does not feel like the Jill Valentine we know. She's foul-mouthed (not necessarily bad on its own) to a point where it doesn't feel like the same Jill I grew up with. She's less likable, less charismatic, and feels like they less wrote her as willful and strong and more brash and reckless. But it doesn't work because that's not Jill.

Nemesis feels less like an omnipresent stalking predator (which he feels like in the original game) and only really stalks you for a brief segment in the beginning after which all his encounters become hyperscripted. In the original, his appearances are varied based on which locations you go to first and which choices you make in the sort of "quick time events" of that era (where you decide between two paths suddenly and out of the blue). This is, in particular, the biggest disappointment for me personally as a long-time fan.

Two major locations are cut out/replaced in the game from the original. In this game, the Clock Tower contains a single fight and the Dead Factory has been replaced by a REmake 2-esque lab. The problem with this course of action is that the Clock Tower and the Dead Factory are such strongly memorable locations that the things that replace them fail to live up to their memory.

The game is also incredibly short. There is a moment where Jill completes her objective of getting the subway up and running to escort civilians to safety and, upon attempting to return, the game diverts her to the sewers and then a construction site for a boss fight before taking her past the RPD and to Robert Kendo's gun shop. As well, Carlos visits the RPD. These efforts feel like very poor attempts to pad out the length of an already extremely short game while reusing assets from the previous game. This results in the game feeling very rushed, the pacing feeling very poor, and the game overall falling very short of the original which it is supposed to modernize and update for a newer generation of players and a newer style of gameplay.

[h1]The TL;DR[/h1]

[h2]Pros:[/h2]
- Easy to 100% for achievements
- Decently replayable if you are looking for a game to learn speedrunning for; runs are quick and simple
- Most characters feel very real and very unique and very good for the story

[h2]Cons:[/h2]
- Lacks true replayability after maybe 5 or 6 runs when you 100% the game
- Fails to live up to the original game in a myriad of ways
- Bastardizes my childhood (this is just me griping, admittedly)
- Feels undercooked and rushed

[h1]The Verdict[/h1]

It is my opinion that, if you get this game for 10 to 15 dollars, it's worth the money, especially if you like Resident Evil [i]and[/i] you like achievement hunting/collecting to get perfect games for your profile. But if you really, really, truly like Resident Evil and are a newer fan to the franchise, my suggestion to you is that you look up a guide on emulating the older games. In particular, you are best served with:

- Playing Resident Evil HD (on Steam)
- Playing Resident Evil 2's remake (and playing Resident Evil 2 on GameCube via the Dolphin emulator)
- Playing Resident Evil 3 (GameCube port via Dolphin emulator)
- Playing Resident Evil Code Veronica X (GameCube port via Dolphin emulator)
- Playing Resident Evil 4's remake and the original version (an HD port is on Steam)
- Playing Resident Evil 5 (on Steam)
- Playing Resident Evil 6 (on Steam)

In Resident Evil 3 you play as Jill Valentine, one of the S.T.A.R.S. members who survived the Spencer mansion incident and occasionally as Carlos Oliveira, a U.B.C.S. member. These 2 are some of the few survivors left in town after the Umbrella corporation unleashed the virus inside Racoon City and their secret weapon: Nemesis. The timeline is the same as the one from RE2, so expect to see some familiar locations.

I remember when I was a child and I played RE3:Nemesis (the original) for the first time, I was terrified to go outside safe zones, the small little environmental jumpscares were too much for that time. I had nightmares for days, so please don't let your kids play this type of games. Anyway... I expected to have a similar atmosphere with this remake and it didn't disappoint me. While the game is short (first run ~6 hours) and they cut some of the old content (probably in favor of that Resistance live service slop), what we had here is a really fun game that delivers exactly the essence of a Resident Evil game. It's a survival horror with scarce resources, interesting puzzles and solid combat where you need to make your way out of the city before it's too late while fighting zombies and a terrifying pursuer that has only one task: to kill Jill. The visuals are amazing, RE engine is incredible when used for this type of games, smaller scale projects, it looks close to Unreal Engine fidelity, but it's insanely well optimized. I also appreciate the addition of the Points Shop, it makes it a lot easier and enjoyable to unlock the "cheats", giving this title a much welcome replayability value.

Now I have some personal nitpicks with this game excluding the small duration. I really hate how the game starts with only 2 rows(8 spaces) of inventory and it's shared with your key items while not having a craft list. I had the same issue in RE2 and I can't understand why did the developers add an unnecessary level of frustration when the other games in the series solved this issue. Another one is the lack of costumes, I don't even ask for them to be unlockable or free, but it would have been nice to get some DLCs. However, this is not a big deal for PC players as the community has some really good mods (and kinky for those interested). A different problem I had was with the last boss, it either feels very underwhelming on lower difficulties or it becomes a menace on Inferno, I didn't find a middle ground. Speaking of difficulties, I'm not a huge fan of having to unlock 2 more, but I really love what they did with Nightmare+, there are more strategic placed enemies that can alter how you play the game, as well as they become more aggressive and Nemesis learns to dodge similar to Wesker fast moves.

Overall, a good Resident Evil game, but a bad Remake. Since it's this short I recommend buying only during a sale, it's discounted very often at -75%.

[h1] [b] [i] Resident Evil 2 Remake's "C Scenario"  [/i] [/b] [/h1]

[h1] [b] [i] ★★★★★★★☆☆☆ [/i] [/b] [/h1]

The remake of a follow-up to one of the greatest survival horror games of all time faced as many hurdles and obstacles as it had opportunities. Resident Evil 3: Nemesis was the 1999 sequel in which the developers decided to go with more action-focused approach than in the second entry, sacrificing some horror elements while pumping up the combat gameplay. That didn't exactly jive with many of the fans of the previous game, but the game was overall received quite well, despite the criticisms of its linearity and dampening of atmosphere. Resident Evil 3 Remake presented an opportunity to remedy many of the issues whiles still preserving the spirit of the original. Sadly, Capcom did not take that road, instead opting to make what would be better described as the either an expanded DLC or a more full-fledged tertiary scenario to the 2019 Resident Evil 2 Remake.

[h1] [i] “It's alright, you go on ahead. I'm not gonna die on you, and leave you in a cold, cruel, Carlos-less world.” [/i] [/h1]

The fact that Resident Evil 3 Remake does not reach the qualities of the fantastic RE2R is evident from any cluster of discussions or reviews you can find online. I'd say most of the complaints are warranted - the game is fairly short, without a proper secondary "B scenario" where you play as Carlos in parallel to Jill's parts where he is absent which makes it a "one-and-done" type of deal without any real degree of replayability. On top of that, it lacks the expansionary nature of RE2R, which did cut out some parts of the original game, but greatly expanded others. RE3R does not do that, instead offering a greatly distilled version of the 1999 classic, which predictably rubbed many fans the wrong way. See, RE3R had the misfortune of falling right in-between two exceptional Resident Evil Remake titles: RE2, which is praised to this day, and more recent Resident Evil 4 Remake, which repeated 2's accomplishments. This made it a stand out, in a bad way. Fans of the second game's remake reasonably expected RE3R to surpass it given the amount of money it made and the success it saw, but instead, somewhat poetically, RE3R is truly an embodiment of both the best and the worst aspects of its 1999 namesake. The original game struggled with lack of proper development time and budget, which made it inferior to RE2's greatness. Funnily enough, this is exactly what happened to RE3 Remake - lack of resources and time crunch saw many interesting things being cut without too many additions to compensate for it. Resident Evil truly is a self-fulfilling prophecy. 

Now here is where I diverge from many of the detractors - despite RE3R failing to either exceed its predecessor or properly expand on the original, it is still very much an amazing addition to the ever-growing monster that is Resident Evil. All of the things that made RE2R great are present, plus some additions to compliment the more action-heavy nature of Resident Evil 3's personality. You can now dodge, which is difficult to get a grasp of but when you do, it feels amazing; the weapon arsenal gets expanded with improved grenade launcher and amazing full-auto rifle along with all of the classics such as Lightning Hawk and Shotgun making a return with slightly more impact. The gameplay is general is immensely satisfying, the game's shorter length at least helps each part of the game to flow from one another swiftly and smoothly enough to be enjoyable. 

Story-wise, RE3R does a decent job recapping the story of the original game while also better connecting it to RE2R, which is happening at the exact same time. It doesn't reach the soaring highs of its predecessor, but stands fairly well on its own in telling Jill and Carlos' stories. I have no real complaints in this department - the custscenes are, once again, great, the voice-cast do a great job and the whole cheesy-but-satisfying nature of the typical Resident Evil narrative has been preserved. I don't even mind the changes done to Nemesis, who now acts in a more cinematic manner, rather than sporadically and spontaneously showing up from time to time. I think they got his threat through fairly well, even if he could have used more screen time.

In the end, you have to go into Resident Evil 3 Remake with proper expectations - if you see it as a large-scale DLC to the second game as opposed to a full-fledged title rivaling its predecessor (which I know it should have been), you will be more content and happy with the end-result, especially if you get it with a healthy discount. Think of it as a separate DLC to Resident Evil 2 Remake and you will have plenty of fun and satisfaction from it before moving on to much better remake of the legendary 4th title.

Resident Evil 3 Remake plunges you back into the zombie-infested Raccoon City, where Jill Valentine is having the worst. week. ever. It's a thrilling, action-packed, and relentlessly stressful experience, kind of like being stuck in a really intense escape room designed by someone with a serious grudge against humanity.

The main attraction, besides the hordes of undead, is Nemesis. This guy is like the Terminator, if the Terminator was a mutated science experiment with a penchant for shouting ""STARS"" and a complete disregard for property damage. He's the ultimate stalker, turning every encounter into a high-stakes game of cat-and-mouse, where the cat is a seven-foot-tall bio-weapon with a rocket launcher.

You'll spend most of your time running, gunning, and dodging through the chaotic city streets, desperately trying to survive while solving puzzles that range from ""slightly inconvenient"" to ""did a maniac design this?"" Seriously, who needs a fancy keycard when you can just shove a battery into a fuse box?

And the zombies! Oh, the zombies. Forget slow and shambling; these guys are athletic, persistent, and surprisingly agile. They're like the undead equivalent of Olympic sprinters, constantly trying to crash your party and eat your brains.

However, amidst all the thrills and spills, Resident Evil 3 Remake does have its downsides. Just when you're fully immersed in the Raccoon City madness, the game wraps up, leaving you wanting more. It's like ordering a delicious pizza and only getting to eat half of it.

Another point of contention is the game's deviation from the original Resident Evil 3. Some fans were disappointed by the omission or alteration of certain iconic locations and sequences, feeling that the remake didn't fully capture the spirit of the original. It's a bit like remaking your favorite movie but cutting out your favorite scene. Personally, I played the original game on PS1 in the last century, but don't remember much of it. I'm also pretty sure that I never finished it.

Finally, while Nemesis is undeniably a formidable foe, his AI can occasionally be a bit predictable. Once you figure out his patterns, he transforms from a terrifying stalker into a slightly less terrifying, but still very persistent, annoyance.

Resident Evil 3 Remake is a pretty good game in and of itself. Just like the RE2 Remake, RE3 has that same creepy and gore covered Resident Evil environment. If you enjoy RE, especially RE2 Remake, you'll almost certainly like this one as there are a lot of similarities. The movement and aiming feels good, with an added dodge/charge mechanic based on which character you're playing, and the balance of available health + ammo on standard feels as good as in RE2 Remake. There is a noticeable drop in puzzles, with most being extremely simple, and more of a focus on combat overall.

One big difference, and imo improvement, is the addition of an in-game store. You have challenges (kill X amount of zombies) that award you points so that you can buy items. Some items are: a better knife, infinite ammo weapons, additional inventory in the beginning of the game, and a costume. With the store you get an easier time picking which items you go after first, compared to RE2 Remake where an unlock you may want could be locked behind a particularly brutal achievement. In RE3 you just save up your points, maybe do a little zombie farming, and you'll be able to purchase the exact unlock you want first.

Another difference is the pacing. In the RE3 story you're hunted by a powerful character throughout the game and he shows up frequently. This, in combination with more basic level design, makes the gaps between boss battles seem very short. You'll regularly find yourself facing the boss again and thinking 'Already?' multiple times. This definitely lends itself to the more combat focused attitude compared to RE2 Remake.

One common complaint is that it's much shorter than RE2 Remake, and I'd have to agree. While the levels look great, they are much less dense than the previous remake's. There's noticeably less looping in levels, meaning you're running down hallways most of the time. I remember getting to the second level and being surprised that I'd completed it within 15 minutes, including exploring. This also goes back to the fewer puzzles aspect, it's mostly just enemies you need to shoot/dodge. So once you get good at that you can brute force your way through levels.

Part of what made RE2 Remake so long was that you had 2 different characters with two stories each. In RE3 Remake you follow one story and occasionally switch between two characters. The combination of the shortness and challenge points does make replaying the game a bit more enticing than RE2 Remake. Once you get an infinite ammo weapon and some damage boosts you'll most likely feel empowered enough to try harder modes. I completed S rank in Inferno, something I'll never even think of trying in RE2 Remake.

Lastly, just like RE2 Remake, the game has RNG throughout. It's not as much as the previous game, but eventually you start to notice it. Late game enemies seem to get the chance to critical hit, taking out 75% or more of your health without warning. This makes a particular late game level frustrating in combination with the simple level design, meaning you have to face these 1-shot-RNG enemies head on. Additionally, bosses will sometimes have stunlock combos that you MUST dodge the first hit on or else you'll be forced to watch your character experience what it's like to be Chris Brown's wife. This can get frustrating when going for certain achievements as it basically turns RE3 into 'Never get hit ever' the game, despite having a health bar.

Overall it's still a very enjoyable game, one of the few that I decided to 100%. People have expressed disappointment at certain levels from the original version being removed, but as a RE noobie I didn't find anything horrifically wrong with the game. It's solid with a few flaws here and there. The puzzles from the first two games are slowly fading away and being replaced with more combat focused game play, but the horror elements are still present. Still a Resident Evil game at the end of the day.

Having not played the original game, I don't know how much this one diverges from the original in how the game/story goes. (Note: played on normal difficulty exclusively)
My first note is that where Resident Evil 2 is almost like a single large metroidvania-style world where you spend a lot of time slowly uncovering parts of a large connected area, this game instead takes you on a journey through multiple smaller areas (though there's still a bit of that metroidvania feel to the design, which I enjoy).
The graphics are great, barring some minor issue that I think stems from a combination of raytracing and the Anti-Aliasing implementation in the game.
Gameplay wise, I really like this take on the RE-series - snappy controls, (I'm using keyboard+mouse), interesting use of the third-person camera (although it sometimes goes a bit lower that it needs to), and there's a fairly decent variety of enemies considering the game's length.
That being said, the game can be fairly short, in 16 hours I've now completed the game three times and done some (but not a lot) of achievement hunting. I'm probably not going for 100% here, but I picked all low-hanging fruit and am fairly satisfied with what I've gotten out of the game.

This, in my opinion, is how remakes can really make an old game/story shine - it's not bloated with extras, it's not needlessly extravagant. Instead, they've cut out unnecessary bits, made the controls way better, and made small changes to the story (as I understand it) in order to make it flow better.

As far as my experiences with the series goes, this is probably the leanest. But even though it's short, what's there is just really, really good.

Taking into account the ending for RE2 and RE3 it just doesn't make sense for Jill's story to be happening before Leon and Claire's. RE3R is worth to buy on sale, but overall a disappointing downgrade after RE2R with some incredibly idiotic design choices.

Nemesis vs. Mister X:
Mister X is just a better gameplay addition in every possible way. Most Nemesis encounters are scripted and in those that are not, he is designed to be an annoyance rather than a meaningful gameplay addition. He does not patrol the area in a logical way, he teleports and spawns at random. He cant be outrun or avoided by good routing, you are forced to either dodge all of his attacks until you reach the next safe zone or stun him on every appearance, which completely contradicts the principle of ammo being limited. When you reach the next safe zone, he will camp on it instead of moving on and giving you room to continue.
Nemesis is lazily made and his design is his only redeeming quality, though you dont get to see much of it, since he pretty much transforms into his next stage after running up and down a linear path twice. 

Zombies:
The zombies, while using the same models as in RE2R, are a plain downgrade. They move and fall through standardized animations without ragdoll-physics that take their environment into account. The body gore has been toned down for no apparent reason, taking away the option to shoot off limbs to reduce their mobility. Despite the reduction of detail, zombies are still portrayed with downgraded graphics already visible past a few meters, which matters a lot more in the open streets of Raccoon City than the confined spaces of the RPD in RE2R.

Dodge:
To deal with threats in tight spaces, RE3R introduces a dodge mechanic, which hurts the game more than providing a benefit. Regular zombies simply pose no threat anymore. Correct spacing was a major necessity for success in RE2R, while the dodge renders it near irrelevant. You can easily run past most zombies and in case you have to take them out, mistakes can mostly be negated by dodging. On the other side, the dodge is too unreliable to consistently avoid Nemesis' attacks, rendering the second option, stunning him, more viable.

Story:
The reduction to one story without crossovers and alternative scenarios makes RE3R much more sensible than RE2R, where a lot of potential was wasted by ignoring consistency throughout at least both perspectives of the main scenarios. Both stories overall are well structured and a few inconsistencies in between both games can be disregarded. The few overlaps, especially surrounding the RPD, actually ended up being the best parts of RE3R. The lack of other scenarios and therefore replayability value makes the game very short though, which is jarring, considering, that the Original game supposedly had a lot more areas that could have been used in the remake as well.

Level design:
The level design is unfortunately heavily downgraded as well. While the RPD of RE2R in particular provided interconnectivity rivaling Dark Souls 1, RE2R is almost completely linear. There are very few puzzles to solve with none of them requiring back tracking and rewarding players for paying attention. The two major "puzzles", the Subway Power Station and the Lab entrance, boil down to searching for some levers. I dont think there was a single moment, where I felt as ecstatic over finding an item for a specific purpose as I felt when figuring out, how the library, clocktower and prison cell in the RPD were connected for the first time in RE2R.

Boss fights:
The boss fights dont only seem more creative than in RE2R, but also profit a lot from the dodge mechanic. While I dislike the choice of a larger health pool, I appreciate the more creative ways of how the different stages of Nemesis are ultimately beaten.

Ranking/speedruns:
The ranking system, which gave you something meaningful to chase in RE2R and rewarded you for skill, memory and awareness, is completely obsolete in RE3R, because the developers decided to allow "cheat"-items like the infinite rocket launcher and not make them reduce the ratings. How you obtain these cheat-items is not designed well either. You can buy them from points you earn through the Records-Tab. The most effective way to get all the S-Tier badges (S+ doesnt exist anymore) is to farm challenges by reloading a specific safe until you can buy the rocketlauncher and eliminate skill from the equation. The decision to make the difficulty dependent on the order in which you buy bonus items instead of the players' actual abilities is ridiculous, especially when there is a perfectly fine system already established in RE2R. Getting platinum - needlessly extended through additional "difficulty"-levels - is more of a grind than the challenge it was before. This might be the biggest reason for why the more active community prefers RE2R a lot over the now much more casual-friendly RE3R.

Graphics, weapons and other details:
While the graphical quality stayed more or less the same in comparison to its predecessor, the details of animations like the already described zombies seem to be reduced as well. Where you could see the shotgun shell fly out of your gun in RE2R, you can only hear the impact on the ground in RE3R. You reload the entire grenadelauncher, when you only have two grenades to put in. Running animations also seem less natural. There are barely any additional costumes for the protagonists and no bonus modes, which were definitely not the most enjoyable part of RE2R, but a welcome addition for variety.

Resident Evil 3 is one of the greatest survival horror games of all time, it balances action and horror brilliantly, features a badass returning protagonist from another one of the best survival horror games, and introduces the grandfather of the stalker enemy.

Of course, the review above was for the original Resident Evil 3, the remake is a very different game.

Resident Evil 3 Remake falls short of its predecessor in the following categories:
Costumes; The original Resident Evil 3 had eight alternate costumes, while the Remake has... 2. In addition to the lower amount of costumes the costumes themselves aren't terrible, but they definitely aren't as exciting as the originals Dino Crisis outfit, as the remake features the worst adaptation of the of RE3 outfit, though it does feature (in my opinion) one of the better S.T.A.R.S outfits being the first time said outfits been featured in a modern title.
Locations; The game omits several locations from the original such as City Hall, The Press Office, The Raccoon City Park, The Graveyard, The Dead Factory, and most jarringly, the Clocktower. These commissions leave the remake world version of Raccoon City empty and unsatisfactory.
Enemies; Just like the Resident Evil 2 Remake, the Resident Evil 3 Remake forgets the giant spiders, while also getting rid of the gravedigger boss fight, leaving Nemesis as the only boss in the game.
Nemesis; The biggest flaw in my opinion is that Nemesis is no longer a stalker enemy, he is scripted and only had one area of the game where he was sort of a stalker, but I don't find this to be too harrowing considering the RE@ remake turned Mr. X, a scripted enemy, into a stalker enemy, so between the games Mr. x and Nemesis changed dynamics, which certainly isn't the worst that can happen.

I just listed a bunch of things I think the Resident Evil 3 Remake doesn't do the best, so what about the things it does excel at?
Characters; Various characters are portrayed so much better in the remake, Jill hasn't worsened or improved in my opinion, she is still a badass who suffers only slightly from not having a definitive Spencer Mansion background in the remake universe yet. Carlos went from being an unremarkable sideshow to a Keanu Reeves-style action star with relatable dialogue as he gets as frustrated with puzzles as the player does, in addition to having pretty neat hair. Nikoli Is a delightful villain who gets plenty of scenes of being a general nuisance and outright unhinged individual with little regard for others, and while his end is a little lackluster, he was entertaining at the very least. Mikhail doesn't have much screen time, but he makes the most of it by his determination to rescue those around him, and in his final moments he stands up valiantly to Nemesis. Tyrell is another character that has a smaller presence, but does his best in his moments to do right and also sacrifices himself to give Jill time to escape her tyrant stalker.
Gameplay; The game has very similar gameplay to the RE2 remake, but with the addition of dodging, which can be finicky, but if pulled off right can be very beneficial to gameplay, the perfect dodge also slows down time and auto aims at enemies weak points for an extra edge in combat.
Extra items; Extra items in RE games are always delightful, but the ones introduced in RE3 Remake are some of my favorites, the Hot Dogger and Raiden look like they're ripped straight out of a sci-fi game and the combat manual, and medallions make the game easier by increasing perfect dodge windows and applying bonuses to combat, defense, and healing.
Enemies; I know I had a section for enemies in the negatives, but while the game did remove some, it also added some, such as replacing the Brain Suckers with Drain Deimos, that are part of the scariest section in the game, the Ne-α parasite zombie, which has a large promiscuously designed parasite attached to its head that can attack from a distance and up close, and the Hunter Gamma, which is a fusion of the Gravedigger and Hunter Beta. 

Ultimately the game has its flaws, yes, but it isn't a terrible game, on the contrary, I find it to be as enjoyable as the RE2 remake, If anyone finds themselves debating on wether or not to get the game, my advice is if you like resident evil, if you like horror, if you like zombies, then you'll like Reident Evil 3 Remake.

Resident Evil 3 Remake was an intense, thrilling experience that introduced me to the world of Raccoon City in a way that kept me on the edge of my seat. The game is visually stunning, action-packed, and immersive, but I did notice that certain elements from the original game were missing, which might disappoint long-time fans, though it didn’t detract too much from my enjoyment.

From the very first moment, the game draws you into the chaos of Raccoon City. The visuals are incredible every corner of the city feels alive, from the destroyed streets to the eerie, tense atmosphere in abandoned buildings. 

The lighting, sound design, and realistic textures made the world feel truly alive and horrifying. The terrifying presence of the Nemesis, the main antagonist, is also a highlight, adding a constant sense of danger. The idea that you never know when Nemesis will appear makes every moment tense, and his relentless pursuit is a thrilling experience.

For someone who hasn’t played the original Resident Evil 3, I was impressed by how the game blends action and survival horror. The combat is more fast-paced and action-oriented compared to Resident Evil 2 Remake, which I really enjoyed. The addition of dodging and the more fluid combat system made encounters with the enemies feel more dynamic.

However, I did find myself feeling a bit lost when it came to the narrative and certain plot elements. I learned later that a good portion of the original content, including iconic areas and storylines, were omitted from this remake. As someone who is new to the franchise, I didn’t realise what was missing, but I can see why longtime fans might be disappointed by these cuts. The game is shorter than I expected, and the lack of certain environments, like the hospital and much of the city exploration, left me feeling like there was more that could have been explored.

The characters in the game are well-developed, and Jill is an incredibly strong and likeable protagonist. The game does a great job of building emotional stakes, and I was genuinely attached to her quest to escape Raccoon City.

The pacing of the game is fast, which is great if you're looking for a quick, adrenaline-fueled horror experience. But at times, I did feel like the game could have used a bit more exploration or puzzle-solving to break up the action.

Overall, Resident Evil 3 Remake was a fantastic introduction to the Resident Evil series for me, even if it didn’t quite deliver everything that the original game did. The fast-paced action, the terror of Nemesis, and the intense atmosphere kept me hooked throughout, even though I recognise there were some content omissions that may affect long-time fans. As a newcomer, though, I found the game to be thrilling.

Resident Evil 2 Remake had stunning visuals, amazing gameplay and was overall a great experience.

Too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bad Capcom decided that making this remake absolutely terrible.

This game, this overpriced, underdeveloped, boring piece of media, took everything that made
Resident Evil 3: Nemesis great and threw it out the window.

In "a few" sentences:

This game is WAY shorter than the original. Instead of the 7-8 hours it takes to beat the original, the R3make can be beaten in 4-5 on someone's first playthrough. Even when it comes to remakes, it's really short. R2make would take the average person 6-8 hours.

By extension, a lot of areas that were present in the original have been shrunk severely, if not removed entirely, making the game feel linear and too straightforward. By comparison, in the R2make, the RPD, Sewers, and most of NEST were all fairly open, with backtracking being (almost) always possible. it didn't feel like a set path that the player can't deviate from, unlike here.

The zombies here are downgrades from the R2make. You rarely see limbs get cut, and they don't get scars from being cut.

The guns feel and sound weak.

Jill is very unlikable here. She comes off as being constantly angry and annoyed. It feels as if she can't go 5 minutes without saying "♥♥♥♥" or "♥♥♥♥". Is it realistic? yeah. Is it in-character for Jill? absolutely not.

The multiple choice mechanic that was available in the original, where you could go different ways, or even get different endings, has been cut, making the game have only one ending.

Nemesis is a joke. He shows up wearing a trash bag on his head in the first 5 minutes, unlike the original, where he was foreshadowed by Brad sounding defeated, having already accepted his fate, with that hopelessness being reinforced by him effortlessly killing Brad outside the RPD, but here, Brad dies to a (completely avoidable) zombie bite, meaning that Nemesis, whose sole purpose is to kill STARS members, does not kill a single STARS member. Nemesis also doesn't follow you everywhere, meaning that you can just camp out in a save room, but you don't even have to do that, since you can down him with just a grenade in Hardcore difficulty. The loot that he drops, is completely terrible, apart for a few (very basic) upgrades for your glock. In the original, you actually got rewarded for fighting him, because of how difficult it was.

Brad, as I said before, dies a very preventable death, but what makes it worse is the fact that it feels as if he's written by an A.I. He calls Jill sounding panicked, but 2 minutes later, he is the most relaxed guy in town. He's completely ok with the fact that there is a basically unkillable monster after him. He does not care that the entire city is filled with zombies. He just casually strolls through as if nothing of note is happening. And when he gets bit, he decides to play hero, acting as if he's saving JIll, while all he did was say the words "back door", pushed her, and said "don't die".

There is a grand total of one (1) unlockable costume in the game. Unlike R2make, where both Leon and Claire had:
1) The original costumes
2) Various stages of their costumes
3) Alternate costumes that resembled the ones from the original
4) Downloadable DLC that made them look like PS1 characters
All completely free.
If you want the classic costumes for Jill and Carlos (Carlos only gets a haircut btw) you have to pay 2,99 to get is as DLC. I'm not saying R2make didn't have costumes as paid DLC, but at least you had some variety for free.

Speaking of DLC, R2make, a game that already had 2 playthroughs (technically 4), and the 4th survivor, as well as the tofu variations, also had the Lost Survivors DLC which had 4 small 10-15 minute campaigns, all for free, by the way.
Meanwhile, R3make, has absolutely nothing. Not even the Mercenaries game mode, that was in the original.

This game is horribly overpriced. As of writing this, almost 5 years after being released, it is 40 bucks, the same price as R2make, and the only reason they have to "justify" it being so expensive, is the fact that their ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Dead By Daylight ripoff is bundled in, which, by the way, barely gets any players.

(Major spoilers for the original and remake until the section where I mention the positives)
Also, you know how in the original, you're mid-way through the game, you call the helicopter, and for a few seconds, you think the game is done, but then Nemesis blows up the helicopter and you have to fight him?
Well, not only does this not contain a Nemesis fight, but it also happens in the first 10 minutes of the game, completely ruining the fake-out, which was one of the most memorable parts of the original.

Nikolai being the antagonist is also not subtle anymore. In the original, you could see him carrying around a laptop and being a bit suspicious in general, but you weren't really sure what he was doing.
Here, the first thing he does, is kill one of his men, and then follows it up by being extremely aggressive to Jill. No buildup, no nothing. And then the game acts as if him betraying you later was unexpected.

Because no game is complete without one, apparently, there is a tower defense segment that is a few minutes too long for its own good.

The Nemesis Fights are not good, with the exception of the first one being passable as "okay". But because I guess Capcom LOVED the 2nd one, they made the 3rd one be exactly the same but this time zombies start spawning and the FOV is zoomed in all the way.

-POSITIVES-
All the voice actors do a very good job and are well-cast.

Carlos is a WAY better character than he was in the original.

The music is fantastic.

The dodging mechanic has been improved and is way better than the one in the original.

Jill says in-game that all this was caused by greed.

The visuals are really good, but that is to be expected of a remake.

Overall I give this game 3 bad remakes out of 10.

Pros:
+ Beautiful graphics
+ Functional environment design
+ Good music
+ Good gameplay. Shooting is satisfying
+ Good inventory management
+ Different guns to choose from
+ The first chapter doesn't overstay its welcome. Thing are kicked in motion almost right away.
+ Playing as both Jill and Carlos is a nice way to tell the story from two perspectives.
+ Things between Jill and Carlos never turn into a cheesy love story
+ Good voice acting
+ Some nice intertextuality with RE2 - Jill meets the gunshop owner before Leon/Claire, and Carlos visits RPD station (although it should've been just a cutscene).

Mixed:
+- Main plot is okay'ish.
+- Environments are different from each other. There's no feeling of repetition. However, there could've been at least one more major location. The environments are also a bit too small (although the sewers area is just perfectly short).
+- Dodge ability exist. Good. However, it's pretty clumsy to use.
+- RE3 main enemy has basically the same design as the main enemy in RE2 - you fight both on several occasions, and both keep evolving into a more horrid monster throughout the story. Although this works better in RE3 (better evolution), there could've been more difference to RE2.

Cons:
- Although the game is in many ways just building on RE2 remake foundation and I wish to give it some credit for succeeding at delivering good gameplay, RE3 has literally the same location of RPD station as in RE2. Yes, there's one thing Carlos does which's direct consequence can be seen in RE2 (blown-up locker room wall), but including RPD station as a gameplay segment is just a no-go. So many things are straight-out borrowed from the previous title. RE3 needs more stuff to make it a more separate, distinguishable experience from RE2.
- The game is way too short, just like RE2 (even if RE2 is longer). I completed this game in under 6 hours. In a way RE3 felt like a large DLC instead of a full-length standalone game.
- There should've been more environments. Exploring streets and a hospital are different from RE2 settings, but RE3 really leaves you wishing for more.
- Brad is bitten like an idiot without self-defense instincts
- The final area is too short
- The final boss is way too easy
- There's no real subplots going on. Everything that happens is seemingly part of the main plot. The story lacks depth.
- While there's some variety in enemies, 4 different enemy types isn't enough.
- When finding out the truth about the outbreak's origin, Carlos didn't tear off the Umbrella badge in his shirt.
- In the beginning, Jill seems to survive for the sole reason that she apparently can barge into someone else's apartment, which's door is open for some reason.
- Nemesis throws Jill around too much, just like most monsters always do in fiction. It takes away realism, considering that the Nemesis could've just crushed Jill's skull on several occasions, but instead chose to gently lift her up and throw against a wall...lol.
- Jill can hear it when a helicopter pilot shouts over the copter's roaring engines and rotors from further away
- It would add realism if an injured character kept holding their wounded body part, but for some reason it always seems to be stomach, even though all the zombies bite in the neck.
- Jill screaming at Nemesis in final boss is a bit cringe. Too many words, too much threatening before action.

7/10 A decent game. Yet I cant give over 7 because of surface-level story, lack of more environments, certain design choices that tear down realism, and because RE3 is too much alike to RE2. This game should've had more to make it feel separate.

5 pros and 5 cons. Thumbs up or down is just my personal like or dislike of the game.
Pro
[list]
    [*] Fast and Fluid gameplay even more so then Resident Evil 2, leaning more into action less so the Resident evil 4.
    [*] Dodge system adds skill based gameplay that feels better then simple spacing and running from older titles.
    [*] Very replayable with lots of unlocks for additional challenges or content.
    [*] Nemesis feels threatening and boss fights with him do not disappoint.
    [*] Visually stunning along with amazing voice work.
[/list]
Con
[list]
    [*] Does not have several systems from the original RE3 choice system, ammo crafting system, and merc mode
    [*] Short even by RE standards even new players will find this done in 10 hours or less blind playthrough, veterans can 
         expect clear times of 6 hours or less if not sooner .
    [*] Several enemies and sections are not present in this version of RE3 killing some much needed variety and game 
         length.
    [*] Once you know the trick to nemesis he is no longer threatening, this is amplified by his lack of presence compared to 
         the original or even Mr. X from RE2

Resident Evil 3 Remake is a reimagening of the original RE3, released back in 1999. Yet again, Capcom does an admirable job of bringing another Resident Evil game to modern day standards. The game focuses on high-octane combat, while puzzles and exploration have a more diminished role than the original. The visuals are stunning; the environments of Racoon City feel alive, player models are highly detailed, and the game makes great use of lighting and shadows. The gameplay is smooth and over-the-shoulder camera angles have replaced the fixed views from the classic, adding a more immersive feel. The portrayal of Jill Valentine in particular is well done, keeping in line her tough and capable attributes, while updating her visually and narratively. There are caveats however. The game feels quite condensed, with ommissions to several parts of the story and locations from the original. The story is faster paced but also a lot shorter. Our main antagonist, Nemesis, was a constant threat in RE3, consistently following the player. In Remake however, most of his encounters seem scripted and overall less present. RE3 Remake may not have hit quite the same way as Capcom's previous remake (RE2), but despite certain issues, this is a solid entry and should not be missed by Resident Evil fans.

Before you consider buying this one, I highly recommend you play Resident Evil 2 Remake. That is the better game of the two, and if you don't like that game, there is a very high chance you won't like this one.

A lot of what made Resident Evil 2 Remake great is in here. There's great combat and gameplay, but the game feels much more combat-focused than the previous game. It's fun fighting the regular enemies and getting from Point A to Point B all the while worrying about being attacked by enemies unknown. However, a huge problem with this game, is that it is not nearly as scary as Resident Evil 2 is.

So, it terms of atmosphere and layout, in Resident Evil 2, you are basically confined to 3 main areas. You are going to explore all these areas have to offer all the while running for your life from sewer monsters, plant monsters and the scariest of them all, Mr. X. 

In Resident Evil 3, the closest enemy to Mr. X would be Nemesis. Nemesis is much more aggressive than Mr. X and much more intelligent. He has a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Rocket Launcher and sneak up on you before you even know it.

The problem with Mr X, is he can be beaten.

My first playthrough was on Hardcore mode, and I was shocked when the guy went down using a single grenade. In the scripted boss fights you can't run from, he is tougher to take down, but there are times where Nemesis is literally holding Jill, (the main character), and instead of killing her, throws her away so she can run from him and his flamethrower.

Matter of fact, nearly all of the boss fights in this game are just bad. Nemesis just continues to get bigger and bigger, but the bigger he gets, the less threatening he feels to fight. There's a difference between fighting someone that is like 3 meters tall and someone that is 15 meters tall. When you are fighting a dude 3 meters tall, he feels like a big bulky enemy that I need to run from at all times. When a boss becomes 15 meters tall, I am no longer running from that boss. If I'm stuck in a place where I have to fight this guy, it tells me with enough bullets I can take him down, and I believe the game suffers because of it.

Where Resident Evil 2 felt like there are three big areas to explore, Resident Evil 3 feels much more linear. While this normally wouldn't be a bad thing, the game is much too short for me to fully appreciate it like I did RE2.

It took me 15 hours to 100% this game. That was three playthroughs in total, which included an achievement which involves beating the game in UNDER TWO HOURS!!

Now, all this being said, it's not a bad game. It's a fun game to play like Resident Evil 2 Remake, but it's not as scary nor is it as long to play. That being said, I would only recommend this game if you are a fan of Resident Evil 2 Remake.

[b]Resident Evil 3 Remake[/b] was a [b]huge letdown[/b] for me for multiple reasons.
It's not entirely bad, there are some good parts in it, but they're not enough to outshine all the dirt beneath it.

The OG RE3 was extremely short to begin with, because originally it was supposedly to be expansion for RE2. so Capcom had the perfect opportunity to expand the game with this remake. But for some odd reason they did the exact opposite and removed bit portions of the OG game and/or reworked 

[h1]The good:[/h1]
+ RE engine just looks awesome. I sincerely hope that Capcom sticks with this engine and doesn't go to that un-optimized slob of UE5 that most companies seem to do nowadays.
+ Moment to moment gameplay is decent fun.
[spoiler]+ Jill is super gorgeous. She no longer looks like a person with deep depression like she did in older RE games.[/spoiler]

[h1]The bad:[/h1]
- It's extremely short. Big portions of the game were either shortened, reworked or completely cut off.
- Hardcore difficulty is way too easy. Ammunition and healing items are supposedly to be scarce resources on Hardcore mode, but the game showers you with those. You never-ever have to ration any of them. (I haven't tried nightmare mode though)
- Dodge mechanic is way too overpowered, because once you get a hang of it you'll never get hit by anything.
- There are basically zero puzzles. The OG game didn't have that many puzzles either, but in this game has even less.
- 2 of the Nemesis Stage 2 boss fights are identical.
- You're done after your 1st playthrough. There are no 2nd runs, different routes with another character or anything like that what RE1R and RE2R had. It took me ~6h30min to clear the game and that's it. No other modes. The game is finished after ~6 hours...

[h1]The Nemesis:[/h1]
If there's one thing that I dislike the most in this Remake, it definitely has to be how Capcom ruined the [b]Nemesis[/b].
He's nothing but a joke from what it used to be in the OG RE3, and here's why:
[list]
[*] Nemesis no longer hunts you like he did in the OG game, meaning that he'll no longer appear at random times. But instead all his appearances are scripted events at certain sections in the game. In the OG game he was constantly on your tail, which made him fearful antagonist.
[*] Whenever he does appear, you're given VERY linear route where you have to run to for few seconds until he stops pursuing you, or you have to clear a quick-time-event in order to escape him.
[*] During early game, when he's still in his Stage 1 form and is pursuing you, a single grenade puts him down for long enough for you to escape from him. A single...grenade. In the OG game you had to unload most of your ammo just to stop him for a second, but in this Remake a single grenade will do the trick. What the hell?
[*] Boss encounters against him are extremely easy as well, mostly because of the dodge mechanic and how powerful it is. It basically allows you to avoid ALL of Nemesis' attacks. They're lame as well, because later on in the game he just runs around like a rapid dog, literally. This ain't Nemesis...
[*] Mr. X from RE2R was way, WAY better antagonist, because he actually hunted the player. Compared to him, RE3R's Nemesis is just bad. What happened Capcom? You literally had the blueprint for Nemesis already with Mr. X's design.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
As I mentioned in the opening of this review, RE3R was the perfect opportunity for Capcom to expand upon this game, but somehow they managed to do the exact opposite and made what was a short game to begin with even shorter.

I was first introduced to Resident Evil on the N64, with RE2.  My brothers and I decided to rent the game due to how expensive its hefty cartridge size was at the time.  Having played games like Winback (RE4 meets Metal Gear Solid), Goldeneye, Zelda Ocarina of Time, RE 2 was a massive step back in gameplay and mechanics.  So after playing RE2 OG for a couple hours, we returned it and never thought about the RE series again until the NIntendo Gamecube remake.

Where RE2 failed RE 1 remake succeeded.  RE 1 REmake hooked me from the get go.  Sure one could argue it was the unprecedented cinematic and artful camera angles envoking mood and emotion alongside a touching soundtrack, but it was more than that.  

The level/world design to this day in unmatched in meaningful and content filled player choice through item/equipment management and route planning,  Each time I play the game I have a totally different experience for nearly the entirety of the middle portion of the game.  Combat was passable and it only interesting quality was weapon choice as the actual act of combat was rather...meh.  

Which brings me to RE2 and RE3 OG, I thought for sure I'd love these games however upon playing them I realized the level and world design has been massively dumbed down and now I was spending a lot more time engaging with the once passable combat system and now tedious and repetitive due to the increase enemy and ammo count of RE 2 and RE 3.  Thankfully RE3 implemented the dodge/shove mechanic but it just wasn't enough to make combat fun...just slightly more engaging.

On comes RE4 OG, Gone is the tone, world design, item/key management, puzzles, as well as the monotonous combat system replaced with a mostly linear and brain dead world design and action packed arcade style shooter with a stagger melee system that is constantly rewarding to engae with.  

RE 5 perfected this system on all levels.

RE6 great on Paper, garbage to play.

So what does all this have to do with RE3 remake, funny that you ask.

RE3 remake is a strange experience and this is why.  

If you played RE3RE on Assisted, Standard, or Hardcore it felt it was disappointing, I agree.  The design of these introductory modes was clearly slapped together last minute when Capcom realized that RE2 fans were not going to be able to handle the difficulty of Nightmare and Inferno modes and it shows.  

This is why I highly recommend paying for the insta unlock for Nightmare and Inferno mode which are clearly the intended ways of play.  These modes not only change up enemy placement but also make them faster, more aggressive, and far more engaging,  You will have to learn to dodge, use knife counters (yep Jill has a faint knife strike that can counter damn near any enemy attack including the Hunters insta kill leap attack), route plan, and manage items.  

RE3 RE is short,  this is a good thing as the quality of encounters and boss design are the highest of the series with plenty of alternate approaches and solutions that will keep you coming back for more.  The pace and flow of the game damn near flawless outside of the opening sequence throught Brad's initial demise, as once it gets going the going is good.

Nemesis (the complaints are based off the initial difficulty setting and not the Nightmare and Inferno modes)

Nemesis is relentless, especially on inferno mode where he can speed up and slow down attacks significantly to throw the player off.  His chase sequences are brutal two steps forward one step back pushes to create distance and time to get to the next safe space.
The boss battles are glorious.  The flamethrower rooftop battle being my favorite and clocktower being the weakest (still fun though).  These are by far the best boss battles of the series, and become even more fun upon replay and experimentation.

I have more to say and will continue to update my review...

Decent game with some highs and some frankly poor/inconsistent feeling parts. It does not compare to how good/consistent/enjoyable Resident Evil 2/4 Remakes were. I've only left a not recommended since Steam does not have an option for mixed feelings.

I have not played the original, so I went into it fully blind and played on Hardcore difficulty. 

I'd say the first half of the game is quite inconsistent and the weakest part. The city parts look just ok visually and nothing really in there stands out. The hub gameplay wise is ok but it's let down by parts that feel unsatisfyingly short/disassociated to the rest of the game such as the insect part and also let down by the disappointing Nemesis moments. Frankly even though it's a hub it just plays in a very linear/directed manner and the Nemesis chases are quite straightforward as well and do not carry any real impact in terms of presence or danger. Revisiting a certain location as Carlos also felt just meh. 

Hospital onwards, I'd say is where the game starts to be a bit more consistent and I was enjoying it much more. Even though the area itself is quite small, it was nice to explore and go back and forth in it, killing the challenging enemies present there. Same could be said for the part that follows after the hospital. Plus visually, the hospital theme helps in terms of being interesting to explore. The boss fights here onwards were also pretty fun to figure out and execute. On hardcore, the lack of ammo gave me a lot of tense moments and I had to be strategic and try to run/dodge past most enemies to conserve it for the harder enemies. 

Overall, you can tell this game was either rushed or had a lower priority given to it by the devs. There is a certain jank to it present all across, be it the QTEs, the scripted chases or the gunplay feeling mediocre.

Story, I'd say is okish. It plays along but feels rushed especially in the first half, and certain moments do not really hit hard. The biggest let down is easily Nikolai. His character is a [i] bad [/i] bad guy. His voice acting sounds like it's very poorly mixed on top of just not having any presence. I always felt actively disappointed whenever he would do things for the story. I was hoping for more of a shade of grey perhaps like Ada or just a more charismatic presence. 
In terms of Nemesis, I feel they overused him a bit, even though gameplay wise he is decent in the second half of the game. Other than that, it's a standard affair, just a different tale present in Raccoon City. 

Visually, as detailed above the game looks just ok and I've already touched on the levels themselves above. Jill's model is easily the best one and the others do not really stand out as much. I feel like RE2/4 remake, even the side characters had good presence both in cutscenes and their ingame models.

Soundtrack is.. well present. Can't say I recall any great parts. I did not complain much either about it to be fair.

The length of the game is also quite short. So that is something to be kept in mind when purchasing it. My ingame timer at the end was 5 hours 30ish minutes and that's a first playthrough on Hardcore difficulty. 

So I'd only really recommend it to people who want to experience everything Resident Evil and want to go through this entry. Others can probably safely skip or be prepared to enjoy a lesser experience in comparison to the excellent RE2/4 remakes.

* While the previous game had Mr. X chasing you around the Raccoon City Police Station making me fear for my life, Nemesis is mostly reduced to a bunch of scripted cutscenes or chase scenes that force the player into running down a straight path... no strategy, no alternative paths, nothing. * A lot of content from the original RE3 was cut. Contents include:
Clock Tower Area
Graveyard Area
Grave Digger Boss
Slider Worm Enemy
Brain Sucker Enemy
Giant Spider Enemy
The QTE where you can select different paths when Nemesis attacks you in the original
* There's a lack of replayability in this game as well due to its extremely short story and... that's it. Most RE games have a mercenaries mode to compensate for that. On the flip side, RE2 and its remake have a lot of replay value due to those games having parallel stories with Leon and Claire. Perhaps if they didn't get rid of the branching path QTE thing that was present in the original game, this wouldn't be an issue.

The Positives:

With all that said, no, this is technically not a bad game but I STILL don't recommend it... at least at full price. My Review of Resident Evil 3 Remake
I never played the original Resident Evil 3, but I do remember watching my little brother stay up all night trying to beat it—with no memory card. I’ll never forget how he lost to Nemesis right in front of the Raccoon Police Station and threw his controller across the room. We were up until 2 a.m. that night laughing (and crying) about it.

The Resident Evil series has always held a special place in my heart, right next to my kid, honestly. The unforgettable stories, the over-the-top villains, and the addictive remake gameplays—I just can’t get enough of this franchise.

That being said, RE3 Remake had some big shoes to fill after the success of RE2 Remake. While I think RE3 Remake is a solid update to the original, it’s not without its flaws—just like RE2 Remake.

Let me start by saying this: don’t believe the online haters. This game is NOT BAD. I enjoyed it from start to finish. If someone says this game is terrible, they’re either trolling or hopping on the hate train for clicks.

Here’s what I loved about it:

The graphics are absolutely stunning—an improvement even over RE2 Remake. The environments in the first third of the game are especially jaw-dropping. Exploring a ruined Raccoon City felt eerie and alive. Think the opening of RE2 but on a much bigger scale.

The voice acting and sound design are top-notch. You can actually hear the music now, and it gets you hyped to blast zombie heads off.

The gameplay is fast-paced and fun, with a great selection of weapons to mow down the undead.

There’s a surprising amount of difficulty options—more than five, compared to RE2’s three—so you can tailor the challenge to your liking.

Plenty of in-game challenges to complete, adding replay value.

But there are some downsides:

The game is short. I finished it in 4 hours and 45 minutes on my first playthrough, which is pretty quick even for a Resident Evil game.

Nemesis, the big bad everyone remembers, is underwhelming. Compared to Mr. X in RE2, Nemesis isn’t as scary or intimidating. He feels more like a scripted obstacle than an unpredictable threat, even though he was also scripted in the original.

Nemesis mutates way too early. In the original, his transformations happened late in the game, keeping him human-like for most of it. Here, he turns into a four-legged beast about a third of the way through, which feels rushed.

Overall Thoughts:

This game is not the disaster some Steam reviewers make it out to be. It definitely doesn’t deserve a 53/100 from PC Gamer. The gameplay is fast-paced, the visuals are stunning, and it has the energy of an action movie. Is it scary? Not really. I think I jumped maybe once or twice, but that’s it.

My rating? 8/10. It could hit a 9/10 if Capcom adds some DLC.

Resident Evil 3 (Remake) is a game that delivers plenty of thrills, but unfortunately, it stumbles when it comes to living up to the legacy of its source material. 
While it boasts stunning visuals, tight gameplay mechanics, and intense encounters with Nemesis, the experience ultimately feels hollow due to one glaring flaw: its brevity!
Clocking in at roughly 6 hours for a standard playthrough, the game feels shockingly short, especially for fans who remember the more expansive journey of the 1999 original... 
What’s worse is that several key levels from the classic, like the Clock Tower, have been completely omitted. 
These cuts strip the remake of some of its most iconic moments and leave the campaign feeling rushed and linear, sacrificing the sense of exploration and dread that defined the original.
Adding to the frustration is how Resident Evil 3 handles Nemesis...
In the original game, Nemesis was a relentless, terrifying force that felt like an evolution of Resident Evil 2’s Mr. X. 
However, in the remake, the roles feel oddly reversed! 
Nemesis is relegated to more scripted sequences, which undermines the tension and unpredictability he brought to the original. 
Ironically, Resident Evil 2’s remake captured that sense of constant dread perfectly with Mr. X’s mechanics, making him feel like what Nemesis should have been here! 
It’s as if the developers swapped their dynamics, robbing Nemesis of his iconic fear factor...
To its credit, the game does shine in certain areas. 
Jill Valentine is given a fantastic redesign and a strong, charismatic personality, while Carlos Oliveira gets some welcome extra screen time and depth. 
The action-heavy tone suits the story, and the encounters with Nemesis are as terrifying as they are cinematic. 
However, these highlights aren’t enough to overshadow the fact that the game lacks substance.
For fans of the series, the remake is a bittersweet experience. 
It’s enjoyable in the moment, but it leaves you yearning for what could have been, a faithful, fleshed-out reinterpretation of one of the franchise’s most beloved entries. 
In its current state, Resident Evil 3 (Remake) is less of a fully realized game and more of a missed opportunity.

Before I begin this review, here are a few things to keep in mind:
The Resident Evil 3 remake directly proceeded the Resident Evil 2 remake. RE3 is, by comparison, lackluster in many aspects. It is much shorter, more poorly written, and generally worse directed than the original. I have 100% completed RE3R and at the time of this review am on my way to 100% completing RE2R. Thus, it is with a moderate level of familiarity with this series that I make this review. In contrast to most RE3R reviews, this critique will keep the importance of the original game (RE3) in mind rather than the success of the preceding remake (RE2R). And again, this game is short for a mainline RE entry. I beat the game in just under 8hrs. There is no reason for why it should take me less than 40hrs to 100% a mainline RE title. Keeping all these things in mind, let’s move onto the review.

OVERALL: 65/100

Fear Factor: 4/10
Shock Factor: 8/10
Atmosphere: 5/10
Sound Design: 8/10
Soundtrack: 4/10
Gameplay: 7/10
Controls: 8/10
Replayability: 7/10
Story/Characters: 5/10
Graphics: 9/10

While that’s not quite an overall score I expected, it's not far below what I'd have predicted.

FEAR & SHOCK FACTOR
The RE series is jam-packed with some iconic scares, and the original RE3 certainly forwards this idea. The remake of this successful and iconic '90s horror game does nothing by way of furthering any sense of fear. It is with much disappointment that I give RE3R a low score for its fear factor. The only things keeping said score above 0 are the adrenaline spikes thanks to chase sequences, delightfully repulsing enemy and boss design, and the entire Subway Power Substation section (which is, you guessed it, short). It is for these 3 reasons that I give RE3R a moderate score for its Shock Factor. 

ATMOSPHERE & SOUND DESIGN
Now for the atmosphere. Thanks to most of the game’s tight hallways full of difficult or straight-up annoying enemies, it can be difficult to discern the game’s atmosphere. In terms of worldbuilding and general atmosphere, RE3R pales in comparison to its 1999 counterpart. That said, some sections of the game (such as the opening 10 minutes and the familiar RPD station) add to the game’s overall apocalyptic theme. It’s almost hilarious that one of the better parts of RE3R was a literal copy-paste from RE2R, and it still wasn’t improved upon. It’s for these reasons, and for the game’s consistent theme, that I give RE3R a mixed score for its atmosphere. There’s little more to be said regarding the game’s sound design than an admission that RE3R is, in fact, a Resident Evil game. Even at their lowest Capcom still delivers the best in action-horror sound design.

SOUNDTRACK
Soundtrack. A major factor which makes so many iconic games so memorable and recognizable. RE3R dared to take inspiration from its 90s counterpart and made a soundtrack that definitely… sounds. Some of the most iconic themes from every title in the RE series are the aptly named “Save Room” themes. RE2R also set a standard of using credits music that slaps. All RE entries have since kept this theme except RE3R. Few songs throughout the game build tension, no boss themes are particularly memorable, and this is the only game in mainline RE that has an utterly unrecognizable Save Room theme. Even RE6 had songs that slapped. It even had an EDM track or two akin to something you might find in Initial D. Regardless, RE3R has one of the least memorable soundtracks in the entire mainline RE series. The only reason it gets any points in the soundtrack category is due to the music’s moderately high production value.

GAMEPLAY
I’m going to split the gameplay category into two parts: One covering combat and difficulty, and the other covering locations and puzzles. This is the only section where I’ll really compare RE3R to RE2R. 
COMBAT & DIFFICULTY
Put simply, the only thing RE3R improved on from RE2R was the combat. Perfect dodges, enemy lock-ons, and other tiny QOL details allow for an easier experience on keyboard and mouse as well as controller, for those who want to seamlessly immerse themselves (as much of an anti-immersion camp fest as RE3R is). RE2R and RE3R are hard. RE3R on the Inferno difficulty features some of the most grueling bossfights I’ve ever come across in gaming. Truly, if I was simply a better gamer, I could’ve 100% completed this game in under 3hrs. But I’ll get to that more in later. The combat is enjoyable, fluid, but leaves you feeling just vulnerable enough on your first playthrough to regularly be on edge. 
LOCATIONS & PUZZLES
The game’s locations, at times, contribute to and take away from this feeling. RE2R nailed the sewers, and despite the fact that RE3R reused many sewer assets and sections, it isn’t quite as riveting as the prior entry. The city and underground NEST sections feel cramped with far too many enemies, on top of Jill’s tendency to be chased by a nigh immovable object. At multiple points in the game, and especially right out the gate, enemies can be more of an annoyance than an obstacle to be overcome. This is seen to a major extent playing as Carlos in the RPD and hospital sections. The puzzles in this game certainly don’t add to the difficulty, but they make their respective areas memorable. As previously mentioned, the maze-and-switch puzzle in the Subway Power Substation is what makes the area memorable (aside from the shock factor of downing herbs to vomit up creepy-crawlies). The Subway puzzle, while extremely simple and typically done within a couple attempts, adds to the memorability of the plot-important (albeit very small) Subway Station. It is with all these factors in mind that I give RE3R a balanced score as far as overall gameplay is concerned. 

CONTROLS
Additionally, the controls are great. Slight upgrades from RE2R for keyboard and mouse users, lock-on highly benefits controllers.

REPLAYABILITY
Time to critique the game’s replayability. As previously mentioned, much of the game’s “replayability” is heaving your head against a brick wall of difficulty until you get lucky enough to beat Nemesis phase 3 on the Inferno difficulty. Inferno is the last of three difficulties offered by RE3R above Standard mode, and as its name implies, it is the closest I’ve come to experiencing hell in an RE game. Most of the game’s “New Game Plus” content is just replaying the already short game on higher difficulties. Actually, strike that. All of the game’s NG+ content is going through subsequent rings of hell. There’s a reason why this is the game that really taught me how to button mash on a controller until the underside of my thumb blisters. Anyway, there’s not much more to say here. As you beat the game repeatedly, you get additional weapons and bonuses to help you through higher difficulties. If you attempt Inferno, you’ll find soon enough that unlimited ammo does nothing to ease the bite of hell’s flames on your fingers during a grind steeped in QTEs and perfect dodges.

STORY/CHARACTERS
Mid is the best word I can come up with to describe the entire RE3 (REMAKE) story. I emphasize the “Remake” because the story is a far cry from the original RE3. Characters are pretty two-dimensional. Tyrell is the only great character which you see more than a shallow outer layer of in RE3R. Carlos is creepy, Claire is the kind of typical campy badass you might expect to see as a side character in one of the Resident Evil live action movies, Brad doesn’t have a presence nearly as significant as he did in the original, Nicholai is hardly seen in RE3R, and even Nemesis can’t hit his shots for the literal life of me. All of these combine to make the overall storyline incredibly weak compared to the first game. Tyrell carried, and the writing is, at the very least, cohesive.

GRAPHICS

Capcom’s Resident Evil 3 Remake reimagines the 1999 classic with modern graphics, streamlined gameplay, and an intense narrative focus. While it delivers an engaging experience, it falls short in certain areas compared to its predecessor, Resident Evil 2 Remake.

The game’s visuals are exceptional, thanks to the RE Engine. Raccoon City feels alive, chaotic, and terrifying, with detailed environments and dynamic lighting that enhance the horror. Jill Valentine’s updated character design and strong personality shine throughout the story, making her a compelling lead. Nemesis, the iconic pursuer, is a relentless and fearsome adversary, although his encounters are heavily scripted, reducing the unpredictability that made Mr. X in RE2 Remake so memorable.

Gameplay is faster and more action-oriented than RE2 Remake, with improved combat mechanics and a dodge system that adds a layer of strategy. However, the game’s pacing feels rushed, with a campaign lasting only 5-6 hours. Key locations from the original, such as the clock tower, have been cut or reduced, leaving the game feeling linear and lacking in exploration. Puzzles, a hallmark of the series, are minimal, further emphasizing action over survival horror.

Despite its shortcomings, Resident Evil 3 Remake succeeds in delivering a thrilling, cinematic experience. It’s perfect for fans of fast-paced survival horror, but those looking for deeper exploration and a longer campaign might feel underwhelmed.

RE3R is a good game, but it could have been so much better.

On its' own, it shares some of the pros with the prior RE2 Remake, though this one suffers from a short campaign with a lack of variations or branching paths, mechanics that were either underutilized or dumbed down from its' predecessor and a lack of any additional game modes.

As a remake, it suffers even more by not living up to the original game it was based on, with missing locations, story beats and other things that made the 1999 classic so memorable, especially with its' handling of Nemesis, who was turned from a genuinely imposing threat that stalked you through almost the entire game with difficult boss fights to an absolute pushover who seemingly is barely taken seriously by the people it's trying to hunt down, whose best moments here are in either RE6 style QTE segments or repetitive boss fights that don't do much with the concepts they introduce.

I recommend treating this as an expansion of sorts to RE2 Remake and I also strongly advise getting this on sale if you can. $40 USD is just way too much for the about 3-4 hours of game you get on a first playthrough; while there are unlockables you can hunt down and achievements to collect, I doubt they'd hold the interest of casual players very long.

With all that being said, I [i]did[/i] enjoy this game quite a bit; even if this is one of the weaker entries in this long and storied series, I still think it's a decent game, though of course your mileage may vary. If neutral reviews were a thing on Steam, this game would probably get one from me.
