Somehow, I like this game even less after replaying it again. It's just not a very well-made game. It's not a good remake either and It's very short too. I wouldn't mind the length as much had it been a great experience throughout but it was not.

Pros : 
- Like RE2 remake, this is a great looking game.
- There are some good scary moments that aren't just jumpscares.
- The characters got modernized and feels more believable (all except one).
- All the performances/voice acting are great. 
- The dodging mechanic is better than in the original RE3 and pretty satisfying to pull off.
- Nemesis's design is great and unique. Very different from Mr. X.
- Nemesis's theme is pretty dope.
- The limited parts where Nemesis chases you are pretty tense.
- Some enemies re-design are also great.
- It has some cool tie-in moments to RE2 remake.

Cons : 
- Nemesis. Just him in general. Everything he does besides the first encounter with him are just scripted events and boss fights. No stalking Jill through the game like in the original or even like Mr. X in RE2. He's easily the worse thing about this game and he's literally the titular character for crying out loud. What a fumble.
- Not a remake, more of a reboot. I recognized nothing in this game that's similar at all to the original. This game could easily be sold as a standalone expansion to RE2 remake with renamed characters and I wouldn't know that it's supposed to be a RE3 remake.
- Reusing many assets and mechanics from RE2 while making them worse. For example, the zombies. RE2 zombies worked because you're supposed to fight them one at a time. But this game constantly throw 3+ zombies at you all at once forcing you to waste more ammo & resources more than maybe you should've. They move around too much and you have to keep track of multiple of them at a time. It made encounters more annoying than terrifying. RE2 zombies just wasn't designed as horde enemies and this game uses them mostly as that.
- Missing areas from the original. Like most of them.
- Uninspired level designs.
- Less puzzles than your average RE games. It's just mostly get keys to open doors.
- Files are too on the nose with the clues they're giving and there's way too many of them. Most of them are uninteresting and doesn't add much to the lore.
- The game relies too much on backtracking to extend the playtime.
- Too linear, even for RE standards. There's just too many one-off areas.
- The combat in this game just feels off. For some reason, shooting feels less satisfying compared to RE2. The weapons feels less impactful. Although critical headshots are still satisfying whenever you get them.
- Too many gimmick/one-shot enemies.
- They got rid of the dedicated sub-weapon slots/buttons for whatever reason making swapping weapons on the fly more tedious.
- The knife got nerfed so hard in this game to a point of it being almost useless (and it still takes up your main-weapon slot!)
- The background sound/music is way too low for whatever reason even tho my volume is all maxed out. Yet the dialogue & sound effects all sound fine. Super weird. It kinda ruined my immersion a little bit.
- Jill being a typical action heroine. "Driving a car off a top of a building? It's all good!" "Took a rocket launcher or a flamethrower to the face? No worries! Jill will walk it all off!" I know RE isn't really a serious series, but this game is approaching RE6-level of absurdity & stupidity with its spectacles & set pieces.
- Nikolai is even more cartoonishly evil compared to the original and feels so out of place in this game.

The best I could describe RE3 (2020) is that this game is feels like one of the "Extra Mode" that you can unlock in RE2 remake except you play it for 4 hours. It feels too arcade-y and lacks any semblance of identity. It's an action game with a horror game skin and mechanics. It's just fundamentally problematic. With that being said, I don't completely hate this game. I liked some parts of this game. I would probably rate it a 6/10 but since Steam only allow for positive or negative review, "thumbs down" describe how I feel about the game the best, I guess.

[h1]Buy it only on Sale or in a Bundle with RE2 Remake[/h1]

While I had fun with this game, I can’t deny that it’s full of flaws and missed opportunities. I haven’t played the original Resident Evil 3, so I can’t fully compare the two, but it’s clear that a lot of content has been cut. Enemies, locations, boss fights, and even core gameplay elements were removed without any meaningful replacements.

What’s worse is that the game also strips away some of the features that made Resident Evil 2 Remake so successful. For example, defensive items are gone. Now you’ll always take damage when grabbed by an enemy. Shooting off zombie limbs? Also gone; anything but headshots feels ineffective now. But the most disappointing change has to be Nemesis. After RE2's excellent implementation of Mr. X, Nemesis is a massive letdown. Instead of being a constant, dynamic threat, he’s reduced to a series of glorified cutscenes masquerading as gameplay, where you just hold "W" to progress. There’s only one section where Nemesis actively pursues you, and it’s easily the best part of the game. Beyond that, he’s just a recurring boss, and most of those fights are unremarkable, relying on gimmicks that make them frustrating rather than fun.

The one notable new addition is the dodge mechanic, which lets Jill avoid being grabbed if you time it right. I also appreciate the five difficulty modes, especially since the harder ones change item and enemy placements to surprise players. The developers clearly put effort into these higher difficulties beyond just buffing enemy stats. Unfortunately, the boss fights become downright tedious at higher levels, especially the final one. Beating it on the highest difficulty without using New Game+ items deserves serious respect.

Speaking of New Game+, it’s one of the few highlights. The in-game shop lets you spend points earned from completing various objectives to buy items that carry over into future playthroughs. Using these doesn’t penalize your rank at the end, which makes replaying the game far more enjoyable. However, it’s disappointing that the game doesn’t include any extra modes or DLC to expand the experience beyond the main campaign.

Overall, while the game has its moments, it falls far short of the bar set by Resident Evil 2 Remake. It’s worth picking up, but only on sale or as part of a bundle.

Pros:

- Carlos is a good character, they could've done a lot more with him, if the game were longer but the sections with him and his dialogue were pretty enjoyable.
- Nemesis Stage 1 feels very scary the first few times you go up against him.
- The incredible graphics allowed by the RE Engine

Cons:

- There is far too much cut content to warrant calling this a game, its more just an addon to RE2.
- Paper thin characters, with not a lot of niche to them
- Encounters with Nemesis all throughout are very inorganic as opposed to the original game.

Do you need to play RE3 to understand the whole story? This version? No. It provides some fun background to some small RE2 characters like Marvin and Kendo, as well as showing us the fate of Brad Vickers, the helicopter pilot from RE1, and Raccoon City as a whole.

TLDR - Ok game, unenjoyable characters and possibly the worst jumping on point for the modern RE games

[h1] A Masterclass in Survival Horror – 9/10 [/h1]

Resident Evil 3 is a high-octane reimagining of the 1999 classic that delivers a fresh, adrenaline-pumping experience while still staying true to the roots of survival horror. From the moment you step into the shoes of Jill Valentine, the intense atmosphere grips you and doesn’t let go. The game shines with its incredible graphics, atmospheric design, and perfectly paced action.

The iconic Nemesis, reimagined here, is more terrifying than ever. This relentless monster relentlessly pursues you, forcing you to think on your feet as you navigate the twisted streets of Raccoon City. The feeling of dread is palpable, and it’s exhilarating to be constantly on the edge of your seat.

Combat feels responsive and satisfying, with a fantastic variety of weapons that can be upgraded for maximum efficiency. The addition of dodge mechanics elevates the gameplay, making encounters feel dynamic and rewarding. While the game offers a more action-oriented approach compared to Resident Evil 2 Remake, it doesn’t lose the heart of the survival horror genre. Managing resources, exploring, and solving environmental puzzles still play a key role in the experience.

The environments are beautifully crafted, from the rundown streets of Raccoon City to the haunting interiors of the hospital and laboratory. Each area is loaded with detail, making exploration as thrilling as it is unnerving.
The voice acting and character animations also deserve a mention. Jill’s determination and Carlos’ charm bring life to the story, and the overall performance makes you care about the fate of these characters, even in the middle of a zombie apocalypse.

If you're a fan of survival horror, Resident Evil 3 is an absolute must-play. While it’s not without a few criticisms—such as its relatively short length compared to Resident Evil 2—it’s still a thrilling ride that will keep you coming back for more. The game may be a bit more action-heavy than its predecessor, but it’s an exhilarating, tense, and visually stunning chapter in the series.

Disregarding the fact that RE 3 is a quarter of the length of 2 with a quarter of the replayability, I was still really disappointed by how poorly it compares to all the other REmakes. Environments are small and shockingly linear, puzzles seem dumbed down, lots of content was cut from the original game, and fails to add anything new that improves the experience.

Nemesis only stalks the player in the very first hours of the game and then is regulated entirely to a lot of cutscenes and some bad boss fights. His second form boss fights involves lots of waiting and dodging until he starts running around the arena for no reason at all so you can use environment to knock him down and then shoot the obligatory big glowing weakspot. These fights were my least favorite part of the entire game and the only part I actively hated.  

This game introduces a dodge that kind of breaks the entire game too? A well timed dodge gives you full invincibility and a chance to auto lock on to the enemy's head and get a few shots in. If you learn the timing, the spacing and resource management that is so crucial to every single Resident Evil game becomes some what irrelevant as nothing can hit you if you do it right. In a game all about not wasting resources this seems like a big oversight since you don't really have to use those precious resources to get to A to B if you get the timings down. 

This compounds pretty harshly with the fact that you never have a reason to return to an area more than twice. First you go through an area without the keys that unlock progression or boxes of items, hit a cutscene / dead end, then you pass back through with the key item and proceed to the next area. Only in the very beginning do you ever have more than one key item that does not go to the same place. There is very little planning or stratagizing of what to take where because the game funnels you through so you get a supreme majority of items by going the most efficient direct route. The game does not look like a hallway but is certainly designed like one.

All that being said, it still looks great and has the advantage of using the same gameplay and mechanics as REmake 2, which was phenomenal. I got it on sale for less than $10 (something it seems to do often) and it is definitely worth that if you have played the others and wanted more. 

In hindsight, it really seems obvious Capcom just wanted to get 3 over with so they can focus on 4, a game that more fans were excited for and turned out much better. They didn't even make additional costumes as DLC outside of pre-order bonuses. For Capcom that is truly damning evidence that they didn't care much about this one.

[h1]Resident Evil 3[/h1]

                                                                             ----------
Capcom’s [i]Resident Evil 3 Remake[/i], released in 2020, is a modern reimagining of the 1999 classic. With gorgeous visuals, thrilling gameplay, and iconic characters, it offers an intense and action-packed experience. However, its focus on streamlined action over survival horror and its brief runtime make it a polarizing entry in the franchise.

[h3]Gameplay:[/h3]
[i]Resident Evil 3 Remake[/i] shifts the franchise toward a more action-oriented approach. Jill’s movements are fluid, and the addition of the dodge mechanic adds a layer of skill-based gameplay. Combat is satisfying, with a good mix of weapon options and strategic resource management.

[i]Nemesis[/i], the titular antagonist, is both a highlight and a letdown. His early encounters are tense and terrifying, but as the game progresses, his appearances become increasingly scripted, reducing his threat level. [u]Fans of the original may feel disappointed by the lack of free-roaming Nemesis moments that made him so unpredictable in the classic version.[/u]

[h3]Narrative:[/h3]
The story follows [i]Jill Valentine[/i] as she attempts to escape a crumbling Raccoon City while being relentlessly pursued by [i]Nemesis[/i], a bioengineered weapon. The narrative is straightforward, bolstered by [i]Jill’s[/i] strong characterization as a determined survivor and [i]Carlos Oliveira’s[/i] expanded role as her charismatic ally.
[u]However, the game trims or reworks significant sections of the original story, including the Clock Tower, leaving some fans feeling shortchanged.[/u]

[h3]Visuals:[/h3]
The RE Engine delivers once again, with stunning visuals that bring Raccoon City to life. From dimly lit streets to grotesque monsters, the attention to detail is remarkable. [i]Jill Valentine[/i] and [i]Carlos Oliveira[/i] look fantastic, with expressive animations and modernized designs. The atmosphere is thick with tension, [u]though it leans more toward action than horror gamestyle.[/u]

[h3]Minuses:[/h3]
The game’s brevity is its most glaring flaw. With a runtime of less than 10 hours and little to encourage replayability beyond harder difficulties and unlockable items, it doesn’t feel as robust as Resident Evil 2 Remake.

Exploration and backtracking are minimal, removing much of the series’ signature tension and immersion.
Several iconic locations and moments from the original game, such as the Clock Tower and more free-form Nemesis encounters, are either missing or heavily truncated.

While [i]Nemesis[/i] is visually imposing and terrifying in his early appearances, his role is largely confined to scripted encounters, lacking the unpredictable threat of [i]Mr. X[/i] from Resident Evil 2 Remake.

[h3]Reviewer's Verdict:[/h3]
[i]Resident Evil 3 Remake[/i] delivers a polished, visually stunning, and action-packed experience that successfully modernizes many elements of the original game. However, its short runtime, linear structure, and lack of survival horror depth prevent it from reaching the heights of [i]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/i].

                                                                                  ----------

[h2]Review in Short:[/h2]
[i]Gameplay: 8/10
Narrative: 7/10
Visuals: 9/10
Replayability: 4/10
Overall: 7/10[/i]

Jill is strapped for most of the campaign and the enemies in the final sequence of the game are no obstacle. In conjunction with the almost complete lack of puzzles, this remake lowers itself to a pretty bog standard action game. It occasionally captures the RE atmosphere.

The biggest disappointment is completely neutering Nemesis and relegating his chase sequences to holding forward and often culminating in a straight up gimmick boss battle of some sort. An iconic tyrant design completely wasted.

As for positives, the game is gorgeous and to be fair, I was never bored playing it. The game moves along at a good clip and doesn't overstay its welcome. It's value at full price is dubious however and I can only recommend it on sale.

Resident Evil 3 is another installment in the famous survival horror series that continues the tradition of previous installments. As in previous installments, players will have to fight for survival in a world infected with a virus and populated by zombies and other dangerous creatures.

Graphics and Sound
The graphics in the game are top-notch. A detailed world, realistic textures, and character animation create an atmosphere of horror and tension. The soundtrack is also top-notch: music and ambient sounds add atmosphere to the game and immerse you in the game world.

Gameplay
The gameplay in Resident Evil 3 is similar to the previous installments in the series. Players control a character who must explore the world, fight enemies, and solve puzzles. The game has stealth elements that add variety to the gameplay.

Plot
The game's plot takes place in an alternate reality where the world is infected with a virus that turns people into zombies. Players take on the role of Jill Valentine, who must save the world from the threat. The game's plot is interesting and keeps you on the edge of your seat until the very end.

New elements
The game has new elements that make the gameplay more diverse. For example, the game has a new enemy - Nemesis, who is one of the most dangerous opponents in the game. The game also has new types of weapons and equipment that help players fight enemies.

Multiplayer
The game can be played in cooperative mode with a friend or other players. This adds variety to the game and allows players to enjoy the game together.

Conclusion
Resident Evil 3 is an excellent survival horror game that continues the traditions of the previous parts of the series. The game has an interesting plot, varied gameplay and high-quality graphics and sound. I recommend the game to all fans of the genre.

Review de Resident Evil 3 Remake: Diversão e adrenalina, mas com alguns poréns

O Resident Evil 3 Remake é um jogo extremamente divertido e viciante, especialmente pelas suas mecânicas de dodge, que adicionam uma boa dose de adrenalina ao gameplay e te fazem sentir na pele o desespero de Jill Valentine ao tentar escapar de Raccoon City. Os mapas são bem desenhados, proporcionando uma ótima ambientação, e a história é envolvente, conseguindo capturar a essência do clássico.

Um dos pontos altos, sem dúvidas, é o sistema de pontos que você ganha ao longo do jogo e pode gastar na loja de bônus. Isso oferece um incentivo extra para experimentar diferentes abordagens e buscar uma gameplay mais estratégica – é uma mecânica que realmente torna o jogo mais interessante e prolonga a diversão.

Dito isso, vale lembrar que Resident Evil 3 Remake fica abaixo do Resident Evil 2 Remake em alguns aspectos importantes. O jogo é mais curto e com menos backtracking, o que resulta em uma experiência mais linear e um pouco menos desafiadora para quem curte explorar.

No geral, Resident Evil 3 Remake é uma ótima pedida para fãs da franquia e de survival horror, oferecendo ação e nostalgia, mas não espere o mesmo nível de profundidade e exploração que encontramos no remake de Resident Evil 2.

As a long-time fan of the Resident Evil franchise, it's safe to say I’ve experienced nearly every entry — from the absolute masterpieces like Resident Evil 4 to the more divisive titles like RE5 and RE6. I’ve loved them all in some way, shape, or form. Heck, even Resident Evil 7 was a welcome shift in style. I’m still looking forward to diving into the remakes of Resident Evil 2, Resident Evil 4, and Resident Evil 8, but there’s one title that’s always stood out to me: Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.

For newcomers to the series or those who never played the original Resident Evil 3, this remake is perfectly serviceable. It’s an action-packed ride with little downtime, which might appeal to fans of fast-paced gameplay. The chase sequences with Nemesis are intense and frequent, and the game never feels too slow. If you’re coming into this fresh, you might have a good time.

However, if you’ve played the original RE3 — or if you’ve come to love its slower, more atmospheric tension — the changes in this remake might leave you disappointed. The game feels short — far shorter than the original, which had more breathing room and a greater sense of exploration. Here, the focus is almost entirely on action and Nemesis chases, which leaves very little room for the puzzles, character interactions, and environmental storytelling that made the original stand out.

One of the most frustrating aspects of the remake is how much content was cut. The original RE3 had more variety in its pacing. There were sections where you could take your time solving puzzles, exploring, and interacting with other characters. The remake trims all of this down, opting instead to ramp up the action. This works for some, but for me, it took away what made the original so special — the balance between survival horror, exploration, and action.

The plot changes also stood out to me as a major flaw. While it’s not uncommon for remakes to take liberties with story elements, some of the decisions here felt like missed opportunities. For example, the death of Brad Vickers, a moment that was genuinely shocking and impactful in the original, barely registers here. Similarly, the iconic Barry Burton appearance at the end is gone, which is another change that felt like a misstep. There are more plot deviations, but I won’t spoil them here. Suffice to say, for long-time fans of the original, these changes can feel jarring.

Looking at the overwhelmingly “Very Positive” reviews on Steam, I get the impression that many players are enjoying the game in isolation, without comparing it to its predecessor. That’s fine, and I can understand why people are giving it high marks. It’s not a bad game, just a mediocre one when stacked against the original. It’s certainly fun in parts, but it’s also a missed opportunity. For fans who grew up with the original RE3, the remake feels more like a fast-paced action game with a few elements tacked on rather than a faithful reimagining.

In the end, I’m going to give the game a positive review as well — maybe not as glowing as some others, but it’s still a fun time, especially if you’re not attached to the original. But, for me, it’s hard to shake the feeling that Resident Evil 3: Nemesis deserved more than just a straightforward action reboot.

[h1]Resident Evil 3 Review – A Rushed Remake that Strays from Survival Horror Roots[/h1]


[h3]Introduction[/h3]
In the world of game remakes, preservation should come first. A remake should remain faithful to the original, honoring its legacy and its fans. If a developer wishes to tell a new story or take a different approach, it would be better suited to a new IP or a fresh installment. With that in mind, Resident Evil 3 feels like a missed opportunity—a remake that sacrifices the soul of the original for a faster-paced, action-oriented experience that lacks the depth and survival tension that made Resident Evil 3 memorable.

[h3]A Misplaced Focus on Action Over Atmosphere[/h3]
The remake’s depiction of Raccoon City has potential, with detailed visuals and a chaotic atmosphere that sets the stage well. However, instead of expanding the back alleys and exploring the city’s grittier side, the game cuts or glosses over key locations that were integral to the original experience. The iconic Clocktower and park area, for instance, are entirely missing—replaced with newer sections like the underground sewer and an Umbrella lab. While new content isn’t a bad idea in itself, it should come as an addition, not as a replacement for beloved elements of the original.

[h3]Resource Management and Survival Elements—Where Did They Go?[/h3]
Resident Evil 3 leans heavily into action, far closer to the style of Resident Evil 5 and Resident Evil 6 than the classic survival horror of its predecessors. Resources are not in short supply, and the feeling of desperation that defined earlier Resident Evil titles is nearly absent here. With only a few isolated moments that truly challenge your survival skills, the game shifts away from its roots, creating a disconnect between this version and the original’s survival horror vibe. For a remake, this is a huge drawback, as it fails to honor the tense, resource-driven gameplay that defined the original Resident Evil 3.

[h3]Nemesis—A Missed Opportunity[/h3]
While Nemesis’ updated design is impressive and menacing, the encounters with him feel underwhelming. The fights themselves lack the intensity and challenge you’d expect from such a formidable foe. Defeating him should have rewarded players with meaningful items or upgrades, rewarding skill and strategy, but instead, the encounters feel more like scripted obstacles than the terrifying, memorable battles they could have been.

[h3]Length and Legacy[/h3]
At the end of the day, a remake should feel like the same game experienced through a modern lens. Unfortunately, Resident Evil 3 misses this mark. Unlike the Resident Evil 2 remake, which, despite some cuts, extended playtime with fresh elements that honored the original’s tone, Resident Evil 3 is actually shorter than its 1999 counterpart. This brevity feels like a disservice, both to longtime fans and to newcomers looking to experience the full scope of this pivotal entry in the series. When remakes are done right, players of both the original and the remake should feel as though they’ve experienced the same game, even if certain details differ. Capcom succeeded with the Resident Evil remake in 2002 and with Resident Evil 2, but Resident Evil 3’s remake falls short.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
Resident Evil 3 Remake is an enjoyable game with stellar production values, boasting top-tier voice acting, motion capture, and cinematics that tell the original story in a compelling way. However, as a remake, it falls short. Rather than faithfully preserving Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, it feels more like a reimagining, losing much of the original’s iconic locations and unique atmosphere. Raccoon City’s streets are condensed, memorable areas like the clocktower are mssing, and new areas feel too similar to Resident Evil 2. Had this been an original title, it would be a solid, if slightly overpriced, action-horror game. But as a remake, it misses the mark on preserving the spirit and survival-horror elements of the classic, making it difficult to recommend for fans of the original seeking a true recreation.

[i]Resident Evil 3[/i] is the remake of the in 1999 on [i]Playstation[/i] released survival horror game [i]Resident Evil 3: Nemesis[/i]. I've never played the original [i]Resident Evil[/i] games on console but after the pretty good remakes of the first and second game I was hyped for this one as well.

Like in the predecessor the graphics are pretty good. I've played with enabled ray tracing and got pretty nice performance even with my [i]GeForce RTX 3070[/i]. There are a lot of graphical settings to tweak and you can also switch back to DX11 mode, if you'll need more performance.

I also like the atmosphere and it's pretty interesting to see [i]Raccoon City[/i] overrun by zombies. Backtracking like in the predecessors is also here but my problem is the leveldesign feels pretty bland, the explorable area of [i]Raccoon City[/i] are basically two different streets with six stores. The other five bigger locations - which one of them is "recycled" from another [i]Resident Evil[/i] game (don't wan't to spoil anything here) are also pretty linear. I've to admit, I do like the fanservice feeling in the "recycled area" nonetheless.
The developers reduced the gore and also removed the ragdoll system. In those situations I wonder why, because I thought those are fundamental elements anchored to the game engine.

Besides the linear and bland leveldesign, the whole game feels somehow rushed - it feels more like a [i]Resident Evil 2.5[/i] or a DLC for [i]Resident Evil 2[/i]. 
The story is boring, it has a short playtime, survival horror is completely gone, there are like two puzzles and the rest is "linear action". And even the action isn't that good. 
Even with a high field of view the camera felt zoomed in and the over the shoulder camera while aiming is pretty bad for open areas and wide spaces.
The developers also removed the "escape mechanic" were you use a defense item if grabbed by an enemy and replaced it with a "perfect dodge mechanic" were you earn a few seconds of slow motion and autoaim on weakspots. 
I've had the feeling, the mechanic also doesn't work very well because on higher difficulties the last bossfight is like a real stunlock party - no chance to escape.

[i]Mr. X[/i] in [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] felt haunting and menacing, also wasn't perfect but in direct comparison, [i]Nemesis[/i] in [i]Resident Evil 3[/i] is a complete joke. All the encounters are scripted and most of the time where you have to escape, you just press "W" and follow a linear route - how exciting!

Look at my playtime, I had fun with the game and enjoyed the zombie and monster shooting in tight dark spaces, but after the remakes of the first and the second [i]Resident Evil[/i] games, [i]Resident Evil 3[/i] wasn't what I've had expected. Some of my friends which played the old [i]Resident Evil 3: Nemesis[/i] told me that a lot of content was missing and in some situations you even had choices to alter the storyline a bit.

[h1][i]Resident Evil 3[/i] feels rushed and unfinished, sometimes even lazy. I had my fun but after the awesome [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] remake I felt like the developers left me in [i]Raccoon City[/i] to die.[/h1]

Resident Evil 3 : By Triple F

The 2020 remake of "Resident Evil 3" by Capcom offers a modern, action-packed reimagining of the 1999 classic, revisiting Jill Valentine’s harrowing escape from a crumbling Raccoon City. Released on the heels of the successful "Resident Evil 2" remake, "Resident Evil 3" aims to capture the terror and intensity of its original while updating graphics, mechanics, and storytelling to align with modern standards. The result is a thrilling experience that emphasizes faster gameplay and cinematic moments but sacrifices some of the depth and exploration that made its predecessor so engaging.

In terms of visuals, "Resident Evil 3" shines, using Capcom’s RE Engine to deliver impressive, realistic graphics that bring Raccoon City to life in disturbing detail. From abandoned streets to dimly lit corridors, each location captures a sense of decay and danger, immersing players in the nightmare. Jill Valentine’s character model is updated with a practical, grounded look that reflects her status as a battle-hardened survivor, and her interactions with Carlos Oliveira and the members of Umbrella’s Biohazard Countermeasure Service add personality and weight to the story. The level of detail in both character models and environmental design amplifies the horror, making every area feel immersive and foreboding.

The gameplay in "Resident Evil 3" leans into an action-oriented approach, distinguishing itself from the slower, more methodical pace of "Resident Evil 2." Jill is agile, equipped with a dodge mechanic that adds a satisfying layer to combat by allowing skilled players to avoid enemy attacks and counter with precision. The combat itself is polished, with a variety of weapons available to handle hordes of zombies, as well as more lethal creatures like Hunters and the ever-present Nemesis. This faster-paced gameplay, while exciting, edges the game closer to action-horror, reducing some of the tension associated with traditional survival horror, where every encounter is meant to feel weighty and dangerous.

Nemesis, one of the franchise’s most iconic antagonists, serves as the heart of "Resident Evil 3," relentlessly pursuing Jill through Raccoon City. While Nemesis appears in scripted sequences rather than dynamic encounters, his presence is still formidable, forcing players into intense, high-stakes confrontations. His adaptability, like using tentacles to ensnare Jill or even wielding a rocket launcher, creates thrilling encounters that keep players on their toes. However, some fans of the original may miss the unpredictability of his appearances, as the scripted nature of these moments makes him feel more like a series of set-pieces than a constant, looming threat.

"Resident Evil 3"’s focus on linear progression over exploration marks a departure from the layered design of "Resident Evil 2." While there are some opportunities for backtracking and finding optional items, the game primarily pushes players through a sequence of high-stakes moments, emphasizing pace over environmental complexity. This streamlined approach makes the game feel more action-driven, with less emphasis on puzzle-solving and resource management. Although this structure keeps the momentum high, some players may find that it limits the game’s sense of discovery and depth, as exploration and puzzle elements have traditionally been a core part of the Resident Evil experience.

Despite its strengths, "Resident Evil 3" has a notably short campaign, clocking in around five to six hours for most players, even on a first playthrough. While the game’s pacing is tight, the shorter length may leave some players wanting more, especially when compared to the more robust content in "Resident Evil 2." To address replay-ability, Capcom included “Resident Evil Resistance,” a 4v1 multiplayer mode where one player acts as the mastermind, setting traps and controlling zombies to thwart four survivors. While Resistance offers an interesting twist on multiplayer horror, it doesn’t quite compensate for the brevity of the main campaign, particularly for fans seeking a deeper single-player experience.

Overall, "Resident Evil 3" (2020) is an intense, visually stunning remake that successfully modernizes the original’s action-horror thrills. While it lacks the slower-paced, exploration-heavy elements of previous titles, it delivers an adrenaline-fueled journey through Raccoon City, packed with memorable encounters and cinematic moments. For fans who appreciate the franchise’s evolution toward more action-oriented gameplay, "Resident Evil 3" is a worthwhile experience. However, those who miss the intricate puzzles and open-ended exploration that define the series’ roots may find this installment falls short of the classic survival horror formula.

Resident Evil 3 Remake: A Thrilling Dash Through Raccoon City’s Doom (And Jill’s Denim Excellence)

Capcom’s Resident Evil 3 Remake takes us back to Raccoon City for another pulse-pounding fight against the undead, with a protagonist whose courage—and curves—can’t be stopped. Jill Valentine isn’t just running from Nemesis; she’s running straight into action, armed with a Glock, an attitude, and a rear view so iconic it deserves its own credit in the ending sequence.

Plot: Zombies, Explosions, and a Clock Ticking Toward Inevitable Obliteration
The story kicks off with Jill attempting to escape Raccoon City’s zombie apocalypse while being hunted by Nemesis, a bioweapon so persistent it makes your clingiest ex look like a saint. As she dodges zombies, lickers, and an absurd number of explosive barrels, Jill’s fight for survival feels like a race against the inevitable—because let’s face it, Raccoon City’s ultimate fate is less a mystery and more a foregone conclusion.

Yes, the nuke is coming. The only question is whether you can outrun it—and let’s be real, if anyone can sprint through an apocalypse while looking that good, it’s Jill Valentine.

Gameplay: Tight Action, Tighter Jeans
The remake leans hard into action, with combat that feels punchy and fluid. Dodging Nemesis’s tentacle attacks? Thrilling. Watching Jill roll out of the way with precision that somehow highlights her impeccable jeans? Unfairly captivating.

The addition of a perfect dodge mechanic gives you a split-second opportunity to avoid danger—while also giving players plenty of moments to appreciate Jill’s, uh, tactical flexibility. Let’s just say Capcom’s RE Engine is working overtime, both in horror and posterior rendering.

Nemesis: The Ultimate Simp
Nemesis is an unrelenting force, smashing through walls and chasing Jill like he’s auditioning for a horror-themed dating show. But despite his monstrous presence, there’s something almost comical about how laser-focused he is on one woman. Maybe he just appreciates Jill’s, let’s say, well-rounded skill set.

Of course, his boss battles are nerve-wracking, but they pale in comparison to the sheer tension of hearing him mutter “STARS” from somewhere just out of sight. (Pro tip: If Nemesis ever looks like he’s about to swing that rocket launcher, just assume there’s another explosion inbound. Seriously, who gave this guy so many explosives?)

Deep Joke: A Nuclear Pun

Why is Jill always calm under pressure?
Because she knows no matter what happens, the nuke will clean up the mess.
Raccoon City: A Doomed Playground
The setting is beautifully realized, though every alley and sewer reeks of inevitable destruction. You’ll explore the city’s ruins, from neon-lit streets to Umbrella’s grimy labs, but the sense of impending doom never fades. It’s like window-shopping for chaos, knowing everything’s going to be in flames by morning.

Character Chemistry: Jill and Carlos, the Odd Couple
Carlos Oliveira, Jill’s backup (and occasional flirt partner), adds some levity with his banter. His mop of perfect hair and cheesy one-liners contrast beautifully with Jill’s no-nonsense determination. But let’s not kid ourselves: Jill is the star here, carrying the game with her grit, wit, and gravity-defying wardrobe choices.

Graphics: Explosions and... Attention to Detail
The RE Engine once again proves its mastery, rendering every explosion, shambling zombie, and perfectly placed pocket on Jill’s jeans with astonishing detail. Even as the city burns and Nemesis roars, you can’t help but notice how well everything is... constructed.

Final Thoughts: A Blast in More Ways Than One
Resident Evil 3 Remake is a thrilling rollercoaster through chaos, destruction, and some very memorable... visuals. Jill Valentine cements her place as one of gaming’s most badass (and fabulously dressed) heroines, while Raccoon City’s demise provides the perfect backdrop for both heart-pounding action and a few cheeky laughs.

Play it for the tight gameplay, the cinematic destruction, and Jill’s, ahem, unparalleled determination. And remember, no matter how fast you run, the nuke always wins in the end. But hey, at least Jill looks amazing doing it.

There's severely little actual game in RE3make. The actual gameplay, when you get to play, is good. It's basically the same as RE2make. But they just do some really terrible things.

The worst offender is without a doubt the neverending cutscenes. There are 21 cutscenes in the tutorial bit alone, and they just keep on going throughout the game. The problem with these cutscenes are that they interrupt the actual gameplay. You play for one minute, then a cutscene starts playing and don't let you play. Then you play for another two minutes, and then there's another cutscene that starts playing, and that one might be followed directly by another cutscene.

There are different variants: The full cutscene that is obviously a cutscene, the seamless cutscene where it seems as if you're still playing but you can let go of the controller(and even skip it), and the "walk and talk" cutscene where you can only walk(not run or interact) while the characters talk to each other(skippable if they talk over the radio).

The game just keeps taking the controls away from you, over and over again, because it wants to show you instead of letting you actually interact. I'm pretty sure there are more minutes of setpieces and story cutscenes than actual gameplay. Whomever was in charge of this game wanted to make a movie, not a game.

The nosdive for this game is so weird after seeing the amazing RE2make. At least it seems they fixed this with RE4make.

I also want to mention how there are certain things programmed into the game that you just might not see because it's the game is short. I don't mind a short game, but did you know the Hunters can randomly leap onto a wall and jump down again to avoid your attacks as part of their movement, and they've got iframes when doing so? I didn't get to see that until my THIRD playthrough! But that's the cost of making the game so short, stuff gets underutilized, and cool work doesn't get to shine. Another cool one was the placement of an extra Licker while playing as Carlos in the RCPD station, and if you're not aware of it or not careful enough it can cinematically(without being an actual cutscene) leap from its position in the ceiling and towards you, and it was one of the coolest moments in the game - even if it killed me! But almost no one's gonna see that because only a handful will play on that difficulty. Not to mention how underutilized the dogs are in the game.

And finally, let's talk about that terrible final boss! The idea and general design for how the boss fight works is fine, I love a good puzzle boss fight. But execution is quite bad. Because the entire boss fight is all about dodging - a secondary, optional game mechanic! And the boss is so fast and deals so much damage that on every difficulty mode it's a sudden jump in difficulty! When you get to him it almost feels like you need to relearn the game. On Nightmare and Inferno he's absolutely ridiculous too, to the point where it's not even fun. You're not fighting the actual Nemesis, you're just fighting the RNG. And that's just frustrating. Having to do perfectly timed dodges up to nine times in a row(yes, nine!), with varying and random timing for each of those attacks, is absolutely ridiculous! And if you get hit once, even if that doesn't kill you you're dead anyway because the next attack comes so quickly it's not possible to go into the menu and heal. 

It doesn't help that it's also obviously balanced for use with the unlockable items from the points shop, which ruins the fun of that as well. Sure, there are some crazy good people out there that can do it without, but there are also people who can beat Dark Souls on level 1, with only starting equipment, taking no hits, all whilst using a dance mat for a controller. And honestly, I probably would've been able to do that easier than fighting this boss on Nightmare.

What I'm saying is that the final boss Nemesis is badly programmed. Really, really bad. And I'm not even gonna mention the articial playtime inflation with the long walkway you need to walk, which often takes longer than how long you actually get to fight the boss, every time you die...

Also, what they did with the "You want STARS?! I'll give you STARS!" line was a crime.

As a fan of the series, I found the Resident Evil 3 remake to be an enjoyable, though somewhat underwhelming, experience. It’s a beautifully crafted game with intense moments and a great protagonist in Jill Valentine. The action-packed sequences are exciting, and Nemesis is genuinely terrifying, but the game doesn’t quite reach the same heights as the Resident Evil 2 remake. The shorter runtime and the omission of certain sections from the original game left me wanting more. While the combat is engaging, the focus on action over survival horror detracts from the atmosphere of dread that defined earlier games. That said, it’s still a solid entry in the franchise and worth playing, especially for fans of the series or those who enjoy action-horror titles.

Story: 6/10

The Resident Evil 3 remake revisits the harrowing events of Jill Valentine's desperate escape from a city overrun by the T-virus. Taking place shortly before and after the events of Resident Evil 2, it places players in a chaotic Raccoon City, teeming with infected creatures. Jill's mission is simple—survive the relentless onslaught of zombies and other biological horrors unleashed by the Umbrella Corporation. One of the standout elements of the story is the Nemesis, an unstoppable bioweapon tasked with hunting down Jill. While the narrative itself stays true to the core elements of the original 1999 game, some sections feel more streamlined, with notable cutbacks to certain areas, especially in comparison to the expanded scope of the Resident Evil 2 remake.

Graphics: 8.5/10

Visually, Resident Evil 3 is stunning. Built using the RE Engine, the game delivers photorealistic environments, highly detailed character models, and some truly grotesque creature designs. The decaying streets of Raccoon City are brought to life with striking lighting effects, dynamic weather changes, and a grimy, apocalyptic atmosphere. The animations are fluid, and Jill’s facial expressions, along with those of the supporting cast, are rendered with remarkable fidelity, enhancing the emotional weight of key moments. From burning cars to decaying storefronts, every corner of the city feels meticulously crafted. However, some areas seem to lack the detail and interactivity present in Resident Evil 2, making parts of the city feel more like backdrops rather than immersive spaces.

Sound: 10/10

Sound design plays a crucial role in Resident Evil 3, and it’s executed masterfully. The unsettling ambiance keeps players on edge, from distant moans of zombies to the heavy footsteps of Nemesis chasing you. The soundtrack ramps up during key action sequences, heightening the tension, while more subdued tracks help emphasize the isolation and dread. Nemesis’ guttural roars are particularly terrifying, making his presence feel even more menacing. The voice acting is also solid, with Jill and Carlos delivering believable performances that elevate the cutscenes. The game strikes a good balance between action-heavy sound effects and atmospheric horror.

Gameplay: 5/10

The gameplay in Resident Evil 3 takes a more action-oriented approach compared to its predecessor. Jill is highly mobile, with a quick dodge mechanic that’s vital for avoiding enemy attacks and Nemesis’ deadly assaults. The game places a stronger emphasis on fast-paced combat, offering players a wider arsenal of weapons. The introduction of Nemesis as a persistent threat is both exhilarating and nerve-wracking, but many felt his appearances were more scripted compared to the dynamic nature of Mr. X in Resident Evil 2. Puzzle-solving, a staple of the series, is still present, but much of it is simplified, which might disappoint fans who enjoyed the more elaborate puzzles of earlier entries. While the core mechanics feel tight and satisfying, the game’s short length (around 5-6 hours for a first playthrough) and lack of exploration in comparison to Resident Evil 2 is a noticeable drawback.

Replay Value: 5/10

Resident Evil 3 has moderate replay value. While the main campaign is short, players can unlock various costumes, weapons, and concept art by completing different difficulty levels and earning points through in-game challenges. The unlockables add some incentive to replay the game, and for those who enjoy mastering difficult encounters, the tougher difficulty settings offer a more intense experience (except for the last boss encounter on Inferno, which is completely dependent on RNG and thus a major frustration point). However, unlike Resident Evil 2, which featured two different playable characters with intersecting but separate storylines, Resident Evil 3 only follows Jill’s perspective, limiting the variety of narrative outcomes and scenarios.

★ Overview:
• Resident Evil 3 (Remake) is a remake of the iconic survival horror game Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, first released in 1999. In this remake, Capcom continues to use the highly successful RE Engine, which was also used for Resident Evil 2 (Remake), to enhance the graphics and gameplay mechanics, delivering a modern experience while retaining the essence of the Resident Evil series.

★ Story:
• The storyline of Resident Evil 3 takes place concurrently with the events of Resident Evil 2, as Raccoon City is destroyed by the outbreak of the T-virus, released by the Umbrella Corporation. Players follow Jill Valentine, a former member of the S.T.A.R.S. special forces, as she fights to survive Raccoon City and confronts the main antagonist, Nemesis—a massive bioweapon sent by Umbrella to eliminate all S.T.A.R.S. members. The story not only focuses on survival but also reflects on Umbrella Corporation's cruelty and their dark conspiracy.

★ Graphics and Design:
• Resident Evil 3 boasts exceptional graphics thanks to the power of the RE Engine. Raccoon City, in its state of chaos, is vividly recreated with detailed lighting, shadows, and lively environments. Character details, especially Jill and Nemesis, are meticulously designed, from facial expressions to movements. The game's locations, from the ruined streets to Umbrella's laboratories, create a tense atmosphere that evokes a constant sense of danger.

★ Gameplay:
• The gameplay in Resident Evil 3 leans more towards action compared to Resident Evil 2. Jill is equipped with more weapons and has increased agility, making the game faster-paced. One standout feature is the dodge mechanic, allowing players to quickly react to enemy attacks, adding more strategic depth.

• The main enemy, Nemesis, is one of the most remarkable aspects of the game. It can appear at any time, relentlessly hunting players, which builds a continuous sense of tension. Each encounter with Nemesis feels different, as it introduces new attack patterns and evolves, keeping players on their toes.

• However, the game's downside is its relatively short playtime, around 5-7 hours, and the lack of challenging puzzles compared to previous entries. This shifts the game more towards action rather than the classic survival horror elements that long-time fans cherish.

★ Sound:
• The sound design in Resident Evil 3 truly enhances the horror experience. The haunting music and realistic sound effects amplify the unease. Nemesis' footsteps or the sounds coming from creatures in the city contribute to the game's tense and oppressive atmosphere.

★ Additional Mode - Resident Evil: Resistance:
• A new feature in Resident Evil 3 is the multiplayer mode Resident Evil: Resistance. This is a 4vs1 mode, where four players try to escape various stages while being hindered by another player, known as the Mastermind, who sets traps and summons monsters. Although the concept is interesting, Resistance lacks depth and faces some balancing issues.

★ Pros:
• Outstanding graphics with a vibrant environment.
• Nemesis is a terrifying and impressively designed antagonist.
• Smooth gameplay focused on action.
• Excellent sound design and music.

★ Cons:
• Short playtime with few challenges.
• Lacks some traditional puzzle elements of Resident Evil.
• Resident Evil: Resistance isn't particularly remarkable.

★ Conclusion:
• Resident Evil 3 (Remake) is an intense action-horror game with fantastic graphics and exciting combat mechanics. However, it lacks the survival horror elements and puzzle depth that fans may have expected. It offers an engaging experience for those looking for a fast-paced, thrilling action game but might not fully satisfy long-time fans hoping for more of the classic horror aspects of the series.

In my RE2R review I called it a 're-imagining' more than a remake because of the changes in content from the original. Well, if that was a 're-imagining' of it's source material then this is a different game altogether. Whereas RE2R re-arranged some areas and expanded some material (Mr. X), RE3R simply cuts cuts cuts cuts cuts. 

	And there's two ways to digest this game. So let's start with the most flattering: without reference to it's source material. 

	As a game on its own it's visually as stunning as RE2R, with just as enjoyable a hunt for key items in modestly sized maps. Zombies all around, with (somewhat) sparse ammo. The story moves at a brisk pace, with Nemesis showing up at times to heighten the action. There's really not much new to say that wasn't said in my RE2R review since this plays identical. Which isn't wild given that it was developed concurrently with RE2R. The PS1 original was action-oriented, and this carries that spirit.

	There's nothing intrinsically wrong with this game when viewed in a vacuum. It's on the short side, but that doesn't make a game bad by default. I wish the city map was larger, and I wish the gun powder mixtures had more than just three mixes. A larger presence to Nemesis would've been nice, but there's nothing I'm really missing here. His action scenes are frantic and well directed.

	Now, let's digest this game as a remake of RE3 on the PS1. Let's dig deep.

	The biggest sin that would make a decent number of people write this off as a failure is changing Nemesis from a constant danger to only appearing during scripted 'run away' scenes. In the original, Nemesis appeared during scripted events, and patrolled certain areas of the map randomly. This gave his appearances a semi-randomness that created constant tension. And because of the static camera angles, when he DID show up you would hear him before seeing him. Given that he's faster than the player, hearing his theme and roar when you enter a room was always frightful. 

	This contrasts to Mr. X in the original RE2, who only showed up in (infrequent) scripted events. Nemesis was an evolution of the 'chase the player' idea. When they remade RE2 they applied the enhancements of Nemesis onto X, making him a constant threat in search of you. But when it came to remaking 3, they downgraded Nemesis to the PS1 original Mr. X game design. He shows up far less frequently, and when he does it's a heavily scripted (and linear) 'run away' sequences.

	Now, the scenes are fine on their own. They look fantastic and provide a challenge. But, again, when viewing it as a remake of 3 it's a total downgrade. I can appreciate X being enhanced in the remake, but he was never crucial to RE2. When it comes to 3, Nemesis is crucial. His name was in the title, after all.

	In the original, the scripted Nemesis appearances often gave the player two choices in how to confront the threat. Time would slow substantially, colors would invert, and you'd be presented with one of two options. You take your pick and the cutscene would play out accordingly. It wouldn't have been difficult to include this, even in a more 'interactive' manner (have the player actually do the thing instead of selecting it in a menu). But I can't say it ruins much. Still, cut content is cut content.

	Moving away from Nemesis and onto the map, they cut a decent chunk of the original areas away. No Clock Tower section at all. RC City Hall is cut (the area behind the gates that looked more like a garden). Graveyard is gone, as is the Park (both areas towards the end). The Dead Factory (the final area) is gone. A lot of the buildings in the city have been removed as well. The Newspaper building is gone, as is the Diner (both locations which had a Nemesis encounter/story content). No gas station (well, it appears in a cutscene). Many of the alleyways and interiors are gone, with their story elements altered or placed elsewhere. 

	To the game's credit, certain sections have been expanded. Previously the Diner had a hatch that led to the sewers. It was a short section, but here it's been expanded into its own map. The hospital section has like-wise received a large expansion. There's a construction site/burning building that is the site of a Nemesis fight now. As well as a NEST lab for the finale. 

	What has happened here is that the story has had a lot of alterations, and it seems like a lot of these decisions were made in accordance with that. The game has more 'action' scenes and 'run-away' maps, which reduce the length of sections in the original or string them together (with heavy alterations). Most noticeably the intro, which has you run through a diner and meet Brad within a brisk 10 minutes. In the original Brad and his death happened over multiple encounters. 

	To its credit, the story is tighter now. In the original Jill was sort of running around until the rail card, which gave her a concrete story objective. You went to RCPD for no real reason other than to get a paperclip. There's more purpose and objectives to everything now. So it's not ALL bad.

	This game was outsourced to a few development houses. You don't usually do that unless the game is a massive undertaking or you're trying to get it out the door quickly for a low price. Supposedly this game was 'developed alongside RE2R', but given the cuts its reasonable to assume that the 'A-Team' worked on RE2R and this received less attention. A shame. But also impressive that the game is as competent as it is. Like I said, without looking at it as a remake it's not a bad game.

	And that's the final verdict on the game. It's really a good game on its own. But as an opportunity to remake 3, it fumbles constantly. It's a good and enticing retelling of the original. Laudable. But as compared to the original so much is missing. The original was more 'action' leaning, but it still had puzzles. I don't remember a single puzzle in the remake. 

	So I'm very much in the middle of it all. I enjoyed my time, I just know it could've been much more. Sometimes a missed opportunity is worse than a bad product, because you think of what could've been.

A great game, yet a very disappointing 'remake' at the same time. 

If this is your first experience with RE3, you'll probably enjoy this game. If you're coming from the original 1999 version, you will likely be disappointed. Unfortunately, since Capcom is billing this game as a remake of RE3 '99, I have to say they missed the mark. 

I do not understand why the dev team decided to jump the shark on this remake. In the RE:1 & 2 remakes, they kept most of the core material intact, and added/modernized as needed. Here, the team decided to completely redo the story, and removed critical game components that made the OG version so special.  Even worse, we didn't even get much in return. Sure, the updated graphics, game-play mechanics (I'm loving the updated 'perfect dodge' mechanic!) voice acting, etc. -- it's all here and is great! Unfortunately, all of this shine simply cannot replace the substance that RE3 '99 had.

It's a damn shame, really, as this a beautiful, competently made (the enemy tethering ranges are pretty janky and easy to abuse, though), and, most importantly, fun game; however, it stings all the more because I know the RE engine could have really fleshed out all the great ideas they had back in '99. Now, we may never see this happen.

How ironic: Capcom had intended for RE3 '99 to be a mere placeholder side-story. Surprisingly, it far-exceeded expectations, and earned that '3' in its title. This 'remake' seems to have removed a good amount of the magic from the original game, rendering us with that 'run-of-the-mill' vision they likely had back then - a baffling outcome, considering they had over 2 decades to prepare.

I adore the Resident Evil franchise, and I've held off on leaving a review for this game since it originally released. I was very disappointed at that time, but for the sake of fairness I decided I'd replay it later. Over 4 years later, I just got around to it. It's as big a letdown now as it was then.

The good things:
- The combat and mechanics have been slightly improved since RE2r. The dodge/counter mechanic is fun.
- Carlos went from an obscure character from the old days to easily the best character in this particular game.
- The RE engine looks amazing as always, though my computer isn't quite good enough to make the game reach its potential.

The bad things:
- The writing behind Jill was really underwhelming. The team made her fit into the "girl-boss" trope, which doesn't resemble her other iterations at all. I'm a huge fan of RE5, and the Jill we get in that game is unrecognizable from this one. Here, Jill is unlikable, arrogant, and largely incompetent. 
- Largely to push the same narrative that encouraged the version of Jill we got, the male characters are also deeply unlikable. They come off as misogynistic muscle bags with very shallow motivations. The only two characters who escape this are Kendo and Carlos.
- Nemesis is not a threat, really. The Tyrant from RE2r was far more interesting as a "stalker" type enemy. This iteration of Nemesis feels more like the Ustanak from RE6, yet somehow lamer. He appears every now and then to be an unkillable obstacle, but you can just avoid him relatively easily.
- A metric ton of content was cut from the original game. Entire levels, interactions, puzzles, and characters. I had never played the original, but even I was able to tell that a lot was missing. I originally bought this game at full price on the xbox one, $60. This really feels like it should've been a $20 DLC for RE2r.

The in-the-middle things:
- This game feels more like Army of Two than any Resident Evil I've played. I adore RE1 through RE8 all for different reasons, so I'm okay with gameplay variety. If you're looking for horror or suspense, you will not find it here. I'd recommend some of the other games in the franchise for that.
- The difficulty is strange. On any difficulty, you'll find that lesser enemies scale as you'd expect, but there are certain times where you will die to one-shot moves that were basically just born from bad luck. RE2r had the same issue, and they both suffer from bizarre hitboxes and hurtboxes. It isn't the worst thing, and sometimes it can work to your advantage, so... it's whatever.


If you want this game, please make the most out of sales and discounts. Even at the reduced $40, it is not really worth it.

Hope that helps!


[Edit: After posting this review, I decided to 100% the game's achievements. I found that playing through the game on the hardest difficulty was pretty fun, and I personally recommend trying out different voice languages on each run. Chinese Jill is adorable!]

When I first dove into Resident Evil 3 Remake, the stunning graphics immediately caught my attention. The RE Engine brings Raccoon City to life with impressive detail, and Jill Valentine’s updated design is both modern and tough. However, as beautiful as the game is, I was left feeling a bit shortchanged by its brevity. The campaign wrapped up in under six hours, leaving me wanting more substance, especially for a full-priced game.

The biggest letdown was Nemesis. In the original, he was an unpredictable, ever-present threat. Here, his encounters feel more scripted, which diminishes the tension. I found myself waiting for his appearances rather than fearing them. The pacing, too, felt rushed, with certain sections—like the hospital and final battle—feeling too short and action-heavy, leaving little room for the atmospheric, slower-paced horror I expected.

While the combat is tight, with Jill’s dodge mechanic adding some strategic depth, the game leans more toward action than survival horror. It doesn’t quite capture the same tension as Resident Evil 2 Remake. Ultimately, while RE3 Remake is polished and fun, it doesn’t live up to the original’s legacy, leaving me wishing for a longer, more tension-filled experience.

I think everyone is already aware of this, especially those who care about the original game.

This is kind of not a remake. It's not a "reimagining" or "modernization" of the old game, like 2 was. 

The game simply received the same name for continuity reasons. It makes use of the characters and a slightly approximate story, but has little or nothing to do with the original experience.

So while old fans may feel slightly disappointed by the far less thoughtful and satisfying approach that the previous game presented, new fans will probably feel quite comfortable with this experience.

It is obviously a much inferior game compared to 2, with a much less interesting and engaging level design and progression, more focused on action and set-pieces than on methodical choices.

All games in the franchise, since the first, have this power fantasy curve, in which the game goes from an oppressive and terrifying horror (more or less), from having few resources and feeling very vulnerable, to complete overcoming this feeling, becoming a superhero of an over the top action film, with a ridiculous arsenal and complete control over his enemies. You start by stabbing and dumping ammo to kill basic enemies that take forever to die and end by blowing up giant abominations with rocket launchers and hand cannons.

In this spirit, Resident Evil 3 is a continuation of the mental and mechanical state in which you end Resident Evil 2. It's not like you start the game with a full arsenal, and the game doesn't skip that curve either, but it clearly expects you to follow a more straightforward and faster pace. They kind of expect you to already be in the spirit of blowing some heads off and move foward. They don't want you to think too much about what you are doing and where you are going.

They even give you the ability to dodge with several levels of execution. For the most daring players to stay right in the face of danger, capitalizing on the benefits of landing critical damage after perfect dodges.

Ammunition still needs to be relatively conserved, but it's way more forgiving. There comes a point where if you play the game too well, you might start thinking it's a good idea to shoot at ammo crates to speed things up.

The boss fights are pretty cool, though. Nemesis fulfills its symbolic role here, even if its usage is a bit disappointing.

And on higher difficulties, the game brings that DMC flavor, with repositioned enemies and new challenges to encourage another round. You definitely need to play the game on Nightmare to have the best experience.

It helps that the game is shorter, too. So if you're already more than saturated from playing the second one, Resident Evil 3 isn't a bad choice.

It's not the most rewarding of the package, and I still prefer the original over this one, but it's still a very competent game. Overall, the game is pretty solid, but it feels like a higher budget dlc.

The only problem I had (And it's a big one), that prevents me from wanting to replay it more times, is that the sound of anything behind my character seems muted no matter what configuration I use. This makes it incredibly difficult to play some parts reliably, especially in the scripted chase sequences against Nemesis.

I literally had to run while looking back if I wanted to have a chance to dodge the giant titan coming at me at 200kmh without making a single sound.

Other than that, while the music is decent, the sound design seems to have suffered quite a bit. Weapons sound like a bunch of stock sounds and the soundscape is pretty poor, with almost no layers at all.

Just compare the sound of this game with the previous or with 7 or the ones that came after to see that something wrong happened behind the scenes.

But, anyway, it's recommended. 

Don't set high expectations for the game, and you'll have fun. It's far from the best, but also far from the worst.

P.S: GOG is bringing the original back. 1 and 2 have already been released. If you've never played the original and don't turn your nose up at old graphics (something that I find inconceivable in this era of indies), do yourself a favor and play it.

Title: A Stunning Revival - Resident Evil 3 Remake

Resident Evil 3 Remake is a masterful reimagining of the classic 1999 survival horror title, and it has undoubtedly set a new standard for remakes in the gaming industry. From the moment you launch the game, you are greeted with an atmospheric blend of tension, action, and nostalgia that makes this experience feel both fresh and familiar.

Visuals and Atmosphere:
First and foremost, the graphics are nothing short of breathtaking. The environments are richly detailed, from the ruined streets of Raccoon City to the eerie corridors of the Nemesis’ lair. The lighting effects create an immersive ambiance that heightens the horror elements, making you feel every shadow creep and every unsettling noise in your bones. The character models are incredibly lifelike, and both Jill Valentine and Carlos Oliveira are portrayed with depth and nuance, perfectly capturing their roles in the story.

Gameplay Mechanics:
The gameplay in Resident Evil 3 Remake strikes a superb balance between action and classic survival horror elements. The controls are intuitive, making it easy to maneuver through tense situations while still offering a satisfying challenge. The introduction of the dodge mechanic elevates the gameplay, allowing for nail-biting encounters with enemies. Facing off against the iconic Nemesis is a highlight, as he tracks Jill relentlessly and forces players to adapt their strategies on the fly. These intense chase sequences are adrenaline-pumping and are beautifully crafted to keep you on the edge of your seat.

Story and Character Development:
The narrative in Resident Evil 3 Remake is compelling, with a well-paced storyline that expertly weaves together action and lore. Jill’s character development is particularly noteworthy; you get to witness her transformation from a survivor to a determined fighter. The voice acting is superb, with notable performances that add depth to the storytelling. The dialogue is sharp, and the interactions between characters feel genuine, adding to the emotional stakes of the game.

Sound Design and Music:
The sound design plays a crucial role in establishing the atmosphere of fear and dread throughout your playthrough. From the distant growls of zombies to the heavy footfalls of Nemesis, every sound is meticulously crafted to enhance the experience. Coupled with a haunting soundtrack that dynamically shifts with the gameplay, Resident Evil 3 Remake delivers a fully immersive audio experience that keeps you engulfed in tension.

Quality of Life Improvements:
The remake incorporates several quality-of-life improvements that enhance gameplay. The inventory system is streamlined, making it easier to manage your items and ammunition. The addition of safe rooms and map hints helps to alleviate some of the frustration that can come from navigating in survival horror games, allowing players to focus on the horror elements without feeling overwhelmed.

Final Thoughts:
Resident Evil 3 Remake is not just a tribute to its predecessor; it is a bold reinvention that breathes new life into the franchise. It expertly balances nostalgia with fresh gameplay mechanics and delivers an utterly thrilling experience from start to finish. Whether you are a longtime fan or new to the series, this game deserves a spot in your collection. It’s a rollercoaster ride of scares and excitement that will leave you eager for more. Capcom has truly earned its place in the spotlight with this outstanding remake, and it stands as a must-play title for any video game enthusiast.

A remake of the original RE3 game, this game offers gorgeous graphics and immersive audio themes to pull you into the world of Nemesis supremacy. A 3rd person horror-survival-shooter game, the player is able to use a spread of weapons and tools to escape a zombie-infested city before succumbing to the evil around them. 

Combat is centered around careful marksmanship and optimizing specific weapons against certain enemies. Of course, the standard run-and-gun or spray-and-pray styles still work, but will quickly deplete your resources, leaving you awkwardly evading enemies as you try to run around them. 
The dodge mechanic can be a real hit or miss for most players, and should best be used as a panic escape option when enemies are in your face; don't rely on it to get you out of trouble, however (balanced this way I'm assuming), as positioning is your best ally. 

Graphics wise, this game is beautiful, even when turned down in quality. The skin/water sheen appearance in particular is quite attractive, leading to a large number of 'popular' alterations on the web; nevertheless, the character details, actions (maybe not the mouth movements), and environment are all pleasing to say the least. Enemies, too, look quite nice, especially during combat and close-up animations. And the cutscenes, phew. Maybe a little too much budget, but I ain't complaining. The only problem I noted occasionally were long-distance graphics, as they would tear in and out; however, those were often the shadows of building signs or smoke, so not terribly important during your playthroughs. 

Audio wise, a notch above standard, but not spectacularly out there. Different BGM's serve to help immerse the player in a particular environment or game theme, and while the chosen tracks fit the gameplay, they are not 'THE' soundtrack, if you understand what I'm trying to say. Still, quite immersive during the run-throughs, and special shout-out to the electrical plant and hospital areas. 

Quality of life wise, the game is quite generous, offering players plenty of loot and supplies if one was to actually search; the earnable shop rewards are quite fun as well, and almost a requirement on the higher difficulties. Makes the game a bit 'easy' so to speak, but nothing says you HAVE to use those infinite rockets.
Loading sections are quite fast, with many loads often taking place during extended map sections (elevators, long corridors, etc), and menu interactions are basic but straightforward.

Infrastructure wise, the game is quite stable, as I did not experience a single crash or even a bug during my series of playthroughs, and was very consistent with its decently fast loading sections. Maybe a few laggy areas, but very rare, and was often due to auto-saving or a sudden reveal of a large map/enemy. As with most games nowadays, high temperatures are most often the biggest issue, and I was hovering in the 50 degrees Celsius region WHILE on undervolting (I use ThrottleStop). Definitely keep an eye on your PC temps (I use Core Temp) as I am most certain your fans will be running at nearly full speed. 

A somewhat short but very stable Resident Evil, a 'solid' game. Nothing too world-breaking, but this game does its job. Might not win game of the year award, but still fun to play through. In my opinion, immersion is probably this game's strongest suit, but if the devs are reading these: a great job nonetheless, and I look forward to continuing to support your future works.
