I really, really wanted this game to be another grand slam like the RE2 remake. Unfortunately, it falls quite flat in comparison, and is a bit of a disappointment overall.

The RE2 remake was a masterpiece both as its own game, and as a faithful recreation of the original Resident Evil 2. It brought the older fans back and rallied all kinds of new ones as well. It combined amazing graphics, audio, and solid gameplay together into one awesome survival-horror themed package. It had different characters to pick from, each offering the player different perspectives to see the story with as they venture into the depths of hell in Raccoon City. There was a variety of game modes that injected a bunch of fresh content into the game, greatly enhancing replay value..

Blah blah.. point is, that game was amazing. The RE3 remake, on the other hand, is not.

The RE3 remake comes up short even in comparison to the original RE3 - only surpassing it in terms of visuals and sound. Everything else seems to be either pretty lackluster, or completely missing. Sure, the environments are nice to look at, but they offer very little to encourage exploration. For example, there are almost no puzzles in the game this time around. You can turn your brain completely off as you trudge your way through this bland hallway simulator, blowing away one zombie after another. 

Yeah, don't be fooled into thinking this is gonna be another blood-pumping, nail-biting, survival-horror epic just because you've played the other games. This is a generic zombie shooter at best, and there ain't sweet ♥♥♥♥ all to be afraid of here. In the original RE3, Nemesis was one scary ass mofo that kept you on your toes all through the game (like Mr. X in RE2). The new Nemesis feels like a step backwards in both aesthetic design and gameplay function. He has been reduced to a mere annoyance that shows up for a few different story triggers, and gets stomped far too easily.

The story and characters are mostly what you remember from the original RE3, keeping it simple like before. The story starts with Jill getting attacked and chased by the Nemesis monster (which will continue to happen through the game). In an effort to reach safety, she encounters a few folks along the way and ultimately teams up with some umbrella mercenaries. The story becomes about securing the vaccine to the zombie virus and potentially saving Raccoon City, while trying not to get killed by Nemesis in the process. It's a simple plot with simple, boring, one-dimensional characters that don't develop in any real way. Carlos appeared to be the only semi-interesting character, whereas our protagonist Jill Valentine and the main antagonist were about as entertaining as white paint.

Before you know it, the journey comes to an end after like 5-6 hours. Again, where RE2 had lots of replay value.. this has almost none. Hooray, an item shop that lets you start with some basic items. But where are the extra game modes? Where are the alternate story paths? Where are the big decisions and multiple endings from the original? None of that exists here. There is almost no reason to play through this again. 

It just feels so half-assed. Could have been amazing.. what a shame.

Update: 

I did go back and play through this again, giving the game another chance.. but damn, what a waste of time and energy that was. It was just as painfully boring and linear as the first run through. There is absolutely no replay value here.

Additionally, I have since gone back to the original RE3: Nemesis for a playthrough. I wanted to see if it's as good as I remember, or if I was being biased due to nostalgia. Turns out that the original RE3 was even better than I remembered. Seriously, it's so much better than this garbage remake in almost every single way (except graphics and voice acting, obviously, but those are the least important parts of a game anyway). 

So yeah, skip this trash and save your cash! Or play the original RE3 instead :)

Especially given the fact that most of its good qualities and mechanics come from RE2 Remake. It feels more like a DLC or a cash grab - as if someone thought, "hmm, we have most of the gameplay already figured out from RE2, let's just switch character models, throw in a few short locations, assemble some level art and switch difficulties to 5 instead of 3 and voila, the game!"
That's not ok. Such low effort games are NOT to be encouraged. And as someone who hasn't even played the original RE3, I can't even imagine the disappointment of the original fans who were looking for a remake of their beloved title. Throwing in metaphorical scraps to the players is just not alright and I refuse to accept such approach.

The opening sequences of the game show me that - there is no real threat, almost ever, as the chase scene is scripted and only requires the player to literally press "W" for a fraction of a second, for a few times. That being said, I still like it a lot. You might call it a guilty pleasure.

There's a lot to complain about. The new dodge mechanic invalidates classic RE resource management since you just dodge past many monsters who'd force a fight/flight choice before, but it doesn't work as a blastathon like RE4/Desd Space since the action is rarely as consistent. This is all exacerbated by the second third of the game going way overboard on linear set-pieces.

However, when it hits the mark, like in the exploration focused areas (streets, hospital), or some of the more inventive combat scenarios (brainsucker maze, sewers) it's intense and memorable

Overall it suffers most from not being able to decide what it wants to be. Is it smart survival horror or adrenaline pumping action-horror? Devs didn't seem to knoww. But the parts of the game that are inspired and creative still shine through and are worth experiencing despite all the balls it drops.

I love the face model they chose for her, including the voice actress who brought her to life. AND SHOULD I EVEN MENTION HOW A MILLION TIMES HOTTER CARLOS IS NOW?!?!?!

Despite the lack of actual content (lol), the action has been explosive right off the bat -- and this was nothing less of a treat for me (as someone who stopped gaming for more than a decade). Overall, the 3D art and design goodness, the unique cinematography whether in the cutscenes or interactive chase scenes, the semi-awkward but albeit laughable dialogues and one-liners (Carlos, I'm looking at you), the superb voice acting, and all the stress it gave me are what's making it worth recommending nevertheless. I can still reconnect with my younger self replaying RE3:N/B:TLE for the Nth time during my playthrough, and for me that is the most important part. [b]And yes, do NOT buy at full price.[/b] HAHA.

(SPOILERS IN THIS PART ONLY RN!!!!)
Story: Being the new RE fan I am. I haven't played the original for RE3 but according to people there is cut out parts from the original. After completing this in 1 day, I can see that. Overall, they kept the premise of the story line. Zombie outbreak in Raccoon city. Nemesis is hunting down S.T.A.R.S members, Jill is one. She gets hunted down by Nemesis. Meets Carlos. Do a bunch of ♥♥♥♥ to get them out of the city. Now, not everything is cut content. The RPD part is new. I believe the original just had Carlos in the hospital saving Jill and that was the only time you played Carlos, now we have Carlos in RPD then in hospital saving Jill. Nice little add-on to the story there.

Gameplay: It's still RE. Shoot zombies, scavenge, craft, unlock stuff. Boss battles, all that. Coming from RE2 remake, Nemesis is a bit more scripted and linear than Mr X BUT he is more deadlier(More on that later). A lot of the typical ♥♥♥♥ is still recycled. Herbs, spray, zombie behaviour, dogs, lickers. All that ♥♥♥♥ but there are a few different zombie types that they added. First off, pale heads are in this. If you never did 'no way out' or 'runaway' ghost survivors in RE2 then you wouldn't know them. Basically, you need heavy ammo so the pistol that holds MAG ammo. They're annoying but one shot to the head if you have that gun. Shotguns work but they'll get up again soon. Hunters (I believe that's what they're called) of all types are new. The gamma ones in the sewers weren't too annoying, you learn their mechanics pretty easily and you just have to be effective with your attack on them. The betas or whatever ones you'll encounter in the hospitals are..... brutal to say the least. Acid rounds are effective on them but they have a shell on their head that you have to break through so fighting them in NEST was annoying but as Carlos it was fine cause he had the AR so just spray and pray ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

Nemesis: As I have stated, Nemesis is a more scripted and linear Tyrant comapred to Mr X. He is also supposed to be an expansion on Mr X apparently. He doesn't stalk you and hunt you down like Mr X does. He moreso just comes out of nowhere and hunts you down. In saying this, he is WAYYYYYY ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ deadlier than Mr X. Stage 2 boss battle was rough but he can stun-lock you if you aren't dodging his attacks with the quickstep or roll (If you can pull it off.). This will ♥♥♥♥ you as you are pretty likely to die quickly if he stun-locks you. The easiest way to get out of a stun-lock is desperately pressing space and going in a direction. You can only pray if that happens. So Nemesis is and sometimes can be busted. So what? Well, it may be the difference between dying or living so just fair warning. Otherwise, his boss battles are what they're supposed to be. Fun yet challenging, stage 2 boss battle had me going insane ngl.

Carlos: He's hot... what else can I say? jk, I have more to say. Despite his looks, Carlos is surprisingly easier than Jill is imo. He can punch or barge through zombies which can be useful in a one on one or Carlos vs Hunter moment. He's more resistant to damage than Jill is apparently and the horde mode felt very much like something I've seen before just changed to fit the situation. HMMMMMM. Anywho, Carlos is just a good character and his sections were easier than Jill's parts were.

Jill: Now, Jill's graphics and looks wise is hot and that's about all for her graphics. Now, gameplay for Jill is a bit weird. Coming from RE2, I forgot about the roll/quickstep mechanic but it is useful. You might just use it to get past zombies but right click/aim after rolling and you can get a slow-mo headshot on the zombie you rolled past. Pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ epic right? Wait, there's more. She is the ONLY character in this game who can lockpick and cut the chains off to access new areas. I guess it's cause she is the character you use all the time but it is pretty fun. She also gets to use some fun guns and ANOTHER MINIGAME TO CREATE SOMETHING. But it is kind of fun to figure it out so good on you capcom recycling that Idea.

Conclusion: Do I think it's worth the full price? No, get this ♥♥♥♥ on sale because off sale is not worth it. Do I think it's a good game? Yes. I probably will play this over and over again. I do want to see how easy assisted mode is and eventually work my skill level up to do the hardest difficulty which is nightmare I think? I don't know man. If I have to give /10 rating, this game gets a solid 8/10 for me. Obviously cut content, recycled content like zombie behaviour and design, and a more scripted and linear Nemesis, does bring the game down in the ratings. But seeing as it is a 5/10 or over it does get my recomendation. Now gamers, go and enjoy this game while it's on sale. Otherwise, wait until another sale or if you DESPERATELY want it then get it off of sale.

They cut this, they cut that. Yes, but they also expanded other parts. Sometimes for the better, sometimes for the worse.  Take off your nostalgia glasses, y'all are expecting something from RE3 it never was.

I couldn't care less about the missing giant worm boss fight, it was stupid on the PS1. I do care for the missing clock tower, which is a weird level to cut out because the entire plot of RE3 was "reach the clock tower to evacuate". But the thing is, the only reason the clock tower was great on PS1 is that it was the only part of the game that felt like Resident Evil.

RE: Nemesis has never been more than a semi-linear action spin-off that got rebranded to RE3 purely for marketing reasons while the actual third part, Code Veronica, was developed by a larger team exclusively for the Dreamcast. Capcom just took this a step further with the remake with more linearity and more action, even including wave defense sections. Which aren't really exciting, and obviously the opposite of what you want when you expect a traditional RE game. But RE3 has never been a traditional RE game. And people have to audacity to give the remake a thumb down because "it could have been a DLC to RE2" - yes, because that's exactly what RE3 has always been.

Ironically, while I loved RE2 on the PS1 and find its remake inferior (although it's still fun and I replayed it few times), I disliked RE3 on the PS1 but enjoyed the remake. Capcom had a team this time that went into a specific direction right from the start instead of going for some compromise between Resident Evil and not Resident Evil.

It's a very straight forward game that's not very faithful to the source material. There's not much replay value and no Mercenaries mode. It recycles lots of assets from RE2, which it did on the PS1 as well. But there are also entirely new sections that were not in the original game, a side character got expanded, and there are some great cross-references to RE2. Which, for some reason, people are pissed about simply because "uuuhm this wasn't in the PS1 version" yeah no ♥♥♥♥ because the PS1 version was rushed.

There's nothing particularly good about the RE3 remake except that it works and it's fun, and I will say the same about the RE2 remake. If you liked RE2, you'll like RE3 as well, just expect a shorter and more scripted experience.

Also Capcom pls bring back Jill, after over 20 years she's still the coolest protagonist in the series. And remake Code Veronica next.

Resident Evil 3 is the remake to the 1999 game RE 3: Nemesis. Building on the remake of RE2, 3 uses the RE Engine to great effect making a photo realistic survival horror game that plays well and can be unnerving at times. I never played the original 1999 title but from what I have been told this is a poor remake of it. As someone that went into this game fresh I can assure anyone else new to it that it is not a bad game at all. 

RE3 takes the gameplay of 2 but makes it more action oriented just like what the original title did. Jill has access to more ammo, storage, and has a dodge roll mechanic similar to what RE6 introduced. It is an extremely fast paced title that can easily be finished in under 5 hours if you know what you are doing. This is the most unfortunate thing about it due to their apparently being cut levels/boss fights, and the fact that the titular Nemesis no longer appears randomly to stalk you throughout the game. Every time Nemesis appears it is a scripted fight and he can be dispatched if you have enough ammo and no how to confront him during these scenarios. It is by no means bad but it does lower the amount of tension the pursuer creates whenever he appears. The other unfortunate thing about 3 is that it is not a very replayable title like previous games in the past. There is a store that you can buy items post game for a next playthrough but it is not nearly as well thought out as previous titles. 

When it came out RE3 was slightly controversial due to the price point it came out and the lack of content it had. While that may be a valid criticism, in 2023 on sale it can be a very value based title for $5 if you are looking to play something that is horror themed and survival horror.

While I do think Resident Evil 3 is a fun game to play, it's hard not to compare it to the quality and impact of Resident Evil 2. 

Resident Evil 3 is not a bad game. In fact, it's quite a fun experience. But it does not live up to the standards set by Resident Evil 2 in terms of its story, gameplay, or puzzle mechanics.

Here are a few things I noticed during my playthrough:

- The game lacks tension -- ammo is plentiful, save points are everywhere, and the linear nature of the game makes it easy to start over from the nearest save point and only lose a few minutes of progress.
- Nemesis only appears in scripted gameplay moments. And when it does appear, all you usually need to do is run forward from a fixed camera angle. It doesn't hunt you organically like Mr. X does in Resident Evil 2, which I feel drastically takes away from any feeling of pressure or tension. (You can more or less tell when a scripted event is about to take place.)
- Enemies are total bullet sponges (good thing ammo is scattered across every corner of every level.)
- The menu UI feels a fraction of a second slower and less responsive than Resident Evil 2.
- Very few puzzles you have to solve in each level, so there's less backtracking and map familiarization needed to progress.

Bottom line: Resident Evil 3 is a fun action game, but as a survival horror game, it's shallow.

After reading many reviews of RE3, my expectations were exceptionally low for this remake. I am a huge fan of the series, however, so I decided to buy it while it was on sale.

I do get surprised by some reviews. There are things I disagree on. Here is what you can expect:
[b]Game length[/b]: expect 4-5 hours of gameplay your first run. The campaign omits many areas and puzzles from the original RE3 game. 
[b]Graphics[/b]: Very good! 
[b]Difficulty[/b]: as much as some areas could be made more difficult, others WILL offer you a bit of challenge. You WILL die. Several times. 
[b]Ammo[/b]: there is abundance of ammo and you probably won't experience the lingering stress of scarcity that we know and love from RE. 
[b]Backpedaling[/b]: the game is relatively linear for being a RE game, correct. But there IS definitely some optional backpedaling to acquire some upgrades.
[b]Replayability[/b]: you can play the campaign 2-3 times to try to beat your initial game time and complete some achievements. That was fun for me.
[b]Nemesis[/b]: encounters with Nemmy are short lived, yet I would argue that they can be intense sometimes. There is little randomness to his patterns of attack. I can see why this is disappointing for some. But he is still powerful, and will definitely be the reason for some frustration as he will kill you. 

I have now played through the campaign twice, and I think the game has recieved way too much negative critique. As long as you accept that the game is 4-5 hours of gameplay your first run, you will enjoy it. Again, I bought it on sale, so maybe that's why it doesn't bother me as much. Try to view it as a DLC campaign for RE2 and you are good to go. If you want to make it harder, play it on Hardcore.

RE3 Remake uses the same RE Engine from the recent titles of the franchise which means a game with good graphics, nice visual effects and a solid voice acting, all condensed into a modern interface.

And that's it. That's almost all and every possible praisable stuff this game can get. Almost everything else is a tremendous disappointment, especially for the classic fanbase.

First of all, the game itself feels and looks more like a DLC from RE2 Remake and not like an original title since many different elements, from items to enemies and models to ambiences are literally reused in a way. 

The game fails to deliver a tense pace due to a laughable Nemesis whose new model can't compensate for the lack of a good challenge, combined with so many unnecessary cutscenes and missable encounters (including the usually bad boss battles) in-game that are easily solved while throwing a single grenade on him (an example of an absolute disregard for the terror that Nemesis should represent - he drops an item and pauses for a very long time, which is enough for you to kill the other enemies nearby, while collecting all the items scattered around and leaving the area, plus not being chased by him afterwards). If at least the Remake had some of the original good encounters, like the one inside the Raccoon P.D., when Nemesis jumps out of nowhere, breaking into a corridor after shattering a window, a moment that freezes your heart and gives you a sense of desperation and unpreparation, the Remake would've been so much better and well-considered by the players. But no, this kind of moment was stripped away and replaced with some cheap ones where you simply press an action button and concludes the scene, without having to think what to do or where to run. In the Remake, you have many scenarios of tranquility and calmness knowing that Nemesis won't be able to follow you properly or break through many rooms as it should. And speaking of action buttons that concludes some scenes, we don't even have those text boxes giving us the decision about to run or to fight Nemesis we previously had in the original game.

The general exploration was ruined in comparison to the original game due to the removal of puzzles (replaced with uninsteresting ones) and an unexplainable destruction of the original street map: whereas in the original game you could walk through different streets using the connections between them while having some options to get from point A to point B, always with a permanent sense of tension, the general areas on the remake are usually linear and without the same freedom to explore. To clarify this specific point, you pass through many classic places from the original game but you simply cannot visit them here ([spoiler]like the Stagla gas station[/spoiler]) like if they were only referenced to somehow but not really being part of the experience which ends up into a tremendous frustration. The number of areas that were removed from the original game alongside their respective puzzles is enormous.

The recreated personality of Jill is awful (and for many people, her recreated appearence too). Take Leon or Claire from the RE2 Remake for comparison: Leon as a rookie who haven't even had a single day on the academy and Claire as a girl looking for her missing older brother. Jill, by the time, had already fought against hordes of zombies and other monsters in RE1 while unscathed thus being a respected member of S.T.A.R.S Team Alpha (a special division of Raccoon P.D.) who survived all that terror and remained investigating the events soon after. And when you put these 3 characters from the Remakes side by side, Jill falls bland. She looks generic, unmemorable, naive (as seen from some decisions she takes) and unexperienced (even more than Leon and Claire, who are always trying to encourage themselves during RE2 Remake). Every other RE game co-starred by Jill itself have a much better Jill than this one, by default.

The replay value is absolutely non-existent, especially when compared to RE2 Remake and RE: Village (both titles using the same engine, as mentioned before). Since there are many places removed from the original game, there is little to nothing that makes you want to play this Remake again because the experience itself isn't memorable.

Capcom had a great opportunity to create an incredible and cherished remake, even more than RE 2, but instead has created a huge disappointment for much of its fanbase and showed how greedly rushed the Remake was.

RE3R has a bit of a weird reputation. My understanding is that it cut content and mechanics from the original game, creating a linear, streamlined experience that especially stung for the fanbase after the runaway success of RE2R. Now, the only survival horror games I've ever played are the three Resident Evil remakes, so I can't really comment on comparisons to RE3, but I can say that if you expect anything like the police station in RE2R, you will be disappointed. On its own merits though, I think this game rules.

I haven't played the original, but my understanding is that in RE2 Mr. X was a scripted encounter while in RE3 Nemesis stalked you (or seemed to stalk you via programming wizardry) throughout the game. In the remakes, these roles have been switched. Mr. X's thundering footsteps are fully ingrained within me. He's a constant ever-approaching threat, closing onto you as you scurry through the labyrinthine station. Nemesis meanwhile is solely a scripted enemy, appearing during certain story moments and for boss fights throughout the game. This could be disappointing if the scripted scenes were meh. Thankfully, they're all lovely. Nemesis is your guide through and the instigator of the total destruction of Raccoon City, smashing through walls as you run building to building trying to escape. That's the real joy of the game: watching Raccoon City burn. In RE2R, the police station was monumental. I got the feeling, running laps around it to open doors and solve puzzles, that it would last forever. Every block in RE3R by contrast is waiting to be turned to rubble. The methodical pace of RE2R is thus quickened in a more action-focused direction, and you don't stay in any given place for anywhere near as long as in RE2R. Nemesis is coming to blow it up, after all.

The story here is also...really good? Jill, who was a bit of a blank slate in REmake, is really efficiently established here as practically a war journalist. She's close to closing in on Umbrella when she's turned into a reluctant action hero after her entire apartment collapses. Something I noticed in RE2R is that when the writing team expands on the original game into new directions, their writing becomes very strong (e.g. Kendo, a heartbreaking interlude that's unique to the remake). Here they're given even more room to breathe, to their immense benefit. RE3R is a surprisingly nasty story, following Jill as she tries to save who she can, and find any way to hold Umbrella responsible for their crimes, all while running, shooting, and swearing her way through the city. The characters she meets are strongly established and there's plenty of twists as the conspiracy unravels. 

RE3R is more than a different game than RE2R: it's its negative image. This is apparent in its mechanical construction (compare Mr. X's and Nemesis' behaviors, which are a microcosm of the games as a whole) but extends to the thematic core. RE2R's story, for as dark as it got, is still a story about defeating the odds. The ending is downright saccharine as [spoiler]the protagonists was into the sunlight, smiling kid in tow, preserving the innocence of a future age[/spoiler]. By contrast RE3R is downright bleak, with various forces conspiring to derail Jill's efforts, and an ending [spoiler]that legitimately shocked me, as the vaccine's destruction rendered all of her efforts null[/spoiler]. A particular comparison I found interesting as I got to the end is that the motivations for one of RE3R's villains is very similar to those of a fan-favorite in RE2R. Under the warm light of the second remake, the character can find the goodness in themselves and do the right thing. Here, things are less kind. These games take place in the same time frame, sometimes even sharing locations, but they live in different worlds. Playing both games back-to-back, however, they interweave with other, creating a larger understanding of the city and the many forces that drove it (for good or for ill). 

I can understand wanting RE3R to take a different approach. But for what it is, and what it wants to be, it's a home run. RE3R feels like a fully realized version of itself, and for me that's the most I can ask from a game.

If you are expecting a well made remake (Like Resident Evil 2 Remake) you are in for a few surprises. RE3 can't quite live up to its predecessor. Almost everything this game does right is packed in the beginning area of the game (downtown Raccoon City). The game's opening sequence, ammo scarcity, jump scares and constant chases by Nemesis (within Downtown area) are definitely its strongest points. 

Compared to the Good old RE3, some story elements were touched to bring them up to modern standards, which was a good call. On the other hand, I was expecting Nemesis to be more of an ever-present thread, Like RE 2's Mr. X or RE 7's Jack Baker or just like Nemesis was on its original run. 

The developers this time decided to remove a lot of the game's puzzles and a whole bunch of areas from the original ([u]Raccoon City Park, Graveryard, City Hall, Press Office, Clock Tower, Dead Factory[/u]), they also removed the branching paths and different endings based on the player's decision during cutscenes, in addition they also removed "The Mercenaries" and decided to rush Nemesis transformations so you are limited to basically two Chases and 4 boss fight with Nemesis, which is pretty much this game's identity. 

This game can be finished by someone new to the survival horror genre in about 7 hours, normally this short of a run time wouldn't be a problem if the game had different modes/reasons to replay (Like RE2's extra main scenarios) but they are not present. 

TL;DR: This is a visually stunning game updated to modern standards that suffers from [b]A LOT[/b]] of cut content and rushes the player to its ending without any sort of reason to replay it. Do yourself a favor a [b]wait for a sale[/b] before buying this game. 

Overall Score: 8/10

Three words: temper your expectations. Now for 600 more:

Seeing as this is the only easy way to experience the story of 3 on PC, you're kinda stuck with this. Fortunately it's a 'good' game, but has a few issues, though they're easy to look past. If you liked the RE2 remake, it's basically the same kind of modernization/streamlining of the original. At times it was too 'cinematic' and trying to be immersive, and sometimes it feels like you're just walking between in-engine cutscenes. Not a huge problem and only annoying to those who have a pet peeve for this thing. Gameplay/control jank is almost excusable in my opinion since it's a remake of a very old game and it adds to the claustrophobic tightness of the environments.

It looks beautiful and runs great, with only a few some weird visual bugs like zombies outside of your current 'room' moving in a lower frame rate (?). The layouts of certain areas felt like they were designed to waste/pad out your playtime (the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hospital) too. No way I'd replay this because it got a little tedious in some segments (the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ HOSPITAL), even though it was overall very short.

That's my biggest complaint; the length. It's only ~6 or 7 hours long (I have ~11 because I took a shower and ate bagels while the game was running). Having never played the original 3, I can't personally compare the two games, but apparently the original is around that length so I guess that's fine. However I did play the RE2 remake, so it's hard not to compare this game to that one. The RE2 remake was closer to ~14 (first run) or ~20 (Claire 'replay' run) and a solidly great experience. Also, this game is $40 full price and $10 @ 75% off (and it used to never go on sale cheaper than $20 @ 50% until recently). I don't like pulling the dollar per hour comparison much anymore, but its price point lends much higher expectations. It still feels like something is missing. This was extremely obvious with the sewers, like if I sneezed I would have missed it. The thought "it can't be this short in the original game" came into my head frequently, and while I do like shorter games as I get older, I had expectations for another experience like RE2 remake.

Nemesis as a enemy will exist forever in the shadow of RE2's Mr. X. That guy was freaky and felt way more 'real' and dynamic. Even though Nemesis plays basically the same role here, the way he was implemented as an obviously scripted force to curry you between QTE cutscenes made him feel annoying and consequently not scary. Some areas of the game blew ass (most boss fights/encounters, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ HOSPITAL, certain enemies with insta-killing attacks, and the dumbass underground warehouse part). The early game in Raccoon City was good though up until the sewers. Still, no part was GREAT, just good.

And that's kind of where this game sits. On its own it's just good. Which is fine, however the previous remakes for RE1 and RE2 were GREAT, so this one therefore comes across as less than.

None of these concerns are enough to give it a thumbs down, mostly because, and I reiterate, that this is essentially the only easy way to experience the story of 3 on PC. Even still, the game itself is extremely overpriced for its length and the DLC is completely worthless. I mean it feels like a DLC for RE2 almost. If I myself wasn't as aware of these issues before playing, I definitely would have given it a thumbs down. Fortunately there were enough comments and reviews early on complaining about everything I just did, so I waited until I could get this for cheap and went it will lowered expectations. At least I got to look at Jill's butt most of the game.

- can't access menu or gain control of character until certain things play out. Example: if you get bitten by a zombie, you can't immediately open menu and heal, you'd have to wait until the zombie finishes the entire attack animation. So let's say you wait as your character is getting up and recovering but you don't know when the menu is available but you're hoping to open it ASAP by spamming menu. Well that will backfire because you might accidentally close the menu as you spam and in that split second you vulnerable for another attack and thus you die. It's a really frustrating ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanic
- difficulty adjustment (DA) honestly ruins the game. You are essentially punished for playing the game. By picking up weapons, healing, and dealing damage to enemies, DA is increased so certain bothersome enemies like lickers will be more aggressive (run faster, aggro quicker, lunge farther, etc)
- there is no way to pause the game while going through certain animations like being bitten by zombies, grabbed by lickers or ivys, or being punched by Mr. X and while recovering by rolling around on the floor. For a game the emphasizes completion speed, it sucks to make a mistake because of the already ♥♥♥♥♥♥ physics and then have to sit through it before you are able to load up a save point. - because of the wonky physics, you'd have to put a lot of time into practicing but you are also forced to waste time through countless mistakes because of the unpausable animations
-speaking of wonky physics, when you are on the floor recovering, your character doesn't stay in a static spot. Instead you are free wheeling to anything that can push you. Before jumping into a review, I do want to clarify that I thoroughly enjoyed this game despite the amount of cut content from the original game. Looking through lenses of a pair of remake shades, I feel this game [i]was[/i] done justice.

What a fun experience this game is to go through! We FINALLY get to see Jill back in action in modern times, and we also get to see Carlos again, too! Seeing them in RE Engine's fidelity is truly a gift, as we get to see them in a whole new way!

The gameplay, too, is certainly refreshing--we get a pretty nifty dodge mechanic that arguably works better than what was provided to us in the original game. Like the original game, you'll have to have some pretty precise timing in order to really utilize the dodge the most effective way possible; practice it enough and you'll be untouchable!

The biggest, most apparent aspect of the game to me was how action-oriented it is compared to RE2 Remake. While there are many survival horror elements in the game, the focal point certainly comes in the action seen throughout the game. There are SO many points in the game that includes an abundance of explosions and one-liners--not that those aren't a trope in Resident Evil games! While I enjoyed the action sequences, they are certainly more common here than in previous installments.

Given that this release was outsourced, I don't like immediately drawing to the conclusion that this is a "lesser" installment of the remakes. Sure, there's a lot of content that was cut from the remake, I still thoroughly enjoyed playing through it multiple times over! And yeah, I am one of the people that makes the claim that RE3 Remake felt more like a DLC than its own stand-alone release; it does feel quite short. Something that I also think, though, is that the original RE3 was also quite short, being able to complete the game only within a few hours or even under an hour! 

My advice, if you'd like to take it: try to look at the game through the lenses of it being its own game. If you focus too much on comparing it to the orignal, or to other installments, then you're going to be quite biased--and then you might see the game too negatively.

Simply put, just try to take in all of the game, and give it a chance! Play it through first, and then make your own conclusion! Especially since its on sale at the time of writing this review ($10 USD), you can't go too wrong!

This game is good. Not the best Resident Evil of the franchise, but you will have a good time playing Resident Evil 3 Remake.

First, I have to mention that I haven't played the original Resident Evil 3 that came out in 1999. So I will not feel any nostalgia about that game.

The things I want to say about Resident Evil 3 Remake are:

1- Nemesis is fun to fight but it feels underwhelming during the story. Nemesis is a menace just during the first section of the game. After that, you will only encounter him in boss fight arenas. I wish Nemesis had a longer "stalker" phase (such as Mr. X in RE2 or Lady Dimitrescu in RE8). Despite that, I enjoyed really enjoyed being chased by it in the streets, he is way more threatening than the other stalkers from the other Resident Evil games. The boss fights are fun too, maybe it is a little bit too easy to win against his stage 2.

2- The story is short. In my first playthrough, I beat the game in Standard difficulty  in 4 hours, while spending a lot of time exploring the streets and collecting every items. Resident Evil 3 Remake feels like it was being rushed during development. I want to explore more of Raccoon City's streets, sewers, and NEST 2.

3- Almost no puzzles. If I remember correctly, there's one easy puzzle at the beginning of the game when you have to select a valid route for the subway and then, nothing else.

4- It might be controversial but I think this Resident Evil has a good replay value. There are 5 different difficulty modes and the 2 hardest difficulties offers different enemies at different locations. There also are challenges that give you points to spend after completing them. These points can be exchanged for new weapons, more health, more inventory slots, infinite ammo weapons, more damage output, recovery items and more. I beat the game more than 10 times and I'm still having fun finding a new way to beat the game once again.

5- Speedrunning the game is really fun. I'm usually not a fan of speedrunning games but RE3R doesn't have long boring phases as we can have in RE Village with Beneviento's House or Moreau's Reservoir being dull to play after the first time.

6- Some cinematics would have been way better to play than to watch and there are some part of the game in which you just have to press W and press left click once.

7- Visually, this game is beautiful. Resident Evil games doesn't disappoint when it comes to graphism. Jill's and Carlos' looks are great, Nemesis looks like the scary pursuer it is.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 3 Remake is a good game that could have been better. You should really give this game a chance and try it because you will have a great time playing it. Not worth the full price, but worth the €15 RE2R + RE3R bundle when it's on sale!

With the release of the excellent (at least that's what I heard) [i]Resident Evil 7, Capcom[/i] rejuvenated its [i]Resident Evil[/i] franchise. Riding that high, they announced a remake of the franchise's second entry, which delivered the best buttchin in gaming to date. It was also a pretty good survival horror game. So, people craved more, and [i]Capcom[/i] obliged — [i]Resident Evil 3[/i] was next in line for a remake.

The hype for the Carlos curls was real!

[h3][i][b]Promesas incumplidas[/b][/i][/h3]
But come release, not even those beautiful curls managed to alleviate the pain of broken promises for many gamers. Cut content, a shoddily tacked-on multiplayer and disappointing Nemesis implementation, alongside the game's shorter runtime, provided people with sufficient ammo to riddle the game into an exquisite slice of swiss cheese.

Nevertheless, I had fun, even more than with the previous remake.

Yes, cut content is a bummer. But after the credits rolled, that familiar feeling of a premature finish was not present — [b]what and for how long the game giveth was adequate.[/b] I won't waste characters on the [i]Resistance[/i] thing — [b]it's an abomination.[/b] As for Nemesis — [b]I prefer him over the fedora merchant, Mr X.[/b] Yes, his sections are scripted, but that doesn't make them bad. In fact, they were excellent — rapid, packed with action and adrenalin. Best of all, he doesn't become a lame gimmick like the fedora merchant, who you can get away from by [i][b]literally![/b][/i] just walking. Good luck trying that with Nemesis — the dude can run, for god's sake! And some of you lot wanted him to hound you constantly through the game's tight and compact levels? You mental?!

As for the 2-hour runtime memes — [b]they're just that, memes[/b]. It took me 6-7 hours to finish my first run on normal difficulty while exploring every nook and cranny. Why anyone would meme a game for being completable under 2 hours during a freaking speedrun is beyond me. And a fair warning to the [i]long-playtime-is-a-must[/i] merchants — give my review a wide berth. I, too, am equipped with idiotic arguments and will clap back at yours. And that's a pinky promise.

So, with that little rant out of the way, let's talk details.

[h3][i][b]A saucy B action movie[/b][/i][/h3]
The franchise was never known for its exceptional plot quality. Thus, expect man-of-culture cutscene shots, big bulging biceps, SFW tentacle hentai scenes, mesmerizing curls, corny one-liners and over-the-top baddies. But that's fine. The story was never the franchise's métier — [b]that be the gameplay.[/b]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2849873266

One word — [b]I-loved-[i]Resident-Evil-3-Remake's[/i]-combat-much-more-than-the-combat-in-[i]Resident-Evil-2-Remake[/i]-because-you-can-dodge.[/b]

Unlike the stiff and puffy-cheeked Claire, Jill is exceptionally agile, thus able to spring away from zombies looking to take a nibble at her silky smooth skin. As for Carlos — [b]he punches things.[/b] [i]"Why dodge when you can punch stuff?" — sensei Segal, circa 2022[/i]. And while not perfect, I did enjoy this more action-oriented gameplay. The game showers you with ammo and enemies to use them on, many of whom are nimble and close the gap quickly, while others utilize ranged attacks. And boy is the monster roster diverse — many even have insta kill attacks.

So, if you wish to survive, you must polish your PP's — [b]perfect dodge and perfect counter.[/b]

And like how you can put distance between you and your toothless grandma before she gets close to thine cheeks, the dodge mechanic allows you to do the same. This is known as a basic dodge. But grandma's still coming! And now, you're backed into a corner. So, how can we avoid grandam's kiss of death now? That's right — wait for the ideal moment to perform [b]a perfect dodge.[/b] So, wait, wait for those saliva-glazed lips to come so close to your cheeks that you can taste them. And just before your cheeks get caressed — BAM! you dodge out of harm's way. [i]Voila![/i] — a perfect dodge.

But you aren't safe yet. Pacificism won't stop grandma — she'll continue to pursue them cheeks. And you're not athletic and agile enough to keep at this forever. So, it's time we stop grandma — [i]permanently.[/i] To do that, we must utilize [b]the perfect counter[/b], which you perform by readying your weapon immediately after executing a perfect dodge. Doing so, you'll enter a Matrix-like slow-mo state that lasts a couple of seconds as you aim at her wrinkly face. Performing this slick manoeuvre will inflict massive damage to grandma, stopping her in her tracks.

And now, I would like to take a moment and praise another area the addition of the dodge improved — [b]the boss fights[/b]. Lame bosses were one of my main issues with the previous remake. They were slow and had predictable attacks with long wind-up time to give my stiff ass a way to scamper away to safety. I don't want that — I want unpredictable, fast attacks and needing to dodge them, damnit! Thankfully, [i]Capcom[/i] obliged, with the dodge mechanic giving them more freedom when designing the boss fights. And playing on the hardest difficulty, the fun factor and challenge these boss battles provided was amplified tenfold, thoroughly satisfying my masochistic cravings.

The puzzles did receive a downgrade. No more convoluted nonsensical puzzles that make zero sense when you think about it. A heart-shaped lock? A secret door under the giant statue in the main hall opened by three discs, all conveniently located in the police station? None of that big-brain stuff here. [b]It's just normie stuff now[/b] — put out a fire with a firehose, turn on generators, click buttons, etc.

Exploration is also pretty straightforward with linear and compact levels. Yes, you'll still backtrack at times — but more often than nought, once you leave an area, that's it, no coming back. I didn't mind this, given we get plenty of unique levels as a result of this level design choice.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2849882009

But despite the more action-oriented nature of the game, [b]the horror vibes are still excellent.[/b] The visual-audio duet is on point, setting up each location's spook flawlessly. The RE Engine once again radiates immersion; dark, gritty, messy, pulpy, but also clean and crips when it needs to be. The amount of legwork it does to breed life to Raccoon City and its undead citizens is tremendous. But it's a duet, and the audio plays an equally important part here, complementing the visuals without missing a single beat.

So, it really pains me to see the horror neutered to this extent. The game actively tries to unclench your goodie hole, of its own volition, by showering you with resources and erecting save spots at every turn. Even if I enjoyed the more action-oriented approach, I still wish [i]Capcom[/i] struck a better balance between action and horror.

[h3][i][b]"Suffering from success"[/b][/i][/h3]
No game embodies this famous passage from the great scholar DJ Khaled like [i]Resident Evil 3 Remake[/i]. In this case, the success of its predecessor. While it exceeded my expectations in the gameplay department, the ball was dropped when it came time to match the tense atmosphere of its [i]onii-chan[/i]. As it is now, while there are some spooky moments, just like food in Africa, the horror here is pretty scarce. Instead, the focus heavily shifted to the [i]shooty shooty bang bang[/i]. But despite this, I enjoyed [i]Resident Evil 3 Remake[/i], and, while not perfect, it's still a decent entry for [i]Capcom's[/i] new remake catalogue.

Plus, you get to gawk at Carlos's new mesmerizing curls.

A worthwhile survival horror game, but pretty rough in a few places and a little disappointing compared to the previous REmake.

The atmosphere in RE3's cinematically-lit settings is still phenomenal and navigating the generally more open areas makes for some gripping exploration. Making calculated shots, planning routes around the map, and weighing decisions about your inventory/resources are all survival-horror hallmarks that RE3 has in good supply. The game comes to a close a little bit too early, but it’s not as if the game failed to tell a complete narrative within the given time. Any shorter though and RE3 may have worked better as a ‘Shadows of Rose’ style DLC.

On the downside, your titular rival, Nemesis, is only ever an engaging environmental threat once and they are otherwise relegated to setpieces and mediocre boss fights. Those scripted moments and their self-contained gameplay fail to punctuate the tension that other portions of the game build so well. And while I'm complaining here, there's also a certain enemy type that is particularly annoying to deal with and some segments don't readily communicate a point of no return.

Overall, RE3make is well-made, compact, and action-packed, but the action isn't honestly the highlight of playing a spooky gun game. It’s still certainly worth playing if the genre and/or franchise is one of your favorites.

Pros
- The change in direction to be more action oriented doesn't completely eliminate the scare roots of RE2 remake, and it's a nice change of pace. Zombie encounters aren't as fun as human encounters in RE4, but it's still a very fun action horror game in its own right.
- Dodge system is an excellent addition and the game gets really fun once you get good at it. If the game were longer, this could have easily been my favorite RE game thanks to the dodge system.
- Letting players choose unlockables with currencies is a very nice idea. Getting specific unlocks in RE2 remake was incredibly stressful. RE3's system allows casual players to obtain many of their favorite unlocks without stress. In fact, since you're allowed to use infinite weapons to obtain S-rank in higher difficulties, getting all unlockables was much more enjoyable and casual compared to RE2 remake.
- The shop has some interesting items that allows the player to customize their gameplay a bit. Some items give health regen, some give more damage, there's an item that makes dodging easier, etc. It's better than the typical infinite ammo unlocks you see in most RE games.
- Nightmare and Inferno difficulties have different spawns, which freshens things up a bit.
- Graphics and overall atmosphere are very nice.
- Unlike RE2 remake, characters no longer use plastic knives. :P

Cons
- The game is too short. Supposedly, they cut a lot of contents from classic RE3 (I never played classic RE3). Even with the shop items varying things a bit, the player is still restricted to the same short campaign. This is a shame because the game is so good.
- Nemesis is disappointing compared to the Tyrant in RE2 remake. There are only a few parts where the Nemesis chases the player and all of these are short scripted events. By comparison, RE2's Tyrant dynamically chases the player throughout many parts of the game. Nemesis was supposed to be the big thing for RE3, so it's a big shame to see it reduced to this.
- Not having checkpoints for boss fights makes it frustrating to learn to fight a boss in harder difficulties as you need to constantly run back to the boss and skip cutscenes.
- Needs a random mode that randomizes the location of items and enemies. Once the player has the game memorized, the game loses its scare factor.

A stunning remaster with visuals highly reminiscent of the 2nd game, with a lot of nostalgia seeing Jill again - I'm enjoying the playthrough as I run rampant with a new Nemesis and an evolved virus.

The visuals, audio, and voicework are superb. Where this game falls flat is the gameplay itself. This remake painstakingly reproduces the inventory tetris and austere enemy design of the original; This, on its own, is not necessarily a bad thing for a remake. When taken as a package, however, the cinematic storytelling and seamless transitions between cutscene and player control only serve to accent the unequal allocation of resources directed towards bringing this game into the modern era. This is further aggravated by the ludonarrative whiplash of repeatedly being chased by a superior threat that, according to the story, is only ever minutes or sometimes seconds away from catching up and then immediately being plunged into a stale encounter designed to be challenging to the standards of 90's 3d gun combat absent any urgency, which incentivizes patiently plinking zombies and then knifing them to conserve ammunition.

The amount of content absent compared to the original game makes it difficult to argue that faithful reproduction was the driving force behind the decision not to refurbish the game design for more modern standards. At least the RE2 remake retains the multiple storylines and bonus game modes that provide rewards for those willing to master the combat system. In the RE3 remake not only is the combat system almost entirely unchanged from RE2 but several of the enemies have also been carried over unchanged meaning that fans of the series start off doubly bored with the combat of this iteration. And of course there is only the singular storyline (abridged compared to the original) and unlockable gimmick weapons left to provide any semblance of replayability.

If they edited down this game's story into a tight 90 minute cinematic I would happily pay $20 for it. However, the amount of tedious anachronistic gunslinging you need to complete just to unearth a small nugget of story makes me reluctant to recommend this game even at $10. If you're going to buy a game then the gameplay should be fun: It shouldn't be a chore that uses cut scenes as breadcrumbs to lure your effort.

In terms of overall quality, this classical style survival horror game falls somewhere in the middle of the whole Resident Evil (RE) series. It is certainly not the best in the genre/series, but also not the worst.

A lot of people directly make the comparison with the RE2 remake. This is expected and justified to some extent. RE3 is a little more action oriented though, and lacks the tension and suspense. RE2 is a more fleshed out experience in all aspects, making RE3 feel more like a third campaign which should have been part of RE2. Although I had the same feeling with the original versions of both games. In my opinion, the original RE3 is also not as good as fans pretend it to be. I always found it the weakest game of the original four RE games in the classical survival horror style.

The modern game engine works wonders in terms of believable world building and playability, compared to the original version with its blocky graphics and clunky tank controls. I love me some classic RE, but the modern public is different from that of the mid 90s and early 00s. Especially from a commercial standpoint, the game design choices for this remake are not as bad as fans present them to be.

The best parts of RE3, are the hectic war zone type opening scenes and when visiting the police station that is also known from RE2. It's quite entertaining to walk around in the police station, while knowing what is going to happen there eventually. This part also fills in some details about specific happenings/objects inside the building. The over the top ending with literally blasting your way through, is also quite satisfying.

The standard price on Steam, is way too much for such a short campaign though. Something which also ignited quite a number of negative reviews. But during Steam sale periods, it should be possible to buy the game at around a 75% discount. Which is a fair price for the amount and quality of the content.

Overall, this is an entertaining ride from start to finish. If you like battling and puzzling your way out of bio terrorism, this game is for you. But please keep in mind that this game does not represent the glory of the survival horror genre or the RE series.

Feels more like a RE3-inspired DLC mission for the 2 remake than a full game of its own.

The remake of 2 took the modernized gameplay from 4 onward, but kept the general structure and pacing of the original, with you exploring more and more of an area, growing familiar with it but feeling suspense each time you run back through somewhere, wondering if this time dogs will burst through the window, etc. This game instead is like if you gave some devs who'd never played the original a 10-bullet-point summary of the game and had them create a generic linear action game that checks those boxes, hitting just enough of the story beats to technically qualify as a remake.

In the original, you first hear about the Nemesis from Brad's warnings, building some tension until you finally see it show up a half-hour or so in and kill Brad in an iconic cut-scene. In the remake, the Nemesis shows up before Jill has even left her apartment or seen a single zombie, you immediately are just pressing a button to run away in the most barebones quicktime event you've ever seen, and they find an excuse for Brad to get killed by a zombie a few minutes later. This really sets the mood for how the game rushes you along at every step of the way.

Raccoon City looks incredible but there's not much to do and no time to spend there. There's always a mission objective and a character on the radio yelling where to go. The puzzles are basically all gone, apart from one or two simplified homages that mostly just give you a box of ammo or some other totally unsatisfying reward. Instead it's, "Jill, run here and pull this switch!" "Jill, bring that doohicky back here!" constantly breaking any opportunity for atmospheric horror. Whole sections and settings have been cut out. A big one is the clocktower, which you almost expect to visit since you can find postcards and stuff talking about it, but then you only get to see it on the horizon, which is almost more of a slap in the face than it not being there at all. You leave Raccoon City much quicker (a shame for how pretty it is) and skip those places to instead spend more time in stock "warehouse/lab" areas, which are always the most bland parts of RE. They don't even let you go back to check on Dario -- no time for any memorable moments, we've got a game to get through.

Sadly this dynamic also warps the Nemesis itself. In addition to his introduction being rushed, he's also a total pushover. It takes one grenade, or one handgun round at a red barrel, to down him. Whereas in the old games these optional fights would get you parts to make cool secret weapons, this time you get, idk, a box of shotgun shells? You can just hit the dodge button and not be bothered by him at all though. His transformation into more monstrous forms comes much earlier too, and he soon becomes a four-legged demon beast that's much less interesting of a foe. Whereas before you felt like the mouse in a game of cat and mouse, watching out for a cunning bipedal hunter as you explore more or less stable settings, now you feel like you're just running a straightforward errand with an annoying chihuahua nipping at your heels.

Overall the game has like, 5 or so hours of content? It also doesn't have a Mercenaries mode to give it more replay value, instead being packaged with Resistance which is its own dumpster fire. It's too bad because the basic gameplay builds on the 2 remake decently, and I wish I could spend so much more time exploring more of those early Raccoon City sections, but there just isn't enough here to justify the price tag. Especially when stepping back into the police station, this game really just reminds me how much better the 2 remake was and makes me want to replay that instead.

RE3 Remake got such negativity from the community that I avoided the game until now, when it finally dropped to a good price in an okay Halloween sale.  I still don't regret not buying it before, but upon playing it I was hugely surprised to find how good this title really is.

To put things in perspective: I've never thought OG RE3 was as good as people make it out to be. It was an okay game, like most Capcom output from that era, but to me it lacked something, it felt like a step back from OG RE2, which was an epic adventure with a compelling story, while Jill campaign had too small of a scope, was just too condensed, and the storywriters couldn't manage to even resemble the previous title in narrative structure, which involved a cast of memorable characters like Claire, Leon, Ada, Sherry, their parents etc. OG RE3 felt like a side episode instead of a numbered title (Code Veronica should have been RE 3, imo).

Having said that, it's obvious that I had zero expectations coming into this and was more open to new ideas and interpretations. First, I enjoyed Jill a lot in this. They just nailed her face model, her personality and expressions - she never appears as annoying as her competitor in the "single heroine carrying the game on her shoulders" department: the rebooted Lara Croft. In fact, Jill manages to show determination but still retaining a kind of charm, which neither modern Lara or Claire are able to do.
Then they get the pacing just right, and great pacing is the trademark of this series, perfected by RE1make and RE4 in their own way each, but also done amazingly well recently in RE7 and RE8. Important to note that pacing was not without flaws in RE2R, as shown by the weak sewer segment halting the flow of that game. This doesn't happen in Re3Remake, which goes along smoothly from beggining to end, with adrenaline pumping and fine tuned gameplay, cool (and some absurdly funny) setpieces, amazing models, animations and action choreography. The soundtrack is also spot on, and I thought it fared better on this game than the  one they composed for RE2R did.

What I must agree with the general opinion though, it's that they could have added more segments from the original. If we had a bit more content in the single player campaign, without hurting the pacing, this might have been the best of the new RE Engine games to me. As it stands, Village is the best from this modern bunch.

By the way, this review was written after completing a blind first playthough choosing Hardcore difficulty from the get go. I believe this is a great manner to experience these games.

Great follow-up to the RE2 remake. While the control schemes and graphical quality are identical between the two games, this one has been reworked into a more fast-paced, linear action shooter. The elements of RE2 are all there, just delivered in different proportions and at a much quicker pace. Puzzles are scaled down, ammunition is plentiful, and you end up blowing through the environments much faster. Controls are buttery smooth perfection - it's probably one of the slickest third-person shooters I've ever played. It's also got some refreshingly self aware, tongue-in-cheek humor that makes the story's inherent cheesiness a lot more palatable.

My one big gripe is the over-reliance on cutscenes. They'll feed you these extended cinematics, then suddenly hand control back to the player for mere seconds... only to yank it right away from you again. It makes the player's input feel totally inconsequential. If you're trying to deliver some dramatic dialogue as a sort of bookend between playable segments, the interruption is acceptable. But why force a player to watch scripted action sequences at all when they could be playing them instead? I can't see much valid excuse for this, as a lot of games (including RE2) have handled this a lot better.

RE3 manages to address all shortcomings of RE2's remake, while delivering a fun experience, that respects the player's time, while providing ample opportunities to enjoy great combat encounters and creative visuals.

While RE2 looked great, what it lacked was variety, as the entire game is basically set in two locations. 3 doesn't bolster a bigger repertoire, but it uses colors, lights and other visual set pieces to make Raccoon City a memorable location.

While combat feels pretty much the same as in 2, controls have been improved and contextual issues are no more. Additional balance changes have made for a better mixture of action and horror too, with more creepy enemies that aim to surprise, instead of annoy. 

The narrative is very fun to follow too. It manages to challenge the main characters in expected, but enjoyable ways. Jill Valentine's comeback is very strong. She's a strong female lead, capable of handling herself, and it's refreshing to see that executed well in a modern game. 

With Mr. X being such an outdated mechanic in 2, some may wonder if Nemesis would be equally annoying in 3's remake. Good news: not at all! He's always fun to encounter, even funny at times (in the right way), and he serves as a great progression marker for the player.

Many have stated that 3's runtime is rather low, but I can't agree. I found the game's length to be just right. The game's fun gameplay and the medium length allows for replayability. It seems that was planned from the start too, considering the types of unlockables that become available after finishing the game. 

Resident Evil 3 is awesome. It's a fun-packed joyride of a thrill, which will stay in your mind, thanks to its classic villain and brilliant visuals. The game manages to wrap up the Raccoon City trilogy in a way that can only leave a player excited for RE4's upcoming remake.

This is a very good game, even if it is impossible not to compare it to the remake of RE2, and this comparison does not work out in RE3's favor. 

I had played and deeply enjoyed RE2 only a week or so ago. It was getting to be Halloween, and this game was on sale, so I decided to pick it up and have a campy horror weekend with it. For the most part, that worked: many of the elements that made RE2 so good are still present here, including amazing production values, good atmosphere, a fun gameplay loop with the item collection, and really quite good combat. 

The act of shooting the 'grunt' zombies in the face is still as good as it was previously, and the fact the game gives you an infinite-use knife and a dodge move that makes you more versatile when you can't afford to shoot enemies, makes it feel like just enough of an upgrade over the previous game's combat to feel fresh. The game also made a good first impression: the opening area looks amazing, and feels open, which is a stark contrast to the oppressive atmosphere of the police station in RE2. 

However, there are also a few gripes I had with this game. First off, the game simply never reaches the heights of the police station from the previous game in terms of level design. To be fair, it is a high bar: the police station was so well-designed in terms of pacing and the way it gradually opened up to you like clockwork over the course of 5 hours, that even RE2's own latter half failed to live up to it. RE3 is more action-y in general, giving you more ammo and clearly expecting you to shoot every enemy until dead, for which in RE2 there simply wasn't enough ammo on the normal difficulty (in my experience). This means the game of finding every single item in a room via the help of the map is somewhat less impactful here than it was in RE2, where I reveled in making sure to explore every nook and cranny to get sorely needed pickups. However, RE3 still manages to be interesting enough in this sense to be satisfying.

Secondly, there are two things I rather thoroughly disliked. [spoiler]The first is that in an already fairly short game, you spend about 45 minutes in areas that were ripped straight from RE2, but that in this game are more limited, with for instance random halls of the police station being blocked off. While I just said the police station was a fantastic environment in the previous game, it feels a bit cheap to just reuse a part of it for Carlos' section, especially when certain corridors are closed off and it feels like a lesser version of something that feels a bit trite to begin with. It gives the impression that they sort of rushed to get this second remake out the door, banking on the quality and reception of the first to make it sell.

The second thing I didn't like very much was Nemesis in general. That sounds crazy, because he's core to the game, but I found the boss fights with him not to be very fun, and I did not enjoy being chased around by him in the beginning either. RE2 already did that with Mister X, and in my opinion did it better. The dodge mechanic theoretically allows you to juke him, but I found the timing on it to be highly unintuitive, both in sections where he chases you in the beginning, and in the penultimate boss fight. Furthermore, the fact he simply will never die becomes a bit tiresome as well.[/spoiler]

That's a big paragraph of complaints under those spoiler tags. This makes it seem like I dislike this game; I do not. Rather, it is a very good game that has some pretty annoying aspects to it as well, which for me stood out extra because I had just played a superior version of practically the same game a week before. Having said this, if you liked RE2, this game is well worth playing as well. I got it on sale, and got six hours of well-made game out of 12 euros. That seems like a very pleasant value proposition to me. Who likes games that outstay their welcome anyway?

Resident Evil 3 remake is fast and intense horror game. But is it good? Yes! Duh.

I loved the original game. It was entertaining, similar to RE2 but somehow felt fresh. And remake is even better. Honestly I enjoyed it more than RE2, although it's a bit shorter but somehow it feels like it has more of everything and also has more action.

You play as Jill and Carlos and...shoot zombies while being chased by Nemesis at times. Why I liked this more? Mister x is the most annoying and stupid thing in RE2 which ruins the game so much that you just download a mod and remove it. Here Nemesis also chases you but only in some scenes, he's not there all the time. He doesn't interfere with exploration and he's actually fun.

Gameplay is pretty standard RE gameplay. You get a map of the current location and explore it while shooting zombies, looking for keys and solving some simple puzzles. The game is more action oriented, you get more ammo, a variety of weapons and enemies also feel well placed and neither are too annoying.
One really good addition is dodge mechanic. Resident Evil 2 doesn't have that and it's so annoying since it makes hard to run past the zombies.

The game also offers great map variety so you never get bored by being stuck in the same location.
Game has several locations, some smaller, some bigger but none of them are annoying. Level design in general is great and there's little to none backtracking.
You still have that iconic and stupid RE inventory system which you need to manage but it's not too bad, although I would like if it just go away. Nevertheless the inventory system makes much more sense.

Graphically the game looks very good. Like really REALLY good. Character models are very well detailed, Jill and Carlos are hot as f***, feels like it's a holywood movie.
Graphics in general also look great, especially with ray tracing on, although it hits the performance pretty hard.
Performance without ray tracing is great, smooth as silk on max settings, fps hovering in the 90-100+ range. With rt on...well...it's worse but not too bad. Game looks even better but is it worth the fps hit? Nope.

Played on 5800x, rtx3080, 32GB @3440x1440.
Native ultrawide support is nice to have finally.

Sound desing matches everything else and is of highest quality. Again it's like watching a good action movie, awesome voice acting, music and overall sound design.

Well it's a short review for a short game. It's a very good game packed with plenty of action, cinematic cut-scenes and holywood'ish blings and bangs. Extremely enjoyable to play through and is a must play for action game fans.

The following feedback is strictly related to the single-player game on Hardcore difficulty; there are no notes about “Resistance” as I did not partake in that multiplayer game.

Short. Semi-sweet. Slightly salty 'bout that

Like everyone says, it's really short. So short that the Nemesis encounters don't have time enough to feel like proper milestones. Short enough that your time in the streets of Raccoon City and your brief foray into the police station don't feel like an homage to iconic locales or a clever trigger for nostalgia. Rather, it feels more like re-using existing assets or deploying cut content from RE2 Remake as opposed to making something singularly appropriate to best fit the (retold) story of this chapter of the franchise. Short to the point that if you paid $60 for this title at release, you probably winced when you finished playing. 

To be fair, even if these implementations were included by design rather than from a lack of options due to squandering time or other resources, much of it would still be in line with the original. Resident Evil 3 from 1999 was pretty short, involved a lot of scenes combating Nemesis broken up by brief intervals of not-Nemesis, and had you return through some signature areas from the previous game. The remake did omit some scenes/locations from the original, but I'm not convinced the inclusion of those scenes would have adequately addressed either of the the problems mentioned above. Specifically, 'so much Nemesis so much of the time!' (i.e., diluted effect for the presence of what is otherwise a fearsome foe), and 'where's muh new scenery for this here new game?' (i.e., reliance on reused geometry and settings, the dearth of new environments compared to RE2 Remake).

On a brighter note, Jill's sections felt like quintessential survival horror. She had just enough resources to contend with her sections of the game but never so many that you felt truly comfortable. You had to: choose when to flee combat or avoid it entirely; dodge often, whether traveling, evading, or standing your ground; you had to juggle lots of threats with limited ammo in tight spaces; all of this with finite healing capabilities... The overall balance of awareness, fighting, and fleeing required for her parts of the game were very well done. Chef's kiss. And Carlos... it was a tremendous relief to have enough ammo so that you had to be a) deliberately aggressive or b) a terminally bad shot in order to run the risk of exhausting his supply. Also, Jill's trash talk during the final Nemesis stage was the definition of crass but still wonderful. The game is gorgeous, drips with atmosphere, and makes the same sparse use of sound that was so effective in RE2 Remake.

So where does this put us in terms of 'to recommend' or 'not to recommend'? The older I get, the less enamored I am with over-relying on the notion that entertainment must be measured first in terms of '$/time = value' with any other metric being inherently less significant. As time for gaming  in my life becomes more scarce, I'm more disposed to make my initial determination something closer to 'value = units of enjoyment/time' with $ as a relevant but less crucial variable. Since the game no longer costs $60, it's easier to recommend in general. But even $40 could be steep for what's on offer, both in terms of amount of game to be played and enjoyment in play to be had. 

I enjoyed my time with the game, but there's simply not a lot of time to be had in the playing of the campaign. My actual time-in-seat was 10-ish hours (had several looooooooong pauses due to the aforementioned scarcity of time able to be dedicated to playing). Those 10 hours, while great, were not as meaningful to me as my time in “Firewatch” or “Soma”, which were of comparable length (and noticeably cheaper to boot).

Sad as it is to do this, RE3 Remake is a 7/10 for my money. Even as a fan of the franchise, $40 feels like too much for the single player game Capcom delivers. A $30 price tag feels more on-point for the 6-10 hours of content on offer, and that re-aligning of quality and quantity would push the rating to an 8.

TL;DR: If you liked the RE2 Remake, then you'll likely enjoy this one, just know that it is shorter, about 6 hours.

When this one came out, I was surprised to see Mixed reviews initially, especially since the reviews for the previous RE2 remake had been so positive. As I read them, I noticed that it was mostly a lack of content and the shorter story that caused this. And while it is true that this game has no 2nd run, not a ton of bonus modes and is shorter than the RE2 remake, I still recommend this one and I don't think those are bad things.

This story follows Jill Valentine, one of the playable characters from the original Resident Evil game, as she tries to escape Raccoon City the night of the outbreak, the very same night as RE2. Because of this, there is some fun overlap where you revisit locations from the last game briefly, but you don't really get to explore quite as much as you did in RE2, so nothing comparable to the many locked doors of the police station. This game also has two playable characters, with you occasionally playing as Carlos, but all within the same playthrough, so no 2nd run here. I think it actually works better. Since the 2nd run in RE2 was a bit of a joke other than the one story part that is different between the characters, I think Leon and Claire should have just switched off and made it one playthrough. I appreciated that they did that here, but I'm not a die hard Resident Evil fan that will replay these games over and over, so what do I know?

While RE2 was more of a scary game to me, this one is more of an action game. In RE2, there were dark, creepy hallways where you never knew what would pop out at you. This one is a bit more straightforward, and the lack of exploration really takes away from the horror that could have been experienced. I can really only think of the first area in Raccoon City streets being close to what was experienced in RE2.

There's also a discussion to be had about the Tyrant versus Nemesis. The problem with Nemesis is he needs a cutscene to introduce himself every time. The scary thing about the Tyrant was that he was embedded in the exploration gameplay. Often you didn't know when or if he was going to show up, and it kept me on edge during RE2. Nemesis probably never made me jump, it was more of a scramble as he was now chasing me and swinging his arms at me or whatever. I understand that they probably didn't want to do the exact same thing, but this also worked well in RE7 with Jack Baker and in RE8 with Lady Dimitrescu wandering the halls, so I definitely think Nemesis could have been done better and scarier.

Speaking of cutscenes, there are a lot here, and I could see frustration from it. In addition to always welcoming in Nemesis with a cutscene, there were parts of the story that you had to just sit back and watch. I don't hate cutscenes, nor did I think they were a problem here, but if you're someone who wants to get back to playing as soon as possible, you might get annoyed by the amount of them.

Performance-wise, this game performed great. Just like RE2 Remake, it is well optimized, getting 100+ fps at 1440p on a GTX 1080, and CPU temps stayed in normal ranges, barely ever hitting 70 C. This does not go unnoticed Capcom, and I give you my thanks.

Overall, I picked this up on sale for $16, and I'd say that price is worth it. I beat the game in 6 hours, and maybe in a few years if I feel like replaying these, I'll go back and play it with RE2. I enjoyed this one, but it is not as enjoyable as RE2, and it lacks the content that RE2 provided.
