I don't have any problems with short games, as long as they are quality and have a fair price tag. Resident Evil 3 is quality, but the price tag is not fair in my opinion. I knew the game was short coming in, but even so it surprised me just how short it was, as I completed it in less than 4 hours.

Even if I were to be harsh and completely ignore the second campaign in Resident Evil 2 - which I don't think is fair, it may not be completely different from the first campaign but it had some new sections, cutscenes and felt different to play as it bumps up the intensity - RE2 still took me longer than RE3, and the two games are basically the same price on Steam.

Continuing that comparison, personally I'm not a fan of the direction RE3 takes towards action compared to RE2. Jill feels like a superhuman in cutscenes and you are given a powerful arsenal, so I feel any sense of suspense is lost as a result. Compared to Mr. X, Nemesis simply doesn't feel threatening in the same way, partly because you feel stronger but also because his AI is not the best.

On the plus side, I think the addition of a dodge makes sense when you're encouraged to save ammo. It's also implemented in a way that doesn't make it spammable and overpowered, which is good. That, along with some better guns does make the boss battles in RE3 better than the ones in RE2.

Once again, the graphics look fantastic in the RE engine and Raccoon City has some interesting environments. Though I do think that the level design is another step backward - I think RE2 was stronger in the sense that it had areas that you stayed in for longer and became very familiar with.

I would recommend this for a low price tag and only if you were already invested in the series because it's a part of the Raccoon City story.

So... The remake of Resident Evil 3, a classic a lot of people love and hold dear in their hearts because of the childhood memories... That may be the main reason of why it got so much hate, although some people say it goes beyond that. Does it really, though?
Let me just take it off my chest: I had a blast playing Resident Evil 3 Remake. Was it was good as RE2 Remake? Hell no. Was it better than the classic game? In some aspects? Sure. For most of it? Absolutely not. But here's the thing, the hard to swallow pills: Not even the classic Resident Evil 3 was that great to begin with. Sure, it was fun, it felt much more complete than this remake. But storywise? That original version was as just as rushed as this one. While the puzzles and the act of coming and going and coming back again gives the sensation that the classic RE3 was longer, if you look at it for real, it really doesn't have a lot to it. If you know exactly what to do and how to avoid the enemies, you can finish it in 40 minutes.
And what about the remake? I think what it really went and even goes against it it's the expectations. We came out of Resident Evil 2 Remake, which was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing and felt more complete (even if they make you redo a lot of repeated things in both campaigns, something that the classic RE2 didn't have) and our expectations for it were huge. In the end, it ended up being rather underwelming and different than what many people expected. Nemesis encounters were much more scripted than the classic, the plot beast went and came much quicker than the original, so a lot of moments that were supposed to be memorable, like they were in the classic, couldn't be properly digested and felt, because the story was going forward at full speed, and we also didn't have a lot to do or explore, the game doesn't make a lot of effort for you to invest on exploration. There was a lot of disappointment and hate.
But now... 2 years later, what do I think of it? This was my first time playing this game, because I finally got a good computer. And I tried to play this game as it is, not accordingly to my expectations and to what I wanted it to be. If you are gonna judge something, judge for what's actually in it. And while yes, the story and the gameplay were super rushed, and some narrative aspects, and mostly gameplay aspects, were disappointing and left a lot to be desired I had a really good experience with Resident Evil 3 Remake. The game felt like those uncomprimised sequels that just wants to make you have fun and enjoy the experience with some big dumb bombastic and frenetic action while mixing a good amount of body horror and ugly monsters. In that aspect, this remake delivers it. It may not live longer in your memory, but I don't think it really needs to be more than that when not even the classic game was more than that. You may have a emotional bond with the original, but not even it was perfect or the most revolutionary game ever made.
I don't mind what this game attempted or didn't attempted to make. Do I wish it was better? Yes. But am I happy with what I got? Yes. It was enough. It kept me enternained and engaged all the way through. Sometimes, that's all what games, movies and books need to do.

I'm a massive Resident Evil fan. I loved the hell out of the RE2 remake, thought they kept it 90% faithful but the stuff they changed made sense for a modern take on an old classic. That said, Resident Evil 3 is my favorite in the entire franchise for a number of reasons. Despite RE3 taking the blame for kicking the RE series into action, I thought it was a nice mixture of horror, drama and action that traumatized me as a kid and continues to entertain me as an adult. I have almost the whole script memorized, I know how to speedrun it, I loved the Mercenaries mode which had you strategically race through the city on a 10-minute timer that gets longer for every enemy kill, every dodge, and every civilian rescued, with 4 characters to play as that have different weapon arsenals.

I knew RE3 wouldn't have Mercenaries mode and is instead implementing the "Resistance" game which is an online multiplayer game capitalizing off of the "Dead By Daylight" trend that everyone and their mother is trying to cash in on (including the makers of Outlast, Red Barrels, announcing their new game will be multiplayer). Capcom would make everyone very happy if they just remastered Resident Evil Outbreak but apparently they'd rather just recycle assets from RE2 and call it a day.

Preface aside, here's my review: the game isn't bad, but it's extremely mediocre.

The entire intro in the remake is different from the original, and it's all a downgrade. Instead of Jill fighting through an urban wasteland crawling with what feels like a hundred zombies, meeting up with her teammate Brad, hearing him warn about Nemesis "coming for us" as he ominously puts it, watching him get slaughtered by Nemesis in front of the RPD before choosing to either fight Nemesis or run inside the building, we instead get an intro with Jill slowly touring her entire apartment (with some exposition in the form of documents for whatever reason) before experiencing a nightmare about her turning into a zombie. She wakes up, gets a phone call from Brad sounding alarmed, and immediately the wall blasts open and Nemesis appears with his face covered by a plastic bag and attempts to kill Jill. No buildup, no tension, just WHOAH FIRE EXPLOSIONS RUN AWAY FROM THE BIG MONSTER IN THESE INCREDIBLY EASY SCRIPTED SEQUENCES THAT HAVE YOU HOLDING FORWARD TO GET AWAY. Then you encounter Brad who JUST SO HAPPENS to be passing by the alleyway you're emerging from (and is now suddenly cracking jokes and sounds very relaxed considering he was flipping out just moments prior over the phone) and you run into a nearby cafe to get away from the zombies. The zombies break through, bite Brad, and he pulls the cliche'd "I'm infected and we both know I'm done for so I'll buy you some time and hold them off knowing I'm gonna die anyway" schtick as Jill runs into a nearby alleyway. Brad was on-screen for all of 3 minutes before they killed him off to advance the plot. Okay.

She picks up a handgun from a nearby zombie and says "Sorry." Jill makes it a regular gag to apologize to corpses for taking their stuff. It's just kind of annoying and she does it multiple times.

Then she runs into a room and meets Dario Rosso, a writer/poet in the original game who had red hair and looked like a chubby dude in his 30's, but this game decided to make him about 70 and balding. Dario Rosso in the original is a super unimportant character, but his vocal performance is superb and he was someone that always impressed me in the beginning of the game. He screams at you at the top of his lungs, mourns the VERY RECENT death of his daughter, and then locks himself in a storage container and says he'd rather starve to death than be eaten by "one of those undead monsters." This Dario Rosso mocks Jill, when she says "I'm a police officer and I'm here to help," he laughs and says "Oh yeah, you're doing a bang-up job." His vocal delivery sounds annoyed and sarcastic, which compared to the original VA sounding on the brink of losing his mind, is a downgrade that let me know immediately this game was going to be mediocre. Calling this game a RE3 remake is a bit misleading, especially compared to the RE2 remake. Fans hoping to relive the classical RE3 experience in a modern setting the same way they did RE2 will be bitterly disappointed. This game is a reinterpretation of the events of RE3 packaged as an action game.

In terms of gameplay, the new RE3 on normal difficulty plays more like RE4 on steroids than a survival horror as the classical RE3. There are several places swarming with enemies. Those places usually have some exploding barrels, generators or are preceded by rooms with grenades or grenade launcher ammo. The message the game passes to its players is clear: wipe out all enemies in that area using all the options that we gave you.

To encourage this behavior even further, ammo in the game is abundant in normal difficulty. You'll have 50 handgun bullets before minute 10. The dodge/parry mechanics are cool, but very op. If you master them early and avoid shooting rooms with 1-3 zombies, you’ll have virtually infinite ammo throughout the whole game. Maybe you have to manage your ammo a little bit better in hard mode since enemies are tougher and there is less ammo available.

Game has few puzzles and as a consequence little backtracking. I think this is a plus if you accept this as an action game. Backtracking in survival horror is always a risk as you probably left some enemies alive along the way. In the cases I had to backtrack in the new RE3, I knew I killed everything in every room and if something new appeared I would kill it as well. There was no sacrifice or planning. So backtracking was boring.

This is a controversial topic and I understand the POV of fans that wished for a more faithful remake, but I don’t mind the cut content. I prefer the new intro with Nemesis making me run for my life, meeting other npcs early and starting a critical quest, than following the same steps as RE2: reach the police station, solve puzzles while a big monster is chasing you etc. I was very young when I played the classic RE3 but I didn’t feel there was a hole in the new game because it cut the police station or clock tower.

I like what they did with Nemesis. Instead of going the same path as Mr. X in RE2 remake, the new Nemesis only appeared in short high paced moments filled with cutscenes, great environments, new controls and character states, or during boss fights. He was wisely used to turn boring walking around into great action sequences. Need to get out of your apartment? Nemesis gives you a hand. Need to traverse a huge bridge? Nemesis helps you to sprint it.

Enemy variety was lacking. Few rooms with dogs, stronger zombies or other types of enemies. Some of them appear only once or twice. 

As a final point, the price tag, which is the most disappointing part. RE3 has one campaign that takes around 6 hours, while the RE2 remake has 2 campaigns and one DLC. RE2 campaign has around 8 hours of content and the DLC has 1 hour. So we’re comparing a 6 hours game to a 17 hour game for the same price. I would argue RE2 has actually around 10 hour of relevant content since there is so much reused stuff between the campaigns and the dlc. I think both remakes are overpriced because for the same price tag you can get RE Village, the latest release that has a 9.5 hour campaign.

RE3 gets overlooked in the wake of RE2. How could it not? RE2 Remake is one of the best horror games of all time. But this is still a solid game. 

Sure, it's more action-y and less survival horror-y, but it's supposed to be. 

It's fun, it's a little more forgiving, and the Nemesis battles are great set pieces. 

If you're looking for a survival horror game, you might be disappointed, but as an action horror game, this RE3 Remake is a blast.

This was a fine follow up to Resident Evil 2 Remake. In fact, it’s a GREAT follow up. It gets a lot of hate because of some of the content and set pieces that were cut, and thus it’s probably a lot of shorter that it could have been, but it makes up for it by being much more frantic than Resident Evil 2 Remake. Coming off Resident Evil 2, where Mr X stalks you, but does so quite rhythmically and predictably, Nemesis is much more aggressive and persistent. There’s no great reveal like Mr X in Resident Evill 2. From the start of the game, you, Jill Valentine, are on the run from Nemesis and he makes himself known. 

I quite enjoyed a lot of the tie-ins with Marvin, Brad and the state of the Police Station from Leon and Claire’s experience. There’s no gravedigger, which is disappointing. There’s no clocktower set piece. No giant spiders. The police station was probably a quick substitute to replace some of these other areas because it was already designed and could have easily just been dropped into Jill’s story. 

Because the pacing is so different than RE2R, it feels more action oriented in the first half. In fact, it doesn’t really become Resident Evil game until the Carlos section in the hospital. There are very few puzzles or areas that need to be backtracked. But I’m kind of glad it wasn’t just a carbon copy of RE2R and they did something to spice up Nemesis.

[h1] Escape Raccoon City Before It’s Too Late! [/h1] 
Resident Evil 3 is a survival horror game developed and published by Capcom. It is a remake of the 1999 game Resident Evil 3: Nemesis. Players control former elite agent Jill Valentine and mercenary Carlos Oliveira as they attempt to find a vaccine and escape from a city during a viral outbreak. The game is played from a third-person perspective and requires the player to solve multiple puzzles and defeat monsters while being pursued by a creature called Nemesis.

    [tr]
        [td]🎮Gameplay[/td]
        [td]Resident Evil 3 is similar to its predecessor. With survival horror elements you must conserve ammo and make every shot count. You have different enemies to deal with, and they can be a true challenge for you. You will find fewer puzzles in this game, and they are extremely easy which some may not like (Myself included). This game is more action paced as well so the horror and tension feels less in my opinion. The Boss fights are extremely challenging though which I was not a big fan of. You will have to test your skills with ammo conservation since Nemesis absolutely tanks your hits, which in my opinion should have been balanced better. [/td]

        [td]Resident Evil 3 Remake’s story is one that is short lived in my opinion. Now I really did enjoy the story segment in this game. It’s really hard to explain how, I guess I'll just send you a list of things they changed or removed that were in the original.
[code][list]
[*]The entire clocktower and Raccoon City Park (including the Grave Digger mini Boss) area are missing. Dead Factory was replaced by the NEST 2 (Which looked pretty boring)
[*]The City itself is only half as big as before, alternative routes and small locations like the Press Building, Gas Station, Umbrella store etc. included.
[*]No randomized enemy and item locations.
[*]No live choices, which further changed the current playthrough in small ways.
[*]Much less encounters with Nemesis, which is also far less durable this time around. One grenade and he is down!
[*]No Brain Sucker, Crows, Giant Spiders and the small Grave Digger babies.
[/list][/code]
Yeah, that's a problem for me. I get that it’s a “remake” and they won’t add everything from the original, but pricing this game at $40 is just wrong in my opinion. I feel like this game was released way too quick. If they spent an extra year on this game, it could have been an incredible sequel to RE2, but it’s not. The story was great, but the game is just way too short and the replayability is small for me.[/td]

Like with RE2, I never played the original version of Resident Evil 3, so the remake was my first full exposure to the game. Overall, I would say that, though it compares unfavorably to RE2 in a lot of ways, RE3 is certainly worth experiencing. It iterates on RE2 in interesting ways, taking a more cinematic, action-oriented approach to its plot, while still retaining most of the survival horror framework. It was refreshing to see the perspective of professionals compared to rookie Leon and college student Claire - Carlos in particular was frequently amusing in the ways he would dismiss the zombies he encountered, while Jill projected strength and confidence throughout, clearly conveying the sense of "been there, done that" that would make sense for her when considering RE1. The gameplay is just as tight as RE2, and the enhanced movement options were a godsend for dealing with the significantly higher zombie volume. Diverse monsters, too, were appreciated, with each new area bringing in new enemies against which you needed to do some quick strategizing. The balance skewed more towards the player, with ample ammo to deal with enemies compared to RE2's stinginess, and I think the end result was a well-executed action game.

The main problem, in my view, is the length. For being the same price as RE2, it's absurd that the game offers a campaign that's basically half as long as either side of RE2, and it looks even worse when you consider that both campaigns are necessary for full context in RE2. For all the interesting setpieces RE3 provided, the fun callbacks and ways in which it tied directly into RE2, given that they take place at basically the same time, I often felt like I didn't have much time to enjoy those setpieces, like I was speedrunning through the game even when attempting to take a deliberate pace. Nemesis is a huge problem in this regard for the early game - the pursuit segments are far more brutal than in RE2, since Nemesis is extremely fast, has long-range attacks, and can use weapons in later encounters, severely stunting your ability to explore Raccoon City (when you're not dealing with an outrageous amount of zombies, anyway). Brevity is fine when deployed the right way, but in the case of RE3 it felt like the story was on fast-forward the whole time, and it left me feeling a little cold.

Overall, however, RE3 is a solid game in its own right, and pairs wonderfully with RE2 to provide a full accounting of the final days of Raccoon City. You can really tell that these games were developed back to back, and a lot of care was put into the connective tissue between them - how much of that comes from the originals, I can't say, since I haven't played them, but I appreciate it either being kept for or added to the remakes. RE3 is worth playing - just wait for a sale.

If you like Resident Evil, particularly Resident Evil 2 Remake, you will definitely like this - as long as you temper your expectations in terms of length. RE3 is about half the length of RE2, but it maintains the fantastic graphics, engrossing gameplay and genuine Resident Evil feel. The graphics settings are a little less straight-forward...

Ignore the VRAM warnings in the graphics settings - they aren't accurate, not even close. You can run on an RTX2060 on "Max" loading a 6GB card with what it claims is upwards of 12GB of assets — it does work. It even averages more than 60 frames per second at Max, though it does dip below that floor occasionally. 

Texture Quality has very little impact on framerate, and any modern GPU (including the lowly GTX 1650) is capable of running the "Balanced" profile error-free, which utilizes the "High (0.5 GB)" preset and looks totally fine. There are also diminishing returns after the "High (1 GB)" setting used for the "Graphics Priority" preset. Likely what's happening if you choose "High (2 GB)," "High (4 GB)," and "High (8 GB)" is you're getting served the same textures, but the game is reserving more VRAM to stream them in—and especially if you're on an SSD, that's a nonissue. "High (1 GB)" works absolutely fine.

Anti-Aliasing is one setting you will want to experiment with, as results vary and your choice will come down to personal preference rather than performance. It has a dramatic impact on the the way the game looks, so if you aren't happy with the  graphics, make sure to change AA settings (TAA for me).

[h1] Could Have Been So Much More [/h1]

I'd like to preface this review by stating that I never played the original on the PS1, I see a lot of people complaining about the lack of the "Clocktower Segment" in this game but for the purposes of the review I'm not going to touch on the comparisons between the remake and the original and will focus solely on the pros and cons of this game as it is.

Firstly, I'd like to say that this isn't a bad game by any stretch of the imagination, the new engine that Capcom are using to create games like RE2 and RE3 remakes and the coming RE4, seem to be the best direction for the game going forward. It felt good to play and I encountered no bugs whilst playing it. 

The set-pieces in the game, much like in RE2, are crafted with love, I might even go as far as to say that this game has better set pieces overall than RE2 in terms of the care that went into them. What really caught my attention was near the start of the game in the subway, I found a little subway vendor shop that just had a bunch of fictional advertisements and magazines that all seemed designed very well, like they were real. I feel like they've done a very good job in this respect, the world does feel realistic and lived in.

The gun-play is the same as RE2, it's very smooth, very easy to get to grips with and doesn't require much skill; which is a good thing, you can just point and shoot and everything feels very good, the style of over the shoulder gameplay in this engine and for this game is solid for a third person shooter.

Graphically, the game looks great, in the same vein as what I said about the set-pieces, the enemy designs look pretty decent, even the new ones that aren't in RE2 and definitely adds to the horror element.

I do have quite a few issues with the game however, although I won't compare it to the PS1 version, I do feel like I have a few things to say about the game as a "Sequel" to the RE2 Remake.

First of all, the "Survival" elements of "Survival Horror" seem to be gone almost entirely. There was absolutely never a time in this game where I felt like I had to keep my ammo for something bigger coming down the line. You get so much ammo the point where you can literally run and gun your way through the entire game as opposed to picking your fights. You never really feel -that- tense for the duration of the game, because you've always got at least five-six mags ready, more or less at all times. In this sense, the game feels more like a Third Person Shooter to an extent, I do believe you can kill every single enemy you encounter and still not run out of ammo; it was a lot more action packed than RE2 and I don't necessarily think that's a good thing.

A small point as well that seemed to have been removed for no real reason is that the zombies can de-spawn when they're killed. This is fine for that one scene in the Hospital but in RE2, if you downed a zombie and left the room, came back and the body was missing. You can absolutely bet money that that Zombie has stood up and wandered elsewhere. So it lulls you initially into this sense of. "Damn I just cleared four in this room and they've all got back up." But this isn't the case, they've just been removed. No idea why they could do in RE2 and not do it in RE3.

Another thing that contributes to the lack of tenseness and survival horror, is that there are way too many save points. Like far -far- too many in my opinion. In RE2 when you found a typewriter and a safe room, it was a breath of relief, finally somewhere where you can take a second to sort your items and take a breather. In RE3, honestly, it feels like there's one every 3-4 rooms. It really takes away from that risk of investing ten-twenty minutes into doing something and potentially dying from a mistake and going back to the save point. I honestly think it's ridiculous, there is genuinely never a fear of dying or losing progress, as the most you'll be set back is 3-5 minutes. This really began to bother every time I'd open a door after saving a few minutes before and lo and behold, another save point. They could have cut out at least half of these save points and it would have made for a much more tense experience.

Another thing I'd like to highlight is the time invested in each area, when you're there. In RE2, you're in the police station for, I'd say, maybe... 60-70% of the game? You go back there a few times as well after initially leaving and you got to know the Police Station very well. RE3 doesn't have this. The game is constantly moving you from set piece to set piece with almost no back-tracking at all, if you think you've missed something. If you progress the story and a cutscene plays, chances are, that shop you wanted to go into and thought, "I'll get it on the way back." That opportunity is now gone. I don't know if the original game was like this, but I felt like that starting zone, where you're in the streets, could have been at least two-three times as long and it would have been amazing. Since there's no Keys to locked rooms like the Spade, Diamond, Heart and Clubs keys, the actual exploration side of things didn't have the same feel as the previous game, it was disappointing that we didn't have a place like the Police Station that was so memorable and we could spend a lot of our time in.

I also want to briefly touch on Nemesis, I felt that RE2 hit the nail on the head with Tyrant/Mr. X, a stalker enemy that follows you for a very good part of the game, especially in the Police Station; when you're back tracking, exploring, or accessing different parts of the police station, you can always hear Mr X stomping about, and occasionally getting a dynamic jumpscare when you bump into him in a corridor. RE3 does not have this. I genuinely thought Nemesis would be hunting me in a more dynamic sense for the whole game, rather than just pre-ordained cutscenes or scenarios where all you do is fight him or run away. It's a little tense during these scenes since you can't kill him but it's nowhere near as nerve wracking as being in a room and hearing something hunting you outside; because Nemesis always knows where you are more or less. Calling back to my previous point about if they just extended the starting zone by a few hours, that would have been great to have a Mr X on steroids, Nemesis trying his best to find you whilst you wander about and explore and do your objectives. I don't understand how they missed the mark on this one when Nemesis is quite literally the epitome of stalker type enemies. Massive oversight.

Overall, I'd give RE3 a 6/10, the game is very short for the £32.99 asking price, if you can get this for £9.99-12.99 I reckon you'll absolutely get your moneys worth, a normal playthrough can take anywhere from 4-7 hours depending on how thorough you are. Like I say, it's not a bad game at all, it just misses what made the RE2 remake so good and I don't understand how they dropped the ball on it. However, it's likely you will enjoy it if you do play it for what it is, I know I did.

[h1]Resident Evil 3[/h1]
A streamlined, modern interpretation of the original Resident Evil 3; this rendition has faster gameplay, a more linear experience, and a heavier focus on cinematic cutscenes. It, however, lacks the terrifying atmospheric tension that the previous remake ever so well established, but that is not to diminish the thrill of action or chase sequences as well as significantly improved boss fights. The visual and audio fidelity remains astonishing, with additional improvements because of the utilization of Capcom's welcomed RE Engine.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
The visuals have improved over RE2, not leaps and bounds by any means but improvements such as character models, facial expressions, and overall lighting. Everything remains thoroughly designed with attention to detail, from the design and creation to the texturing, lighting, and animation. It really shows via the characters, assets, and environments.

Exploration of the various streets and buildings within Raccoon City may not be as frightening as it was in RE2, but that is because of the fast-paced, action-orientated gameplay. That, however, does not diminish that the visuals alone still captivate that affection for Resident Evil and horror, resulting in unsettling and eerie surroundings regardless.

The zombies are visually terrifying and memorable alongside the plethora of other creatures and mutations which roam Raccoon City. The tyrant himself Nemesis, has a spectacular design that keeps on developing, with each encounter growing more ominous and disturbing still. Although it is not only the horrific beings that look great, as do the cast of characters you play and encounter. The models are unique and remarkable; the amount of care put into everybody, even the models you see once or twice, is unbelievable.

[h1]Audio[/h1]
Audibly it sounds great; the soundtrack is good and features some fun reimagined classic tracks from previous installments, alongside creating its new and reimagined score. The guns sound more realistic and satisfying than ever, which can also be said for the environment you are within, from sound effects like water droplets or footsteps to explosions; it all sounds astonishing.

Attention to detail is everywhere, especially when it comes to voice acting. With the cinematic narrative focus, it became crucial to nail the voice acting for the cast of characters, which Capcom did. Each character sounds splendid and has a voice befitting their personality and likeness, whether be it a grim or heartfelt moment, they always pull through and sound genuine. The groans and cries from Zombies still periodically send a chill down the spine. However, this is short-lived, as it is quickly quenched by satisfying death, after blowing the zombie's head.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
The traditional slow-paced action with great prominence on exploration has shifted to a more linear experience focusing on chase sequences, cinematic cutscenes, and much faster gunplay. While exploration does come into play, it feels shallow compared to the previous iteration. It will not be for everyone, especially veterans of the franchise. as it's at odds with the traditional free-roam, slow-paced survival horror that RE2 mastered.

The lack of puzzles, backtracking, areas to explore, and ultimately barely any incentive to scavenge are among the primary reasons exploration feels half-baked. Exploration will of course still reward additional upgrades, herbs, ammunition, and more if the player should explore. But due to the abundance of resources at hand, it never feels mandatory or incentivized.

Gunplay, however, feels fast, fluid, and most importantly fun. The addition of timed dodges allows combat to flow better and feel less clunky. Boss battles feel satisfying and well designed, as it's no longer simply. "run around the boss, and shoot it till it collapses." like in the previous installment.

I do firmly believe Capcom managed to design gameplay with a medium between Resident Evil and the more modern, fast-paced action formula quite well. It is by no means perfect, but it succeeds in staying enjoyable and distinct throughout the journey.

[h1]Story[/h1]
Following the events from Resident Evil 2, Raccoon City is still in chaos, as the virus is rampant, and victims of it arise as flesh-eating zombies that roam the streets. The story revolves around a S.T.A.R.S. member Jill Valentine as she tries to find a cure and figure out who created the virus and why while trying to escape the city with an imminent threat always around the corner. During this time, Jill encounters Carlos Oliveira, a member of the U.B.C.S who is tasked to lead the remaining civilians out of the city but ultimately gets entangled in Jill's journey.

The story is cheesy, albeit enjoyable, and certainly memorable; from the never-ending over-the-top action to the incredibly wholesome moments between Jill and Carlos, it all has personality and enjoyment written all over it. The villain, however, is forgettable, bland, and truly a missed opportunity to take the story to the next level.

[h1]Additional Note(s):[/h1]
Resident Evil 3 is bundled alongside Resident Evil Resistance, which is an asymmetric one versus four Multiplayer standalone game. It is, however, in a bad state as Capcom has abandoned it with no plans of fixing/updating it.

RE3 is a short game, as it's roughly 6-7 hours long with tons of content cut from the original. This fact is barely noticeable for newcomers, as what there is, feels like a solid enough experience. But for fans of the original game, it may feel underwhelming with so much left out, but ultimately still enjoyable, just something to keep in mind.

[h1] Final Thoughts [/h1]
Resident Evil 3 is a flawed yet enjoyable game that improves gunplay, making combat feel fluid and fast, but at the cost of the traditional slow-paced exploration-oriented gameplay and the atmospheric tension that the previous installment had mastered. It is visually and audibly stunning, with great characters, and has an enjoyable story only hindered by its villain. Despite its shortcomings, I do believe it is a good game, worthy of your time whether you are an RE fan or not.

Coming straight off of the RE2R and RE8 I’m sad to say that I did not enjoy this game at all. 

The Resident Evil 3 remake guts the original game down to its barest concept and strips it of all charm in the process. It feels more like an interactive movie than a proper main entry in the franchise. 

Due to its short run time you spend very little time in any particular area and there isn’t much to explore. There’s also an abundance of supplies so you’re never at a disadvantage against the hordes that you do encounter. You don’t really need a map in this game, you will never be lost due to the strictly straightforward space it puts you in and you don’t need alternative routes to avoid the hordes either as you’re never in much danger of them. This could be passable as it’s more of an Action Survivor than Horror but I found it underwhelming. 

This game removes the ability to dismember zombies limbs or use items for self defence against them in favour of its dodging system which is fine. It’s a neat gimmick and again you’re never in an area long enough that dismembering a zombie would be necessary so I get why they cut it. 

Then there’s Nemesis, the bio-weapon that hunts Jill from beginning to end, and the biggest disappointment this game has to offer. 

Put simply, Nemesis isn’t intimidating in this game. Visually it’s a fantastic enemy but due to the fact that it only appears in scripted events it holds no real presence over the game outside of those encounters. You can walk freely, confident that there is nothing you can’t handle in the area around you until you progress far enough to get to the next chase sequence or boss fight with the BOW. Nemesis invokes no lingering tension, shock or panic in this game and if we disregard the higher difficulties that aren’t available when you begin the game, it doesn’t present much of  a challenge either. 

On top of that, the chase sequences feel clumsy. There have been chase sequences in other Resident Evil games before this title but something about this entry just feels janky to play. You’re not in danger of losing of course, but the jarring shifts between what is meant to be controlled by the player and what cool thing the game wants to show you is obvious. There were multiple times in the very first chase sequence where I wish [i][b]I[/b][/i] was doing the cool thing in the game instead of watching Jill do it before they briefly gave the option to press W to take her to the next semi-cutscene in the chase. It was boring. 

There were a few unique enemy types in this game but they’re hardly used. Usually contained to one or two locations at best and easily killed. 

That said, the Drain Deimos enemies were tedious, extremely distasteful and incredibly jarring! After introducing the G-Adults in RE2 that could infect you by vomiting over their victims was it really necessary to force the player to watch an introductory cutscene of one throat-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Jill? What kind of hentai ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is this?

It’s especially jarring as they are contained to only one area of the game and never appear again. They’re pitiful threats that can be killed with a single shotgun blast and the cure to the infection status is scattered about everywhere in the area they do appear in. It feels like a very strange and unpleasant detour to take. 

The game also lacks that many puzzles unlike previous entries in the franchise. There are two safes unique to this game and [i]arguably[/i] three puzzles in total over its full runtime. Initially when you’re given a lockpick I assumed there may have been a mini-game attached to it to make you feel like you the player were the Master of Unlocking but no dice. It’s just an unbreakable item that takes up space in your bag. Wouldn’t want to waste your time with puzzles or minigames now would we?

While completing the game unlocks the options of replaying it on harder difficulties, I feel no incentive to do so unlike the previous entries in the series and I find it telling that the only DLC available for this game is to further remove any sense of challenge from it. 

The plot itself felt like it could have been more but on the plus side the game's graphics are great and I liked the occasional soundtrack that stood out. 

If this were a stand alone title I would feel that it was a perfectly passable but underwhelming experience but as a Resident Evil title it’s just a disappointment and I hope this doesn’t reflect any further games going forward. Maybe I would have been more forgiving if it had been released as RE2R DLC but I would have still been left wanting more all the same. 

TLDR: Visually stunning but lacks substance.

I feel more charitable towards this one than a lot of people seem to do.  Yeah, it does compare unfavorably with REmake 2 on paper, and by all accounts REmake 2 is probably the superior game, but that doesn't make this a bad one by any means.  It's certainly shorter, but it's the length it should be for the story it tells and the linear, narrative, action-adventure romp that it is.  Also, the production values are phenomenal, the pacing and general "feel" is absolutely on point--basically because it has all that in common with REmake 2--and I'm coming at it from the perspective of someone who's never played the originals in the series, so I'm not frustrated by segments missing from the original or etc--so take that for what it's worth.  Nothing feels missing to me, in any case, nor does it feel shorter than it should be.  It's actually just the length I want it to be, short enough it keeps up momentum without running out of tricks by the end.  And seeing as it tends to be cheaper than REmake 2, I think the price difference reflects the difference in duration well, because apart from that it's got all the same level of quality in terms of how it's put together and how much fun it is to play.  The enemies are fantastic, as are the setpieces--I was mashing the screenshot button the whole time.  And the Nemesis made my balls retract up into my body, every single time.  So I pretty much got what I paid for.

After enjoying Resident Evil 2 Remake, I had high expectations for this. I never played the original RE3, but I was told it was probably one of the best ones, so I was thrilled. In my head I had the great story of RE3 together with the idea that was developed for RE2 remake. However, I was in general very disappointed. 

Positive things:
- The dodge action is pretty cold and adds more possibilities to your strategy of surviving and to save ammo (though this latter thing you learn later in the game that is not necessary, you can basically kill all creatures in the game without sweating or running out...)
- New enemies are an extra and a fresh thing, although some of them are testimonial in the game or recycled from RE2R
- In general it is really fun and has a lot of action while having to survive. 

Negative things:
- The game is really far from the original, many parts (basically 50% of it) has been modified completely or directly removed (where is the clock tower section or the park section, for instance). Some other parts are a filler that adds nothing (like the horde section at the hospital...really lame). 
- Many features that were really cool in RE2R are gone. Why you cannot see the health on the screen after you have been hurt, now you have to go to the menu to see your status. I died many times because I did not realize I was in danger. In RE2R you could see your status in game after being hit/hurt. Another important example is the movement and dynamics o the enemies, it was much more realistic and scary in RE2R, for example now you cannot dismember zombies with the knife, or the fact that now zombies have this characteristic movement when they are truly "dead". 
- The challenges are very minor, they were many more in RE2R, it all comes down basically to killing X number of enemies with Y weapon or speed running the game and sections. As opposed to RE2R I did not have any particular reason to replay the game...
- The game is extremely linear. All RE games are to some extent but this one is too much. Except the first part in downtown there is really nothing to explore or to backtrack, no puzzle that requires to take an item to a place you already visited, etc...

Overall I think this is a good game and I do recommend it. It is fun and graphics are pretty good (but worse than RE2R). It has a few improvements and many downgrades in my opinion that makes it something just ok, but that could have been simply awesome. A pity and a wasted opportunity by Capcom. Final mark: 6/10

ORIGINAL THOUGHTS = 07-04-2022:

So, I'm some say 4 hours into Resident Evil 3 [Remake] (2020). It's basically more Resident Evil 2 in many ways, which can be great in some ways & not-so-great in others. If you loved RE2 Remake - well, you'll probably like this game, at least; it's more of that. While it's great that it doesn't change much here in many ways and doesn't try to "fix what wasn't broken", it doesn't really push much forward in RE3 Remake here. It also even reuses some areas from RE2 Remake, such as the Police Station. In many ways, this feels more like a DLC and/or an expansion pack, not a full-blown sequel here. Kind of makes sense here, as this also came out a year later, likely capitalizing on the fantastic RE2R (Resident Evil 2: Remake) from 2020.

A lot of the combat, movement, Inventory set-up & manipulation (grid-like set-up for you to play Tetris with), and whatnot - yes, this is basically taken & improved in some ways (i.e. visually more slick here) here in Resident Evil 3: Remake (RE3R). While in RE2R you felt like you were often scrounging for ammo and it was at a more methodical and slower-paced & all, often with less enemies on-screen on once like other classic survivor-horror games - well, RE3R feels more like an action-game, as you'll often feel a bit more bombarded with enemies and both ammo & action.

Nemesis, who often chases Jill here in RE3 Remake, reminds me a lot of Mr. X here from RE2R, namely in both design & style - but Nemesis feels tweaked-up a bit here in some ways - though, encounters often feels more cinematic & scripted here in this game over RE2 Remake. Again, this feels like they're following a lot of the RE2R formula & copy & pasting it and reskinning basically reskinned Mr. X here with Nemesis.

You won't be mostly playing as Leon here, this go around. Instead here, you'll be playing mostly as Jill Valentine, as this is her story here. Per usual with Resident Evil games: monsters are running amok somewhere; a Virus & out-break has happened; Umbrella Corp. is involved w/ experimenting on humans & whatnot; a cover-up is in the process of happening; and you (as the player) are here to stop this location from being overrun. In this case here, this is happening around & after the events of RE2 [Remake] (2019).

Just like RE2R, RE3R also looks great with RT On - of course, that's provided you have a system that can handle it. If not, you might be better off reversing it back to the old patch without RT, to get much better performance. With a 10700KF, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB SSD, 2 TB HDD, 8GB VRAM on the RTX 3070, W10 x64 - I can achieve 1080p60fps with both RT & FSR On, provided I don't exceed or push things past the VRAM limits of my beefy video card.

So far...I like it, but don't love it. It's good, but not as great as RE2 Remake. More to come, at some point - likely, when I finish it up.

ADDENDUM = 07-24-2022:
Well, at least RE3R doesn't re-use The Police Station an insane amount in this game. Regardless, once it gets back out of the Police Station, it gets into new areas, which are more interesting & different areas again, thankfully. Also, probably worth noting here, as there's a few parts where you also won't be playing as Jill here either, without giving too much away here. Regardless, RE3R really never stops with the constant action here, cinematic cut-scenes, and whatnot. The story's still solid for R.E. title...though, this all w/ the action & story stuff still just never hits the heights of RE2 Remake - and it also doesn't hit the lengths of that game in one play-though either. In terms of length, my first go around here in RE3R took around 7 1/2 hours.

Though, the ending of RE3R is nothing short of crazy, wicked, awesome & epic for the most part...still despite being, of course, anti-climatic and setting-up for another RE game. But, you likely & possibly knew that already - as this'll roll likely right into RE4 (which is awesome & my first RE game, oddly enough) - and we also all know that RE4 is getting a Remake...and on the main stories for RE games, we're now on RE8 a.k.a. RE: Village.

And I'm also not getting into the heavy complaints from RE3: Nemesis fans of say missing content, lack of choice, and other things that RE3 Remake is lacking - which I likely would've loved to have seen here. Luckily, I ain't somehow played RE3: Nemesis, so I can't do those comparisons - but I would love to see RE3 Remake gets DLC's and/or a re-released new version w/ a lot of that missing content, if Capcom would be willing to go to those lengths...since I'd so be cool with more RE3 Remake. RE3 Remake is good, but I'd really like more of it, TBH.

RE3 Remake is good - but still just doesn't top RE2: Remake. And well, RE2: Remake is just going to be very hard to top, as it's actually probably the Best RE Game Made so far...and that's not counting RE: Village, since I haven't played that one yet.

Regardless, even though RE3 ain't as great as say RE2 Remake (the best RE game, IMHO); RE4 (my favorite RE game - and #2 Top RE game); and RE7: Gold Edition (probably my #3 RE game); and RE: Revelations 2 (well, I think that's The Most Underrated RE Game) - RE3: Remake is definitely still worth playing; especially if you can catch it in a sale.

The opening hours of Resident Evil 3 are incredibly effective at putting you on edge. A remake of the original 1999 game, Resident Evil 3 puts the volatile and intense conflict between protagonist Jill Valentine and the unrelenting force of nature, Nemesis, front and center--giving way to some strong survival horror moments that show off the best of what the series can offer. But after that solid start, this revisit to a bygone era not only loses track of the type of horror game that Resident Evil once was, but also loses sight of what made the original so memorable.

Much like 2019's Resident Evil 2, the remake of Resident Evil 3 interprets the classic survival horror game through a modern lens, redesigning locations and altering key events to fit a significantly revised story. Resident Evil 3 doesn't deviate too much from the formula set by the RE2 remake, but it does lean harder into the action-focused slant the original version of RE3 had, giving you some greater defensive skills to survive. RE3's introduction is a strong one, conveying a creeping sense of paranoia and dread that's synonymous with the series, and Jill Valentine once again proves herself to be a confident protagonist to take everything head-on.

RE3 is very much a companion piece to the previous game, serving as a simultaneous prequel and sequel that caps off the saga in Raccoon City. There are even key points in the story that expect you to know of prior characters or locations that tie back to the previous remake. While you won't miss out on anything vital for not having played RE2, some of the previous game's most poignant moments are given more subtext in RE3. You'll eventually cross paths with supporting characters like mercenary Carlos Oliveira, the game's second playable character, along with some other unsavory individuals looking to take advantage of the chaos.

It was fun to see Jill and her allies maintain their confidence and even show some snark throughout the incident, which ensures that the game isn't always so serious. Both protagonists are also given some key moments throughout the story that show off their skills and personality more, which is fun and satisfying to see play out. But disappointingly, RE3's story reaches its conclusion after a brisk six-hour campaign, which is made worse by a lackluster finish that left me wanting. While this is comparable to the original game, the shrinking scope of the remake's plot and locations makes its short run even more apparent.

Throughout the game, Jill Valentine is a capable survivor, more so than both Leon and Claire, and she's well-suited to handle the undead and other bioweapon monstrosities like the Nemesis that roam the city. Along with dodging attacks, she can also execute slow-mo evasive rolls that open a clean shot at the enemy's weak point, which can be especially satisfying to pull off during an intense encounter.

There's a more pronounced emphasis on action and quick reflexes in RE3, which can make the shooting, survival, and exploration loop a bit more engaging and responsive. While this ultimately gives you a greater feeling of control in the field, it's not enough to the point that it makes encounters with the ravenous undead or Nemesis easy. So while you are capable, it's often best to play it safe. Resident Evil 3 tries to stick with the tenets of survival horror gameplay and is generally far more challenging than RE2, due to its greater focus on inventory management and ammo crafting. However, the generous save points and checkpoints ensure you won't suffer too steep a loss after death.

Resident Evil 3 also carries forth many of the successes from the Resident Evil 2 remake, which gives it a leg up for its own outing. As with previous games, RE3 is all about escalation, forcing you to contend with dwindling resources as the monsters--and Nemesis--put the pressure on. Unlike in Resident Evil 2, which quickly took you off the streets of Raccoon City, you spend more time in RE3 exploring the main roads, side alleys, and other points of interest in town.

RE3 possesses an impeccable level of detail for the locations and action during its six-hour campaign, right down to the tense atmosphere and grisly violence. The brutality and devastation in Raccoon City is demonstrated effectively thanks to the vivid and grotesque details as you explore the ruined city. The game also draws your eyes to the many locales that reference classic Resident Evil, which is not only fun to see, but manages to tug on the nostalgic heartstrings.

One of my favorite areas of RE3 is Downtown Raccoon City, which shows off the best that the remake has to offer. As an expansive map, it not only has diverse locations, and plenty of undead, it also displays the dynamic nature of the game's true star--Nemesis. The imposing villain quickly establishes himself as a cunning force when encountered out in the open.

The Nemesis has many tricks up its sleeve, such as using its tentacles to trip you up or turning other zombies into horrific mutations, all of which are disturbing to witness. It'll actively stalk and follow you into places you once thought were safe--bending the unspoken rules of engagement in survival horror to establish its presence further. Nemesis makes Mr. X from RE2 come across as a fedora-wearing goon, and even when you find yourself in a safe space, you can catch a glimpse of the villain waiting outside for you to leave--which stand as some of the most unnerving moments of the game.

However, as the game goes on, it becomes clear that Resident Evil 3 struggles to maintain its poise when the scope begins to narrow, and how blatantly the game relies on recycling many of RE2's tricks and tropes, which now feel less interesting. This has to do with the game's focus on momentum. Just when you're getting accustomed to a location, particularly the extensive and varied Downtown area, a story beat will occur that brings you to the next area, preventing your return. The series' penchant for puzzles are also infrequent in RE3 remake, putting more focus on exploration and combat which can eventually become exhausting.

It can be tricky to balance the elements of both survival horror and action gameplay, as one can easily undermine the other, and unfortunately, this is apparent in RE3. There are many moments where the game's strengths for action and horror shine, particularly during the more open areas where the Nemesis is afoot. Generally, though--especially toward the second half--its attempts to balance both can come across as awkward and uninteresting, and at its worst, they can be jarring. This is especially true with the many elaborate set-piece encounters, where you control Jill as she navigates Uncharted-esque sequences that are highly-scripted gameplay moments that go for the cinematic effect. They often result in tonal whiplash, as you typically transition back into the slower, survival-horror pacing right after.

This is most evident in the portrayal of the game's primary antagonist. Nemesis is at its best when stalking you in the streets. But these sections--while terrifyingly engaging--are fleeting. Nemesis only actively hunts you during the opening section in Downtown Raccoon City. The majority of the Nemesis encounters occur in scripted sequences that lead up to boss fights. In the original game, Nemesis' random appearances kept you on edge. In contrast, the remake's use of Nemesis in the mid-to-late game will likely have you roll your eyes at the prospect of another lengthy and fixed encounter.

Nemesis is undoubtedly one of the most iconic villains of the series, and it's frustrating and disappointing to see it effectively sidelined, coming off more like a standard Resident Evil boss that springs out at story beats. Another side effect of the lack of Nemesis encounters in the game is that it calls attention to the lack of enemy diversity. 

Over all 8.5/10. I highly recommend this game!

It's difficult to review this game without mentioning the RE2 remake, so I won't fight it. Compared to RE2, this game is very disappointing. RE2 started with the original game, built on it, modernized it, and made a definitive version that fits very well with what gamers expect nowadays, whilst still maintaining the spirit of the original.

RE3 did the opposite. It wasn't very close to the original at all except for the basic premise. The story was different, the game route was different, MANY areas and bosses were cut (at least a third to half of the original game), and ALL puzzles were cut. The only puzzles present could be solved by a child and they basically give you the solutions anyways. There isn't any survival horror left, it's just a third-person shooter. You get more than enough ammo on Standard difficulty to kill everything in your way.

I beat the game in 5 hours - and I was stopping to smell the roses. On top of being extremely short, there is basically no replayability either. Unlike RE2's Tyrant, this game's Nemesis is not dynamic. He shows up at the exact same places every time. In fact, the whole game is completely linear, with everything being the same every time. You can't even play as a different character or do a different route like in RE2. Once you've played it once, all there is to do is use points to buy helpful "boosts" in the in-game store, and play the same campaign over again.

The visuals, music, sound effects, and characters were all good. Gunplay still feels tight like in RE2, and you will be doing a lot more shooting in this game, so it's good that it holds up. The Hunter Beta is a good reimagining of a classic enemy. The Hunter Gamma is pretty terrible, and defeating it is more a measure of how well you can shoot a flame grenade into its mouth before getting insta-killed than anything else. The Drain Deimos is not at all threatening, except in the VERY distasteful and unnecessary scene where it throat-****s Jill.

All in all, the game is mediocre if you get it for $20 CDN / $15 USD. Do not buy it at full price. I have no doubt that the cutting of content and dumbing-down of gameplay was for the sake of finishing the multiplayer component. Nobody asked for that, and RE3 was - and still is - some RE fans' favourite in the whole series. I am very disappointed to see them treat the game this carelessly. They totally wasted the opportunity to remake a great game, most likely so they could push the microtransaction-riddled disaster that is RE: Resistance and make more money. Now there is no way RE3 fans will ever get to play a good remake.

Ingredients:

1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie

Directions:

1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

[h1]Resident Evil 3 (2020)[/h1]

[i]Resident Evil 3[/i], the great remake that could have been. I was one of the fools who pre-ordered this game on PS4 thinking it was going to be bigger than RE2R. For someone who holds RE3 Nemesis as one of my top RE games, I have a lot to say here.

To make things clear: as an action horror game, it's [b]okay[/b]; there are issues here and there but it works about 80% of the time at least. As a Resident Evil game AND a Resident Evil remake, it's pretty terrible. There are a couple of ways to tackle this game so I'll be reviewing it from the perspective of one who's grown up playing the original 1999 game.

That being said, this is probably my least favorite RE game and I didn't have that much more fun outside of my first playthrough.

[u]Story + Characters (Possible Spoilers!)[/u]

[spoiler]Most people will mention a lot about how improved the storyline is in the remake compared to RE3 Nemesis and I can see why: it's a lot more focused and streamlined. The plot for RE3R is almost like the original plot, except there's a plotline switch that focuses from escaping the city to getting the vaccine to stop the missile strike from blowing up... Raccoon City?[/spoiler]

[spoiler]The issue I have with this story is that, halfway, it goes absolutely nowhere. Jill makes the vaccine to "save the city" and the vaccine gets destroyed anyway (Jill couldn't care less about RC at the end). Also, aside from other reasons, Jill already has the T-virus antibodies from being cured so this plotline with the vaccine was pointless.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]It's like the RE3R team read a synopsis of the RE3 plot and decided it needed a human main antagonist to show that, "oh, it's not the monsters that are actual evil, it's human greed that's actual evil" except the original already showed these points much better without Nicholai being such a blatant villain with actual subtlety.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]As for the characters, almost everyone in this game has been dumbed down to a certain degree. Jill is snobby and acts way too hard to be a badass, Nicholai may as well be wearing a big white mustache to twirl whenever he's going to do something evil, Mikhail's despair over the loss of his subordinates under him is replaced by a generic disgruntled leader character, Dario is turned from a survivor struck with overwhelming grief over his daughter's death to a complete noodle of an idiot, and Nemesis is turned into an incompetent goofball that only tosses Jill around even when he's got her dead to rights. The only characters who improved from the original were Tyrell and Carlos who is by far the best character out of everyone; anyone who plays this game will LOVE Carlos.[/spoiler]

[u]Gameplay[/u]

This game is [b]short[/b]. That could be confusing considering that most RE games are short, but RE3R is one of the shortest Resident Evil games I've ever played due to the fact that it's the [i]most[/i] linear RE game yet. The reason for why this game can be completed so quickly is that there's not really much to explore compared to other RE games; you never have to backtrack that much because what you leave behind is relatively insignificant and you never have to go back to places for more puzzle solving. My first run was a little under three hours on PS4 and I explored as much as I could.

Given that the gameplay is derived from RE2R, it's still solid. Aiming and shooting feels good, controls are responsive, dodging is fun to do but is situational because enemies will sometimes rush you down from behind which makes dodging based on luck at that point. However, that's basically all there is to say that is good about the gameplay because the pacing that this game goes at does not work with the mechanics. 

Many new enemies you meet are either long ranged or agile which results in you trying to spin your camera to see where they're at and attempting to dodge them. They also range from being insignificant to defeat or being outright drivel. Ne-α Parasites can hit you from nearly across an entire room, Drain Deimos are relegated to one section and are never seen again, Hunter Gammas are almost free enemies considering that one shotgun blast to their mouths stuns them and one Flame Round will kill them, Pale Heads are lazily reused from RE2R's Ghost Survivors, and Hunter Betas are armored and can now randomly one-shot you at ANY condition of health with almost no warning. Dispatching enemies is easy because the game will give you the resources right next to the enemy that is weak to it ([spoiler]example, the Sewer section[/spoiler]) and you are given so much ammo in this game even on harder difficulties.

Nemesis T-Type is the titular enemy that made RE3 Nemesis as memorable as it was. Although he's much stronger than any enemy you will encounter, compared to his original, he is an absolute joke. Mind you, this was basically Umbrella's peak tyrant who could tank 10 Freeze Rounds, take two Rocket Launcher missiles, three Red Barrels, and would still come after you 11 times in the original AND follow you in most areas of the Raccoon City streets. In the Remake, up to Hardcore difficulty, a single Hand Grenade or Red Barrel can down him the fastest. Nemesis only ever truly stalks you in the Downtown area once ([spoiler]after the Power Station[/spoiler]). For him to be anywhere as tough, you basically have to amp up the difficulty to the point where his attack patterns become unfair ([spoiler]final boss, anyone?[/spoiler]).

There is no reason to think about item management at all. There are few key items that are used to progress forward and those that you do get are quickly / twice used (at most) to progress because it's so obvious where to use them. Puzzles are laughably easy to complete (with one puzzle at the end requiring a tiny bit of thought) and are almost non-existent; most "puzzles" that require you to progress will simply be installing key items, unlocking doors, or turning on switches.

It's never a good sign when there are challenges in a Resident Evil game that make you grind hundreds of kills in a series that EMPHASIZES on saving resources, running past a majority of enemies, and killing only what you're required to especially in an action horror game as short as this one. After beating the game, you're left with playing the game on harder difficulties and completing records to unlock rewards, but the replay value is short; I was able to 100% the game within a [b]day and a half[/b].

[u]Graphics & Sound[/u]

I will admit at least that the graphics on RE3R are as beautiful as usual for a game that uses the RE engine. However, I couldn't help but feel that RE2R had much better use of shadows and gore to emphasize the horror aspect and rarely was I ever tense playing this game. Many of the character designs are great; I liked Carlos' design the best and Jill's design is good enough for people to make mods for her.

The sound effects for the guns, explosions, and the chaos of the city are decent as well. Nothing sounded out of place or as if I was shooting out anything weaker or stronger than what the gun looked like.

[u]Conclusion[/u]

Like everyone else mentions, there's an insane amount of cut OG content. In short, about 70% of RE3 has either been changed or outright cut from the remake. To name a few: no Enhanced Ammo, no Clock Tower, no Park, no Cemetery, no Incineration Disposal Plant, no Grave Diggers or Brain Suckers, no complex mixing of Gunpowders and Grenades, no Nemesis-dropped weapons like the STI EAGLE.

It's a damn shame because newer fans will never know how much better this game could have been. Such aspects matter if taking them out removes a lot of depth from the remake and given how easy it is to complete this game in under an hour without speedrun strats, it only goes to show. I would only buy this game on discount and would recommend to RE fans just so you can say you've played it.

Riding off the success of the Resident Evil 2 REmake, RE3 delivers a really great polish to one of my favorite games in the entire Resident Evil franchise. The character designs of some of your returning favorites and the locations themselves are truly top-notch and one of the greatest rides of nostalgia of the past several years. However, Resident Evil 3 can't help but to feel like a rushed product in the midst of RE2's success and the Covid-19 pandemic. The remake of this game seems to be missing several moments from the original game and even erases one of the absolute best death scenes in the entire franchise's history (Brad Vickers vs the Nemesis). These missing moments in the game definitely leaves the finished product feeling much shorter than its predecessor. Though that's something an update and a little DLC could fix, with the release of Village and the announcement of its DLC and the Resident Evil 4 remake, it's unlikely Resident Evil 3 will get the fix it deserves. That being said, it's still a great game, albeit a short one and it begs to be on your digital shelf as Resident Evil has been delivering some of the best survival horror since returning to it's roots in 2017.

Can you spare the time to double back for that weapon upgrade? Should you risk kneecapping this zombie instead of putting it down to spare precious ammo? If that sounds engaging, RE3 is a fun ride you'll want to take more than a few times.

Resident Evil 3 lets you play as Jill Valentine where you are immediately attacked and hunt down by a hulking monster by the name of Nemesis. While Nemesis is hunting you down, the whole city are also experiencing a zombie plague. With a hunky guy named Carlos, it's up to Jill, an experienced and skilled soldier, to survive and save Racoon City from destruction.

I'm not that well-versed in Resident Evil games and usually dislike horror. But I'm warming up to playing this genre after having finished some Resident Evil games mainly 1, 2, and 4. Resident Evil isn't straight up horror, or I like to dub them, "hide and seek horror" like Outlast and Amnesia. Resident Evil is a survival horror where you mainly explore intricated designed maps and search for resources, while having enemies in the way.

Positives first, I like the action in this game. From set pieces to the combat controls, the combat in this game handles very well. Now theres a dodge button, where you can execute a perfect dodge to slow down time and counter the enemy attacking you. Initially its hard to execute, but once the attacks are memorised, encounters can be a cake walk.

That is if you have resources. You can't gunsblazing gun down everything that you see. Ammunition is scarce, hence the genre "survival horror".   This is also the case for other Resident Games that I played. Its good to know where to spend your ammunition and where to just run away. 

The story is okay. I like Jill as a character, and she has a more snarky attitued than her character from RE1. Really shows how much RE1 matures her a bit, since she's already experienced having this zombie thing. I like Carlos. This hunk of a guy is likable. Kinda sad not to see him in other entries, or maybe I haven't noticed (don't spoil me). But the rest are kinda okay, which is a bummer. Not unlike other RE games which have some impact on me.

Nemesis is menacing. But sadly, that's all I can say. I want more of him. RE2's Tyrant kinda eclipsed Nemesis, more scarier and frightening. Meanwhile Nemesis here is scripted to some few encounters and bossfights. But the rivalry and dynamic between Nemesis and Jill are entertaining.

On to the flaws, the soundtrack is forgettable. Usually during the credits are a time to reflect back on your journey, but the credits here played an anime-esque rock song. Took me out of the reflection. Kinda felt outta place. RE2 and RE1's soundtrack are memorable. Probably have to relisten the tracks here.

I've seen reviews on the length of this game. I don't really mind the length as long as its fun. Same thing here, I am satisfied with the experience. But I don't think thats the same to the other RE games I played. All of them have me wanting to replay either to make a faster time or just have fun. Not the same here. I can uninstall it right now and never come back.

I have not played the original RE3, so I don't know how much is changed or different. For me, RE3 feels like riding from RE2's success. Doing the same thing but different. Kinda bummer. I don't know if that is apparent in the OG versions.

Overall, a solid RE game. But some flaws made it dissapointing.

[i]Resident Evil 3[/i] might not be the strongest in any single category out, but hot damn if it's not one of the most consistent entries, too.

A remake of 1999's [i]Resident Evil 3: Nemesis[/i], players step into the shoes of Raccoon City S.T.A.R.S. officer Jill Valentine as she attempts to escape a zombie outbreak threatening to destroy the city; along the way, she unwittingly becomes the partner of a well-meaning corporate mercenary named Carlos, who is unaware of how his employer is directly responsible for the outbreak of undead. In spite of a somewhat complex summary, the bulk of the game flows pretty naturally, with Jill and Carlos attempting to traverse the city and stay alive in the wake of chaos and destruction. Initially comprised of standard, classic [i]Resident Evil[/i] gameplay, the game leans further into action more and more as the stakes of each chapter grow higher and higher. Once again rendered in Capcom's internal Reach for the Moon Engine (or RE Engine for short), it's the most lavishly realized zombie apocalypse the game franchise has yet served up, complete even with ray-tracing, if your PC can handle that sort of thing.

A lot of discussion about [i]RE3[/i] centers around how action-centric the game is, and this is fair, on one level. [i]RE3[/i] certainly asks more from the player in combat scenarios than either prior remake in the series, which can be daunting. What is missed in this conversation, though, is how the increased pacing actually helps the game. While most games in the Resident Evil series err towards either the slow survival-horror school of design or else the action-combat-flavored horror school, [i]RE3[/i] finds a sweet-spot between the two. With [i]just[/i] enough resources to make it through encounter to encounter, it never felt like the game was being easy on me. It's not necessarily strict "horror" per se, but that's fine; it's wonderfully crafted [i]tension[/i], and for the game's relatively short runtime, it's a perfect match. In fact, somewhat controversially, I think the game's pacing actually fares better than the more faithful remake of [i]Resident Evil 2[/i].

If there are drawbacks, they fall into one of two camps, neither being a deal breaker. The first is the Nemesis, a super-powered monster that pursues you through out the course of your Zombie Misadventure. In the original release, it was a more systemic part of the game, organically pursuing your and forcing you to reconsider your approach in-game. Here, it's reduced to a cinematic set-piece, stripped of the same mechanical complexity we saw in the remake of [i]RE2[/i]. What's preserved, however, is a sense of pacing, and while the Nemesis's presence is less felt in the moment-to-moment of play, the times when you face off against the creature are [i]magnificent[/i]. Similarly, some may find the game's playtime too short, and a $40 price tag, a 5-7 hour campaign is indeed short. However, not a moment of gameplay is wasted, and the campaign's pacing never feels contrived. In fact, I think [i]RE3[/i] holds the distinction of being the only RE game I've ever played that well and truly lacks a disappointing third act,.

[i]Resident Evil 3[/i] isn't the strongest game in the series, with neither the adrenaline packed combat of [i]RE4[/i] nor the tight, terrifying horror of [i]RE7[/i]. But that almost doesn't matter. It is almost the ideal version of the game that it [i]is[/i], and that's a rip-roaring, tension-laden, zombie-shootin', survival horror romp through the dying gasp of the most '90s city you can imagine. It's great. Perhaps wait for a sale before picking it up, but rest assured, Jill's escape from Raccoon City remains a superb title.

This game was heavily criticized when it first came out in 2020- almost all of the criticism was around how short the game is, and the lack of an "open world." The same happened when RE3: Nemesis was released back in 1999. Considering that they both followed one of the greatest video games of all time, Resident Evil 2, it was a high order to fill those big shoes. I will go ahead and be the contrarian, though, and say that Resident Evil 3 is still an excellent game with high production value and a TON of fun to play.

The game takes place around the same time as Resident Evil 2- I am always confused by the timeline, because apparently it starts before RE2, but then ends after RE2 ends. There is a portion where Jill is out of commission for two days I believe, which messes up the timeline of the Raccoon City outbreak. The story revolves around Jill Valentine, from the original Resident Evil, who is trapped in Raccoon City in the middle of a T-virus outbreak. A hulking creature, known as Nemesis, stalks her throughout the city- relentlessly, while screaming out "STARS!!!" His mission is to kill all STARS members- the team that uncovered the nefarious deeds of the Umbrella Corporation in the original game. You will be horrified and disgusted by his appearance- looking like his insides have been turned out, with huge pulsing veins and tentacles that he utilizes to grab and suffocate you. Also, he can use weapons! Including a flame thrower and rocket launcher. He is definitely much more frightening than the cold, stoic Mr. X from Resident Evil 2. 

Most of the game's suspense comes from the random encounters you have with Nemesis- if you choose to engage, he can drop valuable items such as weapon upgrades and health sprays. But oftentimes, you can just run away from him, dodging his attacks and using the environment against him. Speaking of- a couple of features have been updated since RE2. First of all- you can dodge enemies by clicking the space bar at a certain moment. They removed the "counter-attack" option where you would stick a knife or grenade into an enemies head if they grab you. This was a disappointing removal, if I can be honest. However, you do switch and play as Carlos at parts of the game, who has different weapons and a different counter-attack. 

There really isn't much to say about this game besides the fact that it's essentially RE2 game play but in an urban environment rather than just the police station. It is not as long as RE2, and not quite as good, but is still a great game and you will have a blast.
