RE3 feels more action than the puzzling horror of RE2. And this is a big mistake. The levels are (mostly) linear set pieces while lacking any true threats. A great deal of the game is played out via awful action movie cutscenes. It spoon feeds you every step of the way.

Levels - Mostly linear, and very short. There's hardly any puzzles, and no real exploration. You can leisurely walk around the levels and pickup every item. Rarely did I have to return to an area with a specific item. RE2 has you revisit areas repeatedly, with multiple puzzles cascading throughout the game. That more "metroidvania" style suits this style of game far better. Giving you sense of exploration as you discover secrets. RE3 is almost the complete opposite.

Enemies - Harder difficulties are supposed to massively improve the lackluster enemies... But those difficulties are locked until you beat each consecutive setting. Nightmare hardly seemed *better* in my opinion. Enemies were little faster, but it wasn't hard to navigate through. Playing through hardcore, I thought it was too easy to full clear levels while being conservative with ammo. I haven't yet played the hardest difficulty, but being forced to replay the game with only a *gradual* bump in quality is questionable at best. Being forced to sit through the awful script, skip the hundreds of cutscenes, and shake my head during what's supposed to be tense nail biting moments.

Nemesis - The main baddy. A super smart Mr. X here to hunt you down no matter where you flee. Viciously using every weapon at his disposal... Except every time you encounter the Nemesis, it's an on-rails section. At one point they weren't even trying to hide it, just hold down 'W' to win the encounter. Half of your time here is spent watching a cutscene of Jill battling the monster. There's only a single moment he inhabits a level with you, but it's insanely easy to full clear the level before meeting him... Which I did unintentionally... I simply had to walk past him to the exit... When you are running away from him, it causes me to eye roll. The threat comes from him hitting you. If he does it can lead to an unbreakable chain stun which can kill you in nightmare difficulty. I understand making an intelligent chase enemy can be difficult, but this is pathetic. He doesn't really feel threatening because he's always paired with a cutscene and a completely straight forward path. His boss encounters are even worse than gimmicks. Literally jumping around the arena like an mindless animal... I expected better from a serious, and threatening enemy. He's supposed to be the NEMESIS, an enemy that hunts you even more fervently than Mr. X. Meanwhile, Mr. X proves to be a real Nemesis. Oppressing your character. Creating enormous tension with those heavy footsteps. Restricting your time in an area as you frantically try to complete a puzzle... Even reappearing in alarming ways. It's likely the incredibly poor level design paired with the heavy action focus made him a movie villain, and not a Nemesis.

Story - It was standard low quality schlock. I didn't really expect much anyway, but some moments were pure cringe. There was also an extremely cartoonish villain who's kind of just there. The final line "it was greed that caused this" felt a little to apropos considering this game is not much more than a cash grab.

How could this game be better? If they had opened up Raccoon City so you could visit the RPD, the hospital, and roam the streets. Attempting to solve a multitude of puzzles that are interlinked between all of these locations... All while the lingering threat of Nemesis hunts you down.

The new remake of Resident Evil 3: Nemesis begins with a literal bang. A giant, monstrous bioweapon named Nemesis crashes through the walls of my apartment, knocking me to the ground. My little handgun is useless against him. His goal? To kill me. And he'll relentlessly chase me through the streets of Raccoon City to do it.

After taking the first of many batterings, I escape, and I'm limping through a dark alleyway. Just ahead of me there are crowds of people sprinting through the trashed city streets, fleeing the zombies that have taken control. I hear only the sounds of endless sirens, water spraying from a busted fire hydrant, and screaming. This is just the beginning and I'm already tense. Game maker Capcom coined the term "survival horror" after the release of the first Resident Evil, for Sony's then new PlayStation in 1996. The genre became known for its maze-like maps, puzzles, limited (and sometimes absent) ability to fight back and heal, and little inventory space meaning players had to run away from monsters more often than fight them.

That changed a little with the original RE3 in 1999, which allowed players to fight back more without ever feeling too in control. Now, 20 years later and following last year's widely-praised remake of Resident Evil 2 it's been completely remade and reimagined. The bare bones of the game remain the same: Raccoon City is overwhelmed by an outbreak of a disease called the T-virus, which turns everyone it infects into a zombie. You're playing most of the game as "Supercop" Jill Valentine, as she desperately tries to survive and escape the infested city while our friend Nemesis stalks close behind.

Jill is a member of the Special Tactics and Rescue Service team (S.T.A.R.S), an elite law enforcement team at the Raccoon Police Department. S.T.A.R.S. was investigating the source of the T-virus, and traced it back to a politically powerful company called Umbrella Pharmaceuticals.

This is a long, complicated story that spans multiple games. But to sum it up without spoilers: Umbrella is super evil. And they really want to destroy all evidence of their involvement in the T-virus outbreak. Jill and her surviving teammates at S.T.A.R.S are a smidge of an inconvenience, so Umbrella has created our stalker Nemesis to kill off all the remaining S.T.A.R.S and cover up their tracks. But other than the absolute basics, nearly everything else changed in the remade Resident Evil 3. The game obviously looks more beautiful with modern graphics and the awful movement controls got replaced with a system more instinctive to today's gamers. This makes it much easier to play the remake than the original.

And the new layers of detail mean we get to know the characters better than ever we see the psychological impact the zombie apocalypse has had on Jill through her nightmares, and the way she falls asleep at her desk, exhausted by her investigation. And any time she takes a gun from a dead zombie or drags one out of a car so she can drive it, she apologizes. The new Resident Evil 3 is an entertaining horror experience. It hooks you into the story quicker than the original and is very welcoming to new players. But there are tons of changes from the original characters, monsters, puzzles, locations, and plot points have all been altered, or in some cases removed. And a lot of the changes make things less scary.

Like previous games in the series, the original RE3 used fixed camera angles. That meant you were navigating Jill from a third-person perspective through an environment you could only see from one angle which made sense with the technical limitations of the first PlayStation but became outdated as technology became more advanced. For the next game in the series, Capcom permanently switched to a more popular over the shoulder perspective, where the camera remains fixed on the character.

But those fixed camera angles made the original RE3 crap your pants scary. Other than audio cues, you never knew if a zombie was hiding around a corner, ready to lunge at you and chase you back down the hall. The remake hides its enemies in the darkness, or behind objects in the room, but its zombies are nowhere near as terrifying as when they were waiting to jump you off-screen. The original game also ratcheted up the tension through its save system. Players had a limited amount of ink ribbons they could use to save their progress whenever they found a typewriter, and the threat of getting killed and losing a lot of progress really upped the stakes. In easy mode, you got unlimited saves.

But now, you have unlimited saves on all difficulty levels (though your number of saves does impact your final grade at the end of the game). You never lose too much progress when you die, which makes surviving every encounter a little less critical.

And one big feature missing from the remake is branching story paths. Like other games in the series, the first RE3 presented players with choices that altered the story and the ending. That meant that even though the game was only six hours long, you could replay it until you'd experienced all the story paths and endings. But you see everything the remake has to offer after one playthrough, and that lack of replayability makes it hard to justify the $39.99 purchase price.

There is a reason to keep playing for fans that want a challenge if you defeat hardcore mode, then you unlock two even tougher difficulties. And despite its shortcomings, it's still a good game; it brings realism and life to a story previously told with limited, 20 year-old technology.

But for what you get, I'd wait until it's on sale unless you really love Resident Evil.

Is it bad? 
No, not really. 
But is it great?
Certainly not.
It *looks* like it's the same Resident Evil 2 Remake formula, just used on Resident Evil 3. At face value, that's correct. But the execution is poor. Some of the features in Resident Evil 3: Nemesis (such as the minigame) are absent, and you're just paying for the story mode, which would be fine (though Resident Evil 2's remake had the original minigames, and DLC minigames) if they innovated a bit more. 

It really sucks because this game came out in the shadow of Resident Evil 2's remake which is absolutely spectacular, and so, it's very easy to compare the two. Resident Evil 2 gave us four very differing playthroughs of the same story, each with two characters and their own unique weapons. For Resident Evil 3, we get three "Difficulty playthroughs" (The first 3 difficulties are the same design, the unlockable two are different) that are barely unique to eachother. Some typewriters and item boxes are absent on the higher difficulties. Ammo is scarcer, items are reduced. Enemy placement has changed and more difficult enemies are placed, as well as more ornery enemies. It's nothing especially unique or different, it's just increasingly challenging. 

Speaking of ornery enemies. Having a suited stranger who can "barely" outrun you at times while you're moving around rooms and confined spaces is tense. Mr. X impedes your progress in a non-linear environment and you can spend a few minutes trying to lead him away from the room you're in. 
Nemesis, on the other hand, impedes your progress in a linear environment. You have to find a way to get past him. His walking pace outruns you. You are constantly dodging attacks just trying to get from point a to point b. This is supposed to be challenging, yes, and it is. But where is the tension? Having someone just dogging your steps all the time attacking you and teaching you how to dodge is just plain annoying. You can nail the dodge down perfectly but it gets old when you're doing it every five fudging seconds just trying to get to where you want to be, zombies closing in.

Oh, right. The linear environment. You're telling me they couldn't innovate and make it a little less linear? They did remove sections from the game, and add larger sections (like the hospital). This is a retelling, after all. Couldn't add new locations? Something to make the game just a little longer? They removed puzzles in favor of a lot more in-your-face action. 
This game was very clearly rushed, and it shows. Jill is missing facial animations during idle (non-cutscene) dialogue, maybe an oversight, maybe they expected you to be looking at her back while she was conversing with Carlos. Interestingly enough, RE2 gave animations for claire and leon to use eachother's weapons. While Jill can use the CQBR (on assisted difficulty or an unlockable weapon) don't try giving Carlos any of her weapons just for fun. 
Many recycled locations from RE2 as well, but it seems like the textures are pretty unpolished using the same graphical settings as RE2. 

What's good about this game? What's not to complain? It's fun. It *is* a fresh take on RE3's story mode, and if you're looking for more RE2, over the shoulder zombie killing with a more action packed spin, this game delivers on that. But don't expect it to match with RE2, don't expect much from this game.

I absolutely loved RE2R on PS4, but I simply can't stomach playing RE3R. The graphics are still top-notch, but it's the gameplay what kills it for me. It's so effing frustrating. 

The regular enemies are unbearably bullet spongy. The regular zombies have a grab attack that is insanely difficult to avoid, has a huge range (far more than what the animation may lead you to think) and they even rotate on the spot to "snap" to you. They sometimes even skip a few frames of animation to latch onto you more quickly. The dodge mechanic is hard to pull of and 90% of the time, I found it to be absolutely worthless.

The insects in an early part of the game are really annoying too. They sneak up on you, hit you hard and sometimes even infect you, forcing you to use a green herb to get rid of the infection.

Later, you encounter a new type of zombie with a parasite on their heads. They have a very long reaching attack and take a ton of bullets to kill. Like the regular zombies, but even more annoying.

Then there's Nemesis. What a massive downgrade from RE2R's Mr. X. He has cheats activated. He can stunlock you after one punch (usually, he punches me three times and I'm dead, without any chance to recover). You can stun him if you damage him enough... but the time he's down isn't really consistent. Sometimes it's a few seconds, sometimes it's half a minute. But that doesn't really matter, since Nemesis can teleport instantly behind you (bypassing his stunned status), rush ahead of you and punch you. He can also grab you from pretty far away with his tentacle attack. Once, I was at the feet of a staircase, he was on the steps and the tentacle clearly went over Jill's head... but she still "snapped" to it and it grabbed her anyway.

It's simply too much for me to find this game enjoyable. A pity.

A great companion game to RE2 remake that extends the lore, story and environment of Raccoon City.  Just like the original RE3,  RE3 remake was always meant to complement RE2 remake (which is why they are always bundled together).  While the game is less scarier than RE2 remake, that doesn't make it any less fun to play (the original RE3 was also less scarier).  The action-based and fast-paced sequences match the intensity of the main antagonist, Nemesis.  Nemesis is greatly updated in this version to be unrelenting, vicious, and almost invincible.  He definitely makes Mr. X and other prototypes look like ragdolls.  While the game is on the shorter side, there are still quite a few memorable/standout moments involving Jill (the escape from the beginning and final boss) and Carlos (revisiting RPD headquarters and defending the hospital).  It would have been great to also include or update extra story game modes such as Mercenaries (from the original RE3).  Overall, if you are an action junkie and passionate about the RE series as I am, this game is a must-play in your library.

As a person who played the Original Re3 as his first Re game... this was a disappointing remake..

I had read a lot of bad reviews about this and only just purchased it to see for myself. 
I don't hate this game but it definately isn't as good as the Re 2 remake and certain falls short of the original Re3 

 It is clear that the development team behind this were perhaps under pressure by Capcom to get this game out asap because you get the impression there are chunks taken out of this game and parts rushed.

Look at the concept artwork it is obvious they did plan to have more locations of Downtown RC and this leads to the biggest let down of this game, unnecessary cut content. 

Downtown seems more or less complete but in the original it feels like a bigger environment, choices of where to go first which impact the story line, nope this Downtown was a linear experience. 
They drew the car park and clearly even designed it with exploration in mind, but you never get to explore it, same with the Stagla gas station. 

The Clock Tower section is completely missing which is a real disappointment. In the original game that was a great middle section of the game, with puzzles and randomising enemies to avoid; depending on what choices were made. In this remake they just seem to jump to the fight in the courtyard. Hang on what about the Clock Tower area, can I just play some re for a moment and explore a remade clock tower? Nope i've got another battle again already great.. And not even that was great..
Oddly enough, the apartment you run through downtown to escape nemesis had clock tower esque doors and walls..

It isn't just the clock tower though is it, it seems if there was an area around the tower and Hospital that was removed, which should be the Park and Dead Factory....
Well they decided, no let's forget the variable looking environment and just go straight in to the Factory and Hospital. Boring! 
Nest 2 just comes across as well we can't be arsed to do anything more now let's re-use assets. Even the concept of Nest 2 shows more interesting areas and even ideas.. Come on Capcom, what happened to the different environments?!

Another gripe I have is what happened to Nemesis? In the original game he practically wouldn't leave you alone for most of the game, in Re3 remake apart from one or two moments he stalks you, other than that he appears in scripted moments and even so, when he does appear in scripted moments the game protects you and holds your hand. You know that something is wrong as soon as the game starts, since he fails to get past the bookshelf...
This is a huge step down from the original pursuer who would take several rooms to lose. 
He also mutates in to an Alien Queen early in the game; yes it seems like an Alien Queen. Gone is the humanoid pursuing monster and now it's just a blob that keeps turning up to taunt you. Personally I would of liked to of seen more of humanoid Nemesis, I rather liked the way he was re-designed and gradually became more mutated, his Stars cries reflected how angry he was getting at losing Jill constantly, like I said though sadly this is cut far too short. 

In fact when I think about it, this game is actually called Resident evil 3... Hmmmm I can see why they removed the Nemesis word!

Puzzles? Well there aren't many if any. The original game had several and even Re2 remake had a lot more than this. Puzzles are good at varying the gameplay and one thing I liked about the original Re3. The only puzzles we get are, inserting jewels, setting a train route with the answer shown and a pointless vaccine puzzle with the solution being press random buttons until it lines up.... Yeah very inventive.

Live events? Nope also gone are the choices and varying routes to take. Would it have taken much to of given us the chance to go to the Stagla gas station or Garage first, to change things up a bit? Nope. The Raccoon Press as well? Nope gone. I mean come on, maybe even change events so Jill goes to the Rpd instead of Carlos resulting in a nemesis encounter, or just Carlos and then the Nemesis breaks through the wall making a Nemesis sized hole... Oh yeah I forgot that is just c4....
 
Any music this time? Well the music oddly enough seemed better in this than the Re2 remake, they remixed some of the original music and re-used it in places and the game didn't seem as silent.

Gameplay? The game plays out a lot like re 2 remake with a few additions. One being a dodge where you can dodge enemies, this was a welcome addition as it was also in the og re3. Imo this is also a vast improvement on the original dodge, it feels more like it works. It also mixes up the gameplay a bit more from re 2. However, the game also likes to hold your hand in a lot of places and you aren't really doing anything! Poison is also oddly removed from this game not sure why?

Boss battles or lack of?
The bosses in this game consists of the Nemesis and the Alien Queen. That's it... There isn't a Gravedigger or anything else. They give the Hunter Frogs gravedigger mouths but that doesn't count, that's just lazy enemy design.
The Nemesis boss battles aren't very inventive either. There is little difference between the clock tower fight and the treatment vat fight, the final battle was a joke. 

In terms of replay value
I feel like you don't really get much for finishing the game or much of a reason to re-play it. The original had a mercenaries mode and alternate paths to take which added replay value, even Re 2 remake had several battle modes. Re 3 remake gives you a shop and some extra guns and accessories you can buy, This is nice but it doesn't make up for missing game sections and a lack of an extra scenario. There is also only one ending, you can't do anything differently or frankly do anything to change the game at any point, as there are no event selections. Pressing a button to do something doesn't count!

The lack of event selections is annoying, anything to vary the gameplay experience? Nope just linear over and over again.

As I said above I don't completely hate this game, there are one or two moments that I enjoyed like the Rpd visit, it neatly ties certain events on Re 2 to this game; although I wish it was Jill going there and having another Nemesis encounter.. 

If you are a fan of the original re 3 you should play this game to enjoy the brief good moments, but i'll warn you it is disappointing what could have been. If you are expecting the same standard as Re 2 remake, even a game as good as or better than the re 3 original you will feel slightly disappointed.   

If you are a fan of the Re 2 remake you will probably find yourself wanting to play the Re 2 remake again.

This game is pretty fun. Some people love the RE2 remake but don't like this game, so you might be asking yourself why that is? Well it's because it plays and feels differently. 
I hopped into this game after beating RE2 remake and thinking it would play and feel the same, just with a different story. But  I couldn't have been more wrong. Both these games use the same engine, so they look and have the same basics as each other, but with my experience RE2 had more puzzles and felt more like an escape room game. So find the missing pieces and put them together to try and make it out of an area. While RE3 has more of an action/fast past feel with some puzzles mixed into it. So big open rooms with lots of zombies coming after you, and more combat options such as a dodge move and more. Which isn't a bad thing at all, but it was just a lot more different then what I was expecting. 
I also think it's a good thing they changed these games up. Because while RE2 was a lot of fun I'm sure it would've gotten boring if they used the same formula and just changed a couple story pieces and sold it as a whole new game. 
So why so many negative reviews compared to RE2? Well I can't speak for everyone but what I could see and relate to is RE3 story feels a lot more forced, and the main part I loved about RE2 is it's rich and thought out story. So what did RE3 do wrong? Well the story feels really forced, like things happening to keep the story moving forward and things that just don't seem to make a lot of sense or fit together well. And like I said before, I do like how they changed these 2 games up, but I don't think an action game is the way to go for a RE game. It doesn't capture the creepiness and "What's going to be behind this corner?" feel at every moment when you can just dodge away from zombies and shoot them in the face 10 times. 
At the end of the day, this is a good game. As the credits rolled on Resident Evil 3’s campaign, I immediately started playing it over again. Not because I felt like I missed anything the first time around – I was as fastidious as developer Capcom encouraged me to be – but because my journey through Raccoon City was so consistently packed with tense monster moments and breakneck-paced fun, and it was so challenging throughout its six-odd hours, that I wanted to jump in and do it all over again with sharper skills and knowledge. My undying enthusiasm for it speaks volumes of the polish seen in this remake, and the finesse with which it manages to tread the tightrope between a confident modern horror and a tonal callback to the original Resident Evil trilogy.
Resident Evil 3 takes place nearly concurrently with the events of the equally accomplished Resident Evil 2, and follows different characters. The endearingly practical Jill Valentine – last seen in the original Resident Evil and its Director’s Cut – is called upon by a roguish Umbrella Corp mercenary by the name of Carlos Oliviera to help save the remaining inhabitants of a demolished Raccoon City from the carnage spawned by the T-Virus outbreak. Of course, nothing goes to plan, and Jill finds herself in a wonderfully labyrinthine, zombie-studded playground where she – and your nerves – must also contend with the threat of an invulnerable monster called Nemesis.
It’s a very classic Resident Evil set up, but then, this is a remake of a classic, goofily fun Resident Evil story -- the original 1999 game. The major story events from the original Resident Evil 3 are all there, albeit rearranged, and the cheesiness the early trilogy is known for is delivered in a charmingly self-knowing way. “How is it no one in the hospital ever noticed all this?” Jill wonders aloud after discovering a massive underground base that isn’t particularly well hidden. Resident Evil 3 is also, fortunately, very efficient in its storytelling; the villain is perfectly villainous, the heroes are all selfless and charming, and cutscenes are lean yet efficiently deliver big dramatic moments. It carries the gameplay swiftly along, in other words, and never gets bogged down in unnecessary exposition.
The chaotic, ruined Raccoon City goes a long way toward bringing Resident Evil’s story and the broader universe to life. Once again working within the RE Engine that powered both last year’s Resident Evil 2 and 2017’s Resident Evil 7, Capcom has done an incredible job in the small details here; from the in-universe advertising (“No Spares in This Game!” reads the tagline for a movie called “Sudden Death Bowling”) to the detritus left by citizens who had to escape in a hurry, to Resident Evil 2-related Easter eggs (“Now here’s a weird f****ing door!” Carlos says upon encountering the Spade Door, which is so significant in Resident Evil 2’s police station) and genuinely compelling in-game notes and journals that give background context to some poor guy’s tragic death and/or reveal a code to open a safe. These are spaces that feel realistically inhabited and then abandoned, full of the sort of detail that had me poring every inch of a room after I’d killed everything in it.
This detail and polish extend to Resident Evil 3’s broader environments, which are stunning. Smashed cars are piled up outside of flickering neon signs, fires lick their way across kitschy storefronts, and broad industrial spaces are eerily empty. Although you can’t interact much with the world unless you are specifically instructed to (this is still a Resident Evil game and is thus inhospitably rigid with its options for touching things) the atmosphere around you is always pulling out all the stops to make you feel vulnerable and small. Not to lean too much into cliches, but I literally jumped at my own in-game shadow more than once.
Like its predecessor, and indeed, every decent Resident Evil game before it, every part of Resident Evil 3’s world feels deliberately put together. No enemy is thrown in for the sake of it, no room is there ‘just because’; at the very least, every room has useful items or a secret. Areas house problems to solve or clues that lead you to other areas and then back again; a fire obstructs one route, for example, and must be extinguished with the help of a part hidden in a nearby building – a building which also houses a weapon that can't be accessed without the use of a tool that's located past the area obstructed by fire.
These tasks might sound video-gamey (and they are), but solving them is never a chore thanks to elegant, interlocking level design that makes backtracking easy. When I say “easy,” I don’t mean “safe,” though, because that corpse on the floor in that building you were in 30 minutes ago, for example, may not be a corpse any longer. Thankfully, the Resident Evil 2 Remake map screen returns, dutifully logging exactly where you saw that locked safe and highlighting if you’ve missed any items after exploring a room.
Item micromanagement is where Resident Evil 3 leans hardest into its old-school survival horror lineage. Like the original (and in RE2), items are your lifeline and inventory is limited, and running back and forth between storage chests to make sure nothing is wasted and certain items are combined in smart ways is a must if you want to survive for long. I rarely ran out of bullets and health – at least during my first run on Standard mode – but this was due to diligent scavenging rather than items being plentiful. As long as you’re careful in Resident Evil 3, you won’t feel like you’re being punished, and that’s the mark of any good classic survival horror game.
A sense of dread as you navigate Resident Evil 3’s puzzle box of a world is not unfounded, as you can be easily caught unawares by a number of deadly nasties. There’s plenty of variety in enemy design here to keep things fresh, such as the spider-like Drain Deimos who will poison Jill with parasites (the cure is to eat a green herb and then throw up), Pale Heads (first seen in the Resident Evil 2 DLC) who can only be downed by a very accurate blow to the head with your most extreme weaponry, and more things trying to eat your brains beyond your garden variety zombie. Even the latter can prove deadly, especially because they feel faster and more erratic in their movements than their predecessors in Resident Evil 2 and can show up in big enough numbers to really overwhelm you.
Fortunately, Jill is a lot nimbler on her feet than Leon Kennedy or Claire Redfield, which gives Resident Evil 3 a more frantic, action-oriented feel than its predecessor (though it’s not all-out-action like Resident Evil 5 or 6, don’t worry). Jill has a quick step move that allows her to sidestep an incoming attack, and when timed just right it earns you a slight slow-motion effect to help you escape. It’s a move I used regularly and compulsively, and it proved as important to the minute-to-minute combat as Jill’s handgun. Some of its best moments involved me getting a jump scare from an unexpected zombie and dodging out of its way via pure muscle memory before lining up a headshot with my shotgun.Of course, Jill isn’t limited to a single gun; she gradually unlocks the classic Resident Evil arsenal (handgun, shotgun, grenade launcher, etc.), and each weapon feels satisfyingly weighty to shoot. More importantly, I used every gun right up until the end, thanks to upgrades to basic weapons that extend their shelf-life significantly.
Like Resident Evil 2 before it, Resident Evil 3’s 2020 remake does an amazing job of recapturing the horror and tension of the late ‘90s original while completely modernizing its gameplay. It plays like a 2020 game because it is a 2020 game. The classic world is brought to life in glorious detail, and smart level design makes exploring it a delight and replaying it almost compulsory. If only all remakes could be this good; bring on the next one.

Un des derniers épisodes de la série qu’il me restait à faire, Resident Evil 3 remake s’est un peu fait attendre sur ma machine alors qu’il était sorti rapidement après l’excellente refonte du 2 sur laquelle j’approche paisiblement la cinquantaine d’heures. Les premières critiques n’étaient pas fameuses : le jeu serait trop court et trop dirigiste. L’achat a donc été repoussé, et puis, trouvé à 8€… Bon, autant mettre les pieds dans le plat (ne faites pas ça littéralement, c’est mal m’voyeeez !), le jeu doit être pris comme une extension de RE2, et est nettement moins bon que celui-ci malgré de bonnes qualités. 

	Graphiquement, il pose sa petite claque sur ma petite joue, le RE Engine est vraiment impressionnant : les décors fourmillent de détails, les effets d’eau sont propres (même si j’attends le patch RTX qui finirait de peaufiner le tout), les textures sont précises et fines, les personnages, humains ou zombis sont crédibles et leurs faciès sont particulièrement bien réalisés, bien mieux que dans RE2 où Claire pouvait avoir une tête issue de la vallée dérangeante par exemple. RE3 offre aussi des effets de lumières remarquables, une flamme d’incendie, une lampe de bureau, ou un spot de couloir n’éclairent pas de la même manière. Cependant, j’ai pu observer quelques scintillements désagréables, notamment sur les personnages et leurs cheveux, avec les graphismes à bloc. Le travail sonore est excellent : les sons d’ambiance, les râles et borborygmes, le doublage de Jill en jeu, les armes… impliquent vraiment bien dans l’action et rendent du crédit à l’ensemble de manière indéniable. La musique par contre est très générique, mis à part le thème des salles de sauvegardes, je n’ai rien de mémorable qui est venu percuter mes tympans.

	Concernant le système de jeu, c’est un copié-collé apparent de RE2 : vue à la troisième personne de dos, inventaire, armes, combat, les seules différences viennent d’un couteau incassable et de la possibilité d’esquiver. Ah cette esquive ! Au début du jeu, véritablement, elle m’a permis d’économiser de nombreuses munitions et herbes de soin ou autre. Mais par moment, ce sera juste « Non » et on se fait attraper malgré tout. Quand elle est parfaite, elle déclenche un effet de ralenti pour placer une ou deux petites balles dans l’ennemi : imaginez quand le ralenti commence à se déclencher et que l’on se fait quand même harponner… Objectivement, le système fonctionne quand même bien mais reste à peaufiner, et l’ensemble hérité de RE2 est déjà excellent donc il n’y a rien de spécial à redire, si ce n’est que parfois Jill rechignait un peu à recharger son arme (en particulier le lance-grenade) sans trop savoir ce qui la bloquait. 

	Un des problèmes dans RE3, c’est surtout le manque de possibilités dans l’exploration, l’idée étant que le jeu est un couloir plus ou moins large mais rien de comparable avec les grandes aires de jeu de RE2. Que ce soit dans les rues de Raccoon City, l’hôpital, le commissariat, le laboratoire, il va franchement être difficile de s’y perdre : les portes sont fermées, les issues bloquées, Jill n’a vraiment pas le choix entre plus de 2 couloirs à la fois. Et pourtant, les level-designers ont pris soin de forcer à faire des aller-retours, un peu ennuyeux, pour rallonger la sauce. Ceci-dit, on ne tombe pas dans les travers d’un Dead Space 2, dans RE3, ne pas tuer les ennemis reste problématique et l’on ne peut pas toujours esquiver pour économiser des ressources en sachant que l’on ne remettra jamais les arpions dans le coin (même si ça arrive régulièrement). Aussi, le jeu n’incite que peu le joueur à aller fouiller, parce que les lieux sont étriqués et parfois un peu vides. 

	Concernant le scénario, c’est nanardesque/20. On incarne donc Jill, protagoniste du premier RE, qui, témoin des événements du manoir et détenant des preuves, se retrouve pourchassée par un zombi tyran créé par Umbrella Company (Parapluie SARL) appelé le Nemesis pour la tuer elle, tout spécialement (Umbrella qui veut tuer Jill pour cacher un secret envoie l’arme la moins discrète possible mais passons...). Alors, la ville est à feu et à sang, il y a des zombis partout, Jill va s’en sortir parce qu’elle est expérimentée et qu’elle rencontre Carlos (jamais vu autant de cheveux sur un militaire mais ok) qui met en place un plan de secours pour évacuer les survivants (qui sont genre 4 dans la rame… bref) par le métro. Mais ça ne marche pas. Alors on se retrouve dans un laboratoire pour récupérer un vaccin. Mais ça non plus ça ne marche pas. Alors Raccoon City est détruite par une bombe nucléaire pendant que nous fuyons en hélicoptère. On va incarner Carlos à 2 reprises, son type de personnage ? Hmm gros-beauf/bourrin ? Infoutu d’esquiver, il met des coups de poings et l’animation étrange fait qu’il reste coincé dans une position imbécile pendant 3 secondes. Ah et de temps en temps, il nous offrira une ligne de dialogue inutile dont il a le secret. Entre temps, on va affronter 5 ou 6 fois le Némésis dans différentes formes avec Jill et ça c’est plutôt bien, même s’il y a bien sûr de la redondance et qu’il a une posture abusivement increvable alors que les combats ne sont pas franchement difficiles à mener. Dans tous les cas, les dialogues sont vraiment peu intéressants, les séquences cinématiques, bien réalisées et magnifiques, seraient suffisantes, mais les développeurs insistent vraiment pour que l’on discute avec notre compagnon de route absent. Donc, Pouf ! Talkie-Walkie, discussion de 30 secondes-1 minute pendant laquelle on marche péniblement sans pouvoir ramasser quoi que ce soit ou ouvrir de porte, parce qu’il est très important de dire à Carlos pour la 4ème fois qu’on a tué le Némésis et pour l’entendre balancer la réplique générique numéro 27. Ce Talkie-Walkie, qui ne servira jamais à, PAR EXEMPLE, essayer de contacter d’autres survivants dans la ville, met en avant surtout que Jill ou Carlos ont apparemment des soucis avec la solitude. Mais dans un RE c’est vraiment ce qu’il faut éviter de trop faire puisque la tension vient de cet effet de solitude . C’est comme jouer avec quelqu’un qui serait observateur perpétuel à côté de vous en disant « Eh beh ! Tu t’en es bien sorti ! J’espère que cette fois c’est la bonne ! Tu devrais continuer d’avancer tout droit maintenant pour déclencher le prochain script ! Au fait Jill, tu veux sortir avec moi ? ». Pour indicateur de l’étendu du souci : les speedruns de RE2 et de RE3 font la même durée à peu de minutes près, alors que RE2 est théoriquement au moins 2 fois plus long, tout cela parce que les runners subissent ces dialogues insipides...

	Mais, le cœur du problème vient que le fait d’avoir autant scripté le jeu et de vouloir nous forcer à suivre l’histoire, impacte directement sur la difficulté du jeu ... Suite et fin de la critique : https://www.senscritique.com/jeuvideo/resident_evil_3/38590850

Back in 2020 I was brimming with excitement regarding the announcement of this remake for very obvious reasons. Resident Evil 2 got a generally well received remake that for the most part captured the exact same essence of the original, but with some added flair regarding its atmosphere, which was pumped with steroids. So how does this remake fair? Well when I went into it back in 2020 I had, I guess, unreal expectations. But when I heard that almost universally, a lot of fans felt the way I did, I knew I was justified with saying this game was disappointing. Don't get me wrong, it still has the beautiful modern grunge that made the RE2 remake work so well, but no amount of visual glimmer can mask what feels like a glorified expansion. Granted the original RE3 was often regarded by some as a sort of “expansion” or “spin-off” but coming hot off of RE2's heels I and many others expected a more opened up/expanded RE2 experience with the one of franchise's favorite baddies Nemesis who looks great in this game but is sorely underutilized, and instead feels like a more scripted Mr. X. Also this game features a LOT of cuts, and when I mean cuts I mean the complete omission of certain parts of the original game like the park and clock tower. I have heard vague rumors that a director's cut was planned to be released, but that rumors hold very little credence to me since it hasn't been confirmed by any official sources. What's even more laughable is how mercenaries was cut, possibly in favor of Resident Evil Resistance, the online game mode that *had* a roadmap that was quickly abandoned. 

But what's my verdict? I think the game is fine for a one time play through and *if* you want achievements then maybe you can grind it out for those, but besides I feel like this game is pretty forgettable as well as underwhelming.

While not as extensive of a remake as 2 was, Resident Evil 3 is a very entertaining and fun 5 hour truncated version of the old 1998 game. It's missing some set pieces and areas, but the action movie retelling is actually very fun and entertaining. At the higher difficulties it is actually very fun to move around. 

Also the Nemesis, while not being a threat on the level of Mr. X, is still fun to dodge, or to interact with. His sequences are very action packed and just as scripted as something in the Uncharted series. 

A lot of the critisicisms that I have seen or read only compare it to the original, or to 2. On it's own the game is a really fun campaign. Maybe on release I wouldn't recommend it at $60, but at the budget price it sells for now it is definitely an easy recommend.

Another thing to note is that a lot of the reviews stating it isn't as good as the original weren't there for the original. The original RE3 was so mediocre. The only saving grace was the Nemesis and even those sequences were really trite and underwhelming. You can't really compare the two since the remake is more of an uncharted type of shooter and the original was a survival horror game made with left over remnants from a spinoff game that never saw the light of day.

It was always hard for me to really put a review on this game. I have loved Resident Evil since the first game. I played the original Resident Evil 3 when it came out, and the amount of times I beat it as a pre-teen are more then I can count on all ten fingers. 

When this was announced, especially after the success that was the RE 2 remake, I was very excited. I wanted to see how much they would improve on this version.

This game is not what I, or judging by what many others have said, expected. 

The game itself, by itself, is good. The mechanics and gameplay is good, and works well. It is almost the same as the RE 2 remake,  with minor adjustments. I feel the new dodge mechanic is better then the old one, and the ability to push zombies off faster felt like a return of something good, as the RE 2 remake didn't have that. The characters are all well played, the voice actors are amazing. Everything looks graphically amazing, with the exception of probably the Nemesis, which honestly I didn't have too much of a problem with how he looked, he just doesn't look as good as the old one.

The problems with the game however, are pretty unique to a game like this. What it lacks, are things that were taken away from the old Resident Evil 3. I try and remind myself that this is indeed a REMAKE, and not a remaster, but some of the stuff thrown out were truly well done in the old RE 3, and are sorely missing here. The game is also, pretty short. Yes, the original RE 3's main game was also about the same length, both of them can be finished in about 4-5 hours. But as the remake, it felt like it wasn't enough, especially since there is no bonus Mercenaries mode. They instead tried to lean on the RE Resistance game, a DBD like game where 4 survivors take on a mastermind and try to escape, in a more RE environment. But that wasn't what people wanted, and even though I also enjoyed Resistance, it honestly wasn't what I really wanted either. 

The game overall is good. No, it's not better then the original. But no, it's not nearly as bad as some people make it out to be. It just lacks about half of what made the original so iconic. Yes, the big deal is Nemesis, and he is here. But the clock tower, the park, the spiders, they are gone. The city seems much more scaled down, at least for where they go. The original, although actually smaller, felt huge because of how it was shown and sectioned, here it feels like a few big places, and then loops and u-turns. Things like, placing the Umbrella facility under the Hospital and indeed of going through a park and adding more area to the game might make sense on paper and in a story like a modern Resident Evil game, but in a remake of a game, it takes out precious more game times, and another fantastic set piece, a few smaller puzzles.

Is it a bad game. No, not by a long shot. I've played waaaaaay crappier games. But, it's not that it's bad...it's disappointing to people who have played the old RE 3 and for newer fans who have played games like RE 7, where it can be finished in the same amount of time, but felt bigger and deeper because of the areas and the way the game progressed and the puzzles you do, or Village where there is so much interesting characters and pieces along with the environment. And unfortunately a lot of people playing this, especially when it came out, were in this category. 

I recommend this game, with a few notes. One, buy it on a sale. Two, if you played the original, throw expectations of specific plays and enemies out the window, it is better this way. Three, remember that this is a remake, not a major remaster, things will be different. And fourth, do you best to appreciate when is very good is thing, compared to the bad. No, these notes wont truly fix everything, but it will help you enjoy this game a little more if you truly decide to pick this game up.

Although I did enjoy this game for the time I have played it, I have concluded that this Resident Evil 3 remake is not worth the price it is currently. Unlike this game's predecessor, Resident Evil 2 Remake, there is absolutely no other content factor to be experienced after completing the main game, due to the fact that the story is the only playable experience. 

Starting off, I'd like to say that I do believe Capcom knows how to optimize a game without making it broken whilst maintaining the good graphics of the RE engine. I played this on a Dell Inspiron laptop, and just like Village and RE2, the game still looked amazing. I was able to play at 1080p with most settings turned to medium, but later on went down to 720p for better framerate. So on that note, the game manages to be perfectly optimized and playable, while being graphically pleasing.

That being said, the way the levels are produced without a sense of backtracking makes the game feel way too linear compared to the games prior to RE3's release. The linearity is akin to that of a COD campaign with that one or two missions that make you go,"That was kinda cool!" and then proceed to stick to the same play style as you continue. The only things that do tend to stand out are the boss fights, which are actually pretty fun. However, they fail to replace to series's staple of puzzle solving (which is absolutely absent in this game, apart from a segment where you align a subway), and thrilling levels pertaining to each game. In RE2 Remake, you had the orphanage and Ada Wong segment; in Village, you had dollhouse. This game has so much potential to be a good, open-area type game. The material is there for a burning city that you have to navigate through in order to survive and escape. Unfortunately, the finished product seems to be rushed instead of managing to deliver a creative and intricate experience that makes want to play it again.

There is also the whole argument that the game also fails to stay true to the original RE3, however I did not play the original game, so it is not in my place to say. I would also like to add that you get this game in the Raccoon City Bundle ON SALE like I did if you don't currently own RE2 Remake. It feels more like a DLC than a standalone game, which felt fitting for being in a bundle.

Overall, you might be wondering why I've pulled an IGN and recommended this game. Well there's a cool Shrek mod for Nemesis.

The team behind RE3 remake was definitely Capcom's B team and it shows in the product. Strong start, but quickly falling into mediocrity, the demo practically gave you the best parts of the game. RE3 classic made a mild departure from 1 and 2 with a more combat focused approach, and this remake follows suit. Ammo is more plentiful thanks to the option to make your own with materials, but not too plentiful as to punish you still for careless shooting. Many say that RE3 is short and...well duh, classic RE3 was short too compared to 2 as well back during their day, but I will say that the remake had many missed opportunities and is clearly missing some content from the original. Entire levels and segments from RE3 classic seem vacant from the remake, and the choice system classic 3 had is also missing in this remake. Its disappointing for sure, especially when Nemesis himself seems to only get less formidable as the game goes on. Nemesis in early game is definitely at his peak with a variety of moves and ability to get lost only to drop from the sky like batman and continue to go after you. Without spoiling anything, lets just say that Nemesis's tricks really start to get limited after a certain point and with that the game's maps become way more linear. Its no surprise that there are achievements for beating this game in under 2 hours, speedrunners could effectively beat this game and refund it under steam's refund policy; the game can be cleared that fast. All that said, its a far cry from bad, just disappointing and limited when compared to RE2. The good points is that it is a nice remake to compliment and complete the whole story of Raccoon City's destruction, tying in all the events of 1 and 2. The early portion of the game comes on strong with putting you in danger and feeling vulnerable especially with Nemesis walking around. Its just a shame that it loses its intensity so quickly after a certain point. Definitely a buy if its on discount.

A divisive title, and despite the time on my profile, I have beaten it. The problem with it is rather complex, and there are better reviews you can peruse. The problem is people are approaching this game from at least four different, but equally valid viewpoints.

1. Is the game good as a Remake of the Original?
2. Is the game good compared to Resident Evil 2's remake?
3. Is the game good as a standalone title?
4. Is it a good Resident Evil game?

Depending on your experience with the RE franchise, the answer will vary wildly. If you're coming into the franchise new, the question you're looking for is #3, to which I can say yes, it's pretty good. It has enough going on to create a horror experience while erring on the side of action from time to time. You'll be treated to a far more action-oriented experience with some lite RE elements. If you've played RE2's remake, then you may be disappointed, as it's much more linear, the stalker aspect is far less intimidating, and less reliant on the horror aspect. If you're a RE veteran, you may be disappointed with the remake because of how far it diverges from the content presented in the original, with several elements missing, and the variety that Nemesis added in the original stripped away.

Is it a good RE game? It retains the core values of what is a RE game, it looks fantastic, and at times it can scratch that explorative survivor element. It's not as good as RE2's remake, it lacks the content that made the original as well as RE2's remake immensely replayable (it's designed to be almost strictly a straight line through clever guidance via game design principles). For what it is, it's a decent play-it-once-and-move on RE title. You can find it for as low as $10-$15, and at that price, I'd say it's worth the shot.

I'm equally disheartened like a lot of people that loved the original, I still have my original copy and it's still a great game. I wish they would've put more into the title, considering the effort that went into RE2's remake, but it's clear they had a B team on the job, as a lot of the personality of RE2's remake was stripped for...some reason. There are youtube videos cataloging the differences, it's really bizarre how much of a downgrade it is, when so much could've just been ported over from the previous project, but wasn't. It's sort of like comparing Left 4 Dead 2 to Back 4 Blood in a way.

Anyways, recommended on the cheap, make a profile on IsThereAnyDeal and keep an eye out.

I'll be honest with you, I've played the original, though say play is a "small" understatement. To this day, it remains my favorite game of all time, and essentialy my blueprint for what makes a good GAME. What makes a good game? Good gameplay. Not looks, not soundtracks, not touching on deep themes or metaphores, though they CAN enhance the experience. The most important thing is mechanics and systems through which the player interacts with the game. It is a feature distinguishing games from other works of art - the audience HAS TO actively participate for the art to... Take place, simply put. And it is not optional, like it may be with music or theatre. It is MANDATORY.
Rsident Evil 3 Remake has very few ways and very little time you may interact with it. Which is not to say more is always more. Minesweeper is a good game that all of us have probably spent more time in our lives playing than we would ever admit. However if we put the same price tag on both Minesweeper and Witcher 3 and let the popular vote decide, I bet we would discover more OBJECTIVE value measured directly with money possesed by the latter.
Resident Evil 3 has mostly the same mechanics as RE2 Remake (takes away a couple of them even), and gives less time to enjoy them. Who would have thought that a police station can cover more space than a whole city? Yup, that's here. There's little to explore, and it shows, blocked passageways, zombies grouped just behind a fence that you can't get to,  having so many fully rendered estetically intriguing buildings with interiors that just scream "EXPLORE ME" cut off from players interaction is bad in and of itself, but even worse is the fact that there are many areas that you go through that are literall passageways to another sections, devoid of any ineraction points beyond next door. Jill's apartament aside from 3 files, and 2 comments has 1 point of interaction. That is all you'll be doing in her WHOLE BLOCK. Keep yourself entertained as you go from door to door like an acquisitor. And there's more of these! Ok, that may be used to spice up the gameplay with a little bit of chase section. But there is very little normal, combat and exploration sections! It's a scam trade off! Look how well it was done in Evil Within - for each on rails chase you get a long c&e section, even RE2R smoothly blended you being pursued WHILE you c&e, and the original did it even better with scripted chase sequences that had a ton of variation and randomnes, WHILE you have to complete an objective - either go from point A to B of find and item and use it in a different spot, forcing you to unfreeze from your panic and use that adrenalin to make bold moves will yourself to make optimal rational choices despite feeling death's breath on your back. There is one, yes ONE such section where you have to solve a riddle, but it doesn't involve item management or allow you to make a mistake and miss a key item.
But there's a dodge button! And it works this time! Which is... Good, honestly. Doesn't make the game too easy, is not necessary to pass the game (on normal), opens up enemies to devastating counters. Fun to use. Satisfying. +1 Point up.
Enemies are... Zombies, mostly. And 4 - FOUR zombie dogs. Gammas are fun. Well thought out enemies, either take'em from afar with the best gun you got, wasting your best ammo, or... Get close and try to shoot their one hit kill hungry mouths. Dance with death, singn me up baby! Betas are deadly too, was never a fan of their design but they can take you out no problem. Bugs are... One location gimmick, and they spawn infinitely, I think. A little scary, a little annoying, but quickly gone, too quickly. But that's the main theme, right? Almost meta. 
And our BIG BAD PURSUER.
His appearance is... OK to me. Just why did they have to replace his iconic leather suit with black foil warapping that says CAUTION (badum tss). Why the bad joke? 
He'll kick your ass professionally for laughing at him though. So don't even try. He'll chase you down and pound you to the ground. Unless... You throw a grenade at him. He goes down in two. Resident Evil 3 is the official remake of Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, released in 1999. Like the previously released RE2 Remake which runs on the same engine, it's now played from a third-person, over-the-shoulder view. You play as Jill Valentine and Carlos Olivera, as they try to escape the city while being pursued by the titular Nemesis, a smart, dangerous bioweapon. Unlike the previous game, there's only 1 version of the story, not 2 separate ones. You switch from Jill to Carlos in the same campaign as the story demands it. Some areas from RE2 are also revisited, like the police station, and provides more context as it takes place a bit before RE2. I still recommend playing RE2 first, though.

RE3 is somewhat more linear than RE2, even in the free-roam puzzle areas, while also having more scripted action scenes. Enemies are more plentiful, and also with more variations like the dangerous reptilian Hunters which can instakill you. But worry not, as there are more ammo as well. Then there's Nemesis, the immortal pursuer. Unlike the slow Mr. X, he is more agile and can easily catch up or even intercept and block your way. The game is faster-paced with more action, but that isn't really a bad thing.

If you ask RE fans about what's bad in this remake, it's the lack of content. Some areas are cut, like Raccoon Park which I would love to see modernized. There are no extra game modes as well, despite the fact that the original one had, making the main story the only playable mode. And while the original one had some choices-matter elements that can affect the endings, you only have one ending here. The only extra feature is the Shop, you get points that allows you to buy powerful starting items by completing the Records section. RE3 is also 30% more expensive than RE2 despite having lesser content, and both games are around the same age when I bought them. 

Despite the expensive price and lack of content, I really like this game, especially because of the enemy variations and more outdoor levels. If you like RE games there's no reason to not buy this. You can still have fun by hunting achievements and records, making your Jill and Carlos better equipped in the future. And then, maybe you can finish the extra-challenging Inferno Mode, with strong enemies and no autosaves.

~ EASY CLASSIC LASAGNE ~

♦ Ingredients ♦

1 tbsp olive oil 2 rashers smoked streaky bacon
1 onion , finely chopped 1 celery stick, finely chopped
1 medium carrot , grated 2 garlic cloves , finely chopped
500g beef mince 1 tbsp tomato purée
2 x 400g tomatoes 1 tbsp clear honey
500g pack fresh egg lasagne sheets
400ml crème fraîche - 125g ball mozzarella , roughly torn
50g freshly grated parmesan

--------------------------------------------------------------------

STEP 1
Heat the oil in a large saucepan. Use kitchen scissors to snip the bacon into small pieces, or use a sharp knife to chop it on a chopping board. Add the bacon to the pan and cook for just a few mins until starting to turn golden. Add the onion, celery and carrot, and cook over a medium heat for 5 mins, stirring occasionally, until softened.

STEP 2
Add the garlic and cook for 1 min, then tip in the mince and cook, stirring and breaking it up with a wooden spoon, for about 6 mins until browned all over.

STEP 3
Stir in the tomato purée and cook for 1 min, mixing in well with the beef and vegetables. Tip in the chopped tomatoes. Fill each can half full with water to rinse out any tomatoes left in the can, and add to the pan. Add the honey and season to taste. Simmer for 20 mins.

STEP 4
Heat oven to 200C/180C fan/gas 6. To assemble the lasagne, ladle a little of the ragu sauce into the bottom of the roasting tin or casserole dish, spreading the sauce all over the base. Place 2 sheets of lasagne on top of the sauce overlapping to make it fit, then repeat with more sauce and another layer of pasta. Repeat with a further 2 layers of sauce and pasta, finishing with a layer of pasta.

STEP 5
Put the crème fraîche in a bowl and mix with 2 tbsp water to loosen it and make a smooth pourable sauce. Pour this over the top of the pasta, then top with the mozzarella. Sprinkle Parmesan over the top and bake for 25–30 mins until golden and bubbling. Serve scattered with basil, if you like.

This is the first bad review I've ever made, and that is sad because I am a fan of the series. I cannot believe that Capcom asked $60 for this, I got it on a deep discount and still wonder if I should've saved my money. This should've been a $15 DLC for R2make- it's a very short, barebones asset flip with little to no replay value that has even less to do with its namesake than the previous entry. It's not that this is a terrible game, just that after playing 1/2/3/CV/4/5/6/7/Remake/R2make I'd put this at the very bottom of the list. Yes, even below the infamous RE6 because that at least had co-op and interesting combat mechanics. For shame, Capcom, for shame!

First off, I'm gonna start by asking people interested to keep an open mind. I hear flak for this game from people who've played it, and people who pretend they've played/don't have their own opinions. Bounce this off of anything else you've read if it help's make up your mind.

For 33 pound? It's a tricky sell. If you liked RE:2, you may still like this as an actionized sequel, though there is less content overall. That's what happens when two games that were originally planned to release as one get seperated into two (for that reason, I'd say the best option is to get the two in a bundle) :^). If you're new to this series or just plain unsure, try and find a cheaper option via sales or other means. I would say make your mind up after this anyway, but we both know most people have scrolled past this review anyway :^).

Oh, and also I haven't played the OG *yet*, so I lack that frame of reference. Chances are, the best thing to do is play both at some point.

Now, I'mma get into labelled specifics. SPOILERS AHEAD

POSITIVE:

+ This game is hella fun. I've played it over six times, and it's one of the few games I actually wanted to achieve 100% because it was just so fun to do so. Yes, there's less gore, but that's for the sake of more action on screen at once, especially in the first half of the game. But once you get to that shop of infinite weapons, or bonus items and a harder difficulty, mixed in with the new rewarding dodge mechanics and bossfights, it has a rush that really sticks with you.

+ This game improves it's dialogue and *especially* the music from what we saw in RE:2. 2 has standout's, like HUNK's Theme 'Looming Dread', but honestly past that I could scarcely remember much of the soundtrack. 3 trump's this with some bangin' tunes, getting your ear far more consistently and really amping up the action. As for the dialogue, I'm not detracting from Resident Evil's famous Narm Charm, but I know not everyone's used to it. The characters here are charming, and I was quite a fan of characters like Nicholai and Mikhail (both the Russian's, funnily enough). RE:2 is mostly like this too, but sometimes something just feels off and it's tricky for me to connect. I didn't have this problem here.

+ Nemesis. Yes I know, and I do agree that he's not handled to his strength's in this game, but honestly I still prefer him over Mr X. Where Mr X walks, Nemesis *sprints*. Where Mr X punches, Nemesis *combos*. The early stages of the game can really catch you in the moment as Nemesis swings in from above and dashes right for you. It's not a matter of just going the opposite direction: can you pull off a perfect dodge, and get some good slow mo hit's and escape to cover? Can you pull out enough firepower to down him, and get some really good handgun upgrades? His bosses (bar one we'll talk about later) are also quite fun themselves, if a bit easy on lower difficulties.

+ Graphics. You saw the screenshots. This game looks fantastic, just like RE:2. This time around it's much more vibrant than the RPD, the Sewers and the mostly sterile NEST, and we get a greater variety of locales in this title too. I won't spoil them all, and whilst it's not like you go to Narnia, but this really help's the pacing. Raccoon City has never looked better. 

+ Replayability. Your mileage may vary, but I loved replaying this game. Nightmare is especially a fun challenge, and Inferno will turn your hair white. Rewards such as Concept Art, Models and money for the Item Shop aren't gonna interest everyone, but in fairness they aren't that taxxing to max out.

NEUTRAL: 

- Linearity. Another thing I don't personally mind, but again it's worth mentioning. Outside of two main segments, this game is rather direct. There are side paths and things to find in them, but you never end up going far. In RE:2, when you're in the RPD in the first third/half of the game, while you may not need to revisit most of it there are some good things to find, such as the Magnum. Here, whilst these two segments do get you some good goodies (including the Magnum as well on difficulties below Nightmare) for exploring, but it doesn't take that long.

- Lack of Puzzles. This can either please you or irritate you. I'm on the fence. Whilst it is nice to have some puzzles and there are a couple here, they're nothing really noteworthy. RE:2 was generally better at this. If you're less fond of puzzles, then here you go, nothing that you need to hold onto for too long.

NEGATIVE:

- Length. Whilst I personally have no general issue with it, I *know* people will disagree as objectively it is a decently short game if you're not messing up that much. That clashes with the price tag. Though in all fairness I must dispute the whole 'RE:2 is longer' thing. Because it really is not that different, I beat Leon's Route A and Jill's Standard Run in about the same time. It does hurt RE:3 to lack RE:2's Ghost Survivor's mode though. It would've been fun to play as Nicholai, Mikhail, Tyrell, maybe even Marvin or Brad. 

- Final Boss. Nemesis' third form and the fourth proper boss fight with him is disappointing from two sides. On Standard and to a slightly lesser extent Hardcore, he really isn't that fast and if you're any way good at dodging he might not even hit you. On Nightmare and Inferno? If you miss ONE dodge, you're dead. If you're lucky you have just enough time to whip out a full-heal or something before you drop it, but without the Iron Defense coins from the shop, Jill is gonna end up a stain on the floor. It took me far too many attempts to beat him on this mode, and it does feel rather anticlimactic after the fight you JUST had with him.

- Nemesis. He really coulda been done better, and it doesn't help that the game isn't incredibly long. In this version, he pops up IMMEDIATELY, he's on the title screen in-fact, and isn't particularly effective at killing S.T.A.R.S members. Infact, the ratio of him killing S.T.A.R.S members compared to U.B.C.S members is 0:2, so it really makes you wonder why they had Brad get himself killed in the first ten minutes to a zombie. Yeah, it gives Brad a heroic sacrifice, but tell me why they couldn't do that with Nemesis. Whilst he does kill Mikhail, Tyrell, and a train full of civilians throughout the game, and it does make it personal, these characters where either injured already or, well, nameless civilians. Mostly, to be honest, I think the lack of build-up ruins him, especially as after you escape him in the Sewers? He doesn't show up outside of bossfights again. Fine bossfights, but he's not nearly as dynamic as Mr X is. That and his model is cool, but not as cool as the old design, but you can just get a mod for that on Nexus.

CONCLUSION:

I love this game, but I can see why some don't, and prefer RE:2. I only made this review because I want to have my own reference of defensive points for when people bring it up and pick it apart :^). I know a guy who pretended he'd played the game and said it was ♥♥♥♥, and wouldn't really say why, only for the next day to admit he'd actually never played it. That felt mildly vindicating :^).

If you get it, I hope you enjoy it. Peace out.

Resident Evil 3 is a modern re-imagining of the original 1999 Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, the remake now having dropped the somewhat awkward subtitle in favor of just the iterator. Having been far too young to play the original game when it came out, I don’t have a great frame of reference for how it compares to the original title. The new title however still manages to be an excellent survival shooter with some purposely older mechanics carried over as a deliberate reinvention of the older game’s mechanics. 

What differentiates new resident evil games (7, 8) from the older titles and even the remakes are less the obvious shift in player perspective and technical accomplishments, and more the emphasis on trial-and-error gameplay, Playing Resident Evil 8 I was never in a position where I knew I couldn’t possibly beat a boss or encounter, as there would often be an abundance of ammunition and health that affords significant margin for error on the players part. There was never a “Correct” combination of weapons and items to beat a boss fight or set piece, if you aimed your shots right and didn’t put yourself in a corner to be waled on over and over, the player would probably survive the encounter. In Resident Evil 3 however, there is a strong emphasis on the one solution the game wants you to use over one the player can organically adapt to if they didn’t bring the right supplies to the fight, either through natural attrition or by saving items in crates for later. A midgame forced fight with the nemesis pretty much requires you to have the grenade launcher on you with the appropriate munitions to shoot at walls to stun the nemesis. Running out of these, or simply not bringing them will basically make the fight impossible. I spent 20 minutes my first time dumping all my pistol ammo, shotgun shells and grenades into the nemesis and didn’t even get to see the second stage of the boss fight. I eventually resorted to the knife, but without stunning the creature, I could only get in one or maybe two measly stabs in before I would have to dodge out of the way, and clearly that fight was a losing one. Eventually I just reloaded the checkpoint, equipped the grenade launcher, and won the fight in under 10 minutes. Now, it’s not like this solution wasn’t foreshadowed, the fight arena is littered with mine grenades and explosives ammunition, and the checkpoint before the fight had a document explaining the creation and use of different explosives, so it’s not like the game didn’t try to warn me what was about to happen, I just wasn’t paying attention. But again, this is illustrative of my point of a single “correct” strategy to playing out encounters. Resident Evil 3 is not at all interested in letting the player find their own ways to beat the game, but slowly refining the playstyle laid out by the rules of the game. Even later when I played through the game again with damage bonuses and infinite ammo, boss fights and set piece encounters still felt longer and tougher than using the original playthrough’s “correct” playstyle.
I’m not opposed to this, forcing the player into a specific mindset and playstyle is a fine way to set up a game, and making me use weapons I was keeping in reserve made my gameplay decisions significantly more freeing. Because If I concluded that an encounter warranted using those two grenades I’d been holding onto, then likely that was the correct moment to use them. Enemy encounters in Resident Evil 3 feel less like a test of my mechanical skill to click on heads, but more a puzzle to solve with the limited inventory I had. Sure, I could use my grenade on this high health enemy, but that would mean a hoard of enemies later might take up more ammo than just dumping bullets into this enemy right now. Early resident evil games were always an exercise in accounting as much as tactical positioning and player skill to aim properly, and even with a modern coat of paint, this still holds up as a core tenant of the game design.
I’ve heard that this game is significantly less survival focused than the Resident Evil 2 remake, and having not played it, I can’t vouch for or against that statement. However, I will say that Resident Evil 3 still managed to make me keep my wits about me when exploring for ammo and healing items more than your average third person shooter. The secondary story in Resident Evil 3 has the player switching from the perspective of Jill Valentine, over to Carlos, an ignorant Umbrella operative who spends most of his time retrieving Umbrella secrets and fighting in the margins with Jill. You even go back to the Police Station from Resident Evil 2, through the timeline is a little fudgy with when you’re supposed to be there in relation to Leon and Claire. The segments with Carlos are significantly more action focused, as your starting weapon is an assault rifle with plenty of ammo, and  the player’s dodge ability is replaced with a big ol punch that can outright kill some enemies and otherwise stun the larger ones. I can’t say I disagree with these segments being in the game, in the initial playthrough at least with Jill, the player is always a few missed shots away from a game over, and playing as Carlos is a nice change of pace. It makes sense his segments feel more action focused, his thematic place in the narrative is to be prepared to fight off the zombie hoard, it makes sense that he wouldn’t be exactly scrounging around for basic pistol ammo and ducking out of the way of every zombie attack.

What this does is give you a taste of what the replay experience is going to be like, part of the appeal of replaying Resident Evil games is the accumulation of power playthrough over playthrough. The first run is a tense survival action game where every shot counts and running from fights is a valid option. The second playthrough is a little less tense since you know where the items are and how to run the level most efficiently. Then subsequent playthroughs can be done with the infinite ammo rocket launcher and boosted health. There’s even an achievement for beating the game in under two hours to give you an idea of how quickly you can clip through with knowledge of the game and it’s solutions.
If you’ve never played a resident evil game before, but have a basic understanding of “Umbrella bad”, then if you’re looking for a point to jump in, I’d say Resident Evil 3 isn’t a bad place to start, although I hear good things about the remake of the second game. It seems capcom is set on remaking it’s older titles for modern audiences and so far the remakes have been knocking it out of the park in balancing the old school game theory while still updating mechanics so it’s doesn’t feel clunky to play.
