[h1]Resident Evil 3, or R3make,[/h1]
... whatever you want to call it does a pretty solid job delivering upon the nostalgia of the original games, while providing an entertaining entrance to the uninitiated. Whether you have played other Resident Evil games or not, the story is easy to follow as the story is complete, from start to finish, of two perspectives on the events of Raccoon City.

[b]Story[/b] is a solid 8/10, fanboys relax, I'm comparing it to modern stories as this is a remake. [spoiler] The bad guy seeming like he's the bad guy but also the Nemesis being your nemesis but not the ultimate baddy is one we've seen many times. [/spoiler] Unrelenting evil becomes a little dull, but if you pay attention to the trophies, the game is aware. It's a complete satisfying story, although I don't quite understand how [spoiler] our male protagonist falls so hard for our female protagonist[/spoiler]. All in all, worth the play if for nothing other than an entertaining story and excellent visuals in cutscenes. 

[b]Visuals[/b] are spot on, exactly what you would expect from a game released in 2020. Scalability is nearly limitless so I would be surprised if you machine can't at least gimp along, or have your face blown off. Crisp, mo-cap is up to par, nobody looks like they need to poo while running. Models of the infected have loads of detail, spend some time looking at them just to see the lengths devs went to. Truly, Bravo. There's a close up scene of an enemy later in game, everything a gamer could hope for.

[b]Gameplay[/b], it's not bad. Get's a little repetitive shooting an enemy in the head 5 times before it drops. However, my biggest complaint comes from not being advised that it really should be played with a controller. The game is mostly linear in combat, enemies in front, nothing crazy...but later on there's a battle that's almost constant Dark Souls level strafing and buddy, that's awful on a keyboard. Imagine one directional button, shift to keep running, and the dodge is shift+space...so it gets intense. obviously you could re-spec. In the same fight, regardless of FOV settings, the camera zooms in on the main enemy so far it undoes whatever setting you may have been playing with. it's enough that it throws off your depth perception and will likely cause you to run into other enemies in the area until you're used to the effect. Personally, I'm a little salty because it threw me off so bad at first that it's the only reason I died playing the game.

Holistically, it's worth playing I picked it up on a sale and recommend you do the same. Playing for eight hours involved quite a bit of exploration and beefing up the arsenal. Considering to achieve "S" rank on normal difficulty you're expected to beat the game in under 2 hours, I'd say it's best to buy it on some sort of sale.

I've never played the original Resident Evil 3, so I can't comment on the criticisms about cut content in the remake. That being said, it is a bit disheartening to hear that a lot was cut out and I can definitely see why that would be an issue for so many people. 

With that aside, this is basically the gameplay of RE2 remake but faster paced and less puzzle heavy. The game is quite short (~5-6 hours on a first playthrough on Standard difficulty), and Nemesis himself just feels like a chore to deal with in non boss fight scenarios (However, the boss fights with him are really well done). Where the game really shines for me is its replayability. I don't know why, but the NG+ style store after completing a first playthrough is insanely addictive. You're given incentive to go back through the game completing various challenges in order to get cool unlocks to use in other playthroughs. The fast paced nature of the game makes these unlocks tempting, like getting the powerful Samurai Edge or ammo crafting companion in order to make more ammo. Not only that, but beating the game on its base hardest difficulty unlocks another, harder difficulty, then another. Because of this, I've been playing through the game multiple times trying to get achievements and Records (the little challenges to unlock points for the item shop). I've been having a blast doing this, and at the time of writing I'm going through Nightmare difficulty, the second hardest difficulty, with an infinite ammo assault rifle, HP regen coins, and attack boosting coins. Key items, consumables, and small paths shift a bit on these harder difficulties too so you can't fully know what to expect with all of this either. I went in to this remake with low expectations after reading all the reviews and controversy around it, but I've been having tons and tons of fun. 

Admittedly, I'm not necessarily the biggest Resident Evil fan out there. I've only played all the main entries (1-8), with my playthroughs of 2 and 3 being those of the recent remakes and that's about it. If you can accept that this game is faster paced and not fully authentic to the original, then you should have at least an enjoyable time with this remake, especially if you like replayability. I would definitely only recommend it on a sale though (~20$ USD), because it would not be worth a full 60$ if you don't end up liking the game enough to keep playing it over multiple times.

Super late edit: I have since played RE3 Nemesis and ouch. Lots left out of this remake, making it feel incomplete. While the remake leaves so much out, I still recommend it on a sale since what's there is fun. However, I really wish this remake had done more. It had a lot of potential that ended up going wasted.

I went into Resident Evil 3 with the expectation that it was short, too much action, and unfaithful to Resident Evil as a whole. I can thank Steam Reviews for that conclusion. 

TLDR: Good story, good graphics, forgettable score, only slightly inconsistent albeit faithful RE gameplay, good general ambience and environment. Don't buy full price, buy on sale.

Disclaimer: Spoilers moving forward

While it only took me 6 hours to complete the game, it definitely felt like it ended at the right time, not too short, not too long. I haven't played the original RE3: Nemesis released in 1999, so I can't say how faithful it was to the main. 
The game looks terrific, as you would hope from a game released in 2020 by a company as reputable as Capcom; and is also well optimized for those who don't have a NASA powered super-computer. 
The gameplay had me torn. Despite the introduction of the dodge (or apparently re-introduction from the OG RE3:N), I felt RE2 Remake delivered less clunky, less "lucky" gameplay when fighting (and avoiding) zombies.
The "perfect dodge" mechanic seems a bit inconsistent. I made an effort to reload saves to try and practice it on local fodder zombies, and was still getting occasionally grabbed even though I was certain I had the right timing. Or I could just be bad. The general camera/avatar movement seemed a bit jittery at times, but was overall smooth. 
Within the story, I never found myself bored within the campaign. I felt like there were always things to do, and I was excited to see where the story was going next (perhaps moreso than RE2 Remake), despite my general intuition telling me Nemesis would certainly be coming back from the dead, once again. I wouldn't call this plot armour, however, as it's established from the beginning that you're gonna have a consistently occurring antagonist. 
One small nitpick I had was with the music, which was not only forgettable, but heightened it's intensity in purely mundane situations. I would be roaming the labs or the hospital, and the music would sound far too intense for what I'm doing, which, while it made me more wary of my surroundings, I felt the choice of music was unfit for general ambience. 
The environment was vibrant and fun, albeit linear at times. I particularly enjoyed the callbacks to RE2 Remake, and also only realized RE3 was a prequel to RE2 like halfway in which was a really cool discovery.

This game hits you FAST and HARD, with a tremendous beginning. It seemingly never lets up, and before you know it...it's over, as nearly everyone else has stated already. As a longtime RE fan since the early 2000s, this R3make does not disappoint! Yes, it is quite short, whether you rush through it or not, but this is most assuredly Resident Evil; from the gameplay, graphics, and experience overall. So, kudos to Capcom for this modern REmake! I LOVED IT...for what it is...but it could have been so much more had Capcom had another year or so to add to its length. Maybe the length is what Capcom wanted all along?  Maybe they wanted to hit you fast and hard...only to be left wanting more...whether that means more Raccoon City goodness, or anticipating more Resident Evil in general. I think Capcom succeeded on both fronts. It's still a bit short though....

Yet, of course I have my own letdowns for this game from what I felt it should have/could have been. My gripes include (obviously) the short length, a lack of a consistent Nemesis throughout the game (I wanted more of him!), those awful Hunters first met in the sewers, hardly any puzzles to solve, and there were no other regular bosses whatsoever! I see Capcom wanted the main threat to be Nemesis, understandably, but there aren't any other big bads here, and when Nemesis shows up, it's ALL him, sure. Nemesis takes the spotlight easily, but since Nemesis didn't show up as much as I thought he would, I was left with a strange RE craving of fighting other bosses, which usually Capcom provides in spades.  Yet, the Hunters in the sewers were quite step up from the pesky RE2 REmake's Adult G-Monsters in the sewers. Both are annoying to me, but the Hunters I feel are the better enemy for the sewers. The G-Adults are probably my least favorite RE enemy ever, so I am glad they did not make a reappearance for this R3make! 

I played on Normal difficulty first, and got a 6 hour 8 minute game play time at the end of the game with a C Rank, and died 7 times. I was enjoying the reimagining of the streets of Raccoon City too much to simply breeze through it the first time. I am sure I can cut that time in half if I hurry through since I have some experience and know what to expect, as it typically goes for nearly any game out there.

I bought this from the Steam Summer Sale for 2/3 off the pricey $60. At $20....you really should consider to buy this if you are a Resident Evil fan or not. I was waiting for a sale price and time to play after the outpouring of poor reviews in 2020.

I am super glad I played this R3make game, and I plan to replay it sooner than later, as this game is not one of the games that I would toss aside after one playthrough. It's probably the RE fan within me that says that! Although, it is hard for me to rank this game among all the other RE titles, as it is usually difficult to decide all that after my first playthrough. All that matters is that I had fun, and I surely did with this game. I don't believe it's the best, yet not the worst. I still have to finish RE6, 7 and eventually Village. 

Ultimately, I wish for Capcom to go even farther next time for their inevitable RE Code: Veronica and RE 4 REmakes. You are in fact REmaking Code Veronica, right Capcom?!?! Please please pleeeeeeeease don't skip that one!

- Thanks for reading if you did, and thanks to Capcom for giving a hearty shot at REmaking RE3!

Resident Evil 3 is the followup to Resident Evil 2, set both before and after the events of the latter. Set two months after Resident Evil 1, you play as both Jill Valentine and Carlos Oliveira, making your way through the recently zombie infested midwestern town of Raccoon City. The catch is, there's a new kind of monster that is hunting Jill; a Tyrant by the name of Nemesis that was sent by Umbrella to terminate the members of S.T.A.R.S to cover up the Mansion incident. As Jill, you have to find a way to escape the city, before Nemesis kills you.

This game does a lot of things really well:

- The graphics look beautiful, just like RE2remake
- The music that plays are updated remixes of the original songs, something RE2remake was sorely missing
- We get to see what was happening in the city before Leon and Claire arrived
- Carlos is hot
- The new points shop is an interesting mechanic where you can buy and keep your items bought there through all playthroughs
- Pulling off perfect dodges is really satisfying to do
- I really liked how they tied in Marvin and how he got bit
- Nemesis

Though despite all the things I enjoyed about this game, there were a few setbacks that I personally didn't like. And while admittedly some of these are nitpicky, these are the things I had issues with:

- The zombies no longer have ragdoll deaths. They all die in pre-determined poses, something I really liked in RE2remake
- Nemesis, as terrifying as he is, becomes heavily scripted after the sewer segment. The thing with the Mr. X Tyrant in RE2remake was that he was barely scripted. Every playthrough with him is different, and while I do give Nemesis points for being much faster, stronger, and scarier than Mr. X, I was really hoping he would remain mostly unscripted like X
- Nemesis also goes down in one grenade
- I wasn't a fan of "NEST 2". I really enjoyed the original NEST in RE2remake because of how different it was. I feel like I could've gotten more around NEST 2 if it were named, say, the "HIVE", and had more to do there.
- The placement of Jill's "You want S.T.A.R.S?!" was honestly quite a surprise to me, though admittedly, that's a nitpick
- Lastly, the destruction of Raccoon City. It didn't feel as impactful as the original cutscene. Instead of getting an upclose view of everything being destroyed, we just see the bombs from afar. That's something that disappointed me as the destruction of RC is such an iconic moment in the series, symbolizing the end of the first 3 games. In the remake, the destruction felt like it was just shrugged off. Jill's reaction to it in the remake ("So long, RC") compared to the original ("Umbrella's going down") also rubbed me the wrong way. It was as if she didn't even care about how many people died in the bombs, let alone in Raccoon City.

Overall, as I feel like this game needed some more time. I haven't played the original Resident Evil 3, but having heard about the cut content, especially the clock tower, I can understand why fans of the original may be disappointed. For what it is, though, I enjoyed this game. I don't like it nearly as much as I did RE2remake, but it was still a treat to play. If newcomers to the franchise loved RE2remake, this is definitely a good game to go to next.

Resident Evil 3 is fun edition to the Resident Evil Remake series, but is not without its faults and divergences from previous titles. Hot off the heels of Resident Evil 2's Remake, RE3 makes use of the same engine and third person perspective, though it does throw a curve ball first person segment in the intro sequence. Despite the obvious similarities in the gameplay and style to RE2, RE3 does also have some notable changes, not all of which I personally cared for. However, I still had a wonderful time playing the game and enjoyed once again stepping into the boots of S.T.A.R.S member, action heroine Jill Valentine.

The start of RE3 is unique compared to other titles. I usually feel that the opening to each entry in the series helps to set the overall tone of the game. I would say that holds true for the most part here. It starts with a well executed horror sequence in first person, before switching to third person and the most intense opening sequence in an RE title I have played so far. As far as tone is concerned, the action segment is the more indicative of the two.

Both RE1 and RE2 handled horror and action, and balancing the two could be difficult. RE3, on the other hand, cranks the dial further in favor of action, opening with flame fueled, screaming chase through a collapsing building and into the newborn apocalypse occuring in Raccoon City's streets. Resident Evil's bombastic B-Movie vibes are back on display, and, though I am personally a fan of the lonely and eerie parts of these games, it was still fun to see and a pleasure to play.

With this said, RE3's main gameplay has seen some changes. While the standard third-person shooting and item collection are the same, your defences differ. The knife and grenades are now full weapons rather than sub-weapons and defence items. In fact, there are no defence items at all. What's more, the zombies seem to be well aware of this fact, as they seem to have become far more grabby. In the place of these items, Jill can dodge with a quick duck or a roll. If you plan on conserving ammo at any point, not that you truly need to, you will learn to juke zombies in short order. None the less, I liked the defensive items more, particularly when doing things like shooting a grenade in zombies mouth, fleeing and hearing it go off, or laying them low to recover my knife. All this is lost, and replaced with command grabbing zombies who like to quick turn and lunge, even when there half way on the ground.

Apart from this, RE3 feels a lot more alive. In previous titles you were exploring lonely, confined areas. There was a creeping ambience, and lonely quality that really set the horror tone well. RE3 takes place in Raccoon cities streets, but visits a number of major locations. It rips half of RE2's police station straight from the previous remake, as well as a similar, but brief sewer section. I will commend RE3, however, for some of the Nemesis sections, in particular the construction site sequence, which really turns on B-Movie gas.

Speaking of the Nemesis, he is a great pursuer enemy, even if some of his segments are trying. His design is far more mutant like than his predecessor, Mr.X with an interesting fusion of meat and metal. In many ways he represents the progression in Umbrella's super bio-weapon solider project, now capable of carrying out distinct orders, vocalization, and using heavy weapons. Even Jill's partner, and the other character you play as, Carlos, is unable to stop it when using the same rocket launcher used to defeat the last two tyrants in RE1 and 2. This helps to drive home how ridiculously un-killable the Nemesis really is. And I loved it.

The Nemesis also visibly mutates, much like G did in RE2, but more so. He too also becomes a huge meat monstrosity, but not before several interesting boss fights, in notably large combat arenas, all of which were fun and an interesting change from cramped boss fights of the other titles.

In addition to Nemesis, several older favourites from RE1 return in good form. The Hunters are back, and third person perspective creates some interesting fights against their speed and endurance. The "White Heads" are creepy regenerator like enemies that will require heavy ordinance to take down efficiently. One segment also sees the return of the mutated fly-like Chimeras, or something like them. The sewers have their own giant bipedal reptiles to deal with. All have great designs and change up some the gameplay over RE3's somewhat brief total play time.

Part of the shortness of RE3 is that there is only one scenario, unlike the first two titles where you picked from two characters. Here you play both as Jill and Carlos during different segments. To be honest, I think this does have some benefits. It allows Carlos and Jill to have very different play styles, with Carlos mowing down lots of lesser enemies with his assault rifle, while Jill tackles the big bosses with high ordinance. Both get fun and interesting investigation and exploration segments as well.

Last, in the case of storytelling, RE3 is somewhat mixed. Resident Evil games are not always seen as great for story on their own, but their fusion of ambience, game play, and charm have often seen them loved none the less. RE3, as I have mentioned, leans on the B-Movie action side of things. However, a part of me wonders if it wouldn't have been more fitting for Jill and Carlos, as S.T.A.R.S member and an unwitting Umbrella security officer to be the ones to uncover the conspiracy behind the G Virus and the outbreak like Leon and Claire did, rather than running around trying to cure Jill and turn Nemesis to mush.

If I haven't sold you on RE3, let me tel you that if you liked RE2's remake there is something here for you. RE3 is a slightly different breed, and suffers both from its hasty entrance after RE2 as well as from its various changes, but it is still great game, and worthy of being played and enjoyed by fans of the Resident Evil series, and of survival/action horror games.

I don't even know where to start. I've had mixed feelings about this RE3 remake.

It has great moments, but it mostly falls short in several areas. The original RE3 is so special to me, and I speak for about everyone when I say that. This remake has no emotional impact, unlike the original because almost every aspect of it was reduced to a shallow, half-assed version of it.

It feels like an interactive movie, but in my opinion it shouldn't. It limited opportunities for the player to explore and feel the gloom and chaos of the situation. It's ridiculous how little you explore as Jill. I couldn't feel for her in this remake. The pace of the game didn't give me a chance to! And it's hard to feel a connection to her because she is too much of a hard-ass. A more hardened version of her would have been fine to me, but one, her dialogue feels unnatural, and two, I have a sentimental attachment to the original version of her. In the original, she's soft, pure and compassionate, yet courageous and capable of fighting for herself in her worst nightmare. This has inspired me so much in my personal life. But in this remake, all of that is washed away for a cocky attitude and lame, over-the-top dialogue, and that put a bad taste in my mouth. I couldn't even see her as [i]Jill [/i] anymore.

Before I get into the cons of Nemesis, one positive note I can make is his new look. The face rework I cannot warm up to, but I really like the caution tape because it dehumanizes him appropriately (I still much prefer his original leather coat and pants in the original though). 

However, Nemesis felt like he was designed to be merely a cameo and nothing more -- "oh look, it's Nemesis! He's the antagonist from the original game that you loved. That's good enough isn't it?"

But no, it's not. Nemesis should not be or feel like a cameo. In the original, he was a force that had a foreboding presence which leaked into nearly every aspect of the game. The threat he should impose on the characters, especially Jill, is absent. For some reason the team behind this remake didn't consider that. He's thrown in, thrown out, and then turned into some mindless creature after an hour of gameplay -- hell his name was even removed from the title of this game. That is all I could think as I observed this lame, superficial take on this once badass and terrifying character. And let's not forget that he and Jill don't even cross each other in the RPD police station... so disappointing that it honestly hurts. There was no love or care shown for Nemesis or the impact that he has.

Even the music felt lackluster. Some of the tracks from the original were recreated, which was great! But their effect wasn't felt at all. Hearing the original "Free From Fear" track was breathtaking and pulled at my heartstrings in so many weird yet wonderful ways. In this remake, however, it was just faint background noise that hardly spoke about the situation the characters were in. It wasn't any more effective than elevator music, and that really, really hurts.

However, some characters were kept the same or made better. Carlos is still cute, charming, and selfless. Mikhail, just as heroic, and I even might prefer this game's version of his sacrifice, at least some aspects of it. I could go on, but these two characters come to mind first.

I'd pay for a DLC with more faithful content just to give this meaningless remake meaning, and a second chance. Definitely not worth $60, at least in its current state (I bought it for 1/3 that price because I had heard it was too short and empty, which surely enough was true). I will probably update this review later.

This is now my 3rd playthrough but also the first time I have played it straight after the OG RE3 and oh boy.. I do want to at least state that is a FINE game, its still fun as is, but if you have ever played the original, it really does frustrate with what COULD have been.

I always felt this one was a disappointment way back on release but now I truly do see all the areas in which it falls short in comparison to its original predecessor.

It's such a shame too, because of course RE2 remake as well as RE4 remake were magnificent reimaginings that paid a LOT of respect for the original entries - and here INSTANTLY I saw how much is skipped/cut out.

For example - within the first 5-10 mins of the game you already meet Brad and go to Jacks' Bar, while also meeting Carlos and the UBCS aboard the train carriage. Some of this stuff only happens nearly 1.5hrs into the original game - after exploring the Uptown and Midtown sections along with the RPD. In this remake, it genuinely feels like a speedrun of OG - and there is no Uptown while the Downtown area has been majorly reduced in size. In addition to this lightning quick pace - there are 4 cut areas (Clock Tower, Park, Graveyard and the factory) with an entire boss being cut out too (Gravedigger). It really is lazy because instead they decided to add in the sewers and NEST lab - which is really just reusing the RE2 Remake assets!!!

It's so disappointing that NEMESIS is mostly just scripted encounters - and because of how quick the game progresses, it feels like you see the guy every 10 mins for the first half of the game. They really missed so hard with this, because Mr X was more Nemesis like in RE2 Remake - in how he stalked you throughout that campaign, as well as his off script AI. The boss fights feel more spectacle based - which is kinda fun I guess?

There is a clear absence of Live Selection - which was such a cool feature of the OG game, and actually made it replayable but now its been axed entirely. Puzzles have been completely changed and removed too. Even the length of this game is arguably shorter than OG - and you gotta consider that the remake has many cinematics/cutscenes so that wasn't really a thing in OG - so in pure gameplay terms it really is lacking there too...

Anyway, there are probably other issues but like I said, the game that we ended up getting is still perfectly FINE and will give you a couple hours of harmless fun - I do really like the way Jill was handled here in design and voice acting too, the dodge is much more reliable here, the chaotic opening in her apartment was great as well as the chaos in RC at the start of the outbreak. The gameplay itself is of course solid as it follows suit from RE2 Remake as well as the visuals and audio design.

I would have to give this 2 separate scores. As a game it's probably a 7/10 because it is fun, and it does do things well. As a remake of RE3 1999 - it gets a 4/10 for me because it is very disappointing as explained above but does a few things well too.

The mechanics are very polished and it's quite fun to replay in order to unlock extra weapons and items. And because of the game's short length, you don't need to commit to a full 10+ hour replay. It's still not a perfect game, but it's worth playing if you can find it on sale.

Plot description:
The plot of the game tells about a girl named Jill Valentine - one of the heroines of the first part of the franchise, who visited Spencer's mansion as part of the S.T.A.R.S. The girl stays in Raccoon City, counting the days until she leaves this seedy town. Here are just all her plans put an end to the thug who suddenly burst into the house, who hunts for all the surviving members of the squad. The girl is saved from imminent death by a mercenary named Carlos, who is a member of the Umbrella Corporation's cleanup squad. He takes the girl to the subway, where it turns out that there is a train that will help evacuate the survivors. You just need to start the food, get the route and so on. Of course, our Jill should be the errand girl, for everyone else is overly preoccupied with their own problems. So Miss Valentine wanders around the city, moving through many locations, solving puzzles and fighting zombies.

My review:
if in the first Resident Evil we explored a huge mansion, and in the second - the former museum, which was converted into a police station, then for the new RE such large levels are a luxury. A couple of Raccoon City districts with tiny shops and a power plant, a hospital with two accessible floors, and a standard laboratory for games in the series. The rest is boss battles (he is alone, you know his name). Accordingly, backtracking has become much less. As well as riddles - if you play inattentively, you may not even notice them. There are fewer safes, locked lockers with weapon upgrades. The need to save cartridges has practically disappeared, because there are always enough of them - with rare, very rare exceptions. The same goes for medicinal herbs and sprays. The gameplay in front of us is still a survival horror. We run around the locations, looking for herbs, cartridges and consumables, from which all this can be crafted, and also trying to somehow spread it all over the cells of the inventory, so that everything fits.

Confrontation between Jill and Nemesis - I thought that he would be something like the Tyrant from the remake of the second part, an immortal monster constantly running after GG. In fact, all the skirmishes with him are entirely scripted. If Nemesis broke through the wall of the house and blocked Jill's path, she has only two options - either use the environment specially prepared for this and escape to another part of the level, or throw a grenade at the monster's feet to stun him and ... also escape. The mutant will not follow the heroine to another part of the location - unless this is a staged chase, but in this case, he will stop chasing according to the script. Boss fights with Nemesis do not require additional description: you are simply locked in the arena, given ammo and healing cures, and offered to put as much damage as possible on the monster.

Characters:
Nemesis (Prime Villain) is an experimental sapient Tyrant created by Umbrella's European division in France, under the direct control of Umbrella's headquarters. The aim of the project was to show that the BOO created with the help of the T-Virus has the ability to retain most of the intelligence, as a result of which it is able to carry out specific orders and orders .. This creature can run quickly and quickly overcome long distances, jumping over the player , and facing him. Also, Nemesis has long tentacles with which he can attack from a distance, knocking him down and pulling him towards him. Already an impressive arsenal, isn't it? But even that is not all. The indestructible tyrant has impressive equipment, including a flamethrower and a huge rocket launcher, which he changes as he progresses through the story.

Jill Valentine (Main Character) - Agent B.S.A.A. and former officer S.T.A.R.S.

Carlos Oliveira is a member of the U.B.C.S. He was a member of the "A" team of the "Delta" platoon. Served as a specialist in heavy weapons. A young Hispanic mercenary, Carlos took an active part in anti-government guerrilla operations in South America. After the destruction of these organizations by the authorities, he joined the Umbrella Corporation, becoming a member of the U.B.C.S. Served in platoon U.B.C.S. Delta was a specialist in heavy weapons and vehicles, making him a valuable member of the squad.

Nikolay Zinoviev - Commander of Detachment B, Platoon Delta, U.B.C.S. According to the character's background, it is known that he was originally from Moscow and before serving in "U.B.C.S." served in the Russian special forces. He is also (behind the scenes) vying with the U.S.S. commander, Hank. During the events of the game, Nikolai meets Jill, along with the few surviving members of his platoon: Carlos and Mikhail. In the first half of the game, he disappears, and until he reappears, he is considered dead.
In fact, Nikolai is one of the leaders who was assigned to monitor the members of the unit, as well as collect combat data on the battles of soldiers with the Umbrella bioweapons. The fate of the character during the game directly depends on the path that the player chooses. In one of the scenes, he is killed by Nemesis, and his body hangs in the air duct. Another possible route: he kidnaps a helicopter to evacuate Jill. At this moment, the player has a choice: try to negotiate with him, during which he will fly away (this is the canon version of the plot development) or choose a battle against Nikolai, destroying the helicopter with him.
Mikhail Viktor is a member of the U.B.C.S. who participated in the rescue operation in the T-virus-infected Raccoon City.

End review:
Overall, the game is not bad, but not good either. I liked the atmosphere of the game, the zombie-infested Raccoon City, the nemesis itself, which constantly appears from nowhere. I didn't like the fact that the game is almost entirely scripted. The game is short, and therefore does not justify its price of 1999 rubles, and in Europe - 60 euros. I recommend playing it, but not for the price.

Resident Evil 3 a third person survival horror and a remake of the 1999 game Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.
The remake features modern graphics and gameplay, so no tank controls or fixed camera angles.
The story takes place two months after the events of Resident Evil and 24 hours prior the events of Resident Evil 2. Most citizens of Raccoon City are zombies now. 
Jill Valentine, a former member of the Raccoon Police Department's Special Tactics And Rescue Service (S.T.A.R.S.), and survivor of the Spencer Mansion Incident (Resident Evil 1) is attacked in her apartment by an intelligent bioweapon known as Nemesis, programmed by Umbrella to kill the surviving S.T.A.R.S. members.
While beeing chased from the this unstoppable monster Jill has to find a way to escape Raccon City as the U.S. government plans to destroy the whole city in a missile strike to eradicate the T-virus infestation. 
Resident Evil 3 has great graphics and good looking character models and environments.
The voice acting and sounds are great.
While the game is a good remake overall from my point of view, it is really short (around 5 hours) which is the result of missing contentt compared to the original game. There are missing areas. This areas include The City Hall, The Press Office, The Raccoon City Park, The Graveyard, and The Dead Factory.
Also The Mercenaries game mode is missing. It was a mode players could unlock after beating the game. Players could play as different characters and needed to reach a goal in a certain amount of time. 
Capcom should have invested more resources in remaking missing areas and other missing content instead of making a bad multiplayer (comes free with purchase of Resident Evil 3) that nobody has asked for. 
59,99 € might be too much for some people in terms of the short duration. However, if it is on sale I can recommend to get this game.

This game makes me sad: I love all the narrative stuff going on but dislike a lot of the actual gameplay.

The good stuff: the script is just great, it might be the best in the franchise even. It's a very focused, tightly written action narrative with really nice character portrayals, good chemistry between Jill and Carlos and excellent voice acting performances. There are no weird tonal shifts like what we've seen in the RE2 remake, it's a step up in every sense of the word and the main reason for my multiple playthroughs. Some great one liners too, love the crap out of everything regarding the storytelling though I'd say that artistically RE7 achieved a bit more.

Pacing, presentation? Top notch too.

The gameplay on the other hand is just weird as hell, overall it plays like a mediocre action game instead of the true survival horror experience the original was. The level design is very linear, there are no puzzles (yes, there are two, both of them braindead so they don't count), a huge portion of the original content is missing (no Clock Tower, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ seriously, Capcom?) and there are no ink ribbons to be found on any difficulty. 

Speaking of difficulty: standard and hardcore are way too easy and hold your hand with checkpoints and typewriters on every second corridor. Nightmare and Inferno modes on the other hand are way overtuned and basically feel unplayable with horrible enemy placements and a huge focus on trial and error. The solution? You can balance the game out for yourself by spending points on items that make your job easier but even then some of the bossfights (especially the last one) will feel insanely broken, and by that I mean "did nobody test this?" broken. 

For example on Inferno difficulty the first boss has attacks that kill you in one hit... so have fun accidentally stepping into fire because of the horrible camera and getting hit stunned for 5 seconds while Nemesis has plenty of time to kill you in one hit. This is a recurring theme and hey, 5 seconds of hit stun would be absolutely fine in a survival horror game but this is an action game that has a ton of leftover mechanics from the RE2 remake, an actual survivor horror game. The result is two very different styles clashing with each other and becoming something that could only be described as inexcusably bad game design. And I've been with this series for long, I did suffer through Code Veronica's tyrant bossfight, died to RE6's terrible QTE sequences a dozen times but those were nowhere near as badly put together as at least 3 of this game's Nemesis fights.

If this was a movie I'd say go buy a ticket because as I've said the story is excellently put together but here's the thing: this is a videogame and a videogame should play well. A really bad remake of a flawed classic.

[h1] Resident Evil 3 [/h1]

From the perspective of someone who had never played the original game, Resident Evil 3 is a difficult game to talk about, and an even harder one to judge. I am fully aware of the many criticisms that have been rightfully levied against this game, but I would also be lying to myself and to you if I said I didn't enjoy my time with it because I did. Much of which can be contributed by the fact that I had nothing to cross-reference due to my lack of experiences and foreknowledge of the original game. Therefore, in the spirit of fairness, I'm going to try and judge Resident Evil 3 from both a personal and objective standpoint and give out a recommendation that is best appropriate for it. As always, I'd like to start by listing all the positives. 

[u] What I liked about Resident Evil 3 [/u]

[b] 1. The graphics [/b]
Just like with many other Resident Evil games that came before it, Resident Evil 3 utilizes the RE Engine, and it looks nothing short of incredible. Unlike what many other people would like you to believe, graphics do matter. Thankfully, this is the one area where Resident Evil 3 shines the brightest, and you can look forward to being enamored by every area you come across in Raccoon City.  

[b] 2. The gameplay loop still works [/b]
There is something about the Resident Evil formula that just clicks with me no matter how many times I played it. The act of exploration followed by puzzle solving and shooting zombies is just as fun as it did the first time. However, it's important to point out that Resident Evil 3 is an action horror game, not survival horror. If you come in expecting it to play like Resident Evil 2, you're sorely mistaken. Survival has taken a backseat for a new emphasis on action-oriented gameplay, and you can see this reflected by how the game has been changed: More enemies, more ammo, a dodge mechanic, etc. As someone who prefers survival horror over action, I still had a good time regardless, so don't be discouraged by the new change in direction because you might just end up liking it. 

[b] 3. Modernization [/b]
If there is one thing I don't miss about any of the old Resident Evil games, it's the constant loading and opening of doors every time I want to enter a new area, and that's just the icing on the cake. Bringing the original experience into the modern era means no more tank control, having an actual proper shooting mechanic, more inventory spaces which equate to less excessive backtracking, and most importantly no more fixed camera angles. These qualities of life changes are immensely appreciated, and I can’t stress enough how much better the game is for it. 

[u] Where Resident Evil 3 failed to meet its expectation as a remake [/u]

[b] 1. Missing content [/b]
The amount of content that was scraped from the remake is simply astonishing. Everything from multiple locations, areas, and boss fights that were in the original game is just straight up missing in Resident Evil 3. This is a colossal failure that has wide-reaching consequences which also significantly affects the overall length of the game making it a lot shorter than it needs to be, and overall making the maps a lot more linear than what it was in the original. I cannot emphasize enough how serious and detrimental this problem is in the overall quality of the experience, and as someone who had never gotten the chance to play the original game, I am incredibly disappointed by the lack of time and passion that was put here in the remake. What a wasted opportunity to introduce new fans to a cult classic. Shame on Capcom. 

[b] 2. Live selection is gone [/b]
 One of the core features that helped defined the original Resident Evil 3 was the ability to make choices that directly impacted the progression of the game. It made the experience interesting, engaging, and most importantly it added much more replayability to the final product; It gave players a strong incentive to replay the game multiple times and provided it a unique experience that no other Resident Evil games since then have been able to offer. In its place now is a shop that lets you spend points that you collected by completing challenges on things such as overpowered weapons and coins that grant passive perks. While this new shop is fine on its own, it shouldn’t be a substitute for what was once a core defining experience of the original Resident Evil 3. It’s an integral part of the game’s identity, and it’s immensely disappointing to see that Capcom felt like it wasn’t important enough to be put in the remake. 

[b] 3. What the hell happened to Nemesis? [/b]
To put it bluntly, Nemesis is a complete and total pushover in the remake. What should've been an ever-present threat which stalks you like Mr. X from Resident Evil 2, unfortunately, became a walking joke of its former self. First and most importantly, Nemesis now only shows up to fight you briefly at extremely specific periods in the campaign, but once you passed a certain checkpoint, it just completely ceases to exist in the game until your next scripted encounter with it. It feels lazy, predictable, and it turns Nemesis into more of a nuisance than an actual threat. Nemesis's greatest strength has always been its overwhelming presence throughout the original game, but you don't feel that at all in the remake. Lastly, what used to be a ferocious and tanky monster that required you to invest an enormous amount of resources just to down it can now be done with a simple grenade. Yup, just ONE grenade. I don't know what kind of bioweapon we got in this game, but it is NOT Nemesis.

[b] 4. Boss fights are underwhelming [/b]
Sigh, as if Nemesis hasn't been through enough with Capcom trying to neuter it at every corner, but it can't even offer you a fun boss fight to save its life. You get to battle Nemesis a total of four times throughout the entire campaign and not once was it ever satisfying. This is the most subjective criticism in my review, but I can't help but feel like most players would agree with me on this. I just didn't feel like much effort was put into this category and consequently, it suffers greatly. What should've been the highlights of the game had become nothing more than slight speed bumps on your way toward completing the game, and that's NOT how players should feel fighting Nemesis.

[b] 5. Puzzles are significantly easier and simpler to solve [/b]
Unfortunately, one of the core pillars when it comes to designing a fun Resident Evil game had also been severely compromised. Puzzles in Resident Evil 3 are more locks than real puzzles. Throughout my runs in the campaign, I think I came across more or less only two actual puzzles in the entire game none of which were particularly difficult to solve at all. This creative decision was probably made to put a heavier emphasis on a faster-paced and action-packed experience for Resident Evil 3, and I gotta tell you, I'm not happy about it. Puzzles have always been a key staple of any Resident Evil game and not only having them be fewer in between but also be made significantly easier to solve is a huge slap in the face.

[u] My final verdict [/u]
This game could've had the potential to be something truly amazing. Regretfully, it’s a game that left many fans disappointed and yearning for justice. For many people, Resident Evil 3 failed as a remake, and it's not hard to see why. Interestingly enough, despite my numerous scathing criticisms, I still found myself enjoying Resident Evil 3, surprisingly. It's a deeply flawed game, but one I still think has something to offer. New fans will be able to experience a much more accessible and modern version of the original game, albeit a compromise version, without having to deal with all of the technical and outdated barriers that the old game poses. Resident Evil 3 is a game that feels much better to play at $20, and as a result, I will only recommend that you purchase ONLY if it goes on sale for a cheap price.

My mind has not changed: this is better than RE2. I know this is unpopular opinion, but hear me out. From what I've seen there are 2 main complaints (aside from the cut content): too linear and Carlos breaking the dynamics.
I agree, that the game is linear, compared to RE2. And I did get a sort of satisfaction from uncovering everything there, solving all the puzzles and stuff. I did like this exploration, although retracing my own steps was a bit boring more often than not. I understand the backlash from lack of the exploration in RE3. But... It works so much better in terms of the narrative.
When I've started playing the game I was quickly reminded of my initial try of the 1st game in latest Tomb Raider series. I pirated it (since there was no demo), played it for like 30 minutes with open mouth and bought it right after with no regret. I had same experience here: I was excited.
RE2 was about "creeping" fear and uncertain danger. RE3 clearly states from the very start: you're screwed if you do not move. This is the point of the story: you are running out of time, you do NOT have time to explore. In this case having a more linear experience makes absolute sense, because it gives developers more control over the experience. And it simply works.
As for Carlos episodes... Yes, they feel slower, but it also works from perspective of the narrative. Think about it, even high-paced action movies tend to have slower moments in them, to provide a breather. Carlos episodes can help with that, although Jill's playthrough has some moments like that as well. And regardless this approach works way better than 1st/2nd run in RE2.
That is why I believe, that despite some minor flaws in narrative in RE3, it's still a better experience. Maybe not "overall", but in terms of the narrative, at least. Again, if you keep in mind, that it has a different focus, different premise, than RE2.

Resident Evil 3(2020) is a remake of the Resident Evil 3(1999), and just like remakes of the RE1 and 2 tries to recreate the old survival-horror classics with new graphics, mechanics and small changes to overall structure. I have to preface this review with the statement that I never played the original Resident Evil 3, and probably never will, since I have no0 way or desire to try and launch without original harware. 

Unfortunately, compared to the incredible RE2make, R3make is kind of let-down. I guess it was released too early after RE2make, but this game just feels underwhelming in a lot of ways.

The story of the game follows Jill Valentine, one of the protagonists of the original Resident Evil. Unlike most of the members of the S.T.A.R.S team, Jill got stuck in Raccoon City during the outbreak of the T-Virus, which turned most of the population into zombies. Making things worse, Jill becomes a target of the unstoppable monster, known as Nemesis, that was created to hunt down and eliminate all of the remaining S.T.A.R.S. members. Thee main objective is simple, get out of the Raccoon City and save as many survivors as possible. With the help of the small squad of the Umbrella Biohazard Countermeasure Service, and in particular Carlos Oliviera, Jill has to leave Raccoon City before it will get wiped out by the epidemic and following missile strike that will destroy all of the living things in the city.
The story by itself is fine. The voice acting is great and characters don't do anything stupid. Nicholai is a wondertful scun of a villain, and Carlos is a great sidekick to Jill. it may lack some slower, somber moments of the RE2make, but considering that this is a different type of story where the main characters race against the clock it's fine.

The graphics are incredible. The first time going through the dying Raccoon City you really get the feel that the world as we know it is ending. The glowing storefronts and dark streets lit with streetlights and police car signals just look great. Zombies roam around trying to eat something on it's path. Later portions of the game feature abandoned hospital and generic secret laboratory, that also look great and full details. Considering the visuals of the game, I have no complaints.

The main roblems with the game are it's direction in gamedesign and levels. Firstly, the game doesn't follow traditional RE formula of searching for keys in an open environment for exploration. The game is mostly linear and broken up into small segments with minimal puzzles and exploration and can be completed in an hour for the first time playthrough and maybe ten minutes if you speedrunning. The exploration that this game offers boils down to tedious backtracking through the same level. There is no interconncted design with shortcuts multiple paths that you can take to avoid danger, only tight corridors and rooms where you have to fight enemies since you can't avoid most of them. The only segment that can remind you of classic Resident Evil is extremely short hospital section as Carlos, where you have to find key items, but it culminates in absolutely stupid defense section where you just shoot down hordes of zombies and couple of hunters.
The game is also very easy and offers no real challenge. i played the game on the hardcore difficulty for the first time, and if RE2make kicked my ass multiple times with it's scarce resources and agressive enemies, R3make is just turns into very boring action game with spongy enemies. 
I will say that I don't have anything against action in Resident Evil or horror games in general. My favourite horror games are RE4 and Dead Space 2. But the fact that the game is built on the foundation of the RE2makewhere you ahd to ration every little thing and be very careful with your resources and inventory space, and just gives everything to you to plow through every situation just kills all tension. There was never a situation where I was actually starved of ammo or recovery items and had to adapt to the current situation. Most of the enemies just rely on gimmicky weak points, that you can exploit to get rid of them. Also one of the most hilarious new features of this game is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dodge move. In short Jill can quickly avoid any attack by stepping out of the enemy's way and it givesyou a brief invincibility window to avoid an attack. By itself in vacuum I don't think it was a bad idea to add this feature, since the game is focused more on action, but where it get's stupid is when you realise, that perfectly timed dodge gives you Bayonetta-style slow motion effect, and with a knife gives you a powerful counter attack. I haven't played the game for a long enough time, but when I realised how this feature works, the only thought I had was "oh no". Main issue is, this opens up so many opportunities for exploites and easy ways out, that a survival-horror game should never have. Second playable character Carlos, has a shoulder tackle instead of a dodge move, which has more of an offensive option instead of defensive one, but timed perfectly with enemies attack it can be used as counter since Carlos punches enemy and knocks them down, opening them up for an attack.
But the main dissapointment I had with this game is front and canter, proudly presented in the first minutes of the game and prominently featured in all of the promo materials of the game. I'm sorry, but Nemesis is a little b*tch in this game. Before playing this game, I thought he was more of a dynamic threat, appearing randomly in different parts of the game to ramp up tension, but in reality he is just a scripted jumpscare that annoys you a little bit and looks kind of intimidating for the first time. On the hardest available difficulty this idiot goes down to a single hand-grenade, drops you a lootcrate and disappears until the next scripted section.
The bossfights are disappointing as well. They boil down to "shoot it until it dies" approach. It's not something you want to see from such a hyped up enemy. He's not scary or intimidating, he's just annoying. The third boss-fight is particularly bad, because it looks like designers realised that this section was too easy and just decided too add zombies that constantly spawn in on the edges of the arena and distract you from bullying Nemesis, that tries to hide from you behind electrically charged containers or something.

the last problem I have with this game is the fact that it lacks in content compared to the other remake. There is no alternative character campaign with a different storyline, no challenging modes like The 4th Survivor or Mercenaries. The only thing this game offers is just higher difficulty levels and some bonuses that can make the game easier if you complete certain challenges. So the game by itslef is pretty short, you have no real motivation to go through unles you really loved the experience for the first time and want it all over again, but harder. i can understand that, but this is really not worth the price it asking for. This is a AAA release asking full price, but giving like half of the content a similar game offers. 

R3make is not the worst game in the series, but it is by far should have been more. i think the game was rushed in development, maybe that's why it feels so underwhelming, but in any case, get it only for a BIG discount and only if you are a die-hard fan of the series.

TL:DR: The remakes of RE2 and 3 are completely different experiences and BOTH are amazing. Buy Resident Evil 2 Remake first, BUT also give this game a chance. 

Resident Evil 3 is an action-packed survival horror game that rapidly transitions from one exhilarating setpiece to another at a speed normally not found in other RE titles. It doesn't let you take a breather for the most part; and when the story MOSTLY revolves around trying to escape the Raccoon City while being stalked by a seemingly unkillable behemoth, this is a GOOD thing. 

Yes, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a longer game, both because of the larger story and the bonus games. 
Yes, Mr. X is a better executed Tyrant compared to Stage 1 Nemesis in the Remakes. 
Yes, Zombies look better in RE2Make. 
Yes, you SHOULD buy RE2Make first. 

And yet, this game got me WAY more addicted than Resident Evil 2 remake. By far. 

IF you are the type of person that finishes the story 1 time and then close the game, then this is NOT worth full price. 1 run through the story is not enough bang for your buck. And it is OBVIOUS, by the greater-than-usual amount of difficulty levels, the very strict time window and restricted amount of saves to get an S-rank on all difficulty levels and how almost every single item in the bonus content shop are basically necessary in order to beat Nightmare and Inferno difficulties (at least for your first time), that the developers WANT you to go for re-runs. 

At its best, Resident Evil 3 Remake: 
- Is a very cinematic experience that can be finished in around 1h30min- 2h (just like a zombie movie) once you master it, making it a very addictive game to replay, since the time investment to enjoy the story all over again isn't as big as the other titles. 
- Provides a very satisfying extra content shop to help give more variety for re-runs. 
- Provides a good enough variety of difficulty levels so everyone can enjoy the game, regardless of skill level. 
- Has very satisfying combat mechanics, with Jill's dodges being the highlight of every gameplay session I have had. 

At its worst, Resident Evil 3 Remake: 
- Needed a stronger opening hour exploring more of the chaos-ridden Raccoon City
-Leaves you wanting more interactive Nemesis that stalks you while you are trying to finish other objectives, instead of an enemy relegated for, albeit fun and varied, scripted sequences and boss fights. 
- Has an FRUSTRATING final boss when fought against in any of the 2 hardest difficulties (BUY IRON DEFENSE COINS FOR INFERNO OR YOU WILL DIE CONSTANTLY). 
- Is a game that will NOT be worth your money if you are the type of person that will play this game's story once and leave it there.

Personally, once I finished the story the first time, I did not stop replaying it, until I managed to complete every challenge and achievement.

I encourage people who did not give this game a chance after reading that the story mode only lasts for 3-5 hours to try it. Because you're NOT meant to play the story once this time. 

P.S: The game's sweet spot, in terms of difficulty, lies on the Hardcore and Nightmare difficulties. Standard and Assisted is way too easy if you are used to playing survival horror games and Inferno can get frustratingly hard, even though you need to have beaten the game at least twice already to unlock it.

It's a really good game on it's own, but as it's a remake, we can't leave out the obvious - the missing pieces. The developers notoriously cut corners for some odd reason (maybe due to time constraints), they chose to remove two entire areas, several different Nemesis encounters, puzzles, a boss fight, a different ending and even an extra mini-game which had huge replayability value, these were elements that made the original such a fan favorite, this decision was really disappointing as it shortened the game by several hours. The atmosphere, pacing, and tension that made RE2 so strong are missing here. The biggest disappointment is how much content was cut or reduced from the original RE3. Areas feel shorter, encounters feel scripted, and the game heavily relies on spectacle instead of meaningful gameplay. Nemesis — who should have been terrifying — is mostly a cinematic gimmick instead of a constant unpredictable threat.

There’s still fun to be had if you enjoy a quick action-focused RE experience, but for fans expecting depth, exploration, and replayability on the level of RE2 Remake, this falls far short. It’s gorgeous, but ultimately shallow — more like a fast rollercoaster ride than a true survival horror experience.

Chances are, if you're going to try this game, you've already played Resident Evil 2. RE3 certainly looks and sort of feels like RE2, but it's missing a couple of things. First, the ominous, creepy tension isn't there. They try to fill that void with extra sound fx that will put you on edge even while you're in the item menu screen, but you'll get over that pretty quickly. There aren't as many choices, or options for exploration. The environments outside don't feel as authentic as they should. There aren't enough puzzles, in my opinion. Compared to RE2, RE3 is on rails. In a lazy attempt to make up for this, they throw in a lot of those cinematic escape sequences followed by a formulaic boss fight. It gets tiresome really quickly. I may have only played a third the way through the game, but that's more than enough to know that it feels more like Diet Tomb Raider than Resident Evil. I found myself just wanting to get it over with, hoping that something rewarding might be around the horizon. Well, my will to get there evaporated before that ever happened.

There are positives with the game, such as a mildly improved fighting mechanic. It looks pretty. If you're into watching the game play itself there are tons of cinematic sequences, a few of which you get to hold the joy stick for. It is tied to Resident Evil 2, so you'll learn more about the virus, and discover context to the events of the previous game. It tries to be like the final 20 minutes of Resident Evil 2 form the very start, so if you really liked the end of RE2, you might just love this game. 

But if you were hoping for ominous, creepy, story-driven, puzzle-solving, exploration... you won't find that with RE3. What you'll get with RE3 is action sequences and boss fights.

My favorite Resident Evil so far was the one the internet told me I shouldn't like. Why?

-I will admit that for a $60.00 game the amount of time you get for your money (about 7-10 hours) is asking a lot, but it is BAD ASS all the way through. The way I see it, this game is more of an homage than a remake. What that means is that they cut out most of the side stuff from the original, which shortened the overall length of the game but IMO makes it completely devoid of filler. Get it on a sale and treat it like a RE2 DLC.
-The new dodging system fixes any complaints I had with the combat of RE2 Remake.
-Voice acting, atmosphere and music are once again a total knockout.
-Story was probably my favorite so far.

What advice would I give?

-Contrary to what I've said for the last two games, PLAY HARDCORE. While Jill's ability to dodge and her arsenal makes her John Wick compared to Leon and Claire, it also has the side effect of making combat a good deal easier on Standard. Hardcore difficulty sets the bar perfectly, allowing you to enjoy the new unstiffened combat mechanics and also not completely walk all over the entire game.

If you liked Resident Evil 2 Remaster or just haven't played RE3, you will love this game. Even for it's length I found it to be worth it. Now I'm on to RE4 or RE Zero. Haven't decided yet.

RE3:Make is an honestly really solid game. It plays well, is visually fun, it's just solid. But it's also flawed. And it's flaws are hard to ignore. Many of the things that made the original game (A short, but wonderful game) awesome, well they're missing. First and foremost, the remake feels like things were scrapped on the alter of expedience. To get it out they clearly cut out sections of the story, boss fights, hell the entire decision making system when encountering nemesis. That last one is more a personal nitpick, but I think it's important cause of how it feels having to make those decisions. Even so, it's the things that feel cut or missing that bug me. 

This is especially frustrating as it feels like they were cut to allocate money towards the easily monetized resistance game. A game I have no interest in and will not bash here, but which I will say should not have been made to be included with this game. Anyone who says that resistance was free is lying. With how sadly short and somewhat hollowed out 3 itself is, the price you pay for it is a price paid for 2 smaller games, not 1 full game and a bonus. 

And that's my biggest issue. The lie that resistance was a free bonus, and not something made by a separate team that you are paying for in addition to the cost of 3. It's not a bonus, it's just the other part of your purchase, even if you wanted a better 3 remake.

In the end, issues aside, I think that, on a discount, RE3:Make is well worth it. I don't regret buying it at full price. I think the game is excellent if flawed and hollowed out some, and would have benefited from some solid DLC expansions. I just think it's dishonest and unreasonable of them to act like resistance wasn't just the other portion of the game. To pretend you were buying 3 and getting a bonus, instead of a small game called 3 and a small game called resistance.

Next time capcom, maybe devote the budget to one game or another, instead of splitting the budget to make 2 lesser games.

This is going to be an unpopular opinion. I had just played original RE3 over before playing this so I could freshly compare the two games. RE3 original is the better version, but not by much. This however is a better remake than Resident Evil 2 remake was. 

Let me start off by making a pros and cons list

[b]Pros[/b] 

[list]

[*] Graphics are fantastic, as well as performance
[*] The dodge system is MUCH better than original 3
[*] Unlike RE2R the zombies did not feel like bullet sponges as much. This could be partly due to the weapons in the game but I did not feel like it took 13 headshots to take down zombies in this one
[*] I felt like the story was better and rearranged pretty well over original RE3
[*] Scenes were removed, but scenes were also added. It was very clearly a reimagining of RE3. I felt like there were enough new scenes or boss encounters to make up for most (but not all) of the removed scenes from the original
[*] The final boss fight specifically I felt was really cool, and it felt pretty hyped when I defeated it. 
[*] I really enjoyed the story in this game over most entries in the series

[/list]

[b]Cons[/b]

[list]

[*] Just like Resident Evil 2 remake this game removed one of its most unique features from the original. The different options you could take in the original game was entirely removed. While this wasn't as big of an impact as Resident Evil 2 removing the Zap system and mostly ruining the need for B scenarios, it was a disappointment. RE3's choices were small in comparison, but I still found the fact that they were missing to be a disappointment. 
[*] The removal of the clock tower was on the disappointing side. This game is on the shorter side so any cut areas hurts its over all value. RE3 original was already on the shorter side.
[*] Not enough back tracking. This game felt a little more like a linear Uncharted style story than it did a Resident Evil. While I think it executed this extremely well, it could have done the same with more back tracking, item hunting, and puzzle solving and been even better. RE3 original had some very good back tracking. Not a huge knock but a knock against it none the less.
[*] They should have kept the bonus modes from RE3 in there. There are some cool after the game bonuses like the store, but I'm not sure if it can compete with the removal of The Mercenaries. 
[/list]

The game is, as you've heard, woefully short and lacking in puzzles. Considering that the original RE3 had its fair share of shoehorned filler content, though, this remake isn't as egregious as naysayers love to vapidly repeat. As a remake it does fall considerably flat in several areas, but it stands tall in others and functions as more of a reimagining than anything. The story is cohesive and effective, if simple, and both the mechanics and ammo economy are well-designed around the more action-oriented level design. The fear factor is lowered considerably, but it still has its moments. My biggest gripe with this game is similar to the "short game bad" argument that spearheads the crusade, but it's more of a wish than an actual complaint. Carlos, Jill, and especially Nemesis are beautifully recreated and given excellent VAs as well as detailed models. They are downright iconic, but have so little screentime that it leaves me hungry for more every time I finish a run of the brief campaign. Even RC itself is gorgeously iconic, and it makes me cringe to think of how much we missed out on when we could have had a semi-open world Raccoon City to explore with the narrative crossroads and roaming Nemesis encounters vis a vis the original RE3. All the same, hope isn't lost. This is a great game by itself, and remakes of remakes are known to happen. Maybe ten years from now we'll have a proper, exploration-heavy RE3 iteration that blows our collective minds and takes its rightful seat among the greatest video games of all time.

I didn't pay full price for this game, so my experience is purely through the lens of someone who only paid $20.

Overall, it's a lean and mean action horror game well worth a sale price. As a remake goes, it's not particularly faithful but that also doesn't really alter the end product. Hero beat Snot Monster, The End. 

Here's all that matters: 

- Jill is a badass who is not here for your sh!t. She's instantly recognizable as RE3 iteration of Jill, but this time not dressed like a Raccoon City sex worker. Her dodge mechanic is also useful, if a bit inconsistent. 

- The monsters all got amazing modern updates (particularly the Hunter Gamma), but the obvious star of the show is Nemesis himself. He always scared the crap out of me in the 1999 game, but they just nailed him in this remake and somehow made him more imposing and intimidating. I know that a point of contention is Nemesis encounters are purely scripted and Mr. X has a more dynamic AI. That style of AI worked better for RE2, which is a much more methodical and complex game. Nemesis is an aggressive menace that matches the tone of this game. In OGRE3 I didn't care for Nemesis's mutations, but I really dig what they did with him here. He's still just as agile and fast, while also being the size of a small bus. His final form is nothing short of breathtaking.

TL:DR If you paid $60, that sucks and this is definitely not a $60 game. This definitely felt more like $40 title (like Uncharted: The Lost Legacy) or a paid expansion. For what I paid, I loved it. Probably even more than RE2, because I paid full price for that and have only felt the need to play Claire's campaign. I'm already on a second run of RE3 so I can farm all the points that will eventually get me my unlimited rocket launcher.

I hate leaving a bad review for a Resident Evil game, and it took me a while to come back to this after completing the game.

When i first completed it, my initial reaction was:  [i]" holy crapzombies that was shorter than i expected."[/i] And i really didn't know how to feel about how underwhelming the whole experience itself felt at the time, i kind of just forgot about it and moved on to another game.

Now with Resident Evil Village literally over the horizon (okay so about 8 or 9 horizons), I started thinking about this game again, and it kinda clicked suddenly.  I now know why this game was so bad and why RE2 Remake was so good.  

RE2 Remake was its own thing, and didn't have anything else production-wise vying for control over what got worked on and when; even those extra pieces of DLC were still just making use of things already worked on within the main project, and that game feels like it was given the time it needed and deserved.

RE3 Remake does NOT feel like it was given even a fraction of time and effort RE2 Remake was given, and it's easier now to see what may have caused that; that nonsense multiplayer Resistance game that was shoehorned into the price tag.

It would be interesting to find out what project started before what; Did they begin working on RE: Resistance BEFORE RE3 Remake? or side-by-side, or after?   Now it's no secret what Resistance was meant to be; it was Capcom wanting to cash-in on the wildly successful [b]Dead By Daylight[/b] IP, which is a 4 versus's 1 Survival Horror game which pretty much consumed all of Steam back in 2016.

I cannot help thinking this is why RE3 Remake felt so bare-bones compared to what came before it, because Resistance came bundled in for Free with the purchases of RE3 Remake... because... of course it did.  Now whether RE: Resistance is good on it's own merit's is really besides the point, I just couldn't help but wonder how much better this whole game could have been if there wasn't a Multiplayer project attached to it.

Now granted, for what RE3 Remake is and what it does, it's not bad or anything, it just feels like the bare-frickin-minimum effort on the Developers part, and it probably wouldn't have... if Capcom didn't feel the urge to give us a standalone 4-vs-1 multiplayer game no one even asked for.

This actually makes me a bit worried for Village if i were to be honest, because they did the same thing with the upcoming Re8(Village), which is a numbered entry, and i kind of hate them for doing that with a numbered entry.

I know this seems a lot more like a rant than an actual review, but again, there isn't anything necessarily terrible with the actual game, it just felt like WAY too much content hit the chopping block that it feels like a incomplete Resident Evil experience instead of a buggy mess or the like.
