As someone who considers the original RE3 one of her favorite games of all time, I'm a bit conflicted.
I'm leaving nostalgia at the door (for the most part) for this review. Some of the points I make in this review are slightly exaggerated so don't take it too serious.

The Good

1 - The graphics like usual are stunning as hell, just like the last two entries. I found myself wandering around just to look at all of the amusing stuff that they left laying around. I especially loved the part where you just get to walk around in Jill's apartment for the start of the game and all of the visual story telling on display inside there, great stuff. On repeat plays, I'm sure I'm going to be finding new stuff with each one and that's a huge plus in my book.

2 - The Dodge mechanic is definitely improved from the original (Something that was so obtuse you may as well have never even bothered trying to learn it) and it's satisfying as hell to pull one off and counter attack with three shots. I found myself trying to bait dodges just so I could get that slow-mo effect. It's especially a lot more satisfying when you're playing as Carlos and you just deck creatures in the face. It's so stupid, I love it.

3 - Although I prefer Jill's original look (mostly due to nostalgia) I feel like they did a fantastic job with her design in this game. I especially love what they did with Carlos (my favorite aspect of the remake). He's just a straight upgrade in my opinion. Capcom had a weird fixation of making all of the male leads look exactly the same with subtle differences between them for a little while (Leon, Carlos, Billy and Steve) and it was really weird. It was great to see them just dump that and go for something completely new.

4 - The weapons (especially the grenade launcher) are all really fun to use. They did away with the mine thrower and just kinda made it an attachment to the G. Launcher and that's probably what it should have been in the first place.

5 - I love what they did with Nicholai. He was always a conniving bastard that you just loved to hate, but here he was tuned up to 11 with his facial expressions and his warped idea of "self preservation."

6 - The soundtrack is great. I'm glad to see that music made a return to this title instead of the choice to just use ambient music for the most part in the RE2 Remake. The remixes they made of the original score sound so natural and I'm honestly impressed with how well they just wove everything in. The final boss in particular just knocked it out of the park with it's remix of the final boss theme.

7 - Nemesis having more weapons is just awesome. Seeing him run around with a flame thrower doing borderline Flame Shoryukens is something I never knew I needed in Resident Evil.

8 - Speaking of Nemesis, his design is great. Just this mangled monstrosity that's stitched together in a hurry. I wouldn't call him an improvement on the original design, but I accept him as just as good as the original and I'm honestly happier that they didn't just copy and paste him.

9 - Jill and Carlos' dialogue is just the best. That's really it. They rule.

The Bad

1 - I guess the first thing I should mention is that the game is a lot more action oriented, which is fine. The original RE3 was a lot more action oriented so it would make sense that the remake do that as well. However, I feel as though it was perhaps a little TOO action oriented. I'm more into the puzzle and survival element of these games and found it a little more than irritating that the game not only encourages action play where you kill every single creature you run into. They seem to have gone out of their way to actually punish you if you try to play like previous titles in the series. (Ex. Run around zombies instead of fight them)

One example that I seemed to run into a lot was that if I tried the strategy of running around zombies, there seemed to often times be a zombie conveniently tucked away in a dark corner I couldn't see who'd surprise me and push me back into the crowd, basically leaving me doomed after I shoved him off. I quickly learned that this wasn't the way you should be playing this game and accepted it's action elements, but I was still sad to see that I couldn't play the way I wanted to. (Something I still could do in the original RE3)

2 - They took out the little moments where you got to make 1 of 2 choices. Not a huge loss, but it was at least fun to see how things turn out on repeat plays.

3 - Jill didn't say the classic STARS line in the game. Or rather, she DID say it, but not at the appropriate time. C'mon guys, if you're gonna have her say it at least make it at the right time.

4 - This one is minor and probably only happened to me. There's one section of the game that you can potentially get stuck in because of the auto save feature. The fight with Nemesis while you're at the Clocktower requires the grenade launcher to get past. However, being the RE Veteran that I am, I keep just the pistol with me for the extra space in case I need it. So I go into this boss fight and find that I need the G. Launcher to get through, but "Uh-oh, I can't go back." because the game auto-saved and I'm stuck there. So I had to load a previous save, it wasn't THAT bad, because my last save wasn't too far from that area, but it was still pretty irritating and I feel like it should have been coordinated better that you were gonna need the G. Launcher. Or at least, somehow make it possible for you to go to your item box mid boss fight or something. (idk, I'm only here to complain, not make solutions)

The Ugly

1 - Cut Content... so much cut content. There are so many things missing from this game. From iconic locations, such as the Clock Tower, The Park and most of Raccoon City. Not to mention that we didn't get Mercenaries Mode. Which is just abysmal, considering that the whole concept of Mercenaries Mode started with RE3. I'm okay with change when it comes to remakes, sometimes it can make things better, but a remake should only add to it's original source material, not take anything away. (That's just my opinion though) I speculate that Mercenaries Mode was sacrificed for Resistance. (Something nobody even asked for)

2 - Going back to Nemesis. Aside from the great things I stated in the "Good" section, he was kinda lackluster. He wasn't nearly as much of a threat or in your face as the original. He's mostly just reserved for scripted events and that's it. He was heavily scripted in the original RE3 too, but he had some moments where he was slightly unpredictable, which is what made people love him. (Well, at least me)

He also doesn't say STARS as much. Or maybe he does and he just doesn't say it as clearly. (I could probably use a new pair of headphones)

Conclusion

Even though there's a lot wrong with this game, I recommend it and proudly hold this in high regard within my Resident Evil collection. I'm a Resident Evil super fan and I love every single numbered entry in the series. (and the Revelations games as well).
If you're someone who's played the original RE3, don't expect the bang up job they did with the RE2 Remake. RE3 was rushed like hell and it definitely shows.

It took me six hours to complete this game first time. Six hours with me taking as much time as possible analyzing everything. Every document, every display, repeatedly backtracking for items (as I'm an aggressive item hoarder that won't leave behind anything... for any reason), standing around doing nothing, etc. Again, totaling six hours. Six. Hours. What?

First things first. Nemesis. Anyone remember the original Resident Evil 3's title? Resident Evil 3: Nemesis. They were in the name of the game. For damn good reason. The Remake? I... don't really remember seeing much of Nemesis. I'm being completely honest. I had so little engagement with the Nemesis that I honestly forgot what game I was even playing -- that the Nemesis even existed. The demo for this game... I thought people were joking when they said that's all the engagement you really got with the Nemesis in the final game. Well, they weren't lying. That's basically it. That's about the only general area of the game any stalker mechanics *might* be in play. And I say might, because, to be frank, Nemesis is a giant pushover. One grenade and they're out; dropping a useful item / upgrade. I swear to God the first proper encounter I had with Nemesis was 5 seconds. Nemesis shows up, I toss a Grenade, they're out. "Hi Nemmy, bye Nemmy. *waving as I go on my merry way*" If added up all the time I was actually being stalked before I casually put them down as a passive annoyance, I'd maybe get like 30-40 seconds throughout the whole game. Every other encounter with Nemesis is just a scripted cinematic scene where you just run away on a pre-determined path or just watch someone else take care of them (where originally you'd have fought them). And then the occasional boss fight.. where Nemesis poses almost no threat to you at all.

Now, I understand the original game had scripted areas where Nemesis would appear, but I need to call out obvious BS here in the reviews where necessary. By comparison: In the original game, Nemesis was up your ass almost constantly. Either you put them down for some reprieve time to do some things, or you had to worry that any second, sometimes without warning, a pissed off super-Tyrant would come Usain Bolt sprinting through a door ready to plant their fist up your backside. And they were occasionally weaponized, for casual encounters. Not some scripted chase sequence. No, your ass was fighting them, room by room, while dodging rockets until they ran out and decided your buttcheeks were bongo drums. And they didn't go down with a single grenade. No, try an entire arsenal (multiple grenade rounds, shotgun shots, dozens of handgun rounds) just to put them down for a *little while*. And the original game had butterfly effect options with some of your Nemesis encounters that would impact the flow of the game to varying degrees. While not a super huge thing, it's nonetheless not a thing in the remake. Stop trying to equate the "scriptedness" of these titles. They aren't the same. They aren't even on the same plane of existence. Either you need to replay the original game, or you're lying. They are not comparable.

I was expecting fun new twists with the Nemesis this time around. New ways to screw with you. An even more intelligent and relentless killing machine. But unfortunately, he gets outclassed by Mr. X from Resident Evil 2 Remake... because at least they had a presence in that game. In fact, they were a huge upgrade over the original. But I digress.

Now, Raccoon City. It's incredibly linear, and has little presence (unlike the original). Certain enemy types have been removed, abilities reduced, or relegated to their own tiny area of the game (still no spiders or crows, though REMake 2 did that as well). No branching pathways, much of the city being inaccessible outside of cinematic / scripted events, any and all puzzles entirely removed. At least a third of the original city is completely gone, or reduced to setpieces you can only view from the outside. Like the clocktower. Used to be its own mini-mansion with an evolved form of Nemesis chasing your ass. Now? You get a boss fight with a very different, uninspired, Monster Hunter version of the Nemesis in front of it. That's it. A certain bug monster boss and its relevant areas in the city have also been nixed from existence.

In the original game, the city itself was like a giant version of the RPD. Except instead with a ridiculously oppressive version of Mr. X lurking about.

I knew I was going to be disappointed with what Capcom had on offer after critical reviews came out. I decided then I would only purchase this title on steep discount, if at all. Well, now that I have, I can't say that I exactly hate it (which is what I was expecting), In fact, I actually had some enjoyment playing through R3Make. But, not like the original game. There was some neat new documentation, a new lab, and some interesting character developments and insight into Umbrella's involvements domestic and abroad. Taking the game as it is, and disregarding the original title. It still works in its own way. I can imagine playing through it again through the harder difficulties and messing with unlocks, as combat had its moments. And the graphics are gorgeous!

I want to be as fair as it makes sense for me to be. And honestly, if you can view this Remake in similar light to the RE Chronicles games, then there is definitely some fun to be had. It's a consolidated highlight-reel version of RE3 with hugely upgraded visuals. And, while not necessarily an on-rails shooter, it does feel like it at times. In short: It's Resident Evil 3: TL;DR Edition. But I cannot allow myself to review R3Make this way, as this was not the sales pitch for the game. The original game has to be considered. The full $59.99 price tag has to be considered. And to this end, I'm sorry, but Resident Evil 3 falls very short. It fails in almost every metric that made the original great. And where RE3 does succeed is greatly overshadowed by its shortcomings as a remake. It feels almost as if it lost its soul.

I'm not including RE: Resistance into this review, because, who cares? Maybe I'm missing something, but, seriously. Why? I didn't even bother installing it. RE isn't about multiplayer.

If you want to get Resident Evil 3, please wait for a huge discount. Don't buy it for full price. It's not worth it. I might even have recommended this title if it were permanently discounted.

[h1]Original Review (Was thumbs down):[/h1]

I was writing down notes as I played.  I'm going to stick to bullet points. Resident Evil 2 Remake was a solid take on the original.  If I had to take a random guess I’d say it feels like they cut out about 30-40% of the original game.  But, they did such a quality job remaking that remaining 60-70%, and they added in cut content from the original plans for 2 which was great.  In a complete 180, Resident Evil 3 Remake is missing like 90% of the original game.  It is extremely linear and short.

[h1]The game skips past or flat out changes multiple things I enjoyed from the original game, such as:[/h1]
	-Player choices causing different outcomes to certain situations, adding replay value.
	-Nemesis used to feel like a threatening pursuer you had to escape from, not an annoying scripted obstacle.  He moves at Mach 9, giving you literally no time to react.  Plus, the levels are so linear at points that there is clearly only one way they want you to go, which Nemesis will often end up blocking.  That was so obnoxious.
	-The man who locks himself in the truck in the beginning of the original game, and coming back later to find he’s turned.  You just run past him in the beginning and never go back there.
	-The bar in the beginning of the game – you can’t even explore it, it’s just in a cutscene.
	-Carlos placing Jill on the altar in the church while he tries to find a way to help her.  This was such an iconic moment in the original that they 100% cut out of this remake, opting for Carlos to bring Jill to a hospital instead.  The whole gravitas of the original moment for me was that Carlos places her on the church altar because it was nearby.  He didn’t have time to bring her somewhere else because he had to act quickly to save her.  The remake completely misses the mark there.  That altar is even in Resident Evil: Operation Raccoon City.  Why wasn’t it in this full blown Remake?  Come on…
	-They had a chance to give Brad more of an important role in the story before he gets infected, but they killed him even faster this time than in the original.  What a waste of his character.
        -Countless puzzles are missing.  RE 2 Remake was missing some puzzles, notably towards the end, but at least the RPD was fully realized.  

[h1]Next up, the stuff I just straight up didn’t like and/or things I thought were done really poorly:[/h1]
	-Way too much action in the beginning.  The game moves way too fast and is completely on-the-rails for far too long.  Just let me play already!  It's a drawn out chase sequence with Nemesis until you get to the Sewers, then it [i]finally[/i] slows down. 
	-I don’t know if this is a bug or what, but frequently if a zombie grabbed me while my health was on “caution,” the game would seemingly enter the “danger” health state while I was doing the qt event to get them off of me, causing them to initiate their death grab animation and kill me.  
       -They removed a great quality of life thing from Resident Evil 2: seeing your health go down when you get grab-attacked.  Why in the world didn’t they keep that?  You can’t bring up your inventory while stunlocked/grappled either, which this game [i]really[/i] needed.
	-The classic style menu asking if you want to pick up an item only appears the first time you pick up a specific kind of item (green herb, handgun ammo, etc).  For successive times picking up the same kind of item, it swaps to a quick-pick mode where as soon as you press A, the item is put into your inventory.  This does not account for accidental button presses, or boss fights where you’re trying to quickly pick up a first aid spray on the ground, but end up picking up the handgun ammo right next to it instead, filling your last inventory slot and causing frustration.  It was likely supposed to make the game feel faster, but it conflicts with the core mechanics the game embodies.
	-Facial animation sync during cutscenes, and multiple animations overall are far worse than in RE2 Remake. 
	-Carlos’s character has been altered so much he's basically a different character.  In the original he was compassionate and a bit dorky.  Now he’s like Mr. Macho man and flirts with Jill [i]constantly[/i].  I was like dude, chill!  They got most of the other characters in 2/3 remake right, but I don't think they did Carlos justice.  He's not a terrible character on his own, but he's not a good reinterpretation of his original version.
	-The writing/dialogue is corny and uninteresting.  There was a cutscene moment where Carlos sees Jill, and despite having a clear view of her (she has not changed her hair or clothes) he asks “Jill, is that you?”  It's written like bad anime.
        - I had a lot of problems with the first phase of the final Nemesis fight.  It’s the one at [spoiler] the end of the game in the umbrella lab where Nemesis runs on the walls in a circle. [/spoiler] I had what seemed like a camera bug where the camera would zoom in and stay that way so Jill took up like a whole third of my screen real estate.  Also, I didn’t realize I could use the tesla coils to fight him off until the loading screen told me.  It definitely felt like something you’re supposed to do for the fight once I learned that information, so why didn’t they make it more clear?  Plus, the zombies spawning in made an already annoying fight really irritating.
	-And finally, the games poor implementation of the original's dodge/evade mechanic.  Not only was putting it on RB a bad decision because in RE2 remake that was the swap ammo type button so I kept accidentally pressing it (why didn’t they just make it LB if they got rid of sub-weapons??), but also the game does not teach you that the dodge will be something necessary in the game later on.  It seems like an optional, situational thing that you could use to avoid zombies who were getting too close, but not something you ever had to rely on.  However, all of a sudden, in the endgame fights you [i][b]have[/b][/i] to use it frequently and your timing has to be [i][b]perfect[/b][/i] for it to work [i][b]at all[/b][/i].  Plus, the audio/visual cues for the attacks you have to dodge are really bad.  If you’re going to give me a fraction of a second to react to an attack, there has to be some kind of clear tell that helps me memorize it so I can be ready.  This was very irritating to me, because I love Soulsborne style games, but I didn’t realize I was supposed to be playing this game as if it was one.  If the game had taught me how to use the dodge, that would be one thing.  But, it doesn’t.  You pretty much never have to use it for the majority of the game, and if I was supposed to be using it more the game did a pretty bad job of making that clear.  I didn't even know Carlos had a punch instead of a dodge until a YouTube reviewer mentioned it.

Overall, Resident Evil 3 Remake doesn’t hold a candle to its source material like Resident Evil 2 Remake did.  It feels rushed and poorly designed, which completely blindsided me.  It lacks a significant amount of content yet still has a $60 price tag.  They had a chance to correct the flaws of the original Resident Evil 3 to make something great, but they messed it up.  They made something inferior, a shell of the game it’s inspired by.  Capcom, please give your studios enough time to do remakes correctly.

Despite its SIGNIFICANT flaws, I do think this one is worth picking up. The key for me was to play through once on Assisted (Easy) mode, to get used to the game mechanics without having to replay the first few stages over and over while I figure out how the hell I'm supposed to play this one.

The bad: difficulty scaling... isn't really a thing in this game. The earliest stages are the hardest ones. Monsters, including bosses, don't get much tougher as you progress through the game, but you do get stronger weapons to blast them with. This is complicated by the fact that aiming with a controller can be unintuitive and frustrating, though I did get the hang of it eventually. The upshot to all this is that if you can make it past the first boss fight, you should be able to complete the game without too much trouble. 

The good: that said, the game looks amazing and the cinematic cut scenes mesh seamlessly with the gameplay. As a big fan of horror movies and novels, this was enough to get me over the imperfect mechanics. It also helps that it isn't a huge time investment; playing through the whole story in under 3 hours is doable, and even newer players can likely do it in under 5. New Game+ options aren't bad, if you like the idea of blitzing through the game with a machine gun with infinite ammo.

It's also worth being aware that, unlike other RE games, this one doesn't really have any puzzles to speak of. At least, nothing more complicated than *combining a tape recorder with a tape*. It's pure shoot-em-up. Whether this is a good or bad thing depends on your preferences, of course.

A survival horror experience set in the Resident Evil universe, you'll be chased by an unstoppable creature.
You play as Agent Jill Valentine (and a second character, at some point), trying to survive a collapsing city under the effect of a strange and horrifying virus.

I enjoyed this game. Finishing it multiple times on the PS4 and now once again on PC, I still had fun with it. Gorgeous graphics, solid voice-acting and great combat. RE3 Remake sets out to be an amazing adventure, but falls a bit short on the puzzles and length. So, if you enjoyed RE2 Remake or you enjoy a solid action/survival/third-person game, this game is a must buy. Though, I'd wait for a sale to compensate with the lack of length and replayability.

In short: REmake 3 is unfaithful and a downgrade to the original game and due to the lack of a severe amount of in game content. it's simply not worth the justification of a full priced AAA game. If you still haven't gotten to play RE3, you're better off playing the 1999 version instead. 

If you still wish to buy this game however, I recommend when it's on sale.

Longer version: After playing this, I wanted to try out the original Resident Evil 3 Nemesis to see how it compares to the REmake, I heard the criticisms and the backlash it first received so I thought it'll be a good try to give it a shot. I realize now, REmake 3 is nothing more than just a cashgrab of the original. 

[h1] What REmake failed to accomplish. [/h1]

To put it short, there is lots of cut content that didn't make it from the original game, Most notably are the mercenaries and civilians are randomly seen throughout the game, an entire explorable location removed and only use as a quick boss fight segment, some crafting elements have been cut, etc. 

The playtime due to this is way too short, I've only beaten the game in just about 6 hours, and I usually would take my time playing the game without having to rush it. The game feels completely linear and too easy, puzzles aren't exactly has challenging and the all the "threats" in the game aren't not as intense compare to the other RE games. 

Speaking of threats, I wanted to talk about Nemesis himself and oh man, he got shafted hard. I hadn't played the 1999 yet, so I never go the chance to see what it's like to against Nemesis, considering the RE community really hyped him in the original due how terrifying he was. However, after REmake 3, it's definitely not the case. The main issue for me was, unlike Mr. X from REmake 2, Nemesis felt and was completely scripted in events you would most likely expect, the chase sequences are not has terrifying compare Mr. X and I even found myself laughing at times where Nemesis felt like a complete pushover and just overall silly play against. 

Although, after playing RE3 1999, Nemesis' presence is very different, while it some occasions it was scripted, he still gets me off guard and overall was actually quite scary. 

[h1] How does the game itself plays? [/h1]

Quite good actually, I love REmake 2 and this game still uses the game mechanics and functions making it a solid gameplay experience. If I would rate based on gameplay and graphics, it would be a 9/10 game. Especially the improvement of no fixed camera angles and tank controls. 

But this does come back as I said earlier about the playtime duration, because this game is very short, you'll won't be able to engage as much it has to offer, even the replayability of it is lacking. In this case, just get REmake 2.

[h1] Closing thoughts [/h1]

I still like this game even though of its issues, it still have some decent things to offer, I love the mod support it has and its community, but I can't for the life of me recommend to people who never got to play RE3, if you don't mind dated looking graphics I heavily recommend getting the original and if you do have the original on PC or plan to get it, you can get the Resident Evil 3 Nemesis: Restoration Project where the game quality is improved and some QOL are added, it works on Modern PCs very well too. 

Other than that, just for a sale on REmake 3 if you do still want this, while the game is short, it's not bad by any means just not as good as the original.

[b]Summary[/b]
This game is not as good as RE:2 and is absolutely not worth $60. But strictly speaking, it's not a bad game either.

[b]The Bad[/b]
[list]
    [*]Nemesis = sad
    [*]Dodging = bad
    [*]Length = short
    [*]Story = Carlos
[/list]

[b]The Good[/b]
[list]
    [*]I mean it's still Resident Evil, and it's a pretty enjoyable one too
[/list]

[b]Nemesis[/b]
Easily the biggest disappointment in this game is that Nemesis is nowhere close to being as fun as Mr. X. Aside from some brief moments near the beginning of the game, Nemesis does not really hunt you across the world, and is basically relegated to being a boss that you fight several times at certain key points in the story. Nearly all of the encounters with him that aren't a boss fight are scripted sequences (ie cutscenes) that involve no decision making, which is quite boring and sad, since Mr.X was easily the most thrilling part of RE:2.

[b]Dodging[/b]
Simply stated, dodging isn't very fun, and is vastly inferior to the system it replaced. RE:2 did something totally ingenious with the "zombie shakeoff" mechanic, where you had to sacrifice a secondary weapon (knife or grenade) to escape a zombie bite. This is totally brilliant because choosing to sacrifice an item rather than take a hit added a lot of strategy and additional tension to the game (survival horror itself is all about the tension of item conservation, after all). Ultimately, I suspect that Capcom removed this system in RE:3 because some players struggled to avoid getting hit in the last game, partly due to the expectation that they could always fight off a zombie whether they had any items or not. Well, I strongly feel Capcom should have doubled down on their old design, rather than revert to the old "tap to escape" system. Resident Evil is most fun when it's about survival horror, not superhuman agility and quick-time powers.

[b]The Length[/b]
This game is indeed pretty short, and while I strongly believe this doesn't make or break any game, it is unfortunately still the primary reason that I can't recommend anyone to spend $60 on it. I hadn't played RE:2 in about two years since I played this one, and I am certainly not an expert, but according to my end-game stats it took me only just over 6 hours to beat the entire game, and only 8 if you include Steam's generous playtime counter. Unlike RE:2, this game has no alternate storylines or side-missions (although, you can unlock special items by replaying the game). To make it worse, certain level designs from this game are wholly recycled from RE:2, which had already exploited all of its levels to death via additional missions and backtracking. In short, there is nowhere close to the amount of content in this game as there is in RE:2.

[b]Carlos[/b]
I could write a ream about how good Leon's story from RE:2 is, while acknowledging that Claire's story is not particularly strong. But this review is about RE:3, and unfortunately, by comparison, none of the characters in RE:3 are memorable or convincing, and the camp value in this game has been kicked up a notch with the addition of Carlos: a fairly brain-dead beefcake who essentially acts as Jill's romantic interest and partner in this game. What little character development he experiences essentially boils down to his discovery that by working for Umbrella, he is working for the Bad Guys (shocker, right?). Jill is equally disappointing, since apparently her personal journey is all about learning to kill people to save lives? But she's already an elite cop, not to mention a survivor of the "Mansion Incident", so that makes very little sense. The game's antagonist has no character at all; he is a Purely Evil hired goon who wants money, and he dies before he can even explain who hired him. Snore.

[b]The Good[/b]
I've spent practically all of this review ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ about the bad bits of this game, so here at the end I'll leave the good bits. Well, what can I say? This game may have no Mr.X, it may have disappointing dodging mechanics, it may be short, and it may be less memorable overall. But in truth, many of the small things that added up to make RE:2 great remain in this thoroughly decent game. When I started playing this game, I was surprised when I quickly found myself enjoying it, and I don't regret spending two afternoons playing it all the way through. The complaints I listed above are certainly serious enough to make this game a major letdown, and I would certainly knock it down 1 or 2 full grades below the masterpiece which came before it. But does this make the game totally bad? Of course not.

Remaking is but a commercial strategy aiming to provoke and reconcile nostalgia of various kinds. In RE's case the original versions were back then prevailing mostly among teenagers, who by now have been grown-ups with sufficient budgets and willingness to go through their childhood experiences once again - the playing of RE franchise included. One basic standard to grade a remade is therefore to what extent it managed to keep the contents while elevating the form. Bluntly this can be discussed from two aspects: Does the remade stir feelings players once had playing the original one? And if so, is the remade presented in an up-to-date acceptable way. 

On the former regard, would say RE3R has done well. Throughout the gaming one can easily recognize many featuring elements of the original version, such as the business man who locked himself in van so as to die of hunger rather than infection, the piano tune played once the character reaches a check point, and the item synthesis system whereby following certain formula two different stuffs synchronized yield a third. Combat logic proves of the same vein as the original’s - no shoot without aiming first. Nice try of the developers to remake outfits and appearances of the protagonists so that they could charge for the classic ones. To me it is not within the scope of DLC but of tax, for most guys driven by the nostalgic incentive would of course expect to see the very acquainted characters dressing in the same costumes. The DLC hence is a tax imposed on gamers who wish to play with characters dressing familiarly. Nice try all in all. The price no high, the outfits nicely done, and thus the charged not too irritated. Modelling of the protagonists are delicate, still there’s a shift of style on Jill’s appearance – from a decisive, oriental female to a much more western and feminine one, presumably compromising with the taste of both west and east. Anyway, it is fancy. 

The second question aforementioned is mainly about graphics. Particle effect (flame for instance) and water look a little bit of weak, and all the other aspects quite good. This secures the game’s status as an up-to-date acceptable product. 

Content preservation and acceptable form together make a remade of average standard. To achieve excellence there need to be things which have quality beyond players’ anticipation, and it better be something core to the original. Under RE3R’s circumstance that points to the modelling of protagonists, especially Jill’s, which is, from the perspective of either community or personal feeling, indeed a success. This alone suffices to justify the remade a constructive one.

In summary, RE3R is nicely done, genetically homogeneous with its prototype, and graphically out of expectation.

As someone who is a long time RE fan, watched all their films as well as played most of their games. I would really give a big round of applause to the development team. 

I never understood where the hate is coming from. I see most people would compare this to RE 2 remake and complain how short this game is and the lack of mercenary mode make it looks like a complete rip off. I would somehow agree that not having bonus mode ( other than resistance ) make this game lackluster but I don't think it's inferior to RE2 in any way. 

This game introduces dodge mechanic which allows player to quickly dash through places and complete key quest of the game quickly. But that was not the original intention of this mechanism, it's meant to avoid danger. Not sprint through the game. 

If people would take their time to explore every single details of this game, you would see how magnificent and beautiful it is. 

The main enemy in this game - Nemesis, is also known as pursuer. Nemesis, in its literal meaning, means the arch enemy of someone. Greatest of them all. I think the design of nemesis fits this term itself. From the beginning it will stalk you all the time and constantly evolving to give hell to players. Experience the real fight by playing inferno mode. You won't feel the real challenge if you play it on standard as bullet is in abundance. 

In terms of character design and dialogue, I feel that it's really genuine and well designed. Jill never believe in Carlos in the beginning but seeing how their relationship improves over time really gives you the chill. It's really well done. 

If there's one thing I would improve in this game, is perhaps when Jill gets infected by the T-virus. If you read the comic, when Jill gets infected, she actually find herself back in the mansion facing all the enemy. Plant 47, yawn etc. This would be awesome if the dev team could just add part of this into the game itself. That would really make the game so much more complete. 

Another thing that I would improve is adding multiple endings to the game. Nothing too different as I dont want to cause  the dev team any extra work. But making a few small tweak is fine, for example, if you don't shoot nicholai in time, Carlos could die but Jill shoots Nicholai right back, ending the game. So that's a different ending. Of course it's just an example. 

All and all, I would give this game a 9/10. Really well done. It's not a complete perfect game, but it's hell of a game. Would recommend it any day.

This is a hard one to talk about. Coming off of REmake 2, I could feel a similar passion buried deep in this game. They wanted to make it fun and, if they were given the time and resources, would've made it fun. There were ideas to let you explore Raccoon City here and reward you for going out of your way, much like exploring RPD in REmake 2. The entire Power Station segment proves that they know how to create thrilling moments. Heck, they even made me like Carlos a little, a character I sincerely could've done without in the original game. I want to love this game, I really do, but the things it does right aren't enough to balance out what it does wrong: the anemic replay value, cut content from the original game, the removal of Live Selections and the feeling that the best part of the game is the first third of it. Once you're into the sewers, you're basically in the lesser parts of the game. Not terrible, but not as great as the first part.

Even if a particular segment in the hospital is made a million times better by looping Bonnie Tyler's I Need A Hero through it.

And that's the hardest part. What R3make does wrong isn't necessarily its own fault. Anyone who reads the Steam page may find it suspicious that this remake is bundled with a 4v1 multiplayer game "for free". Even more suspicious is the fact that REsistance still gets (or got, I haven't checked recently) updates while R3make got...nothing. A soundtrack and five dollars to unlock all the bonuses from the store. The game Capcom really wanted to make here was not the game the fans wanted. As much as I say I enjoyed R3make when I first beat it, the slow realization of what I really played through crawled up into my mind and makes this potential-filled game the disappointment it is: Resident Evil 3 should've been the main attraction, but it was treated as the side show. 

And here I thought Paul W.S. Anderson treated Jill with disrespect, but between zero mention of her after RE5 and this, Capcom might've done worse than him. Don't buy this game; just play REmake 2 again.

For the gameplay, it plays similar to RE2 but the focus is definitely more on the combat and numerous boss fights against the Nemesis, which is IMO its weakest part.

The scripted escape runs from Nemesis are annoying and the boss fights are problematic because the ways to kill the boss are not all that intuitive. The game gives a general hint as to how to kill the boss, but in practice, following that hint requires very specific weapons or even very specific ammo, used in a very specific way, which is not always obvious. I spent way too many attempts unloading enough ammunition to kill the boss 20x over, yet it refusing to die because I didn't trigger that one specific cutscene where it would take like 10x more damage out of nowhere. There's also way too much reliance on timing your dodges accurately to avoid powerful boss attacks which can chain-stun you and basically kill you without any counterplay if you failed the first dodge.

But other than the boss fights, the game is very similar to RE2. Exploring a bit of the city, taking out the occasional zombies and learning more about the lore is enjoyable.

I wouldn't recommend paying full price for the Single Player story alone though. Grab the game on a sale. 7 hours of game time is not worth $60.

It's pretty, it plays well mechanically, but the original game feels lost in this remake. 
As with the RE2 Remake, the models representing the main characters have strayed too far from the originals for my taste, and the unlockables feel too grindy.

The challenges make the game feel like a series of segments rather than a fluent game. It sounds weird, but I feel like hidden criterias suit horror games better, because they tend to feel quite arcadey otherwise.
Resident Evil 4 did this perfectly in my opinion, because you didn't expect unlocking the handcannon from attaining an S-rank on every Mercenary map, but you did, and it was unironically one of the most exciting moments I've had in a video game.
Being presented with every goal in the game at once and knowing there's nothing beyond that spoils a lot of the fun for me.

TL;DR, it was a fun & pretty game, and I would give it a 5/10, but I was also immeasurably disappointed, and my day was ruined.

This game has many upsides and many downsides; more downsides than upsides.
It clearly lives in the shadow of Resident Evil 2 Remake, and makes many downgrades to design along the way.

While I do think the story, cinematics, and encounters are fantastic: the level design lacking in comparison to the game before it. Part of RE2R's charm was that it didn't take control from you in what you needed to do or needed to go, and while RE3R [b][i]tries[/i][/b] not to do that, it does it far too often by limiting where you need to go to OVERLY limited and narrow paths that pale to the RPD Station from RE2R.

I'm more often thinking: "Am I about to be in extreme danger by turning this corner?"
and not even because of Nemesis, but because of the terrible back-steps in common enemy and level design.

[u][b]Warning: [/b] Heated Rant About Enemy Combat[/u]
The zombies in RE2R are predictable but not in a bad way; I guess Capcom thought they were?
Their solution: Make zombies EVEN MORE resiliant to bullets than they were before.
If you haven't played RE2R, I'll make it short: zombies often ATE bullets for lunch. I've literally had to RELOAD on them to keep them down [i][u]and they still don't die most of the time[/u].[/i] Making any worse than it already was effectively makes them bullet sponges. The worst part of it is: it doesn't even stop there. Zombies ALSO don't react to being shot, so thanks to the [i]almost always[/i] tiny areas that you find yourself in (which says a lot considering that RE2R took this into consideration), you're incredibly likely to get cornered and then bit because [i]there is no defense mechanism in place to prevent it[/i] after RE2R already takes under consideration that this is a very possibly scenario. I get that RE3R probably didn't have the disposable knives that RE2R had [i]but this is a remake for a reason.[/i] If you're going to to buff the zombies beyond what even makes sense for a zombie game, at least have the decency to give the player a fair way to combat it. Mashing A with next to no perceivable benefit just because it was decided to give the player the ability to dodge or punch in select scenarios [i][b]does not make up for it.[/b][/i] You're far more likely to get chain-grabbed than effectively get out of it when everything is taken into account.

[u][b]Rant Over[/b][/u]
That said, the [i][b]open nature[/b][/i] of RE2R's level design is what puts the world into the player's hands rather than forcing them to what can feel like: "push W or up left-stick to beat game."

I can't even remember a single puzzle in the entirity of the game, which is strange, considering the age of RE games we're talking about. It honestly felt more like a frustrating interactive movie than a zombie-horror survival, which RE2R somewhat leaves the impression of. RE2R doesn't try to be difficult by putting bullet sponges in your path, it's difficult because there are enemies [b][i]on the way to actual difficulties.[/i][/b] Thus, RE3R's difficulties are artificial rather than natural.

[b][u]CONCLUSION[/u]: [/b]
It's a good game to play once, but I honestly can't see myself ever playing it again, because it just took everything I loved about RE2R and threw it out the window.
Definitely not worth $60.

And don't even get me started on this game's pistols compared to the last one's: [i]they're trash.[/i]

Resident Evil 3 (1999) is and always will be my favorite Resident Evil game, and it's the first one we (me and my siblings) played when we were young, scared us senseless back then what with all that Nemesis chasing you around in a creepy infested city. 

This remake does bring back a lot of what was there in the original - the atmosphere and the monsters are still as eerie as ever, while improving on a lot of things like ofcourse the visuals and audio, cutscenes and characters etc, and then offer some new experiences with a faster paced over-the-shoulder gameplay. It's a really good game on it's own, but as it's a remake, we can't leave out the obvious - the missing pieces. The developers notoriously cut corners for some odd reason (maybe due to time constraints), they chose to remove two entire areas, several different Nemesis encounters, puzzles, a boss fight, a different ending and even an extra mini-game which had huge replayability value, these were elements that made the original such a fan favorite, this decision was really disappointing as it shortened the game by several hours. Given how good the game is at this state, those missing pieces would've made this a masterpiece.

Although it's a really botched remake, what we got here is still a really good game albeit a short one. If you played the original, and/or Resident Evil 2 remake, or any Resident Evil game in general, then you should definitely try this, the action alone is worth playing.

I feel like Resident Evil 3 remake (R3make from here on) is like if you took the RE2 remake and mixed it with the action and pace of RE4 or RE5, you would get R3make. It's pretty good if you understand that and expect that. It's certainly not as good as the original Resident Evil 3 on PSX, but if you like silly action it's great.

The problem is that the original RE3 made Nemesis an ever-present threat that could appear at any time. RE3 also originally had moments where you could choose what action to take, and they would actually impact the story and what would happen next. None of that appears in the R3make. If you enjoyed the tension, art direction, and soundtrack of the RE2 remake, you will not be disappointed in this as long as you temper your expectations. You can tell that the creators of R3make looked at the original PSX RE3 and recognized that RE3 was a more action-oriented game than RE2 was, and thought that was what players would like to see expanded upon and enhanced in the RE3 Remake. While that was true of the PSX RE3, it certainly wasn't the thing that made people love that one. RE3 was always more of a side-story than a mainline game (despite the number) and so it was the changes to the core gameplay with the choices and the looming Nemesis threat that really made it stand out. Not the action. That said, R3make is still a fun mindless action game, and if you go into it with that expectation, you will not be disappointed.

With such an explosive first hour, one may think it's set will blow its predecessor away. In a disappointing twist of irony it manages to reverse much of what made the previous game great and over-does almost everything along the way. First though, to give much due credit, the detail and work done on everything graphics is stunning, a luxury for my eyes. I am aware this is a remake which likely constrained the rather weak plot, but issues go far beyond that; this is a completely new game two decades later. The problems begin with the audio that seem to not be just a me problem. The bass on gunshots is weak, feedback of hits don't have impact, voices are sometimes hushed and Nicholai's voice actor is pretty bad. The previous game's difficulty could be felt where here the game makes sure you can't lose. This is of course besides the boss fights where the movement is painfully slow and no matter how many times you press dodge your character will just eat a hit. It may be just a preference but the puzzles seemed to lack content, feeling more like a jigsaw than a rubix cube, requiring brain activation. The overlapping plot with the previous game is very welcome but what isn't are some strange holes, awkward decision making and clique moments. To give one more comparison, it is two thirds the length of the previous game, but feels longer, has more cuts scenes, and doesn't have a second story line. I know the reason for this is the development largely going toward the over-the-top cinematics that might look great but you don't control it. Towards the end they commit the sin of bad quick-time-events and cut scenes are either noticeably sloppy or over done. Unfortunately the badass factor couldn't sell me here, the insane action moments can't top the simplicity and beauty of the last game.

I'm not one of those gamers who enjoys ticking off every singe check point on the map; sure, I did it for the Witcher 3, but very few games are able to maintain the Witcher's level of quality after sixty plus hours (Cyberpunk 2077 apparently failed in that regard). So if a survival zombie action game thrills me while only taking about a week or two to play (I game about 40 minutes to an hour five days a week roughly), that's great. That being said, I think RE 3 would have benefited from some expanded sections. The opening stage in downtown Raccoon city begs for more areas to explore. Still, the relative brevity of RE 3 improves its schlocky narrative (it's good schlock, though) because it really feels like Jill Valentine and Carlos (your two player characters) are in a race against time. There's no fiddling around collecting cosmetic items or beating frivolous challenges; this is a story-driven action game, with a big game zombie called Nemesis frequently poking his hideous head into your business like a classic horror villain who just refuses to die. I do think he loses some of his effectiveness after he mutates into a bestial fleshy xenomorph, but he's a constant presence, although you'll always know when he's about to drop, due to the level design opening up and filler enemies clearing out (with the one exception of the downtown stage). An impressive amount of terrible creatures are out to eat Jill (and Carlos), including nasty rape spiders that ram parasites down Jill's throat (gee, I wonder where they cribbed that trope?) and pale naked zombies that resemble the monster from Pan's Labyrinth. Jill, a former Raccoon City cop who's on the run from Nemesis, looks almost lifelike; indeed, it's more than a little disturbing to watch her get thrown and beaten by the aforementioned beasties. We're approaching real-life fidelity in games, and certain questions are raised when your abused protagonist actually resembles a living human being and not a bunch of pixels. So is RE 3 torture porn? I don't think so, but Carlos, a hunky special ops soldier with ridiculous hair, never gets a mutant proboscis shoved down his throat. All that being said, RE 3's mix of bullet scrounging, awkward controls (both Jill and Carlos move like they're drunk), and light puzzle solving makes a tense, tight action game that I recommend, if you can get it for about twenty or thirty bucks. Apparently, this is a much condensed remake, and several sections were cut from the original game, but if you care about that, then you probably know already whether or not this game is for you.

“Resident Evil 3: Nemesis” embraced the survival horror elements of its predecessor while shifting its focus onto an action packed experience, resulting in an exhilarating campaign that added plenty of new ideas to the RE franchise. This game however, is “Resident Evil 3” the modern remake that fails to capture the magic of both the original game and the franchise it belongs to. RE3 is a lacking remake, but even without that context and standing on its own legs, the game fails to be a particularly enjoyable or memorable experience, making it hard to recommend playing it.

[h1] Returning from RE2 [/h1]
The greatest strengths of RE3 are almost entirely owed to Resident Evil 2’s Remake. The outstandingly detailed world is back and pushes the RE Engine to the max, with large intricately detailed areas populated with the same insanely elaborate zombies appearing in a much higher quantity, all of which still dynamically fall apart in response to your actions. This game is a graphical achievement and never fails to look stunning. 

The traditional RE gameplay returns here too, although it’s implementation isn’t quite as strong as prior entries. The same focus on inventory management returns to deal with the bigger threat, although with a greater emphasis on character switching and linear environments, the survival elements don’t feel nearly as fleshed out. Exploration and resource management take a back seat, leaving a lot of moments to feel like nothing more than a generic shooter.

The new mechanic on the block is the dodge function, and it’s kind of a mixed bag. On one hand, dodging an attack feels amazing to pull off in a tight situation, providing levity in the game’s higher enemy count than most RE titles. On the other hand, dodging becomes far too reliable compared to the standard evasion in other RE titles and often mitigates dangers too heavily. It’s also used poorly in boss fights, basically required for higher difficulties in which you have to pull off multiple dodges in succession to survive, resulting in uninteresting fights that rely too heavily on precise execution from the player. RE3 does have it’s occasional charm, but most of these moments are overshadowed by RE2’s more interesting and far stronger execution of the same ideas. 

[h1] A Mediocre Campaign [/h1]
The content original to Resident Evil 3 feels lacking to say the least. 3’s approach to level design was far more linear than the series had seen before, but composing the game of shorter open sections as opposed to the singular massive area still allowed for plenty of strategy and resource management. 

The remake gets this right sometimes. The opening town section, although massively shrunken from its original counterpart, is probably the best display of slowly uncovering more of a map while having to deal with the precarious amounts of enemies in constricted space. Exploring the town feels great, you barely get a glimpse at Raccoon City in RE2, so having the freedom of navigating the city streets is refreshing and I really wish this area had taken up more of the game. The hospital section later on, also fills these requirements, providing a short but decently open section that feels very standalone from the remainder of the campaign. 

The rest of the areas that tie RE3 together are completely forgettable, the multiple sewers and [spoiler] the returning police station [/spoiler] are extremely straight forward, providing no variety for player freedom like the other areas do. Areas are also often capped off with atrocious boss fights that employ frustrating gimmicks or constant dodging on top of suffering from the traditional RE problems of being slow, high health enemies that take far too long to kill. 

All of these faults are prominent within the finale,  a very bland location that provides nothing new to the series that’s just a pain to navigate and features some of the most boring bosses I’ve ever faced. These issues combined with the campaign's extremely short length really hurt replayability, as there are so few moments to enjoy compared to what will play out almost exactly the same every time. The shop that lets you start runs with different items is a nice touch, but it doesn’t save the campaign as a whole.

I left RE3 with no desire to return to it. With the few hours I got out of it only providing joy on the rare occasion, I didn’t see the point in suffering through the worst parts of the games to access those moments again.

[h1] Cut Content & The Nemesis [/h1]
It’s unsurprising “Nemesis” has been removed from the game’s title, considering the enemy no longer has that drastic impact on gameplay he once possessed. Nemesis starts off pretty great as basically an enhanced Mr.X. He moves faster and employs more attacks to catch you off guard, he’s an amazingly threatening presence for the game’s first couple hours as he shows up from nowhere to torment you.

Unfortunately after a couple major encounters with him, he’s shelved almost exclusively for set piece moments that lack the tension or fun his moments in an open world had. What made Nemesis so fun in the original is how he kept reappearing as a constant threat over and over again. These appearances may have been scripted, but his harassment through the campaign gave you a constant sense of unease as they were pretty unpredictable on a first playthrough. 

The option of fight or flight in the original gave the campaign a lot more variety too, as both responses provided rewards of unique items or more resources respectively. Nemesis in his current iteration starts off amazingly, but quickly devolves into a boring mechanic that’s constrained by the game’s design. Nemesis really needed to be better if they wanted to save this already lacklustre campaign.

I don’t think RE3 needs to be defined by the game it’s remaking, but notice needs to be paid to the insane amount of cut content. Multiple significant areas such as the park, parts of the town, the clock tower and the factory have been either removed entirely or replaced with boring counterparts. Many enemy types are no longer returning too, which I don’t think is as bad, but definitely adds onto the existing feeling of what's missing.

The biggest cut to me is the “Live Choice” system, which gave you 2 options to choose from in many intense parts of the story, I cannot believed they removed this. What provided variety (and strategy in later playthroughs) to the campaign has been completely deleted with no counterpart to replace it. It wasn’t a complicated system at all but it added so much to the game and I cannot justify any reason to delete it other than a lack of development time.

The features that made the original RE3 stand out from other titles in the series are either downgraded or completely removed here. As it stands, there’s really nothing unique about this entry.

[h1]4/10[/h1]

Resident Evil 3 is an uninteresting game by its own merit, but it becomes especially disappointing compared to its predecessor. The botch job done here leaves me wishing for easier access to the original, and leaves me very concerned about the RE4 Remake. I’d only recommend this if you really want some more of RE2 specifically, but otherwise I’d give it a pass.

With Resident Evil Village just around the corner I decided to go back and play Resident Evil 3, a game that I missed at launch. I have played nearly every main line Resident Evil game but somehow, I skipped both the Resident Evil 3 Remake and the original Resident Evil Nemesis. I have enjoyed this series immensely and have been really amazed at how well they have transitioned out of the weak middle years of Resident 5 and 6 to create some amazing new games in Resident Evil 7 and the Resident Evil 2 Remake. 

Resident Evil 3 takes place concurrently with the events of Resident Evil 2 though you see the city from a different perspective. That of Jill Valentine and Carlos Olivera. Jill is simply trying to escape the city and expose Umbrella as the cause of the outbreak while Carlos is an Umbrella employee with mysterious motives. Unfortunately, this remake does not quite live up to the high bar set by its predecessor.

It is quite a bit shorter than Resident Evil 2, which was already a short game and my playthrough took around six hours. A single playthrough of Resident Evil 2 by comparison was around 8 hours and the game gave you incentive to playthrough multiple times. 

The game also feels considerably more streamlined. It lacks much of the exploration and backtracking that made the police station so much fun in the previous game. While the city streets are interesting the locations are limited, and it feels much more on rails like the game is holding your hand. You even visit several of the same locations but in a much more truncated and limited fashion. An already short game has about a third of its run time spent on existing locations.

The expected enemies all show up, zombies, lickers, and hunters but the biggest and most constant threat is the Nemesis. This giant tyrant like monster is present through much of the game and makes up nearly every boss fight of the game. While it does not chase you for long periods of time like Mr. X in the previous game, it does show up frequently and provides some exciting set pieces. I did find several of the boss fights against the Nemesis easy and overly long and I wish the game had a bit more diversity in these fights.

If you have played the Resident Evil 2 remake the gameplay is nearly identical here with just a few small tweaks. You have a dodge move now which is useful for evading the weaker enemies and makes boss fights that much easier. The selection of weapons is good and how they are divided between the characters makes sense, but you get a ton of ammo and supplies, and the game starts to veer more into action game territory and away from survival horror. There is also a multiplayer component that plays like a cross of Resident Evil and Left 4 Dead, but I did not enjoy it that much and only played a few rounds.

The graphics are quite good, though much of it is ripped right out of its predecessor. The performance is spectacular, with my RTX 3080 and i7 10700k I was able to run the game at 3440x1440 with every setting maxed out and maintain a constant 144 FPS. The sound and music are also both quite effective at create a scary and tense atmosphere.

Overall, this is an enjoyable entry in the series but the lack of content and depth and how similar it is to the previous game make it difficult to recommend at full price. Luckily, this game can be found on sale frequently for $20 and at that price I think it is worth checking out especially if you are a fan of the series looking for more.

In RE3, I really felt like this was just a cash grab Capcom thought fans would rush to get after seeing the success of the RE2 remake. The puzzles seemed very similar to RE2 (can't really fault the devs for this since I realize some game series have signature puzzles). The story seemed a bit rushed, with not a lot of backstory if you were to take this game as a standalone game. I never really understand why Nemesis was after Jill, other than some photos and dialogue hinting as a backstory. Graphically, I was able to run the game at max settings with 150% rendering, which made the game look really good, especially during cutscenes. Character models and animations also felt very well polished with little to no noticable errors. Also, I'll admit it, Jill was smokin hot, but her voice actor did a good job portraying her character. All in all, I can't recommend this game because of its short length and lack of replayability, but above all, because it feels like a blatant cash grab for very little work.

Wanted to get thru most of the difficulty modifiers before posting. This game is unfortunate in several ways. First is replayability. It is so linear with next to no variations (some different item locations on the higher difficulties but no layout differences). There aren't any changes to cut scenes, and there just doesn't seem to be a reason to go back to periodically replay, which I can easily do with the good Resident Evil titles. 

This transitions into the second problem, which is value/amount of content. There are no bonus game modes, just the story. I had a very good time with RE2 remake, and mentioned in my review that this game could be a good DLC. That is the only way I would have given this a pass, was if it was a DLC for the RE2 game, because as far as I am concerned, it is just a 2 hour campaign that ranges from so easy that you feel like the Nemesis to so infuriatingly hard with countless necessary garbage perfect dodges and lack of resources that the infinite weapons (which it does not punish you for using) become mandatory, unless you are Carcinogen. My respect to you lunatics that S ranked Inferno without Infinite weapons or combat modifiers. 

Third is how gutted this feels compared to the original. RE3: Nemesis was never my favorite game of the series, but I respected the decision moments, the ability to strategically avoid fights, and the PACING of the game. None of that is here. Characters and the Nemesis are all introduced in the first 10 minutes of the game. Brad's death is now slow and off screen, a complete waste compared to how it was utilized in the original. All that is left is a bare-bones story flying at 200 mph that doesn't leave much of an impression.

Last, and most important, is Nemesis. There is one 10 minute sequence where Nemesis is not a scripted encounter in the game. All other instances are scripted runaway sequences with instant fail modes, or boss fights. The boss fights themselves do a decent job of escalation. I personally felt the last fight was unnecessary and on the harder difficulties was a garbage frame-perfect dodging mess. Seriously whomever decided that last fight needed that many insta-fail quick dodges really needs to play test it and ask: IS THIS FUN AT ALL? During the unscripted 10(ish) minute section in the streets, there is really only one question: do you have two or three grenades? If you do, that section is a easy. If you don't get ready for Nemesis to drop out of the sky (literally) right behind you, constantly. What made Mister X good in the RE2 remake was that it never felt like pursuit continuity was broken. Was it perfect? No. But if he went thru a door on the first floor and you were up on the third floor he didn't magically kick the door open behind you one second later because line-of-sight was broken. That is the one unscripted sequence of this game. If Nemesis isn't stunned, and line-of-sight is broken, get ready for shenanigans. That is, in my mind, bad programming. 

Were there good parts to the game? Sure. I liked the hospital sequence. I liked the second-to-last Nemesis fight. I liked the power station bug nest sequence. Are these enough to recommend the game? No. If you buy, do it at a discount. This game shouldn't cost more than good DLC.

This is a great standalone experience that is sadly ruined by wasted potential, cut content and multiple endings.

If you have never played the OG RE3, you wont notice those things or even care about them, but you will notice how short the game actually is, it takes you around 4 hours to complete the campaign, and thats basically 95% of what this game has to offer, it has little to no replay value and the game doesnt have multiple endings like RE2 Remake.

So before I even review the game for what it is, I have to tell you that its not worth 60$, especially for people in poorer countries, grab it on g2a or somewhere for 15$ or less, because to be fair thats how much this game is worth.

The game itself is a lot of fun. It takes a more action oriented approach as opposed to previous RE installments which were more focused on survival horror aspect of the game, which is not everyones cup of tea.

The game is placed in different locations in Racoon city, including the police station from RE2, but its not that big of a deal since you wont spend too much time in it regardless.

In basically every area you will face Nemesis and different opponents that pose a threat, with each and every Nemesis encounter providing a different challenge to overcome. 

The main issue I have with Nemesis in this game is that he just doesnt feel scary for some reason. Wherever he attacked it almost felt like a puzzle to be solved (with which weapon should I take him down with), instead of a fear that should be overcome.

The story is pretty simple and straightforward and I feel like this game does a pretty good job in telling it, primarily because it has a lot of cutscenes and cinematics in it, which some people like.

In terms of game mechanics and the gameplay itself, its basically the same game as RE2 Remake, with minor differences.

So if you liked RE2, chances are you will also like this game, but before you buy, make sure you know what you are getting for your money, and that is a very short game with little to no replay value.

Overall, I will give this game a positive rating because it was mostly an enjoyable experience for me, but I completely understand other complaints and arguments against it.

Like Resident Evil 2, I didn't play Resident Evil 3 when I was growing up, so I kinda missed out on the original "unholy trinity" of Resident Evil games. But this new remake of RE3 is an absolute delight - gorgeous graphics, cool story (very over the top at times, but so much fun), and very relevant themes (a need for a vaccination, distrust of authority). It also continues the story of Jill Valentine, one of the key characters from the first game. I admit I couldn't get into the first Resident Evil game, from the tank controls to the weird camera angles to the hammy dialogue, but RE2 and 3 are more my cup of tea. In fact, in many ways RE3 improves on RE2, minimizing the frustrating puzzles and providing a more action-oriented gameplay experience, which we continue to see in later games and incarnations of the series. And boy, is Nemesis something ("STAAARS") - he makes Mr. X in RE2 look like a walk in the park. He looks like a Clive Barker Cenobite (the Chatterer) but acts like the Terminator, a seemingly unstoppable superhuman bioweapon, and within the first five minutes, you're in the thrilling heat of what continues for most of the game. The chase scenes with Nemesis, which are usually scripted, actually didn't terrify me as much as I thought, but they are thrilling and get the adrenaline going (those sewer toad things scared the hell out of me though lol). The game is also a sequel and prequel to RE2 of sorts, featuring (another) revisit to Raccoon City's infamous police station (it's never a good idea). It shows a bit more of what happened to Brad Vickers from RE1 and Marvin's backstory from RE2. While RE3's more open-world exploration is not as frightening as RE2's survival horror (or their best game RE7's), it makes for a much more fun and engaging game. As per usual, Umbrella Corporation is the poster child for corporate corruption and insidiousness, and perhaps a critique of late stage capitalism in their exploitation of labour and resources. The endgame also features a search for a vaccine, which I felt was quite timely and relevant given our current situation. The search for the vaccine is not only an important quest-narrative within the game, but it also raises questions of ethical distribution and uses. Our engagement and interactivity with the vaccination process as Jill, particularly in the wake of a city plagued with the zombie pandemic, is crucial, and I think it affirms our own connection to the success of a vaccine and believing in its possibilities. Unfortunately, my game was buggy towards the end and thus I'm unable to finish the game, but wow, what a great game and definitely one of my favourite Resident Evil games to date. RE3 is a buried treasure, and this remake is especially worth seeking out. On a side note, I wonder too if Nemesis embodies the persistence and invasiveness of a pandemic infection? Just thinking about how he mutates and persistently stalks Jill Valentine through most of the game.

- Enemy placement and behaviors also don't change. They just become more spongy and hit harder. And with wonky hit detection on several enemies, getting one-shot can lead to pure frustration.

All in all, it feels like playing a remaster of an old game with a few modern twists than a remake. And with only 3 infinite guns to unlock (pistol, assault rifle, rocket launcher), there aren't many good reasons to replay the game.

Resistance? What Resistance? I'd be happier if they'd taken Resistance back and given me infinite grenade launcher instead.

So, I recommend this game, but only if you catch it on deep sale, maybe at 60% off or more.

Complete and utter disappointment. When it comes to re-telling the story, RE3 gets shafted everytime, just look at the RE3 re-telling in the Umbrella Chronicles game. Well, RE3 gets shafted again, after the masterpiece that was Resident Evil 2 remake. That game's antagonist, Mr. X, opened a world of possibilities to make Nemesis the unescapable threat that he was in the original Resident Evil 3 game; a relentless pursuer who wouldn't give you a moment to breathe unless you found a save room or managed to knock him down. Unfortunately, he's pathetic in this game.

First of all, his appearances are scripted, only at a certain point will he actually chase you and that's barely for a third of the game. It's like the game blew its load right at the beginning, no build up, no suspense, Nemesis attacks Jill in her appartment right at the beginning. Cue a little chase scene in the apartment building then you're out in the streets. When finally the game begins to feel like its classic counterparts, it all crumbles when you discover that a single hand grenade will knock Nemesis out cold. No difficult battle that costs you lots of resources just to have a breather, you throw a single grenade and he's down and you get an item. Sure, he comes back later but for a while, you can practically erase it from the game until a script brings him back. Really. They reduced the series' most iconic monster from a relentless, indestructible pursuer to a pushover that won't bother you for a while after a single grenade. Disappointing.

And once he transforms, he's relegated to a generic scripted boss monster who appears for gimmicky boss fights. Avoid his attacks, use explosives, stick a mine on his path when he starts running on the walls. Later on, the exact same boss fight but in a different environment, plus zombies. And finally he becomes a huge mass of flesh with glowy weak spots, which you shoot to stun him so you can reactivate generators to charge up the rail gun. Just like that, the great Nemesis becomes just another obstacle, Birkin wasn't even the star of the show in RE2 and he still had more interesting encounters than Nemesis did.

I could go on about the rest of the game but it's nothing special. Find keys, manages ammo, do some ridiculously easy puzzles and so on. The monsters are fine but not very impressive, the Cerberus make an occasional appearance but sometimes you forget they are in the game. Hunter Gamma is now just a big, lumbering monster that can eat you but are easy to kill, if a bit tanky, regular Hunters now have some kind of face protection which you must destroy before you can do headshots. Drain Deimos are only there for a negligible portion of the game and sadly, the Gravedigger doesn't even make an appearance. And Capcom even recycled RE2's Pale Heads for the later parts of the game, which are nothing more than tougher zombies.

Overall, it feels like little budget and efforts have been put on what should've been a great remake of a fondly-remembered entry in the Resident Evil franchise, RE2 had set the bar high for remakes and the fanbase's expectations were soaring to the heavens but what we got is a short, uninspired adventure that does little to live up to its classic counterpart's name. Capcom wanted once again to put ressources on a multiplayer game nobody asked for inn the form of RE Resistance which, I admit, have not played and don't intend to. RE2 Remake could -without the nostalgia glasses- considered a better version of a classic survival-horror experience but in the case of Resident Evil 3, stick to the classic. And take a look at my playtime: That's how long my first playthrough took and I had no reason to replay this. Only get this if it's on sale, you're not getting a bang for your buck and it doesn't deserve to be played for much more than curiosity.

While this is a good game it is not a true remake of Resident Evil 3: Nemesis. Some key differences and other weaknesses specific to this game are:


[b]- Focus on Action:[/b] More action packed than RE2:Remake and doesn't even comes close to the original RE3's survival horror gameplay, ammo and herbs are very abundant. 

[b]- Short Playtime:[/b] I finished RE2 Remake in about 8 hours, finished this one under 5, and I was combing the environment from top to bottom while playing both games.

[b]-Missing Content From the Original:[/b] Smaller city section, no restaurant where you had to make a choice when Nemesis shows up ( decision system has been removed as well ), no factory, no Raccoon park, no clock tower and Giant Spiders that housed them, no Gravedigger boss and some other minor omissions.

[b]-Lack of Puzzles:[/b] I counted two "puzzles" in this game, one is extremely easy and the other can be brute-forced with ease. There is one more but I don't count "inserting three items to their three slots" a puzzle.

[b]-Mistreatement of Nemesis:[/b] In the original, Nemesis didn't show up immediately but when he did, it definitely made the player feel helpless. You had ammo and herb shortages constantly and it was generally not a viable option to take down Nemesis. He could stalk the player throughout different sections, attack from everywhere anytime. In the remake, Nemesis shows up immediately, you run away from him in a very scripted section and then he disappears. He then shows up a couple of more times and after a boss-fight he mutates, this takes place two hours at max. The early mutation makes him lose his iconic look very early and instead you spend the rest of the game dealing with his new, Xenomorph looking form. Also, no one seems to afraid of him in this game, Jill constantly makes fun of him and taunts every chance she gets. I am also not a fan of his new look. He has a very slim waist, wears trash bags and has a weird looking nose. "The nose makes him look more human!" arguement made whenever someone criticizes his new look is a tired quote used by unimaginative people that can't come up with their own defense regarding the design.

[b]-Jill's Personality:[/b] Jill is somewhat unlikable in this game. She swears like a sailor and tries to act tough in weird situations. The writers failed to make a believable and grounded tough character and instead make her spew one-liners hoping those would stick.

[b]-Writing:[/b] Compared to the original the writing seems very childish in Remake. Nearly every note has a cynical tone to them, something that was also present in RE2: Remake. Everyone swears a lot and act like action heroes. Jill calls Nemesis a ♥♥♥♥♥ in one encounter, instead of acknowledging the direness of the situation. Makes the tone shift constantly.

[b]-No Ink Ribbons:[/b] There are no ink ribbons in the game, even on Hardcore mode. They should have at least been exclusive to the Hardcore mode, just like RE2: Remake.


After all these criticism why am I recommending this game? Because, while it is not a good Resident Evil 3 remake, it is a good Resident Evil game. I love both classic and modern RE games and this one is another quality modern style title that is worth playing. If you are looking for a faithful remake of the original, you will be disappointed, if you view this as another modern RE title, you will enjoy it.
