Obviously this is a mechanically good game. It builds pretty effortlessly off of the redesigns the series saw during the "Revelations" games. Still more actiony than they used to be but with enough tension and skill required that - on harder difficulties - you'll be fairly puckered on a playthrough.

While I do recommend it, there is one glaring fault here: the length. There is FAR too much cut content of the original Resident Evil 3 for it to go unnoticed. The clocktower portion is just a... weird, samey bossfight with Nemesis cosplaying a licker for all intents and purposes. Where the Resident Evil 2 really brought the gasoline to the car to keep Resident Evil going and allowed for a phenomenal remake, I feel like this one has far too much cut content and diminished character interactions and a severely crippled gameplay length to be worth $60. $40 would be more appropriate.

For those who like replayability, there is a substantial point system involving items and costumes - including Jill and Carlos' old outfights and weapons such as Jill's fairly iconic (I know) Beretta 92. A must-have for anyone who can't stomach the sight of some generic little glock in Miss Sandwich's strong hands. It does also come with a half-baked Dead By Daylight style 1x4 multiplayer mode which is equal parts trying too hard, populated solely by people who are high enough level to exploit the systems at play, and abandoned by the developers so they can go screw around with the noticeably inferior first person series' new multiplayer mode.

I can only recommend this in good faith because of what they did right - but it's also what they did right off of the assets they largely made for Resident Evil 2 Remake and because the characters themselves were always lovable to begin with.

Running away screaming is not the first instinct anymore, like with Mr X, and it's a massive flaw – running is what actually makes you scared, not just slimy tentacles and a guttural growl. By turning around and hotfooting it, you admit that you are inferior, weaker, vulnerable; triggered by these unpleasant realisations, fear kicks in. 

★ Speaking of anticlimactic stuff, consider several most intense moments in the game where all you need to do is... [u]press and hold a single button while looking at the screen[/u]. I dreaded getting the RE3 remake for a while because I had heard so many bad things about it. Not only that, but quite frankly, I never liked the original RE3. I played through it once years ago, disliked virtually the entire game, and never touched it again. I far preferred the original RE2, and when the RE2 remake came out, I was blown away by the improvements to it, and it was my favorite game in 2019 as a result. Unlike many, I don't do nostalgia, though. If I loved a game when I was younger but it is lacking, I will turn my nose up at it. For example, now that the RE2 remake exists, I will personally not bother to play the original RE2 because the remake does the overall game so much better for what I want in a game that I have no reason to play it again.

I actually remembered so many locations from RE2 when playing the RE2 remake. However, when playing the RE3 remake, I didn't recognize even a single location. After finishing the remake, I pulled up a YouTube playthrough of RE3 and skipped around in various chunks, finding that the RE3 remake - as best I can tell - is an attempt at building a coherent explorable area containing small businesses with flavor/personality in a "less is more" mentality, as opposed to the original game's philosophy of "give them ALL the alleys!!!" I was so bored watching the original RE3 clips. Alley after alley after alley, with some generic rooms and buildings, lacking the tightly-packed, content-stuffed, prolonged "intimacy" that the Spencer Mansion and the Raccoon City Police Department possessed. The city areas you travel through multiple times on the RE3 remake do the best I believe could possibly be done to imitate what makes the aforementioned RE1 and RE2 locations so enjoyable.

But I digress. I suspect the best way to determine whether or not you like the game is to ask yourself the following questions: did you like the RE2 remake? If not, don't get this. If you haven't played that and like action horror games or other Resident Evil games, then play it. Did you play RE3 and nostalgia is the most important thing to you in gaming? If so, don't get this because nothing shy of an almost identical replica of the original game would please you, and this is not it...which I believe is for the best. Would you dislike this game if it is shorter than the RE2 remake? If so, then don't get this game. If you still haven't been "disqualified," so to speak, then you might enjoy this game if you're into Resident Evil games and liked the RE2 remake. This is basically more RE2 remake in terms of gameplay, with a couple new features (craftable grenades, a couple of new enemies, dodge/punch mechanics), but it's in a city rather than an awesome structure like the Spencer Mansion or Raccoon Police Department, and a few things like some puzzles. a clock tower fight, and a boss fight against a big worm have been cut. There's still a fight beneath a clock tower which is pretty well-designed and better than most original RE series boss fights, but there is no pleasing the most adamant of nostalgia junkies if you change something like this.

I believe the developers did a great job of trying to make the game fun and interesting, despite the bland alleys and backrooms of the original RE3 which made me hate that game in the first place. It's unfortunate that RE3 was set in the streets in the first place, which effectively caused the RE3 remake to require a significant chunk of the game be set in city streets, but I think they did a fantastic job with a bad situation. The original game was in the bizarre situation of wanting to be more action-oriented, but being so stuck in the trappings of RE2, which was designed around a tight, lovingly-designed building. RE4 rectified this situation by making numerous locations you sometimes don't visit more than once, but they're all so very flavorful, memorable, and avoid giving the player a tiny inventory and requiring save room boxes, thus permitting the player to be on the move while still doing some inventory management.

I'm getting off track again, but in short, I was surprised to find that I kinda loved this game. I hated the original RE3 and this game redeemed the premise and general story of RE3 for me. All the nostalgia junkies and folks who paid $60 for it will likely not be happy with it, but I have already lost count of how many playthroughs I've done, and it's just a blast. I preferred the RE2 remake, but this one's still pretty darn good. I'm greatly considering it for my favorite game of 2020 right now, unless something else comes to mind that I liked better. Anywho, I hope this helps you decide if you do or don't want the game. Even if you decide against it, hopefully at least something I said helps you make your decision. =)  Given the length of the game, I probably would suggest getting it on sale for at least half off, or a deeper discount. I think the game really should have launched at $39.99 given the new things it offers and the game length, but that's just my opinion, of course.

However, fans of the original and 2019's Resident Evil 2 Remake might be disappointed to find this game lacking in puzzles, resource scarcity, and as a result, fear. Frankly, I'd sooner recommend this one to fans of Naughty Dog's Uncharted series.

With an impeccable sense of pacing, a laser focus on action, and one of the most striking antagonists in gaming history, I can easily assure you that Resident Evil 3 is an absolute blast from beginning to end. Jill and Carlos are an absolute joy to the ears and eyes thanks to the unparalleled presentation of the RE Engine. And the game is never a bore when desperately avoiding the unkillable Nemesis who facilitates some of the most well-crafted and exhilarating set pieces and boss fights the franchise has to offer in one of the most high-octane games I've played.

In short, Resident Evil 3 is a great time but I'd recommend waiting for a sale or price drop.

As I wrote in my [url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198275281641/recommended/883710]Resident Evil 2 review[/url], Capcom made each Resident Evil game distinct from each other, even both RE2 and RE3 are the remade of classic Resident Evil. While RE3 keeps most mechanics of RE2, it is much more action-packed and fast-paced because not only you are constantly chased by Nemesis, who compared to Tyrant in RE2, is much faster and able to jump and run, normal enemies are also more aggressive and agile. Take zombies as an example, they have a wider attack range, which means harder to slip through. And when they lie on the ground fαking death, it is harder to knife them down without getting bitten. To counter that, the game introduces the dodge button replacing the old sub-weapon (knife and hand grenade) button. It is hard to master, but once you did, it can be very helpful. Additionally, enemies are less bullet spongy in general - only take about 4 to 5 well-placed handgun bullets in the head to put a normal zombie out of misery for good. That said, you might want to consider whether it is worth killing them. Unlike RE2 where you wander around the same places a lot making cleaning some areas a necessity, RE3 reduces a lot of backtracking and many locations are one-time only, due to the much simpler and more linear map design.

Capcom also made other changes for a better Resident Evil experience: graphics have been upgraded – it looks sharper, more colorful and beautiful and full of visual details while still comes with great optimization; inventory has been optimized to be more handy; safe rooms now have a soft and relaxing music like The Evil Within, which a nice touch to relax the nerves a little bit, etc.

But not all the changes are welcome, at least for me: when grabbed by zombies, you press left mouse to reduce damage; it has quick-time-ish events in certain circumstances requiring you to either smash or long-press buttons. I am not a fan of these two changes for functional but more for personal reasons. The first one lacks visual feedback making me feel I was smashing button for nothing. It is also just a step backwards compared to being able to shovel a knife or grenade into a zombie’s mouth. For the latter, I hate QTE in general, thereby naturally it is not my liking. On top of that, there is no dedicated sub-weapon button. I use knife very often so it is very inconvenient that I had to switch back and forth in the inventory after I acquired four weapons. 

If I have to make a comparison, I am definitely more fond of Resident Evil 2. I can’t really blame Capcom because this is how remade works – even the original RE2 is better than RE3 from what I heard. Still, I had tons of fun playing Resident Evil 3. Jill is such a badass and Carlos is a very likable character and I like the gameplay. I heard people complaining a big part of the original was cut from the game causing the game to be too short. I never played the original and cutting is definitely a shame, but it is not as bad as it sounds – 6 to 7 hours for the first playthrough, and if you want to turn every stone like me, you are looking at about 8 hours. 

You can still find other points not to like this game: pacing is a mess for those who don’t understand how Resident Evil games usually work, as they trigger chase scenes too early and get interrupted leaving areas unexplored or items not gathered; Carlos session is arguably the worst part of the game since the game just plies up zombies and even has a siege like the cabin level in RE4, which feels more like a generic zombie shooter and can obviously frustrate a lot of people; animation is kind of lazy for always reloading six rounds into the grenade launcher even you don’t have six; as well as simplistic map design, inventory management and puzzles. But on the flip side, Resident Evil 3 is still an utterly satisfying experience. It has enjoyable shooting, intense horror atmosphere, refined mechanics, fun gameplay, superb graphics, great sound effects, likable characters and a simple story that works. Of course, you can take my words with a grain of salt cause I am obviously a big fan of the series. Nevertheless, I don’t think anyone will regret playing it.

Resident Evil 3 (this version) is a hack job filled to the brim with excessive quick time events and horrible cutscenes. The graphics are fine but the game and the gameplay feels incredibly short and rushed. Almost like I'm playing a demo of a game. The biggest flaw of this game compared to RE2 is the exploration, puzzle solving and overall critical thinking revolving around the player is just non-existent. Almost like the game caters to a bunch brain dead idiots. Many sections felt like a tutorial and the game practically screams at you what to do. I almost expected every single objective to be posted across your screen so it could be even more obvious than what it already was. 
Even sections that could be a spot where you take your time rush the player forward because you are constantly being chased throughout the entire game. And unlike RE2 where Tyrant could show up at any given moment, RE3 was painfully obvious about it. Making quick saves and having the player walk into sections that clearly meant a scripted event was going to take place. The boss fights were annoyingly easy to the point where it more of a chore and it wasn't very thrilling. 
If you want a game to be horror or survival for that matter then you have to set up an atmosphere to do so. RE3 comes as a system shock to anyone that played RE2 because there is no atmosphere of survival or horror. The game insists upon itself and with flashy cutscenes and graphics and quicktime events that are practically useless. The most obnoxious ones are scripted movie sequences where the player needs to press a button to basically drive the cutscene forward. Why not just play the cutscene why force a player to push buttons for the sake of being "interactive".  Other quick time events are awful like repeatedly tapping a button when being pinned by a zombie only to have that same zombie bite you in the neck. I spent the whole game wondering if I was even doing this mechanic right because RE2 allowed you to avoid the attack while RE3 throws up the middle finger and shows its glorious scripted cut scenes wasting your time watching your character being bitten and thrashed around. 
The only improvement I've seen in this game over RE2 is that your pistol will actually crit from time to time and kill a zombie instantly. Its like the developers have no idea what their own fan base even is. Cutting out huge segments from the original game. Fixing mechanics that didn't need to be fixed and making other mechanics more frustrating and annoying than RE2. Overall I hated most of my experience with this glorified action based over the top lackluster video showcase of a game. Most items felt pretty much useless and the game gives you an incredible amount of resources and its almost not worth the effort to even seek them out. They might as well just given the player unlimited ammo and made the entire game a linear A to B game. There is very little to practically no strategy involved in this game. I just hope people don't actually seriously enjoy this burning dumpster fire of a game. It might as well have been DLC with the content provided. Don't waste your money on this and if you wanna see the story then get it on sale.

Resident Evil 3 is short and action-packed adventure that I enjoyed from start to finish.

It's very hard not to compare this game to Resident Evil 2 Remake.

Gameplay - RE3 is very basic when it comes to shooting mechanics and design. You cant do much to zombies besides shoot them but there are some environmental objects like barrels and generators that are used but they are very rare. The reason why its enjoyable is because your not given much ammo for most of your weapons. This forces you to optimize your way through the game. Why use a full clip to kill a zombie when one or two bullets will knock him to the floor and you can run past him without harm but ill need to come back through this area again so maybe i should.... Having to make quick decisions on your feet with zombies on your heels is what makes it so fun. The main problem is that they don't fully utilize that design philosophy throughout the game. Whenever they don't design the locations or scenarios around this, the game suffers. The game has autosaves and unlimited saves on the normal difficulty which is unusual for this series and further pushes it from that optimal gameplay design. Some of the weakest parts of this game are sections were you play as Carlos. Carlos is a special agent whose able to use a fully auto assault rifle. Almost all of the tension is gone while you play as him since you run around blasting zombies with ease. It isn't necessarily bad, but the character movement, aiming and impact of your shots just feels out of place. Don't get me wrong, landing a perfect dodge with Jill is very satisfying but for every perfect dodge there's an awkward moment when I feel like my dodge should of registered and it doesn't or I dodge an attack unintentionally because i just happened to walk in a specific direction. When it works, RE3 requires you to make quick decisions under tense situations and the result is thrilling. When it doesn't, your stuck wondering if your just unskilled or unlucky. Also, the Nemisis shows up in very scripted moments. It can be a slight surprise to see him but he isn't that much of a threat most of the time. 

Graphics - The RE engine is fantastic. The character models and animations look so detailed. Cutscenes are always a treat. You'll get an occasionally cheesy line but it wouldn't be Resident Evil without it. Looking at you Jill Sand-which! Environments are also so wonderfully creative. Dark and moody streets and corner stores to cold and mechanical labs. Every space designed with such great attention to detail. All the enemies and bosses look so amazingly detailed and appropriately frightening as well.

The story is about 5 hours. I felt no need to replay it but there is an item shop and multiple difficulties if you do decided to go another round. Not worth $60 but for $20 or less, this is a good buy. 

As a fan of the Resident Evil series, this is a worthy addition.

Resident Evil 3 Remake is a fantastic action game that delivers an adrenaline-fueled experience, even if it doesn’t quite match the survival horror tone of its predecessor. It’s not necessarily fair to compare it directly to Resident Evil 2 Remake because they are fundamentally different games. While RE2 leans heavily into survival horror, RE3 shifts gears and focuses on fast-paced action, quick-time events, intense boss fights, and heavier weaponry like assault rifles.

The gameplay is undeniably fun. From dodging Nemesis in heart-pounding encounters to blasting your way through hordes of zombies, every moment is packed with energy and excitement. The addition of mechanics like the dodge move makes combat feel faster and more dynamic, perfectly suiting the game’s action-oriented design. The boss fights, in particular, are a highlight—each one is intense and cinematic, keeping you on edge.

That said, the game is short—too short to justify its original $60 price tag. The story content feels a bit sparse, and you can’t help but wish the developers had included more areas to explore or fleshed out the narrative further. It’s a thrilling ride, but one that ends too soon. Despite its brevity, what’s here is polished, engaging, and undeniably fun to play.

Visually, the game looks incredible. The RE Engine once again delivers stunning graphics, from the grimy streets of Raccoon City to the detailed character models and terrifying enemy designs. The sound design and voice acting are top-notch, adding to the immersive experience.

If you go into this expecting a pure action game rather than traditional survival horror, Resident Evil 3 Remake is an absolute blast. While it could have been longer, it’s a well-executed and exciting reimagining of the original game. And I, for one, am looking forward to more Resident Evil remakes in the future.

...well, it's not horrible, but I wouldn't recommend playing it unless you really love Resident Evil. I can't speak for how faithful it is or isn't compared to the original RE3: Nemesis, having not played it, but I didn't care for the minor changes from RE2: Remake. Shifting from resource-based counters (IE, countering being grabbed with a consumable knife or grenade), RE3 Remake moves to dodging and button mashing. The dodging never felt quite right to me, and reducing the resource management in favor of more combat with more enemies and more instant-kill opponents didn't increase tension or excitement for me. It just left me frequently annoyed.

It's not all bad, that being said. While the level design is linear to a fault, I did find just barely enough little nooks and crannies to make exploration fun. The graphics and art direction are both still excellent, and the early encounters with Nemesis were really fun, even if I felt like the later ones got a little predictable and moved away from what made Nemesis cool in the first place. I liked Jill and Carlos a ton as characters, and the story - while simple - kept me going throughout.

Heck, the combat changes do clearly have a place. A later fight where I actually ran out of ammo against some hunters led to a really tense sequence where it was just me versus the last guy, dodging and striking with a knife until it went down. And that's kind of Resident Evil 3 in a nutshell. Some really great classic survival horror moments of overcoming impossible odds, and some solid spectacle mixed in with a bunch of okay-to-annoying zombie shooting action that only lasts about 5 hours total. Take that how you will.

For better or worse, the Resident Evil 3 remake is the poster child for "weekend game" with its overemphasis on linear areas and action. Puzzles and backtracking are few and far between and don't come close to what you might expect from your typical Resident Evil title. That doesn't sound very compelling, does it? However, what this game does, it does very well. For starters, it's absolutely gorgeous, improving on the already beautiful Resident Evil 2 remake (especially the hair). Thankfully, the gunplay is also a high point. Everything feels smoother, faster, compared to its predecessor from a year earlier, which also meant Nemesis animated and behaved in ways that continued to surprise me throughout my playthrough. 

The final time for my first playthrough clocked in at about 8-9 hours. Yes, it's easy to run through the game in less than two hours, even as someone who struggles to hit the par time for S rank in these games. If you like to take in the sights and explore, however, I don't think my initial time is too far from most. All the talk around launch about the playtime is partly why I waited so long to buy it. If I had paid full price I'd probably be upset by the short length and lack of meaningful extra game modes compared to RE2 (and the original RE3, I'm told). 

Length and puzzles aside, the biggest complaint would be the areas that were cut from the original. This was already a divisive game back in 1999 so I don't understand why Capcom wouldn't do everything in their power to correct the game's image and give it a legacy worthy of recent games. Time, money, and the impending release of RE4's remake are obvious answers but in a perfect world Capcom would have given these games more time to breathe, along with a higher budget. If you expect your customers to buy into a $60+ game at release it's fair to expect a product worthy of that price.

Our Resident Evil hot runner has a confession to make. Despite renting a Playstation back in the day for a sleepover fueled by Water Joe (caffeinated water), this is the first Resident Evil game he has completed.

While reading reviews and fretting over whether or not the game was worth the price equivalent of a large Domino's pizza (remember to avoid the Noid!), it became clear that nerds were beachin' about the short length of the game. However, this is exactly what appealed to our hot runner and eventually got him hooked on the series.

You can tell from the RE3 game trailer that its graphics are a main selling point. This became even clearer to us when returning to RE3 after beating the RE2 remake released a year prior. In comparison, the character models in RE3 look more realistic and inventory menus/gameplay are much smoother. RE3 also has improved defense over earlier games with Jill's "evasive slip" move and Carlos' show-stopping "mega punch".

In short, we highly recommend this game to anyone who is curious about the Resident Evil series but does not want to take it on as a part-time job. Our first run took approximately 6 hours and was later refined to 4 hours the second time through. If you are skeptical about this "short" game being worth your time, please consider that Resident Evil games are perfect for multiple play-throughs.

Also, do not be concerned about missing items when "blasting" through this game. Due to limited inventory, it's not always advantageous to collect every single item. This may come as a shock to you if you've recently played games like Disgaea or Forager where compulsive item hoarding is rewarded.

Out of all the original resident evil games 3 was always my favorite.  So when I saw they were indeed remaking 3, and especially after how incredibly well they did with 2, I was extremely excited!  Would've preordered the collector's edition if it hadn't sold out in like ten seconds.

But then the game came out and I played it.  It's a travesty.  They truncated the game, cutting out at least a third of the original content, and what they left they changed so much the game is virtually unrecognizable as the third game.  They kept a few characters, sure, but the story and even locations are basically entirely different.  This is not Resident Evil 3 in any way.  It's just some bull with almost no content and a couple kind-of familiar faces.

If you're interested in this game because it's a remake of 3, don't waste your money.

Let me be clear, the Classic is the better game. I do enjoy this game though. It is super short and you should absolutely not pay full price for this glorified DLC. That said, it is enjoyable.

There isn't anything hard about getting all the achievements so if you want to do something like that, it'll take like 20 hours or less if you are efficient. I messed around and enjoyed the game.

Pros: 
-It's pretty. 
-I experienced little to no bugs/glitches or issues with the game.
-It gives you the basic RE3 story if you are a Resident Evil story person.

Cons:
-Short game, like insanely short for the price you pay. Like 3 hours tops with lots of just bumbling around. If you don't like replaying a game that doesn't offer more story based on your choices this is a replay killer.
-Missed mark when compared to RE2 remake. They had wonderful source material and made a game that is procedural with little surprises or character growth.
-Despite great game play, the game gets really redundant. See above comment. The changed item/enemy locations in higher difficulties fails to spice the game up enough for replayability. 

Verdict: Great game for 20 bucks, but lost the excitement the Classic carried in spades.

I always felt like “This is a story that could have been told in the random notes in other games”. Well, now I believe this is a story that NEEDED to be told. Not in 1999, rushed-to-release to capitalize on the success of the first 2 games, but as a true gaming masterpiece of 2020. When the world around us is falling apart to a super terrifying virus it was only appropriate, in my mind, that RE3 was released right after stay at home orders were issued in my county. I played this for an entire week straight on Ps4. I purchased it again on steam recently, for a quarter of the release price, to play it again for my full RE canon adventure, and I don’t regret buying it twice and beating it 13 times total. This game has everything I like about video games.

A lot of people say it’s not a “faithful” remake. I don’t agree with those people. I understand a lot of people have different things they like or look for in video games, especially remakes of “Classics”. This game takes the drawn out and poorly paced source material of the original “Nemesis” and makes it a streamlined, graphical powerhouse that puts all other RE projects to shame. I gave the RE2 remake a 9/10. That game was great, but all it really did was take an already great game and make it modern. RE3 remake took a mediocre action game from 20 years ago and transformed it into something amazing.

[h1] “Come on, you creepy-ass stalker! You want STARS? I’ll give you STARS!”[/h1]

RE3 is a VASTLY different game from Nemesis while still maintaining all the important things from the original. In fact, I don’t think RE3 is a remake at all, but more of a re-imagining, and it is better off for it. Much like looking 20 years back at things you did and said when you were young and rolling your eyes thinking “Ugh, what was I thinking? I was so stupid at 16”. That is this game. I feel like Capcom looked back at Nemesis and thought that [i]very thing. [/i]

[h1] Story [/h1]

RE3 covers the events of Racoon city from a different perspective than Resident Evil 2. While this game's timeline intersects with RE2 at many points, even with certain locations like Kendos gun shop and parts of the RCPD from 2. It tells Jill Valentines’ story and what she’s doing while the city is burning around her. She wakes up in her apartment after a terrible nightmare caused by the trauma she faced in the Spencer Mansion in RE1. It’s several months later and she is struggling with normal daily activity. With obvious PTSD, having been removed from STARS, and obsessed with bringing justice for what happened, Jill has been having a rough go of it. Set to leave Racoon City in just a few days, Jill gets a phone call. It’s Brad Vickers, the helicopter pilot from STARS and he says [i]“GET OUT”[/i]. The game begins with a literal [b]BANG[/b] and it doesn’t stop, ever. You can tell already that this will not be the RE3 you know. Pursued relentlessly by a seemingly indestructible creature known as Nemesis, Jill just can’t seem to catch a break. Jill meets up with Carlos from the Umbrella Biohazard Countermeasure Service, and together they attempt to escape the city.

[h1] “Are you kidding me? Are you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ kidding me?! You guys are the ones who caused all of this [/h1]
[i] -Jill, finding out Carlos is U.B.C.S [/i]

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

Just like the RE2 remake, RE3 completely transforms the original into a modern gaming experience. Gone are the tank controls, camera angles, polygons, and all of the rose tinted staples of the original game. Replaced with, in my opinion, a vastly superior action/horror game that takes the source material and makes it something fantastic and unique. This is an action based Third Person Shooter, and I see people saying it isn’t anything like the other REmake, and they are right. Developed alongside (not after) the RE2 remake, you can tell this is a different approach, and it shows in the gameplay. 

They have added a MUCH NEEDED dodge button in this game, allowing Jill to get out of a tight spot with ease. Your knife is now an actual weapon and doesn’t break all the damn time. Jill moves faster than Leon or Claire, making the game seem much faster paced, and it is. While RE2 leaned more towards the horror side of Resident Evil, RE3 definitely takes a more action packed approach. Here's the thing though, it suits this story so much better. ♥♥♥♥ is going down. These aren't a few creatures roaming around in a building. It wouldn’t make sense to have a dark and tense atmosphere and small locations when the entire damn city is burning around you. Helicopters are falling from the sky, signs are falling off buildings, hundreds of zombies and other monsters are openly roaming the streets filled with bodies and burning vehicles. This game is more on the lines of a thriller, because it can still manage to scare you without hiding a creepy monster on the ceiling of a dark room.

Gone are the multiple campaigns and forced multiple plays to get the “True story”. You beat this game once and you get the full story. However, UNLIKE 2, I beat this game multiple times by my OWN choice, because it is just so satisfying to play! Yes, it’s a bit shorter, my original Standard difficulty run of RE3 took 6 hours, while 2 took me 8. That’s where it stopped for me in RE2. I played each campaign once [i](Because I felt like I HAD TO)[/i] and got the “TRUE ENDING”, but I full-on [b]mastered[/b] RE3, and I don’t do that with games often. I’m not a speedrunner at heart. I don’t play a game 10 times just to be good at it… however with RE3 [i]I did.[/i] I beat this game, on inferno difficulty [i](The locked difficulty AFTER Nightmare)[/i] with an S ranking because prior to this I had earned enough points in my previous runs to purchase an infinite ammo rocket launcher. This is not a microtransaction or anything, it’s simply earned currency for earned rewards, and it felt awesome. The game even lets you use the cool rewards you’ve earned in your new runs and doesn’t penalize you for it. THANK YOU!

[h1] Performance [/h1]

Much like the last REmake, RE3 gives you a huge amount of graphic, audio, and visual options to screw around with. I got this game looking gorgeous, running at 60fps + on 1440p with a mediocre PC gaming setup. It seems so well optimized I dare say this is one of the best running games I’ve ever played. Period. I ran into ZERO bugs, and had ZERO crashes. The controls were tight and intuitive. I played with KB/M. The audio in this game is top notch. Whether it’s the creepy background soundtracks, the action sequences with thumping orchestral music, or the gunshots ringing through the air and zombies moaning from the streets, it’s just so well done. I was fully immersed the ENTIRE time, even on my final run through, after knowing exactly what was going to happen and when.

[h1] Summary [/h1]

I could keep going on and praising how great this game is, but Steam has a character limit. I find it much harder to write positive and glowing reviews like this than I do negative ones where I can just point out what the issues are. This game gave [b]ME[/b] a [i]perfect[/i] experience. Will it be a perfect game for everyone? Nope, no game is.

[b]Overall Score: 10/10[/b]
[b]Why Buy?[/b] This game is insanely fun with a lot of additional stuff to unlock.
[b]So there is nothing bad about it? [/b] It’s not a 1:1 remake of the original game and is less horror, but it’s exactly what RE should be. If that bothers you, skip it.

Thanks for reading [i](if you did)[/i] and please let me know if you found this review helpful at all!
Cheers!

First off, this game does look great and plays great. It is an excellent remake of a classic Resident Evil title and is worth a buy if you are a big RE fan. That being said, this game is extremely short and suffers from a lack of overall content. This is due to several cuts of content including some systems from RE2 Remake and entire levels from the original RE3. The game's recommended speedrun time is under 2 hours to obtain an S rank, if that tells you how short the game is. 

The game also suffers from a lack of replayability that the RE2 Remake had. There are no other routes like that one had, just a single cosmetic outfit, some upgrades, and some infinite ammo guns. Every playthrough will have the exact same experience with no additional modes or post-launch support like RE2 had. Overall, there are several downgrades from this RE2 to this title that show an evident lack of development time. 

If you just completed RE2 and are looking for more, this will only satisfy you for a very limited amount of time. If you are a hardcore fan of the series, then I would recommend buying, just not at a $60 price tag. I wouldn't recommend paying more than $20 for this short, but sweet experience.

[h3]Opening Excuses[/h3]
RE3 was never my favorite. Short and relatively linear, it had little to no plot, puzzles or replay value and was less suspenseful than its predecessors. As well as much more action-oriented, to the point that it introduced a dodge mechanic. Wait a minute... this is exactly it, but remade for modern times! Preposterous! In all seriousness, It's only fair to judge the game by today's standards, but let's admit that as a remake it's pretty damn faithful. 

Too faithful for its own good, or should I say for its price tag. I don't deny it, but I also don't buy the common "I loved RE3, but I hate the remake" position. As shown above, most of the arguments some people make against the remake apply to the original as well. The games have the same length, the same replay value, share most of the problems. Is this remake really bad? It happens to be worse as a deal, but it's still a good [strike]DLC[/strike] game.

My sincere condolences to people who expected more after playing RE2 Remake and paid the full price at launch. You did nothing wrong and suffered greatly, so others could make an informed decision later. It's hard to imagine your disappointment when after beating the game in a few hours came a realization that there's nothing else there aside from a couple of new difficulties and some stupid multiplayer crap that nobody asked for. I'm sorry to hear it, but I'm not here to carry out this stale vengeance for you.

[h3]Characters & Voice Acting[/h3]
The game adds a lot to the series' lore, but its simplistic story isn't something to write home about, and the "main villain" is so obviously telegraphed that it isn't even funny. However, It doesn't mean that I didn't like any of the characters. I wouldn't call Jill and Carlos as fleshed-out or well-written as Leon and Ada, yet I found them very likable. Jill combines badassery with femininity and Carlos is a sympathetic guy all around. They don't have the chemistry to be lovers, sure, but just enough of it to stay best buddies for life. I envision them having a couple of beers together, not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ one another, which is fine by me.

RE2 already had well-established characters with quite a personality to each of them, so good voice acting felt only natural. Here, however, it's so incredible that it saves the characters from feeling like mere cardboard cutouts almost single-handedly (impeccable facial animation also helps). Even a second fiddle like Tyrell ended up being memorable. There're a few great lines in this game, but most of the legwork was done by the actors. Who are evidently talented, passionate, and in spite of how little there was to work with, managed to elevate their characters to new heights. Color me impressed.

[h3]Sound & Visuals[/h3]
As for the graphics, for the most part, the game looks crisp and glossy, special effects are popping, the environments are even more lively and intricate than before. Occasionally a blurry texture or two might pop up. It doesn't seem to have anything do with the textures not loading, looks more like they've accidentally used the wrong assets (from consoles?) in a few places. In terms of sound, nothing new here, too - the zombies moan hungrily, the shots crack loudly as they leave the barrel and land with a satisfying thud. Basically, if you've played the previous remake, you know what to expect.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
Would I change a few things, starting by giving Carlos a separate campaign or giving Nemesis a bit more freedom of thought? I probably would. But when it comes to the lack of non-linearity, the thing people complain about the most, I was happy to see it replaced with variety. Why are you booing me? I'm right. Here, specific gameplay elements get frequently introduced to serve their purpose and never be repeated again, which isn't necessarily a bad thing.

I think that this approach worked in the game's favor, in particular, for the bugs' labyrinth, chase sequences, and the sewers. Although paradoxically, I would love for the latter to last longer since the giant fish monsters that dwell in there are simply awesome. They've become my favorite monster design in the whole series. In terms of favorite environments, I could never get enough of RE's labs. The mix of sterility and pestilence is inherently unsettling.

The dodge mechanic kinda trivialized most of the regular zombie encounters. But it also replaced the lame "bite insurance" system, meaning that having a knife or a grenade in your inventory doesn't automatically shield you from being bitten anymore. More importantly, it allowed to make the boss fights not just less clumsy than before but also super-fast and intense. I loved these fights, despite some of them being slightly drawn-out. That Pinky\Amalgam\Mommy from Braindead was a hard nut to crack! And Carlos's final standoff was a neat callback, too.

After not quite feeling the pressure on Normal in RE2, I opted for Hardcore this time around. Playing on a higher difficulty should've made sense of my resource-saving pathology, an old PTSD stretching from the very first game. By the end, I was still left with an abundance of ammo and healing items like a dumbo. Yet, at least I died quite a few times... without losing much progress thanks to the generous autosave system. Anyhow, the game kept me reasonably focused and tense, which is how it should be.

A few additional small things to appreciate:
- Hunting for treasure is still very satisfactory - you lockpick stuff, look for codes and cards to get your hands on weapons, upgrades, and precious resources.
- Protagonists get more bruised and unkempt as the game goes. It isn't anything new, but I love that feature.
- No Ink Ribbons, ♥♥♥♥ them.
- Grenades MVP. Hint: save them for the bosses.
- Panic-inducing predicaments that catch you off guard are as well-designed as ever.
- Little to no QTE shenanigans, which is rather relevant to me since I just replayed RE4.

[h3]Closing Excuses[/h3]
The sheer fact that this review is mainly comprised of excuses kinda speaks for itself. I know, right? Does it make me a Capcom fanboy or something? It seems like all I do is roam about defending mediocre ports and half-assed remakes of Resident Evil. And this isn't even my favorite series of theirs, believe it or not! That place in my heart belongs to Phoenix Wright for which I'd kill in cold blood.

Anyway, let's face the facts: RE3 re-hashes its own boss fights, some of the plot elements (looking for a vaccine), and flips some assets (police station) from the previous remake. Yet, it bears repeating that this is what RE3 always was. Also, all of it sounds much worse than it really is. What we have here is an action-packed, pulpy flick that bleaks in comparison to any of Capcom's games of late, but introduces a couple of neat gameplay changes and is a blast to play in spite of its flaws.

Overall, what little there is in terms of content is well-crafted and delightfully entertaining. I get it, you guys wanted more content than there ever was. Hell, I wanted more content than there ever was! But as Marlo from The Wire once said: "you want it to be one way, but it's the other way". Yes, I'm telling you (us), who is going to buy the game at a hefty discount or already did, to deal with it. Come on, people! Don't tell me these 6-9 hours of fun aren't worth 20-30$. They most certainly are to me.

Resident Evil 3 Remake: A Butchered Shadow of a Classic

Capcom’s Resident Evil 3 remake isn’t just a disappointment, it’s an outright disservice to fans of the original. What could have been a faithful modernization of one of the most tense and action-packed entries in the franchise instead feels like a soulless, stripped-down cash grab.

First and foremost: the content cuts. If you loved the original game’s diverse environments. The clock tower, the park, the newspaper office, forget them. They’re gone. Entire segments that added depth, atmosphere, and pacing to the 1999 classic have been gutted with no satisfying replacement. What’s left is a linear, barebones sprint through set pieces that feel like deleted scenes from the far superior Resident Evil 2 remake.

And let’s talk length. This game is shockingly short. We're talking five to six hours on a first run, and that's being generous. For a full-price title, that's borderline insulting. There's no real incentive to replay it beyond unlocking cosmetics or slightly tweaked difficulties. Compare that to RE2 Remake, which offered two full campaigns, intricate puzzles, varied routes, and meaningful replay value. RE3 doesn’t even try.

Then there’s Nemesis. Remember how terrifying he was in the original? Unpredictable, relentless, showing up at the worst moments? In this remake, he’s a glorified scripted boss fight. You’ll rarely feel hunted,  just dragged along for the ride. His potential as an iconic antagonist is completely squandered.

In short, Resident Evil 3 Remake feels more like an expansion pack than a standalone game. It lacks the care, complexity, and polish that made RE2 Remake such a triumph. What we got is a hollow imitation, a shiny but shallow facsimile that seems more interested in rushing players through than letting them soak in the horror.

Resident Evil 3 (2020), despite being a remake of one of RE's titles from the 90s, feels more like a spin-off of Resident Evil 2 (2019), it's remake predecessor, than an outright narrative deserving of its own entry. Despite its lineage in the same horror and puzzle stylings of its predecessor, the tone of Resident Evil 3 is, from the get-go, an action oriented affair.

That's certainly not a bad thing. In fact, there's a lot of moments in RE3 where you're reminded, quite wistfully, of Capcom's capacity to present a dynamic, dramatic narrative, more mindful of its villains and heroes than the creeping dread of RE and its sequel (finding a great balance, in my view, in RE4). But the result produced in Resident Evil 3 is the tone and pace go hand-in-hand and you quickly find yourself flying through environments in Raccoon City. There's a lot that I like about that though and having a greater diversity of environments (and spending less time in the drab corridors of underground Umbrella bases) is always a plus. Coupled with the relentless pursuit of Nemesis (not quite as meaningfully relentless or memorable as Mr X though) is a great, cinematic struggle between Jill and the villain.

I'd certainly say that the length of the game is a bit of an issue, depending on how much you're willing to pay for Resident Evil 3. While the game does provide incentives to fall into additional playthroughs, it doesn't quite have the spread of base content that Resident Evil 2 arrived with. Emphasising this is the uneven split between Jill Valentine and Carlos Oliveira. The writing has the purposeful charm to turn its cheesy 90s progenitor into a sincere but still fun narrative, but this is a much more singular story all together, passing back and forth between the two characters a handful of times, without the benefit of another run of RE2 as Claire/Leon, giving you 6-8 hours of playtime depending on your speed. I finished my first playthrough of RE3 in a little over three and a half hours.

So my recommendation here is largely conditional. If you liked Resident Evil 2, you're likely going to enjoy this too. For its regular price of £49.99, it's an absolute no-go. For the present discount (with the showcase of RE8), £16.49 is reasonable enough, but I wouldn't pay £20 for this.

I really enjoyed it, partly because the RE Engine is absolutely beautiful, there's some great performances from the voice actors across the board and the narrative, while a bit begrudgingly straightforward, is still fun and moves along well enough to fit its pacing and tone. No one can doubt the earnest efforts of Capcom to try and reinvent these games and shape them into experiences for a new generation, that's something to be celebrated over everything else, as it's not something we've ever been fortunate enough to see done so well, so consistently.

RE3 is RE2 but worse in every way.

If you played the remake of 2, you should remember how its level design complimented the Tyrant. The entire police station was designed to always give players a way to not get closed off, regardless of which keys they had. Tyrant would simply not enter rooms which would trap the player, like save or interrogation rooms. RE3 by comparison, is so linear, Nemesis needs to teleport, spawn, despawn, and leave the playable area through scripted events in order for the game to be navigable.

The Nemesis itself isn't great. He cuts through walls, elemental hazards, and secondary characters with ease, but is utterly worthless against the player character.

The linearity of RE3 refocuses its gameplay from a context of resource scarcity into a power fantasy. With few to no optional areas to collect from, the game must leave a lot of resources directly in the player's path. Too many. The shooting mechanics are just as fun as they were in the last game, but there is no concern whatsoever for things like using too much ammo on a weak zombie or taking a hit that was avoidable.

The story isn't any better. Your good characters are naively, stupidly good. Your bad characters are cartoonishly bad. [spoiler]And it all culminates in a tired moral that people have already told to death for decades.[/spoiler] Play this game if you enjoyed the shooting in RE2 and want more of that, but don't pay more than $20 for it.

As a long time RE fan, especially the recent RE2 remake, I went into RE3 with the same anticipation and enthusiasm as I usually do with this series. And, whilst shorter than it should've been, I came out on the other side mostly happy with my 6 hour playthrough. 

From a visual standpoint, the game is a real spectacle; bright neon lights shine vibrantly onto cold burning alleys and streets, Jill's torch creates a tunnel of vision in pitch black sewers and dimly lit buildings to create an atmosphere packed with fear and tension. Along with the impressive visuals comes expertly crafted sound design that never falters in giving the game world a feeling of necessary realism to match the mood and feeling of Jill's surroundings. Distant groans of the undead or the pulse pounding footsteps of Nemesis come together to elevate the realism of the environment. 

The game's narrative fit the standard for a typical RE game, not really doing anything too unique, though the overall focus is around survival horror/action so this doesn't harm the experience. The main gripe people have with this game is it's short length in comparison to RE2, giving the RE3 remake a feeling more akin to an expansion as opposed to a fully fledged title. The in-game store unlocked after beating the game's main story does add a lot to the replayability factor of the game, allowing access to new weapons, items available earlier than usual, or straight up cheat items, all of which are sure to add a few extra hours onto your all round game time. 

Overall, the RE3 remake doesn't push the bounds of an RE game like the RE2 remake or RE7 managed to do, but does provide a smaller scale story experience that is worth a play through if you're a fan of the series (though I'd definitely wait for a sale to avoid buying at full price).

Pretty decent, but not amazing. What most people say definitely applies. It's a more linear, action focused version of Re2 Remake. I'm not gonna talk too much about the game's shortcomings in comparison to Re2, because far more people than me have already done that, better than I could. So here's my take on the game as someone who never played the original, but loved Re2 remake and put over a 100 hours into it:

I think it's still worth playing if you're a resident evil fan. I still love the graphics, it still manages to startle me from time to time and the added dodging and counterattack mechanics can be very rewarding although a bit unreliable(then again, maybe it should be to increase the horror factor). It strays maybe a bit too far away from the story of the original. Re2 remake did too, but Re3 remake might have gone too far. Although I still appreciate certain subversions of the original story without giving away spoilers. The game does recycle a fair few assets from the last remake and you will be able to tell. Sure the original trilogy recycled a lot, but it feels a bit more blatant here. Also, they removed ink ribbons even on hardcore. Why Capcom? It made the game less tense when I felt like I could save-scum frequently. It might also be a bit less balanced imo. I ended the game with so much surplus gun powder, but very little healing left. Speaking of the ending, It's ending was a bit disappointing, there's plenty of epicness during the climax, but it ends on a bit of a low note. Could have easily replaced the last moments of gameplay with a cutscene. Not as strong of a finish as Re2 remake imo. There's lots of spectacle here for sure, but maybe a bit too much for a survival horror. 

Nemesis is less scary than intimidating, they really wanted to make him out to be a superpowered mr X, but they tried too hard. The unpredictability of Mr X made you dread running into him. Nemesis is more scripted and theatrical, he usually just comes out from nowhere and forces you into a planned scenario where you must fight or outrun him. It just does not build anticipation like Mr X does. I just think the game has a slight identity crisis, where it's not sure whether it wants to be Re4 or Re2 remake. It's still very much a fine game and if you're thirsty for more of what Re2 remake had to offer, you should at least be OK with this game. But it's really not as good as that game and should have been better really. Grab it if it's on sale, otherwise, only get it if you're really curious, like the more action focused aspects of RE, or you're desperate for more Re2 remake gameplay

Just a few months ago, I FINALLY got around to playing the OG R2 and 3 because I wanted to compare them to their remakes, and now I understand what the issue of R3make was. They literally cut FIFTY PERCENT of the game. The OG R3 had twice as many areas as the R3make did, including the ones that were already in the R3make. The reason why R3make felt about half as long as it should be is because it IS half as long as it should be. I've also heard many people talk about how upset they were that the Clock Tower and RC park wasn't in the remake, and now I understand why. While I was playing those parts myself, I began to realize how much cooler those parts could have been in this remake. This was for sure just another cash grab for Capcom. Now like I said, there are definitely some good parts to this game as well. Below is a brief breakdown of game elements for R3make.

Gameplay - 8/10  - The game is fun and enjoyable.

Length - 3/10 - For obvious reasons. Game is way too short and many areas feel rushed.

Story - 6/10 - The story is engaging and enticing, but doesn't give to much about why we care about the characters or what they are going through.

Characters - 7/10 - Personalities of some characters could be worked on a bit more. I thought the small relationship/exchanges between Carlos and Jill were a bit cheesy, but it turns out that's just the way it was in OG R3 too, and that's just part of Resident Evil in general.

Graphics - 10/10 - The game looks amazing and very realistic.

Puzzles - 2/10 - 2 points for LITERALLY only 2 puzzles in the entirety of the game, both of which are INSANELY EASY

Replayability - 5/10 - The records and item shop give the player a reason to continue playing the game and grinding after they complete it, but it feels like an excuse just to encourage the players to keep playing the game. 

Enemies - 4/10 - Literally all the zombies are copied from R2make. Just a few new ideas were put in play, and many unique enemies from OG R3 were cut. Nemesis is also incredibly scripted, and he barely has a purpose on the easier difficulties. The 3 boss fights in the game are extremely repetitive to one another.

Assets - 5/10 - While there a some unique items/objects/assets in the world of the game, most of them were also just copied from R2make. 

Additional content - 2/10 - What happened to mercenaries? Where's the extra game modes? I was also hoping this game would have some DLC coming out later like the other recent RE games, but it never did. Also NOBODY WANTED RE RESISTANCE

Overall score: 52/100

Let me preface this by saying this game is often compared to its predecessor, RE2 Remake, and that game is clearly superior to RE3's Remake.  Therefore, I think it would be unfair to rate this game without judging it independently from its counterparts, so I'll do that at the end.

RE3 Remake is probably one of the most beautiful and graphically jaw-dropping games of 2020, so if you're expecting a AAA experience, you'll be getting Michael Bay with this one.  This means a linear plot with lots of action, scares and explosions.  It hearkens back to the more action-packed versions of Resident Evil, so it many senses, it keeps the adrenaline flowing.  The new actress that the modeled after Jill is gorgeous, and I really like how they chose someone who had natural beauty without makeup.  I beat the campaign in about 6 hours, with 7 hours of total gameplay, so this was worth the bundle I paid for both RE2 and RE3 on sale.  And for those of whom who say it has no replay value, I beg to differ.  There are plenty of challenges you can still earn, and the Jill outfit mods at least make it "interesting".  This is a game worth playing, especially if you enjoy RE lore.

However, every criticism I have of this game stems mostly from its comparisons to RE2 Remake.  I can only presume much of its shortcomings were due to a need to devote resources to the new Multiplayer mode, plus monetization.  Secondly, RE2 isn't better because the campaign is longer, because both games can be beat in 50 minutes during world-record speedruns.  RE2 is better because it maintained the formula of the original: Puzzle-solving and route-planning.  That formula, coupled with constant tension and scares, seems to produce the greatest dopamine release in gaming.  Whereas, RE3 is just constant tension and scares without any release.  It doesn't force you to "go back" and deal without something you're trying your best to avoid. 
 We're just always left hanging and subsequently raging in RE3 as we die from a horde of zombies.  The reason why people will often say RE2 has more replay value is because the puzzles and backtracking often challenge us about how do these things more efficiently.

All-in-all, I recommend.

It's a much more action focused title I would argue and the linearity of the level design and the story constantly propel you forwards at a breakneck pace, which further reinforces this point. It's in strong opposition to RE2 which let you explore the environments and navigate the story at your own pace more often than not. RE3 is also MUCH shorter than RE2 clocking in at around 5-6 hours for a first time playthrough instead of 10-15 for RE2. Overall, Resident Evil 3 is decent and worth a buy if you enjoyed Resident Evil 2 but ONLY at a discounted price somewhere around the $15-$20 mark. *(7/10)*

At a fairly reasonable discount (50%+) this is a no-brainer. At full price it's still a spectacle, albeit an expensive one.

Positive - 
Mechanics wise its a solid evolution of the previous RE2 remake (2019), with a now workable dodge mechanic and a much faster feeling protagonist (Leon and Claire ran pretty slowly). Its gun play is fun and challenging when under pressure, especially on the higher difficulties of Nightmare and above. 
Visually its the best of the series so far, with excellent work on the characters from top to bottom, and the environments have a level of detail that rivals its origins of the PS1 era pre-rendered originals. Voice acting is good throughout - although no one has managed to quite nail that Nemesis growl of STARS since the original.

Mixed - 
Its so short. It appears that the devs have cut approx 1/3 of the original game content, meaning we have lost most of the early game uptown gameplay, the park, graveyard and dead factory. I see why they did it this way for story flow, but it has the effect of making it feel rushed in terms of the story compared to the 1999 classic. 
Nemesis has a good introduction and early game combat, with some good set piece battles to spice things up, but once you board the train he becomes a completely set piece boss with no pursuit and no real tension. Its disappointing to see such a reduction of his presence in game, and it really has a knock on effect of his role in game. He's much less of a threatening enemy that can pop up anywhere in this iteration.

Bad -
No Mercanaries mode! Its been replaced by a 1V4 multiplayer game for free - Resistance. While this game is fun and a good time in its own right, it simply does not have the same appeal of he originals' race against the clock and resource management of Operation: Mad Jackal. 
Lack of bonuses - although this game has an excellent collection of development art, a model viewer and a nice collection of unlockable bonus items, the lack of costume items compared to the 1999 original (and the RE2 remake for that matter), is a disappointment, especially as some of these costumes are locked behind  paid for DLC (boo). 

Overall thoughts - 
I have enjoyed my time with RE3 in spite of a lack of content compared to its source game. The flow of gameplay and amount of unlockables and challenges to beat make for excellent replay value. I will continue to perfect the game and obtain the coveted S+ ranks.

Resident Evil 3 Remake is a great game but, severely underwhelming remake. BUY THIS GAME AT A DISCOUNT!!!!!!!

To start lets discuss why it is a underwhelming remake. This is because, it cuts vital features to RE3 that made it unique Resident Evil game (similar to Resident Evil 2 Remake). This cut content being live selection, multiple endings, epilogues, mercenaries, enemies, a lack of puzzles (and this is huge as puzzles are a staple of RE), and iconic areas, character fates, files (such as Jill's Diary), and boss out of the game. Also some unlockable costumes are missing (by this i mean the variety of costumes in the original game. Here we are relegated to 3 costumes (2 if you don't spend extra money)). Is that a bad thing yes, it very much is a bad thing because the game is not being remade but, reimagined. Remakes should take what was once there improve on the old and add new ideas to the lore of Resident Evil (similar to how Resident Evil Remake did in 2002, that's a perfect remake). Also they really managed to under utilize Nemesis which is a shame. Now with all the negatives out of the way lets get to why you should buy this game. 

For starters lets talk about the story. Not much to say here but its good. Its the same story as the original with some liberties taken. It a high octane story that takes you on a mad dash to escape the city. Thats really all that can be said.

Next lets discuss the gameplay and level design. The game play is very satisfying it is a huge improvement over RE2make with the aiming feeling slightly better than RE2make and with the introduction of the dodge mechanic it makes the game even more of a joy to control Jill or Carlos. You really feel like elite operatives and not rookies like Leon or Claire (but those two are amazing still). As for the level design it is linear but, don't let that discourage you (this is not a bad thing). The level design does an effective job at making you feel a seriously since of urgency to complete objectives in order to escape from Raccoon City. They masterfully pepper in explorable areas that do not overstay its welcome and gives you a taste of classic RE with a modern twist to it with a decent level of back tracking and more sensible puzzles which rewards you for putting in the effort to solve puzzles and backtrack. 

On to the characters, they are very well written. Jill and Carlos (this character is at his best in the Remake) share a dynamic relationship that starts of cold but gradually evolves into two people that trust each other and have each others back in this nightmarish scenario. The U.B.C.S. supporting cast has been overhauled and given a great amount of development than they received in the original.

Lets talk about the enemy variety. While many enemies and a boss were cut RE3make does a excellent job with the enemy types in the game. From Zombies to the big guy himself Nemesis the developers do an excellent job at making each enemy menacing (especially at higher difficulties). Ill let you discover them for yourself but, my favorite B.O.Ws inhabit the Sewer and hospital. 

Lets talk about Nemesis. He is under utilized BUT, how the game s set up to basically be a high octane game of cat and mouse he serves his purpose. He is fast, powerful, and menacing. Every form of him looks amazingly grotesque and he forces you to learn the crucial game mechanic the dodge. Yes, he is more scripted as (and bear with me) this game really drills in the sense of urgency that hey you need to get out of the city as fast as possible. Unlike the old game where they tried to capture that but fell short due to the layout of the game coupled with the puzzles and heavy back tracking. To keep that sense of urgency yes you do lose the dynamic feeling he had in the old game but, he is utilized just right to fit what the game is trying to convey which is an increased level of urgency. And for the love of all that is holy please master the dodge as it will save you at higher difficulties. Also at higher difficulties practice with Chris Redfield's (WOOOO MY BOI COMING IN CLUTCH) S.T.A.R.S Manual it helps you get dodging down.

The weapon selection is very good. Every gun sounds and feels different and is very satisfying to use and eventually upgrade. The thing I enjoy about the weapon selection is that they fill distinctly different between Jill and Carlos. I know that sounds silly to say like dude every character weapon selection feels unique to the character but, to that I say it feels especially unique in this game. Each character weapons go to show you where each character came from in a sense. Let me try to explain, Jill's Arsenal is comprised of a collection of guns just lying down on the ground. It really gives the sense she is just bare scrapping by as she traverses the city while being haunted down. Improving as she finds parts to upgrade her arsenal to become deadlier. Juxtapose this with Carlos' Arsenal which is very streamline it doesn't change. its more than enough to deal with every threat that comes his way. It in a sense adds to each character in a way that no other RE game has  before.

Now lets wrap this review up it getting pretty long unlike this game. Lastly lets discuss the length of the game. Obviously the game is very short. On my first play through it took me a little over 5 hours to get through and that's because I stretched it out by pretty much finding all files and weapon upgrades. But, if you just play through it once or a few times but, aren't very through it is very noticeable. I put over 30 hours into this game as i am an achievement hunter and do enjoy speed running the game. Something a lot of people do not do. Its no secret due to time constraints a lot was cut and yes Capcom needed to delay this game to add content to it. At first glance the short nature of the game seems it lends itself to speed runners and achievement hunters. But, what if I told you it lends itself to players that want to master RE3MAKE. You see due to the short nature you will play through the game more mastering the dodge and completing the challenges in the game. These unlock special items that make the game easier and these items can be used on the harder difficulties (and yes playing the game on the higher difficulties offer more replay value as it tests your skill). The over all goal of RE3MAKE is to be able to play inferno without the use of special items and be able to S rank it. That's where you get your bang for your buck. But, like I said not everyone wants to do that or even enjoys doing that.

So with all that said this game is not worth 60 dollars for anyone. Its worth 30 for fans who enjoy the challenge of repeated replays of Resident Evil (a la speed runners and RE Fanatics). But, for the average person that just wants to experience Jill's last escape once maybe even play through it once or twice don't spend more that 20 bucks on it. Always wait for a sale on this game. Because, if you spend 60 bucks on it i will say your getting ripped off.

PS: The soundtrack and graphics are fire!!!!

It would have been ok being an expansion pack to the previous game. Get it on sale if you are a fan of RE series. Otherwise I suggest that you just play RE 2 Remake, detailed reasoning below.

Character design:
Character design  is on par with the previous game. Highly detailed models and memorable characteristics.
Monster design:
Only a few new enemies that aren’t straight are pulled from RE2 Remake. This isn’t all that bad, but you can count the number of these monsters with your fingers since the game is so short. The main enemy in the game (Nemesis) is well designed and I personally like him more than previous games mr.X design vice.
Map design:
 Game starts strong on map design with city streets with few stores to explore which were given crazy amounts of detail. Unfortunately this is short lived. The attention to details also disappears after the first 30 minutes of gameplay (including cut scenes).
Gameplay:
They added a new feature that lets you dodge zombie attacks with a button press, which is a welcome addition and an improvement over the last game. They also changed how the knife works. It now has unlimited uses, but you can't use it anymore if you are getting bitten. Near the beginning part of the game they introduce the most annoying mechanic I have ever seen on a video game called “parasite”. That reduces your movement and makes the screen go red with parasites. I almost wanted to stop playing during this part. Luckily it is quickly over like the rest of the game.
After completing the campaign you get higher difficulty modes and a shop that lets you buy unlimited ammunition guns. The difficulties make the game of course harder but also change enemy placement somewhat from what I saw. Not enough of a reason to play the game again in my opinion.

This remake stays true to the original by being as disappointing as the original once was.  Excluding RE1make, cutting content in these Resident Evil remakes seems to be a common trend and unfortunately for RE3make the original was such a short game to begin with that cutting content means cutting a 6 hour long game into a 4 hour long game.  That being said the game isn't as bad as some people say but being a remake of a game that was a step down from it's predecessor is a recipe for disaster and it doesn't help that the Devs focused work towards the bad parts of the original and did away with the good parts.

The crux in this remake is that Nemesis is a complete ♥♥♥♥♥, he somehow succeeds in being less threatening than OG Mr. X despite the massive improvements remake Mr. X had.  They were able to achieve this seemingly impossible achievement by catering to Mr. X complainers and making nearly all of Nemesis' encounters scripted and sparse; there is only one point in the game where Nemesis dynamically roams around the map searching and chasing you like Mr. X did in RE2make and it happens to be the best part of the game but it's a very short (around 4 minutes-long) section.  Afterwards, Nemesis progressively becomes less and less of a threat to the point where his appearances are secluded to only boss fights; the Nemesis of this game isn't worthy of it's nickname as 'The Pursuer' when the once useless Mr. X is a better pursuer than Nemesis is.  Excluding the first form, all of Nemesis' original forms have been cut as well and replaced by a licker-like 2nd form and a massive blob-like 3rd form that doesn't really make sense in terms of the lore of the series.  I personally don't mind these forms but the 2nd form has 2 rehashed boss fights that get old quickly and the reduction of human-like, weapon wielding Nemesis is overall damaging to the game and the image of Nemesis since being able to wield weapons was what made Nemesis special and superior to the other, more primitive Tyrant variants.  The biggest crime of them all is that the iconic, rocket launcher-wielding Nemesis only appears for a short 3 minute-long, on-rails section that is easily skippable.  During combat Nemesis has a wider variety of moves than Mr. X and is able to TOD combo you like the original but it doesn't matter since the existence of the perfect dodge mechanic and the fact he gets downed with just one grenade makes him a non-threat; it's a very low cost to the player and is always beneficial since he drops upgrades and ammo.  Remake Nemesis feels like an absolute joke yet he's so easily fixable by increasing his dynamic appearances, increasing his health to not be downed by a single grenade and lengthening his first form screen time, chalk it up to the Dev's design decisions, they chose poorly.

In terms of cut content, they cut the first section of the game by making it unexplorable, removed a vast majority of the puzzles and removed one of the most iconic areas in RE, the Clock Tower.  This is a sorely missed opportunity to increase the appearances of Nemesis and and while they do add some new content, the content cut is much more.

Now onto the gameplay and level design, the game barely passes as Survival Horror.  Meticulously placed Key items strewn across a labyrinth-like map is how classic RE likes to create Survival Horror by pure design as it forces you to backtrack to areas and continuously encounter enemies you've already seen before that eat more bullets than you are given.  This forces the player to make both a micro and macro decision with each and every enemy encounter in whether to kill them or  risk running past as not killing them will result in the player not only risking themselves presently but also in the future, that is Survival Horror.  The threat in RE games are zombies, but for classic RE games the threat can be anything, even say guinea pigs and the games will still be Survival Horror because the games are Survival Horror by design.  This approach to level design is what makes the maps of RE so memorable; the placement of every item and enemy is memorable thus making the game as a whole an incredibly memorable experience.  RE3make only barely passes in doing this in sectioned parts of the game, in the main area of the game for example, the city section, the majority of the area is optional, there's really only one mandatory place in the area that you backtrack to once or twice and you're done with the area which is so unlike classic RE and the original since the first main area is usually the most well designed, labyrinth-like area that you spend time on for the majority of the playthrough.  The areas after are linear with the final 2 areas being the only areas in the game that follow the classic RE design philosophy.  This is the main cause of the game being so short.  In terms of ammo, you get so many you won't know what to do with it.  Jill is a walking armory and you don't even need to use the plentiful ammo she has since she breaks ankles with her perfect dodge mechanic.  You can run past everything with absolute ease due to perfect dodge and it honestly could have easily been fixed if Nemesis just appeared more to mess with your rhythm and deplete your resources.  The game as a whole leans more towards Action Horror than Survival Horror which is kind of fine considering the original started leaning more towards action but the original for the most part was still Survival Horror; this game is more RE4 than RE3 though thankfully is not as action heavy as RE4 as it's final 2 areas save it's dignity.  

The massive shift in genre makes sense when you find out the development team for this game is M-Two, a team primarily consisting of staff members formerly from Platinum Games which you may or may not know is a company that primarily makes character action games such as Bayonetta and Metal Gear Rising.
