So let's throw that out of the window. It took me almost 6h30m to beat the game on the Hardcore difficulty. And that should be the difficulty to play this game if you want the closest experience to the original.

Action oriented? Well what do you know, the original game was the first entry in the series to lean on a more action oriented gameplay. Resident Evil 3 had Jill Valentine roaming around with a machine gun and a rocket launcher on her back pocket, giving zombies absolute hell. This is no different, even had more thriller/horror elements in contrast to the original.

Campaign is fun. It's short, but full. Not much backtracking, not much roaming around, you mostly have an objective and you know where to go, what to do. There's always something going on around you and the game never gives you the chance to take a break. It holds you, and never lets go until the very end. 

No need to keep this any longer. It's a good game. Don't let people tell you otherwise. It's the same as the original. Short, action packed, and fun. It's the Jill Valentine and Nemesis we know and love.

Honestly my only issue with this game is the fact that its way too easy. I haven't tried the Nightmare difficulty but Hardcore difficulty was an absolute breeze. I only had difficulties beating Nemesis on the last part i think and that's only normal.

Let me start off by saying, yes, RE3 is fun imo. I am not a pro at RE games, I love taking my time, and soaking in the surroundings. That being said, I am a very slow gamer on top of that. I beat the game at little over 6 hour mark. It shows 24hrs, well, I will get to that later. Still, I do not blame ANYONE for wanting to pay less here. The 6hr mark is spot on with my Leon A run (RE2). But considering you at least had a story B to run along with it, with albeit, slight differences, inflated that run time to about 10hrs. At 60 bucks, with gorgeous graphics and sound overhaul, I could verify the price point. But here, I can see why ppl were upset. 

I got the game half off, so the pain isn't teeth deep. So Ill say it plainly, I would NOT spend 60 on this game. Wait for sale, as I did. 30, or less, I think is OK (if your impatient). But if you can get it for 20, or less, that is perfect. The above being said, let's tear and rip apart, RE3!

The sound
The design is once again, top notch. From wind billowing through the empty rotting streets of Racoon City, to the difference running on the recently moist concrete road VS hard wood flooring in some random, most likely infected persons home. Even to the opening and closing of a rusted door VS the futuristic high tech sliding sound of metal doors is very well done. Top marks almost all the way around, it really allows the world to pop, and keeps me invested! Now, to the reason why I said "almost"... Weapons. I don't know who does the music and surroundings, but bravo! Whoever does the weapons, well, not.... bravo (don't judge me). It is something I just cannot understand, y'all are right there! Just make some tough sounding, mean biting, flesh ripping, pew pew sound effects, and I would be over the moon excited! RE2 suffered in this department too, tbf. But at this point, I give up Capcom, you seem content on BB guns. I just hope someone there comes around and revamps the sound of the weapons, and allows gamer's to have ear orgas.....

Graphics
No surprise here! RE Engine is a sight to behold! It really is perfect for RE style games (I mean, it was obviously built for it, but yeah). Except no less then RE2, but taking place outside REALLY showed a new side of this engine I was not expecting. Cop cars emergency lights, and the street lights pop with life. Neon sides cannot go missed, doing as they do in real life, catching your eye without even trying. Puddles reflecting the whatever is around them, almost like a mirror image. This game KNOWS how to bring a world to life. Even chomping off the heels of RE2, they still managed to beat my expectations. You will not be disappointed. 

The Story
RE games, at this point, are not hard to follow. That isn't because the story is given its due. No. Its because you pretty much already know it. I kind of hate this fact because this game jumps around like a rabbit doing a fat line of cocai.. I get the Devs and original players get it, and don't really need more. But this was MY first time playing RE3. A game I have wanted to play with a passion for so many years. I actually had one of those life moments, when it feels like your heart skips a beat, once I found out RE3 was in fact coming after RE2. There are some characters I still don't fully understand. Characters not given the right amount of time to be fleshed out. Capcom just made the bad and good guys stereotypical and called it a day. No double cross, or anything for that matter needed. I am not saying change the story, but RE2 was able to give everyone their time, although some seconds long. Some where even built around the atmosphere alone (Chief Irons office). RE3 is as simple as it looks. I just wish they would have taken this remake and done something with it. That is all I am saying. Granted, you at least get a beginning, a middle and an end. Which is something in this current gaming world.

Acting
Nothing to say here....... Except this this was spot on! I am a simple guy, so maybe that is my issue. But everyone came prepared and delivered beautifully. From Jill, Carlos, and the rest. I really cannot tell you a time I wanted to laugh, or rolled my eyes of the cheesiness. This was acting done right! Please, keep this up.

Things I did not like
DODGING: Not the worst, but very hard to master (for me anyway) and you absolutely feel great when pulling it off. However, there IS clipping, and rubber banding. I would figure in a more slower paced game, this would be ironed out. But there were enough times of my character going right through the enemy. Which is usually followed by the enemy getting an insta-meal by taking a chuck out of my leg! Other times, I would dodge / hit, and yet, the zombie would get the grapple still. The parry is not by groan, or their arms length, it is by their lunge. What I do like, is zombies can lunge from a foot, 6, to sometimes, 2 inches away. Really giving you a sense of needing to be a timing master! So timing these correctly can be tough. Nothing wrong with that, but there times I know I got the timing but was still bit. My best example was when I tried to parry and punch the enemy. But my character shoulder slammed instead. The zombie on the other hand, got the grapple somehow, but was flung off of me before dealing damage. In the same motion, my character went from a should slam, into a punch. The zombie was hit by the shoulder slam (because that is what was done fist), but some how flung FORWARD like they were punched in the back. It made me feel the dodging can be a crap shoot of what comes of it. Which in a survival horror, isn't good.
LENGTH / PRICE: Not going to speak much, but I am reinstating to be clear. I REALLY wished the city section and hospital was longer. It could have balanced the game, which in turn, the price. 
CUT CONTENT: Again, I never played the original, but I do read reviews. It wont take you long before someone else brings it up. I have read, three locations have been cut from the game. Funny, how I feel the story jumped around a bit, well, this is most likely your culprit. Look, this is never good. Capcom, if you needed more time to develop a game, let us know. For a masterpiece, we can / should wait as gamer's.

So in summary, RE3 IS  a good, fun, thrill ride! It's not too scary, so for beginners, it's a good place to start. I love how the interwoven the station and you actually got to see some back story before Leon, and Clair (from RE2) show up. In fact, I would say, if you buy RE2/3, play 3 first, then 2. But as much as I give praise, I also see the length and cut content and think of what could have been! The station, again, is a prime example of detail that I love to see! I am not sure if the Devs were cut short, for RE8, or if they were happy with what they had, but I kind of feel this was abandon while being a work in progress. Because of that, I stand beside it being a fun game. But beg you, wait for a good / great price first! 

No matter what though, if you buy, I hope you enjoy!

As a fan of the series since the release of RE1 on PlayStation more than 25 years ago, after finishing my first playthrough of this game on hardcore difficulty, I have concluded that this game succeeds where the RE2 remake (REmake 2) failed. It honors the original in a way that REmake 2 doesn't.

RE2 is one of the largest and most replayable games ever made; especially for its time. So when REmake 2 finally released and it was so short and lacked a true 'B' scenario as well as having weird continuity errors in its story and some awful boss fights, I was disappointed in many ways.

My general feelings going into REmake 3 were apprehensive and not very hopeful. I can safely say that I was surprised by just how much I enjoyed this game. RE3 holds a special place in my heart; Nemesis—himself—specifically. To address the elephant in the room, yes; they did go in a totally different way with the redesign. They've gone for more of a Western horror theme than a Japanese horror one, which some purists may not be able to look past. Fortunately, I don't count myself among that group.

One reason this game is so much more successful as a remake than REmake 2 is the fact that the original (RE3) was never intended to be a mainline entry; it was actually a short experience compared to its predecessor. Capcom knew this; evolving from the "4th survivor" mode in RE2, they invented what became a series mainstay: "Mercenaries mode" as an unlockable bonus mode to compensate for the game's shorter length.

If you were not aware, no, there is no Mercenaries mode in this game. Capcom instead packaged a multiplayer mode that was made externally by a Korean development team; as far as I remember, and at the time of writing this, I have not played it.

(This game being the length that it is is not a detriment; the original was basically the same length. In other words, the length is not anywhere near as big of a factor in this remake as it is in REmake 2.)

Another absent feature is the "choose-your-own-adventure" moments from the original. This is another strong point of contention for fans of the original.

As there is no getting around the absence of both of those arguably integral features, this remake, when judged solely as a remake, is an abysmal failure; however, when judged completely as its own thing—a story-driven survival horror game—that simply carries the name of its predecessor, there is a well-crafted and intense, story-driven experience here.

Firstly, the mouse and keyboard (M&K) controls are fantastic. This game handles beautifully on M&K; because of the aiming mechanics in this game, having a mouse to aim with doesn't act as an "easy mode" either. The menus are fully M&K supported and are perfectly accessible. My only gripe with the controls is that I was unable to find an option to reverse the mouse scroll for the weapon wheel—small gripe, admittedly, but worth mentioning nonetheless.

As for the changes between REmake 2 and 3, there are several small, yet very significant changes to the mechanics that make this game a more enjoyable and consistent experience than REmake 2. The zombies now have a clear death animation—reminiscent of those from RE Zero. The dodge mechanic takes some getting used to; but it does not detract from the experience and also does not cheapen the game in an annoying way. It can be mastered and abused, surely, if you have the skill to do so; but for me—not a try-hard—I don't find myself reliant on it to get through the game.

While the third act goes in a different direction than the original, the game had earned enough goodwill from me that I was willing to let it be what it wanted, without too strong of a purist bias. The single ending and excluded levels and enemies also get a pass from me for the same reason. That said, I do wish Capcom would have included the graveyard and the worm; notably, the rundown, dilapidated feel of the original is absent from the game. I had a similar gripe with the lab level in REmake 2; it was replaced with a shiny and clean looking redesign. The same holds true for this remake. Though, again, that was a stylistic choice, and one that REmake 2 went with previously; so it would be reaching to expect the art style to change for this game.

The biggest surprises for me were seeing the Nemesis actually drop cases with weapon parts and ammo; I honestly did not expect that to be carried over from the original at all.

I was also very happy with how this game treated the return to the RPD building and how it changed the ending of Brad Vickers' story. Both were handled well; the game acts as a companion piece to REmake 2 in ways I never expected. Which again gets into why I feel that this game was so much more successful as a remake than REmake 2. It honors the original while also offering a new retelling—a "spin" on the story of the original. This was also expressed by the producers of REmake 2 in interviews; but I didn't feel that any of the story changes were all that clever or surprising. They felt like they were used as ways to shorten the experience or acted more as a result of the new style rather than as an homage in recognition of the original. TL:DR: The changes in the story here earn their place.

The cast of characters is fully realized and far more interesting than those in REmake 2; Nicholai and Tyrell are standouts.

Jill is a more endearing hero than REmake 2's Claire as well.

The zombies are fantastic here and can be frightening in their relentlessness.

The set pieces are immaculately designed; the experience as a whole has some harrowing moments.

Without spoiling anything, I can say that this game, if nothing else, acts as a showcase for why Capcom has chosen to skip a Code Veronica remake in favor of a RE4 remake.

All in all, Capcom has really done this lifelong fan proud.

For the first time in years, I'm actually excited for where this franchise is going.

Having another remake and a continuation sequel (RE8) in the pipeline simultaneously—as well as a Netflix live-action show in the works (starring Wesker's daughters—a strange choice)—fans of the series have a lot to look forward to over the next few years.

Resident Evil 3 Remake was my first time experiencing this part of the series, and while I enjoyed it, it never quite reached the standard set by the Resident Evil 2 Remake. It’s a entertaining horror-action game, but it feels a little too slight to stand at the same level as its predecessor.

The presentation is one of its strongest qualities. The visuals, environmental chaos, and cinematic direction do a great job of selling the atmosphere, especially in the opening. The character performances and animations also help the story stay engaging, even if the short runtime leaves some moments and characters feeling less fleshed out than they could have been.

Gameplay leans more into action than survival horror. The core third-person shooting still feels good, and additions like dodging and environmental hazards give combat more variety. Switching between Jill and Carlos also helps keep the pace moving. That said, the game often feels more streamlined than satisfying. The environments are more restrictive, the problem-solving is lighter, and the enemy and level design don’t create the same tension or depth that made Resident Evil 2 Remake more memorable for me.

I feel noteable issue was value at launch, not necessarily value now. When I played it at debut, it felt short on content, replayability, and overall substance for a full-price standalone release. I still recommend it to fans of the newer Resident Evil style, but at the time it left me with the feeling of a high-quality expansion rather than a fully substantial package.

The best way for me to know if I enjoyed a game or not depends on how much I can pick it up again for a replay and I have to say that this game gave me little reason to play through it again for several reasons.

The first being the strictly linear gameplay which removes any kind of choice the player is able to make. While the choices given in the original title made little impact in regards to the story (there were still minor changes and outcomes) it at least put pressure on the player to make a decision which opened up extra rewards should you choose to execute them. 

The second being the near removal of puzzles. Resident Evil is synonymous with terrible, janky puzzles and the original was no exception. The removal of these felt like a part of the heart and soul was removed in order to accommodate the linear, action gameplay and is sorely missed.

The third being the changes to the story itself. The introduction of the Nemesis in the original was a build up to an ominous being which hunts STARS after you encounter Brad in a diner whereas in this there's no build up. It simply happens and I find that does a huge disservice to Nemesis. Elements are shifted around, old locations are removed and those put in their place have a very lazy approach. At this rate, there will be a RE game where you just start in a NEST and have to find your way in to the NEST of the NEST.

Fourth being the disservice to Nemesis himself. Right from his introduction I feel like Nemesis was such a wasted opportunity especially after Mr X. He's scripted to be suited for the linear gameplay which makes him far less menacing than Mr X in RE2R, he looks awful and his boss-form fights are incredibly uninspiring. This is easily the most disappointing aspect of the game because it undermines what was once an iconic villain and turns this omnipresent threat in to a corridor hurdle.

Last but not least the city setting. For a game which puts emphasis on the sprawling city of Raccoon City you actually explore less of it than you did in the original which is a shame since it would have been great to see more or at least feel as though you're at the street level as the events are unfolding.

The game itself isn't terrible it's just a shame that it happens to be Resident Evil 3 Remake especially when Capcom knocked it out of the park with RE1R all those years back and RE2R not long ago. I gave them the benefit of a doubt that lightning could be caught a third time but something happened where they allowed the developers to have too much creative freedoms which essentially wiped out most of the source material in favor of this which only hurts them because now many are less enthusiastic about additional REmakes if this is what we can now expect.

Riding the coattails of one of the best remakes ever created you couldn't blame anyone for being hyped to play REmake 3. I was impressed with the demo, despite noticing a few minor flaws, and was exited to play a tense horror game where a large murderous threat could be lurking around every corner.

What I was served was far more action-oriented and event-driven than what I was expecting. You feel like you always have to move forward to either the next area or to get away from Nemesis and moments of silence and tension are rare. With a campaign length of about 6 hours REmake 3 makes for an entertaining action game with a good cast of characters, including Nikolai who is one of the most evil and well acted villains I've ever seen in a videogame.

The "minor" flaws I noticed in the demo became far more pronounced after playing the full game. A remake is supposed to expand on what worked in the original and improve upon the elements that didn't. This game cut a large section of the original game, removed the puzzles entirely and reduced Nemesis from the terrifying stalker Mr. X was in REmake 2 into a never-ending chase scene with the occasional arena boss fight and quick time event thrown into the mix. Though I certainly had fun playing the game I found the overall experience to be shallow and disappointing.

Not a terrible game, it stills has some of the great gameplay feel and action from the RE2 Remake, but the problem is that is way to short (yes, I'm aware that most RE games are not that long and are supposed to be played multiple times, but this one is particularly short, around 5 hours in the first playthrough, the whole campaign), it also has terrible pacing and most of the nemesis encounters are terribly scripted. This game fails to capture both the quality of the RE2 Remake as well as the original RE3.

Let's start from the beginning. The first hour of the game is great, you open up with the city infested by zombies and you have to traverse a lot of open ground with many puzzles, enemies and places to explore, this is the same place from the demo (which I think it's great and was the thing that sold me into the game) and this is also the place where you will encounter nemesis for the first time, he is fast, strong and relentless, I loved my first encounter with him because it manage to really made me feel threatened and scared of his presence. In general exploration, resources and combat felt fantastic in this area and sadly it all went downhill from there.
The rest of the experience is mostly linear (except for the hospital area which has a little bit more exploration) and the rest of the nemesis encounters are bosses and scripted ruining sequences. Checkpoints become way too close to each other given that the maps aren't that big or generally well designed and the game becomes just a 3rd person shooter with zombies given that suddenly the game starts giving you tons of ammo and you normally end up clearing dozens of enemies without a worry for the resources, it's just not that fun and it really goes against the pacing of the previous installment and the original title.
It lacks the encounters options and narrative choices of the original, and it also just straight out skips most of the content from the original PSone era title and it’s just too focused on action, it actually manage to remind me of the game design of RE 5 and 6 (although this one is a lot more bearable than RE 6). I will say that I liked the characters of this game and their interactions better than the original, still, it´s an RE game, so it’s not like we are talking about high quality writing to begin with.
The game looks amazing, the RE engine still really keeping up even against other AAA titles, action gameplay is solid and mostly really fun and unlockables give some replay value to the game, yet, the problem is that while an entertaining experience, it's just really a disappointing sequel and just a terrible remake that fails flat on its face when it comes to do justice to the original Resident Evil 3.

Extra note: Given that I have now finished the game a 100% (this note is after I wrote the rest of the review), I must say that it’s a competent action horror title, but only on standard and hardcore dificulties, nightmare and inferno modes are just super ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, super artificial and frustraiting dificulties and in the last boss fight against nemesis is pure RNG, forget about resources, healing and everything else, you need to do trial and error and get really lucky, it’s horrible and in heavy need of a nerf. It feels as if it just didn’t get enough testing and polish and was thrown in the game at the last minute of development, it’s inconsistent and most of the time just down right broken, this boss is really one of the worst ever designed in the whole series. 

So, I don’t hate the game, but it’s just not worth a 60$ price tag, it has problems, really big ones, but the gameplay loop and presentation are great, still, it feels more like a DLC to Resident Evil 2 Remake rather than its own original title, I would only recommend buying it on a heavy discount.

Sadly, I am giving this one the thumbs down. I don't think it is a terrible game, there is a lot to love about it in fact, but I am left feeling quite unsatisfied because of its flaws. It is a great game in a lot of ways, but it is also a huge missed opportunity.

The things that I loved about it:

- the sense of atmosphere throughout the game
- beautiful graphics
- excellent music
- the characterisation of Jill and Carlos. I found them, and the rest of the characters in the game to be very well done.
- the Downtown and Hospital sections of the game
- the gameplay. controlling Jill and Carlos feels the same as Leon and Claire in RE2R (with minor tweaks). Less puzzle/exploration than RE2R, but still quite enjoyable.
 
Things that were not great:

- there's an insane amount of cutscenes in the game
- there are many cutscenes and scripted sequences that require you to 'press forward' or some other button. These sequences are annoying, unnecessary and immersion breaking. To give an example, if you want to start a new game, it takes about 10 mins of skipping cutscenes, rushing your way through areas where characters are talking to you, just to get to the start. It is very tedious after your initial playthrough.

- it feels as though there is not enough game here.

Now I have to explain the point above because a lot of the complaints have been about the games length. Yes, the game is short, but many games are, and it is not always a problem. RE2R is not that much longer than this one to be honest.
The difference here though is that RE3R just FEELS a bit hollow. It needed a bit more meat on the bone.

There is a lot of talk about the cuts and changes, and although I don't put the original on a pedestal (I've only played it once and it is not among my top RE games), Capcom really did cut too much in this instance. It really feels like you play through downtown, breeze through the Police station with Carlos (I thought returning to the station would be cool but it is one of the weakest parts of the game and can be wrapped up in about 10 mins) and then bam, you're at the hospital and it feels like you're at the end of the game already (and you basically are).

When I heard there were big cuts I did not care at all as I thought they were just streamlining the story and it would work out. No, the game really needed at least one more significant area to feel complete. The only areas that seem to have had serious thought put into them are downtown and the hospital. The sewers, police station, and nest 2 are not particularly interesting and very brief.

I am giving this game a negative review, not to say 'don't play it', but more to let people know that one way or another they will likely end up unsatisfied with this game (yes, even if you buy it on sale). Like I said, there is a lot to love about RE3R but it is baffling why so many resources seem to have been put into creating showy 'cinematic' sequences while the overall quality of the product was neglected.

EDIT 2: More thoughts on the game...

So now that I have played the game a third time (on nightmare) I have a little more clarity on why this game is unsatisfying overall.

Apart from the stuff I have mentioned above, the game also kind of has an identity crisis.

On one hand, it has the same inventory/weapon system as RE2 Remake, but it actually is more similar in structure to RE4. Despite having similarities to both of those titles, it is simply nowhere near as good as those.

RE4 is extremely linear for a RE game (technically it is a different genre of game anyway), but it is absolutely brilliant at what it does.

RE2 Remake may have a few deviations from the original, but it perfectly captures the essence of old school RE gameplay.

RE3R is somewhere in between and doesn't do the greatest job of it.

Also, a huge difference between RE2R/RE4 and RE3R is that the more you play RE2R & RE4, the more you appreciate them, take comfort in their brilliant design, and discover new ways to conquer them. The more I play RE3R, the more obvious its shortcomings become.

In fact, RE3R probably is most similar to RE5 (not a good thing), but sadly, RE5 is probably the superior game at the end of the day.

After playing the game a few times, I strongly believe that the team behind RE3R simply did not have the resources to do it right. It kinda feels like they designed a bunch of environments, some of which are BEAUTIFUL (downtown), and didn't have the time to really figure out how to utilise them in an interesting way. Perhaps some areas of the game were intended for exploration but to save time and get the product out they relegated them to backdrops for set pieces that required minimal input from the player.

It is possibly that the clock tower was originally intended to be a playable and significant part of the game, but they had to wrap things up and just leave it as a backdrop for a boss fight. It really feels like something went wrong during development and things were simplified to hasten production.

Last thought: Nemesis kind of feels out of place in this game. Now as I said earlier, the original RE3 is not super precious to me, but they made his presence a lot less interesting in the remake, because it feels as though Nemesis does not exist in the same world as the player.

What I mean is, because you only encounter Nemesis in boss fights here and there after the downtown section, there is no sense whatsoever of being hunted. It feels like Nemesis is just some weird thing that shows up for the sake of having a boss fight. In other words it could have been replaced with anything and it wouldn't change the game at all. It is a shame, and it just adds to the subtle feeling of dissatisfaction.

[h1]A thrilling companion to last year’s Resident Evil 2, Resident Evil 3 is the fitting, if a tad short, closure of the Raccoon City saga we were looking for.[/h1]

When last year’s Resident Evil 2 hit the shelves, it did so to universal acclaim: the game was praised as a faithful reenactment of the original’s story and atmosphere while bringing the gameplay to turn of the decade standards. Thus, when Resident Evil 3 was announced, the gaming world held its breath in expectation of what the team behind Resident Evil 2 would bring. The end result, however, ended up being a tad underwhelming for many players around the globe. That is not to say that the game is bad; far from it – in fact, it is a remarkably good game, and one that lived up to my expectations as someone who played the 1999’s original (and which happened to be my first Resident Evil ever) but the standards set by Resident Evil 2’s otherworldly quality overshadowed Resident Evil 3 beyond any possible redemption.

You play as Jill Valentine, S.T.A.R.S. operative and veteran of the Arklay Mansion Incident that took place during the events of the first Resident Evil. The game starts one day before the events of Resident Evil 2 and ends some day and a half later. Thus, it plays as a sound companion to last year’s iteration, following the travails of Jill as she traverses zombie-ridden streets during the ill-fated final days of Raccoon City. Her quest, unlike that of Resident Evil 2’s Leon S. Kennedy or Claire Redfield is distinctively personal: hunted from the onset of the game by a mysterious and seemingly unstoppable creature, the Nemesis, Jill has but one goal: to leave the city alive. In her quest for survival she will come across a bunch of characters, most remarkable of which are those of the Umbrella Biohazard Countermeasure Service (U.B.C.S.) forces sent by the nefarious eponymous corporation to cover their tracks  and their responsibility in the city’s undoing. Aided by the mysterious Carlos, an U.B.C.S. agent, she tackles the job of assisting civilians and looking for a vaccine while thwarting Umbrella’s insidious plans and evading her relentless pursuer. It is a chronicle of the suffocating death throes of a city that is long lost and how two souls amid its chaos do whatever it takes to survive. The anguish is palpable, the urgency of the situation looming ever closer, and that is what the game manages to capture so neatly: its atmosphere of inexorable destruction in the wake of the outbreak that ravaged the city. Not only is the game great in conveying its aura of dread and despair, but it does so with probably some of the best graphics I have ever seen and a fitting musical arrangement -I will however say that I missed the opportunity to have the original’s music and sound effects, much like Resident Evil 2 did. Gameplay is also downright superb and just what one would expect from a Remake of Resident Evil 3: an action-packed horror game.

Yet for all its brilliance the game has been criticised for a multitude of things, most of which I feel are undeserved. First and foremost, the game has been criticised for the scriptedness and predictability of the Nemesis, especially when compared to Resident Evil 2’s Mr. X. It has been one of the more recurring remarks, yet one which I find rather unforgiving and unfair: most of the brilliance of last year’s Resident Evil 2 stems from its borrowing the original Resident Evil 3’s Nemesis mechanics and not the original Resident Evil 2’s Mr. X’s. Had the new Nemesis’ behaviour been cast using the same mould as the original’s, we would have ended up with a rehash of last year’s Mr. X, which would have fared poorly in the innovation department. Add to that that in an attempt to spruce things up, Nemesis was furnished with a myriad of abilities that if coupled with Mr. X’s ubiquitous, relentless pursuit would have made the game a frustrating exercise of constant obliteration by the game’s signature creature. The game has also been criticised for its lack of replay value which I also believe to be an unfair by-product of Resident Evil 2’s first and second run mechanics; while these were present in the original iteration of RE2, the original RE3 offered a story which branched out differently according to the player’s choices throughout the game. Such a mechanic (as welcome an addition as it would have been) would have been insanely expensive to implement on 2020, as it would have entailed crafting many times the quantity of assets that the game ended up having; it, simply put, would not have been feasible from an economic standpoint.

The game, however, does have its flaws: some of the best and more memorable areas of the original are either nowhere to be seen here or have been downright down-sized: the whole original segment that saw Jill run from her apartment to the RPD on the original is non-existent. Instead, Jill is outright ambushed by Nemesis on her apartment and evades it from the very first seconds of the game. What follows is a rather linear and heavily scripted flight from the creature that ends up with the main character being saved by Carlos… and this not even 5 minutes into the game! One does not need a keen eye to realise that what amounted to the first quarter of the original game has thus been butchered; scrapped altogether. Accordingly, Jill never sets foot on the RPD (though Carlos later in the game does) which was a sad departure from the original’s memorable sections in the erstwhile police station. The game does compensate for the loss of these by offering a significantly larger (and creepier) hospital segment as well as a brand-new NEST 2 Underground Facility. In shaking up the makeup of the game so profoundly, it feels more like a reimagining of Resident Evil 3, and not quite a remake. Moreover, for all their freshness, even these areas cannot compensate for Resident Evil 3’s true shortcoming: it is awfully short. A casual gamer playing on standard difficulty will have finished the story within the 5 hours mark on the first playthrough. Successive playthroughs for achievement-hunting will amount to lengths as short as 1 hour and 20 minutes, which borders on the ridiculous, even for Resident Evil standards. Its excessive reliance on linear levels hurts the game as well, lacking the sense of opennes that characterised the original. Finally, it is worth noting that whereas Resident Evil 2 had a plethora of skins and costumes to choose from, Resident Evil 3 offers only the default appearances for both Jill and Carlos as well as Jill's S.T.A.R.S. outfit as an unlockable. It is worth noting that you can buy a DLC comprising of an attire reminiscent of that of her original Resident Evil 3’s one as well as the traditional Carlos hairstyle. Contrary to most players, I dearly recommend that you get this DLC, especially if you played the original like I did; it costs a meagre price to pay and will go a long way in conveying that sense of nostalgia that you are probably craving for.

Yet none of this can detract from the fact that this is a good game, and a remarkably good one at that. Truth is, had it not been for the fact that Resident Evil 2 -simply put- emptied the creativity well, Resident Evil 3 would have had much more to offer in the originality department. Not only that, but Resident Evil 2’s insane level of quality set the expectations bar way too high for this game to reach, let alone surpass. Yet it deserves to be considered for what it is:  while it cannot be mistaken for a survival horror game (as Resident Evil 2 Remake undoubtedly is), it is more than a worthy companion to last year’s Resident Evil 2 and a sound 3rd person horror shooter that will appeal to those nostalgic for the original Resident Evil 3 and for newcomers to the series that are hoping to complete the Raccoon City story arc.

Resident Evil 3 is a remake of the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis developed and published by CAPCOM Co, Ltd.

If you're expecting another great remake like Resident Evil 2... this isn't it. Loads of cut content from the original, no branching paths, more action oriented and [b] INCREDIBLY [/b] short and a stupid, tacked-on multiplayer mode

Also, why on earth does your main villain (which was also featured in the original title) do not pose any threat whatsoever. Mr. X in Resident Evil 2 was more threatening then anything posed by Nemesis in this version, whereas in the original he posed more of a threat

Double also, Nemesis in this version feels more like a nuisance and a constant annoyance, who just flips and pushes Jill around constantly (which by the way, by the amount of times Nemesis flips her around, she would have been dead within the first five minutes of the game's opening)

Also, I'd just like to add why... why... why on earth does Jill feels more sexualized? Such as the camera panning in to where it comes close to her buttocks or the way certain creatures treat her in a very innuendo type of way (people who have played this game will know of a certain area of the game where it feels like something out of The Human Centipede... why?), just... why?

The game offers some nice graphics, although some ugly glitches here and there, it is pleasant all the same and is an amazingly looking game thanks to the RE Engine

The game does suffer with some repetitiveness at certain areas of the game but an okay game nonetheless

Resident Evil 3 overall, however, is an okay game to play, yet sometimes repetitive and it does get boring if being played for a long time, but is an okay survival horror game to play in short bursts!

But as mentioned previously, if you're looking for the next great Resident Evil remake, CAPCOM squandered that with this remake and that is an utter shame and a pure waste of 60 EUR for a game that should have had it's full price slashed in half with the amount of content they included...

When Capcom announced the remake of [i]Resident Evil 3[/i] after the success of the [url=steamcommunity.com/id/atisz2/recommended/883710/]Resident Evil 2 remake[/url], I was doubly excited. First, because I was eager to play with another good game and secondly because I never played the original [url=en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resident_Evil_3:_Nemesis]Resident Evil 3[/url] from 1999. 
The remake received harsh criticism shortly after its release mostly by some youtubers/influencers. I would like to make it clear that while it indeed has some shortcomings and may appear a bit rushed, it is just as great as RE 2 was.

As Raccoon City succumbs into chaos during the T-virus outbreak (the game takes place before and DURING the events of the 2nd part), with most of its citizens already turned into zombies we step into the shoes of Jill Valentine once again, one of the main protagonists of the first [url=steamcommunity.com/id/atisz2/recommended/304240/]Resident Evil[/url]. Being closely observed by the corrupt police chief she decides to leave the dying city while she still can. After receiving a phone call from a colleague, she's immeadiately attacked by a large humanoid creature who's intent on killing all the prominent members of Raccoon City Police, who might know something about the origins of the T-virus. As she barely escapes with the help of a mercenary named Carlos and while running for her life from the seemingly invincible monster, she must also search for the vaccine against the deadly virus, before she runs out of time.

The game follows in RE 2 Remake's footsteps by revitalizing the survival horror category (which the series partially lost from [url=steamcommunity.com/id/atisz2/recommended/254700/]Resident Evil 4[/url]) while maintaining the action oriented gameplay which wasn't present in the original (RE 0-3) parts. The successful combination of the 2 is largely assisted by the immersive over-the-shoulder view and the fact that the entire game takes place during the nighttime.

steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2143970682

Our arch enemy is the titular Nemesis, who - while resembles - is quite different from Mr. X.. This time we don't have a swiftly walking giant in our tracks, but an unnaturally fast creature that can easily outrun or grab us. As it chases us and (re-)emerges from time to time, fighting zombies without him being on our tail actually becomes a refreshment. Or rather it would be, since ammunition for our guns is very scarce and by 'very', I mean it even by RE standards.
While we find plenty of additonal once useable items, such as grenades and flash grenades, these can no longer be used as last resort self-defense items. What we can do against zombies that are about to grab us is a new feature Jill possesses, dodging. If we manage to time it right, by pressing Space, Jill can perform a perfect dodge, which slows down time giving us opportunity to do a counter-attack (by aiming immediately after) if we have the knife (which no longer breaks, thank goodness) or a firearm equipped, the game automatically aims at the head of our enemy, providing time to place a few headshots. This would make playing with Jill easier than it was in Leon's case, but it doesn't really, since the zombies are more numerous this time and dodging is often our only 'weapon' against Nemesis (actually at most of the chase sequences we can - and we SHOULD - turn and 'fight' him, since by bringing him to his knees, he 'drops' suitcases containing precious weapon upgrades or some ammo, just like in the original).
What makes our job definitely easier is that we no longer need ink ribbons to save at the typewriters present at most hubs which connect areas. These 'save rooms' still provide shelter, but since Nemesis' emergence is scripted at most points, these will only grant short pauses where we can catch our breath.
Just like in the original game, the bossfights consist of fighting the various forms of Nemesis at certain sections of the game. Flame grenades (which are usually pretty much useless against zombies) are a safe bet during these encounters. Nemesis is also capable of turning zombies into more dangerous 'tentacle headed' variants, that can hit us from a distance. The 2 new type of monsters include a very annoying parasitic insect and the sewer-residing 'gamma'.

While most of the criticism RE 3 received comes from the fact of how short it is, it's not entirely true. The highly esteemed remake of the 2nd part can be beaten/'speedrun' even under an hour (!). What made RE 2 seemingly longer was the Claire scenario (which only slightly differed from Leon's part) + that both paths could be played by both characters. By skipping these, RE 3 indeed appears shorter, but it wouldn't be a fair comparison.
My personal grudge is that the Raccoon City downtown area consists of basically 4 (!) roads with roadblocks and a few little alleys. One of my hopes was that this time around we could explore a larger portion of the city that plays a key role in the Resident Evil series, instead of the boring sewers and underground laboratories present in all RE games. Sadly, we can't.

On the other hand where the 2nd part fell short, the Ada & Sherry segments, RE 3 shines by giving us control over the Umbrella mercenary, Carlos. This happens twice throughout the game, both times when Jill loses consciousness. For me these parts were the highlights of the game, since they brought back the old survival horror atmosphere of both the remake and the original series very effectively. With Carlos we get to explore the Raccoon City Police Station (hours before the arrival of Leon) with all its perils and an eerie, abandoned hospital full of fast moving hunters. We also get separate item boxes (Jill won't be able to access them, so there's no need to keep those extra healing items) and his own unique machinegun which - even when fully upgraded with a special scope and a grip - is unfortunately a rather weak weapon against the mentioned hunters.

steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2147449640

Other elements still function as they did before: item combinations, gunpowder mixing to create different types of ammunition, weapon upgrades and a minimal amount of those boring puzzles. There are also QTEs (quick time events) and while there's a fair amount of time to perfom these (especially after we got used to dodge effectively), I still managed to die due to one right at the end of the game, where I was least expecting it :/
And for some reason limb/crippling shots don't seem to work as well as they did before: a zombie will probably rather die after a dozen of leg shots instead of actually losing the leg... so with the help of perfect dodge I highly recommend going for headshots.

The graphics engine is retained from [url=store.steampowered.com/app/418370/Resident_Evil_7_Biohazard/]Resident Evil 7[/url] and the visuals are maybe even better than in RE 2 with some quirks and rough bits here and there. While the main characters are elaborate, some models such as Tyrell or the hunters (their uniform dark green colour doesn't feel right) don't reach the set standards. For me the face model choice for Jill was also a bit strange, I would have preferred Sienna Guillory instead.

I had high expectations towards [i]Resident Evil 3[/i] and it didn't disappoint. While it has its fair amount of shortcomings, most of these were also present in RE 2 remake. The attention to small details such as meeting old characters or (re)discovering the origin of the destroyed wall in the RCPD bathroom also make the game unique and memorable.

PROS
+ superb survival horror atmosphere, especially with Carlos
+ Nemesis provides an abundant amount of surprises
+ excellent visuals, plenty of cutscenes
+ good voice acting
+ references to Resident Evil 2

CONS
- only a few roads and alleys represent Raccoon City
- dismembering zombies doesn't really work anymore

RATING
8/10

Really solid survival horror experience, but not a lot of content and replayability compared to other Resident Evil installments. RE3 steps away from the openness of RE0, RE1 and RE2 with more linear level design that doesn't involve much backtracking or puzzles. The game seems to expect you to fight enemies more than you would be expected to in the previous titles, but the game definitely gives you the firepower to handle anything thrown at you. You also have more capability to avoid enemies mid-combat, with a perfect dodge-roll for Jill and a perfect counter for Carlos. The enemy design and diversity is well done as with most RE games, forcing you to fight them differently and with different weapons in your arsenal. Nemesis provides amazing tension throughout the game. As you would expect, he appears at the most inopportune times to make your life miserable and make your objectives more difficult to carry out. The threat that Nemesis poses always looms over you in the beginning portion of the game, when he is in his first stage. The boss fights with Nemesis are engaging and a fun challenge, and they demonstrate what an interesting bioweapon he is. The character interactions provide corny one-liners and charming interactions, and the story rounds out the beginning three Resident Evil games well. Having played RE4 and RE5 before this game, it's easy for me to see that this is where RE games started to take a new direction, with more level-to-level based design rather than placing the player in an open setting like the mansion and having them explore their surroundings. Personally, I like both types of Resident Evil experiences, but regardless, this game should cater to fans on either side of the spectrum. However, I do think the game is lacking in content, since there is only one route in the game while most RE games have at least 2 routes. The game seems to attempt to make up for this by adding an additional difficulty, Nightmare, and of course the game comes with the multiplayer game RE: Resistance. Resistance is good additional content for sure, but Nightmare is not a good enough replacement for a route. I never played the original RE3, but as I understand it did not have a second route, so not adding a second route is probably more faithful to the original game. Nevertheless, I would hope that a remake would dedicate itself more to adding content that adds to the original content of the game it is reimagining. Regardless, RE3 is a great survival horror game, but it might not be worth 60 dollars.

To preface this review: I never played the original game (Resident Evil 3: Nemesis) released in 1999 for the Playstation. As such, I played this game for what it is as a standalone, not in comparison to what it was back in 1999 nor to the Resident Evil 2 Remake from 2019.

The Resident Evil franchise is known to have coined the genre “survival horror”, which is known for its maze-like maps, puzzles, inventory management, and ominous ambience. Players are crippled through limited ammunition, health, or speed to add to the players lack of control. However, the game does introduce some new gameplay elements, perhaps inspired from games of the Dark Souls genre, such as performing perfect dodges that reward players with a window to counter attack.

The narrative of the game ties in with those of the rest of the games in the franchise and fits the classic zombie movie trope. Raccoon City is infected by the outbreak of the T-virus, which turns everyone into zombies. You switch between playing as one of the two main protagonists of the game – Jill Valentine, who is part of the Special Tactics And Rescue Service (STARS) and Carlos Oliveira, who is part of the Umbrella Biohazard Countermeasure Service (UBCS) – as they try to survive and find the vaccine for the virus. You aim to defeat the pharmaceutical conglomerate Umbrella, who is responsible for creating and releasing the virus. At the beginning of the game, you are immediately thrown into action as you are pursued by the biological weapon of which this game is known for: Nemesis.

Character development is also very well executed. Jill is put in imminent danger and beaten down so many times, a sign that despite being the main character, she is still human. Carlos flirts with Jill quite a handful of times and shows that he actually cares for her. Carlos’ comments on how weird the doors are in the subway station and mentioning how our tax dollars are used to pay for art further pushes the idea that our main protagonists are human just like us.

The thing that I immediately noticed was how visually stunning the graphics were. The game provides no shortage of scenes that make you feel like you are watching a movie rather than playing a game. One thing I really respect and appreciate is Capcom’s attention to detail. You can zoom in on a wall and observe its textures or focus in on a book and read the text legibly. I noticed that they put more care into every character’s expressions. There are also many scripts and books scattered throughout the game that you can read to gain further information on the lore.

To cater to players of all demographics, new players and veterans alike, the game offers five modes: Assisted, Standard, Hardcore, Nightmare, and Inferno. On Assisted mode, you get an extra assault rifle with auto aim and health regeneration. You will only unlock Nightmare mode after you beat Hardcore mode and Inferno mode after you beat Nightmare mode. In Inferno mode, everything is altered. All the enemy and item location from previous modes will be changed, so you cannot depend on clearing it off memorization of past playthroughs. There are less save points, no auto checkpoints, less ammo/healing items, and you will die after 1-2 hits from enemies. This emphasizes the need to learn how to perfect dodge. These five different modes greatly increase replayability. Resident Evil games were never “long” games to begin with, as players are encouraged to speed run through playthroughs, learning which items are essential and which routes are optimal.

This game is hard, but fair, and I appreciate that. There will be times in the game where you forgot to pick up an item, exhausted too many bullets, or were low on healing items. There will always be enough ammunition and healing items scattered throughout a boss arena to progress you through the game. It is Capcom’s attention to these gameplay details that have drawn me to play more of them!

Albeit a “short” game with a single playthrough of around 5 hours, this game gave me around 40 total hours worth of play, including the time it took to complete the hardest difficulty with S rank and to achieve a Platinum trophy for the game. After your initial playthrough, you will unlock an item shop in which you can complete challenges to unlock points for purchasing additional in-game items, such as an Infinite Ammo Rocket Launcher. With the introduction of these gameplay elements, this promotes more replayability and flexibility to different play styles and strategies.

Now for a few gripes that I do have with the game. Although the Resident Evil series is meant to be replayed as well as speed run, the replayability aspect does get dry very fast. With each subsequent playthrough, the game definitely gets less and less exciting and fun as you mostly know what to expect and do. Unless you are a hardcore gamer trying to achieve a record-speed run time, you would probably cease to play through this game after two or three runs. The boss fights in this game are also somewhat underwhelming, with very scripted and expected appearances, which takes away from the survival horror aspect of the game. The price for this game on release, $60 msrp, is also a very steep price for the amount of content you get, even though you do get the online multiplayer game: Resident Evil Resistance included as well. At the end of the day, I still had a lot of fun playing this game and am looking forward to the next game in the series :D!

Here's the issue with RE3. Not only did it have to successfully reimagine the original Resident Evil 3, it had to compete with Resident Evil 2 Remake which was released early last year in 2019. RE2 Remake established a pretty great survival horror experience using the newest version of the RE Engine, so expecting RE3 to come close or surpass RE2 was going to be a challenge, because the overall setting and theme of RE3 was much different compared to RE2.

RE2 was focused on set locations such as the Police Station, Sewers, and Umbrella's Nest. RE3 had more unique locations but the time you spend in each location was much shorter, so it is much harder to achieve a lot of that constant backtracking that existed in RE2.

The original RE3 was also slightly more action oriented, so they added some new elements into RE3 like the perfect dodge and counter attack. To compensate, you couldn't use protection items to prevent bites like from RE1 or RE2, so if you get grabbed, you're going to get bit.

As far as the game itself goes, it was above average. The gameplay was obviously very similar to RE2 Remake, but still felt a bit easier because perfect dodging was too easy for me. The new stalker threat, Nemesis, was way too scripted, he didn't chase you as much like Mr. X did in RE2, so you're not going to be feeling much threat with his presence around. Some locations were cut too like the clocktower from the original RE3, but some areas were also expanded, like the hospital.

The length of the game compared to RE2 Remake was also a few hours shorter. In my opinion, they should have added the cut areas to the game to extend the main story, it still felt too short. The initial Raccoon City phase should have been much larger as well, it felt like you didn't get to explore much of the city at all except a few places. They should have included more streets, shops, and points of interest.

The puzzles were very weak in RE3. For an RE game, I hope Capcom actually listens to the fans and improve upon this for future games.

Graphics, audio, immersion, all these things are really good. One minor complaint is that the blood/gore effects for zombies have been toned down compared to RE2R.

The boss fights are alright, nothing too spectacular, it's typical Resident Evil boss fights that you are used to. They have a few mechanics to understand and once you get into the rhythm, you can probably do it with your eyes closed.

One good thing RE3 has over RE2 Remake is that there is a shop system where you can purchase some new items to help you on your second playthrough. There are 3 difficulty modes upon starting RE3R, but you unlock 2 more harder ones once you beat the game the first time. To unlock the final hardest mode, you have to beat the game again on the new difficulty to unlock the 5th and final difficulty mode, so there are 5 total modes. The shop system has certain unique items that you can use during the game, and to earn credits to use in the shop, you have to complete certain objectives/challenges during a playthrough of the game. The first item I unlocked was this fire dagger which burned zombies and other enemies if I stabbed them enough times. This was better than the standard knife for obvious reasons. You can also unlock special coins that, when held in your inventory, can boost your attack power, defense, or regenerate your health. You also can unlock new weapons. Use your points wisely. This whole system added more replayability to the singleplayer experience.

I'll give this game two separate ratings. The first is a professional rating of the game based on what the devs did and didn't do. The second rating is my own personal opinion, which can differ from the professional rating.

Professional rating: 7/10 - As an RE game, RE3 was lackluster, simple, and pretty short. Characters, gameplay, graphics, were decent, but Capcom could have done a much better job like they did with RE2 Remake.

Personal rating: 8.5/10 - I still enjoyed the game and can forgive some of its faults. I liked many things about the game such as the new enemies, the environments, and some of Nemesis' behaviors. The locations towards the end of the game gave me the creeps.

Thanks for reading.

This game looks spectacular. It is a super fun game to play. But I'm gonna say this straight, the game is super short. It took me between 5 and 7 hours the first run through, and then I've played it 2 or 3 times again, which took me little less than 2 hours each! But knowing you're paying a price a bit high for a game of this length, everything else I have to say about it is great. It looks nice, it plays nice, and it keeps my faith in the franchise together with the RE2 remake.

[b]Graphics/Performance:[/b]

The graphics on this game look fantastic, with great textures and effects, and a great level of detail on the surroundings. The characters design is excellent, and even the changes from the original are well received on my end. And for those who don't love the new Jill design, you still have the old character design as an extra! And both look great on the game (I know, I played it like 4 times, had to do something different). Also this game is very well optimized. Same as it's predecessor. It's a game that runs on very low system requirements and performs perfectly. Also, playing around with the settings, I can tell you that it even looks nice on lower settings. But playing on max-settings, I've never felt a frames drop on the game.

[b]Gameplay:[/b]

The gameplay on this game feels super realistic and easy to learn. The shooting goes smooth, it's easy to aim and every weapon feels good on your hands, to take out wave after wave of brain seeker zombies. The puzzles are perfectly placed and easy to resolve, so you can get back to the action fast enough. I didn't feel at any time that the game was glitchy or seen any bugs. Capcom has really achieved a great game here. In the end the gameplay is rather simple, but it's exactly what it needs to be for this game. You have some level of crafting and different ammunition, as you might expect from a remake of the classical game. And the achievements are fun to go for, with quite interesting rewards, though I must say: Despite the fact of unblocking infinite ammo and weapons is fun to achieve, playing with infinite ammo takes out a lot of the fun to the game.

[b]Story[/b]

The story of this game is great, as you should know if you played the original on your childhood. It has some fantastic plot twists and the story develops on a great way. I won't give any spoiler, but I must warn you that some details on the story (some more important than others) change from the original. But all in all, it feels the game makes justice to that old game that had us sticked to our console (or PC on my case). If there is a con to the story, it's its' length, as I already mentioned. And that is the only reason that made me feel I paid a price too high for this game. The game is excellent though. The acting is also pretty good.

[b]Veredict[/b]

This is a great good looking game, and if you loved the original and are not tooo picky, you'll probably love this one too. It's an excellent game to have in your library and I totally recommend you to buy it... just, maybe wait until you see it on a good offer. I must admit I enjoyed more the remake of RE2. But still I enjoyed this one a lot too, and I will replay it even once more at some point. This is an 8 out of 10.

Honestly even as someone who recommends this game I can not just wave away all the valid complaints of other fans. Its true that its way too short, its missing areas from the beginning, and its over priced for what is a campaign with a tacked on multiplayer. That being said this isn't a bad game by a long shot, and it's not even what I'd call lazy. The voice, level design, animation, and story is still given the same amount of care as Resident Evil 2 Remake. With the areas that were cut or changed the story never really suffers from pacing problems. You have to remember that RE3 original was substantially short as well comparatively to RE2. This game was always going to be short. I personally agree that this probably would have been better as a DLC to RE2 but I feel they added enough new enviroments and mechanics that maybe the choice of making it a seperate game was called for. There are some things that this game even has over the original in terms of retelling the story to fit with the current game's stories and contexts. The redone RPD section, hospital, and its climax all are really solid, and help stream line the original Raccoon City games into a more cohesive story. The game is definately more linear than RE2 as well. No real backtracking (but this was pretty much the same for RE3 to be fair) making the experience be one unbroken campaign. What this leaves is a pretty fun adventure from beginning to end that can be beaten in a day. My recommendation is buy it on sale, probably around $30 is fair,  though I bought it at full price and don't feel too much regret. I should mention Resistance as one of the few people to have seemed to have played it in this review section. It's okay. Its not bad, apparently when the game launched there was a cheating problem but the game has seen a substantial drop in active players in general so I have never personally seen cheaters. The matches revolve around a player as a mastermind trying to kill the other players before they can beat several stages of trials. The other players are survivors that need to beat every stages goal while trying to stay alive. The matches are short and they can be fun if the other players are actively talking and helping each other. It feels like a shorter, match based, version of Outbreak Files 2. Its not something I'd buy on its own but its not really hurting the game with it's inclusion.

[b]About:[/b]
Resident Evil 3 is the game from the famous CAPCOM survival horror franchise and, pay attention: it is a remake inspired by Resident Evil 3: NEMESIS, a PlayStation classic released in 1999, following the same line as the previous remake of series, Resident Evil 2 Remake.

[b]Plot:[/b]
The game features Jill Valentine as the protagonist, a police officer who is trying to escape Raccoon City while being chased by NEMESIS, a kind of biological monster created by Umbrella Corporations to annihilate S.T.A.R.S. members, in order to erase sensitive information about the organization.

[b]Gameplay:[/b]
The game basically uses the same recipe as Resident Evil 2 Remake – the gameplay has been completely modernized and optimized for the current generation, with a very high quality and simplicity. For those who played the PlayStation classic, it must be easy to recognize some scenarios, characters and enemies, but in a less hostile and more unfolded way. The game does not have the Resident Evil 2 Remake campaign system selectable, having only a linear campaign, which by the way is very short and without many twists, being able to finish the game in a time of approximately 4 ~ 7hrs. Just like in the classic, Jill Valentine meets Carlos Oliveira, a veteran soldier linked to the U.B.C.S. - Umbrella Biohazard Countermeasure Service. Instead of being playable in a separate campaign, he has his moments dedicated to the story unfolding. The gameplay is very similar to that of the previous remake: Armed combat, map exploration, items and weapon systems, etc. However, there are some caveats that need to be mentioned: You no longer have the system to get rid of a zombie with the knife, the game has an own avoidance system from Jill and Carlos, which is very efficient, but does not work very well in some moments due to the delay of the movement itself when performing it. The inventory remains small, but the game's loot system is much more generous compared to the previous remake (which was a better experience for me) and the game's puzzle system, so striking in the series, is almost not present, unfortunately. By the way, I would almost forget about the game's “icing on the cake”: Nemesis. At each encounter with the biological monster we have in the game, its 3D model is different, revealing various forms of the villain during gameplay. Moments of mild distress when running from the villain and pretty simple battles do not make the star of this game bad, but it leaves a lot to be desired in relation to Mr. X, the villain of the previous gameplay, who has scenes of real despair and quite difficulty in the battles against the monster, leaving the player really immersed in the villain, something that is not repeated here. Regarding the scenarios, they really are very good, but he gives the impression that they just “copied and pasted” the previous remake, without much news, graphics improvements or easter eggs inside them, really unfortunate. On the other hand, when it comes to the new scenarios on the “otherside” of Raccoon City, we can see that the city has more life: shops, staircases, pharmacies, train station, etc. Really done with great care, with vibrant colors on the signs of the stores and the giant head of Mr. Charlie on top of the Toy Uncle store really makes a splendid contrast between the destroyed city and the scenery, something really magnificent.

[b]Graphics:[/b]
Speaking of the most delicate part of the game, the game really is a cinematic work, from which you can easily recognize the high realism of the facial hair and hair in high definition of the characters when the game abuses the close-up on them. The facial expressions in different dialogues with the protagonists are really incredible – movement of the eyes, mouth, eyebrows, movement of the arms, create several possibilities of reactions within cinematics. The physics, dynamics and 3D models of the characters are really mind-boggling, as are the animations, the carnage in killing a zombie and the effects of blood. The depth of field in the transitions between gameplay and cinematics and the field of view itself, really make a game a great work of art. The shadow effects are dense and realistic, as well as softened, respecting their position while an animated model or object moves. The screen space reflection that are based on rasterization that only invert the image of what is visible on the screen is very good, as it is an extremely common technique in the world of games, having only a few errors in specific moments, which could be corrected with technologies like raytracing. The game also has a lack of fluidity in the animations of the long hair of characters that have it, like Carlos for example, they have a strange physics and framerate, as well as the shadows of the zombies in the scenery background, which gives a somewhat contrast how weird in the game. The game has some artifacts in TAA (Temporal Anti-aliasing) technology, which uses the previous frame to correct the knurling of the next scene, and this happens when there is a sudden change in the change of scenery, nothing so noticeable that it interferes with the player's experience. When it comes to the PC version, the game is extremely optimized, and runs even on computers with simpler configurations. I experienced the game in Ultra quality in Full HD, with the resolution scale at 130% and locking the game at 60 frames, using the DirectX 11 API and I didn't have any crash, bug or sudden drops of frames during the gameplay, despite many reports from users who had problems with bugs and crashes in the game using specific AMD hardware.

[b]Soundtrack and dubbing:[/b]
Unfortunately, the game has no voiceovers for my country (Brazil), but it has subtitles in my language and they work perfectly well. The soundtrack of the game is good, appearing only in times of greatest distress as in battles against Nemesis. The dubbing is good, with the exception of non-American characters, like Mikhail and Carlos, who have an extremely strange and poorly worked native accent, spoiling the immersion with these characters a little during some cinematics.

[b]Is it worth it or not? [/b]
It's worth it if you're really a fan of the saga. Even for those who, like me, have not had the opportunity to play the PlayStation classic, they will have an immersive, pleasant, simple and even frantic experience sometimes. What is not worth it is the value: the game, until the date of this review, continues to cost the price of its release: $ 59.90, however, if you don’t really care about it or manage to buy the game in some sale, go ahead. In summary the game is very good, leaving something to be desired such as its short gameplay time and lack of puzzles. However, it is undeniable that the game still has the Resident Evil experience in vein.

[h1] Intro [/h1]          
Resident Evil 3 is not an unenjoyable game, but I can't in good conscience give it a thumbs up. It's more of a cash grab by Capcom than anything. Capcom rushed this game instead of giving it the proper time to be developed and fleshed out. RE3R has a lot of content that's missing from the original Resident Evil 3. In reality, the original RE3 was short, you could finish it in 5 hours or so, but it had actual replayability. You could redo the campaign and go through different areas that you didn't see in your first playthrough because of choices, and even have different endings for the game with different characters surviving or dying. The original also had Mercenary mode, which added even more replayability as well.

 [h1] Gameplay & Mechanics [/h1]

Sadly, the current RE3R misses out on the replayability bit, and once you finish the game, there's almost no reason whatsoever to go through it again. It's a once and done kind of game. It's even shorter than the original RE3, and you can finish the game in 3-4 hours. If I had to compare it to Resident Evil 2 Remake, I would say it pales in comparison in many ways. Because at least with RE2R, you were able to feel that the game was well developed and that Capcom had put a lot of time and effort into the game to make it replayable and enjoyable with different branching paths. They took the original RE2 and remade it with care while also improving on the original game. RE3R doesn't do any of that, and Nemesis is a literal downgrade from the original RE3 game. He's scripted and barely shows up, in the OG RE3 he was randomized. He would show up at random times and attack you, and he was definitely more menacing and scarier in the original than he is in the remake. He's not really scary in the remake. He's more of an annoyance than anything else. I actually found Mr. X from RE2R to be a lot scarier than Nemesis was in the remake, which is just depressing. The gameplay is pretty similar to RE2R, but now you have an unbreakable knife and a dodge ability that makes you evade attacks from Nemesis and zombies alike. It's a nice addition, and it works well, but other than that, the gameplay is almost the same as RE2R. However, there is one big difference between the two games though, RE3R is mostly an action game and isn't horror focused like RE2R was, so you're going to be seeing a lot of action and less of the atmospheric horror feel that you got from RE2R.

 [h1] Graphics [/h1]

How about the graphics? I can tell you that the graphics are as good as RE2R because they obviously use the same engine, but sadly the game was downgraded when it comes to dismembering the zombies. You can no longer dismember zombies like you did in RE2R. I feel it was downgraded to allow the consoles to run the game smoother since the areas in RE3R are a lot bigger than RE2R, and they do throw more zombies at you to deal with, so they downgraded the game just so the consoles would be able to run it well. I'm also not a fan of how they redesigned Jill's model. I feel the new face doesn't look remotely similar to the original or previous games. I won't dwell much on this point because it might be subjective, but overall I was not a fan of the new redesign.


 [h1] Resident Evil Resistance [/h1]

The game also came packaged with Resident Evil Resistance, I personally feel it should have never been bundled with the RE3R, and it should have been a separate game that's f2p or has the same model as Dead by Daylight. It took development time away from RE3 to make this game, and I feel it wasn't needed. RER, as It's currently, is a mess, the game doesn't have dedicated servers, and It's solely reliant on p2p hosting, which comes with its own issues. The game has many game-breaking bugs and glitches that the devs are very slow to fix, and it also relies on a loot box system to unlock items and cosmetics, in 2020 I can't for the life of me understand why this mechanic still exists for progression. I haven't delved a lot into Resistance, but my early impressions are not good.

 [h1] The Good Parts [/h1]

Now, what are the good things about the game? Well, I can tell you that the action bits are enjoyable, and being in open areas feels a lot different than RE2R and gives you a different atmosphere than the previous game in a good way. Also, having to deal with hordes of zombies and other enemies all at once definitely puts you on the edge of your seat and can be challenging. Sadly, that never lasts long because the action setpieces are short, but are definitely the most memorable parts of the game.

 [h1] Conclusion [/h1]

All in all, Resident Evil 3 Remake is a forgettable experience, and a missed opportunity by Capcom and the game isn't an improvement on the original like RE2R was. Capcom took the short route for this game, and it shows. It's such a shame, this game could have been so much better, but greed won out in the end with Capcom. 

My overall rating for the game is 6.5. I can only recommend buying this game if it's on a big sale. Otherwise, It's not worth the full price tag at all, and you would be wasting your money for a game that only lasts for 4-5 hours tops with almost no replayability whatsoever.
