This game should be called RE 3: The Director's Cut, with 'cut' being the operative word here. Yes cut-content and an embarrassingly short campaign is the item of the day here, coupled with a shallow and incredibly sub par multiplayer mode in an attempt to save face. 

At its core, RE 3 is unquestionably a fun third person shooter. Shooting zombies and hitting Nemesis in the face with a bazooka has never been more satisfying. Jill and Carlos feel good to control, especially given how third person camera angles can sometimes be hit or miss with mouse and keyboard (I go back and forth on it personally, but this game feels good to control no matter what you're using.) Plus in comparison to the playstation, the controls here are a godsend. I had almost zero technical issues to speak of, which is good seeing as how this game barely had a 2 year development cycle. 

But there is no way i can justify anyone buying this game for $60, i feel cheated and i spent $40 on this game! Replayability for this game is low to average at best, with that replayability being present solely due to higher difficulties and its short length, not due to any desire or feeling like you could explore the game further. Compared to the far superior RE 2 remake, my experience felt like i was zooming through a tunnel in a car at 100 mph, with barely any time to take in the gorgeous environments and characters that i see fading in my rear view mirror. The next thing i knew, the game was over. I'm not gonna go into how much content this game cut, there are plenty of other reviews on Steam alone that have covered that. To keep it short, the cut content is A LOT. For context, the original game had 8-13 hours worth of content, this game has only 5. So, faced with a deadline and a lack of content, Capcom decided to make a foolish mistake that a lot developers do: pack in a "free" multiplayer mode that is more shallow than a kiddy pool. Overall, the multiplayer feels superfluous within a series that is almost solely single player, serving only as extra padding and a justification for its 60 dollar price tag. If it was a choice between the cut content and the multiplayer mode, i would pick the cut-content every single time.

Like what did you expect me to use this multiplayer for Capcom, to wipe my butt with it? I would but I'm afraid that my butt cheeks would chafe. [h1] [b]Resident Evil 3 (Remake): A Thrilling, Action-Packed Survival Horror[/b] [/h1]

The [i]Resident Evil 3[/i] remake, released in 2020 by Capcom, brings the 1999 classic to a new generation with updated visuals, reworked gameplay, and a more action-oriented experience. While it successfully reimagines a fan-favorite, it doesn’t quite reach the same heights as its predecessor, [i]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/i]. Still, [i]Resident Evil 3[/i] offers a highly engaging, atmospheric ride that will please both longtime fans and newcomers.
[h3] [b]A Reworked Survival Horror Experience[/b] [/h3]
The game follows Jill Valentine, the iconic heroine of the [i]Resident Evil[/i] franchise, as she navigates the chaos of Raccoon City during the outbreak of the T-virus. As she struggles to survive, she’s relentlessly pursued by the terrifying Nemesis, a hulking bio-engineered monster intent on hunting her down. The remake delivers tense encounters with Nemesis, which are a hallmark of the game, and elevates the stakes with dynamic action sequences.

Graphically, the remake is stunning. The environments are beautifully detailed, from the burning streets of Raccoon City to the dimly lit, abandoned buildings. The lighting and sound design contribute to an oppressive atmosphere, maintaining the series' trademark sense of dread. The redesigned models for characters, especially Jill, are incredibly lifelike, making the game's visuals one of its strongest aspects.
[h3] [b]Faster, More Action-Driven Gameplay[/b] [/h3]
One of the most significant changes in [i]Resident Evil 3[/i] compared to its original is the shift towards more action-based gameplay. The remake features smoother, faster combat, which makes Jill feel more agile than in previous entries. The combat is more refined, with more responsive controls, allowing players to quickly dodge and counterattack enemies. This makes encounters with both zombies and Nemesis feel more intense and thrilling.

However, the shift to action did lead to some complaints from fans. The original [i]Resident Evil 3[/i] was more focused on exploration and survival horror, and the remake reduces the amount of backtracking and puzzle-solving. As a result, some players feel the remake loses the slower, more methodical tension of the original game, opting instead for a faster-paced experience that’s more in line with the action-heavy trends of modern gaming. The game can be completed relatively quickly, taking around 6-8 hours to finish.
[h3] [b]Nemesis: The Relentless Threat[/b] [/h3]
Nemesis remains one of the game's biggest highlights. His pursuit of Jill is constant and terrifying, creating a sense of urgency throughout the campaign. While his AI is not as unpredictable as it was in the original, his presence still serves to keep players on edge. There are moments where Nemesis will burst through walls or unexpectedly show up, turning an otherwise quiet moment into a pulse-pounding chase. It’s a thrilling and memorable aspect of the game that reinforces the survival horror experience.
[h3] [b]The Downsides: A Shorter, Streamlined Experience[/b] [/h3]
While the remake succeeds in its action-driven gameplay, it does take some liberties with the narrative and pacing. Some areas and characters from the original are missing or significantly shortened, which may disappoint long-time fans. The game feels shorter compared to [i]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/i], and the lack of additional content, such as the original’s more intricate puzzles and exploration, might leave players craving more.

The multiplayer component, [i]Resident Evil Resistance[/i], is included but doesn’t stand out. It’s an asymmetrical multiplayer experience that feels like an afterthought compared to the rest of the game, offering little value to those seeking a strong multiplayer experience.

[h3] [b]Verdict[/b] [/h3]
[i]Resident Evil 3[/i] is a thrilling, fast-paced remake that retains much of what made the original a classic but modernizes it for today’s audiences. While it focuses more on action than the slower, survival-horror atmosphere that fans loved in earlier games, it still delivers an exciting, visually impressive ride. The game succeeds in its presentation, combat mechanics, and Nemesis encounters, though its shorter length and lack of exploration may leave some feeling unsatisfied.

For those looking for a concise, action-packed survival horror game, [i]Resident Evil 3[/i] is a solid choice. However, if you're seeking the more meticulous, slower-paced tension of the original, it might not fully hit the mark.

[h1]No Rescue is Coming[/h1] 
When the Resident Evil franchise debuted in the spring of 1996 it was a revolution. I remember playing the original, fresh out of its big black PlayStation box, and having my 9-year-old brain zapped into a euphoric mesh. It was the first time I’d really played a violent video game. My parents, blissfully unaware of the flesh-eating murder rampage going on in the next room, had just purchased a PlayStation for me that Christmas. To them, video games still meant Pac-Man and Mario. And I was completely fine with them believing that. They couldn’t know what was happening back in that room. They couldn’t know it was video game history. They couldn’t know that borrowing from previous, but lesser-known, survival horror video games came something called Resident Evil. And the medium evolved because of it. 

There would be no more Pac-Man for me.

[h1]Who is my Nemesis?[/h1] 
A quick jumpcut to modern day. A married, slightly overweight, balding 33-year-old is picking up the controller for another go-around with Jill Valentine. The remake of the original 1999 classic Resident Evil: Nemesis is out, now titled (perhaps a little confusingly) Resident Evil 3. What I am introduced to in the 5–6 hours or so of gametime is a title that puts the exclamation mark on the viability of remakes – particularly remakes that are recycling game formulas long considered archaic. What was reintroduced to in 2019’s Resident Evil 2 remake continues to be buffed out and refined here.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2159388941 

The difference – and I think this may have affected many peoples’ opinion on the RE3 remake – is that this game crosses genres. Leaning heavily into an action-oriented experience, RE3 is more interested in delivering set pieces littered with environmental spectacle. Ammo is more plentiful, enemy encounters are denser, the whole game feels, frankly, easier than its RE2 predecessor. Lastly, Nemesis is the replacement for Mr. X and he doesn’t hunt you like in RE2. Story-wise, yes, but not mechanically.

These changes can be alarming because they create potential for a watering-down effect. The more action, typically, the less horror, as the game inadvertently (or on purpose) ends up over-empowering the player. 

Jill isn’t locked in here with Nemesis; Nemesis is locked in here with Jill.

[h1]Survival Horror Meets Bazooka[/h1]
It's something I should have had a problem with. After all, isn’t the entire point of going back to the roots of Resident Evil to recapture the original horror magic? Well, yes. I suppose. But the story of RE3 is buffered against that rationale because this isn’t Jill’s first rodeo. She is a veteran, a bio-weapon killing machine, as she is the original heroine of the mansion incident. She’s our Batman. And when the action gets a bit over-the-top, the game effectively switches from the player controlling Jill, to our new hero, Carlos. More survival horror elements transpire while controlling Carlos, which, either by happenstance or on purpose, makes sense narratively speaking. He doesn’t know what Jill knows. That is to say, he’s actually the rookie here. And it’s a nice change of pace to have the player take control of another protagonist for an actual reason. And for more than five minutes (ahem, RE2 remake, ahem).

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2159389795

Another explanation why I don’t mind RE3 wading into something more action-based is that the RE2 remake didn’t always do horror particularly well. Chief Irons was laughable. And Mr. X’s bumbling presence was just as likely to annoy as frighten. So why not? If Capcom’s RE Engine is also conducive to action, why not blend both genres? 

The gameplay is done in the same style as the RE2 remake, with slight variations in systems. It’s played, almost entirely, in third-person. Jill, unlike our other Resident Evil “supercops,” is equipped with a new dodge roll and a knife that no longer breaks. This knife is mainly used for prodding zombies, ensuring they are down for the count (I miss the pooling blood from yesteryear). And it’s possible to get proficient enough with the dodge roll that it renders some encounters, possibly even with Nemesis, a bit trivial. In one boss fight, whether through luck or skill, I was never touched, thanks to rolling. 

Again, perhaps we’re a bit too empowered?

[h1]Ghost Stories[/h1]
The actual story of Resident Evil has always been silly, so don’t expect that to change. But it takes itself very seriously. There’s zero winking to the audience, and the voice actors do an excellent job of delivering pathos when it matters. Even when their lines are a bit cringy, the actors still manage to sell them. In particular is Jill, who somehow convincingly delivers lines that compare Nemesis to a “creepy stalker.” And she really makes it work! It seems entirely character-based, and adds verisimilitude to the action that is unfolding. Simply, it made me like her.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2159389171 

This isn’t new, but the story also wades into environmental and journal-based delivery of narrative beats. I’m not sure why they coincide, but when an RE story is less horror and more action-oriented, the journal entries seem to matter less. The result is the series’ weakest readable collectibles. Perhaps it’s because many of the horrors that unfolded with the T-Virus outbreak are typically documented so well in the notes you read (I still have some memorized from the original RE), and this game isn’t as interested in why the outbreak occurred and unfolded? But there’s nothing, story-wise, that RE3 does wholly wrong here. Jill is a veteran to this world. Leon and Claire weren't. It makes sense they’d have more to learn. 

Regardless, pitfalls are avoided. And there are no gaping continuity errors like existed in its predecessor. Truthfully, RE3 actually does a better job of preserving and respecting RE2’s continuity than RE2’s conflicting scenarios did in the remake. And it also manages to deliver tiny nuggets of the events that will later lead to the action in RE4. 

Having played most Resident Evils, I think the story works as well or better than most of what we’ve previously encountered, but...  

The issue most people who played the original Resident Evil: Nemesis are going to have is that the game strays incredibly far from what one might expect a “remake” to do. As someone who has beaten RE:N many times, it was a disappointment not to see some of my favorite moments resurrected here. Don’t expect this to satisfy nostalgia to that end. It’s not interested in doing that.

It’s also not a very long game. My entire first playthrough lasted about five hours, which is something consumers should be aware of before making the purchase. In terms of the pacing, it makes sense. There’s really no reason, in a game stuffed with so much action, that it necessarily needed to go longer, but “quality over quantity” becomes debatable when we’re discussing a mere five-hour playtime. Particularly coming off the heels of another remake that had content ranging two to three times longer, depending on the player.  

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's divisive. It doesn’t walk the steps of what it supposedly remade. And it’s short. This could be a deterrent for anyone spending money on this, expecting it to recapture the same thing I was capturing as a 9-year-old all that time ago.

But consider what it is instead of what it is not: An action-packed night through a zombie-ravaged city, playing as an armed-to-the-teeth video game icon, using an innovative engine that retools classic Resident Evil systems. 

To me, it sounds like a helluva way to spend a night in Raccoon City.

If you are looking for a game that played like the RE2 Remake, then sad to say that this is not what you're looking for. If you are looking for a nostalgia hit with updated graphics, then this is still not what you're looking for.

The RE3 Remake is an action-packed game, but most of the action you will be doing is dodging and dying; especially if you want to play on hardcore mod to unlock nightmare mode. 

The knife and grenade mechanic of stuffing these items into zombie mouths when you get grappled is no longer part of the game. The controls feel a little like trying to make a sharp turn with a big rig truck as you tend to swing wide no matter what your mouse settings are, and the aiming for your starting handgun in general does not feel good. I have tried with aim assist off and on - it makes no difference.

The claustrophobia the game seems to be trying to create also does not mesh well with how much action is going on at any given moment. There IS an FoV slider, but at this time it remains grey'd out in my options regardless if I am in game or starting from the menu. This has to be a bug, but the way the tight quarters and cluttered space are, I doubt changing the FoV would do much aside from throw off your sense of perspective.

And this last one is a bit nit-picky, but Carlos no longer has his Hispanic-American accent. Mikhail kept HIS accent, but Carlos now sounds like a Chad. I'm not certain why they thought to do that.

I will say that the game is beautiful, and the story explains some of what the original RE3 did not, but I was personally hoping for another experience like the RE2 Remake provided. Bullet sponge zombies regardless of head-shot accuracy are not particularly fun.

I could play on easy mode instead of normal or hard, but I feel like I would be babying myself. If you want tense action from start to finish, this game probably is what you are after - but be warned: the controls are not as precise as they should be.

Resident Evil 3's remake fails to respect its source material and feels like a rushed cash-grab to capitalize on the recent popularity of Resident Evil 2's remade success. While it acknowledges some of the original Resident Evil 3's features, it lacks the ambition of both its original and the respect Resident Evil 2 Remake gave to Resident Evil 2.

To understand why Resident Evil 3 remake received a downvote, it's necessary to attain the perspective of playing its original. The original Resident Evil 3 had many unique aspects nonexistent in its remake. First, there are no decision prompts affecting the path Jill takes to the ending; it's a linear experience. Second, there are almost no puzzles, besides one near the end and some basic "where do I go" mazes. Third, some prominent stages are also omitted, such as the clock tower, although the clock tower is featured as a brief background set-piece and via an in-game newspaper file, which is even more insulting as it proves Capcom's developers knew the clock tower's significance. Finally, the most egregious sin is the remake's treatment of the Nemesis.

The Nemesis in the original mastered the art of balancing semi-random and scripted encounters to keep player's guessing. His behavior closely exhibited enemies from Haunting Ground (aka Demento) and the Clock Tower series. This made the Nemesis an unpredictable threat who seemed to dynamically roam Raccoon City, providing different experiences on subsequent playthroughs. In the remake, none of this applies; he's entirely scripted and is largely relegated to boss fights, scripted encounters, and cutscenes. Ironically, Mr. X from Resident Evil 2's remake behaved closer to the original Nemesis! It's appropriate Resident Evil 3's remake does not call itself "Resident Evil 3 Nemesis," like its predecessor did, but rather is simply titled "Resident Evil 3." It's as if Capcom knew they didn't invest enough attention into the Nemesis system.

Jill Valentine also returns as the story's protagonist, but she isn't the same Jill from previous games. This Jill has a rude demeanor, and when she's not on a bad mood swing, she's hurling profanities; this is not the Jill most of us grew up with! What ever happened to the positive-minded Jill from Resident Evil 1, who after almost getting crushed like a "Jill sandwich," simply laughed and thanked Barry for saving her? There are better ways to exhibit character strength than displaying a negative attitude.

After completing the game, there's little incentive to replaying. There is no Mercenary mode as seen in the classic Resident Evil 3. Again, there's no alternative in-game decisions seen in the original Resident Evil 3, and unlike Resident Evil 2 there isn't an alternative character to replay the game with. There are new difficulty options which mixes up some of the item and enemy locations, and in-game unlockables, but it's a lazy way to artifically inflate the game's replayability. There's a free add-on called Resident Evil Resistance, but it's a broken mess and has mostly negative reviews.

There's still some fun to be had with Resident Evil 3's remake. If you enjoyed Resident Evil 2's remake, then you'll get more of the same. For better or worse, it's a carbon copy of Resident Evil 2's remake, which is appropriate given the original Resident Evil 3 was planned as expansion content to the original Resident Evil 2 before being made into a fully-fledged title. What's unforgivable is this remake reeks as a rushed cash-grab. It fails to understand the significance of its source material while blatantly omitting several of the original's key features. If you're a Resident Evil fan, I'd still recommend it for the gameplay, but if you're looking for a remake that respects the original, then you'll be sorely disappointed.

Final score: 4/10.

Resident Evil is a franchise that needs no introduction. I've been playing these games for over 20 years, and the original Resident Evil 3 is one of my favorites in the franchise, so you could imagine how excited I was when I heard that Capcom was remaking it. 

Before I bought this game, I read some of the reviews for it, and to my surprise, people were review-bombing it. Why? Because they say that it's too short and that it isn't a true remake, as the game lacks some content from the original game. So, are they right? Well... yes and no. I have played this game twice. My first run on Standard Mode took around 6 hours. My second run on Hardcore Mode took just 1 hour and 25 minutes. Yes, this game can be short, but it can also be as long as the original, if you take your time to explore, as I did in my first playthrough. I do agree with those reviewing it that say that this isn't a remake, but I disagree with them giving it a bad review because of it. Bad reviews should go to bad games. This isn't a bad game, at all.

Though this game can be short, it does have some replay value. There are challenges that you can complete to earn points that allow you to buy weapons, tools, and upgrades for your characters, after you beat the game for the first time. This will help you on more difficult runs. Also, there is a multiplayer game, aptly named Resident Evil: Resistance, that is a separate installation, but comes "free" with this game. I haven't tried it yet, but I know enough about it to know that it isn't a Mercenaries game.  

As far as performance goes, this game is well optimized, as long as you don't go messing with the image quality or the volumetric lighting settings. Wow, they're demanding, even with an RTX 2070. My only performance concern was a little texture pop-in, but it was few and far between, and I'm certain that it's an issue with DirectX 12, which is notoriously problematic.  

Overall, I'd give this game an 8/10. Though I prefer the original, I really do love this game, too. I'd recommend buying it at a $40 or less price point, which is what I paid for it.

I usually don't write reviews, but as a long time fan of the series, this has been the most disappointing Resident Evil game since RE6. RE2make wasn't perfect; it had it's mistakes, as did the original RE3. I still was super hyped for this game as I did enjoy both of those games. This remake dropped almost everything unique and interesting about RE3 and altered what it kept in a way that left much to be desired. The first minutes of the game created an engaging atmosphere that showed promise, but that atmosphere got smothered by the barely interactive first encounter with Nemesis. For a game that already feels so lacking it is frustrating that some of the most intense moments of the game are cinematics of Jill get chased by Nemesis.

It usually takes me at least 8 hours to finish a Resident Evil game the first time around. I always explore, take time to think about things, make mistakes. It took me about 5 hours to finish this game, and that includes all the above and me just leaving the game idling for a bit. There was just too much taken from the original that was not sufficiently replaced. Gone are several puzzles, brain suckers, the Grave digger, spiders, The Clocktower, Graveyard, Park, City Hall, freeze rounds (rip), Mercenaries mode, the live selections, Barry's appearance, multiple endings, and so on. Nemesis was intimidating for about 5 minutes during the first part but was ultimately less dynamic and terrifying than in the original or Mr. X in RE2make. Nemesis, THE Resident Evil pursuer, being less dynamic than Mr. X is such a let down. Additionally, I felt like there was more time with the U.B.C.S. in the original, and that Nicholai was more interesting as well. 

Perhaps this lack of content was to be expected. This game came out a year after RE2make, and was being bundled with the multiplayer game (which I have yet to try as it just reminds me that Capcom will never give Outbreak another chance). However, the original Resident Evil 3 offered more with a similar time frame. of development. It is truly disappointing that this is the experience that newer fans will have of what Resident Evil 3 can offer.

Overall good game, but not as good as RE2 Remake.  As a matter of fact, I can copy/paste most of my review from that game, as little has changed gameplay-wise and aesthetically from that.  See below for that, as well as a “What’s New” section added to each category:

GRAPHICS: Realistic facial expressions, environments loaded with personality (just like the original PS1), great detail in everything ranging from the monsters to the weapons. The game looks too sweet at 1440p, 144 fps.

What’s New:  Nothing, really.  Everything is identical, even many of the zombie character models, background objects, weapons, items, etc.  There are a handful of newer monsters, including “yours truly” from the game’s cover art, but that’s it.  Still looks great, but don’t expect to be wowed again.
`````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````

SOUND: This to me is the key element of any horror game. The eerie sound of silence mashed up against a subtle air vent rustling, or was that a monster growling........? Uh oh, better approach that corner carefully in case something tries to eat me. The score kicks up in intensity when you engage in battle, which further fills the situation with dread. The only negative I can say about the sound is the voice acting (or should I say script) almost sounds like a teenager wrote it at times. The voice work itself is great, but there's waaaaay too much swearing to the point where it just feels overplayed. A good "F-you" can give a situation that needed punch, but it loses meaning when it gets thrown out every other sentence.

What’s New:  Again, nothing much.  The sound continues to get the job done, but many of the same sounds from RE2 Remake are recycled, making for less of a fresh experience.  You’ve heard many of those groans and shrieks before, but there are still a few audible surprises that might get you.
`````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````

GAMEPLAY: The most important part of any game. This being a remake of the original RE2, comparisons will naturally be made here. Gone are the tank controls, in favor of the RE4 style over-the-shoulder view. Therefore, combat is more particular and aiming based, allowing the user to perform head shots, or slice off limbs, or come up with other creative ways to stop the undead. The overall environmental layout mirrors that of RE2, including some of the puzzles, though they do kind of hold your hand in some spots to guide you to the next objective. Controller and keyboard/mouse options both play wonderfully. Added is a much welcomed "Assist Mode" that can help players recover health automatically over time, aim assist in hitting critical areas on enemies, and generally easier difficulty. For those who enjoy punishment though, the Hardcore difficulty gives players just enough ammo, health items, save opportunities, and harder enemies to get through to claim victory. The end of each game is graded based on the difficulty, time, and number of times saved on a scale of C through S. Obviously getting that S will earn you better goodies if you're skilled enough to achieve it.

What’s New:  Yep, you guessed it!  Nothing much is new here either.  You’re still solving puzzles as usual, though there seems to be even fewer compared to the RE2R.  Was there a time in crunch in finishing this game or something?  I wrote a guide for solving RE2R’s puzzles to help me speed run, and that thing took up almost 4 pages (including diagrams).  This game:  less than half a page!  The few puzzles that are in this game are pretty simple, and combat is just a continuation from RE2R.  You’ve seen this and played this before.  Of course, there is a different story behind this game which takes slightly different twists and turns compared to the PS1 original, so this aspect will be the main highlight for playing.
```````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````

REPLAY: As you can see by the number of hours I poured into this game, there's a lot to see and do! Being a master at it, I'm now able to get through the game on Hardcore difficulty in less than 2 hours, but my first playthrough was closer to 7 hours. There are 4 different scenarios in the main campaign to play through, so you can see where all that time goes. After the main campaign, there are additional Ghost Survivor challenges to complete, as well as weekly challenges issued by Capcom. To fully 100% the game, you're tasked with performing certain challenges to unlock all the artwork, character models, and infinite weapons. Some challenges are as easy as "Shoot a zombie in the head 10 times" or as hard as "Get S+ rank on Hardcore mode".

What’s New:  Well, get ready for a big difference here.  I fully 100 percented this game in less than 40 hours at the time of this review.  There’s less content here compared to RE2R, so a good speed runner can finish this game in less than 1.5 hours easy.  After that, you unlock a few more difficulties and that’s it!  No extra scenarios or special gameplay modes, which is kind of a downer since the original RE3 was known for that fun Mercenaries Mode.  
```````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````````

If Resident Evil 2 was a yummy pizza with extra toppings then Resident Evil 3 is a calzone - still yummy, but a much smaller portion. This game is really short, like [b]really[/b] short. You can finish a first playthough in under six hours, and second in less than half of that, easily.

Despite its length, RE3 is excellent. It's action focused this time around, but it still retains the horror elements that defined RE2. This campaign takes place in the same locations as RE2, but in areas different enough that it doesn't feel like a copy and paste job. The creepy abandoned hospital was a great original location - I just wish there had been more to explore.

The Nemesis encounters are mostly scripted Kool-Aid wall smashing sequences, which personally I preferred over Mr X constantly bursting into rooms mid-puzzle in RE2. They've also added a dodge and punch mechanic that gives you the mobility to avoid a Nemesis attack or zombie bite, and counter a Hunter swipe with a jab. If anyone from Capcom reads these reviews, please go back and add this into RE2. Zombies with a six foot magnetic grip are super annoying, this makes the situation fairer and the gameplay more fluid.

There's also an in-game shop, which thankfully is only tied to challenges that can be completed throughout the campaign. It's a nice touch that you can reload a save game, mow down some zombies, die, and then reload your save and still unlock the challenges. The items for purchase include new weapons, infinite ammo, skins and various attack, defence and health improvements. You'll want these trinkets to blast your way through the hordes on a second playthrough.

Basically RE3 is fantastic, just don't spend more than £15 if you don't want to feel ripped off.

Resident Evil 3 is a beautifully moody and dramatic retelling. Gameplay has you take control of the Iconic Jill Valentine and Carlos as they face the latest threat caused by the evil Umbrella Corps T-Virus. While this game is shorter than it's predessor it still offers up plenty to do, from exploring for the clues to open all the safes and breaking into lockers and locked rooms. Gameplay feels quick like you are being pushed along to the next area and it's unfortunate that it may cause some to miss out on some hidden goodies and zombies feel like they have had a bit of a boost and not so easy to kill this time around giving players enough of a challenge should they not be paying attention fully to their surroundings. Visually the game looks gorgeous, with deep, dark and moody tones complmenting the richly detailed environments. Offering up reworked characters and a new outfit for Jill and a new hair do for Carlos though in honesty we at XA prefer the originals models for both and decided to play using them instead. With the undead also getting plenty of TLC they look deader and more dealier than ever and that brings us on to Nemesis himself, the big tank looks as horrifying and intimidating as he should.
With all the good there is some bad. Firstly, aiming, this is quite noticeable and more so when using Carlos, you will see he appears to not look down the gun bit more into the butt of the gun, I feel this is something that should have been picked up on and make to look a bit more realistic, while not game altering in anyway at all it is just a slight visual annoyance. Secondly as mentioned above the game can feel at times a bit driven and feeling rushed to progress through the game, with puzzles / mazes feeling more simplified to push you along and ultimately spending less time in an area to find stuff and appreciate the detail. Overall: RE:3 May not be as good as the game it's retelling but as a game on it's own merits warrants the kudos and hype it's gained. I would suggest highly to anyone looking into the horror genre for something to play. Really looking forward to what the already announced Resident Evil 0 Remake has up its sleeves!

Re 2 was my favorite in the franchise from the original series. I had played pretty much all of them except 6 and 3, as people had told me 3 was bad (back in the day from those around me) and deterred me from ruining my experience with 2.

Come the announcement of Re 2 remake and success, it seemed like Re 3 remake was on the horizon, and sure enough we get the announcement that it'll launch within a year of Re 2 remake's release... This already had me extremely concerned, but with Re 2 receiving a lot of attention to detail while not being afraid to take some stuff out and add others, I kept high hopes to the design decisions.

I even went as far as to dust off my Mother's old gamecube, grab myself a copy of re3 original, and play through it a couple of times to make sure I had enough experience from the original game under my belt. Playing it now, I then felt some heavy regret having never given the game a chance before. The varying outcomes to certain situations, (dogs vs crows coming out of bus is a small example) the dual choices during tons of nemesis encounters, and the overall fear factor that nemesis put in you that game was fantastic. The puzzles weren't tedious imo, but they definitely made you take in your surroundings and focus on what you can do at the time. It was always me wanting to take the next step, and thus the game play felt like I dictated where I went and when certain puzzles were solved.

Finally this remake comes out, I had it pre-ordered and a good 20 hours off work. Within minutes, I realized I was not going to enjoy this game. It's not the action at all, in fact I think some of the action really helps set the mood of "Jill's final escape" since some of the city scenes were extremely brutal during the beginning of the original game, and you definitely had that feeling of "♥♥♥♥♥ gotten out of hand, I need to be careful" while trying to maneuver through the infested racoon city. But the amount of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ content that they cut from this game between choices, progression, and even flat out zones missing and puzzles completely cut made me feel like I wasn't "escaping" racoon city. I was being taken on a tour of what the DEVELOPERS wanted to see, not ME as a player. I was never given the chance to explore or go the paths I wanted, because there was only ever a right and wrong path to this game. The boss fights are a joke and dare I say, extremely zelda like where It's just a one two three sequence of the same ♥♥♥♥ over and over again. Acid nemy in the original game was an extreme pain, but it still felt way better than acid nemy in this game.

The only saving grace that I can give this game would be Carlos' RPD section (not including the hoard fight at the end). This section was the closest I ever felt to that original re-style exploration and fear of having to search around, find different things, ask yourself if you wanna enter that room again, and general light puzzle solving. It was one of the more open areas of the game in terms of exploration.

But the fact of the matter is that I can't excuse how short and uninteresting this game became when it started holding my hand in what directions to go, and removed nearly all of those nostalgic puzzles and areas. No park, no clock tower, no dual choices, and the few puzzles they did have were just finding something along the way and wasn't really a "find". The final fight is complete ass. 

5/10. If you have any amount of love for the original game, I would recommend against buying this title and sticking to better remakes like Re1 and Re2. (re1 being my favorite remake) If you've never played Re3, I think it might hold up as it's stand alone game, but the replayability just isn't there like it is for Re1 and Re2 in my opinion, and with it already being an incredibly short story (averaged about 5.5 hours compared to the original game where i played for 7.5 on my first play through) you may feel like you aren't getting your money's worth compared to other $60 titles.

This issue comes from how linear the game progresses, as well as how short most areas are. The linearity means there are almost no puzzles to add any depth to gameplay, or to break up the action. 

Regarding the gameplay, the game still feels great, and the dodge mechanic is a welcome addition to me. The real problem lies in how enemy types are handled. I noticed very early on that zombies aren't much of a threat, but rather an inconvenient obstacle to avoid. Lickers, Hunters, and Gammas are encountered, but they are poorly utilized, with predictable placement and move sets. Being a more action focussed game means that enough ammo is always at hand to dispatch these "difficult" enemies as well. Unfortunately, the most poorly handled enemy is Nemesis. He is under utilized throughout the main gameplay and easy to avoid. He's kind of a joke. Annoyingly though, he can't help but interrupt almost every cutscene for the first half of the game. 

I should say that all of these aforementioned issues result in a game that just isn't scary.

Of course the biggest criticism that everyone has already covered is the short length of the game. I won't go further.

It's a solid addition to the Resident Evil Remakes with everything feeling almost identical to the original, including it's many flaws. 

The story is nothing to write home about and seems to have been cut short given RE3 included a multiplayer addition which also feels unpolished. Combat dodging is included this time around and action is increased just like before. However the mechanics of dodging feel more tacked on rather than an addition with much care and thought. No tutorial on how this system functions and IS a core part of the game play will frustrate players of RE2 not expecting it. It's simply put a trail by fire until you get the hang of it. Nemesis also is a constant threat, which makes for some good chase scenes,  but with that comes the issue of not getting the chance to explore the map properly, or take in the rich atmosphere the designers have so carefully crafted. 

So why on earth would I review this game a recommendation despite it's many flaws? Simply put its expected. RE3 came out to some very similar poor reception itself when it first launched. Many players were used to RE2 and it very opposite tone and pacing and felt sideswiped when RE3 came bashing through their doors. Issues such as dodging, story, and questionable game design were also all issues many had back when this was first released. These issues were expected to be fixed in RE3, but rather than fixing them the developers simply took away some features and added others that really did nothing to change the overall problems the first iteration had. For example RE3 if you can believe it had branching pathways in the first game that seemed to be Capcom trying to diversify their series and change the statues quo up.j Which came with mixed reception. RE3-Remake had multiplayer tacked on which also much like branching pathways in the original came with mixed reception. Both however seemed to have taken away from the core development of the game as a whole which in turn makes both feel very identical despite development choices being changed up. 

Regardless the game is fun and enjoyable with much to like as there is much to hate. RE3 divides the resident evil fan base just like it's original. Some enjoy the spooky horror and slow pacing while others found the fresh new fast paced action style of RE3 to be a breath of fresh air. As the games progresses into more action I hope however Capcom aims to retain the horror that made the original series so iconic. If not they may find themselves running the same issue the series had prior.

Jill Valentine has to get out of Raccoon City while evading the relentless Nemesis. Where this game excels is in those first half exploration and chase segments, those tighter boss fights and the idea that your resources might actually be finite. By the second half of the game things are a bit rushed, your cup of bullets doth runneth over and Nemesis won't be chasing you until the designated boss arenas. To a deeply flawed point this game is linear. It is so linear you're forbidden from rotating your camera at times during "Press W to Live" sections. Still, I love that first half. You're encouraged to replay the game with a host of modifiers, including extra difficulty modes past Hardcore that shake up item and enemy placement and a shop that offers you extra gameplay features like regenerating health, easier dodges or infinite ammo. These don't count against your ranks in the higher difficulties and I find the idea of sequence breaking in this on rails experience to be a good laugh.

I can recommend it as a 7/10 but it's really a shame. I could feel a sense of forlorn despair as I walked by the placeholder for the cut clock tower section and across the gorgeous little waterfront area, a simple resource gathering hub before another boss arena. Is this all it would have taken to have another RE2R masterpiece? A few more months, a second extended exploration area with some loops and branching paths, some more time to have fun with Nemesis Form 1, the star of the show?

[h2]Summary[/h2]
Well done hospital area, dodge mechanic, graphics, weapons, difficulty settings, and boss fights. Missing puzzles, boss fights, large areas, live choices, and haunting nemesis. Short length, and might have wasted the only opportunity RE3 had for a great remake.

[h2]Intro[/h2]
In terms of a RE game, this is a good and short addition to the series. In terms of a remake of RE3 (and a fully priced RE game), it falls short on enough areas to prevent it from becoming a great remake. Most puzzles and some iconic areas have been removed. Horror has been toned down (compared to RE2R at least), and action has become a larger part of the game.

[h2]Pros[/h2]
-Hospital changes: the hospital was really well done and works well with this remake(and was my favorite section of this game). 
-RPD: I like the way they connected RE2R with RE3R in RPD. Also, [spoiler]RE2R safe codes are the same here.[/spoiler]
-Dodge mechanic: is a good addition and adds another element to learn for the game.
-Graphics: game looks great, but it’s expected since it’s using RE engine and shares assets with RE2R.
-Weapons: includes most of the weapons from the original game (although I’ll miss my freeze rounds), adds some cool unlockable weapons, and the weapons feel good to use.
-New enemies: the added enemies ([spoiler]sewer big boy and orange heads[/spoiler]) are well done and work well with the dodge mechanic.
-Difficulty modes: lots of difficulty modes make the game easy or hard, depending on how much challenge one craves.
-Boss fights: boss fights (although few) are solid.

[h2]Cons[/h2]
-Puzzles: most of the puzzles have been cut leaving only a couple of puzzles. Puzzles were one of the main elements that made this game standout back in the day. Sadly, in the remake, puzzles make up a very small portion of the game’s identity.
-Boss fights: while the boss fights are well done, there are [spoiler]4 boss fights, and they are all against nemesis (worm boss was removed). Also, the 3rd and 4th fights are right after each other (after you beat 3rd boss, you walk down a hallway and you reach the save room that’s right before the final boss). [/spoiler]I feel like they could’ve added some cool things to separate these fights better.
-Missing large areas: two large areas removed from this remake are the clock tower (one of my favorite areas of the game) and the park. 
-Missing live choices: original RE3 was shorter than RE2 (specially since it didn’t have multiple scenarios), but adding live selections meant each playthrough would be a little different. This game omits them, so each playthrough is exactly the same.
-[spoiler]Predictable nemesis: nemesis appears in set areas and doesn’t really haunt you. Original RE3 improved over the original RE2 in terms of the nemesis haunting you randomly. RE2R furthered improved this. But RE3R took a step backwards.[/spoiler]
-Missing ink ribbons: they add another layer of resource management and tension; because then, you can’t save after every small task to play it safe. This increases the fear of dying, and therefore, fear of the enemies. 

[h2]Neither good nor bad[/h2]
-Points system to unlock items: can’t decide if it’s good or bad. Adds artificial replayability, but mostly for collectors and fans of the series. 
-Electricity restoration area: I like how they changed this area over the original, but they removed its puzzle, so I’ll put it in the ok section.
-Carlos in RPD: can’t say if it’s a positive or a negative decision, but it fits fine in this game.
-Combining mine thrower with grenade launcher: while it’s unfortunate to somewhat lose a weapon, I think it works well like this. 
-No poison/blue herb: [spoiler]only one type of enemy (kind of) poisons you, and you have to use a green herb to heal.[/spoiler]
-No original sound option: I really liked this feature in RE2R, I wish they had added this here too.

[h2]Final thoughts[/h2]
On its own, this game is a short and fun RE experience that should’ve been priced as a (standalone) dlc to RE2R. But, looking at it as the remake of RE3, I feel it’s hard to recognize it as such at times.
You can experience the entire game in one playthrough of about 5 hours. While this game is around the same length as RE2R for one playthrough, RE2R has multiple scenarios and extra game modes, which more than double its game length. In addition, this game uses the same [spoiler]RPD location as we had in RE2R and shares assets for sewer and lab areas with RE2R[/spoiler]. These things should’ve given them more time to not have to remove the missing areas. 
Had they included at least the clocktower and the park area, I think this could’ve been a fantastic game. I feel like capcom tried to ride on the success of RE2R and cheaped out on this one. Now, RE3 has lost its opportunity to have a great remake that it deserves (perhaps forever).

I wish I could join the chorus of negative naysayers, but I actually really do like this game and I don't know who all these speedracers are, but it definitely took me a minute to get through and it felt very worthwhile. The game is just as gorgeous as the RE TWO MAKE, but graphics and scenes appear even more polished and smooth. Characters, monsters, and surroundings are stunningly detailed. Screen space reflections seem to be on the whole much more improved, except for, oddly enough, in the police station. Sound and orchestrations are all excellent here as well. A lot of the things I liked about RE2 are absent here. The masterful and brilliant pacing of RE2 was its biggest strength. This game's tempo does fall in-line with its environments, but because it shifts a lot, it means that the other thing I really like about RE2 is missing here as well--the tight resource management. Resources were very limited in RE2 and it was oh so satisfying to barely eek by in a lot of the situations, that "felling the last zombie with your second to last bullet" feeling is gone from this game replaced instead with "should I carry two full backup clips of auto-rifle ammo or one?" As a long term Resident Evil fan I sincerely recommend this game to fans of the series and newcomers alike. It's a survival horror with some FPS elements thrown into the mix, and a good one at that. 
The most important thing to know if you're fan, however, is that this is more of a retelling of the story rather than a faithful remake. Just keep in mind that the story elements were changed and if you can embrace it, you were enjoy this game quite a lot.

What I loved:
1. A bit of an inside of the post-trauma episodes from RE1 in the main character - I wish it was elaborated on even more. 
2. Introduction of Carlos much earlier into the story with a bigger agenda - gives him more  of a character.
3, Raccoon City looks sickening! 
4. The whole art style is really on point.
5. Jill's outfit makes much more sense than what she was wearing in RE3 original. I know many people had an issue with that, but I sincerely don't understand why - Jill's a special grade cop, not a go-go dancer. 

What I am unsure of is the entire Nemesis changes they made. On one hand, he was just as sweet and loving as in the original, but his evolution was changed dramatically and somehow diminished his intelligence I think. He felt more like a trained and driven animal rather than an intelligent monster. 
I think I liked both versions because they were in the end quite different. 

What I didn't love:
1. Jill's hair. It looks like she hasn't washed it in ages.
2.  Game's length  - it is relatively short. i beat the story without rushing it in around 9 hours.  What I think the story could have benefited from would be the inclusion of more post-traumatic episodes for Jill's or any elaboration on the effects the past events had on the heroine to flesh out her character. 
3. Reuse of the RE2 remake assets. I felt like the game explored too many similar locations as the RE2 and while some made sense - the police department for one - others could use a different setup,. Like the sewers. While I loved the enemies in the zone, I really think this could have been done literally anywhere else.

Now to start I’d like to say I don’t think this game is terrible, or even remotely bad, like some people out there are a saying, I believe this game is still very solid. I think people are more just disappointed than anything else, which I think they’re right to be since I can say with confidence Resident Evil 3 is nowhere near to being as good as its predecessor. But why is that? In this review, I'll be discussing my beliefs on that very subject.

With that now out of the Way, I will say this. The story is honestly decent and it’s definitely a fun time, however, due to some of the game's shortcomings like its very short run time which is at around the 5-6 hour mark, On top of the game missing a significant chunk of content from the original, I can say this title very much feels underwhelming and lacking content. So if any of these things are important to you, I would suggest waiting for the game to go on sale or something. Now with that over here are some specifics.

Gameplay: 
The Nemesis: The Nemesis, in my opinion, is by far the weakest part of the first act. When you first run into him it feels hectic and fun just like with the previous games, big bad guy Mr. X however, this sense of anxiety and fear quickly turns into frustration, and annoyance. As he likes to teleport, sprint, and generally do ridiculous ♥♥♥♥ all over the map the moment you get out of the line of sight of him. I don’t know if this is really how he’s supposed to act or if this is just bad design.

Quick Stepping: To go more in-depth I liked this mechanic, I thought this was a good implementation to the game. Since honestly nothing else in this game feels as good as getting those perfect dodges and counter attacks in boss battles. But if they continue to use this in future games I would highly suggest they give players more time, and opportunities early on in the game to teach them how to use it effectively.

The Enemies: Zombies A.I in this game is well executed, in my two playthroughs I never felt like I was unfairly killed when it came to the normal zombies. The other enemies on the other hand I can’t say the same. Specifically the [spoiler] Hunter Alphas [/spoiler] in the sewers and the [spoiler] Hunter Betas [/spoiler] in the hospital. I cannot even begin to tell you how many times I wanted to stick my head in a furnace while playing my first playthrough on Hardcore mode. Both of these enemies have instakill attacks, which are nothing short of infuriating when they hit these attacks on you, forcing you to spend another 10 minutes trying to kill them with no ammo since they keep throwing these bullet sponges at you. Thankfully with the quickstep system, it is possible to dodge these attacks, but the game oddly doesn’t really do much to teach you how to use this system but instead opts for you to kinda figure it out which led to much frustration especially when playing on a harder difficulty.

All in all, I enjoyed Resident Evil 3, and I can definitely recommend it, but only really if it’s on sale since I feel like we don’t get nearly enough content here to justify the full $60 price tag. I rate Resident Evil 3 a 7/10

[spoiler]Resident Evil 3 takes place around the same time as the events of Resident Evil 2, and follows series regular Jill Valentine who is one of the two playable Main Characters of the Original Resident Evil. And as someone who's played through all the mainline resident evil games (except 6 because ♥♥♥♥ that), I can say as a character I thoroughly enjoyed my time playing as Jill Valentine.

Main Protagonists: When it comes to the two main protagonists Jill and Carlos I honestly liked them and thought both were well voice acted and had good chemistry when in scenes together because the games very short run time I think players including myself aren’t given a realistic amount of time to get to know these characters and begin to form a connection to them like you would with characters you were given time with like Jole and Ellie from The Last of Us, or Nathan Drake and Sully from Uncharted. [b] Beforehand [/b]

I have played Resident Evil 0 (HD), 1 (HD) and 2 (Remake) before this. So my review might by a bit biased by those games.

[b] Story [/b]

Resident Evil 3 takes place in paralel to Resident Evil 2 (Which plays 2 months after Resident Evil 1). You are Jill Valentine, a member of S.T.A.R.S, and a survivor of the mansion incident back in the first game. You swore to defeat Umbrella but failed. Having all this knowledge about the mansion incident, Umbrella sends Nemesis, a modified Tyrant, to defeat her and the other remaining S.T.A.R.S. members.

[b] Gameplay [/b]

The gameplay in Resident Evil 3 is similar to Resident Evil 2, but with a few changes. You only have one story (Jill's story), a dodge feature (Which you should use a lot, by the way), and a knife that doesn't break (Yay)

[b] Performance [/b]

I have an i5 3470 and a GTX 1060 6 GB with 16 GB of RAM, most settings were on the highest (With exception of the ones that exceeded my VRAM) and I am sure it ran 60+ fps for 90% of the time. This game is really well optimized and looks beautiful.

[b] Additional notes [/b]

Resident Evil 3 contains Resident Evil Resistance. Resident Evil Resistance is a mixed bag, I haven't tried it out much myself, but people say it is riddled with hackers. Also, keep in mind that Resident Evil 3, just like Resident Evil 0, 1 and 2 (I don't know about the ones after 3) do not support 16:10, it will just add black bars at the top and bottom.

[b] Conclusion [/b]

Resident Evil 3 is great, I loved the story, liked the gameplay, and the time it took me to beat it (almost 12 hours) gave me enough gameplay to be satisfied. The graphics are great, the sound is extremely well done. However. I think it lacks compared to Resident Evil 2. Resident Evil 2 overall felt more like a Resident Evil title thanks to its mansion scenario and truly nerve racking rooms and areas. What Resident Evil 3 truly lacks are the puzzles, the creative enemies. The Nemesis boss battles get tiring quick as a pattern is quickly visible from my experience of playing. However, it is still a great game, it provides an atmosphere rarely found in modern games in my opnion. If you have enough money, buy this one and Resident Evil 2. But, if you are short on money, I recommend Resident Evil 2 instead.

This game has mixed reviews because it gives mixed feelings.

If you never played the original RE3, but enjoyed the RE2 remake, you'll probably enjoy this game. I'd recommend waiting for a sale if you can (I did). I wouldn't pay more than $40 USD.

I will say this, this is a good game on its own merit (ignoring its predecessor). I've beaten it multiple times (already beat Inferno and obtained all achievements on the Xbox One version) and enjoy playing it. It has its faults, but it's not a bad game by any means.

The game looks beautiful, the cinematics are well done, the voice-acting is good (especially for Resident Evil). The game recreates several parts of the original RE3 beautifully, and the soundtrack is an amazing re-imagining of the original game's score (better than the RE2 remake soundtrack). The gameplay and control is well-done, with the same setup from the RE2 remake. It moves and plays smoothly. 

Also, the characters are well done. Carlos is awesome, Jill is in great form, and Nicolai and Mikhail are enjoyable as well. And Brad has a great screen presence and redemptive story-arc now.

That being said, there are shortcomings to the game, namely in its length and the unfortunate loss of classic areas and gameplay elements. 

Two extremely memorable segments from the OG RE3 (the dead factory and the clocktower) have been cut. The dead factory is here nor there, as it's been re-imagined in a pretty neat new lab segment. But the missing clocktower is sorely missed. The uptown area (immediately surrounding Jill's apartment) has also been reduced to a walking-simulator set piece, and cannot be explored like in the original game. No more spending time in Dario's warehouse crafting ammo or looting supplies, no more forked paths moving to/around Bar Jack (Bar Jack is just a backdrop in a cut-scene now). You spend less than 5 minutes in this area of the game, whereas in the original it was a good 10-20 minute segment that really let you soak up the atmosphere.

The zombie animations and gore have been toned down, which is hard to grasp given this is a PC release. I'd get that for consoles, but I feel like modern PCs could handle the extra zombies ragdolling. The zombie gore system in RE2's remake was so amazing, it's crazy they left it out. It's immersion-breaking, and really hurts the tone the game is trying to set (or could have set, I guess). 

Also, Nemesis surprisingly does not feel nearly as intimidating as he did in the OG game. He doesn't compare to RE2 remake's Mr. X either. There's only one small segment where he's actively pursuing you, and it's not enough. I actually found myself purposefully dallying about just to extend this segment and enjoy it more. So much wasted potential here it hurts. 

And my last gripe, the puzzle-solving has been dramatically toned down. The RE series is known for its campy, horror-gothic exploratory puzzle-solving, and RE3 lacks this. It also lacks the open-ended, choose-your-own adventure level-design and is extremely linear compared to previous games. 

So, again, it's not a bad game. It's competent, but it misses the mark. RE7 and RE2 were great and were a promising return to form for the franchise. It was disappointing to see this game just barely fall short. You can unlock concept art in the game and see for yourself how close they came to really pulling it off. I don't know if it was design-choices, or CAPCOM executives rushing development, but there's definitely a layer of world-building, level-design, and overall polish missing.  I honestly think some dedicated modders can make this game into what it was meant to be, and I'll be looking forward that. 

If you catch the game on-sale and like Resident Evil, go for it. But I would NOT pay 60 bucks for it unless you just truly adore the series. Again, it's not a bad game, you might even say it's good, but it could have been GREAT.

No content will be added to it, even though RE7 and RE2make got tons of post launch DLC's. No side mode, no mercenaries, no alternate scenarios, no ghost survivors. No S+ rank, meaning S rank (which you can achieve using cheat weapons like unlimited rocket launcher, that you can now just buy instead of being a reward) is the highest grade, which means there's no point in trying to legitimately beat Inferno under 2h30 as it gives you no reward for doing so. Think about that. A costume menu with no costumes in it. The original had more costumes just for Jill alone.

I never got around to completing the original RE 3 so I can't properly judge this one as a remake. Nevertheless I enjoyed this one. The basic gameplay is pretty much the same as 2 with a few twists. There are no more defensive items but the character of Jill gets a dodge button to compensate which when timed properly gives you a perfect dodge, slowing down time and automatically aiming at the dodged attacking enemy's weak spot for a few seconds. Carlos doesn't get a dodge but a short shoulder charge which with the proper timing can be used to parry an enemy's attack with a punch knocking him down and similarly to Jill slow down time for a few seconds. The campaign is more action packed with more enemies and generous ammo quantities, it is more linear with backtracking significantly toned down from 2 giving it a seemingly shorter duration. The fact that there is less variety in extra modes doesn't help either. It feels like the game would have benefited more from splitting the story of the 2 characters in seperate modes like in RE 2. Other than that I really liked the design of the characters, especially Nemesis. Unfortunately due to the shorter duration of specific segments Nemesis seems to be underutilized and not as big a threat as the tyrant of RE 2 was. Unlockables exist in the game in the form of extra items which can be exchanged for points won awarded through completing challenges and help spice up another playthrough. The sound design is great and the music is more prominent including remixed tracks from the old game. Graphically the game looks great and it is very well optimised. Definetly pick it up on a sale.

Okay, with my bad history with remakes, this game was a welcome change of pace. I really enjoyed this game, and was more than satisfied with it. But a few notes for those eyeing this title:
1. This game is a remake, and that's okay. Playing a remake is like listening to a remix of a popular song. If you're playing this for a nostalgia trip, expecting it to be exactly the same, you're going to be disappointed. This isn't exactly like the original, but that's to be expected. The whole thing (like Res-E 2's remake) has been rebuilt from the ground up. You'll likely enjoy it either way.
2. The gameplay is okay, and not very different from Res-E 2 remake. But there is significantly more wiggle room to avoid enemies.
3. The whole game can be pretty short (between six and eight hours, if you're doing all the exploration). Unless you're playing on a higher difficulty (like hard and nightmare) you can breeze through a lot of areas. Enemies are manageable on the lower two (easy and normal), but can still pose a threat.
Overall, this game is pretty well-crafted. It's not exactly like the original, but it still has a lot of charm. There are a lot of familiar areas, from both the original and the previous game. It is, admittedly, fairly short, but it still has a few good qualities. Overall, 8/10.
UPDATE: After playing through this title again, I realize I have one gripe about this title: The Hunter Betas (the lizard-creatures you encounter in the hospital) feel really annoyingly designed, and are more of an inconvenience than an actual threat. That, and this game's replayability is more suited towards speedrunners and completionists, and the occasional nostalgia seeker.

Like Resident Evil 2, this remake brought back the nostalgic feel of the old games. The character design updates made sense, the combat was good, and this time it focused way more on Nemesis and his dogged pursuit of Jill. Among the things this game did right:
 - it made Nemesis way more aggressive and terrifying, because you literally had no idea when he would show up, and when he did he was fast. 
 - The dodge system finally got the fix it needed from the original.
 - They did a good job of expanding Jill's intro so we had a better idea of what she has been up to since the Mansion incident instead of just starting her off in an alley.
 - All the characters have well done updated appearances.
 - The segment where you play as Carlos did a good job of having a different dynamic and play style from Jill.

The things I wish they improved, 
- late game is super straightforward and easy. 
- I wish we got to explore more of the town, like in the original.
- They cut a lot of areas short, or completely out from the original game.
- They cut mercenary mode, which is a real shame.

Despite the balance of pros and cons, it still scratched my Resident Evil itch, and felt like another step in the right direction.

[b]TL;DR:[/b] Capcom has jumped the shark again. Resident Evil 3 is not a bad game. It is (almost) as enjoyable as Resident Evil 2. The big issue, and what keeps me from recommending it, is that this is a 6 hour game with a $60 price tag. While a single play through of Resident Evil 2 takes about as long, there were multiple story routes you could pick from plus multiple extra modes to keep you entertained. Resident Evil 3 on the other hand, has one story mode and an unlockable store which allows you to purchase in game items with in game currency. I have heard that a lot of content was actually cut instead of being remade and remastered as well. While there is little "wrong" with the game, this feels like a huge step back from the amazing remake we got with RE2 with the same big price. Get this one on sale.

[b]The Good:[/b]

Mechanics: Not much to say here other than the core game is pretty much the same as it was in RE2, with some not so great changes.

Graphics: Same as before. The game looks just as great as RE2.

Nemesis: I actually prefer the Nemesis in this game to Mr. X in RE2. Nemesis is much less of an annoyance and more of an actual threat in this game. He is fast, has multiple ways of closing the distance with the player, and he can very easily kill you if you are not careful. He is not a constant presence at certain points in this game like Mr. X (which quickly became annoying), but only appears at certain points briefly. I still think it would have been better to have Nemesis show up randomly for short periods of time, but this mechanic is an improvement from RE2 nonetheless.

Environment/Level Design: We get to explore the city that is shown very briefly in RE2, and it looks great. The levels are sufficiently different from RE2 to keep things fresh, and the developers have done new things with their design. We also get to revisit some of the popular locations seen in RE2 like the police station and gun shop.

Boss Battles: They are more diverse and less annoying than they were in RE2. Nemesis has multiple different versions of himself, each somewhat similar to the last but each requiring their own strategy to beat him. This is a vast improvement to the boss battles in tight, enclosed spaces in RE2 that regularly devolved into run and gun. These actually take some strategy and skill to win, not just timing and spatial awareness.

Story: I think the story here is a little better than standard. There are hints of paranoia and self doubt relating to Jill's virus exposure, which allows for some interesting exploration of her character and how the situation is affecting people. Jill's history with the virus and the police allows for some good moments too. Unfortunately, these elements are quickly left behind after the beginning of the game but they are nice to have and help set up the game and its conflict.

[b]The Bad:[/b]

Action Cinematics: A huge amount of the action that happens in the game is restricted to cut scenes, especially encounters with Nemesis. These are cool, but if I wanted to watch an action movie well... I would watch an action movie. It is not clear why so much control is taken from the player when it would have been fairly easily to program these cinematic encounters as controllable moments.

Quick Step Mechanic: There is nothing wrong with the mechanic itself but instead with how they chose to go about implementing it. They got rid of the secondary weapon system in RE2 which allowed players to equip knives and grenades alongside their main gun in order to use this system (with the same key bindings). This was not a good choice since the secondary weapon system found in RE2 greatly reduced time spent in inventory switching between weapons. In RE3, it was very annoying having to manually go into my inventory or take up a quick slot to equip knives and grenades. There is also no way to use a secondary weapon to break grabs in this game like there was in RE2. I am not sure why this mechanic was removed, but with its removal a huge part of the strategy in the game was taken away as well. I am sure they could have found a way to keep both, there are plenty of un-utilized keys.

Blue Herbs?: What happened to these? Did I miss them all? I did not find a single blue herb in the entire game, and the poison effect seems to have been replaced with parasite. This effect only appears once and very briefly in the game, remedied by green herbs instead of blue. It would have been nice to have this herb in RE3 as well since it adds a damage mitigation dynamic that would have been very helpful at certain points of the game. It is strange they were not put in the game.

Atmosphere: It is hard to say why exactly, but the atmosphere of this game is significantly less scary and tense than RE2. I have heard that RE3 always had more of a focus on action, but its hard not to draw unfavorable comparisons to the RE2 remake which so masterfully balanced action and horror. It also does not help that at no point in the game did I feel like I was low on resources. There is ammo and herbs everywhere, and it is hard to feel threatened when you always have another herb or another clip on hand at all times.

[b]The Ugly:[/b]

Resident Evil Resistance: This is a whole other tangent, but the multiplayer game that comes with RE3 is poorly realized. I could be saying that this game, while appearing to be hastily pushed out by CAPCOM, is a surprising amount of fun especially with friends. Instead, I will say that the game is a buggy, laggy, exploitable mess. All it takes is one person, especially the master mind, to have a trash connection and the entire game falls apart. People walk through walls, enemies teleport on top of you, health melts away in lag spikes, etc. Basically, the game is unplayable as it is and very easy for cheaters to take advantage of. This does NOT help justify the price of the game since it can hardly be played online.

Cut Content: From what I have read online, the original RE3 was already very short. It is puzzling then why the developers chose to cut additional content from the remake. There really is just no excuse for this. There was already a very short amount of time between the release of RE2 and RE3 (1 year 2 months), so it would not have been a big deal to push the release off a few more months to get all content remade.

Characters: Aside from the opening half hour, the characters are not particularly well written. There appears to be some effort on the writers part to make the characters a little more fleshed out than they were in the RE2 remake, but Jill comes across as a mega-♥♥♥♥♥ princess who needs to be saved multiple times by Carlos. Carlos can get a bit creepy in 2020 with his multiple unwanted flirtations with Jill.

The Price: As stated above, $60 is a big ask for a game with 6 hours of content. The game comes across as a lazy cash grab.

I feel like this game gets a bad rap for no real reason. Sure, its pretty short if you know what you are doing, but the original was quite short as well, as is the Resident Evil 2 remake if you run straight through that. Nemesis doesn't chase you all the time, but the Tyrant chases you constantly in RE2 remake and that is honestly just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ irritating, not intimidating or scary. Being chased constantly might be scary for about 10 minutes, but once you get used to this large creature literally just WALKING at you menacingly, it just becomes an obstacle, not something to actually fear, but rather something to just avoid.

He has a few good moments like when he breaks through the wall occasionally, but because he is CONSTANTLY after you in the exact same way, he becomes a chore, not a scare. Nemesis on the other hand, is constantly changing up his tactics. First he is just running after you, then he upgrades the zombies around you, then he uses a weapon, then uses the same weapon in a different way, then once all that fails, he straight up just changes himself completely to come after you harder than ever before. THAT is intimidating. A relentless creature that overcomes death itself to rip you to shreds, not once, but several times. The Tyrant is just a guy who chases you, occasionally punches you in the face a single time before you run straight past him as he tries to seem tough by cracking his knuckles and his neck.

The main reason Nemesis is a better antagonist and generally scarier than Mr. X is that he has variety. Mr. X does the EXACT SAME THING throughout the entire game from start to finish with the exception of the very end when he becomes more akin to the Tyrant from the RE1 remake. Nemesis on the other hand, as I said above, employs several different tactics to kill you. He LEARNS, he is more than just a machine that follows a singular command. He is a living, thinking creature with a single-minded resolve to accomplish his mission, no matter the cost, no matter what he has to do.

All in all, this game is well worth its price and while it is a bit more of an action horror game than survival horror, if you love a disastrous atmosphere with constantly building momentum that eventually culminates in a crescendo of strife during a boss fight, this game is undoubtedly going to hit the spot for you.
