Now let me start the drawn out bit by asking a simple question. Who bought "RESIDENT EVIL 3" specifically for "Resident Evil: Resistance"? Cause I sure as hell didn't. Part of what hurts this game is that the price tag is being inflated by a supposedly free game that's locked behind the purchase of another game.  I'd likely be much less judgmental of the game's lack of content if it weren't for the fact I'm essentially ignoring half my purchase because it does not interest me. I bought RESIDENT EVIL 3 for RESIDENT EVIL 3, and the amount of content in RESIDENT EVIL 3 is downright pathetic. I beat this game in one sitting the night it came out and while its not uncommon to beat Resident Evil titles in only a hour or two after multiple playthroughs, this game feels much more empty than previous titles.  The nicest way I can describe my feelings for the game is that they're charging full price for what is essentially a DLC for RE2 and another title I have no interest in that's getting all the post-launch DLC support. Where's my Clock Tower DLC? Where's the Raccoon Park/Cemetery DLC?

Even Nemesis, the dude who's supposed to be bringing in the crowds, is quite underwhelming in the remake when he exhausts his bag of tricks and its already quite limited. Part of what gave original Nemesis his charm was how much of a game changer he was. He was the first enemy in the series who could pursue you from room to room. He could drop in on you completely unannounced if RNG had it out for you, outside of scripted encounters he is meant to show up in and this trait made him freaking terrifying in the original.  He could meet you at different locations depending on your choices during the story and almost every encounter with the brute was a complete nail biter. Ironically, it feels like RE2's Mr. X does a far better job at this in his remake. Modern Nemesis is a total bore once you have him figured out. If anything he's a literal stalker and Jill's short temper with him by the endgame is a completely appropriate reaction that I felt as a player. There's no degree of randomness to Nemesis this time around. He's almost entirely scripted, not counting the "open" city segment in the very beginning that was showcased in the RE3 demo. The rest of his encounters are very much scripted, including the final boss fight which is ok at best on normal and hardcore difficulty, and completely insufferable in nightmare/inferno mode. He just doesn't feel as unpredictable and omniscient as he did in the original. 

On top of all this, there's also no Mercenaries: Operation Mad Jackal equivalent in the remake and that feels like a travesty, considering RE3 helped make Mercenaries a staple in Resident Evil games, even though you could perhaps argue RE2's extreme battle was the first instance of that.

I don't know what else to say other than RE3 fell well short of my expectations that were partly set by RE2 being such a wild success. While I wasn't expecting a point for point remake kinda like how RE2 wasn't a 1:1 remake, I was expecting more than we got. And again, I really need to hammer on the price tag. If this game were much cheaper, or perhaps a DLC for RE2, I could be more forgiving towards it. Thing is I need to judge the game on what I bought, and what I bought was ultimately a disappointment for what I paid.

Some positives? I like the remake's take on Jill and Carlos. They feel like they have chemistry in the remake and I do like how their relationship changes as the game progresses. The game's beginning minutes are a first person look at Jill's apartment before she begins her "last escape" and I love the things they did in this segment. Visually its a very good looking game and it performs fine on my setup. I guess technically its a solid game but it really is lacking in content and my lack of interest in Resistance doesn't help the sour taste in my mouth.

If you're a hardcore fan or you REALLY want this game, I won't say don't get it. There are fun moments here but they are incredibly fleeting. I feel like the dealmaker/breaker will be whether or not you see yourself playing Resistance. I don't so the game has less value to me seeing as how I'm paying to play RE3 and some game that continues to go uninstalled in my account. I would wait for a sale or if you absolutely can't wait for a good RE fix, I'd recommend RE1 or RE2 first as they're both cheaper and feature more content than RE3. RE7 gold is also a pretty good time with tons of content. I can also recommend RE4 but I'm stretching the limits of "horror" there.

The company takes the RE3 storyline, but some plots and scenarios are absolutely changed. A few scenes are cut out, like Park, Clock Tower, and the later becomes a background landmark only. One of the representative creature is absent too, Grave Digger, whose concept is obviously blended with the original Gamma Hunter. Not to mention Crow nor Spider because both were not existent in RE2 Remake anyway.

The Raccoon City town session is definitely a big letdown, for fans, even for new players I assume. The demo already presented most of it. In anticipation of exploring more, there is not much of the rest in the final release. Compared to the original, the remake is even much small scaled. A waste of an opportunity to reconstruct its look of Raccoon City.

But to be fair, there are new marvels. The new Beta Hunter which is made even more threatening and lethal, after all, it is a mass-product bioweapon. Gamma Hunter is more distinctive. The another NEST of Umbrella facility. The new designed Hospital scene is way better than the original in my opinion, with a little stressful atmosphere that makes you a bit jumpy. Carlos becomes a much interesting guy. During his playthrough, you can hear his comments toward surroundings a lot, and some of them are really funny.

As my experience, RE3R is fast paced, unlike RE2R, after managing to S rank all five difficulty modes, without any bonus shop items. It is ultra harder than RE2R hardcore mode. Since RE3R kind of "derailed" from classic RE style, it focuses too much on action, especially when you go on Nightmare or Inferno, Dodge is what the game forces you to master, particularly during the final Nemesis. Just when on Nightmare you gotta to make 90% perfect dodges through a sequence of actions, the Inferno puts you for the remain 10% to one slap death. This is completely why Calling it [b]Derailed[/b], for the classic REs which never require players to be 100% perfect in aspect of action control. Even those so called action shooters 4, 5 and 6 may not that terribly designed. Somehow I really doubt whether or not the developers have played the original, or they just dished out what they think a real challenging game. Thanks to the satisfied face of Jill after defeating final Nemesis during the cutscene, and the touching good-old rearranged ending song, I found myself some relief from these unbelievable absurdities.

RE3R is totally a fun game and still recommended for people who like some challenges, but as mentioned above, it is also a disappointment, for fans of the franchise. RE3R, is a linear action-horror game, utilizing assets from its predecessor RE2R, a survival-horror game, mirroring the original RE3's development. RE3 is somewhat divisive as a game, being a shorter, content light, more action oriented game with a full price tag, compared to previous titles in a franchise of survival-horror games with a large array of ways to play, and content to enjoy. Its fundamental nature has crossed over completely in this remake. However, these things do not inherently make it a bad game by any means, just a more niche one. It still very much promotes replayability with unlockables such as skins for characters, new weapons, character upgrades, as well as a concept art and model gallery. This is a good practice taken from RE2R and expanded on slightly. 

Subsequent runs of the game are also notably different, and i think this is where the game shines in comparison to RE2R. Its short nature allows runs to be refined to incredibly short stints of time, memorizing item and enemy placement, learning the quickest routes, etc etc. All of these things could be done in RE2R, yes, and its DLC allowed for it more specifically with the 4th Survivor, however i feel this is a far more compelling experience than DLC. 

I recommend this game completely, as i enjoy playing it immensely, and will continue to do so, and refine my gameplay. However, i can understand that its shorter, partial-asset flip, more action oriented nature can put people off, and to boot its full price! To those with such a sentiment, i understand, and would recommend purchasing it during a sale.

TL;DR, good game, sorta niche, buy if you like action-horror and speedrunning, get on sale if you are on the fence.

I'm really disappointed by this game. Of the remakes so far, RE3 had the most to benefit from a remake, particularly with the OG slant more toward action, modern technology could have allowed the devs to expand the scope of the chaos and flesh out the Raccoon City outbreak as one of the most pivotal events of the RE lore. But instead of iterating on the highly successful "puzzle box" slightly linear but branched exploration gameplay loop of the classic trilogy/RE2make/RE7 they go back fully to the button prompts, scripted, "on-rails" set pieces and no-backtracking philosophy of RE6. Why?!

It's extremely frustrating because you can see glimpses of this game's potential with better technology. For example the updated dodge mechanic, more refined shooting and the switch to the over-the-shoulder camera perspective make combat way more enjoyable. Whilst I am still in the camp of preferring fixed camera angles, if the franchise insists on retaining boss fights (weakest aspect of the series in every game IMO) then the switch to third person is more beneficial in that regard.

Graphics and sound design are obviously also a huge step above the original, the game looks amazing and the soundtrack is more prominent than it was in RE2make. Whilst that's likely just a different artistic direction, I think making the soundtrack more prominent again is the right move.

I also do want to mention how well all the characters are done here. Jill, Carlos, all the UBCS are all done extremely well, and their interactions are natural, leaps and bounds above the stiff 90s video game dialogue. Jill and Carlos feel like they have a legitimate relationship and play off each other really well. It's a huge credit to the refined mo-cap technology (another incremental but important step up from RE2make) and the performances by the voice actors. I get the OG fan criticism of Jill's personality change, but I reckon how Jill is written and portrayed in RE3make does just come down to personal preference. My only major sticking point on characterisation in RE3make is how quickly they trivialise Nemesis as a threat calling him all kinds of names. I reckon it's just dumb and never makes him feel scary.

So with such great modernisations of the RE3 cast you'd think that the devs would also devote the same effort to Nemesis. Nope. I think to sum up how Nemesis is mistreated in this remake, its important to put into context how Nemesis is implemented in the core gameplay loop.

This is an extremely linear game. It's not an open world, or even linear branching like the RPD. RE3make had the opportunity to give us a modernised, expanded Raccoon City with a free-roaming Nemesis AI. Think Mr X on steroids, instead of stalking you in just the RPD you have to contend with him for a few city blocks and all the interesting details in-between. But instead of that, we get a single cross section of a street about as large as the RPD B1 map. It's two parallel streets in the first section of the game. You've seen the city in the demo. As well as the extent of the dynamic "being stalked by Nemesis" portion of the game. That's it. And that's why Nemesis is so under-utilised and relegated to scripted quick-time sequences. Because there's nowhere for him to go to actually do anything! Even if the RE3make map had been expanded x3 times and was completely empty, at least that would give the player (and Nemesis) room to breathe and allow players to have more tense pursuits with one of the most prolific antagonists in the damn series. As it stands, Raccoon City is just constricted and suffocating.

The linearity of this game and how scripted everything is is also reflected in the opening segment of the game, which is a complete chore to do more than once because you get no control or freedom to do anything. The game starts very promising with a PTSD first person sequence (hardly explored thereafter) that starts in Jill's apartment. You're given a moment to look around her room before Nemesis smashes in through the wall. No build up in tension, no ominous conversation with Brad about being hunted, no wandering freely through the streets toward the RPD on edge, Nemesis just shows up immediately and you're stuck holding forward in a bunch of scripted escape sequences intercut with cutscenes. This lasts for a good 10-15 minutes before you're finally through all of the chaff and you can finally play the game. It's really bad. For repeat playthroughs you have to do this song and dance every single time.

It's ironic, in the modern day where "open-world" is a trope tacked onto some games to pad them out to make them feel more substantial than they actually are, a game that actually desperately needs to be expanded is restricted. OG is superior in every way in this regard, hell I may get crap for this but ORC is a better rendition of Raccoon City than what we get in RE3make. Nemesis is one of the most iconic enemies in the series, and with so many side-story takes of the events of the Raccoon City incident (UC, ORC, Outbreak) you'd think when finally given the opportunity to fully explore a location as important to the lore as the Spencer Mansion, it's just completely diluted. It's an enormous disappointment.

Other criticisms and unnecessary changes; no ink ribbons on any difficulty, maps don't use the same detailed item icons (they use this flat generic 'item-type' design instead of telling you specifically what the item is), no backtracking, no defensive weapons (the knife is now something you equip in a weapon slot and use as a weapon), and of course another big negative is no Mercenaries mode. And then theres the cut locations which have been mentioned many times by other reviews.

RE3 is my favourite of the OG trilogy, but RE3make is the worst remake by far. It's too much like RE6 in all the wrong ways, and it's made worse by the enormous potential this had, and following on from the RE2make which was a fantastic game in its own right, and a fantastic remake of my least favourite of the OG trilogy.

For old-school RE fans, I'm not even sure I'd recommend waiting for a sale. The shooting is tight, it looks stunning, but just way too much has been cut. There is nothing traditional Resident Evil about this at all, which is what you'd expect from a remake. This is a post-RE4 Resident Evil, which isn't [i] necessarily [/i] a bad thing, but when you're pitching your game to be a remake of one of the OG trilogy you better damn well make it that as a bare-minimum. This also stings just that little bit extra with all the potential promised by the amazing RE2make and its implementation of Mr X, and just how pathetic Nemesis is by comparison. Really, really disappointing.

There were many warning signs during the development of this game; Jill's redesign, the game supposedly being developed by a "B team", no Mercenaries mode and a rushed development schedule to name but a few, so this game's shortcomings came as little surprise to me as a longstanding fan from the PS1 original days. The game's got all the hallmarks of a rushjob thrown out the door to clumsily try and capitalise on RE2 Remake's success and fan goodwill. "Hey RE2 Remake was great, so RE3 Remake will be too, right?"

I'll do a rushjob, bullet-pointed review to match the game:
- Sound mixing often lacks the "oomph" of the RE2 remake. The terror of having Mr.X hunting you down with heavy, foreboding footsteps has not been replicated in this game (or at least sounds very poor comparatively on my 5.1 setup).
- The game shares RE2 Remake's problem of assuming you want to play with a controller even when you're using a mouse and keyboard, so expect your idle controller to be vibrating away happily until you manually turn it off
- Jill's new outfit is uninspired, thankfully an approximation of the original is available which looks much better and is more in keeping with the original.
- Encounters with Nemesis early on lack impact as he can be one-shotted by a single grenade.
- In 2020, particularly with RE2 Remake's Mr.X stalker framework having already been established as a proto-Nemesis, I was expecting a much more dynamic Nemesis with encounters that could happen more organically (think the alien from Alien Isolation). This was far from the case. I've no clue what happened during development but the devs definitely indicated early in development that this remake would be more open than the original (and presumably Nemesis would take advantage of this). The game is anything but open, so presumably something happened during development that caused plans to change. Nemesis has no stalker-mechanics like Mr.X from RE2, you won't hear Nemesis actively hunting for you - because he can't. His appearances are linear, scripted affairs, you'll always know when he's around because you're either in a boss fight with him or a brief evasion sequence leading up to cutscene/boss fight. Nemesis feels incredibly primitive in terms of what he can do outside of boss encounters. As the namesake of this game his systems should be an advancement in every way from what we saw back in the original game, but they really aren't.
- Nemesis has essentially been neutered and held back from what could have been his true potential to a series of scripted encounters, likely as a byproduct of babies whining about Mr.X "ruining" RE2 Remake due to his constant stalking the player through the police station.
- Nemesis' forms are more varied than the original, Jill has amusing quips to make throughout the game about this, but I felt he lost him iconic look far too quickly in this game.
- Voice acting of a high quality throughout with one or exceptions here and there.
- The game is as short as you've heard, I clocked in 5.30 hours upon finishing my first run and I wasn't rushing.
- The choice system from the original has been completely removed, the game is far more linear and streamlined as a result. It feels incredibly railroaded compared to the original due to these missing divergent paths, this and the missing Mercenaries mode harms replayability.
- Ultimately the game feels like a rushed cash-in, cynically hurried to market without a team that loves/understand what made the original great, chiefly to quickly cash in on fan goodwill towards the previous remake. Capcom may well be heading down the wrong path again

This game was a major disappointment on many levels and demonstrated to me that it was just a lousy cash-grab with the 'Resident Evil' label slapped on it. Minor spoilers will be made in this review!

1: Gameplay

This isn't much of a pro, it's more or less the same as the gameplay seen in the Resident Evil 2 remake, so I understand why they would follow the 'if it ain't broke don't fix it' mentality. However, one prominent feature this game added was a dodge mechanic which was an interesting mechanic and worked well and complimented the general gameplay. My only real downside is that it made the player feel TOO in control and confident when encountering enemies that it strays away further from the traditional survival horror seen in the original game. The return of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ QTEs was unwelcoming. One particular gameplay segment that I absolutely despised was the horde mode part defending Jill in the hospital, really put me off and the zombies evaporated as they died what was up with that!? I would've love to have seen a fixed camera angle and tank control alternative for this game as it would've added to the experience.  

2: Story/Soundtrack

Now without delving into the narrative of the game, it is clear having finished the game that many segments seen in the original game did not make the final cut in this remake, which his a damn shame. Playing through this game's story felt more like playing out a Michael Bay film than it did a survival horror experience. These is one particular scene in this game where this became apparent to me, it involved Jill 'Balls' being shot at with a rocket launcher by Nemesis and then plot armour happens. If you've played the game you know the scene. If this 'remake' included every cut segment seen in the original game and even added more content it certainly would've helped fleshed out the game a lot more. Otherwise all you really have is this disposable AAA C grade cash-grab with no replayability which is what this game at this current state is. The soundtrack was not very memorable at all and I believe the soundtrack from the original game only just released on steam for a hefty price A MONTH LATER. This should been included in the games release as an option!

3. Nemesis/Enemy AI:

Nemesis was the most disappointing element of this game and it's sad to say that they truely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up an antagonist that is meant to be super intimidating and downright terrifying like in the original. Nemesis presented very little challenge to me throughout the game and was just an annoyance than an actual threat. I didn't like his redesign, made it look like it was wearing a garbage bag and his facial design was just dumb to look at, if they'd just remastered the original look for Nemesis that would've worked just fine. Plus the animation of Nemesis kneeling down when wounded made it even less threatening and just made Nemesis your ♥♥♥♥♥. Now the enemy AI was an absolute mess in this game compared to the Resident Evil 2 'Remake', there were particular moments where the Zombie AI in particular would just mope around aimlessly trying to find me when I would just be standing a metre away and they would just walk circles.

4. Conclusion

Overall, I was very disappointed with this 'Remake' of the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis and doesn't deserve to be called a remake. A re-imagined version sure, but a lacklustre and piss poor effort. If you're on the fence on getting this game don't shill for it now, wait until there is a either a massive price drop or don't bother playing it. I personally don't think this game is worth the time at all I would instead suggest you play the original Resident Evil 3 Nemesis, a true survival horror classic!

While RE2make was very much a survival horror game with some modern third person shooter trappings, this game feels like the opposite. This is a modern "cinematic" third person shooter, first and foremost and I consider every change from the design sensibilities of that game to be a clear downgrade. 

This doesn't really feature the classic RE exploration loop where you work your way back and forth through the map, slowly opening up new routes, making meaningful decisions about navigation, hazards, and resources. There are basically no puzzles to speak of. There ARE tons of tedious Cinematic Set Pieces™ and canned stumbling animations in response to pointless scripted explosions. It even has several scenes where "W" (or controller equivalent) is displayed prominently on the screen to make you feel like you're doing something (holding W). The Nemesis sequences are all linear hallways or marginally interactive set pieces. The final boss ends with a QTE finisher. I don't consider this a spoiler because it wasn't really that cool 15 years ago when developers thought this kind of thing was amazing next generation game design and it sure isn't now.

Continuing in this direction is the awful new dodge move, which you primarily use to execute a last second timing roll and slow motion quick draw move. I have no idea why people enjoy this kind of fake skill mechanic. I would much prefer straightforward, readable collision detection that lines up intuitively with the models and their animations. Hell, even a standard dodge roll that just works consistently. You know, instead of the only thing that matters being the frame timing window when you pressed the special avoid damage button. Of course many of the enemies (and bosses) are clearly tuned for this, with extra magnetized attack animations that lock in from 10 feet away to force you to hit the arbitrary slow mo timing unless you've maintained serious distance and continue to back-pedal. Most of my deaths were the result of obnoxious instant kill moves.

So, in brief, my problem with this game is not that it's short. My problem is that it's yet another tedious modern AAA cinematic action game. It would fit right in as a PlayStation exclusive. I can only hope the series will not continue its backward slide towards the wannabe western AAA garbage dark ages between RE4 and RE7. Weird how they never made an RE5 or RE6.

To put it in a nutshell: this game is only if you want to experience a very slapped together, "guess we have to do this while we have the assets, code, and map data from RE2Make" type of Resident Evil 3 remake that's missing a lot of the heart and soul of the PS1/DC original.

The whole purpose of a remake, in my mind, ever since I played Metroid Zero Mission on the GBA so many years ago, (back when games actually came out finished and there was still creativity in the industry) was to add content, not take things away or make a glorified square object look like a clock tower and be all like "hurr durr, there's a clock tower, normies won't complain, hurr durr. We made Resident Evil 7 and RE2Make (and maybe DMC5? Doubt that's the same team though), surely they'll let us off the hook for this one, amirite, m8s?"

Sure, the game looks and sounds better, no doubt about that, but that's every remake/remaster (*coughs* glorified port) nowadays. That's just the expectation. I mean, c'mon, not as many people would have bought Metroid Zero Mission back in 2004 if it used the same NES graphics, but added in everything from Fusion/Super Metroid in terms of functionality and re-designed the game's challenge and structure along with the new content that game had.

And considering that there's been sources talking about a RE4 remake (because there's not enough ways to play that game already, and apparently, not enough mods to make the game look good enough for normies now), do you really have confidence that they'll do a good job with that game, if it's actually real and not just some confusion about that RE8 Village demo that shared a similar premise, but with some weird Werewolf-esque monsters or something?

This game really isn't that bad.  It looks friggin great and I enjoyed exploring what I could of Racoon City while I was there which in turn is the reason I have 10hrs on play instead of 6.  For as quick as this game came out just after RE 2: Remake it's got a lot of good stuff in it. 

One thing to note is that Nemesis is not Mr. X and will not follow you around like Mr. X would.  Rather he shows up for scripted events and several escape sequences most of the time your fights with him are either in boss fights or QTE events.  In some ways he feels watered down and is kind of easy to fight if you have the right weapons.

For my playthrough I stuck mostly to handguns and a whole lot of knife usage.  I never saw the need for the shotgun and really only used the grenade launcher for the Nemesis battles.  The zombies are still the same fodder as ever and can be somewhat threatening if they get into groups, they even play possum most of the time.  You can stab them with the knife when they are on the ground,  It makes it very easy to kill some of them before they get up however it also allows you to easily tell which zombie is going to wake up later on.   These kind of zombies you can stab and have them bleed but can't actually kill because you aren't meant to kill them and they don't even wake up until they are scripted to.  If you stab a body on the ground and nothing happens then that body isn't going to do anything.  

Outside of regular Zombies, you have the zombie dogs which show up in about two locations once early on and again near endgame.  You get at least a couple of variants of hunters.  Both of which which have one hit kill abilities if they manage to get close.

There is cut content, such as the central park area and the clocktower.  Hell we only gain access to one restaurant which is a doughnut joint.  The concept art has a bar but you never see the inside of it in game.  The puzzles are completely gone and have been replaced by a couple fetch quests.  Outside of that I don't recall what other areas may have been cut.

The controls are the same as RE 2 which isn't that bad, You will be picking up a lot of stuff and have to learn to manage your inventory so you don't run out of space.

Now do I think it's worth 60 dollars?  Perhaps not.  again it has cut content and the multiplayer segment was kind of dead the last time I tried it out where I quit after waiting around 10 - 15 minutes to get into a quick match as a survivor.

In short:  It's a decent great looking game that has what feels like a tacked on Multiplayer mode and would reccomend people try it out, most likely when it's a little cheaper.

This game is a mixed bag to me and its hard to judge becouse of that, in the end I will judge the whole game not just what I enjoyed about it.
The game is short on content, and the content that it has feels unfinished in some respects.
At some point I had to open a text file and write down some of the bad things that I encountered while playing, becouse there was so much of it.
In short the game feels rushed and unfinished for the price they ask for it.

[b] Pros [/b]
+ World looks amazing
+ Music and sound is great
+ Voice acting is great
+ Story telling is amazing both dialogue and text files

[b] Cons [/b]
- Has some bugs (not game breaking for me)
- Loot locations and amounts make no sense
- Fight mechanics have flaws, bossfights break immersion
- Scripted dammage that you can't avoid & animations that you can't break
- Some mistakes were made in the worldbuilding and cutscenes
- Game slows you down to drag out content
- Short 4-12 hours of gameplay (vast pace vs search everything)


[u] World and Sound [/u]
The game has a great feel to it, eerie yet enticing to enter and explore. The grafics are on point most of the time, and fit a game of this time. Comming from a franchise that is great in city design, this game draws from that and does not disapoint. Some areas will be familiar to those that played RE before, yet felt new and refreshing enough to me.
The worldbuilding has some flaws where the developers have most likely used props from previous games, there isn't much of it, but it was immersion breaking to me at a few points. Where a sign or poster is such low resolution that you cant read it, while every other sign or poster arround it is newly made and high resolution. There is also a point where you pick up a picture frame commenting that Clair is in it, while the picture only shows a group of male soldiers.
The Cutscenes are mostly well made and realy add to the game, however there are points where a weapon gets trown away and disapears in that same cutscene, and someone shoots with an empty gun without picking any ammo up.
Loot is in the weirdest places, where a locked weapon save or crate got a single box with a few rounds of ammo. While a hospital treatment room has grenades and ammo on the food and treatment tables. Healing items aren't always spread arround logicaly, you might get tons of healing items at places where there is no combat, yet where there is combat you might struggle finding any. Some loot is randomized, this might be the issue.
I have also noticed that some paper maps can be interacted with, and will update your digital map, while the exact same type of maps in other places can't be interacted with.
Some areas are blocked in a stupid manner with small objects or ankle high plates of wood blocking large openings or passages. You can't jump over logical items/places.

The sound and music in the game felt great, from the background music to the voiceacting, it realy pulled me into the game.

[u] Gameplay [/u]
The gameplay is realy a mixed bag for me, its challenging and engaging, yet at the same time flawed and annoying.
Zombies heads have hitpoints, yet every zombie has a wildly different amount of hitpoints, some might take 2 shots, while the exact same type of zombie might stand up again after 12 shots. There is no animation nor model in place for a dead zombie only for critical hits, so the player gets no feedback what so ever.
The combat finds place in a lot of confined places, sometimes as big as 3-4m2, yet you can't aim at your feet, this becomes a problem when you need to make sure a zombie stays down.
Zombies dont react from getting shot in most cases, and attack animations can't be broken. 
A downed zombie that is not dead can be shot without reacting, while slashing a knife at that same zombie makes it stand back up, as if you hurt it.
Zombies have attack animations that take arround 3 seconds and can't be interrupted, even longer if you get hit, yet the game tells you to click your left mouse button to ''break free'' when a zombie grabs you.
Zombies will break through doors that you have to open with a handle or doorknob, while doors that you push open (like in hospitals) they can't get through and walk away from. Creating a wierd sight, when you stand in a doorway and move forward and backwards.
Boss fights are just mini games of hit and run, loot scattered in the boss fight area breaks immersion. 
Becouse of attack animations, you can get stunlocked or blocked from moving.
The dodge mechanics are terrible and for me immersion breaking, you run faster than you dodge out of the way of an attack and even stop walking or running for a while afterwards, just standing there casualy like nothing is going on, breaking down the speed of gameplay.

The game throws a lot of items at you to open doors, passages and containers, and its inventory management I quite enjoyed, yet you have to sellect the items to use every time from the inventory, where a simple 2 second cutscene would have worked better.
The game also stops when using those items, even if you are in combat.
Those items have to be discarded manualy every 30+ of them, while you magicaly know you can't use them anymore for the rest of the game for some reason.

The game feels like its made to slow you down, and with its limited amount of content that makes sense.


[u] Bugs [/u]
The game has rendering bugs, that happen when you go through a doorway into a new room, showing a dark grey void before rendering the area again. This happens a few times and i have managed to reproduce it every time. The game also has some locations where the camera clips through walls, and the game glitches objects in the map sometimes.
A finished AAA titel priced at 60 euros, with only 4-12 hours of gameplay, should not have bugs in it, especialy those that could have been fixed by playtesting.

[u] Replay value [/u]
The game can be replayed at a different dificulty setting, with some starting items and/or to unlock achievements. No actual content will be added to the game, so this wont be for everyone.

[b] Verdict [/b]
This game is a strange one, where some of the development team have delivered content well and truely beond expectations, other parts seem unfinished or rushed. The game also feels like it hasn't been properly playtested, or the dev team didnt have a gamer on board that looks at details.
I cant recommend this game with a straight face, so i wont. Did i enjoy the game? Yes i did. Was it becouse i already love the franchise and gametype, absolutely.
Do i recommend this game, to someone who wants to play RE for the first time at any price point? No.
Do i recommend this game to someone who already likes the franchise, yes for 8-12 euros to someone who is mildly interested. And maybe 20-25 euros if you are a die-hard fan, but be warned that you might get disapointed.

Resident Evil 3 Remake is the reimagination of the 1999 Resident Evil 3. You play as Jill Valentine, trying to escape the zombie infested Raccoon City, while being stalked by the B.O.W known as Nemesis. As this game leans more towards combat, you will fight against zombies, mutated monsters and Nemesis itself much more often here, though flight is still a wise choice most of the time. Unlike RE 2 Remake, items such as knife and grenades are now occupying your weapon slot instead of being the defensive item to protect yourself from attacks. Instead Jill gets the dodge button, which, it time correctly allow to evade any attack perfectly without taking any damage, while being able to aim and shoot at the same time.

Like in RE 2, you need to find key items to progress, while trying to evade attacks or outright being killed by zombies, monsters or Nemesis. There will be instances where Nemesis itself will chase you with whatever it is holding or has become, making it hard to outright escape him, though you can slow him down or incapacitate him to buy some time, or even get some loot in the latter case. The dodge button, while risky to use if mistimed wrongly, its a boon when done right. At higher difficulties, you will need to master this skill to survive.

Visual wise, Jill looks really good here, so does Miguel... I mean Carlos. Raccoon City looks really nice as well. Combat is fluid, especially when you get that perfect dodge, since you can do an attack during the dodge animation, while everything slows down. Kinda like bullet time, you know. Some side characters, where you may barely know in the original, now gets more personality. At least its not a side character that exists just to be killed off. Some monsters looks utterly terrifying compared to the original version, like the Gammas.

Now the downside... Where to start.... Remember Mr X in RE 2 Remake? Yeah, his presence in RPD is way more intimidating than Nemesis stalking you in his human form. Because of the linearity of the levels, you just don't feel Nemesis stalking presence as much as you have in the original. Many things were retconned or removed outright, such as the park, Gravedigger boss, Clock Tower, Brad, event choices, even puzzles. At higher difficulties, perfect dodge is pretty much a must, since you either get two shotted, or worst, one shotted by pretty much anything. This is the most frustrating part of the game, where the last two difficulties kind of rely on you using the item shop to make it through. Special shoutout to the worst final boss in RE history. At higher difficulty, his attack patterns and speed changes drastically, so prepare to play Dark Souls: RE edition and die. Repeatedly. For a AAA game, the content is pretty short. One main story, and the replay value is just to unlock the infinite weapons and perks, and artworks. No other game modes like Mercenaries or so currently.

Overall, I would still recommend this. I enjoyed it, but not as much as RE 2 Remake to be honest. You can get this game, but wait for the price to drop. I would also suggest to start with RE 2 Remake, just to get the gist of the gameplay, despite RE 3 taking place slightly earlier than it chronologically. Do note that Resident Evil Resistance is free with this game, if you are interested in some kind of mastermind multiplayer PVP kind of game.

Praise Point #1: Right off the bat, I noticed the degree of world and character detail is slightly improved over RE2make, and that the action is much snappier.  And you can dodge in this game!  It's a great mechanic, and in a realistic twist, the inconsistently shambling zombies are tougher to dodge cleanly than more conscious and precise foes, like Nemesis or the hunters.  Everything is fun to fight for different reasons.   

Praise Point #2: Carlos, despite his silly salon coiffure, is a teriffic character to play as.  Whereas Jill follows up a perfect dodge by centering her crosshairs automatically on an enemy's weak-point, Carlos pulls a genuine Chris Redfield, letting fly a haymaker of boulder-smashing magnitude and sending foes flying.

Gripe #1:  Zombies.  While the action is quite a bit better, it's disappointing to see zombies recycled from RE2make -- and even more disappointing is that severed limbs no longer fall off and leave a nice gooey mess, but now simply [i]vanish[/i] into thin air.  If one thing in this pretty, slickly playing game can actually be called "cheap," it's this.

Gripe #2:  Brevity.  The game is way too short for the price.  I can see this being an upscale DLC for RE2make, not a full-on $60 game.  That said, it's only a "three-hour game" if you blaze through it as quickly as you possibly can; if you spend any time [i]at all[/i] soaking up the details, collecting missable ammo and items, or practicing the dodge mechanic, you should get at least six.  This kind of length was common back in the PS1 days; perhaps we've all been spoiled by meaty games with [i]loads and loads of [b]content[/b][/i]. 

A great game in the final estimation, but Capcom could have made it better and longer -- perhaps another half-year in the oven would have done the trick.  Buy it at a reasonable price, enjoy it, and don't agonize over what could have been.

(This is very minor gripe, but I really miss classic Jill, the one with the sleepy blue eyes and the ample bottom; it's not that nuJill [i]isn't[/i] beautiful, but it's really hard to see her as the same character I've controlled over these many years.)

Developers never learn.  Capcom hadn't exactly slam-dunked the release of Resident Evil 2 but the game was meaty enough, pretty enough and revamped enough to excite many hardcore Resident Evil/horror gamers.  Upon completion of Resident Evil 2, many gamers were hungry for the release of the sequel: Resident Evil 3.  Even more excitingly, the game was going to be every bit as satisfying as its precursor but was also supposedly packaged with a gorgeous multiplayer mode that would add even more hours of gameplay.  Resident Evil 2 sold really well and the assumption was that Capcom would do everything in its power to funnel those funds to replicate the process with Resident Evil 3.  Not so.

Resident Evil 3 has simply staggeringly beautiful models, with sharp, realistic animations and nigh-photorealistic textures.  The game looks sumptuous in 4K and it positively bleeds atmosphere.  Possessed of great sounds, a solid soundtrack and good voice acting, Resident Evil 3 seems to have caught lightning in a bottle again.  The game runs at Ultra/4K at a solid 60 fps.  Unfortunately, the game isn't nearly as stable, with issues afflicting my drivers for half my playthrough, resulting in pronounced and onerous screen flickering.  Additionally, the maps are tiny, with areas of Raccoon City amounting to 2-3 square, shuttered blocks.  I still remember my profuse disappointment when I finally broke into a toy store, only to discover a 10x10 room with minimal secrets or loot.

Gameplay feels good, with third person controls operating beautifully, especially with the expanded dodge animations/controls.  Unfortunately, some of the enemies rush you quickly, resulting in camera issues although, thankfully, this doesn't happen often.  Apart from the technical issues, weapons and gunplay feel really good.  The same can't be said about the enemy AI, with several enemies losing track of you through a simple, open doorway.  Additionally, Nemesis exhibits a more event-oriented AI, rather than the roaming Mr. X AI from Resident Evil 2.  While this kind of behavior can be tense when he pops up as a surprise, boss battles tend to be more formulaic and less stressful than the preceding game's boss encounters.

The story is about as absurd as it gets.  Worse still, the game's plot has become more action-oriented than that of Resident Evil 2.  In some ways, it feels like the same type of descent that the Resident Evil IP experienced in its slide towards Resident Evil 6.  The game is phenomenally short, completed in about 6-8 hours, with minimal reasons to replay the campaign.  Some character and sketch galleries acquisitions could lead to a replay.  Some more determined players may want to attain certain achievements but most players will play this once for 6-8 hours and never touch it again.  Large areas from the original game, like the clock tower and spiders have been completely excised.

The multiplayer is pretty, runs well and has minimal glitches but, unfortunately, bad design and a poor UI mar the experience.  Playing as the evil RE scientist can be fun but the gameplay often progresses far too quickly to weigh strategic options carefully or to employ complex tactics.  Playing as survivors is a frenetic mess, with little communication and little strategic application outside of running and gunning.  I doubt I'll get more than 2-4 hours out of the multiplayer.  This problem is compounded by empty lobbies that compromise online play, less than 2 months after release.

Overall, Resident Evil 3, is a sad addition after the inspired Resident Evil 2.  It feels abridged, small and lacks the hours of gameplay that the predecessor revels in.  It feels like a lazy release and a poor celebration of a true classic Resident Evil game.  It's still a wonderously cinematic experience with jaw-dropping graphics and I recommend that anyone pick up the title for 30 USD or less.  It's not worth 60 USD however and at the current price, it's a bad bargain.

R3Make is just like ordering mashed potatoes without gravy; I was fed with what I was craving for, yet it missed something substantial for me to be fully happy with the meal. The game just did not feel that immersive and engrossing, because for the price, I was expecting something that would make me internalize the things happening in the game. That "immersive factor" was what scared me in the previous remakes they had. While the game did have its fair share of merits that made in enjoyable, I think the content is the glaring flaw of this game. 

For the graphics, the it cannot be denied that R3make spared no expenses from making the scenery; the ruined city is detailed and complex, yet intuitive enough for you to get around quite easily. Even though the map was in an open area, it still made me feel claustrophobic from the tight spaces it had throughout the game, which is no easy feat. Overall, there is nothing much to nitpick about the graphics because it did a great job of creating an open, yet packed level.

The mechanics are smooth, and it did not get in the way in the horror-ness of the game. While the dodge mechanic is seemingly easy at first glance, it requires practice to pull off properly. This means that players cannot abuse it, which would have dampened the impact of the game otherwise. The aiming is smooth, and the inventory mechanic was improved compared to its predecessor. In other words, the mechanics removed the "chores" that would have been unnecessary for game play, and it implemented a mechanic that benefits both beginners and pros alike without turning the game into an action game.

The content was supposed to be crowning point of the game, yet it flunked it horrendously. The story was too short compared to the other games, and it lacks any sort of replay value other than a completionist gameplay. Once you're done with the game, you're just done. There are no side stories or anything that would have fleshed out the game more. The linear story means once you've seen the game, you've seen it all. RE Resistance may be created to compensate for that, yet it just feels detached and awkwardly tied with the game itself. Perhaps I might be being unfair here because RE2 had those modes where you are offered alternate perspectives within the game, but a 5-6 hour linear story is just not enough to distinguish itself.

In short, I regret buying this game. I wished I spent it on ACNN instead because I felt unsatisfied with how they delivered the content. It's just too linear and limited for me to truly immerse myself.

Remember when RE4 let you choose between 4 different handguns with their own unique specs to add replayability and experimentation? Those were good times.

After beating the game you can unlock new weapons but they’re so overpowered they’ll trivialize the challenge making them a non-option for a serious replay.

[h1]So i‘m gonna be one of those unpopular opinion puffins and say that RE 3 (2020) is better than RE 2 (2019).[/h1]

First and foremost: I‘m not a die hard old-school survival horror RE fan.
I only watched a friend play the original RE 1 and 2 on his playstation back in 1996. I remember 10 years old me finding the RE 1 intro cutscene pretty scary and disturbing back then and since then the series was burned in my brain as that super scary and violent zombie game series. But the first RE i actually played and completed myself was the PC Port of RE4 back in 2007 or 2008. That’s when i really started to love the series and played every major entry since RE 4 as long as it was released for PC. Consequently i‘m a fan of the more recent, action-oriented RE titles that started with RE4. I played the remakes of RE 1 and Zero too, and watched Let’s plays for the classic RE 1, 2, 3 and Code Veronica, but apart from that the only nostalgic memory i have for RE are the memories of 10 year old me described above. As a result, i‘m not one of those survival horror purists that hate every RE post RE 4 or Code Veronica. Since i got into the series so late and never played the first three classic REs, i basically enjoyed almost every RE game ever since (yes, even RE 6). And maybe that’s why i enjoyed the RE3 remake even more than last year‘s RE2 (which was fantastic as well and one of the best games of 2019).

Compared to RE2, RE3 is a lot more linear, straightforward, action-orientated and fast-paced. There is little to no backtracking and compared to RE2 the amount of puzzles is kept to a minimum here, maybe 2 or 3 very easy ones during the entire game. The focus clearly lies on the various encounters with nemesis, but compared to the almost unvulnerable mr. x, who randomly stalked the halls of the police station in RE2 and could lurk around every corner, nemesis is a joke. The fights against him are heavily scripted and every other time or so you are basically forced to fight him anyway, because it’s made up as a boss fight.

but apart from that, i really welcomed the faster pace and linearity of RE3. While RE 2 was not significantly longer than this, it had a couple of sections which i felt were dragging a little. The level design and pacing of the story in RE 3 however keep things fresh and after finishing the game in about 5 1/2 hours i felt it was just as long as it needed to be and left me satisfied at the end. Neither was the game so short that i wanted more of it, nor was it so long that it left me bored and oversaturated.

Technically, the game looks and sounds fantastic as well, even though the grafics saw no significant overhaul since RE2. Music, sound effects and voice acting are decent at least and the grafics (especially the character models) are rich in detail. the level design encourages exploration (where possible) and rewards it with atmospheric and very detailed environmental design. The game can be quite demanding on higher settings, but if you have the proper hardware it runs very stable and smooth. I did not experience a single crash or slowdown during my playthrough.

So, is RE3 objectively better than the RE2 Remake? Probably not. For many RE fans it will certainly stray too far from the beloved survival horror roots again, that were revived in RE7 and last year’s RE2. But for people who like a little less puzzles and a bit more action, RE3 is probably the better choice. I personally enjoyed it a bit more than the RE2 Remake.

I'd have to say after playing Resident Evil 2 very recently I found Resident Evil 3 quite underwhelming. There are things to like, but it felt like a decent step back from Resident Evil 2. The game definitely has pacing issues as it felt unfinished. The game performs well, and looks spectacular, but the game really is very short. I knew something was off when you were running through the city during the initial outbreak, then all of a sudden you were met with a nest of monster bugs. Didn't the outbreak just happen today? Where could they have come about so fast?

In terms of gameplay, it plays fine. If you played Resident Evil 2, this would be very familiar. Only differences is now you get a nifty little timed dodge roll you can do if you hit the space bar at the right time.

Now let's talk about the titular character Nemesis. It's basically the culmination of Umbrella's Tyrant program. But I found him more of an annoyance compared to Mr.X from the previous game. In Resident Evil 2, what made Mr.X so intimidating is that he's basically a giant wrench in the game design that forces you to do things that would be against your interests. Zombies in the way? Can't wait around! Mr.X is after you! Lickers are prowling about? Maybe you could sneak pa-NOPE! RUN! X GONNA GIVE IT TO YA RIGHT IN YOUR ASS UNLESS YOU LEG IT! 

In Nemesis' case, he is much more mobile than Mr.X, which with the already somewhat (I think intentionally) clunky controls can be a tiny bit annoying. He also has a tentacle that can grab you across the room and pull you over to him. I can tell you I wasn't the least bit scared of Nemesis while Mr.X was very unnerving and I'll tell you why.

Nemesis is very incompetent, both to his own stupidity and Jill's plot armor. Nemesis gets access to a boat load of weapons, in addition to being an Übermensch built like a brickshithouse. He is faster and stronger than  any human, and gets access to a flame thrower, and even a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rocket launcher, and yet a (Sure, highly trained, but with RE2 trying to be a bit more grounded it is pretty ridiculous) woman can give him the run around and even fight him off? In RE2, it makes sense, since all the monsters are moreso mindless creatures acting on animal instinct. Mr.X is just a big huge brick that burst through walls because he's not a smart allec. He just wants everyone in Raccon City to die, and he will keep trying no matter what.

And in Jill's case, she manages to survive situations that would seem find in Resident Evil 4,5, and 6, but in the more grounded universe of the reboot it definitely is out of place that she can get hit by a rocket and get sent flying, or that she can slowly walk away with a wounded comrade, TURNING HER BACK ON A PSYCHO KILLING MACHINE FRANKENSTEIN MONSTER, and then Jill proves she was in the right as the Nemesis creature kills the comrade, not the PRIMARY TARGET WHOSE MURDER IS ETCHED IN IT'S DAMN PROGRAMMING. No, the randy is what he goes for.

You also play a significant part of the game as Carlos, a mercenary who was hired by Umbrella. I actually really enjoyed these segments, and even found him a tiny bit more enjoyable than Jills (Partially because Jill reacts to everything with mild confusion and annoyance, such as a giant bug monster puking maggots down her throat). There isn't much of a Part a Part B story like in Resident Evil 2 (And it was virtually nonexistent than outside of a few levels), so Carlos is more of a back up character for Jill.

TL;DR: Too short, not enough puzzles, and not nearly gripping as RE:2.

Game Length:
I'm gonna say what everyone else has already said. I never played the original, but it's obvious this game caters to that niche group that did. I'm not gonna say what I'm about to say because others have said this in other reviews, but rather because it is blindingly obvious when you do play it yourself: there is a lot cut out here. Now, I don't know if it's because I played RE:2 which had SIGNIFICANTLY more content, but you can tell when you play RE:3, that each area was holding back. As if there was more to that area, more puzzles, more story, but it just wasn't handing over the goods. I bet this is because Capcom rushed this out of the door. On a related note, because each area 'holds back' and 'has less content' it is incredibly short, with only 5-6 hours worth of gameplay. You could essentially buy it, download it and finish the game all in 1 day if you had the internet speeds for it. It's disappointing that the game costs $92, because it sure as ♥♥♥♥ ain't worth it. I could buy The Witcher 3 with a third of that money and get over 100 hours worth of decent gameplay. I know it's unfair to compare TW3 to RE:3 because they're completely different games, but what I'm trying to say is that it should be priced accordingly. In short, this game is less of a standalone game, and more of an expansion to the previous remaster. 

Puzzles:
There are much fewer puzzles in this game than in RE:2 and because of it, I found it hardly captivating. Towards the end, I found I was just playing to see it through. The thing I loved about RE:2 was how many puzzles there were; different items unlock different things. You get a key with a spade on it, and you think, 'Oh ♥♥♥♥, I know what that's for!' so you end up going to every room with a spade symbol on the door, unlocking it and seeing what's inside, only to find another item that gets you excited again and makes you say the exact same thing. You don't get nearly as much of that here. Not only is It n't nearly as much of a special moment, simply because there are much fewer items to find, and even fewer special areas, but there are not nearly as many complex puzzles. I can only recall 1 decent puzzle, and it is in the beginning area and it gives you neat little items. You'll know what it is when you find it.

Nemesis:
Watching the trailer, this guy was scary ♥♥♥♥. If I thought Mr X was bad, this guy must be a whole other ball game. Wrong, not really. He looks scary, but he's basically just Mr X with a reskin, if you ignore the boss fights that is. He is not NEARLY as scary as Mr X, simply because he only arrives during cinematic moments. Mr X could be around the next door, and what's that? You hear loud booming footsteps outside the room. And what else? There is only one exit and the Tyrant is literally outside? Better be quiet as ♥♥♥♥ and not move, and pray to hell he doesn't walk in. Those are the experiences that made Mr X terrifying. Not knowing if he was in the next room, the room below you, or just around the corner, only having the sound of his footsteps to tell if he was close. It's impossible to be scared of Nemesis when he only ever shows up in cutscenes, chase scenes, or anything overly cinematic. It becomes less of 'Oh crap, it's Nemesis!' and more like, 'Oh... it's Nemesis'. It's a shame because he looks totally badass.

Summary:
The game isn't bad, it just needed a lot of improvement before it could be said that it was a great game. RE:2 was great. RE:3 is just mediocre. It's harsh, but it's true. The biggest let down overall, despite everything is the puzzles for me. I don't mind playing a short game, especially if it's reasonably priced, but without the puzzles and the items and all the running around exploring each room, the experience is ruined. That's the appeal for me on the Resident Evil games: never knowing what's next, what's in the next room, and figuring out how to solve the next puzzle.

[h1] This Review Will Contain Spoilers [/h1]

Ok, before I begin my review for this, I just want to say that I normally don't write reviews for games. I usually play a game and then I move on because reviews don't matter to me, but this one is different. I really need to review this one after beating it last night for the first time on Standard difficulty. This review is going to be a combination of pros and cons, as well as comparisons to the original game it's based on since I have played both games.

[h1] Graphics, Effects and Lighting, and Optimization [/h1]

So right off the bat I really liked the visuals. The RE Engine does an amazing job with making things look so realistic. The effects of explosions combined with lighting against objects looked really cool and flashy, and the shadows to me looked a lot better in this one compared to the Resident Evil 2 remake. Also, the game seems well optimized; I didn't experience a single frame drop, and had everything set to almost their highest settings before the game warned me I was exceeding the VRAM required.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

Overall I thought the gameplay was really solid. Controls were just like Resident Evil 2 remake with the addition of an improved dodge button much like what was in Resident Evil Revelations 2, which the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis didn't have. If timed correctly, you can do a perfect dodge and then get locked onto a spot that is weak to an enemy. In the original game you had to flick the control stick or push the action button while aiming at the right moment, but it could be hard to pull off, and sometimes you could easily dodge towards danger if not done correctly. Another thing I felt is that the game is more fast-paced compared to the original, but I didn't feel it was like Resident Evil 6 with extreme over the top moments and questionable action sequences. Both Resident Evil 3: Nemesis and Resident Evil 3 2020 are more action oriented games compared to the original Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 2 2019. Also, this game packed in a lot more zombies in quite a few areas, which really added to the tension and you had to choose when it was best to kill them or ignore them.

Now a few things that felt weird in this game is the guns didn't feel like they packed much of a punch compared to the Resident Evil 2 remake. Handguns felt very weak, and zombies seemed to take more bullets to the head. Also, shooting off limbs is a lot harder to do in this one unless you're using a shotgun, but even then they didn't always pop. Another thing, which I will also touch more on later in the review, is that this game did feel shorter compared to Resident Evil 3: Nemesis. Even though I beat it at a standard playtime of 4-5 hours, it is a lot shorter than that. Now the original game was short as well, but this one is by far a lot shorter than that game.

[h1] The Story and Cut Content [/h1]

So much like the original you are playing as Jill Valentine who must escape Raccoon City which has become overrun by zombies and other creatures unleashed by the Umbrella Corporation. You start off at her apartment just like the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, but this time you actually get to start inside her apartment before the 'S' hits the fan. This is where the game starts to take a completely different route from the original source material the game is based on. Instead of Jill fleeing her zombie infested apartment, she is [spoiler] greeted by a B.O.W. (Bio-organic weapon) called Nemesis which was unleashed upon Raccoon City by the Umbrella Corp to hunt down and kill any S.T.A.R.S. members remaining in the city. [/spoiler] After you have escaped the apartment, you run into Brad Vickers for a short time, but then, unlike the original game where Brad [spoiler] warns you of an unknown creature that is after S.T.A.R.S. members, and later killed by Nemesis in front of the Raccoon Police Depart by Nemesis, [/spoiler] he [spoiler] sacrifices himself to the zombies at Jack's Bar so that you can escape. [/spoiler] After all that, the game then becomes nothing like the original game. Instead of going to the Raccoon City Hall to [spoiler] fix up an old train car to escape to the clock tower for extraction, [/spoiler] you instead go to the [spoiler] Raccoon City subway and meet with Carlos and the rest of the U.B.C.S. (Umbrella Biohazard Countermeasure Service) to help them get one of the subway trains full of passengers out of the city. [/spoiler]

I could go on and on about all these story changes, but I'm just going to list off everything that was in the original that was cut from this game. [spoiler] Way too much of Raccoon City was cut; You spend more time in Raccoon City in the original game compared to this one. The warehouse, the restaurant, the parking garage, the Raccoon City Hall, the Raccoon Press office, the Raccoon City Park, and the water treatment facility is GONE. Even though in this whole game you're in Raccoon City, you honestly won't feel like it after a while. A lot of the new areas that replaced those I mentioned are indoors and within reach of each other when you do go outside. After helping Carlos get the subway train ready you're no longer going to be exploring much of Raccoon City. Also, just like the Resident Evil 2 remake, they cut out enemies. You will no longer see those snake/worm-like creatures that had a chance to poison you, no more giant spiders, and no more crows. They even cut out the giant worm boss fight. [/spoiler]

So to go back to the story, it is very underwhelming compared to the original. It just didn't feel as engaging, and it didn't have nearly as much lore. You got Nemesis chasing you in some fixed areas like the original, but he [spoiler] transforms way too early and it doesn't make much sense. His final transformation was the worst and fastest boss fight I have ever completed in a Resident Evil game.  [/spoiler] And with all the memorable moments that made up the original cut from this game, the story has been drastically changed. Yes it all ends with a [spoiler] government cover up and a missile completely wiping Raccoon City off the face of the earth, but the ending just didn't have a big impact on me like it did in the original game. There's even a quick and forced scene where you have to shoot a certain character to end the game which felt very out of place. [/spoiler]

[h1] TL;DR/The Verdict [/h1]

While I did enjoy this game as another installment in the Resident Evil franchise and graphically it looked amazing, I felt this was not a good remake of the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis. Too many memorable moments were cut as well as enemies and areas. I wish Steam had a neutral review instead of a thumbs up or thumbs down because I feel that's what this game deserves, but for now I will have to give it a Not Recommended review. If you're a new fan of the Resident Evil series and did not play the original, you will probably like this game. However, for fans of the original and have been following the series, this game has very little in common and strays far from its source. Buy it on sale.

This does have 2 extra difficulties which I see a lot of people saying is the end game content. Nightmare and Inferno. They change enemy locations, make them 10x more aggressive...aaaaaaaaand that's it. Nothing else is done with it. There was a moment where the Tentacle Heads fall from a bridge onto the streets, a bunch of them. Coulda made the situation you were in very hard and...oh...you ran into the building because when they fall they have a 5 second grace period to attack you. That happens a bunch. Harder enemies in earlier locations will be completely skipped, and very easily too. Coulda done something like new enemies, maybe RE3OG cut enemies on the harder difficulties. Nothing of the sort was done. Nightmare and Inferno isn't really worth it since you're just gonna be seeing the Tentacle Heads used way more than they were used on the earlier difficulties.

Many, and when I say many I mean hours of content, areas were cut from the game. It's not surprising. REmake 2 came out a year ago. They started work on REmake 3 when they were almost done REmake 2. And it very much shows. They cut a lot of corners in this remake. Areas like the Clocktower and the zoo just...gone. Oh sorry, you can go to the Clocktower...and when I say go to the Clocktower, I mean go right outside of it and fight a Nemmy dog boss and that's it. The Clocktower in the original was at least a good hour worth of content, which is still baffling to me that they cut it considering there's a pamphlet RIGHT before the Clocktower area saying how the building is pretty much rotting and falling apart. When I first found that and read it, I instantly thought we were gonna go in there, find Nem, and maybe break a pillar and make it fall on him. Maybe the floor would give under Jill and...just...STUFF. Nope, you never go in there. You just have a fight with him and it's off to the Hospital. So many missed opportunities with many different areas. But that just leads me to believe this game wasn't just rushed, it was mishandled so poorly.

They didn't cut the Hospital from the game too surprisingly, however, you play as Carlos with his Peashooter of a gun against one of the hardest enemies (The Hunters) in there, with his very buggy Dodge command, which is just him punching. However, it doesn't register most of the time. It's not like Jill's where you use it during the attack animation of the enemy, you use it BEFORE the animation. But even then it doesn't matter. Hunters will instantly get up and hit you, probably even 1 shot. Then you do a Tower Defense to protect Jill for 5 minutes and...that's the Hospital in a nutshell. Even tho I talked so bad about it, I liked it more than the original hospital. The original was just a straight line and you're out of there within 10 minutes. Took me a good 30~ minutes in the new hospital. So...yeah.

The opening streets of Raccoon City in the remake are...so...GOOD. It's what I wanted from this game. It's what it did so freaking well. It's what RE3 is all about. Being chased by Nemesis on the streets of a burning town. What more can you ask for? That's the issue tho, there's a lot you can ask for here. You're on the streets for about 1 1/2 hours, and only 20 minutes of those is running from Nemesis. And that's such a shame because that was some of the most fun I've had with a RE game.

And I don't wanna miss talking about Nemesis considering this game is all about him. He's great in the remake, then he's beyond bad. When he's chasing you in normal humanoid form, it's the most fun thing ever. He's BEYOND threatening. So much so that Speedrunners are still getting stomped by him and runs are being ruined. He's way more aggressive than Mr. X. I remember my very first playthrough that I did on Hardcore, my first actual encounter where he breaks through a wall, I died there over 10 times. I even tried to cheese him in a safe room and it ended in such a clenching way because I got cocky. It was beyond fun and I would do anything for a REmake 3...REMAKE where it's only that. He's used in the streets roughly 3 times, then gets a rocket launcher where that part is very easy, but whatever, at least they included it, and then he comes back and is a boss with a flamethrower. Cool! I don't mind if it's a mix of him chasing and then a boss fight. However, after this fight, you see him with the rocket launcher (the part I was saying is very easy), then he's gone. [i]RESIDENT EVIL 2[/i] provides better horror atmosphere and immersion but [i]RESIDENT EVIL 3[/i] delivers better action and might be more fun to play during core gameplay.

Resident Evil 3 - Remake is nothing short of a huge disappointment and double so coming after the very strong Resident Evil 2 - Remake.

RE3R removes almost everything that made the original game stand out from it's predecessor and what we end up with is a very watered down action like RE game focusing on set pieces.
The horrifying Nemesis, this games Mr.X for those of you who are most familiar with the RE2R game is nothing short of a laughing joke. Compared to the original game where he was a menacing threat that stalked you from room to room and not going down without a ton of effort can easily be dispatched in this game with a single hand grenade.
Without spoiling too much he also mutates very early into the game and not only that but his mutated form is more goofy than scary and not only that but also way easier to handle.

Gone are also the "branching paths" from the original where you would be able to alter parts of the story by making different decisions which greatly added replayability, there is no replacement in RE3R and not only that but they also removed the originals random elements like enemy types, placements, items and so on which made almost every playthrough slightly unique in one way or another.

Fan favorite locations like the Clock tower and the dead factory are also gone and are replaced by a longer hospital section and extended sewers which in my opinion does nowhere near make up for it in interesting locals at least. Gone are also the majority of puzzles, there is little in the way of puzzle solving unless you count finding a notepad with a safe/locker combination.

Last but not least the game is a very short experience clocking in at only 4-6 hours for a first playthrough and that is counting collecting everything and exploring the little side areas that do exist. With the lack of replayability it's hard to justify paying 60€ for such a short game and had they not removed areas from the original game and kept all the random parts it would be much easier to justify the price tag.

Now some of you are probably thinking that I am being unfair to the game by comparing every little detail to the original and that is a fair point but needless to say I loved the Resident evil 2 remake despite it not being completely faithful to the original simply because it tried to add new interesting things for the player where as RE3R brings little new to the table for all the cuts it makes.

That is not to say I hate the game and think it's awful because it's not an awful game, not even a bad one. I do however find it very mediocre at best and the things it expands on over the originals is little else than better visuals, voice acting and expanding a bit on character development which is it did well but those things are not enough to make this game anything more than another average Resident evil title.

If I were to put a score on it it would have to be a 6/10. Slightly above average

[h1] Written Review [/h1]
Resident Evil 3 is more of a Remake than a Remaster, but that's not a bad thing.

The game aims to retell the original story, and hits most of the key plot points, but takes liberties along the way. Things are cut, while also added. Including areas, enemies, scenes etc.
The game by no means replaces the original. It just accompanies it. 

The game is set during the fall of Raccoon City. The city is realised beautifully with the RE Engine. It really looks gorgeous with all the neon lights, and wet concrete.

Gunplay feels really good. And I think the game did a great job at ambushing you with zombies quite frequently.
There were a lot of times where zombies sneak up on you from behind while you're already being swarmed. I really enjoyed these intense moments.
Many old enemies have also been reworked to be way more scary and interesting.

The layout is probably one of the most linear Resident Evil games I've played. You'll only have to backtrack a handful of times, and only if you want to collect everything.

There really aren't that many puzzles at all, which disappointed me. And the game was quite short. I beat it in 6 hours, and that's with checking every single nook and cranny. Although it's worth mentioning that the original was around the same length too.

I also didn't really find it scaryl. But, I felt the same about the original. The setting just isn't the same as a creepy mansion or police station. I also really wish they used more music in these remasters. Outside of the beautiful save room music, you don't hear anything, and I think those older songs helped build atmosphere so much.

Now, this wouldn't be RE 3 without Nemesis. 
Well, he's back, and as spooky as ever. There are things I liked and didn't like about how he was handled in this remake though.

He didn't really feel like a staple, like in the original.
He wasn't this ever foreboding, scary (and annoying) monster that he used to be. In the original, there were areas where he just pestered you for ages, similarly to Mr X in RE 2 Remake.

In RE 3 Remake, that only really ever happens once, and your future encounters with him are limited to scripted chase scenes. 

Now, I don't think this was necessarily a bad thing. I think with the overall pacing of the game, having him linger everywhere would have really slowed it down. That's not to say I wouldn't have liked a FEW more scenes like that, but this brings me onto my next point.

In this remake, he is a LOT more relentless. So if he lingered, it could maybe end up being too frustrating.
I remember more or less effortlessly gliding by him in the original. In this game, he genuinely is frightening to be chased by. 
Aside from his scary new look and sounds, he also plays with you more than in the original. Just when you think you've gotten away, he might grab you from offscreen with his tentacle and pull you closer.
Or simply jump right infront of your path. 
These new moves made him feel a lot more real and threatening, which was super intense, and scary.

The game brings in some new set pieces and boss fights with him too. I'll refrain from talking about them to allow you to discover them, but I think they do a much better job at keep the player engaged with more interesting fight mechanics than in the original. 

In the end, I really enjoyed his presence in this game, while I would have like to have a bit more of it overall.

A feature that came back from the original RE3, is the counter mechanic. You can dodge roll with Jill, and block and punch with Carlos.
In this remake you can even get a bit of slow-mo for 2 seconds to get some easy shots off.

As for the narrative, the voice acting is great, as well as the facial animation. People are written pretty realistically, and it really brings the whole thing to life.

The overall story is more linear now. You can't make any choices in the game, and Jill feels less neutral, and more like a developed character.
I personally liked it, and didn't mind the scrapping of multiple endings and choices, as that's not what I play RE for, but thought it was worth mentioning for those that would care.

In the end, although I do wish it was longer, and it has some shortcomings like the absence of puzzles, I overall loved playing through this remake. I think players old and new will both find a high quality campaign here, if you like what you hear from the rest of the review.
