If you're looking for your Resident Evil fix then this is a fine choice, it's fun. It's definitely belongs in the camp of "good Resident Evil games", so if that's all you're worried about then I suggest you try it out. But if you're curious about how the game compares to the original Resident Evil 3 then stick around, because I have a lot to go over.

- Nemesis. So here's the thing with Nemesis in this game, he sucks. Every single one of his encounters is scripted, he's easy to dodge and even easier to knock down. On assisted through Hardcore difficulty his stage one form can knocked down with a single grenade or explosive drum, and even on Nightmare and Inferno his attacks are still too easy to dodge and it only takes two grenades. He's still a threat, sure, but he simply doesn't compare to his appearance in the original game, or heck even Mr. X in the RE2 remake is a greater threat. That's probably the thing that bothers me the most, it's like Nemesis and Mr. X swapped roles or something. See, in the original Resident Evil 2 Mr. X only appears in the B scenario, and even then only in specific areas with attacks that're easily dodged, he's hardly a threat worth remembering. In the original Resident Evil 3 on the other hand, Nemesis also has scripted encounters, sure, but he can show up at random, and he'll chase you until you either knock him down or lose him. They really did my boy dirty in this remake, he's still cool but man is he a paper tiger by comparison. 

- The dodge system. See, in the original RE3 the dodge mechanic was a half-baked mess that took a lot of practice to pull off consistently, and even then sometimes it just wouldn't work. Naturally it's not fun when one of your core gameplay mechanics sucks to use, so in this remake they put a lot of work into fixing the system and it shows. Instead of having to aim and press the action button at just the right time, now you just have to press spacebar within a (very lenient) window of time. In addition, if you're aiming while dodging, you're also rewarded with slo-mo and your aim locks automatically to a weak point on an enemy. My only problem with the new dodge mechanic is that now instead of being half-baked it's too easy. It's very easy to pull off a perfect dodge, even by accident, and the slow-mo aim thing just makes things even easier. But the other thing is playing without the dodge is tough too because for some reason Capcom took out two key defensive measures in the game, which I'll get to right now. 

-Blue herbs. They're gone, completely gutted from the game. In fairness there's no poisonous enemies in the game (which is pretty lame, why take that entire class of threat out from a survival horror game), so I guess it's redundant to have it. But the thing that weirds me out the most about this decision is the fact that in the remake of RE2 they introduced an armor status that applies when taking mixed herbs that contain blue herbs, it granted poison immunity and reduced damage taken in general. That made strategically planning when to use mixed herbs in order to have armor a fun addition to the game, and now that entire mechanic is absent, replaced by the dodge. 

-Sup-weapons. This entire system, present since the remake of RE1, absent. The weapons are still there, but you can't have them as an emergency weapon any longer. This takes a lot of the strategic options out of game entirely, and now you must either dodge an enemy or risk taking damage. 

-Enemies. Sliding worms, crows (Again!), brain suckers, small spiders and giant spiders (Also again!) are now completely absent from the game, along with the Grave Digger and the optional Nicholai helicopter boss fights (neither were fantastic boss fights but that's just less content in the remake). In fairness we do get some new enemies in the form of parasite zombies (slightly stronger base zombies with a ranged attack and unique grab attack), pale heads (stronger, faster and more durable zombies with regenerating health), and lickers make a cameo in the police station (you only fight two on Assisted through Hardcore, and deal with an additional two in the police station and two more in the hospital if played on Nightmare or Inferno), so that’s cool I guess. Zombies themselves are actually easier to take down now, and instead of going for the legs like the RE2 remake I recommend you aim for the head (critical hits are more common in this game). The ones that have the strangest return are the Drain Deimos, they’re completely different from before. They only appear in one area (the power sub-station), are small, fast and deal pretty decent damage, take only one shotgun shot regardless of difficulty but make up for it with endless numbers, and have a unique grab attack that results in Jill having parasites implanted down her throat (in a really weirdly sexual animation). All having the parasite status does is make your screen all red and weird and slow your movement down to a snails pace. It’s cured with a green herb, and is obnoxious more than anything else. I’m honestly fine with this new drain deimos, that’s one less hunter clone I guess, but it just sucks that they’re only in one area of the game. I also like how the Hunter gammas are now, too. Instead of being just another hunter clone they’re now pretty different, being a large, slow damage sponge with an attack that’s easy to dodge but a one-hit kill if it lands. So overall it’s sad that the enemy variety is reduced, but at least the enemies that are present have been improved in one way or another. 

- Locations and puzzles. The clock tower interior, entirety of Raccoon park, most of the dead factory and large chunks of the downtown and uptown areas are now absent from the game. Most of the puzzles the original RE3 had to offer are now gone, as well,  and the overall length of the game is shortened now too. I guess there’s an argument to be made about trimming the fat, but I’m sad that many of these classic areas got the axe instead of the remake treatment.

Weapons. I’m actually pretty happy with the changes to the weapons for the most part. The M37 Western shotgun has essentially returned in the form of a semi-atuo shotgun upgrade (though I would’ve loved to see the dumb lever-action in the remake), and the STI Eagle is basically the starting pistol upgraded, but the grenade launcher has been somewhat reworked. The mine thrower has been rolled into the grenade launcher in the form of mine rounds (which only appear in like two areas in the entire game, but like the original mine thrower they’re not very useful anyways so its’ fine), and freeze rounds are completely gone. I’d be sad about that but the freeze rounds were expensive to make and only really good against select enemies and Nemesis, and since Nemesis is so lame in this remake there’s no point in using the freeze rounds. The magnum is now an eight shot Deagle instead of a revolver and even has an upgrade now, so that’s cool. The only weapon that’s strange is the G18 burst, it’s a 3-shot pistol you get pretty late in the game and while it’s good, I don’t see why it couldn’t just be a fourth upgrade for the G19 pistol you already have as opposed to a separate weapon. It’s particularly good on the final boss, though, so even though it’s less accurate I would use the G18 burst over the upgraded G19 in the endgame if I were you. The hot-dogger knife and Rai-den weapons are really really cool, and fun on a bun to use, so if I were you I would make those two items some of the fist things to buy from the store after beating the game the fist time.

Overall, I'm not happy with a lot of the decisions Capcom made with this remake, and I honestly think it's too easy. But it is still a good Resident Evil game, which feels so good to be able to say. Ever since Resident Evil 7 the series has really experienced a renaissance, and even if this remake is a misstep it's still fun.

The 2019 Resident Evil 2 Remake, which I played on PS4 therefore can't review on Steam, is a near-perfect game. Literally the only criticism I have of it is that it's not particularly ambitious - it's a little backwards-looking, melding a more well-designed version of the original PS1 game's Zelda dungeon-esque progression with modern over-the-shoulder third person action and the state of the art visuals & absorbing atmosphere of the incredible RE Engine. Populating the levels with the shambling, slow-moving enemies from the classic RE games but making them work in a modern context is maybe it's cleverest trick, but overall, RE 2 is great simply by virtue of taking a safe, can't-miss pitch for a game and polishing it to a mirror shine.

This game is not as good as that one. This one has a heavier action focus and simpler levels, and the balance feels a little off in parts. It's still quite good though. Take this review as a Resident Evil 2 recommendation. If you haven't played Resi 2 Remake, and you like horror games, Dark Souls, or even something like Zelda (and reckon you have the stomach to play a spooky Zelda), you should absolutely grab last year's remake. In fact, if you've never played a Resident Evil game before, that's a great place to start. It's not that expensive these days and goes on sale often.

Then, if you really, really liked the remake of Resident Evil 2, and are hungry for more, maybe think about grabbing this one on sale.

I'm gonna give this a negative review but I'm mostly neutral. I feel a negative rating would have more impact though, so, thumbs down it is. Also, this is a long one...I've got feelings about this and they're getting vented.

I liked the game. Especially the first playthrough. I was jazzed for the game, RE3 was my favorite in the OG days, and I played through this is in one sitting. Enjoyed my time. Went in for my second playthrough and...started to think...

Nemesis really sucked. Like, really really. He's only in a "chase" mode for one small portion of the game and the rest is weird scripted QTE events and boss battles. When he's in "chase" mode, he really does come after you, which is great, but that leads to quick bursts of fighting then you either beat him, or die and reload. If you beat him, you move along, and he comes after you again for another quick burst of fighting. Rinse, repeat. You never...feel...his presence in the game. 

With Mr. X, it was different...he stalked you...he was slow, deliberate and practically unstoppable. Those footsteps. I F***CKING cowered in the safe room in RE2, waiting for him to leave. COWERED, whimpering and crying to myself. Pep talking to even move. IN THE SAFE ROOM. I think they actually messed up a bit with making Mr. X like that...cause it stole a lot of Nemesis' thunder. Now, we can't help but make the comparison. And Nemesis *doesn't* compare. 

This is by far the biggest disappointment in the whole game. I was absolutely hyped to see them do, "Mr. X on steroids." And Nemesis bursts through the wall and faceplants in front of you. (Figuratively, he doesn't actually faceplant.) You can literally walk circles around Nemesis and he can't hit you. You can escape Nemesis by climbing a ladder. You can kite Nemesis around small objects. One grenade on normal difficulty downs Nemesis in his "chase" mode. Hunters are more dangerous than Nemesis. Zombies are more dangerous than Nemesis. 

The rest is the usual crap: cut content, no real puzzles, very short (beat it in 3 hours. 8 hours of total game time for THREE playthroughs). Over all, I just...don't understand what happened here. I don't get it. They had it. RE2:Remake set a fantastic foundation and they had the OG RE3 for a solid blueprint. I hate to say it, cause I'm not fan of it in most games...but...this game...it needed FILLER. I just wanted to BE in Raccoon City trying to survive but the game was just balls-to-the-wall 100% gogogogo. This game should have been double the play time with the Park and Clocktower and another "city" level before you meet up with Carlos. With Nemesis *in* the levels actively tracking you and not just showing up randomly to fight. Slow down the pace by 10%. That's it, I just designed the damn game for them.

 Did they cut corners to get it out quick? Did they try to change it up too much and end up shooting themselves in the foot? I would have waited another year or even two if it meant getting more content!! And that's what sucks, now, it's basically set in stone. I doubt they'll add DLC that'll implement more levels. If they do...it better cost nothing. Cause I ain't dishing out another penny for content. $60 is what you're getting for this, Capcom. And I already feel like I overpaid by $30. If they come out with a Clocktower DLC for $12.99, I'll riot. I'll do it. I'll go outside and flip cars.

This is a review from someone who has NEVER played the original RE3. I believe this relieves me from any subconscious bias I could have or expectations.

The game is good. It's also unfair. Without spoiling anything, it is very hard to play the game without getting damaged, especially unless you are using the cheat weapons after clearing. It is a short game, but has decent replayability mostly down to unlocking items you get from points for completing challenges in the game. With an infinite launcher, I have beaten the game in less than an hour, but it took me beating the game 5-6 times to get it. My first playthrough was 4 hours, the 2nd was 2 hours. For 60 dollars, that can be a tough pill to swallow but you also get the fairly fun RE Resistance multiplayer game too, which has quite a few characters and is pretty well done and unique. 

Mechanically speaking, the game feels clunky at times. Characters aren't the most responsive to your inputs (I swear sometimes I have to hit reload 5+ times to actually get the reload to happen which I don't feel like was in issue in RE2) The game is meant to be more fast paced than RE2 and suffers more from these controls because of it. You can also be stunlocked and killed in what seems like unfair ways because you get caught on a piece of scenery that is knee level. Even with infinite ammo cheat weapons, expect to get damaged at least a few times because of this. Dodging is not very intuitive and you'll find yourself spamming the dodge button to traverse short distances faster and not actually dodging enemies with it. This changes in the higher difficulties though, as against bosses you will likely die in 1 hit and you need to hope and pray your dodge timing is correct. 

I don't know what it's missing or added from the original game, but as it's own entity, it's a solid game that's short but has decent replay value from challenges that let you unlock more items to make other challenges even easier. After that, you have RE Resistance to play which definitely seems like will be suffering from major balance issues in the long run if it survives, but is fun nonetheless. (Large player level discrepancies can shift the dynamic entirely from a easy match to absolutely impossible to do anything).
Not the RE3 I had hoped for, but if you ignore what it was supposed to be its still a fun game

RESIDENT EVIL 3 REVIEW: 

Another classic Resident Evil game by CAPCOM getting the "remake" treatment. So to start off, this is not a bad game. Although it has it's problems it was still quite enjoyable to play through. I'll list off my issues with the game first; 
. Game length - I completed the game in under 5 hours and I was taking my time and watching cutscenes.
. Cut content - Changes made were mostly cutting a lot of story and classic areas from the original which made story progression feel rushed.
. Set pieces - Too many scripted set pieces in the game that also affect the games story progression by making it feel forced and rushed.
. City section - The Raccoon City sections feel small with not much reward for exploring the area.
. Nemisis - Nemisis seems to show up mostly in scripted set pieces or finale boss fights so his terrifying presence starts to wear off.

Now the positives for this game would be;
. Graphics - Similar to Resident Evil 2 Remake, RE3 has incredible visuals using the trusted RE engine.
. Main Characters - Jill and Carlos are amazing in this game, clever and funny dialogue makes them easily likeable.
. Replayability - Due to the short game length it is easy to hop back on to replay the main story and complete challenges to spend points on the in-game shop.

I do recommend this game but not at the full retail price it is currently going for. Wait for a good sale price before deciding to buy.

Let's break it down a bit. Resident Evil 3 is not a bad game, but it is also not the perfect remake, having to follow in RE2's very successful remake release it was a tough call going in and I feel like Capcom made several mistakes along the way.


The Good:

- Not among the list of these mistakes is the fact that RE3 remake is action based, anyone who says this as a complaint about the game has clearly never played the original at all. RE3 original was the most action orientated of the original trilogy and I believe Capcom did a good job of continuing to capture the feel of this in the remake, even keeping in the dodge mechanics was a nice touch.
- The characters, they completely nailed the redesigns, the personalities and the dynamics of every character from the original. Jill was a pleasure to see, play and hear. Jill's relationship with Carlos was done perfectly. Carlos is the overall nice guy we know he is with his quirky humour, Mikhail is still the absolute G we remember him to be and Nikolai is every bit the villain we wanted him to be.
- The gameplay is smooth for the most part, but there is some jankiness here are there.
- Another visually stunning masterpiece, every you see and can interact with looks incredible.


The Bad:

- Lack of unlockable costumes and mercenaries mode, come on Capcom. The original RE3 had a plethora of costumes to choose from, these either could've been directly translated from or expanded upon from the original. No new Jill Regina costume makes me sad :(
- Extremely linear gameplay... the original didn't have a massively expansive area to explore I will give you that, but the remake just feels like it's completely on rails. You could've put the game on a 2D flat plain and it would've felt the same to play.
- Nemesis implementation could've been better, the way he teleports around the player (and I mean literally teleporting) in order to be imposing is more annoying that it is scary. Also his lack of ability to enter stores etc and just standing outside looking at your just completely removes the suspense. I was expecting Mr X 2.0, not Mr X 0.5.
- Loads of original content was cut or shortened down, also fan service was not there at all. I was fully expecting the experience of going to the RDP building as Jill, when it didn't happen I was more than disappointed... The only part that felt fully fleshed out/expanded upon was the hospital area which was actually quite fun.
- The puzzles... wait... what puzzles? There are basically no puzzles in this game, an RE game for god's sake! And the ones that are there they just have the answers directly in front of you, or you can just face roll your keyboard/controller and solve it in about 10-15 seconds.


The Reasons:

I feel like Capcom took a leaf out of the CoD/Fifa book here and was trying to get another RE remake out in the wild while the iron was still hot from RE2. This could've been that the development time was so long for RE2 and they didn't want to risk a lull whilst they had the same amount of development time put into RE3. Or it could've been due to it's multiplayer counterpart RE:Resistance, to be perfectly honest my thoughts are that Resistance was probably meant to be it's own title but Capcom knew that it would've died on it's own, so by coupling it up with RE3 remake they guarantee not only "sales" for it but also a player base that will at the very least check it out even if they have a low retention rate afterwards.

There is no doubt that this remake was massively rushed and it saddens me greatly that that's the case, RE3 always held a strong place in my heart and I was truly excitedly for it's revival for many reasons. To ultimately be disappointed is quite a blow as such as large fan of the series... Does this mean I don't love it? No, I love it but only because I'm a fan of RE.

TLDR; The game isn't bad, but it fell well short of what it could have and should have been. I don't know the reasons for this, but I know this was a rush project and I hope they don't do the same thing for the next one. Don't mess this up Capcom, please.

Do not take the big red thumb of doom as a sign to frantically avoid this game- this new REmake is neither stellar nor terrible, and I will offer you some pointers as to why.

1) Presentation and maniability. As its predecessor, the new Nemesis looks quite fine and plays accordingly, the dodge being a useaful feature instead of the chore it was in the original. 
Jill is now longer outfitted like an escort-girl and it is a pleasure to move through the iconic city of the saga- albeit the adventure is way too short. 

2) Story and atmosphere. Here's a shy attempt to justify why Jill was still in the city while she knew full well a new catastrophe could happen and Umbrella and Irons were out of her. She wanted to investigate a little more, alright, but the all "Umbrella control everything in a 100000+ inhabited city" is still foggy at best, and the manner the quarantine is handled doesn't make a lick of sense (why would Leon still go to RC if, as shown in the opening cutscene, a quarantine was officially broadcasted on TV ? How come really no one reacted faster and contacted the outside about the zombie plague intensifying, when they were already article about gruesome murders a few months ago ?). 
The rest is not much better story-wise, while the characters are duly "upgraded" from the B-movie vibe that the original had (Nicholai's portrayal is quite good), the return of the legendary "combat data" that no one sane would buy is ridiculous.
Yes, I know, story never was RE's forte, but please, if you want to make your game more serious (and so it appears) working on plot holes, consistency and some modicum of believable content would be appreciated.
One example : like in the original, at one point, Jill is infected by Nemmy and is down for the count.
For half a day. Now in the original, Carlos was there and immediately put her in a safe zone while searching for the cure. Here, she's 3 meters away from the not-really-down Nemesis, separated by a convenient herse. How the heck Carlos needed half a day to reach her ? Why Nemmy didn't finish the job ? 
I know it can be quite subjective, but it kinda kills the mood and the more I had to suspend my disbelief, the less I was into the game- and certainly not scared. 

3) Nemmy, the big guy himself. You know, the one who gives its name to the original game ? Well, last century it was understandable for Nemmy to be scripted. Here, it's just lazy. Escaping him is rarely hard and some of the scripts are downright poorly handled. Example : early in the game, he chases after you and you are forced to go through a storage box room, while chatting with Carlos, completely halting the chase. 
Thanks Nemesis, it is really courteous of you to stop destroying walls and letting us advance for a while without fear !

4) Boss fights. Now, the REmake² was not brillant with those, and it's not better here. Nemmy mutates way too soon in a more bestial form- but not more efficient. Circling the plaza while easily avoiding its attacks and throwing mine-rounds from the grenade launcher to stop him while he runs itself in a circle like a stupid lizard and then shooting the weak point is not a fulfilling experience. 3rd fight is more or less the same with convenient electrocuting tanks instead of mine-rounds.

5) Remake aspect. It quite changes from the original and while giving more screentime to Carlos (he investigates RPD, not Jill) and shuffling the event's order is fine, cutting the Clock Tower, erasing the Worm mini-boss and investing more time in the lab under the hospital and forgetting about the facility might be more for saving up time and ressources rather than being creative. 
Now, I'm not saying that finishing the game in a biohazard waste disposal was better, but at the end of the day, it's just less content. 

6) Puzzles. In the original, they sometimes felt more like tedious/nonsensical obstacles than seamless actions to progress or interesting challenge. I mean, the emblem affair for fetching a battery hidden in the mayor's statue, all that because you are in the sole city in the world with battery-operated elevator- not the game's shining moment.
In this remake though, either you have nothing to replace it, or some attempts so shallow it feels like an obligation. The earliest example, setting a route for the subway train, only need 5% of your brain potential and one awakened eye to complete in less than 30 seconds. 
So the "obstacle" part remains- like the obnoxious part where you have to fetch 3 replacement fuses in a warehouse designed but the usal madmen. Alas, one must confess it's par for the course for many horror games. 

7) Replay value. By finishing a run and completing in-game challenges, you earn points to spend in a shop in order to ease your future ordeals. A fair concept and useful if you want to complete the harder difficulty modes and getting S-Ranks ; you can for instance buy items boosting your defense, superior weaponry like the good ol' Samurai Edge, an extra pouch, etc. 
I'm not fond of the system (mainly because it means you would have to beat the game again and again, which would become stale for me given the level-design) but I can definitely see the appeal- just note that some challenges might be quite long to achieve.
I mean, killing 80 ennemies with the Magnum, when you acquire it very late and can fetch/make about 20 bullets per run ? Bleh. 

Despite all its flaws, it remains a competent, if not adventurous, action game- no, definetely, I have a hard time feeling the horror in there, but to its credit, the original RE3 was the point when the series took a first turn towards more action. 
In the end, it's more accessible than the original and will allow more people to enjoy it. But veteran of the series or newcomer, the full price is just indecent. 
Price eventually become irrelevant as time go on, what with sales, bundles and normal price reduction over the years, but it still stays a factor, and as far as I am concerned, inclunding a multiplayer mode really do not warrant such a price. 
Let's just hope Jill will get a better treatment in a future, all-new game...

[h1]If RE2 Remake is survival horror, this is action horror. Like RE2 it is beautifully realised, and it really manages to match the nostalgia I had for the original RE3. [/h1]

RE3 Remake is a different beast to RE2 Remake. A simpler more cut down narrative and leaning more heavily into action than the previous game. 

[u]Gameplay: [/u] Similar to RE2 Remake - 3rd person over the shoulder action is a very welcome change from the original, puzzles are now minimal, and the environments are somewhat more linear than in RE2, with less backtracking over multipath environments. Despite this, the opening act of the game set on the streets of Raccoon city feel less cramped and claustrophobic. This is assisted with the addition of a dodge mechanic which allows for more mobility around threats.

[u]Visual:[/u] RE3 Remake is beautifully realised, with high attention to detail applied to the environment, even parts that most players might never even notice unless they are looking for hidden secrets. I also preferred the updated character designs for Jill, Carlos and Nemesis (Although original outfits for the protagonists are available for those who must have it). Enemy design has a similar attention to detail with damage models being very satisfying to witness during combat. 

[u] Sound: [/u] In game sound is extremely satisfying, from footsteps to explosions, fleshy sounds and voice acting, all work very well to match the action film feel of the game.

[u] Narrative: [/u] Somewhat akin to a blockbuster film. It is all for the sceptical, stereotypes and set pieces and leans into these appropriately. Doesn’t take itself too seriously with characters making comments about Resident Evil logic. 

[u] Note: [/u] This is quite a short game, and it appears the developers definitely built the game with replays in mind, not for alternative endings (of which there are none, mores the pity) but because of unlockable harder difficulty modes, unlockable weapons and equipment, challenges and end of run scores. Normally I don’t go in for this kind of thing because I’m more of a narrative guy, but it was compelling enough for me to play through and finish everything in the game. 

If you are only interested in a single playthrough then you would likely finish the game in about 10 hours if you were playing for completeness, but the game can be completed in under 2 hours if you are doing a speed run and missing everything non-essential.

Oh, Capcom... why must you play with my heart? It was easy to assume that R3make would be another great title, following two of the best titles in the history of the series and made on the same engine - but alas. All Capcom had to do was remake the game the same way they made RE2, but instead, they chose the route of a 'reimagining'. Indeed, this is less a remake of RE3 and more of a mis-marketed standalone expansion for RE2, loosely based on a few of RE3's concepts. A lot of what you'd expect is missing here - ink ribbons, limited ammo, mercenaries mode, zombie physics, dismemberment gore, diverging plot points, defensive weapons, most of the original locations, and most of the puzzles are all absent. In their place is a mostly linear action-oriented game which feels like a compromise between the RE2 remake and the action-oriented approach of RE4. Like the original RE3, this was released just a year after RE2 - but since AAA games in 2020 require a bit more development time than they did back in 1999, this edition feels like even more more of a rushed cash-in. This title is the first casualty of Capcom's newly planned yearly release schedule for Resident Evil, and it likely won't be the last.

One of the the things RE2 did incredibly well was expand the original campaign without affecting the pacing, but the opposite happened here - the campaign was reduced and sped up. The original RE3 had 5 overarching areas - the city, a return to RPD, a clock tower, a hospital, and city outskirts. Of the 4 areas that are unique to RE3, the outskirts (park & factory) have been cut entirely in this remake, as has the indoor section of the clock tower - only the boss fight in front of it is represented here, albeit unrecognizably. The city areas are heavily cut and hardly resemble their original counterparts. The cut areas have been replaced by scripted chase sequences and new segments which allowed for more asset recycling from RE2 (more sewers, more NEST). And the recycling doesn't end there - for instance, music is reprised from (the original) RE2 and the item boxes from RE7 return here without any alteration. Other details feel unfinished, like the laser reticule - a red dot which looks like it came straight out of MS Paint. New enemies sometimes show up in only a single section of the game, never to be seen again. All of this adds up to an experience which feels oddly budget in spite of its AAA production values.

All of this could have been forgivable if the game still provided the wonderfully tense feeling that I seek from Resident Evil, but the only time I felt it in my first playthrough (on Hardcore difficulty) was in an optional item-gathering sequence at the end of the hospital, following on the heels of a pale imitation of RE4's house seige. Otherwise, the game is designed like an on-rails shooter that just happens to retain a few design elements from RE2, and this is reflected by the game's perfunctory plot pacing. Everything happens a lot faster right off the bat, with Nemesis being introduced almost immediately and Jill meeting the Umbrella team less than 10 minutes in. By contrast, the original game built up to the first Nemesis encounter, and Jill spent a bit of time in the city on her own before encountering the Umbrella team. The game breezes through the heavily cut city areas, which is a shame, because they're the only part remake which feel true to the spirit of the original.

It's hard not to imagine the missed potential here. The city could have been the game's main selling point - a big, open area, filled with puzzles and vastly expanded from its original scope - but instead, it was abridged. Relative to RE2, this makes little sense - how does it take longer to explore one floor of a police station than it does to scrounge through several city blocks? Granted, RE3 was always about running more than getting to know a space intimately, and they've dialed that up here, but in practice that just means that most areas in the game feel underutilized and underdeveloped. This change in focus is reflected in the abundance of ammo and the focus on combat. There's a new dodge mechanic (that's thankfully a lot easier to use than in the original title), and quite a lot of emphasis is put on dodging and rolling here - special retaliatory moves are hidden behind perfectly timed dodges. Defensive weapons have been replaced by a quicktime event used to reduce zombie damage. In essence, the moodiness of RE2 has been replaced with RE6's incessant floor-rolling.

The star of the show here is, of course, Nemesis, whose redesign looks rather... unfortunate, to my eyes. His face his covered with a trashbag at the start in order to later provide a dramatic face reveal, but said reveal ends up providing a sinking feeling instead of the intended fear. Replacing his facial scars and stitches with a nose makes him look significantly goofier and less menacing than his 1999 counterpart, and his Alien3-inspired 2nd stage is far more cliche and uninspired than his original transformations (more angry dog than intelligent stalker). Looks aside, only the brief city portion has him stalk you like Mr. X - in the rest of the game, he is relegated to scripted chase sequences and boss battles (providing more of what was arguably the weakest part of RE2's remake). Even in the city, he ends up being more of an annoyance than a terror, chasing you at high speeds, jumping in front of you, and knocking you over with his tentacle. Despite how overpowered and scary this may sound, it feels like the developers had no idea how to make this a fair fight, and instead opted to artificially reduce the difficulty. For instance, he never attacks you after knocking you over, and instead lets you recover for a moment and get up before attacking you again. I never expected Nemesis to be so principled and considerate!

On the note of surprisingly friendly things, hardcore mode is considerably less hardcore here than it was in RE2. The game frequently autosaves (allowing you to easily get away with saving less than 5x) and there's practically a typewriter and item box in every other room. The frequency of safe rooms removes the need for most of the inventory management and also makes it quite easy to retreat to safety. There are 2 unlockable difficulty modes after Hardcore - Nightmare and Inferno - but they still autosave, lack ink ribbons, and feature frequent safe rooms. Enemy placement is different in these higher difficulties, and the pacing of the city area actually works a lot better in Nightmare - provided you skip the brash cutscenes, this is the closest this game comes to providing a classic Resident Evil experience. The feeling is short lived, as nothing much can fix the game's lackluster back half. By the time I reached the final boss in Nightmare and discovered that the only way to defeat it was by mastering perfect dodge, I was ready to call it quits.

These difficulty modes provide all of the game's replayability. To incentivize replaying, completing challenges gives you points which can be used to purchase things like stat boosting items, new weapons, and weapons with infinite ammo. Many of the challenges involve killing large numbers of zombies, often with a specific weapon. This grinding is yet another way I was reminded of RE6.

RE3 isn't as bad as Revelations, but the fact that this game appeared in what seemed to be an era of renewed focus for Capcom makes all of this sting that much worse. RE3 remade in the style of RE2 could have been a glorious thing to behold, but thanks to this game, we'll never get to find out.

Resident Evil 3 was probably my most anticipated game of 2020. It being my first Resident Evil game I played as a child, it pains me to say that the remake falls rather short of both the original, and the previous remake. 

In the first chapter of the story, what should have been a sprawling cityscape nightmare, we instead get a linear and straight forward tour through 2 streets and a couple buildings, a tragedy considering the clear effort put in to make these few areas look as good as they do. Where as in the previous remake, you found yourself revisiting old areas as you acquired new equipment, allowing for a different approach to puzzles and challenges, in this you often only visit each area a single time, leaving the game feeling a bit hollow, and after having killed whatever undead abomination resides there, these areas too begin to feel a bit safe.

Nemesis, one of the few truly terrifying aspects of this game, only chases you for a brief time. Setting a theme for the rest of the game, only to be immediately dropped once you leave the area. Being unaware of when and where Nemesis will next appear, be it breaking through a wall or straight up falling from the sky really created a sense of danger absent from the rest of the game. After this you can count on every interaction with Nemesis to be a scripted event or cutscene. 

Many things present in the original are absent here, leaving to me wonder just how much of a remake this game is. With so few similar concepts between the two, calling it a remake almost seems like a lie. By the end of my first playthough I found myself surprised. Having recognized the end was approaching it left me wondering where the rest of the original game went. 

That being said the game isn't entirely awful. It just feels empty. More like a companion piece to the previous remake, but with the price point of a standalone game. If you feel the need to buy it, it would be better to do so when it is on sale.

----------------------------

[b]Things I do like:[/b]
[b]1. The continuity nods[/b] - really good way of exploring the context further of the events occurring in RE2. [spoiler]Brad and Marvin's scene was my favorite.[/spoiler]

[b]2. Inferno mode[/b] - it's artificial difficulty but it gets the job done of putting you in a nice tense state especially to shake off some of the staleness that comes from replaying the story.

[b]3. The cheesy lines[/b] - good old RE campiness apart from the Jill problem that I've mentioned above. [spoiler] "GET OFF MY TRAIN, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" [/spoiler]

[b]4. Carlos[/b] - Ballsy. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. By far the character that benefited the most from the remake. I wanna see more of Carlos in the future games after this one. [b]5. Just some good RE gameplay[/b] - I feel like most of the flak this game receives is from the comparisons that it's going to get. [b]Final notes:[/b]
This game gave me great vibes coming from the original. It's different and it tried to be fresh, and I can appreciate that. The problem for me is that some of the fundamentals of what made the original great were highly diminished (Nemesis and the environment's overall atmosphere in particular).

First a disclaimer: Resistance is a free game bundled with RE3. Because of this, I do not consider resistance's additions in this review. Now for the review:

Here's the thing.

I have a hard time deciding on Yes or No for this game. The game is really, *really*, fun to play. From a gameplay perspective it's a huge improvement on RE2 Remake. Trading defensive weapons for a dodge system makes sense for Jill as she's shown to be afraid of being infected or being a carrier (as indicated by files found at the very beginning of the game). The weapons feel really good to use, with one exception (and you can upgrade it to mitigate the issue).

The issue is content. Resident Evil games are notoriously short, and this game is short for a Resident Evil. A lot of content from Original RE3 was cut out entirely (though we did get a couple areas more fleshed out).
If you take your time you might take 4 hours on your first playthrough. I'm regularly clearing the game in 90 minutes, and to put that in perspective the record for speedruns on the hardest setting is ~55 minutes at time of writing.

RE3 comes with Resident Evil Resistance, which is a game I have very little interest in. If it was possible for me to take the dev time spent on RE:Resistance and give it back to mainline RE3 I would do so in a heartbeat. 

tl;dr: If you're good with playing the same game over and over for fun/earning unlockables/speedrunning/etc., RE3R might work for you. Otherwise wait for a sale, this game is great but there's not enough there for $60.

Ok let's lay out the facts here. I'm an older guy and I've played and loved literally every single RE game released (with the exception of those awful gun survivor games). I even liked RE Revelations!

Either way though when the RE2 re-release came out I was extremely excited for it, and it did not disappoint.  A full retelling of the story with everything still in the game and everything was EXACTLY like it was in RE2 (ok maybe not exactly, but close enough to feel validation for the 60 bucks you spent). It made you want MORE Resident Evil remakes.

This one though? Where do I start....

First thing you'll notice is the insanely short amount of time it'll take you to beat the game. I mean really, it's insane. There really isn't a lot of depth in this game compared to the others. I know the original Nemesis wasn't exactly the most expansive game but it seems like the remake is cut in half by comparison! It cuts out entire areas (no spoilers here, guys. Sorry) and shortens the already brief game by a LOT. To anyone who played the original RE3, you'll feel cheated simply put - like they sold you half a game.

Secondly, the much favored mercenaries mode - gone. No mention of it, nothing. So nothing really to speak of there at all. If it's DLC - who cares? We still had to pay 60 dollars for a half finished game.

Also, it seems like the fans were LAST in mind for this remake but at the same time were counting on the nostalgia factor to boost sales. I'm not much one for lip service to fans in remakes of tv shows or movies but if you've played the original Nemesis or even watched a speedrun of the game, you know there's some lines in there that the fans love. You won't find them in the remake. Anywhere. Would you remake Jaws without "we're gonna need a bigger boat" in there? Hell no. I have no idea what they were thinking about that one.

To sum it up, I'm an old-ish guy compared to the majority of steam users. I played the original RE when it came out and obsessed over it, toiled the entire summer RE:CV came out to save up for a Dreamcast just to play the game, did the same again a year or two later to get Gamecube for RE4 and again years later to get an Xbox360 just for RE 5. I've consistently been a lifelong Resident Evil fan and did whatever I could to play the next game, now it just feels like they're phoning it in. God knows i'm not interested in any more remakes after this halfassed attempt they put out, let's hope RE 8 will change how I feel because I'm a little ashamed I paid 60 dollars for bad retelling of a story we already knew. I've spent probably approaching the thousands for the systems to play the games on and the nice, deluxe editions too since I loved the games so much. But now? I feel embarrassed I even paid 60 dollars for this.

Please don't let this be a sign of things to come from my favorite franchise.

The game plays more like a horror/action movie, which isn't necessarily a bad thing (see RE4). The main Nemesis fights are varied enough throughout the game that seeing him again doesn't grow old, but he's less of a looming threat in-game and more of a plot device to string location changes together. The map structure also takes a hit due to, and although the story covers more ground in Raccoon City, it feels like a bunch of half-baked layouts when propped up next to RE2. This also makes items like the bolt cutters feel a bit shoehorned in for the sake of tradition than something that will one day open up your map to bigger and crazier things. 

The main emphasis in this game is it's set pieces, which definitely feel a lot larger and spectacular than 2. This, mixed with the time-tested success of Resident Evil's base mechanics do make for an alright game, don't get me wrong. The issue is that with having previous experience in Capcom's landmark titles, it's hard to not stack the game up against the potential of what it could have been. So much is cut out compared to it's source material, and instead of building something better it just regurgitates disappointment into a capable game engine. Stacked up to the best RE titles the game is probably a 4/10, but with the right price point and it's own merits in mind, I'd give it a

It's not a bad game but i can't recommend it at full price, it's way too expensive for what you get.  The campaign can be beat in about 8 hours, that's if you explore absolutely every nook and cranny. It has very little replay value unless you like the ultra hardcore difficulty modes or want to unlock all the collectables, you get a few unlimited weapons you can buy post game with points but there's nothing new to see after your first playthrough.  As a completionist it took me 20 hours to do everything, and I wasn't trying to do it with any speed so i'm sure if you want to speed through the 100% you could easily do it in <15 hours.

The short campaign length wouldn't be so bad if there were multiple routes or areas to explore but after the first area you spent the majority of the game just walking through straight corridors. All the other Resident Evil games are short but there's new things to see and discover, areas or rooms you may have missed. In this game you see everything your first playthrough. there's nothing new to see or do after the first time, no exploration. There's also next to no puzzles in the game, they're a staple of Resident Evil games and seeing them all but removed was another disappointment.

Nemesis is a complete push over and can be defeated in literal seconds if you have the right equipment or ammo (outside of boss fights). He only shows up to stalk you in the first area of the game and when he does show up his appearances are scripted and he's only there to rush you to get to the next story beat. MR X is a lot scarier and feels like more of a threat than Nemesis does at any point in this game. He's not scary, he's not difficult and more of just an annoyance.

Despite all the negatives this is a good game on your first playthrough, it has some fun set pieces and good voice acting and looks absolutely gorgeous. The survival aspect against the zombies are fun and the new Jill  is witty and hilarious.

If you can get this for 50% off or more i'd suggest picking it up, you'll have fun blasting you way through. At full price though absolutely not, unless you really want to play Resistance and think you'll get a ton of play time out of that, personally i thought it was boring.  The game is insanely overpriced for what you get, which is a campaign fun for one playthrough, with no replay value.

Seeing how RE2's remake turned out pretty good last year, i was hyped that maybe my beloved RE3 would get the same treatment now. When announced at first, that did seem the case!! Now this remake turns pretty fun on it's own, but also pretty dissapointing compared to both the original RE3 bossness aswell as the RE2 remake. Here's why:

Muh nostalgias, muh rants:
As soon as i saw the achievement "Escaped Uptown" pop up after a lineair setpiece i could already tell: Gone are the hub-like areas, mazey streets and alleys, and instead there's mostly lineair sections to race through. At most, only 2 areas could count as a hublike area, and along the way, pretty much all of the puzzles are axed aswell. Perhaps they tried to address some of the backtracking that the original had? But i liked the way one could tackle obstacles in different ways through each playthrough, roaming the streets at will and all... Alot of the iconic area's from the original are also gimped or just removed altogether (along with THAT one bossfight) And there's little or no content to replace it. This is doubly frustrating compared to the treatment RE2 got last year. Now don't get me wrong, 2019's RE2 cut some corners too, but certainly not as drastic as this RE3 remake did. After a little while, this remake just says "F' it, im gonna do my own thing now" which is pretty jarring. Now Nemesis, the titular big bad is still pretty powerfull, but also depressingly scripted. He does dynamically chase you along like in the original RE3, but here it's like... only in 1 area? Most of the time he just harasses you in lineair setpieces and bossfights. The setpieces and bossfights are still thrilling on it's own, but it's not quite the same... Mr. X was done better in RE2 remake, so did it prove too hard to one-up him to Nemesis-tier throughout this whole remake? This makes me pretty salty about the RE3 demo too because what was shown there was pretty much the best part of Nemesis and Raccoon City's streets in this entire game. (Not wanting to spoil to much, there is one other area i really liked) Sadly, the whole game doesn't feel as open ended as even the demo suggested it to be, which is just dissapointing and again, very frustrating.

Muh value:
It's also frustrating to see that the game is quite short, but instead they added in RE: Resistance, a game i have no interest in playing. (I still prefer RE: Outbreak with it's co-op breakout scenario's, thank you very much). So they shoe-horned Resistance in for "free" but it probably makes up half the asking price of this package, because RE3 by itself is in no way worth the current €60 retailprice. I've completed the standard run in 7 hours, which is pretty meager in itself compared to my first run in RE2: 9 hours and 30 something minutes. (Alternate A and both B's scenario's not counted). I certainly wasn't rushing it and theres also no live selection system like the original, so even if you would compare it to RE2 remake's lacklustre approach to it's original A-B system, there's still no branching paths here anyway. (Except for maybe different enemy/keyitem placement per each difficulty?) There's no Mercenaries minigame either, and on top of that, many assets are lifted straight from RE2 and even RE7 (which RE2 admittedly also did with RE7, but still added more then RE3 did). For example, Carlos's M4 feels like a remodeled version of RE2's MAC-11 because i can't remember this 5.56 rifle being this surprisingly weak in the original RE3. And why does the Desert Eagle fill in as the Magnum in this game? Where's that badass S&W Magnum? Was Jill not in the mood to give some heavyduty STARS, wheelgun style?? Or was it just easier to copy-paste Leon's Desert Eagle from RE2... You see, it doesnt ruin the game, but alot of these design choices sure feel really lazy for such a short and expensive game. RE2's assets were probably created with RE3 in mind aswell, so if they didnt go all the way with this RE3 remake, I can't help but feel that RE3 should've been a add-on campaign for RE2. Certainly not bundled with Resistance for full price... Maybe they will add content later, like the ghost survivors content in RE2R? Maybe a proper Mercenaries minigame, or even extra chapters to well... you know... let you play in the area's they left out of the game? Would be nice but i doubt it will come.

The good parts:
I could keep ranting on forever about how this game is missing so much from the original. I could, but i won't (or i'll try at least) because i did actually genuinely enjoy this game!!  As i completed the game, i instantly started a new run on a higer difficulty, which i never would have done if i truly hated this. Raccoon's streets (what little there is of em) look and sound absolutely amazing, just like pretty much every area that did make it into the game. Like RE2 remake, it's still a beautifully crafted game and unlike RE2, i felt RE3 uses more of it's original golden soundtrack aswell, like the saveroom theme, Nemesis chase theme, the ending credits etc etc. Alot of the things that actually DID made it into this game were pretty good, and it was surprising that even Dario is in there too. Once a minor but loudmouthed character in RE3, he's inseparable from his hideout-container once again, and he has almost the same voice lines from the original, word by word. Actually, most of the characters are done pretty good aswell. RE2's sweet mechanics are back, with a few additions to help out with the actiony approach of this remake. The knife wont turn dull like in RE2R and there's a dodge feature that works more reliable then the original RE3's tricky dodge system. And if Jill times her dodge perfectly it lets her instantly lock on to an enemy's weakpoint and fire/slash away (Yes it works with the knife too). Carlos has a similiar system, but bodychecks enemies instead to clear some space. Time it perfectly and Carlos will do a Chris-style haymaker that will knock even the mighty Hunter Betas flat on their asses (it's actually really good on Hunter Betas in particular). He can also follow that up with an instant lock-on, just like Jill. [spoiler]Speaking of Hunters, they were done pretty well i think, and the Hunter Gamma's are now way slower, but even more disgusting. The Alien-like spiders that replace the Drain Deimos are horrifying too, but are sadly underutilized...[/spoiler] woops, there we go again.

Conclusion:
So with the really lineair pathways and Nemesis chases, this short remake is not quite what i have in mind when i think of Resident Evil, let alone it being comparable to it's original source game... Maybe it is best summed up as an abridged version of the original, with a much faster pace and tighter, more action orientated controls and a stubborn attitude with doing it's own thing every now and then. it's pretty fun in it's own way, as a more thrilling agression-rush, especially if playthroughs on every different difficulty DO end up changing the keyitems/enemy placements completely.

This game is great, but a definite downgrade from last years Resident Evil 2 Remake. The game is a bit short, lacking certain areas from the original, and underutilizes the Nemesis character. However, at the time of writing this, Capcom has recently released an online survey asking players for their opinions, and it seems a lot of people are in agreement that it could use another area and some more of base Nemesis. So, here's hoping for the best.

Gameplay-wise it's more of the same from Resident Evil 2. Defensive items have been removed in favor of a dodge move, which honestly makes the game a little more challenging at times, since it relies on player timing and reaction speed, rather than having the right item equipped at the right time.

There's also plenty of replay value, with different challenges to complete for subsequent playthroughs, which gives you points you can spend to unlock new weapons and items, such as the infinite rocket launcher.

I do recommend this game for anyone who enjoyed last years Resident Evil 2, but unless you are a huge fan of the franchise or are interested in the Resident Evil Resistance multiplayer game (which comes bundled with this), I'd recommend waiting until its on sale or the price drops a bit.

I was on the fence about buying this because of the reviews for it. I think most are. But I decided to bite the bullet and grab it now at full price.

I wrote out a huge review and decided that I needed to just make it quick and gritty. At the end of the day anyone thats reading this just wants to know if they really need to plop down 60 bucks for this game. So lets get down to it.

[b]Is it pretty, does it use next gen graphics?[/b]
Yes, yes it is and yes it does. It's gorgeous. I use a gosh darn nVidia GTX 750 and it still looks pretty. The new RE Engine that Capcom has been using since 2017 is really amazing.

[b]How well does it recreate the original RE3?[/b]
There's puzzles missing, Story choices missing, and I think there are some baddies missing too. But this will only affect you if you're a returning RE3 player from 1999. Otherwise its a great follow up for those of you who jumped on the train with the RE2 remake.

[b]EDIT: So there's a substantial amount of locations missing from the original, which mean there's quite a few puzzles missing, AND...well, one big bad monster missing. The clock tower, town hall, park, and factory are gone to the wind. With the graveyard gone, we miss out on the giant worm that is the Grave Digger. But I think we can do without Crows and Giant Spiders. 

[b]Is it as short as they're all saying?[/b]
So I haven't technically beat the game yet. I have 3 hours in, at least 1.5 of those are actual playing the game. I just got past the Subway segment of the game. I estimate it'll take me about 5-6 hours to complete. That's with taking my time, collecting all items, exploring all the nooks and crannies if you will.

But please keep this in mind when making your purchase. The original RE3 was all panned as being Short. The requirements for S rank games are based off how long it takes for you to beat the game and how many saves you used.

[b]EDIT: 7 Hours, thats running around, looking at everything, looting everything, dying like a scrub to Nemesis in a particular boss fight. After completing the game you open the shop, allowing you to buy items that you normally get through the playthrough to streamline and make it faster, but also allows you to buy crazy weapons too (Infinite ammo gun, a knife that catches monsters on fire, a rocket launcher.) Replaying the game because I want to buy everything in the shop and get the S rank.[/b]

2.5 hours is the minimum time for a Normal play through to get A rank. 

This game was meant to be played Fast and Furious on a second play through. 

[b]Will you change your review, when you complete the game?[/b]
Sure will, [b][u]SURE DID![/u][/b]. I know the story and what should come based on my life in '99. So I look forward to seeing the rest of what they did to tweak the game.

[b] Is it worth 60 bucks?[/b]
As of right now, I'm still leaning towards "Maybe wait for a sale..." mentality. Don't get me wrong, the game is fun and beautiful. I like it alot. But something feels off. With the RE2 remake, they really made it punch hard. There was a gravitas to the RPD. If that makes sense? Raccoon City, in flames, and carnage has its own feel, but it also feels like its missing something. It's ow~
[b]IS IT WORTH 60 BUCKS?![/b]
The base game is worth 50 I feel. But it comes with Resident Evil Resistance, a team based game where 4 people face off against a mastermind. I'm definitely feeling it, and I like was I see, and it's totally worth about 10 bucks of fun. So in my minds eye, its totally worth 60 bucks for a game and a minigame, if you will. 

But I'd have much rather paid just that 50 for just the base game.

[b]EDIT: In conclusion, after beating the game and finally coming back to do this. My stance remains the same. If you want to buy it full price, do it. You wont be disappointed, unless you're some weird RE3 purist that needed everything to be brought into the remake as is.

I'm going to try and be as unbiased as possible, but it's difficult to do so with the fact that I hold the original RE3 on a tall pedestal. As such, my expectations were much higher. This was an OKAY remake. There were things it did well, but the list is about as long or longer for things that were lackluster. This review is going to be about the ♥♥♥♥ it failed at.

Many environments were either left out/barely explorable/too simple/very linear. The grand majority of puzzles/backtracking was removed, which normally would be a boon. HOWEVER, what this did was remove many opportunities for events to occur/events to be played out differently depending on route chosen. As such, the encounters with our lovable hulking stalker have dwindled to a tiny amount of appearances in a tiny area. 

As for character development, holy ♥♥♥♥ Nikolai. The original had him come off as abrasive initially, but now he struts in, twirling his curly mustache from start. And the whole Carlos/Jill chemistry is still very forced/rushed.

Choices were removed. There's a lot of replayability that was removed. The game overall felt exceptionally rushed. I was going to be fair about areas that were added/expanded on, but you're either rushed through them at breakneck speed or the amount expanded felt that it didn't make up for the loss of other areas. 

And rather than attempt to expand on the main campaign, maybe even offering the ability to play entirely as other characters through their scenarios with things they were doing during Jill's run, rather than giving us modes that existed in the original after beating the game, we get slapped in the face with 2 harder difficulties than hardcore which don't really add that much to the campaign at all. Don't even mention RE:Resistance. Nobody asked for a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ 4v1 multiplayer game that was 'packaged' alongside this feeble attempt at a remake, Capcom. Know what you could've done with that time? Given RE3 the same love that the RE2 remake received, or reserved this kind of effort for an Outbreak remake.

TL:DR

If you can look past the lack of choices, dynamic events, decent suspense/pacing, MERCENARIES MODE, you might enjoy this remake. But you're probably better off playing the original, regardless of the tank controls. Here's hoping Capcom learns from this atrocity, but I doubt anything will be fixed.

(April 8th, 2026) Coming back to this nearly 6 years to the day later, I have to say I'm a little sweeter on this game now. I just replayed this and the 1999 version back-to-back with my spouse, and while I do think my old criticisms remain valid, I think my expectations were simply far too high around the release date. I really, really liked the RE2 remake, and that love hyped me up quite a lot for this one.

This game is missing a lot of what made the 1999 version special, but I think it's still in the same spirit. The 1999 version was a spin-off made concurrently with Code Veronica. It bridged the gap between bigger mainline releases, and kept fans occupied while 4 was being developed, which would come to revolutionize third-person action games entirely. This is the first issue, as this remake was marketed as another big entry following 2019's RE2 remake, not a spin-off that was originally intended to keep the studio's release dates from getting too far apart.

The 1999 version has a great setting and appealing graphics, and Nemesis kept the tension pretty high. It was fun and engaging to make those little narrative decisions and figuring out strategies to deal with him while making progress. He adds a great layer of friction on top of dealing with the normal enemy types and navigating the levels. However, it's short (only one disc, unlike the original RE2's two discs) and the story is very simple. It doesn't really advance the overall narrative, it's really just... what Jill was up to during the outbreak, and how she escaped. That's basically it.

The 2020 remake has a great setting and appealing graphics, and Nemesis keeps the tension high... when he isn't aura faming in a cutscene, forcing QTE's like it's 2010, or chasing you twenty feet into the yet another cutscene. It was engaging to deal with him in open gameplay when he sprints towards you at 60 miles per hour, but the actual segments where you're free on the streets and not just running from scripted sections to more cutscenes make up a tiny fragment of the game's runtime. It's lacking the key components of randomness and organic tension we had in the RE2 remake and the 1999 version of 3. It's also quite short, and the story is very simple. It doesn't advance the overall narrative, it's really just... what Jill was up to during the outbreak, and how she escaped. That's basically it.

I do want to say that I loved the voice cast here in the remake. Great work all around, and the slight tweaks to the plot made it a little more interesting. The revamped dodge mechanic was also pretty fun, if not poorly explained on how to use it to its full potential.

Ultimately, it's lacking soul. I still enjoyed it a lot more upon replay, but I do prefer the original. That's not nostalgia talking either, I played the 2020 remake first! Both have their place, and this game is worth playing for fans of the series (provided you get it on sale).

Albert Wesker may have very well summed up this game with his description of the Tyrant in the first Resident Evil - "Premature".
Resident Evil 3 (2020) is not a bad game but then again it's also not a great game, which is strange because Capcom always pushes for the highest quality in terms of campaign, content, story, and replay value. Even more so if you're expecting a remake from a game from nearly 20 years ago. Unfortunately, with key plot points missing from the original, the game suffers a dtwo hit punch story logic and play length.

One of the longer games in the RE collection, RE3 remake is surprisingly short. Within 3-4 hours, you've escaped the city and defeated the biggest abomination Umbrella has created. And what's left from a replay standpoint? Well, nothing much really, aside from Hardcore and Inferno modes which feel like nothing more than a test on your ability to use the perfect dodge. The game also introduces shop items to make subsequent run throughs more bearable but it doesn't reward you rank wise (i.e. S+) for not using it. In addition, the game does come with Project Resistance, an online mini game meant to appease the multiplayer community but I'm sure that could've been substituted with a hybrid campaign/multiplayer edition of The Mercenaries. The game play is exciting with Capcom continuing to orient survival horror and third person shooter but after a while the surviving part of the game becomes tedious. The boss battles with Nemesis are no longer about the player fearing the Pursuer but more about getting enough ammo for the next all too soon battle.

For a fan well acquainted with the series it's safe to say that there were a multitude of improvements that could've been made for this well anticipated remake especially after the praised received for the Resident Evil 2 (2019) release. Structure and story wise, RE3 is not so much symmetrical with its original 1999 incarnation nor its sister installment of RE2. Key components of the original game utilized Raccoon City as a character in itself as much as the RPD/Police Station in RE2 or the Spencer Mansion in RE. In the original we got to see how distraught the city was due to the viral outbreak and the mass panic, the obstacles it has caused for Jill/Carlos, and provided an intricate layout of where important landmarks and puzzle pieces should be. The vast openness of Raccoon City almost served as a hunting ground for Nemesis with the only warning being the low toned violins of and those heavy footsteps. With the remake the city is just, well, there. Raccoon City became this vibrant yet destroyed mix of NYC and Seattle but it's more like a neighborhood in a little sandbox. No claustrophobic alleys, no far fetched pieces to puzzles or clues, the neighborhood almost plays a shill to Nemesis letting us know when he's about to pop up in the short lived city portions of the game. 

The game should receive some praise to how it reinterpreted certain portions of the game's character arcs and segments. Carlos' hospital was a great rendition as it was clear to see the entire sequence received more love from the design team with its eerie environment. For one the beginning is a great illustration of Jill's surprise attack by this super bio weapon and yet it also ties in nicely the beginning of the original where Jill escapes a burning building. It would've been more logical if they had reintroduced Jill's RPD segment and Brad's death at the hands of Nemesis to help illustrate her perpetual battle with Nemesis but this obviously paved way to give Carlos more say in the story and to connect points in RE2. 

When comparing the character arcs and scripts of the original it's easy to see that significant portions of the game's play through were modified heavily or were just flat out missing, thus affecting the length and logic of the story. Capcom made itself some obvious missed opportunities to incorporate more fear, action, and story development. The entire Clock Tower Segment is replaced with a boss battle early on eliminating the plot point of Jill and Carlos struggling to get a signal to safety after escaping the Monster once. On another hand, Jill meets and collaborates with UBCS from the fifth minute of the game as opposed to the end of the first third making it seem that Jill is more compliant than she should be towards other paramilitary operatives.

The Resident Evil 3 remake is worth a play but for fans of the original they shouldn't expect much compared to its predecessor. If Capcom let this one sit in the incubation tube longer and gave it more time to reimagine key plot points compared to the original as it had done in certain segments, emphasized more incentive based replay value, and included the anticipated Mercenaries mini-game, the remake would've received an overwhelming amount of praise from critics and fans alike. We can only hope the next remake, which ever it may be, will certainly make headlines.

Die-hard fans will complain about this remake. Like RE2:Remake, it is not a verbatim copy of the original.

Regardless of the (lack of) details, the Resident Evil 3 remake is an excellent game. 

It is more action oriented. The puzzles are not difficult, which can be a disappointment to some. The scare factor is there, but not very much. The environment and map design are beautiful. There is some back-tracking involved, but the scenery is constantly changing as you progress through the game. There are also two difficulties higher than “Hardcore.”

You essentially play as Jill and Carlos. They each have their respective segments, with the main focus being on Jill.

Ammunition is abundant. It will be hard for you to run out of ammo, unless your aim rivals that of a potato. There are achievements and challenges that unlock an in-game currency that allows you to purchase in-game bonus weapons and items to help with your play-through.

Many players complain about the length of the game. It is considered a short game by the majority, and rightfully so, if you pick up story/necessary items only. Because of the constant stage/scene changes, the game does not feel as short as it actually is. 

Regardless of its flaws, this remake is the action shooter that it was intended to be during development. This is most likely to cater to new-comers to the franchise that aren’t keen on the eerie/dark item-management atmosphere that most of the original RE games had. 

Worth full price? If you really want it to be

Worth sale price? Yes. You also get RE: Resistance; a co-op 4v1 stand-alone game.

This game is a re-imaging of the events from the original game. Some of the original content was cut in lieu of new environments and enemies so that the game isn't an exact carbon copy. It plays with your expectations in a good way. Nemesis doesn't overstay his welcome and there are a lot of attainable unlock-ables, even for the casual gamer for extended replay-ability (if your not a die-hard horror buff or into speed-running). This remake, like the original, is a lot more action-packed compared to RE2R.

RE:Resistance is fun but is in need of major balancing and in some circles, a complete overhaul.  The PC version suffers from long match-making queues. Presumably it is due to players upset with the package pairing of it with RE3. Which means that the overall value of RE3 is worth about $40 and Resistance being about $20. If you are less likely to play Resistance, i'd wait for a sale/discount to purchase RE3 as a solo title.

Overall, I would rate the game an 8/10 for a solid action-packed survival-horror experience. It would be higher if it included solid DLC like RE7 or more content from the original for that epic nostalgia feeling we received akin to RE2R (as a hardcore fan of the series).

Despite my favoritism towards classic games I never actually got around to playing the original Resident Evil games, except for RE4 of course, so after playing the demo for RE2: Remake I knew I had to get that game, and now comes the RE3: Remake, let's see if it can do for RE3 what RE2: Remake did for RE2.

PROS;
-Fantastic graphics
-Nemesis is terrifying in cutscenes
-RE2 Remake gameplay (mostly)
-Jill is awesome

CONS:
-Game is [strike]waaaaay too short for $60[/strike] a little short for $40
-Lots of reused assets from RE2: Remake
-Once Nemesis is actually in the game he's not very scary
-Some of the nitpicks from RE2: Remake have become problems
-Dodge mechanic is fairly wonky
-Choice system from the original game is gone, missed opportunity to improve it
-The entire clock tower segment from the original game is missing, resulting in pacing issues

RE3: Remake is a fairly fun game, and seeing our classic resident evil heroes in the RE engine is a real treat, from the lighting to the textures pretty much everything graphics-wise is beautiful, this jump in graphics has also made the main enemy, Nemesis, much more terrifying especially in the cutscenes, hearing him bellow 'STAAAAARRRS' as he chases down Jill with a chunk of a building really instills how scary this monster is supposed to be, all of this combined with the RE2: Remake gameplay should make for a good game in theory. In practice however, this game feels like a let-down, I ended up finishing this game in about 6-8 hours, and that's with me taking my time and exploring every nook and cranny for supplies. It was while I was looking around for stuff that I noticed pretty much all of the zombie models are reused models from RE2, I know this is common practice to speed up the workflow but here it's done to a frankly ridiculous degree, so much so that I feel like I'm playing an expansion pack rather than a separate game, I've since learned that both remakes were made concurrently which explains this however I still feel the quality suffered a bit as a result. Meanwhile even though Nemesis is incredibly scary in cutscenes once he's actually in the game he feels like a discount Mr. X rather than the terrifying relentless terminator he's supposed to be, it seems like he can't take as much punishment as Mr. X which is probably an incentive to take him down so you can get the supply crates he drops, this is a mechanic carried over from the original and in theory it sounds like a good way to add more depth to the game, but in practice this turns a nigh-invincible terminator into what feels like an elite enemy in a MMORPG, you do a total of 4 boss battles against him but they weren't tense like in RE2, it just felt like an extended session of ring-around-the-rosie. This is further amplified by the RE2-style gameplay, the fact that you don't have the option to use a healing item when you pick it up like in RE4 still annoys me, it wasn't that much of a problem in RE2 but now with the more action-oriented gameplay (especially in the Carlos sections) the severely limited inventory now hampers the game rather than enhancing it, made even worse now that there are 4 different types of grenade launcher ammo. I wouldn't be complaining about the healing item thing if I wasn't getting grappled so much because I tried to use the dodge mechanic, how the dodge mechanic works is if an enemy is about to attack you, you can press W, A, S, or D and hit the spacebar and Jill/Carlos will dodge in the corresponding direction, [strike]the only problem is once they get to the end of the dodge animation they freeze for a second before doing whatever you're telling them to, this has the effect where a zombie will lunge at me, I'll dodge, and it lunges at me again before I can even move and I get grappled anyway, making the game even more frustrating[/strike] it turns out that this happened because I wasn't executing a perfect dodge, however the timing on this perfect dodge is either incredibly tight or buggy because I wasn't executing it half of the time resulting in the previous incorrect critique, there is an in-game unlockable that fixes this problem so I genuinely don't know if it was intentional or not. All of this wouldn't have been enough for me to give a thumbs-down review, but the final nail in the coffin is that the choice system from the original game is completely absent, in the original RE3 you'd have encounters with Nemesis and the game would freeze and give you a choice, usually either run from Nemesis or fight Nemesis, most of these choices didn't change the overall story arc and were kind of pointless but it still gave the player some sort of agency over their actions, it made it feel like we were in Jill's shoes debating whether to try and take this monster down or flee to safety, and now that it's gone I can't help but think they missed a chance to improve that system and remake it better, however without it all that's left is a visually stunning game that feels too short, they could've fixed the length issue by including the clock tower segment but for some reason that was cut, leaving only a pamphlet hinting at it's existence and resulting in a pacing issue where we only get to have 1 boss fight with Nemesis between the Carlos sections.

All in all while the game was fun the fact that a core mechanic and segment is missing entirely makes this experience fairly underwhelming, it set out to update a classic game to the modern era and what we got was an expansion pack for RE2: Remake, I'd still recommend it if it ever goes on sale or if the price drops to $30 or so but until then, unless you're a hardcore fan of Resident Evil, maybe think twice about buying this.

P.S. After this game has been released there's been talk of a remake of RE4, and after the release of this game I'm kind of hesitant about a remake of 4 since imo that was one of the best in the series and remaking it feels like they're just trying to remake all of their games as fast as possible.

UPDATE: After learning a couple new facts and hearing about the price dropping to $40 I've decided to come back and update this review, While I do think most of my points stand the $40 price tag has definitely softened my critique, reducing it from "don't get this game at all" to "Maybe skip out on it if there's something else you need the money for", ideally I think a $30 price tag would be a bit more reasonable thanks to the game's length.
