In a remake of the finale to the classic Resident Evil trilogy (before Resident Evil 4 started down a new path), Raccoon City returns torn up between a deadly virus, its own citizens and the mysterious and powerful Umbrella corporation. Similar to the 1999 original, half of the events of Resident Evil 3 (RE3) occur before those of the 2019 Resident Evil 2 remake, and the other half after. The overlap between the two timelines is particularly evident around the police station (where we finally learn how Marvin was bit), and at Kendo's place (another homage). 

On the upside:
-The new RE3 features stunning visuals and rich, beautifully detailed environments that feel ominous and immersive. Devour all the stunning visuals RC has to offer! The return of a number of familiar enemies and villains is welcomed, although the collection is by no means expanded.
-The inclusion of a new quick-step dodge system is an excellent addition and the controls feel connected, involved and agile.
-Jill Valentine is a much more rounded, engaging and likeable character than either Leon or Claire from RE2. This iteration of Jill may be my new favourite Resident Evil character (having played the entire canonical series).
-Carlos has undergone some massive improvements since his last appearance in the series, and it's about time (goodbye corny 1999 Carlos).
-Nemesis is a noteworthy, well... nemesis. His pursuit is not as ever-present and creeping as Mr X in RE2 (who felt like he was constantly on your tail), but he is larger, faster, more aggressive and more intimidating when he does jump into the action. His evolution through boss fights into menacing final monster is impressive and well-executed. For a boss fight worth frustration and a racing heart, try the final boss fight on Inferno difficulty.

On the downside:
-The campaign is short. Really short. Across 6 runs, my originally chilled 4h50min was reduced to under an hour (albeit with the help of some helpful additions acquired with achievement points).
-While the action is good, there is a serious lack of puzzles that formed a large part of the foundation of early RE games. Where are the cool puzzles, Capcom?!
-The original RE3 featured story choices that altered the game and the endings. Here, there is really only one ending (arguably two if you REALLY refuse the no-brainer choice the game forces you into). This is a serious under-delivery of an otherwise excellent game and seriously cuts replay value.
-Past the early phases of the game, this is really a very linear experience, often underscored by cinematic click scenes that really have neither alternative nor challenge.
-There are some weapon modifications and the usual arsenal, but I miss some of the bizarre customisation options that really allowed one to decide how you want your weapon to behave (I want my lever-action Western Custom M37). Shotties should be fun to fire. Period.
-As many others have pointed out, the trade of Mercenaries mode for 4v1 Resistance is just not acceptable. Surely the addition of both could have been possible? It feels like the 2019 RE2 had a little more body to it.

RE3 is both a worthy sequel to the 2019 remake of RE2, and a worthy remake of the original. For a reality check of how far gaming has come in 21 years, check out comparisons between the 1999 and 2020 RE3s, particularly the final boss fight. With that said, RE3 is a good addition to RE2, rather than an evolution of it. It's very good, but it could have been so much better, especially at the premium price. Still very much worth a rainy weekend, and then some.

As obligatory introduction for those unfamiliar with the series, Resident Evil 3 (2020) is a remake of the original game released in 1999. Resident Evil 3 (1999) (hereon referred as OG RE3) had interesting developement history as it was supposed to be a spinoff that turned into a sequel for various reasons, and it had features not seen in the series before - and more actionised tone than the games before that; long before Resident Evil 4 was a thing. At its core it still had the same formula of gameplay of finding items, solving basic puzzles, inventory and resource management and not getting brutally killed by whatever was around, and whatnot.

For starters, I do not consider Resident Evil 3 (2020) (hereon referred as R3make) a bad game - as I could name plenty of objectively worse games but it certainly is disappointing and pretty weak remake as a whole. At worst it aggressively skirts the line of mediocrity and meh. Doubly so accounting Resident Evil 2 (2019) was pretty good remake in my opinion. 

What I consider the biggest issue is the game's habit of trying to force 'awesome' scripted events in your face to establish big sack of garbage that is after the main character is supposed to be a threat. I do not consider somewhat more scripted approach a bad thing, but when it turns the basic gameplay flow into game of guess the point of no return and guess how many triggers you bypassed because the developers somehow forgot to make the big sack of garbage actually menacing long-term. I am not sure is it due conscious design decision or they could not figure out how to implement x\y\z properly. But when supposedly menacing threat is more interested pretending to be anime villain who teleports around rather than brutal, aggressive stalker-hunter and only way they achieve even that is scripting and railroading the crap out of it, I begin to question how the ♥♥♥♥ they managed to do that? OG RE3 handled it better, and even RE2make's well-known troll functions better in same role considering the devs were not busy scripting the crap out of it every few seconds in vain attempt to establish a threat... long after it ceased to be a threat.

As R3make progresses towards the end it shows rays of light of more organic gameplay and - gasp - actually feeling like you are not entirely railroaded and may have to look around bit more to find out how to progress. I personally found those the most enjoyable moments of the game. Unfortunately inbetween when it feels more like a game and less like interactive cutscene or walking narrow corridor setpiece into another setpiece involving big sack of garbage which seems a cointoss whether it actually wants to hit you or simply walk menacingly or pretend it wants to do something, plot events piles up like an avalanche that one minute ago you dealt with a setpiece then you have obligatory bossfight in very conspicuous boss arena more suitable for running in circles (which also conspicuously renders the boss helpless, minor spoiler here) and after maybe few minutes of gameplay that feels almost like paced another obligatory sequence that could almost be good if there was more flow to it - and the big sack of garbage could be threathening. Oh, and maybe few minutes later? Another scripted setpiece brought to you by big sack of garbage.

If you are going to make something like that, make it more organic and do not cop out by making over 90% of its function due to scripts that one can practically hear "Psstt nothing personel Jill" in the background. Especially if you took the wrong door and big sack of garbage was about to punch, dodge was done pre-emptively and would've been death only it just despawned because they never taught the big sack of garbage to open certain doors into area(s) you only visit once. Or maybe twice by accident. Convenience and balancing challenge vs frustration is understandable, but so is understanding the game has quite abusable dodge mechanic and perhaps introducing better flow and pacing to the game.

OG RE3 did that much better. So did RE2make. I was looking forward to see how R3make differs from the original, and there are some moments where it feels pretty interesting take on the source material. But when perhaps the primary selling point fails to provide organic threat and the game is keen on slapping it in the player's face like self-insert fan-fiction character, and it overshadows other parts of the game as if to highlight everything that is wrong with the game, to quote a certain known eyeglassed old-timer on the Internet.

Another clear example is when you are 'introduced' to a group of survivors near the start, the original characters just point to another room where you can see the people but that's it. I'm not saying this is a bad game overall. But it's a bad $60 2020 game. It's a bad RE3:N remake. It's a bad successor to RE2 Remake. If anything of that would have been different, I would recommend it. But it's just too much.

Case A: A bad $60 2020 game.
The game is outdated. It's a very short liniar game that does not add anything new not only to a gaming in general, but does not even evolve Resident Evil as a series. Even Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice, a 2017 "indie AAA" game feels like more polished and thought-through experience for half the price. RE3R does not offer anything that would justify the price. And no, Resistance does not do it either, it's unnecessary addition that nobody asked for.
That being said, it would be still be ok and I would still recommend this game if not for ---

Case B: A bad Resident Evil 3: Nemesis remake.
I'm not talking about fixed camera + tank controls (though I would definitely prefer it). I'm talking about the feeling of the game.
Do you remember when in RE3N you would find an item and had no idea what it does? You would have to explore the map and find the next step you're supposed to do. This is gone. Every key item is obvious and located close to the place you need to use it at, almost making it pointless to have the item in the first place.
Do you remember how in RE3N Nemesis could appear anywhere and you would have to down him and run away until he despawns? Not anymore. It's now completely scripted chase sequences that ruin all the experience. Sure, you have a tiny moment in the begining where he pretty much can appear, but it's so short, it almost does not count. And it's definitely not half the game as in was in 1999.
Huge sections of the game are gone. Clocktower, City Hall, Park. Lots of smaller locations are gone too, like Newspaper office, Restaurant, and many more. Spiders are gone (as they were gone in RE2 Remake). Gravedigger is gone (!!!). I'm sure more other enemies are gone too that I can't remember right now.
The story is reshuffled. Jill no longer goes to the RPD, Carsol does. Nemesis no longer kills Brad, Carlos does. Carlos no longer goes to the Hostpital and back, he is teleported in and out. The story is based on RE3N, but only slightly. It does not even have that iconic timer at the end!
Puzzles are gone except for, probably, one. The whole feeling of where do I go next gone - you always know where do you go, game is totally liniar. It's so disappointing it makes me mad.
And just to add insult to injury ---

Case C: A bad successor to Resident Evil 2 Remake
This is very unexpected, but the game in a downgrade from RE2R. Both in gameplay and in graphics. RE2R was an open world compared to RE3R. Despite being far from the original RE2, it still handled oldschool RE2 mechanics well enough to be forgivable, but RE3R just abandons them altogether. Even the RPD office is no longer explorable, they turned it into a short corridor.
Zombies are no longer dismemberable. I heard it's because RE3R will have more zombies on the screen, but it's not true. I'd go ahead and say RE2R had more zombies on the screen, especially in 4th Survivor mode (where are my Mercs minigame from original?) Zombies lost their ragdoll physics. If in RE2R they realisticly fell on environment, now they lose their model right after death. They can fall through walls, through each other, you can walk through them as if they are not there. And on top of that, they now despawn after death, while in RE2 they stayed forever.
Speaking of Mercs, they didn't even bother to add epilogues! Just few pictures after you beat the game - it's gone. No multiple endings, no nothing.
Mr X is more Nemesis-like than the Nemesis is.
And for some reason they removed the subweapons. When zombie grabs you, there is no way to get away from it. It's been in all remakes so far, why did you ditch it? Oh, you added a button promt that does nothing? Cool.
Finally - they managed to lower the graphics. The classic REEngine mozaic on hairs is now so much more visible it's irratating. The environment is now bigger and you can enjoy the 3FPS distant zombie animation so much more in this game.

This game should have costed $20. My dissapointment is immeaasurable and my day is ruined. Thanks for watching.

I am posting this review as a comparison to the original game (mostly) and listing where it compares favourably or unfavourably below.

TL;DR: Good game but short. Recommend buying on sale.

Better:
- The plot in this remake is much better than the original which was weak (especially in the second half).
- Characters are much better written in this game than in the original where they were always quite bland.
- Graphics are obviously much better thanks to the REengine, environments look better and the characters no longer look like waxwork figures.
- Introduction is so much better compared to the terrible opening of the original.
- Dodge mechanic for Jill is good, it requires skill to pull off but is satisfying when a perfect dodge is executed. That being said Carlos dodge mechanic is quite poor (see below).
- There is more enemy variety in this game than in last year's RE2 remake.
- The enemies also have more interesting mechanics which are unique for each type.
- I like the inclusion of the shop, it makes items more accessible to people generally and there is quite a lot of variety.
- The nonsensical time frame and plot hole regarding MB from the original is corrected and nicely linked to RE2 (There is a nice eater egg in this game calling back to a secret in the original RE2 game).
- The clock tower has been removed which from a plot point did not make any sense and which from game play perspective was the weakest part of the original with a terrible boss fight with Nemesis's first form.
- Nemesis encounters are intense and well executed.

Worse:
- Definitely short (I recommend buying this on sale if you want the most bang for your buck).
- In the original Carlos section was about 10% of the game, in this its more like 40%.
- Generally Carlos sections are weaker than Jill's, there is definitely a feeling of padding with more zombies being created just to add artificial difficulty.
- Carlos's dodge mechanic is poor and unwieldy (reminds me more of the kick and attack mechanic of RE4 and 5 but not at all well executed).
- There is an issue of pacing at one point, where you take control of one of the characters just for one boss fight before switching back to the other.
- The starting city area feels too short and the randomness of being able to run into Nemesis is over too quickly.
-Shame to lose the cemetery section and gravedigger boss.
- No mercenary mode.

The amount of content on offer may be on the thin side, but this re-imagining of RE3 has it where it counts. Yes, some sections were cut, but other sections like the hospital were expanded to make up for that. Your enjoyment of the main campaign will likely depend heavily on how closely you wanted this game to stick to the original material, as many things have changed, though there are still a lot  of homages and references to the original RE3 to satisfy older fans like me. The quality of the campaign is very high while it lasts, although it does drop off a bit (but not disastrously, by any means) after you escape from Raccoon City. I don't know if I can recommend this at full retail in good conscience unless you're a huge resident evil fan and love the idea of a RE game running on RE2's engine that leans a little bit closer to RE4's play style while still usually feeling closer to RE2 overall. That said, if you're afraid of not getting your money's worth, just wait for a sale. If you can get this game for $30 or less and you liked RE2 then I think you'll be very, very happy with your investment.

I originally gave this game a thumbs up, but after having done everything there is to do in this game, I can't give it one anymore. This game was designed to be a cash grab, and that's all there is to it. Speed running it can take 2 hours, so it's hardly worth the price. Then Capcom decided to announce that it was done with the game. No clocktower, no park, no graveyard, and much more. So much cut content forever lost. I’m disappointed with this remake. My first run through I walked from point to point more than half the time, and spent an excessive amount of time just looking at the environment for nostalgic sake. It took me 5.5 hours. An average nonspeed run would be sub 4 hours, and prolly closer to 3 as you memorize the item and enemy positions. To get an S rank in assisted you need to clear it in 2.5, standard is 2, and hardcore 1.75 hours. There are no additional play modes. There are no alternate story lines, or alternate endings based on decisions. Several areas and “quest” where eliminated from the original game. 

To compare this thing to its predecessor RE2, RE2 you needed between 2-3.5 hours for an S rank clear time. This isn’t that much more than RE3, but you also had two different characters with very different story lines to play. And each character had a secondary play through mode for a total of 4 total time lines you could enjoy.

The lack of major puzzles makes the game feel a lot like RE6. It’s all about just running around, shooting zombies, and progressing the story that ends all too quickly. There are several small issues that may or may not bother some users. Lip syncing for example is atrocious for a triple A title. RE2’s limb cutting was removed from RE3. That means head shots really are the only way to go, since body and limb shots will do less total damage and serve no function purpose as far as disabling the target. Downed zombies also will no longer be there an hour later as you explore the place. they will simply disappear within minutes leaving a pristinely clean area were you had a blood battle 3 minutes ago.

The character models when aiming a weapon are pretty bad. When Jill attempts to point her shotgun at a target 20 feet away or so it’s aimed so low it’s almost comical. The reticle is huge and will encompass the entire zombie torso at that range, yet if you look at the angle of the shotgun in her hands she’s aiming around the targets feet. For someone that owns and has used firearms for a long time it’s pretty immersive breaking to go to aim at a targets head and notice Jill’s gun is actually leveled at their waist or thigh. Its likes she’s too tired to hold the weapon fully upright and is just resigned to being zombie chow. Maybe this is Capcom’s way of trying to show Jill as a weak and defeated character… more likely it was just some animator that didn’t check their alignments and it somehow got blessed off by a less than spectacular quality control.

Oh I almost forgot pathfinding and zombie AI. So in RE2 zombies could follow you into almost any room (other than safe rooms). They would chase players and eventually lost track and then stand in place or mill about. In RE3 zombies are locked to specific areas. Most of the time if you open a door and see zombies inside a room they will be unable to leave that room. If you just stand in the doorway you can shoot them all without any fear of being attacked. Often when this happens the zombies won’t even react to being shot. They sometimes won’t even turn to look at you as you slowly pick away at their health from that doorway. If you enter the room and engage them only to find out you’re in danger of being swarmed, no problem! You can just casually walk back out the door and the majority of the time the zombies will completely lose agro the second you enter the doorway and will return to very specific default locations. Each zombie has its own “standing place” and anytime it loses agro it will automatically move to that location and stand immobile. The whole standing place is most noticeable in the hospital. It even works on several of the hunters. Of the two hunters in treatment, the one furthers from the door for example can never leave that room and will auto loose agro the second you walk through the door. The closer one can leave the room, but rarely will and you have to try pretty hard to bait it into going through the door.

Now for the good. Despite all its failings RE3 is still a fun game to play in terms of gameplay. Boss fights are fairly quick paced compared to RE2. One nice note was the number of zombies on screen at any given time has gone up to the point where it’s “almost” a zombie game. 1-3 zombies in a large room does not a threatening hoard make. That was a major failing in RE2, glad to see were getting more. That’s…. really about all I have for positives.

Wow... I Have been sucked into the RE world now since January when I first beat RE1. Now before continuing with my review for the newest release in the franchise, RE3 Remake, I'd like to give some background.

   After beating RE1, I went on to play RE2 Remake; and with 20+ hours into RE 2 Remake, I can safely say it is one of my favorite games ever. Everything about it was perfection to me. The graphics were of course gorgeous, and the overall atmosphere of the game combined so well together. The story keeps you asking questions and as the whole thing unfolds it really is pretty damn cool but cheesy in the best way possible. I LOVED the horror/creepy atmosphere and then later in the game the campy and goofy vibes started coming in and it worked so damn well.
   The gameplay? Sure its a bit simple, but adding in the idea that ammo is scarce and somewhat hard to come by, blended really well with all the zombies you had the choice of killing or avoiding. My most favorite detail of the game came down to the maps in which you have to explore/backtrack to be able to progress through very fun but easy puzzles. Now while the puzzles are quite simple, the addition of zombies constantly threatening you AND Mr. X stalking you really made for an overall great experience. Ok speaking of Mr. X... lets talk about that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!
   So, MR. X is this big mofo who follows you the entire game and only has one goal: to kill you. The first time I played through RE2 remake, I literally ♥♥♥♥ myself when Mr. X was first revealed. Within 15 minutes of meeting this big heckin chunker I said to myself, "wait is this bald DILF really gonna follow me around for the rest of the game"??? By the end of the game, the answer to that question was YES. The one question I still need answered is how big is his ♥♥♥♥?? Everything about Mr. X was so exciting, from hearing his footsteps coming closer and closer to you from another room, or being cornered by him and having no choice but to take a fist full of X GONNA GIVE IT TO YA, each encounter was so exhilarating and never really got stale until my second playthrough.
   Now here's one of my favorite aspects of RE2 remake, that sweet sweet sweet second playthrough. Now truthfully, the second playthrough isn't all that different from the first. Sure you play as a different character, but besides a few different gameplay moments/cutscenes, its basically the same. THAT'S PERFECTLY OK. The reason it being ok is because since you know all the puzzles and all the little areas, it truly is a joy trying to get through the game in a quicker playthrough. This is because there is a timer implemented in the game for those who are interested in doing their own little speedruns. With the addition of different little gameplay segments and cutscenes, it really is worth it playing through it a second time. Oh and when you're done playing through it a second time? Go play through it all again a 3rd and 4th time on hardcore to see how quick you can beat it on that difficulty! Damn, just thinking about it, I might go back and do ANOTHER playthrough myself. I mean hey, I have only put 20+ hours into that bad boy.

Alrighty... Now that we've got THAT mouthful out of the way, Lets talk about why we are actually here: RE3 Remake.

   Let me start off by saying I love this game. I really do. This is the thing I hate though: it is nowhere close to being the masterpiece that is RE2 Remake. Why do I hate that? Because I hate comparing things, especially these two games because while they are in the same series (which is why i'm comparing them to begin with) they are two completely different beasts, or should I say Tyrant ;). 

   Now don't get me wrong, I actually am glad that RE2 Remake and 3 Remake are different, because that just means they didn't want to do exactly the same thing again. Sure it has the same engine, graphics, gameplay mechanics and atmosphere as RE2 Remake, but RE3 Remake is, I guess, a different style of game? For example: RE2 remake has you in the police station for a large portion of the game, having you backtrack and go into all the different rooms to complete different puzzles, all the while making sure you don't use all your ammo. Sure RE2 Remake gets more "linear" later in the game but it ocassionally puts you in a new area with new puzzles and areas to backtrack. RE 3 Remake on the other hand, does none of that. Like none at all. MAYBE right at the beginning of the game, but this area only lasts 40-50 minutes. RE3 Remake is an action/thriller game. Plain and simple. It's just that. 
  While that is ok that its different from RE2 Remake, I personally found RE2 remake more enjoyable than 3 because of this. RE3 Remake has the player run through Raccoon City, unfolding the mysteries that started in the original, but in a linear, action oriented blockbuster video game. With quicktime events and many many MANY cutscenes I personally would have loved to play through, it all just felt a little bit soulless. I hate to say that, because I still enjoyed it, but it just felt like a game I have played hundreds of times. Especially add all of that in with the fact that it only took me 6 HOURS to beat the whole thing. Oh and this time, I really don't feel the need to replay through it again. Will I? yes, because I love this franchise. It's just that besides the love I have for the series, I have no other reason to replay it.

  Overall, the game added more to the RE story which has me DYING to play the next, RE4 :). I just wish it had some more depth to it and was a tad bit longer and had a bit more replayability. I understand they wanted this to be different from 2, which I am glad they did that. I guess I wish it was a different different from the different we got. Does that make sense? Ah who knows. Anyways I still loved this game and highly recommend it to any other RE fan.

 You aren't an RE fan? What you need to do then is buy RE2 Remake IMMEDIATELY no matter what it costs, its worth any kind of price tag. Then wait for RE3 Remake when it goes on sale.


TL;DR: RE3 Remake is a fun cinematic thriller with enough action to please someone looking for a quick 6-7 hour long adventure. Not worth $60 UNLESS you are a hardcore RE3 fan. Nowhere close to being as good as RE2 Remake.

The level design, enemy placement, upgrading system, and boss battles all felt really lazily designed and uninspired. Nothing felt new, or really interesting. There are literally tons of reused assets from re2 remake ([spoiler]
like the section where you visit the RPD for a brief level[/spoiler]).  It's also super predictable at many points, where you can tell when an enemy is gonna show up  based on how the level is designed ([spoiler]especially in the sewer level and in the Nest[/spoiler]). Sure, there are some fun moments sprinkled throughout the game ([spoiler]like the zombie swarm and penultimate boss fight[/spoiler]), and the gameplay as such is fun as always like it was in re2. But unlike in re2 remake, where by the end you were super pumped and felt super satisfied taking down the tyrant / Birkin who was a thorn in your side your entire story, here I just wanted to get it over with just to get it over with. By the end I didn't care because I never really connected with the characters (whose stories are never really developed), or really found Nemesis to be that scary or intelligent. Nemesis just shows up, and unlike how you may have thought based on the demo, [spoiler] you really are only chased by him in the beginning of the game [/spoiler](the aspect of the game I was most excited for and I feel cheated about). The rest of the encounters are scripted, and you can skip them as they're cinematic. I don't care that it's a more action oriented game with less puzzles - I'm all down with that. But this game just lacks a spirit - feels rushed, and cynically made. Really disappointing.

This is going to be a hard review for me to write because I love this franchise dearly and have for nearly 20 years now. I have to say that if you are on the fence about buying this game, I would suggest waiting for a sale. There are some things I really did not enjoy about this game:

1). When I first heard rumors about this game being remade, my mind went crazy with the possibilities of how Raccoon City would look in modern day technology. However, what we got was the very small portion of the city to really explore, and ya know, do Resident Evil things.  But, throughout this whole play through, I was grasping for more, anything on exploring Raccoon City like the original let us do 21 years ago. 

2). The overall sense of feeling rushed. The game legitimately skipped almost the entire first portion of Resident Evil 3, I would say all the way up to the point where Jill meets Carlos at the gas station to do the puzzle for the trolley. Now I do not know if the rumors are true, that Capcom was working on this and RE2 Remake and this at the same time, but it sure as hell does not feel like they did because Resident Evil 2 Remake is vastly superior. Throughout the whole game it just feels rushed, being unable to explore with too many linear sections involved. 

3). The treatment of Nemesis. Do not get me wrong, I loved Nemesis new look in this. However, the boss fights with Nemesis, were really bad. Without going into spoilers because, this could be a potential spoiler especially for newcomers of the franchise. But his involvement in the game is vastly inferior compared to his previous version of Resident Evil 3 in 1999. The other thing that I really did not like is how easy he would go down, just absolutely no challenge from him whatsoever, providing no incentive to bring him down. Just really disappointed with this too.

4). The lack of memorable locations and puzzles. The lack of basically the entire first 1/3 of Resident Evil 3 was not here at all. The complete injustice done to places like the park, the gas station, the clock tower, and even the lack of the major puzzles. Especially the one where it is now reduced to a bonus machine. To me, all the awesome locations and puzzles were just done a complete disservice from the original game. Also, something like the Dead Factory was a location I was very much looking forward to, and that was pathetic. Just so terribly done with the re-imagining.

5). The game is easy. I played on normal, and I only died a handful of times only because I made some stupid decisions or I was not sure what to do. Nemesis, when chasing Jill, when using a certain weapon will go down instantly. Making him less threatening than he actually is and he is suppose to be, he's a Tyrant that uses weapons and can run at his victims. The zombies are less bullet spongy this time around, which I guess can be a plus, but makes them less threatening this time around compared to Resident Evil 2 Remake. 

6). I could bring up the fact of how short this game is, but all the old school Resident Evil games are pretty short too. But in 2020, they could have done so much more with that, especially not cutting out almost half the game that was in the original 21 years ago. 

7). A particular boss battle that I was hoping to see make a comeback, but unfortunately it was not provided for us. 

=======================================================================

-Graphics:  9

Neutral: Dodge makes the game a lot easier than RE 2: Remake

Neg: The physic is definitely a step down from RE 2 Remake.  There is less of the following: destroying body parts, less blood / gore, infinite zombie hoard? Also personal, but Capcom, you don't have to keep making profanity laced videogames.  You don't have to curse to look cool, this game being one. 

-Replayability: 7 
It's telling that the last challenge you can get (beating all the challenges) is aptly named "Bye Raccoon City" or something similar.  As much as I like the game,  I have like 5 or 6 challenges left & when I am done (should be able to finish it in a day), I may not play as much, if at all. This game is on the shorter side.  on the 1st play through, I played at an extremely leisure pace, trying to memorize the layouts, & trying to find everything, & it took me about 8+ or so hours. Story length, puzzles and lock picking

Despite its short length and shortcomings I enjoyed this game, but I still can’t recommend it at full asking price. I never played the original RE3, however from what I’ve read and watched in videos, some content was cut here, specifically the park and tower levels. I completed my hard core (nearly 100%) run at 11 hours (8 hrs 57 mins of successful playtime, according to my final score card). I became very aware of how fast I was moving through the story once I started getting advanced weaponry and mods so quickly. The game doesn’t waste time linking some of the maps together like in RE2, once you get past an area and the big event happens to move you to the next and you won’t be returning.

There is a shockingly low amount of puzzles here, and they are easily guessed or straightforward to solve. The game tries to slow your progress via lock picking to cut off loot and extra areas on the map, however this feature feels tacked and somewhat immersion breaking. It’s weird to see the same yellow lock on everything, from stores to a simple lockers (there is a map with a little bit of lock variety, but I won’t mention why due to spoilers). Its lazy to have most of your locks be solved via lock picking, at least in RE2 you had different types of keys.

Nemesis

From what I’ve heard from people who have played the original, they are all saying Nemesis pursued you more, and is really scripted here by comparison. I completely agree, I never felt pressured in my play through, in the few segment(s) when Nemesis does endlessly chase you I had already cleared most of the map aside from a few lock picking areas which meant all I had to do was get to the next story objective, and since the maps are not that big it really cuts Nemesis stage time short. After about mid game Nemesis is purely a benched and scripted boss, only showing up when you reach a certain checkpoint. This is a bummer, I’ve heard people talk about how much Nemesis puts MR X to shame, yet my experience with MR X in RE2 was superior in terms of unrelenting tension and harassment. 

Difficulty, knife durability, ink ribbons, and quick time events

I completed the game on hardcore difficulty and the overall the game was too easy. There are plenty of red explosive barrels or electric fuse boxes in the early city areas, allowing you to conserve ammo and clear or disable 3-4+ zombies in a single shot. Once I downed enemies, I could use my knife to slash and stab them on the ground to confirm they were indeed permanently dead. If they are faking they would react and try to get up, most of the time I can kill a zombie with my knife before they can counter attack. 

That’s the other problem I had with this game compared to RE2, the knife has infinite durability. Now initially I jumped for joy at the idea, but after an hour of play I realized how much it reduced my difficulty experience, even on the hardest starter setting. The game gives you time to breath and clear downed enemies without much trouble, which means that backtracking through areas littered with dead enemies rarely has that tension because you can just stab and recheck they’re dead without cost of durability, or if you can remember who you fought and confirmed killed via knife check, you can run through confidently. Only occasionally does the game pull a cheesy moment in which a dead enemy you haven’t fought yet but have already stab checked, will rise up; this is usually done by some kind of progression check. In RE2 you had to choose how to use your limited resources, be it ammo or knife durability. Often this meant you would have to leave enemies alive in areas to get through and just stun and dodge when backtracking through those areas of the RPD, that stress and tension is mostly gone in RE3; in part because you never stay in the same map for long due to the games length and always forward motto. 

It’s also sad that the ink ribbon feature didn’t not make a return; it made saving your game in RE2 another scarce resource on higher difficulty, adding a risk versus reward for holding off on saving for as long as possible and potentially losing play time if you died. In RE3 you can save as much as you like, and the save locations are plentiful on most maps, the only downside is too many saves impact your final score after story completion. 

The dodge mechanic is very inconsistent in my play through; often causing death in moments where I could swear I timed it right. This is especially annoying in boss fights and against specific enemies that can execute you with a single special attack that is poorly advertised. There are difficult spikes in this game that caused a lot of frustration, one in particular that took over an hour of repeated deaths to get past because special enemies are more spongy at higher difficulty.

Most of the QuickTime events were no problem and very straightforward. However one in particular quick time event caused several deaths that felt cheap. Without spoilers, the prompt was to press “W” over and over to avoid death, but no matter how fast I spammed it I kept dying. Turns out the prompt had some white circle around it that expanded outward (which all of these quick time prompt have). So I always thought it was cosmetic, when in fact it meant hold the key down for a brief amount of time. And I had to does this prompt over a dozen times for that frustrating sequence. I can tolerate quick time events if they are straightforward with clear advertised timing, but some of these are just too vague. 


Resistance multiplayer

I didn’t even touch the multiplayer mode as of this review because the streams I watched sucked any interest I had in trying it out, specifically it lacked what I wanted out of a resident evil game, survival horror, tension, limited resources. In the few hours of gameplay I saw, the mastermind spawned enemies or traps right in front of survivors. Time to kill zombies was too quick, and the gun/ammo store made it seem too arcade like. 

Overall impressions

Having never played the original RE3, I enjoyed the story for what it is, but it’s just too bad the content is so limited, as it feels like RE2.5. Nemesis while restricted, goes through some cool evolutions throughout the game, with a few exceptions. I would recommend this game if it was 30 to 40 bucks, but if price is of no concern then you will enjoy what limited content is here.

If RE2 (2019) was a master class in remaking an old game, RE3 (2020) was something made by people who just went to lunch with the RE2 dev team. Whole areas of the original game are missing, it's extremely light on puzzles (I think there are only two or three in the game), the 'story path choice' system is gone, Mercenaries mode is absent, the new enemy gimmicks are clear reuses in many cases, and Nemesis is in less of the game than the original and most of his segments are set pieces. 

Similar to the original RE3, it feels like this was made in a rush and by a different team. It's also quite short, and with limited replay value. And it has DENUVO, if that's a concern. 

This is not a $60 game, but it is a decent purchase if you can get it on sale between $30 and $40.

If you enjoyed RE2 Remake, you'll likely enjoy RE3 Remake. It feels like an expansion pack. It's way shorter than RE2R because there's only one campaign. There are also some gameplay changes that may be considered improvements or flaws depending on your tastes.

Let's start with the Nemesis. Unlike Mr. X, who felt like an ever-present threat, Nemesis is mostly relegated to highly linear and scripted set-pieces. When he's chasing you, he's harder to escape because he has ranged attacks and will jump in front of you if you get too far away. His encounters do have more variety than Mr. X's but they're far less scary because you know they'll be short-lived. If you love cinematic set pieces, you'll enjoy Nemesis more than Mr. X. If you're looking for a more fear-inducing experience, you'll be disappointed.

The gameplay itself is more action-oriented than RE2's. In RE2, you had to spend resources (i.e. bullets) to stun or knockdown zombies to get past them. In RE3, you can just dodge roll past them and that trivializes most zombie encounters. In addition, RE3 is far more generous with ammo so if you really want to just kill everything, there's little reason not to. Puzzles have also been reduced considerably compared to RE2.

Finally, RE3 lacks the sense of place that RE2 had. You spent most of RE2 inside the police station. In many ways, it felt like a puzzle box as you unlocked new areas and learned the quickest routes to where you wanted to be. In RE3, there are more distinct levels but they are much smaller and far less layered than the police station in RE2. The first area is the most open-ended and does offer areas to be unlocked but you'll unlock them all within the first few hours. RE3's pacing is definitely tighter than RE2's and you don't spend much time in each level.

Overall, I enjoyed most of my time with RE3 but came away a bit disappointed. It has a greatly reduced scope than RE2 yet has the same price tag. RE: Resistance also comes with it but I'm pretty sure that'll be dead within a month. I wish they had cut Resistance and invested those resources into RE3 instead. I can't quite recommend the game at $60 but it's worth picking up at $30-$40.

Resident Evil 3 sets a great inital impression but after a while you begin to notice all of its short comings and why the turnaround time from RE2make to RE3make was so quick. Let's keep this short and sweet. 

Graphics 9/10: RE engine is a magical thing for Capcom and they need to utilize it everywhere, I will knock it for a ton of reused assets from RE2. I understand its the same time frame but man... You know that saved them a hell of a lot of time and money on production.

Gameplay 7/10: This is where it get's weird. I almost want to drop this to 6/6.5 if you have affinity towards the original RE3. That game used to scare the living crap out of me because of how random it was. This game is not random. It turns into a corridor fest. It almost feels like a step back from RE2 and a step way way back into PS3 era Uncharted style games except even more linear. This is one of my biggest negatives for this game. Once the magic sort of fades you realize what you have gotten yourself into. 


Controls 10/10: This game feels like butter on keyboard. I've always played controller but man forget that with how crisp it felt playing with a M/K setup. Didn't miss my sticks at all. 

Sound 9/10: This game sounds great. Pop on some high quality headphones and you are pretty much set to go. 

Story 8/10: It's compelling enough. Carlos reminds me of Keanu Reeves. Jill reminds me of Gina Carano. The game has a solid push of forward momentum even when it slows itself down for backtracking. There are TON of cutscenes. I thought i was watching a movie instead of playing at times but it was all entertaining if you are looking for action/adventure.

Additional information that sways me final impressions: There is a lot of scenarios in this game where it feels like... if you make one mistake, the game is completely over and you will be punished without hesitation with a cheap kill. There is a particular room with 4-5 particular bad guys that do not behave in the manner that they do in the rest of the game where you COULD lose almost all of  your ammo and the game gives you no real warning about it. If you re-enter said room the enemies all reset to their base positions as if nothing happened repeating the chaotic cycle of trying to escape them in very bad position stacking for your dodge move as Jill. This was a major instance where I though the game was unfairly balanced towards the player and slowed the pace of the game and the fun factor way way down. It happens in a few spots where it doesn't seem to be necessary or called for and it just ruins the pace of the game a little. 

Final Verdict!

I'm sitting at a 7.5 to 8 on this one. I would highly recommend this if you are paying less than 60. USD 30 would be the perfect price point especially with RE Resistance isn't part of anything you will play. But for a first run of 5 or so hours at 60... and some of its short comings I think you could honestly wait for a sale here!!! 

Happy Gaming!

As a fellow who played the Original Resident Evil Series, I've always been a fan of the classic horror series the games are known to provide. Finished this game in 8 hours, and I have to say, I love the way the game was done. 

Firstly, I wasn't expecting the game to be an "exact copy" of the original. If it did, I would've immediately lost interest mainly because I would know what would happen next. Roaming through the narrow sections of Raccoon City, really emphasizing the disaster that the T-Virus has plagued on the city, it's what scared me as a kid (classic series), and it still did with this game. 

Nemesis scared the heck out of me during the classic series, and seeing him being able to block my path, and prevent me from progressing, it's the kind of expectations I wanted from Nemesis. A beast whose goal is to only see you NOT walk out of the city alive. Sure, the game leaves obvious hints on when you should expect him, but when you're running on critical ammunition, and need an extra boost to confront that beast.. you'll be very grateful for those hints.

Going back to the Raccoon Police Department gave me nostalgia from the classic series to today. To some folks, they think that it's because the developers were being lazy, but if you really pay attention, it really ties the strings together. From understanding why Marvin Branagh meant what he said to, "Don't make my mistake. Take them out, or run!", to understanding why the safety deposit locker room was open, to understanding why there is a huge hole in the wall in the shower room (and a busted pipe). The point is, if you've played the previous game, it makes more sense.

All-in-all, the game is a masterpiece. It gave me the opportunity to replay a great gem, and I hope we can see more in the coming future.

My review is based off of several points of view..

[b]1. Comparing RE3R to RE2R:[/b] RE3R is a HUGE downgrade. Key features such as dismemberment, rag-dolls, critical shot system felt like it was missing. RE3R is significantly shorter then RE2R and RE3R reuses A LOT of assets from RE2R. RE3R is significantly more linear than RE2R. I'm not exactly sure why a lot of the amazing features RE2R had were cut from RE3R. RE3R also attempts to loosely connect itself to RE2R with really half-baked Index/Codex/Notes. Large portions of the map from RE2R were completely reused in RE3R with little to no variation added. 

[b]2. Comparing RE3R to RE3 (Original):[/b] RE3R is missing a lot of content and features that the original RE3 had. I did not expect RE3R to be a 1:1 remake. However, I did not expect hours of gameplay to be cut, nor did I expect RE3R to deviate so far from RE3. RE2R managed to capture what made RE2 so memorable, while adding a new refreshing aspect to the game. They had it right the first time with RE2R, so I was personally saddened to see how RE3R turned out. 

Below are content or features that original RE3 had, but did not make it to RE3R.
[list]
[*] Lack of branching paths and backtracking. 
[*] Lack of costumes. Original RE3 had a boutique unlock with various types of costumes.
[*] You never enter or explore RPD as Jill. Only as Carlos, which does not make much sense.
[*] No Puzzles and all the safe/locker combos are reused from RE2R. 
[*] Missing the following areas - Clock Tower, City Hall, Park, Newspaper Office, Restaurant, Graveyard/Gravedigger, Dead Factory area (Mind you it was added near the end of the RE3R as a small segment tied into Labs). 
[*] Story progression is extremely fast and a lot of the original story has been changed or does not make sense in RE3R. Area progression and who did what was changed up a little bit. 
[*] Brad was done dirty and died to a zombie bite, rather then getting his head ventilated by Nemesis in front of RPD. 
[*] Missing Mercenaries mode, which was a really fun game mode.
[/list]

[b]3. As a standalone action game with Resident Evil Lore:[/b] As a stand alone game ignoring both view points mentioned above. The game was a fun action packed game and looked graphically amazing. I enjoyed the new take on key enemy types such as Nemesis and the Hunters. However, as a AAA title it still felt very short and the pacing did not feel right to me. I really did feel that the game was on rails per-say and had no real reason to explore or backtrack. Due to the shortness of the game, you get rewarded pretty early on with upgrades and get them in plentiful amounts. 

One thing I do want to add is they did so some things right in my opinion - I liked how they designed Jill and liked some of the voice lines she got. They gave her some sass and spark, I about died at B- Can't Swim part of the game. 

Overall I cannot recommend this game at full price. The game feels like a half-baked DLC overall. It is kinda a shame because the RE engine is an amazing engine. With the amount of reused assets used from RE2R and key features from RE2R cut, in my opinion, it is hard for them to justify the current state of the game. This game could have very easily been way better then what they produced. This game felt really half-baked and rushed. I liked some of the elements they added or redid in this version, but it isn't enough to win me over. 

If you want a action game with some RE lore in it - buy it. 
If you wanted a proper sequel from RE2R - do not buy it.
If you wanted a remake of RE3 that was similar to the original - do not buy it. 
If you want to play the remake and come up with your own opinion - wait till it goes on sale.

Remember when Resident Evil 5 came out and the feelings everyone had when it did? In many ways, this game reminds me of that. When Resident Evil 5 came out, there were complaints about it cause of how it measured up to its then seriously popular predecessor, Resident Evil 4. It was significantly shorter and some of the gameplay changes just weren't up to what everyone had hoped it to be.

This feels about the same.

Resident Evil 2 (REmake2) was an AWESOME game, and it was everything I think most hoped it to be. This game....well, given how there was so much we were hoping for and looking forward to, I think they dropped the ball. This game feels about half the length of REmake2, if not a LITTLE longer than that, and a number of places we remember from the original were cut. There aren't any options that change up how the story progresses (the Live-Choice Selection thing from the original), so the path you go on is the path you go on, no deviation. So to be blunt....I'm pretty disappointed as far as where my expectations were for this.

So why am I giving this a yes? Well....expectations aside, what IS here is pretty darn good, in my opinion.

There are some differences in the pacing compared to the original, such as Nemesis being RIGHT on Jill's tail as soon as the game opens up, but after a bit, it does settle into exploring and trying to find a way to get out of the city. I did like how open the game felt and that while there isn't much "off the beaten path" so to speak, I was rewarded for taking my time to check for things and explore. Yeah, that kinda ends once the train is taken but that happened in the original too. I especially liked that there's more sections to play as Carlos. Given that he was the secondary protagonist of RE3, his section was almost woefully short. Here, he feels more fleshed out as a playable character and I liked that. There were also nods to the previous game in the RPD, which on the one hand was a little silly...but on the other was a pretty cool attempt to tie the games together.

Basically, if you liked the gameplay of REmake2, then you'll like this....it's basically the same, albeit a bit shorter. It IS fun, it IS a nice remake attempt, and I DO love the music, some of which are awesome remixes of the original tunes (honestly, I was pumped when the final battle music against Nemesis swelled up. LOVED it)

My rating: 7/10
What's here is good, so if it's a question of if you'll like that, then no fear. If you liked REmake2, you'll have fun with this since it's more of it. But the reason it doesn't get such better from me is cause it's somewhat lacking in comparison to the original. There's less areas, less monsters, and it's just nearing the final act when you really start digging into it. Granted, I do believe a game should be based on its own merits alone, but given how hyped we all were for this game, I feel this is justified.

It's not RE2make, but I think it's a good game. RE2make was challenging and did a much better part of being a holistically survival horror experience, where this game tends to lean more into the action shooter side a little more (but no so far that it's like RE4-6). 

Pros: Great visuals within the new RE engine. The dodge mechanic in this game is something I really wanted in the RE2make and gives players another option if you're willing to accept extra risk to save ammunition for where it's really needed. Character-wise, they did a great job making Nemesis into the ultimate Tyrant that it's supposed to be. And personally, one big improvement over RE2 as far as post-game goes: [spoiler] Rather than having the S+ rank requirement for unlimited items, the game focuses on a new points based system where completed in game challenges reward points where you can spend them on the unlocks you want. Completing RE2 on hardcore with the S+ rank made infinite weapons incredibly boring because it was clear there was no need for them anymore once you've mastered the game to that point, and I found they became useless after half an hour of play with them. [/spoiler]

Cons: The game is short. RE2make took about 10+ hours to complete on the first playthrough; this game took 4. Unlike RE2make where Mr. X is this omni-present behemoth that can burst through at any moment, Nemesis follow a linear pattern and follows scripted appearances. I relate it with Dead Space; sometimes the fear of not knowing whether something is coming or not, is better than the fear of something that's right in front of you. Nemesis is an awesome tyrant, but because of the forced linear pathing, it loses a bit of its luster. 

Overall, RE3 is a fun game. If you don't go into it expecting another RE2, chances are that you'll enjoy it.

Side Note: I sincerely hope for the devs to work on a Code Veronica remake in this engine, keeping the same style as RE2. I think there's a lot of potential for that game to shine in the new engine.

TLDR: Is this a good game? Yes.    Is it a good Resident Evil game: Yes.      Is it a good remake of Resident Evil 3: Nemesis?........................Not really. 

Not compared to what RE2R was to the original, at least. Sure, there were some changes made for RE2R compared to the original, but they were very minor and on the whole it was a faithful modern adaption of the classic. Everything that was seminal for story and layout was kept. Not so much the case with this one. Here's some good and bad from my perspective:

Good
+some unique features from the og are present(dodging zombies, explosive barrels)
+character models are gorgeous and expressive, as expected. Everyone looks great, particularly Jill and Nemesis.
+the areas that are present are decently atmospheric(however don't give me the same vibes as the og)
+gameplay is a satisfying extension of RE2R
+another win for the legacy of Jill Valentine, resident badass.

Bad
-Nemesis, as a game-presence/mechanic, was straight up neutered. Only shows up for scripted moments, cutscenes, and parts that bottleneck you into progressing to the next section(no backtrack).
-Typewriters every other room it felt like, on top of autosave even on hardcore
-no ink ribbons on hardcore
-Very short. I purposely drew out my gameplay to elongate the experience on hardcore mode. Still super short, could prob speedrun it in a couple hours.
-the areas that add variety to the cityscape are nice, but shockingly short lived. In fact, you won't have to stay anywhere long enough to start wishing you could leave the oppressive atmosphere of said area.
-many story beats are different that either change memorable parts from the original or just omit them entirely.(Brad/Nemesis in front of the RPD, raccoon park, clocktower, etc)
-even with all the scripted Nemesis encounters, they couldn't bother with the timed choice events from the og.
-did I mention this is basically a hyper-condensed rewrite of the og?

Starting with what stinks, this game does not capture the soul of the Playstation original. At first I thought the intro to Nem in this one was sweet, until I saw how they handled Brad in this one. After beating it, the easiest way to put into words what's missing(aside from entire sections) is one important feeling always present in the og:  dread.

The build up to Nem in the original was great, and the dread/tension stays for the whole game. In this one, the game proves rather quickly he's not always stalking you. I believe there's one part where you can choose to make it hard on yourself by allowing Nem to chase you throughout the city map(super small), but that's only if you're trying to put off moving on to the next part. Other than that every encounter is a one and done. The demo section is what I'm talking about(again, if you're smart you can just straight up do everything you need, trigger him, then move on). So yeah, Nemesis is more of a boss fight/cutscene setpiece, not a gameplay mechanic/presence.

The cut sections speak for themselves if you've played the og. I hated Raccoon Park, and was looking forward to hating it all over again. It's completely removed. 
The clock tower was a tense section as well, almost entirely removed, but somewhat present only as a background kind of 'nod'. 
There are parts that were stretched out, and one might say they compensate for the cut areas. Not at all. They were repurposed areas from RE2R, and don't lend to giving RE3R the identity that makes it stand on it's own as a memorable RE experience. This game is very actiony, which is fine, but the atmosphere would have been better if the game wasn't constantly pushing you into the next area before you even know what's up. 

I gave it a thumbs up because it's still fun, feels and looks good, gives me another Jill campaign and is run on an amazing engine. I wish I could give it a thumbs down as a remake, however.

This is less a remake of RE3 and more a sequel to RE2R, if you get what I mean. A similar yet different beast than RE2R.

Pros:
-Game looks great and feels great to play. RE2R veterans should feel at home, mostly.
- Escape items mechanic has been replaced with a dodge mechanic. Fiddly, but feels good when you do it right.
- An interestingly different, albeit underutilized pursuing enemy. Nemesis is different from the Tyrant (Mr. X) in RE2R. He doesn't wander around and he's a lot faster, meaning you generally have to escape from him or beat him down - either because the game tells you to, or to get optional rewards like gun parts and ammo.
- A reasonably long campaign. Shorter than RE2R considering that there's no "side B" other than doing harder game modes. But it does add more difficulties, harder ones over the initial "hard" mode, if you're into that. 

Cons:
- Nemesis is pretty cool at first, but he doesn't really last long. Like him as a cool trenchcoat-wearing pursuer? Better enjoy that while it lasts.
- A nice homage to the RPD from the previous game that is unfortunately rather short. Not that it's unexpected, I believe it's like that in the original game too, but it felt weird seeing it again but with doors that the game never acknowledged as actually being doors at all, rather than being "locked".
- Weird moments here and there when opening a door causes a cutscene to play out that moves you into a new area with no way to return to the previous one. Save often and loot everything you can as you go, or you might find an unexpected cutscene decided to move you to the next area or even the next map with no way to go back.
- Limited costumes. I enjoyed these a lot in RE2R, giving Leon and Claire new looks for playing the game and in cutscenes. So far though there's only preorder costumes and one additional costume for Jill when you beat the game for the first time and unlock it.

Overall: a different flavor than that of RE2R. If you enjoyed the previous game, you'll probably like this one - but it does depend on how you feel about the various changes made, and how much they matter to you. To me, they didn't matter much - I enjoyed my run and will definitely be going back to do a harder run soon.

After last year's stellar Resident Evil 2 remake, I was excited to finally get the opportunity to play through Resident Evil 3 in what I hoped was that same love and care. And I think this game provides it.... mostly.

Pros:
Combat is stellar in this game, using the already great combat mechanics from Resident Evil 2, this game expands on that by providing a perfect dodge mechanic, which when executed, also gives you an opportunity to retaliate and shoot at an enemy's weak spot, or dodge and uppercut with a melee weapon. This provides interesting opportunities where you can potentially avoid contact with any enemy.

Jill is a wonderful character, foiling very well with Carlos, and the writing overall is an extremely fun level of camp-ness without feeling underproduced, like scenes in the original version of Resident Evil.

Presentation wise, the game is incredible to look at, and the enemies have the right amount of disgusting detail put into them.

Nemesis is a fun antagonist, and the boss fight's against it's various forms are all extremely well done, and bring new mechanics with each of them.

Each area doesn't overstay it's welcome. You get just enough time to explore each area and taking the time to find every secret.

What I didn't like.

I do echo the sentiments of people who agree that this game feels short. I think what's here is wonderful, but it does feel like there's an area we're missing. I could debate that this game, with the clock tower area brought back in, can rival Resident Evil 2 remake's single playthrough. 

While I'm still planning on playing through this game again on the harder difficulties, I do think not having the dynamic choices leads to a lack of replayability for the game, which could turn people off.

Finale
Overall, I thought this game was wonderful.  However, I don't think everyone will share my sentiments. Compared to the previous game, which I could recommend easily at full price, I do think it's the right call to wait for a sale for this game. At 30 dollars, I think this game is an absolute steal.

So Resident Evil 3 is was the only mainline RE game I never beat as a kid. I don't even remember why, but I just never beat it. I finished every other one since, so I was very excited when this was confirmed to be coming out so soon after the incredible RE2 Remake.

Having only finished the campaign once, (I'll most likely play through again on a higher difficulty soon,) I can safely say that this remake is pretty on par with the original RE 3. Which is good and also kinda bad.

So for anyone that doesn't know, the original RE3 was basically an asset flip because of how quickly CAPCOM was demanding a sequel after the major success of RE2 in 1998, RE3 coming out in 1999, Because of this, a lot of the content had to be scaled back, parts were bloated to increase the runtime, etc. 

The game has it's fans and sold very well, but my main problem with this is: why the ♥♥♥♥ would CAPCOM do the same thing twice?
What could have been the definitive Resident Evil 3 experience ends up being a fairly straightforward retread of the original. Which, if you couldn't tell by my play time, does not make for a very long game. Which is fine, I just wish Capcom had left this in the oven another year and really made something groundbreaking like their previous efforts. 

2 major complaints I want address though: 

-Nemesis isn't very scary at all. There are one, maybe two times in the whole game where him chasing you isn't scripted, once you realize this, he really isn't much of a threat. With all the hype Capcom put on the this guy being the Mr. X 2.0, it just blows that he's not that at all except for a few shining moments in the early game. Oh, and I'm not sure what they were talking about him being able to chase you into saferooms, but I never had this happen to me once. Maybe it's on a higher difficulty and I'm talking out of my ass. Moving on, 

-People saying this game is very action orientated: no ♥♥♥♥, that was what the original was like too. I don't know why people keep saying this about the remake, but frankly a stupid ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ complaint if you know literally anything about the original. 

Overall, if you're a hardcore RE fan, you've probably already bought this honestly. But I really can't recommend this game to anyone other than them. You probably won't get a lot out of it, and the 60$ price point is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥' steep for a game you can finish in an afternoon. RE Resistance is fun and nice added bonus for picking up the game, but it suffers from a lot of problem Dead By Daylight suffered from (Looking at you hosts with 9000000 McDonalds Wifi ping,) and frankly it can turn into a bit of broken cluster ♥♥♥♥ at times. 

I do want to be clear, I did enjoy this game a lot, and I'm glad I finally got to finish it, but I also can't help but feel disappointed from the very rushed feeling experience. I don't know, maybe that's just Resident Evil 3 in a nutshell and I'm just missing the point, but after finishing the game, I felt like I only ate half my dinner and was still hungry for more.

TL;DR: Recommended on sale, but not recommended at $60. I really liked it, but I didn't $60 like it. Read on for details. 

In a perfect world this game would've been sold as a giant expansion pack DLC for last year's Resident Evil Remake 2. It feels perfect for that role, but it works less well as a standalone $60 game. I really enjoyed it, but I also see it as a glorified DLC that could've easily been sold at $40 for REmake 2. The additional pricing probably has something to do with Resident Evil Resistance, the multiplayer mode that's being bundled alongside it. 

The shooting and action gameplay is very well done in this game. It feels polished and satisfying, there's a reasonable amount of challenge here, especially with the "Hardcore" difficulty, which should really be renamed to "Normal" as it's well balanced. The visuals and sound work are beautiful also, just like in REmake 2. The engine really shows its quality here. 

This is a lot like a Universal Studios theme park ride. The action is terrific, if too scripted and linear at times, but the real meat of the gameplay involving puzzles, exploration, and hunting for key items to open up new areas is too sparse. You get to go to several interesting areas, but they don't last very long because they aren't very large relative to the areas in REmake 2, or even the original Resident Evil 3. The content that you get to play is excellent, but all of the major areas of the game could've used a few extra rooms and an additional puzzle or two so you aren't constantly jumping into new areas just as the last location was really getting good. 

I really liked the original Resident Evil 3 and I played it about a month before this released. I'm not the kind of person who really cares that much about whether my nostalgia strings are pulled, I'm open to new ideas and creative takes on old favorites. I just want the new creation to be good and enjoyable for what it is, if nothing else. There's a lot of stuff in RE3 that's not present in this remake, but there's also a lot of new stuff that's awesome. Other reviews have already spoiled these details so I'm not going to get into specifics, but I will emphasize that the remake's main issue for me isn't that certain old locales, items, and enemies aren't given 1:1 perfect recreation here. 

The problem I have is that what REmake 3 does do very well is still missing a lot of its potential, namely the classic Resident Evil exploration, puzzles, and key item hunting stuff I mentioned above. The action/shooting gameplay and audio/visual presentation is excellent, and there's plenty of it, but the rest is lacking a bit. Even if all of the original game's areas were here, unless they were the same size as they were back then, and had some puzzles and key item hunting to pace them out properly, the game would probably still seem lacking even with their inclusion. 

I don't need my nostalgia fed, I have the original RE3 for that. I did want to see this remake achieve it's full potential, though. It comes close, but in its current form it plays like a $40 DLC for REmake 2 that gives us a Jill/Nemesis scenario to go alongside Leon and Claire's scenarios. If you view it in that light, it's one of the best DLCs/expansions ever made for any game. If you focus on the $60 price tag and think of it as a full standalone title, it's still good, but it falls short of what could be. 

Wait for a sale, think of it as a standalone RE3 DLC for REmake 2, and you'll be good to go. $40-$45 seems good to me, and that's what I'd like to have bought it at.

I'd like to start off by saying that I never played the original when it came out, so please take my review with that in mind!

From the opening moments of this game, you can tell this isn't a standard Resident Evil game. The opening is brash, in your face and heart pumping. From there, the game continues that breakneck pace all the way up until its relatively quick conclusion. From start to finish I genuinely adored this game, while also acknowledging it is missing some of the things that make Resident Evil, Resident Evil. For a comparison, this game is definitely more in the vein of Resident Evil 4 than 2 and that's ok, because for Resident Evil 3, it just works. With that out of the way, let's talk about what works!

Pros:

- Graphics

This game SHINES in the RE engine and I must say it's one of the most beautiful games you can get. There's gritty realism that really makes you feel like you're IN Raccoon City

- Story

I felt this Resident Evil had a tight, concise story that had some great behind the scenes elements for RE2 and set us up for what I can only assume would be a Code Veronica remake. I actually think the world building in RE3 was much more developed than RE2.

- Gunplay and unlocks

I'm putting these together for a few reasons. The weapons in this game are very much mostly heavy weapons, which makes you feel stronger heading into the late game and sort of takes away from the "scariness". I think the unlockable weapons is such a nice touch and allows you to spend points how you see fit to unlock what you like. This is a great feature and I wish RE2 had this!

Cons

- Story length

While I said the story was a strength, I must admit it was painfully short. I tried taking as much time as I could, but my first playthrough clocked in at just over 3 hours and it felt like nothing I could do would delay the speed at which I was approaching the end.

- Linear design

While this ADDS to the conciseness of the story, I fear that this game lacks what the original Resident Evils have: multiple paths and hidden secrets. For the most part, you can spend a maximum of 2 hours in the first third of the game exploring before it puts you into a linear path for the rest of the game. This was the biggest letdown for me.

All-in-all, I felt this was a strong remake that plays fantastically well with infinite replay ability based off the sheer "fun" factor. I felt so much joy running through the game and the world. I just wish there was MORE of it.

After the popularity of the Resident Evil 2 remake, people were eagerly waiting for a remake of 3, particularly since the former had some hints about the latter's possible development. It was later revealed that a remake of RE3 was indeed in production much to the fans rejoicing. Now it's finally released, and there seems to be a lot of backlash towards the game, based on what's clearly a bunch of unreasonable expectations, likely a product of the quality of its predecessor.

So I'm going to go into detail about the game as I respond to the game's major criticisms, many of which I personally believe to be unwarranted.

[b]1) The game is too short! - [/b] While it's true that the [i]campaign[/i] is short, this isn't necessarily a negative thing. Much too importance is given to a game's length, as it by itself and with no other context was a synonim of quality. True, you can squeeze 40 hours out of an open world game, but you'll spend 20-30 of those hours just driving from place to place, a couple more hours hunting hundreds of useless collectibles and the remaining playtime will be done in nearly identical missions. RE3 is short, sure, but there's [i]no padding[/i]. The campaign is carefully designed for a tight experience that never overstays its welcome, and there's a lot of visual storytelling that goes in the level design. Also, I need to note, the original RE3 was short too. In fact, if we compare both the old RE2 with the old RE3 and do the same for the new ones, the old one was shorter in comparison.
[b]2) The game is too linear! - [/b] This is a relatively fair criticism. RE2 was linear too, but since the majority of the first act is set in the police station and you can more or less go around the place in any order until you find a roadblock it seems a bit more open. RE3 is actually the same, and in fact it has two open areas, but they're much shorter than the RPD, even combined, and too far from each other, while in the rest of the game you're constantly changing scenery, so it [i]looks[/i] more linear than RE2. Another reason is that there are a couple of features removed from the original: differing paths and alternate endings. The differing paths were ocassional quick time prompts that allowed you to choose one of two actions and that would affect how you dealt with a threat, and might cause you to do better or worse. They were nice breaks from normal gameplay that allowed for some extra minimal replay value, and I am a bit sad that they're gone. I don't care about the alternate endings. They're pointless in a continuing series like this one that's going to pick only one as canon anyway.
[b]3) Not enough puzzles! - [/b] This one seems like a silly complaint. Resident Evil puzzles usually come in three varieties: click a bunch of buttons until you happen into the solution, wait until you find the file that has the combination and enter it or find the colored object to insert into the colored slot. They were never anything special and there was no penalty for failing. You can claim they add some flair to these games, but this isn't Professor Layton. Lack of puzzles isn't really something worth talking about, and it feels like people are just looking for reasons to complain.
[b]4) Nemesis isn't random enough! - [/b] This is entirely true. Save for his pursuit of you in the first open area (incidentally, the one from the demo), every other Nemesis encounter is scripted. This wasn't like that in the original game, where besides the scripted appearances, Nemesis could just show up at any time while you were exploring. But the reality of the situation is not as simple as laziness. If you check reviews for the previous game, even between those who loved it to death there was one clear complaint: that Mr. X was too annoying. Sure, it was scary at first, but then it started to become a problem when you just wanted to grab an item and you couldn't shake him off, or you wanted to reach a place and he kept popping up. The way this game handles Nemesis seems to have born from both an intention to address this complaint and a desire to keep Nemesis different from Mr. X, who was already feeling too similar to the old Nemesis. So instead of making him random they simply chose to make every one of his encounters different, so they're all more memorable. I think it's a perfectly fair trade-off, and people should stop pretending this game is removing stuff without adding anything in its place.
[b]5) Too many locations removed! - [/b] While it's true that the game removes a couple of locations from the original, it also adds a couple more and expands on the other ones. It seems like, again, people are just looking for reasons to complain.
[b]6) Too many enemies removed! - [/b] Sure, the Grave Digger is no more, and neither are his offspring, but in their place we have an extra couple of boss fights with Nemesis (which, again, are always different) and the more prevalent and powerful blind zombies. There are no crows, but those were already gone from RE2 and no one complained. Giant spiders are no longer here, but we have Lickers making a comeback. People keep harping on what's lost and very conveniently forgetting to include the stuff that replaced it.
[b]7) The game is too action oriented! - [/b] I mean, sure, but that was also the case for the original. RE3 was always the more action-based game in the classic series.
[b]8) Less dismemberment! - [/b] This is outright false. Zombies can be dismembered as easily as in the previous game.
[b]9) No Mercenaries mode! - [/b] This is correct. Instead of Mercenaries we have Resistance, which is a multiplayer mode. I haven't tried this mode, so I can't speak of its quality, but if you don't care for multiplayer you're likely to be upset.

I have no problem with people being critical of a game. I certainly am, all the time. But criticism has to be [i]fair[/i]. Taking the time to attack this game for stuff that's missing while entirely ignoring all the new stuff that's replacing it is silly. Criticizing it for stuff that was already part of the original or the previous remake while those weren't criticized for it is unfair. And you can call this game many things, but "lazy cash grab" isn't one of them.
