Hear me out, [b]while I did have fun playing this game[/b] and will likely do more playthroughs for achievements and unlocks, I cannot recommend this as a remake to resident evil 3. This is not a step back from RE2. This is a series of backflips and a bad sign of things to come for the series. Capcom is starting to make the same mistakes as they did leading up to re6 already.

If you're expected RE2 remake quality, avoid. If you're a big fan of RE3 and yearn for a remake, avoid.

First, there is so much cut from the original. So many locations are gone, and practically every puzzle is gone except for one at the end of the game. No, putting jewels in that apparatus in the train station isn't a puzzle. Even key locations like the clock tower are gone, and a decent amount of the original took place in the clock tower. But now it's just a backdrop for an encounter.

The game is surprisingly linear. Areas are small, and you're typically only moving in a single direction. There are a few times where you have to go back and forth between a couple of places, but even then there are times where certain paths are cut off forcing you to take a certain path. You're only in an area for a short period of time before you're moved somewhere else. 

It feels too action oriented. I get Jill is experienced, but I'm given abundant ammo and healing items to the point where I struggled to pick up key items because of all of the healing items i had. I was playing on Hardcore too, and even that gave me unlimited saves and checkpoints. After beating it, another difficulty unlocked which makes enemies more aggressive, and there's one after that. So maybe fans can get the experience they wanted, but only after you've done a few playthroughs and all of the key events are revealed. I could gun down every zombie without worrying about resources. There's also way too many cutscenes, many of which feature QTEs for some reason. While this part seems nitpicky, I can't help but get reminded of the games that tanked the reputation of the series.

Nemesis is wasted. He is far too scripted and any sense of threat from him was immediately gone when I realised this. He only appears in certain story segments and sure, while he pursues you until the next one, he is easy to avoid and easy to take down. Despite Mr X being a pushover in RE2, he was terrifying the first time he appeared and I remember not leaving the saferoom for about 10 minutes because I thought he was nearby and would wreck me. While he is scripted in the original, it's been over 20 years now and RE2 got it right. I think there was only one occasion where he caught me by surprise because I could just *feel* like he was going to pop up in these convenient corridors and I was right almost every time.

Despite this, I still had fun. It's a good game in its own way, so if you don't care about a faithful remake or just need more resident evil then I think you could be happy buying this, even with its incredibly short game time (4h 57m on hardcore, first playthrough, and checking every room) However there is no love for the original here, and signs in this game point to Capcom making the same mistakes that led to RE6 and the series being a laughing stock.

Overall, it was an enjoyable game. I liked being able to play another Resident Evil zombie-slayer puzzle-solver wanna-be-a-hero game. If you're looking for that simple, short and fun Resident Evil playthrough, then this game might be right for you. It has a followable plot with cool characters and personal interactions. It even references back to previous games. Stop reading here if that's for you. If not, let's talk about what could be better. This game wasn't nearly as good as RE2 or RE7, unfortunately. The repeated boss interactions lacked thrill and variety as it was the same chase every time. You hardly need to conserve ammunition or health supplies (I played Standard mode). Also, the puzzles were fairly easy to solve. Even the side ones and locks that you keep in the back of your head weren't very tasking. I will concede: Once you know how to play a Resident Evil game, you know what you're getting into when you come across a gem or a familiar area or any puzzle for that matter. On top of the length (which was too short), it would have been nice to get to know our side character a little more. Dynamic duo action was lacking here and the chemistry and build-up between the two characters wasn't too interesting either. Lastly, I find the plot to have severely lacked in information, cutscenes, and, well, STORY. It's the same concept the whole way through and the background that is given is too shallow for players to become wrapped up in. [b]TLDR[/b]/What could improve this game: varying styles of boss battles/interactions (such as the alternate ways to DEFEAT the boss as seen in RE2 or the different greater bosses as in RE7), more in-depth puzzles (there was a lockpick at one point and it would have been more interesting to scatter picks and let players learn to use them, break them, and limit them instead of letting it be a basic key), and a longer; deeper story (such as taking time for players to form bonds to the main and side characters and providing a thoroughly compelling Umbrella activity/monster/goal to surmount). Hopefully future games can learn from these mistakes and continue provide fans with the awesome, thrilling Resident Evil experience that they deserve. Nevertheless, I, myself, am a simple gamer who just appreciates a little more. I had fun being the hero and absorbing all of the plot details that I could. I sincerely hope that you do, too.

I was extremely excited for this game but I cannot deny it is a disappointment. Longtime resident evil fan, played all the games except 6, loved the RE2 remake despite some issues. The RE2 remake honestly made me FEEL something. The something was palpable adrenaline and terror. I thought it was incredible. When I heard they were remaking the 3rd game too, I was ecstatic. I could hardly imagine that same tension of being hunted blown up to the proportions of Raccoon City. Sadly, this is not what you get in this game.
The city has been DRASTICALLY cut down. More than half of the city locations are straight up gone. After a QTE-laden intro where you run away from Nemesis, you get to the demo. The tram-car mission. If you've played the original you might be thinking "That's not right, a bunch of stuff happens before the tram car." Not anymore. What was in the demo is essentially the entirety of the city you get to explore. No restaurant, no gas station, no pharmacy (there is a pharmacy but it's just a tiny nondescript building, not the whole sequence it used to be), no bar (it exists only in a brief cutscene), no weird mayor statue or gate puzzles, no newspaper building, no clocktower (it's seen in the distance but never visited), no park (and by extension no graveyard), and no maze of streets to get lost in. You get just that area in the demo. Then it's straight to the substation, restart the subway, and leave. You know what all those city exploration sections were replaced with? A. BRAND. NEW. SEWER LEVEL. Everyone's favorite environment. Not the eye-catching, beautifully neon Raccoon city streets, but the bleak, grey sewers. The sewers played a VERY BRIEF role in the original during the first encounter with the worm boss (which is also gone), but in the remake it is its whole own section, congratulations. 
I kept waiting and waiting thinking "Oh maybe they just mixed up the order of events like they did a bit in RE2 to make it more exciting for old players, I'm sure these locations will pop up soon". They don't.
NEXT UP, PACING. Because there's so much less content, the pacing is VERY FAST. This doesn't allow any tension to build up which is a terrible misstep. The RE2 remake left me with heart palpitations. Slowly exploring the police department, you build up an intimate knowledge of the layout of the station which then becomes your only weapon against Mr.X. You have to navigate using your judgment and memory of where you left enemies alive to find the best path. It is SO. SATISFYING. SO TENSE. Well executed and properly built up, giving the station itself so much life. I was expecting the same level of graceful execution in Raccoon City. Having to memorize streets and routes in a bigger area to escape an even more fearsome enemy. The City itself SHOULD have been its own character, like the station. Instead you get that one section. And instead of a continuous, heart-wrenching chase like Mr.X gave, you get a handful of chase SEQUENCES which are infinitely less scary. Just hold the run button. Wow. Incredible. The only time there is an active chase is during the sequence that was in the demo. Such a disappointment. Also you get TWO hip pouches and a shotgun upgrade WAY TOO fast. But I guess it had to be fast since there isn't much game to stretch out the upgrades over.
That chase as well was disappointing because of my next point, the characterization of Nemesis. Nemesis looks goofy. He basically teleports to where you are during the chase. Rather than being stalked by a menacing presence, he just poofs to your location no matter what. When he arrives he either does a superhero landing or this skater slide into the area that looks so silly, especially when he was behind you two seconds ago. Really breaks the immersion. Sometimes he'll shoot out his tentacle and spiderman swing away, on god. Also thought it was poor choice to introduce him at the VERY start. Would have preferred him to be built up more. Like, in a monster movie, you don't SHOW the monster right away, it takes away a lot of the mystery. I liked the idea of his face being covered at first, but he loses that during the intro very fast. 
Next, DIFFICULTY. It is wildly easy. Upsettingly easy. I played on Hardcore and the first thing I notice is that they've removed ink ribbons. Some people online don't have a problem with this because they argue, "it was just a waste of an inventory slot," but I'd object. Ink ribbons inherently alter the gameplay experience. When you have unlimited saves, it is so easy to save the game, go out and do one little thing, then come back and save again. You can play very safely without consequence. When ink ribbons are introduced, saves become much more significant. The more you do after saving, the riskier things become because you could die and lose a lot of progress. This can add so much more tension when you're arguing whether or not to save before or after you go out to grab some bit of ammo you missed or something. If you use the save, you're going to have to go collect that ammo again everytime you load from there. If you don't save, you risk dying on the way and losing a lot of progress. It just adds more decision making, which in turn adds more stress and tension. Oh also there are checkpoints. So if you die you might not even restart from your save. What's even the point, man. 
Next, there were just not enough  zombies for me to ever feel in danger. Not once did I feel like I might not be able to make it. While the original had a lot of tight alleys that were PACKED with zombies, here most of the zombies are wandering around large open spaces,  making them easy to avoid. If there is one in a tight space, you always have more than enough ammo/healing items to deal with it. I don't get why they wouldn't make better use of this fancy engine. If you're going to have these big open spaces, why not render in a mob of 25 zombies or something. Make something threatening that requires me to actually reevaluate my routes. If there ever is a large crowd of zombies, there is always a red barrel or generator to shoot, making quick work of them.
Unlimited saves, checkpoints, barely any zombies, the nemesis encounters are mostly QTE run sequences. 
Just. How do you mess up this bad. 
The game feels like it barely carries any of the weight that RE2 did, feels more like a DLC for RE2 than its own game. 
OH AND ANOTHER THING, this really got me. They misused the most iconic line from the original so badly. 
You know the one. "You want stars? I'll give you stars". That line, originally spoken by Jill after blasting Nemesis apart with a railgun, as she deals the final blow by shooting him in the face. It's cheesy, but man it felt so good in the original. It's triumphant and really seals your victory over this unkillable monster. 
VERSUS
Jill returns to the subway because it's ready to go, but Nemesis is chasing her. She realizes if she boards the subway, she'll endanger the other passengers, so she sprints off in another direction. This begins another heavily scripted chase scene with Nemesis. When the chase starts, he's right behind you so it's very easy for him to land a hit. As the chase starts, she delivers the line. Why? It just. It makes no sense. It felt even more out of place considering I was already limping when the chase started and after Jill said it Nemesis just decked her in the back of the head. So silly, so out of place.
I fear the devs rushed this A LOT. Maybe to strike while the iron was hot since everyone loved RE2. Or they were forced to tack on that multiplayer mode nobody asked for and that stole time from developing the real game.  It could have benefited massively from another year in development. Play it if you've been waiting for it, but be prepared for disappointment if you're a fan.
Things I did like: What's LEFT of the city looks beautiful. Jill and Carlos have great characterizations. The final blow on Nemesis was satisfying. That's all.

This hurts me, because I really wanted to like this game but it fails in almost every possible way. It's a bad remake, it's a bad Resident Evil, it's a bad sequel to RE2 remake and it's a bad game in general. 

Bad Remake:

They didn't respect a single thing from the original RE3. RE2r took some liberties, but at least hit a lot of the right spots of what made RE2 RE2. That's not the case of RE3r. It doesn't care for recreating a single place or moment from the game it's supposedly recreating. Classic epic moments are changed for rushed and generic cinematics, including the iconic death of a character at the entrance of the R.P.D. and the introduction of certain BOW. 

The new appareance for the characters is generic and boring, Capcom used yo have some of the best character designers back then. These ones are tame and bland. 

They even used the "classic" RE3 outfits of the characters as pre-order only bait. Only to find out at last moment they went prude with Jill's skirt, changing it for a skort, a ugly combination of a skirt with shorts. Carlos Oliveira's classic is even worse, limiting itself to only a bad hair change that looks more like a mod made in five minutes. 

But the worse offenders of this point are the locations. I can't understand how they did it, but they managed to avoid including almost all of the scenarios of the original. No restaurant, diary, clock tower, park, graveyard, gas station, park, among others of the classic places. That wouldn't be bad if they were replaced for scenaios that are equally as cool but... I'll enter into more details about this later.

Also one of the things that made RE3 so interesting; the multiple options and paths that change the story or even enemies that appear later on, all that is gone too. This used to influence on where Nemesis appears, the character you'll encounter, and the parts of the story that will be revealed to you first.

And the cherry on the cake, no "Mercenaries" mode. RE3 was the one that introduced this classic mode into the franchise. One of the most enterteining parts of the original game and future entries is no doubt the "Mercenaries" where you have to survive and earn rewards for the main game, having different levels of chalenges depending of the character you choose. This was an evolution of the "4th Survivor" mode introduced in RE2, and it's a shame is nowhere to be found.

They gave us RE: Resistance instead. An online game nobody asked for and no one would have buy if it were on it's own.

Bad Resident Evil:

Theres's little to no exploration in this game, eveything is a bunch of hallways that most of the time are one way only. No atmosphere nor tension. 

The puzzles... there are almost none, except for one or two very easy and not very imaginative ones. 

The survival horror is non existant, there are plenty of ammo even in the hard difficulties, so there's not inventory management either. 

The evading move is simply broken, making almost no enemy a threat, specially Nemesis, who telegraphs his attacks with entire seconds of anticipation.

No ink ribbons are needed, to save the game, and the game is full of checkpoints, so there's no fear of dying at any moment.

Bad sequel to RE2r.

This is simply a downgrade from the previous entry. The gore mechanics and ragdolls of the corpses are gone. If a limb of any enemy is cut, that limb simply dissapears instead of falling to the ground.

RE2r had plenty of the things people like about a Resident Evil, puzzles, exploration, survival and armosphere. None of those things can be found in RE3r, you'll only run forward, sometimes shoot, sometimes evade, and repeat. 

The only good things this takes from RE2 remake are the graphic assets it recycled. RE3r uses the same zombie models and animations from the previous game, so there's no new designs. It even adds an annoying sewer level that was not in the original RE3, nothing but a bunch of hallways  with enemies that kill you in one hit, this scenario was made only to have a lazy excuse to rip off the sewers graphics from the previous game and to avoid creating some new assets. The lack of imagination put in this is simply astounding.

Bad game in general:

It doesn't recreate the classic RE3 but It doesn't create anything new or interesting either. Only a bunch of boring hallways to shoot or run from monsters once in a while, and there are plenty of games that do this better, including it's predecesor. 

At the end, if it was on it's own, it'd be mediocre at best, but as a Resident Evil, it's among the worst entries I've played, even worse than some of the black sheeps in the franchise.

The Good:

He shoulder charges and can actually counter attack some times if you time it perfectly, knocking enemies down allowing you to reload or take some shots. Jill's dodge doesn't have offensive capabilities, but it will slow down time depending on the situation, allowing you to line up that perfect shot.

Gun variety stays true to the original, pretty much. I can't remember if Jill had a revolver or a deagle in the original. Either way, she does have an identical weapon selection. Handcannon type pistol, normal pistol, shotgun, and the grenade launcher.

A new addition in this game, is the point system. I haven't really gotten to spending any points yet, but these are used to unlock things, much like RE6's system. You don't have to collect points in game though, they're awarded to you for achieving certain feats in the game. In RE2, feats like these would unlock things like character art and models in the model viewer. This time around, these feats also net you points, allowing you to unlock things like costumes, infinite weapons, alternate pistols, extra inventory pouches, defensive buff coins, etc. 

The Bad:

They changed the inventory management for whatever stupid reason. In RE2, you could pick up items and combine them all in one motion. Not here. Ugh, this one irritated me. Now, instead of being able to combine herbs when picking one up, it will force you to pick it up, then go back to the inventory screen just to do that. I hate it. Picking up items feels clunky in this game, in that if you don't have an item similar, there's like a 2 second delay going from the pick up, to actually seeing it in your inventory. The only time this doesn't happen, is for example, if you have a stack of ammo already in place. It will allow you to just pick them up without seeing the inventory screen. New items seem to always trigger the menu delay. 

YAY! Remember when the knife was actually good? Yeah, well it's back to it's former glory...........of being absolutely terrible. Now one could argue, it might have been a little too strong in RE2, and no one would contest that. They nerfed it a little too much imo, especially now that zombies can quickly attack you as they get up. You have to time your slices now, and get ready to get out of there when the zombie readies for the attack. You will NOT be using this on any boss either, nor anything outside of a zombie. At least the knife had it's glory of not being total crap at least for one game.

Speaking of the knife, sub-weapons have also been nerfed. Things like the knife, grenades, and flashes are all categorized as primary weapons. This one hurt me as well. You no longer can use these to escape grabs and they take up 1 of the 4 weapon slots you have available to you. I don't understand this one to be honest. They went through all that trouble to include it in RE2 only to completely remove it from this game. My guess is, "they already have a dodge, so lets take this away." 

Some set pieces have been completely cut from the game. The clocktower section is gone and so is the worm fight, those are just the ones I can remember from the original. There could be more. Kind of a bummer tbh, I thought the clocktower was kind of iconic in this game. The worm fight, I ain't upset with. It was a filler part of the game anyways, and the boss itself is really corny and was really easy to get past.

Carlos' section, ugh. His assault rifle, isn't made for hunters. I can't recall their full name, but they're not the ones who can eat you. They're the ones with the claws. These things are on crack in this game. Super fast, can OSK, and they now have a weak spot after you shoot them in the head a bit. This is where my problem is. Carlos' AR is very weak against them otherwise, and the way they move it's pretty hard to hit them in the head. I died so many times to these things, I got very frustrated. Add in the fact the hospital is VERY CQC oriented, you will have a bad time against these the first couple of times, especially if you don't have grenades available. I must have gotten OSK'd about 5 times in that section in my first run on standard. Jill's shotgun is so much better at killing these things.

The UI is basically unchanged from 2. It doesn't bother me too much, but it would've been nice to see something fresh here.

Nowhere near enough depth as RE2. RE2 has 4 different playthroughs, this game has 1. That's enough said. I don't know how much replayability this game will have in the long run unless they plan on releasing some sort of DLC. Based on Capcom's track record, this probably will be it unless they choose to add another "Tofu" type speedrunning DLC. God I hope they don't add that. I will add that the game plays very differently on the unlockable difficulties, Nightmare and Inferno. Enemies are more aggressive, which seemingly makes dodging easier for whatever reason. Easier difficulties, the dodge seems less consistent. Enemy spawns also change on the harder difficulties. Example, say you know a zombie spawns in a certain location. On harder difficulties, that enemy will change from a zombie to say a Parasite version, or even a licker or something. Enemy spawn total increases slightly here as well. 

The multiplayer that come along with it most likely means, this is it for the main game, and by most accounts the multiplayer game leaves a lot to be desired. I doubt I will touch the multiplayer game, but I'm definitely gonna play this game for as long as it keeps me attached.

In short, it's a good game, but much like most sequels I don't think this game will match the gem that is RE2, much like the originals back in the day. Still worth every penny, you can feel confident in your purchase.

EDIT (Final Word): So I have roughly 40 hours on this game already, and can consistently beat it under an hour and a half, along with having every achievement and every shop item. That time is without legit speedrunning it, grabbing everything. I beat Nightmare in an hour and 45 mins the first time through, while getting an S on it straight away. Same thing for Inferno. The modes add a little replayability, but if you're not a professional speedrunner, I can see plenty of people not even playing those two difficulties and getting bored of the game faster. Still a good game imo, just not what RE2 was when it comes to replayability.

This bums me out more than anything to say, but I personally cannot recommend this game at its current price unless you are more interested in Resistance than the actual remake itself.

I played the demo and thought it was FANTASTIC. I really liked the way the game felt (and still do, for the most part). I couldn't wait to get into the full game. RE3 is the game I'm least knowledgeable about, so I was really excited to see it from an updated perspective. But there are so many story elements straight up missing from this game. I won’t go into excruciating detail here as there is already another review with a huge list of all the missing content. But unfortunately all that we are left with feels like a bunch of hastily stitched together set piece battles with one or two branching pathways thrown in to simulate depth.

I don’t mind the action-oriented gameplay, I don’t mind certain pieces being omitted, but I beat this game in under four hours on my first playthrough. [i]Four. Hours.[/i] I swear I was not even trying to rush through the entire game. There just wasn’t a lot there. But it's so unfortunate because I really enjoyed what [b]was[/b] there.

As far as gameplay goes, the zombies don’t go down quite like they did in RE2. They seem to take many more hits to the head to drop, and don’t stagger nearly as often to allow you to slip by to conserve ammo. It seems to be deliberately done to encourage use of the new dodge mechanic, which I have to admit is a little clunky. Sometimes zombies will lunge at you and you’ll get hit despite dodging because the game decided you didn’t dodge correctly. Sometimes the direction you dodge seems important, but other times it seems up to chance whether you get hit or not. This applies doubly so in boss fights.

Nemesis encounters in the early game are pretty cool. He definitely fights harder than Mr. X in RE2, and you’ll definitely need to take advantage of the environment to avoid him. Sometimes though he will do things that rub me the wrong way. For example, you’ll look back behind you and he’ll be a good 30 or 40 feet away, and then in the time it takes for you to pan the camera to look in front of you again, he’ll have mastered time and space and drop down in front of you with no logical way to have ended up there that fast. 

All in all, this just feels like such a missed opportunity. I enjoyed what was here, and enjoyed my time playing it, I just feel like for what the money I spent there should have been so much more to it. I feel like the big argument there is going to be “Well technically for the money you spent you bought two games, so the remake obviously had a lower budget than if it came out as a standalone release.” And I feel like that is a fair point. But with how little we got, I can’t help but feel a little salty about my purchase. This feels like it should have been a $15 DLC expansion for RE2. 

Finally, I honestly can’t comment on Resistance. I wasn’t very interested in it before launch, and now all I can see when I look at it is a leech that took development time away from making this remake better. It honestly feels like Resistance is the game they wanted to make, but knew it wouldn’t sell well on its own, so they had to bundle it with a remake of Resident Evil 3 to push sales. Maybe it’s good, maybe not, but it isn’t my kind of game anyway.

Lemmie preface this before my wall of text, the RE3 remake is not by any means a bad game, however, if you're going into the RE3 remake expecting the same length and replayability of RE2 remake, you're in for a bad time. 
  
   Even though they're priced the same, there's not nearly the same amount of content in this one. With a lack of alternate routes and no side modes, there's little reason to go back and play the main story again, aside from revisiting the same areas of the game with key items and weapons you can buy from the store, which is unlocked after the end of the game.

   The atmosphere is arguably more beautiful with an an abundant use of volumetric lighting and light rays illuminating the dark streets and alleyways of Raccoon City. Audio is about on par with RE2, but has issues with Nemesis when he's after you. Speaking of that mean ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, he doesn't have the same overbearing presence that the Tyrant did in RE2, as the only times he's actively after you is in scripted chase scenes, and when duck into a safe room, instead of walking away, he simply puppyguards the entrance, waiting for you to poke your head out. 

    The newly introduced dodge mechanic is very handy, also too handy, making it where in most situations, it isn't worth it to fight zombies, leading to an abundance of ammo. But with this excess ammo, it just doesn't feel good to place a round into a zombie's head, it has no weight, the zombies don't flinch nearly as much as they did in RE2 making it seem like your trusty sidearm is nothing more than a mere peashooter. 

    RE3 is still a fantastic game, but there just isn't a whole lot there to take in, the main story took me about 5 hours to complete, while I took my time back tracking for goodies that I would eventually never use. Overall, it's a good game, but I just can't justify spending full price for the currently provided experience, maybe if there was post game content or alternate paths like in the original game, I would say otherwise

[h1]Another Resident Evil game without survival or horror[/h1]

This is an embarrassing step back from RE2 and the original RE3. As many reviews mention, the amount of cut content is staggering, but the biggest problem is that what's there is either bad or mediocre. The storyline and dialogues are aggressively bad. Sure, the original trilogy had plenty of cheesy dialogues, but they got all the story-telling beats right, while this one makes everyone sound both whiny and overwhelmingly smug at the same time, and rushes you through the story from beginning to end.

Most of it is incredibly linear. The starting area is the most open part, and it's still tiny and extremely gated. For some reason, a large percentage of items are inside "piñata crates", which only serve the purpose of wasting a bullet if you don't carry the knife with you. You will swim in ammo, and the game fails to have any atmosphere (and uses "scary violins" to an eccessive degree, where are good soundtracks these days?).

There are too many dialogues and cutscenes, which often repeat the same themes or info (I can't believe how many times Jill is chased in a cutscene full of explosions and falls, seems like Uncharted or modern Tomb Raider). Everything is spoon-fed to you.

Combat is also atrocious. The Nemesis has a few attacks that can stun-lock you to death (giving you only a fraction of a second to open the menu, which means you'll probably mash, open and then instantly close the menu, and then die). Particularly fun is if there are zombies around and you get hit, shoved into a bite, and hit again during the bite animation, killing you (3 hits is usually all it takes to kill you).

The dodge is spotty, and inconsistent, outside of the Nemesis. Many enemies either run or teleport when you aren't looking at them, covering distances that are simply impossible with their usual meandering.

I could go on and on, but at this point I am too disappointed to care. RE2 remake had its issues, but at least it was enjoyable, here dying for a minor mistake is the norm, you are pitted against zombies in large areas (which does them no favors), and everything generally feels clunky and uninspired. As soon as they stray more from the originals, it becomes evident that Capcom has no idea of what to do to make a good survival horror.

If you’re a newcomer to this part of the Raccoon City saga, you’re going to love this game. Or if you didn’t like the story in the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis, this might finally do the September 28th-October 1st romp some justice for you. But if you’re like me and you loved the OG RE3, you might just be in for a big disappointment.

Resident Evil 3: Nemesis was tied with Resident Evil 2 for my favourite classic entry in the series, so it was a given that RE3R would dissatisfy me, right? No actually. RE2R didn’t dissatisfy me at all; it took all that made the original great and made it better, fleshed-out the story more than I could’ve ever hoped for. But what the hell is RE3R all about? RE2R followed the original narrative closely and faithfully, but RE3R is just a gigantic mess.

So many story elements have been cut from the remake, along with the majority of the fun logic puzzles; several tedious lever-pulling, fuse-switching and battery-pushing tasks take the place of said puzzles, to great disappointment. The characters aren’t terrible (except for some very pointless cameos from RE2R) though several were underused for sure, and Jill misses out on a lot of character growth that she experienced in the OG RE3. And now, the biggest issue, at least for me - the pacing.

The story moved far too quickly, all the acts seemed to blur together, especially with the cut plot elements/areas, when compared to OG RE3, and it was all over in a matter of hours. I’m also highly critical of the play style, the game felt far too much like RE6 for my liking, too much emphasis on action/shooting, rather than survival horror. The only real horror parts, were the appearances by Nemesis, and these “jump scares” were really overcompensating for the lack of an authentic horror feel in the game.

Nemesis himself is very disappointing, he’s like Spider-Man, disappearing into the sky, using his tentacle as a grappling tool, only there are no really tall buildings to speak of, so he just looks like superman taking off. And then when he comes back down, he’s like something out of Titanfall, just falling straight down out of the clouds in front of Jill.

Capcom, you got Resident Evil 2 Remake so so right, so my question is, on the back of its success, how the hell did you get Resident Evil 3 Remake so so wrong? Thank you so much for giving us back real Resident Evil in 2019, only to turn around and take it away again the following year.

This game isn't worth it. I had fun with it but you can tell it was made in just over a year. 
There's so much content missing from this game compared to the original and the game is very linear compared to the RE2 Remake. This thing just feels rushed.

My first playthrough was only 4 hours with 1 hour of that being cutscenes.
As it is currently, this game at best should've been a 20-30€ DLC to RE2 Remake.
But even as such I don't think this cliffnotes remake of RE3 would've really gone over any better.

I also really dislike that because the game is already so short, with only a single route that is split between two playable characters, Jill and Carlos, you don't get this same sense of scope and grandeur that you'd get from the other entries excluding RE6. You're not going on a journey here with a single survivor and sticking with them for 8 to 10 hours as you guide them to safety. I more feel like I had just played through a trailer for a game.

But I could've been okay with the short length. After all Resident Evil games are meant to be replayed. Yet they also managed to ruin that aspect too. The earlier entries would invite you to master the game. See if you can beat it on a harder difficulty, maybe you can do it faster this time too. Beating these challenges would then reward you with infinite rocket launchers and the like. Unlocking them felt like a badge of honor. But here, after beating the game you now unlock shop where by beating the game several times nets you coins that let you unlock the rewards in any order you want. Not only does this shop spoil all the rewards you can unlock, it also makes them feel less special since now skill can be replaced with just grinding for coins. It's this that killed my interest to immediately start the game over once I beat it. That and the scripted chase scenes that I forgot to mention earlier which look cool but don't add much of anything to the game and only serve to highlight how linear it is.

There are also no other unlockable modes to speak of. Instead you get a "free copy" of Resident Evil Resistance included with your purchase but let's be real. Bundling it with RE3 Remake was the only way Capcom can hope for this game to have any legs to stand on. They probably learned the hard way with Umbrella Corps that nobody wants to buy their PvP Resident Evil multiplayer games so you might as well give them away for "free" and hope for the best. Why they can't just make a new PvE Outbreak game is beyond me.

But yeah, Resident Evil 3 Remake. Expect it to go on sale soon. It might be worth it at a very heavy discount but that's a strong maybe.

Main differences between REmake 1 and 2:

Location:
Much like the original RE3 was significantly more action-oritented than RE2, so is the case with the REmakes.
You don't spend most of the game in a single building. While RE2 had you exploring the police station and getting familiar with every nook and cranny, RE3 has you breezing through multiple city streets, business, and homes while barely taking a glance at any of them.
There is very little traversal over the same terrain.

Camera work:
The game is also much more cinematic. Lot of "run toward the screen" segments, like you would see in Uncharted.
Whereas REmake 2 put the camera over your shoulder, and for the most part just left it there.

Visuals:
People have said REmake 2 is more graphically impressive. But I think it's a bit more complex than that.
In REmake 2, you got a close look at everything. There wasn't a whole lot on the screen at any one time, so the designers could get intricate with the details. Molding every room to perfection, and making every body unique.
REmake 3 has to render a lot more. There are more explosions, buildings on fire, wide open city streets, massive facilities. So while the images individually are less impressive, there's a lot more to look at. And the specticles are a lot bigger.

Main Characters:
The protagonists are also significantly different.
REmake 2 followed Clair and Leon. One a civilian, the other a rookie cop. This was their first experience with life-threatening danger and zombies. So there is a significant difference between Clair and Leon at the start vs Clair and Leon at the end.
Jill, however, has seen all this before. Sure, giant blob monsters are new, but she knows the deal. Even Nemesis isn't completely new, she fought a Tyrant at the end of REmake 1. She even calls it Tyrant by name. There isn't as much character development, because most of her development happened between the 1st game and this one.

Tyrant:
If you were hoping Nemesis would be more of Mr. X, you'll be disappointed.
Nemesis is not Mr. X.
Mr. X was an always present, oppressive force over the second part of the game. You could always here him, and he was always in the background. He hunted you organically, searching room from room. He didn't always know where you were, and sometimes you might even get the drop on him, but you could never fully beat him. Shooting at him at all was an exercise in futility. He was an absolute predator.
Nemesis is more like the rolling bolder in Indiana Jones. He's a cinematic setpiece. He 'hunts you,' but only in scripted sections. His boss fights are pretty impressive, but therein lies the key point. He has boss fights. Multiple.
Nemesis is an enemy to be fought. Not feared. You'll run from him in highly scripted, Uncharted-esq sections until the game tells you to stop. Every one of his appearences will be announced with a cutscene, he'll never get the drop on you. In every one of his apperences, he always knows where you are, there's no hiding.

Pacing and Atmosphere:
This is probably what will make or break whether you like the game or not.
The difference between REmake 2 and 3 is night vs day.
REmake 2 put you in a single building, gave you an objective, and sent you on your way. You could spend hours trying to accomplish the same goal.
Progressing was mostly on you to do. You needed to figure out where in the police station you needed to go. Which rooms needed to be explored, which puzzles needed to be solved. Which battles needed to be fought.
In this way, almost every time you get hurt, it's kind of your responsibility. You made the calculated risk. You chose to move forward. You do it to yourself, and that's what makes it hurt.

REmake 3, on the other hand, it always pushing you in a direction.
You never spend more than an hour in a single location, or getting familiar with a place. You will always know where to go, there are no puzzles. You plan for the short-term, how to get around what's directly in front of you, rather than planning routes to travel and areas to avoid. Enemies go down in a fraction of the hits that they did in REmake 2. An RE3 zombie on Hardcore has about the same health as an RE2 zombie on Assisted. And you get access to shotguns, assault rifles, and grenade launchers incredibly early and with ammo in abundance.
You will take damage a lot more often. But you will have healing items to match it.
You'll face more enemies in a level than inhabited the entire RPD station, but you'll have enough ammo to kill every single one.
There's more adrenaline, but very little fear.
It's basically the HUNK bonus game, except stretched out to 6 hours.

And lastly, I think Resident Evil: Resistance should be destroyed.

In what ends up being a more action packed follow-up to it's predecessor, Resident Evil 3 hit's a vast majority of the marks it needs to in order to be a formidable game in the franchise. From the gut wrenching encounters with Nemesis down to the fine details of Raccoon City, I found my time with Resident Evil 3 to be mostly enjoyable albeit short.

What's sure to please fans are the nods and liberties taken from the 1999 version of the game. Plot points and connections between Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 3 are more fleshed out and cohesive. We see events unfold that explain the story in great detail, and Capcom is to be commended for not being afraid to alter the universe they created over 20 years ago. I found the reworking of the third act worked very well, and found myself thinking how much more sense it all made.

That's not to say that Resident Evil 3 isn't without issue. It's the shortest game in the entire franchise that I can remember, and while I want to equate that to me not wanting to put it down, I have to admit I was desperate for more... a lot more. Simply put, Resident Evil 3 forgoes a lot of the charm the other games carry in that it eliminates a vast majority of puzzles. Rather than wondering around the city dodging zombies while looking for clues and solving riddles, Resident Evil 3 puts a pistol in your hands and says "have at it". Don't get me wrong, I love putting a bullet in a zombie's temple, but I found that I wasn't being challenged to uncover any mystery along the way. By the time I reached the third act, I wasn't even asking questions to myself anymore and just assumed that as I progressed things would be made clear to me.

Resident Evil 3 is worth your time. For those who say the replay value doesn't exist are only saying so because Resident Evil 2 offered multiple campaigns and a full ending upon beating the game with a 2nd play though. I'd argue that speed runners will find far more variants in Resident Evil 3 than they will with Resident Evil 2. The dodge mechanic in particular adds a level of time save that isn't seen in their other titles, making it all the more exciting to see what you can make for yourself. There's also a shop that allows you to spend currency for your next play through in order to give yourself additional advantages. To date, I've seen the game beaten in under an hour (it's common among the speedrunning community in a Resident Evil game to be sub-hour).

Resident Evil 3 will offer you challenges and a great story that ultimately will leave you wanting more, but in a good way. 

Who knows, maybe the success of this game will tilt Capcom into remaking 3 additional titles: Outbreak, Code Veronica, and Resident Evil 4. If you're a Resident Evil 4 fanboy who wants that game to remain untouched because you think it's gaming perfection, let me remind you that Ramon Salazar is still a thing, and the introduction of quick time events in video games is the true plague that came out of that game.

Gameplay wise Resident Evil 3 plays much more fast paced and skill bound than Resident Evil 2 did, bringing a requirement to make quick decisions on the use of items and ammo to the table and requiring the player to decide which items are worth using up in the next 5 seconds to stay alive.

There is a noticeable difference in the style of game play between the two games, for sure. Where RE2 brought a lot of hallways filled with zombies that you could take the time to put down one at a time, Resident Evil 3 ups the pace by providing the player enough supplies to handle any situation and then removing a lot of the time needed to use it all. You might have 45 9mm rounds ready to go at any given moment, surely enough to take care of any zombies in your path with a few head or knee shots, but you as the player will need to decide whether you have the time to do so, or if your best off moving fast and using up a few shotgun rounds to advance quickly before you are destroyed from behind.

Resident Evil Resistance Review -
I'm only recommending this game because it's a pack in title with the purchase of Resident Evil 3 Remake and cannot be purchased seperately at the time of this review. Because it's a packed in experience you'll feel obligated to play it after your short time with the main game in the package. This game feels unfinished, unpolished and is loaded with problems and balancing issues. Some of these problems can be fixed with time but the most damaging problem is the health of the game community wise for the long term. This game tries to imitate the popularity of Dead By Daylight by spicing up the formula Resident Evil style. I like that we get some nods to familiar characters of the series as villains, and some call back puzzle sets from old games. But the charm fades away quick after you figure out the game and essentially "solve" playing as the survivor. Becoming familiar with every playable environment is very easy, and it makes the game very predictable. By my 10th or so time running through as the survivor I was sprinting from spot to spot, dodging most enemies along the way with ease and finishing objectives before even my teammates knew what was going on, if they were new. The traps and zombies that the mastermind can place are trivial annoyances at best. You're never short on recovery items or ammo making it simple to move on from any hiccups to completion. This game almost feels like a "How fast can you get to the end experience" rather than "Survive the mastermind and escape with your life" which I'm sure the latter was the intended game play but the former is what we got. 

I can't say it isn't fun to play, but it does become boring after about 5 hours. I enjoyed playing the survivors and learning the masterminds different tricks while I was figuring out the game. But I'll go back to my statement of saying I "solved" the game and know how to get my team to the end with relative ease. The only times I'm failing is when everyone on my team is new or someone drops out. A big problem I had the entire time was my connection to the host, which caused lots of lag, stuttering and janky gameplay. I never dropped from a match though. A lot of other players I played with said they had a lot of lag too. And unfortunately for the mastermind this is very abusable. You can exploit a lot of attacks coming at you by taking advantage of the lag. I want to say I hope it gets better, but as Resident Evil fans know the history with RE titles and multiplayer isnt great. Looking at you, Umbrella Corps, Operation Racoon City.

1. The RE Engine is AMAZING!!! The graphics are so realistic that it's unbelievable.

1. REMOVED Nemesis's first appearance at the R.P.D. killing Brad. (Even if he was bitten, and nemesis had been already reveled, that scene had to be in game, in the original game Brad is wounded, but he's killed by the nemesis anyway.

3. Park and graveyard removal, same with Spiders and the Grave Digger.
4. After the power station, where the hell are the drain deimos???!!!!

Extreme downsides:

1. REMOVED classic scenarios (Jill at R.P.D. and the Clock tower.) - I don't get it. So many opportunities for RE2 scenes here, why not let nemesis punch those holes? we were expecting that since re2(2019) release! Before you hate on me for leaving a bad review, hear me out. 

This is a great game. It is beautiful and very well optimized and it feels like you pick up where you left off in Resident Evil 2. The problem this time around is it feels more like a DLC more than anything. 
Zombies are the same models from RE2 with a few reskins, though poorly rendered if you are too far away. 
They are bullet spongy as hell like usual so the best thing you can do is use the new quick-dodge feature that the game introduces and avoid fighting them most of the time, which I thought was a great alternative rather than having to waste loads of bullets on them. (Usually 7+ headshots on Standard difficulty unless you are lucky to trigger a critical headshot). 
There are no puzzles this time around, only 1 or 2 throughout the whole campaign that aren't complicated to figure out at all.

Now that that is out of the way, let's talk about Nemesis....
They tried to create something worse than Mr.X and they suceeded, not in the good way though. 
Not only will he constantly appear to "chase" you, but he isn't even a threat to you. With Mr.X you know that you won't be able to stop him unless you have a flashbang or grenade to stun him, with Nemesis, you can literally just dodge him or shoot him until he leaves and after about 1/3 through the game, he won't even chase you anymore and he will just turn into another boss that you fight 2 or 3 more times before the game is over, making the first part of the game that introduced him as a scary big boi you have to run away from, pretty pointless. 

Finally, the length of the campaign. Now we all know, Resident Evil 3 wasn't going to be as long as Resident Evil 2, the original wasn't either. But here we are looking at a 60€ game that offers you roughly 5 hours of content if you take your time to collect all loot and collectibles in your playthrough. To me, that doesn't seem fair for the pricetag. If you are all in it for the story, this is a great game that offers quite the cinematic experience, but if you are here for a game you can play for hours and hours at a time with loads of replayability, you might want to look for something else.

[h1]Overview[/h1]
[b]Resident Evil 3[/b] is a remake of the original 1999 game with the same title. However, it is not a 100% accurate recreation of the original, more like a re-interpretation, since several mechanics and chapters have been changed significantly compared to the original. RE3 takes place in the dreaded Raccoon City, where a virus engineered by Umbrella Corporation got out of control, unleashing death and mayhem upon all. Players impersonate STARS agent Jill Valentine, and also Umbrella agent Carlos in other chapters, living their parallel stories as they try to escape the madness of a doomed city.

🟩 [b]Pros[/b]
[list]
[*]Absolutely exceptional graphics, animations, effects and art direction. Raccoon City never looked better.
[*]Excellent gameplay system that merges together classic Resident Evil mechanics with modern twists.
[*]Very good challenge level on Hardcore difficulty, with tough and deadly enemies aplenty. Efficiency is key.
[*]Tough bosses: on the hardest setting you WILL need to save up as much as you can to defeat them.
[*]The multiplayer spin-off Project Resistance is included with the game, for those interested.
[/list]
🟥 [b]Cons[/b]
[list]
[*]Ink Ribbon saving was completely removed. Old-school fans of this mechanic may not like this change.
[*]The dodge / counter-attack mechanic is not always reliable, can get you killed sometimes even if you timed it right.
[/list]
[h3]Rating: Excellent[/h3]

On the good side, RE3 Remake has much to boast. First of all, as already seen with RE2 Remake, Capcom delivered again an amazing quality visually speaking: from highly detailed models to realistic textures, animations and art direction of environments, Raccoon City is a sight to behold. This added to the nostalgia of fans is a mix as good as Red and Green herbs. The gameplay merges well tested mechanic of the series with reworked ones: for example there is a dodge / counter system that works in a way not seen before, while the crafting and combat stay true to the series' usual.

Challenge level on the hardest setting, Hardcore, is definitely solid as even the lowliest enemies will take few hits to kill you, while more dangerous ones can outright 1-shot you at full health. Resource conservation and avoiding unnecessary fights become pillars of gameplay, as resources will be needed mostly for the tough boss fights ahead. Nemesis proves to be lethal as ever, with both chase sequences and boss encounters against him, each time in a different form.

On the bad side instead, the complete removal of Ink Ribbons even on the hardest difficulty will surely upset the most veteran fans of the original RE3, making it an ON/OFF option would have been a better compromise. The reworked dodge / counter mechanic is powerful but especially with Carlos it proves to be unreliable and will get you damaged or even killed several times, which can be frustrating. 

[b]Overall RE3 Remake is an excellent modern transposition of a cult classic, even if it's not an exact 1:1 replica, it still manages to deliver the atmosphere, feeling and satisfying gameplay elements that make the series great. Playtime greatly differs by approach, difficulty and skill: it took me 9 hours to complete the game on hardcore, and fully explore every location very accurately. This time may be less, with lower difficulty and/or if you choose to be less thorough with item collecting and secondary areas.[/b]

[h1]In-Depth Breakdown[/h1]
🎮 [b]Gameplay Analysis[/b]
The gameplay is divided into Exploration, Combat, Character Management and Puzzles.

[b]Exploration[/b]
Is done on foot, and in this RE compared to other chapters is more linear especially early on. In each chapter there are several areas barred off by some kind of obstacle such as locked doors, chains, fire and so on: finding the right tool to unlock them is essential to progress. being thorough pays off, as each non-mandatory area often holds extra ammo, resources and healing items you will surely need later on, especially in boss fights.

Other than that, there are some collectibles to destroy and secondary puzzles for extra rewards. While exploring, certain areas can spawn new enemies or change their layout based on what happens, so the path you're used to might not always be there later on. However each area has a finite number of enemies, they do not respawn under normal circumstances.

[b]Combat[/b]
In RE3 Remake is a bit more faster paced than what seen in RE2 Remake. While normal zombies are as slow as ever, other enemy types and bosses are often fast and deadly, and this is where the dodge / counter mechanic comes in. By pressing Space or Right Click at the right time, it is possible to completely dodge (or deflect, with Carlos) an enemy attack, to then counter it in a slow-motion fashion that helps you aiming. If done right it can be powerful but the timing feels off and inconsistent, not much reliable especially with Carlos. 

There are various weapons from pistols to grenade launchers, each has a distinct feel and adapts better to specific situations (elite enemies, single enemies, groups of enemies...), all of them can be modded if you happen to find the right mods, often hidden behind secondary puzzles. Ammo is sometimes of different types, as in the grenade launcher, with different effects. Enemies hurt like hell and even the weakest ones will be a serious threat. Boss fights have multiple phases and attack patterns, and are very challenging.

[b]Character Management[/b]
Is done via the inventory panel, which stops time when opened. There you can organize items, most occupy one slot while some two. Combining materials to save space and obtain better items, such as ammunition or herb mixtures, is both efficient and recommended in terms of space. Safe rooms, scattered throughout levels, offer a safe place to save your game, stash excess items for later in the Item Box and prepare yourself for the fights ahead. Saving is unlimited even on the hardest difficulty, needing no Ink, which might upset some fans but is not a big deal in my opinion.

[b]Puzzles[/b]
Are not so many compared to other RE games, and those present never are overly difficult. Mostly puzzles are about collecting a series of items to use in a place, or inputting a sequence in the correct order. Many of them are secondary and offer great rewards, such as mods or inventory expansions.

🔩 [b]Technical[/b]
[u]PC Specs: RTX2080Ti, Ryzen 3900X, 32GB RAM DDR4[/u]
There are no stability issues, bugs or other problems to report. The game runs perfectly in 1440p, 85Hz with maxed out settings. Optimization is quite good for the graphics delivered, with fast loading times and no stuttering or popping of any type.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
RE3 Remake is overall an excellent reinterpretation of a legendary classic, both on gameplay and visual levels. A recommended purchase for fans of the series for sure, and for horror aficionados in general. It's really damn good.

This remake feels and plays different than REmake 2 did, but that doesn't make it any less enjoyable.
The dodge mechanic has been improved by leaps and bounds. It still requires precise timing and each enemy has its own timing, but once you start getting a feel for it, you'll find new ways to dodge and conserve ammo; Jill can easily dodge past a group of zombies with a few well timed rolls, and Carlos can easily eliminate zombies only with a knife by punching them into the ground.
The story is much more linear than the original RE3's was, but it's much better paced and told: the characters feel much more human and relatable than in the original.
It's quite a treat to explore Racoon City in this game; the town and other environments look incredibly and if you like trying to find all the little items and collectables, then you'll be greatly rewarded for doing so.

That being said, the game is not without its flaws: the gore and dismemberment were toned down from REmake 2, Standard Mode feels fairly easy, Nemesis isn't as present as he was in the original (but when he does show up he's still a fun challenge), and I've come across an odd glitch where, every time I load the game, it thinks I'm starting a New Game, forcing me to go through the setup menu and skip the first cutscenes, until I'm able to press Start and load my save.

Overall it's an incredible game, fun, beautiful graphics, responsive mechanics and gameplay, and a treat for fans of the original. Definitely an 8/10 for me, it would've been better with the multiple choices from the original one and a few tweaks, but it's still one of my favourite games from this year.

Resident Evil 3 is a great game that ultimately feel like a mixed bag. This is a game that wears its action game lineage on its sleeve, literally starting with an Uncharted-esque escape sequence. There are a fair few sequences like this, where you're required to just push forward to escape the Nemesis. The fact that Nemesis spent more time in scripted chase sequences than free-flowing gameplay disappointed me. I feel as if the T-103 in RE2 was a more constant threat, and a lot more memorable. That being said the fights against Nemesis (sans maybe one) are really great. 

The changes to gameplay are pretty excellent across the board. The new dodge feature has been implemented pretty well, and the new enemy redesigns are great for the most part. The best part about the game is by far the changes to most of the characters, with nearly everyone being expanded upon and made into much more interesting people. Carlos in particular pretty much steals the show. 

Something a lot of other people have asked is whether there's enough content to justify the asking price. It's maybe a six hour game for most people, though like any RE game this is replayable with weapon unlocks and higher difficulties. However, the lack of any extra modes and just one unlockable costume is pretty inexcusable. Unless you're highly interested in RE Resistance, I'd suggest getting this heavily discounted if you're the type to play a game the one time.

Warning: Vague Spoilers ahead.

So, I will start off by saying that I'm a relatively recent RE fan. I got into the series around 2017 and I've played REmake 1, REmake 2, RE7, RE4, OG RE2, and OG RE3 before getting to this game. I love and have a fair experience with this franchise, but I'm not nostalgic for it either. I'll simply say that this game is pretty good, albeit not a very robust REmake. 

I'll say one of the biggest problems with this game respective to the original RE3 its structure. Several explorable areas were cut from this game, and mostly  not for the better. Granted, some of the areas that remain are expanded a bit and one area is replaced with an alternate setting, but it's still rather distracting. Now, in contrast to the RE2 REmake last year, I have played the original RE3 before playing this game. I wanted the context of the original game in mind when going through this one. Even when I played the OG RE2 after playing its REmake, I didn't mind the few areas that were cut because they were very minor or conjoined to a more expanded area in the REmake, so it didn't feel as though that much content was lost besides the alternate A/B scenarios. It was far more noticeable in OG RE3 and it almost makes the game feel too short.

Now, the criticisms don't end here, there's still more. Another issue is that unlike the RE2 REmake, this game is less puzzle-oriented than its original counterpart. For RE2 it was the opposite. The puzzle solving in OG RE2 was more shallow than the RE2 REmake. On the opposite end, RE3 REmake's puzzles are not as complex and dense as either those found in OG RE3 or RE2 REmake.  It's not a deal breaker, but it's still disappointing. The game also has a couple of action set-pieces that are a bit evocative of RE4-6. Which is appropriate given the action-based nature of the original, but one section proves to be a bit too much.

Now lets start on the positives, what was kept. As far as I've been made aware, the random ammo and health placements are retained in this game, along with Nemesis dropping loot for taking him down. The enemy variety surpasses both RE2 REmake and the original

Now as for some other positives. The dodge mechanic is much better than in the original, though it does require practice. Nemesis is amazing, though a touch underutilized. His entrance was great and his boss fights were pretty stellar, if a bit long. The areas that were kept are very nicely designed. The game, if anything, never drags, it has a pretty breakneck pace.

Now as for the story, it's fairly close to the original, and does a good job at adding a some more depth and chemistry to the characters. This is one of other the few things I'll say that this REmake handles better than the original.

The graphics are great, all the characters look amazing and the environments are very beautiful and benefit from the extra color present than in the REmake 2. The one downgrade is that the dismemberment is not as robust as RE2 REmake. This game also ran great at 1440p, 120+fps on my GTX 1080TI paired with an I5-8600K.

The verdict: A bit disappointing as a REmake, but has just enough positives to be a great game. If I had to rank it relative to the rest of the games I've played:

Adore: OG RE3, REmake 2, REmake 1 
Really like: REmake 3, RE4, OG RE2
Like: RE7

Here's my SPOILER-FREE review of Resident Evil 3 Remake. It'll be a long read, so sit tight and enjoy.

I can't even properly put into words just how much fun I had with this game. The original Resident Evil 3 was always my favorite videogame of all time, but I never thought the Remake would be even better in literally every aspect.

Visuals and Sound: The visuals and stuff being obviusly better, I need to say this: The soundtrack is literally (somehow) even better than the original game. Unlike the Resident Evil 2 Remake soundtrack, Resident Evil 3 only took the music and remastered it with actual instruments, making them sound so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing. They put a lot of love into re-creating Raccoon City and you can tell. The atmosphere alone already makes you FEEL like you're in Raccoon City - which Resident Evil 2 Remake kind of failed to do. The boss-fight music is absolutely amazing and I'm immediately adding the final boss-fight theme to my Spotify playlist.

Characters: Every single character in the game feels realistic, loveable and charismatic, even the bad guys. Carlos finally feels like an actual main character instead of a sidekick. They made it so RE3 is no longer "Jill's game", but she actually shares it with Carlos now. I liked the way the story made you switch between the two sometimes, to see what the other one has been up to.

Gameplay: While the dodge mechanic CAN feel a little overpowered sometimes, there are enemies that will downright hand your ass to you if you try to dodge them in return. The weapons feel good and very different. Some are better and some are worse depending on what situation you're in. Nemesis also feels like the biggest threat I had yet to be chased by in any Resident Evil game. He's intimidating, cool looking and overall the best Resident Evil monster design I have ever seen so far. The game is well optimized for PC and I didn't notice any framerate issues at all through out my whole playthrough. The puzzles still feel like puzzles, but are way less tedious or nonsensical than they were in RE2 Remake.

Extras:
-The final Nemesis bossfight is one of the most epic moments in videogame history and you'll absolutely see what I mean when you get there.
-Jill goes through so much character development throughout the story of the game, which is amazing. They tried to do the same in the original RE3, but couldn't due to the limitations for cutscenes and voice acting at the time.
-I didn't agree well with some of the story changes, but they were so minor and didn't change it too much, however while I preferred the original deaths of some characters, the deaths in the Remake feel a lot more natural and logical, which is a plus again.
-Carlos has got to be one of the coolest Resident Evil characters after this Remake. I hope to see him in spin-offs or future titles like this again. Perhaps even with Jill?
-I have to say it again: The Soundtrack is absolutely magnificent. It's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ART what they did.

Note: I compared Resident Evil 3 Remake a lot to Resident Evil 2 Remake, mentioning that Resident Evil 3 is definitely the superior game. That doesn't mean Resident Evil 2 is a bad game at all. Keep in mind that Resident Evil 2 was an absolute masterpiece and if you hear me - the biggest RE nut on here, say that RE3 tops even RE2, that should say a lot about the quality of this game. The only downside is that I beat the whole game in 5 hours, but I do have to say that it felt nice regardless. The pacing was right and every part of the game actually impacted the story and I much prefer that over 9 hours of gameplay from which 4 is just backtracking or filler ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that could've just been avoided.

I waited 20 years for this remake and the waiting paid off. Resident Evil 3 was always my favorite game of all time. Now Resident Evil 3 Remake is. Amazing job again, Capcom. I can't wait for future Resident Evil projects. Thank you for the remakes of these masterpieces.

[b]I've been waiting for this game really much.[/b] I finished it in one go and I have mixed feelings about it. I can't help, but compare it to RE:2 remake in certain aspects. Graphically the game is astonishing and also very well optimized, especially compared to RE:2. Never once did it drop below 60fps for me and I didn't play it on a high end system. The game was on a very high setting. However dismemberment is no longer present in the game. You can blow off heads and limbs, but not to the awesome degree you could in RE:2. Some enemies afar have very blocky animations. This must be an RE engine thing or optimization. It was also present in RE:2. As a sidenote: disable screen space reflections. You'll be doing yourself a favor. It looks disgusting in most cases and on a lot of surfaces. Really, see for yourself.

The game is mostly fast paced and you won't be doing a lot of backtracking, unless you're like me and you want to pick up every item there is. I played on Standard difficulty first and it wasn't too much of a challange. There were times I had so much ammo, it couldn't fit in my pockets and I obliterated almost all enemies. I died a few times against hunters or in boss fights, but once I figured those out, it was a breeze.

This time there's only one playthrough, just like it was with the original and that's fine. The game's length is typical of most resident evil games. It took me about 6-7 hours the first time, taking it slow and exploring every corner there is.

[b][i]My greatest disappointment was[/i][/b] the fact that three of my favorite areas were just simply replaced by others. [i]There's no Clock Tower, no Raccoon City Park and no Dead Factory![/i] There are other areas instead. I feel that there were a lot of places, where the developers simply re-used a lot of assets from RE:2 by modifying them a little. This'll be very apparent in the final area of the game.

There is however a lot of fan service in the game, which is a huge upside. You'll notice if you know the original inside out. 

All in all, this is a very decent game and it's definitely worth playing, if you're a fan of the series. My first game in the series was RE3: Nemesis on the PS1, so I have fond memories of the original. Honestly, I don't know if I'll be completing it as much as I did that. But it's worth a shot if you liked RE:2 remake.

Oh and Resistance is neat, give it a try as long as you're willing to actually learn the mechanics.

[h1] Resident Evil 3 [/h1]

Way too many things were cut from the original game to excuse how unbelievably short this game is. The story was [i] fine [/i]. Just barely. It served the purpose of wrapping up RE3 and tying up the two Raccoon City remakes. It felt even more rushed than RE2's story (which I didn't even think was possible but hey, here we are) and mostly boiled down to set-pieces spaced out by busy work. You have action packed set-piece sequence #51472 and then you stop in an area to travel all around it to get a key item to continue. Rinse and repeat. There is no sense of exploration, no sense of turning over every stone to get supplies to help you because unless you're playing on the two "super duper hard difficulties" you only unlock after beating the game, the game is piss easy even on Hardcore. The only times I even died was to one enemy's instant kill attack that's pretty cheap but excusable. The dodge is easily abused anyway to get some quick, free kills. And after the campaign? Any replayability at all? No. Not even close. You have unlockables you can purchase using points collected from challenges you can complete while playing the game and that's it. Maybe harder difficulties spice things up a little bit, moving around items inconsequentially, but the beats are the same and the paths are the same with absolutely no changes on subsequent playthroughs. This should've been a DLC for RE2 Remake. What a waste.

[b] TL;DR: [/b] Not even close to worth $60. $30 would be the absolute most I'd pay for a product like this. RE2 felt like a passion project, this seems like a rushed cash-in. Get it on sale.

Cons:
-No traditional FCA (Fixed Camera Angle)

-There's no Freeze Round in RE3 Remake, even though it was Nemesis' weakness
-FoV may look claustrophobic in 32:9 aspect ratio
-Running DirectX 12 Renderer seems to run slower than DirectX 11 which I highly recommend to run in DX 11 API for more performance
-Long-distance zombie background animation transition was rendered as low as 30 frames per second.
-Ragdoll & Gore physics have been toned down, compared to RE2 Remake
-Missing lots of puzzles and iconic locations such as Raccoon City Hall, Dead Factory, Park, Clock Tower, etc.

-No Blue Herb this time. Just Green Herb and Red Herb
-Game can be finished under 5 hours if you understand the gameplay elements, excellent resource management, time it correctly in order to execute perfect dodge/punch, 
-Gameplay was more focused on action-oriented shooter, but still retains survival horror elements
-Missing original soundtrack from RE3: Nemesis (1999)
-Unfortunately, there's no classic Mercenaries Mode included
-No Ink Ribbons in Hardcore, Nightmare, and Inferno Difficulty
-Classic outfit can only be obtained by pre-order bonus for now, but will eventually be sold as DLC in the future at certain price point.
-Incorporates Denuvo Anti-tamper DRM but don't fret, Capcom will eventually remove it in the near future

Verdict: We all knew that Resident Evil 3 (2020) was outsourced to different Japanese developer studio such as M-Two Inc., Redworks Inc., Bee Tribe Co. LTD, Buzz Co. LTD., during the development project of Resident Evil 2 (2019). For gameplay-wise, it was heavily focused on action-oriented shooter, but still retains survival horror elements which is more or less loosely inspired by RE3: Nemesis as well as RE4, RE5, & RE6. For instance, if timed-correctly as Carlos, he literally punched/parry zombies/B.O.W.s just like Chris Redfield from RE5. As for cinematic cutscene, it was inconceivably fantastic! Characters and voice acting sounded believable and passionate. What I'm very disappointed was that Capcom didn't include the original soundtrack from RE3: Nemesis (1999) as well as classic Mercenaries Mode which got replaced by online game, RE: Resistance which doesn't feel challenging and rewarding. Also, there's no memorable music which I really missed it from classic Mercenaries Mode, otherwise it doesn't keep me motivated; in other words, there's no momentum nor replayability. In addition to that, it's missing Ink Ribbon save for Hardcore mode which I don't know understand why Capcom made their decision in terms of gameplay-wise. But all in all, RE3 (2020) was an amazing action-shooter, survival horror game.

Since I haven't played the original Resident Evil 3 I can't comment on any of the cuts made from that game to this remake.
That being said, this game is structured in such a way that I didn't really feel like there were many missing pieces. A lot of transitions to different areas are accompanied by time jumps which did feel a bit annoying as I would have loved more video game to play, but ultimately it didn't damage the story. Because of the time jumps the story moves at a break neck speed and I completed my first run after a little over 5 hours having gone over almost every nook and cranny. Unlike the RE2 remake, this game only has the one campaign, so unless you are a fan of the series / you enjoy trying to achieve higher ranks, or replaying the game on higher difficulties, I recommend you wait for a sale.
If you do enjoy putting in several runs then, like RE2 remake, this game has 3 difficulties for you to tackle from the start: Assisted, Standard and Hardcore. What's new this time around is that after you beat the game on Hardcore, you unlock Nightmare difficulty which makes enemies hit even harder, has even scarcer resources and, like RE7's Madhouse difficulty, changes the placement of certain key items. Beat Nightmare and you unlock Inferno difficulty which just makes everything hit even harder and resources even scarcer. Once you beat the game for the first time you'll unlock a shop in the main menu where you can spend points you've earned from completing records challenges on helpful items that will give you an edge when tackling these new difficulties.
Now, when it comes to gameplay and tone you'll find that this one is a lot faster paced than the previous one. Not an issue for me personally as RE2 is focused more on a rookie and college student solving the mystery of what's happening and creating a tense atmosphere, whereas here it's about a member of an elite task force (with previous experience fighting zombies) trying for survival and looking to escape the city. Lore-wise, all good if you ask me. However, because of certain cuts that have been made in the technical department, which I assume was for performance reasons (limbs explode instead of fall off, no ragdolls and things like that), it does feel like this game could have used a bit more time in the oven. 

Overall I do want to say that the remake of Resident Evil 3 is still a good game, though not as amazing as the RE2 remake. Does that mean it's a step backwards? It depends on your perspective. I don't think so as both games were going for a different direction and focus. I'm a little let down by how short it is, but the game knows what it's going for with a more fast paced and action packed focus, just like the original I'm told, and it executes that very well.
