Like the original, RE3 takes a more action-oriented approach. That doesn’t mean that you won’t be solving puzzles or having a lot of eery downtimes, but when compared to Resident Evil 2, those are in less quantity here. The story also has a sense of urgency the previous one didn’t, with the (formerly) titular Nemesis posing a more involved threat than RE2’s slower, more patient Mr. X. So let’s get on with it!

(Full review - https://www.techquila.co.in/resident-evil-3-remake-game-review-pc-ps4/)

Like the last game, you’ll find most of your time wandering around darkly lit corridors or streets, trying to put together pieces of a puzzle that’ll grant you access to locked off areas. It’s a linear game, but with tons of replayability and player freedom. I played the opening area (the same one from the demo) about 5-6 times for our performance benchmarks and they weren’t the same experience always. Throughout the map, you’ll find many locked off areas or collectible chests/treasure boxes that need special equipment to access. With just the right amount of open-ends in the map design, it becomes instantly addictive to find and solve those puzzles. Oh, and shooting zombies in the head to never gets old, until you run out of bullets.

Although the game is quite linear in terms of story progression, the maps don’t strictly adhere to that. You’ll quickly find yourself memorizing map layouts and floor plans as you bounce around the streets/corridors to find the next key or weapon equipment. This is where inventory management comes back into play. Like the classic games of the past, you’ll have to consistently manage what you have in your (invisible) backpack. Be it healing herbs, keys, guns, ammo or mysterious collectibles, you’ll have to make snap decisions in the heat of battle about keeping or discarding them for the greater good.

Resident Evil 3 makes yet another case for Capcom’s immense talent in updating the classics to a modern standard. Everything from the characters to the visuals, the atmosphere and the addictive gameplay loop here reflect the original game’s big ambitions. The story here gets some nice tweaks along with the freakishly awesome design of Nemesis, which newer players will also find rewarding.

REVAMPED REVIEW to better reflect the current review climate of this game:

Before diving into the Resident Evil 3 remake review proper; you must first understand the history of Resident Evil 3 development process because in a bit of irony while the Resident Evil 2 remake went above and beyond it’s original – here, it’s sort of history repeating itself but with lesser content than the original.

So what was cut? Well a lot - too much to list here to keep it short and sweet; they favored a more linear and simplistic approach rather than going balls to the wall in this remake attempt. I wouldn't be surprise if this falls under very to mostly positive to mixed by the start of summer time.

So, for the gamers of the modern generation of gaming? What is Resident Evil 3? It is the third game in the Resident Evil 3 franchise starring another iconic RE character: Jill Valentine; you must outrun the Umbrella man-made monstrosity: Nemesis all the while escaping Raccoon City. 

Besides the audio, visuals, and intense atmosphere; what else is there? Well, that’s about it. Again it’s more of the same with a different paint job and new interior parts – there really isn’t much else the game is offering (at this current time) unless they plan to do a UBCS DLC and a sort of Ghost Survivors story thing they did with Resident Evil 2 remake where you played certain characters during the events of that horrific night. At any rate, this review is mainly for the single-player only. Why? Because the PvP mode: Resistance isn’t out yet proper and it’s more or less Dead by Daylight with a Resident Evil spin on it with only Mr. X and the zombies as the horror monsters.

That’s about it – should you buy this game? here’s my personal take:

If you wanted MORE from this remake and that should be the main focus is the "more" factor. If you want "more" as i mentioned then play the second one, wait for the third to go on sale and hopefully added DLC and a refined & tuned up multiplayer mode if you are into that sort of thing. Resident Evil 3 remake is not a bad game, I believe that the hype train was just too damn high (and the price tag) for this one after the success of the Resident Evil 2 remake – and well, we can’t win all the damn time.

I will only give it a thumbs down at this current time. And then change it when or if DLC content like Ghost Survivors from the RE2 remake is added for this game.

I wasn't necessarily the target audience to pre-purchase the new and improved RE3; I'm not certain I did the right thing or not... I never finished RE7 or RE2, but still bought this fancy-assed RE3, just in case I needed the game intro's timely meta head-trip about a intra-national quarantine via simulated pre-rendered news scenes. Wash your hands, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The masks are next to the "green herb", just to the left of the 9mm rounds.

The new engine [i]is[/i] beautiful and comparatively light on GPU resources vs. perceived graphical fidelity, which makes both me and my new 43" 4K monitor happy. In a troubling development, I was certain there would be ray-tracing options for nVidia users, though I'm not certain why.... it just seemed to make sense to me that some gorgeous ray-traced reflections and shadows would kick the sexy up a level. Of course, they're not here!  I'm probably the only person who expected this, but still. 

As far as the game play goes, the dodge mechanic alone makes it better for me, as the lack of such an option in RE2 was incredibly depressing. Anything I might say here about gameplay is somewhat suspect, since I've logged a grand total of two hours before penning this review. I will say that trying to conserve ammo and run past violent, virus-infested citizens of wherever in RE2 was annoying, but dodging is rather satisfying in RE3.

But seriously, I am sad about the lack of support for nVidia and ray-tracing, especially after reading an article about the development team really spending absurd amounts of time targeting advanced graphical options (though in retrospect, I think this was "advanced graphical options for a 4-going-on-5 year-old PS4 Pro console") around the time of the RE2 launch. Once you get used to well conceived ray tracing implementations (Control comes to mind first) it is difficult to go without it, and might very well take the visuals/effects which are so important in a narrative sense to the new RE remake family to absurd new heights. Imagine a set piece escape where you get away from insane infected grocery-store shoppers via two right turns in an alleyway, only to dead-end into an empty main street storefront back door (locked, naturally). The zomboids are nowhere to be seen after that last right, but as you're trying to break into the full-length locked door, you gradually see your next death approaching in the guise of  subtle 2-nounce reflections ray-traced in the glass door, partially obscured by your own well-lit character. I see endless possibilities for this in RE7, RE2,  and RE3.

The sound design gets honorable mentions as well, it truly conceived and executed brilliantly. The music is mostly just "appropriate" rather than spectacular, but the totality of the sound design/imaging is positive and contributes much to the atmosphere of the game. 

If you dig Resident Evil, well, you know you should already buy it. If you've never really played a RE title before, or haven't played one since 2004, maybe check out RE2 first.

After clearing the game 3 times now my views are still leaning more toward negative, but a bit more mixed. The only difficult segment of the game is the city, once you're through with this part everything is laughable. After you arrive at the clock tower the game has a point of no return, as in, once you start the boss fight you're locked into it via the autosave, that is unless you created a save before the fight. My biggest complaint isn't the game has points of no return, it's the fact it has autosave and zero ink ribbons, this is incredibly disappointing as ink ribbons are iconic in the franchise and taking them away on all settings is harsh. Also at this point, Nemesis is no longer in the city, and you're at the half way point of the game. You don't even explore the clock tower or fight the Giant Worm, adding more to the amount of content that was removed. 

You really don't need to play the game on higher difficulty settings. All special unlocks are purchased via points you get from simply clearing the game, this means you can run Assisted as many times as you want and unlock all the items. The items include unlimited ammo weapons, attack buffs, defense buffs, health regeneration, upgraded knife, Samurai Edge, ammo creation tool which was in the classic, perfect dodge buff, skins, and other items. Unlike RE2R the game removing higher difficulty rewards is even more damning as that was the reason to go and play it those settings.  

I will say the 3rd and final Nemesis fights are better then the classic, the 3rd fight is a rehash of the Clock Tower fight, except you shoot electric panels to knock him  out and follow up with free gunshots. The classic had you bait him to valves you had to open and he gets sprayed. The final fight is Nemesis in a giant mass of organs and weak points, you hit them, get the railgun and kill him. In the classic, you had to bait him in front of the railgun and blow him. These fights were improved in this and is about the only thing I can say was better, as I hated those fights in the classic. 

I really believe a lot of  the classic was gutted to make room for Resistance, RE3R is shorter than RE2R and the lack of classic content being cut, and the glaring fact Nemesis doesn't stalk you like Capcom claimed. They said he could enter safe rooms, and know where the player is at all times, and adapt to that. This isn't the case at all, since he's only present in one area, the game blocks off your routes as you progress, and spawns Nemesis at natural choke points. 

If you like the game, that's great on you and I'm happy a lot of people are getting to play this that didn't get to enjoy it in 90s. But as a Resident Evil vet, I'm sad to say, this game could have been better.

First and foremost let me state that I'm not recommending it because the game is bad, or it has wonky controls, or like my review of the demo where the game crashed, no. The game is way more refined then the demo and much more stable, it's exactly what the game should be. But I'm not recommending it based on the underlying issue that the game does less but with more. So let me explain.

I logged 104 minutes in the game so far, with a little under two hours the game is clearly doing a 180 on following the original Resident Evil 3, in such, the opening to the game is different, the sequences that lead to meeting certain characters, is also different, and so far two certain key events that happened have played out entirely different. Now when you compare this to Resident Evil 2 Remake, that game is almost identical to the classic version, with some changes, but not in the scale of RE3R. So don't expect having that same nostalgia feeling you had with RE2R.

When you peel the game back a bit, it's very clear that Capcom had two different philosophies with how they wanted to approach RE3R. At it's core, it's exactly what RE2R was, but the game deviates from how RE2R played. As Jill, you're dodging nonstop, and this mechanic is what removes the tension the game naturally creates, and shifts the game back towards the "Action Horror" style they wanted to get away from. While it's true Jill could dodge in the classic, it was much more difficult to pull off and required a bit of time to master, where as in RE3R, you hit space and the direction you want to go, dodging zombies is very easy, and is Nemesis for the most part, and you can do it whenever you want, unlike the classic. And because of that, the biggest threat in the game is weakened, Nemesis.

In the classic he was fear instilling, from his iconic S.T.A.R.S call out which he doesn't say as often or as creepy, to his ability to close large gaps, and combating required planning, he was what you played RE3 for. Now in this remaster, he doesn't look as intimidating, he flies around like Venom, he can mutate zombies, throw punch combos, and if you plan on fighting him, he falls to his knees like Mr X, and you can break his logic and cause him to unload in some cases. Capcom in the first hour put so many explosive barrels and electrical hazards in places he spawns, that you have no fear fighting him, because he can get shocked and knocked out from these traps. You have no fear of him and that's bad considering RE3 was much more tense then RE2. 

But this is just been my impressions from nearly 2 hours of gameplay, with a lot of things changed, I expect the rest of the game to be largely different, maybe in the end it will be more tense and less action. But ultimately, the game is fun, just don't expect to relive the classic game, it's much more then a fresh paint of coat, or teaching a old dog new tricks. It's revisioned not remastered.

Okay after 25 hour of actual gameplay, I will go into details and how I really feel about this game, this game feels like a whole new, it hardly represent the original, with the downgrades on gore compared to the previous remake of Resident Evil 2, making the game feel a bit stiff and raw, the game feels more like watching a movie than playing a game.

The game felt "alright" from the start up to flamethrower event which was shown in the trailer and the gameplay video, that was probably the only boss fight that I was getting intensive on it and died on it many times due to starting the game on hardcore and I was doing it blind, but after that boss fight, the game started to be rushing events like no tomorrow.

Too many content has been completely removed, the clock tower part with the puzzles it had, the park, the whole gravedigger worm boss completely removed due to "making the game realistic", at least 1 hour of game play has been removed right from the start of the game and you just meet up with brad the next 1-2 min starting the game.

Crafting ammo completely been reworked to be very simple, which is another hit but it wasn't as big, downing Nemesis isn't even worth the ammo you will waste as he won't drop anything iconic as the original, mostly 2 weapon upgrades and the rest is ammo for regular weapons.

The puzzles.. almost all the amazing puzzles that been represented in the original are gone, the entire game has only 2 puzzles that has 1 route you can always do and move on, there is no randomizing on them as well, which was super disappointing to know and see my self.

All of above is a thing and the most upsetting thing for me that really pissed me off big time is.. Nemesis crawling form or dog form, just why the heck? like is that the BEST idea you could come up with? making him run around like a dog, what the hell capcom?

I can't describe how mad I get everytime I see that form when I replay the game like I really want a mod or something to give that form more iconic look or just make it the the normal nemesis with weapons or anything, this felt like a huge insult to the fans and huge slap to anyone that even felt any nostalgia for nemesis 2nd biker form with twitching tentacles all over his body, how DARE you ruin that?

Seriously this alone killed my mood off when I saw it, not to mention beating that form was a piece of cake, I died multiple times to the flame thrower fight but this one I got it on my first try on HARDCORE difficulty like come on, are you kidding me? I just really can't swallow that form, it's so upsetting design.

The semi dead factory fight.. just like the above.. huge disappointment on that weird non sense form, BUT the final fight compared to the original was fine, I loved that fight it was fun to do and I admit I struggled on it a bit, even the mechanics was cool to do and dodging etc, still I was hoping if they sticked to the original more instead of making it an obvious fight, that fight was awesome not gonna lie.

The ending.. how you miss this good opportunity to make a bad and good ending to the game.. is beyond me, like it was right there but again WASTED opportunity.

Do I recommend this game? that's a hard question, as of right now, I really don't recommend it, there is not much to do after you beat the main campaign in the hardest difficulties, and there is no news from capcom of anything such as free dlc, or even paid dlc to add something or even a small mode to do as the mercenaries from the original which also been completely removed with no word of ever returning it back.

Amazing reinvention of Resident Evil 3! I am so glad, I am living in an era where people can play and experience this amazing journey of a game! Although, not without it's own set of faults. Personally, I enjoyed this RE3: Remake way more than RE2: Remake. However, I find both games to be amazing as a long time fan of the series!

***PROS:***
- Fluid survival horror gameplay similar to last year's RE2: Remake with some improvements like dodge and perfect dodge which adds to tense moments. I highly recommend to start your first playthrough on Hardcore mode and not Standard.

- Loved the soundtrack and use of sound effects! It really set the perfect ambience for this game. This is a major improvement over RE2: Remake as it had really quiet and dull moments in the audio department.

- The boss fights! Yes, they were not hard or super challenging but, the way they were presented just makes Jill feel awesome and a true badass!

- I never found a single dull moment in the game at all and no boring backtracking as compared to RE2: Remake.

- Nemesis is more terrifying than ever! And does not overstay in the game chasing you all the time like Mr X did. To be honest, I found it really frustrating on RE2: Remake that Mr.X keeps chasing you. Whereas Nemesis chase sequences created tense moments and fun to deal with in the game even though those sequences were too little and between.

- Many people seem to be complaining RE3: Remake to be a linear game. I totally disagree with this. This is a Resident Evil game not some open world backtracking adventure. I am glad this game has minimal amount of backtracking compared to last year's remake.

- Most importantly! You can acquire Chris Redfield's Field Combat Manual! Time to punch boulders into oblivion baby! xD

***Cons:***
- Unfortunately, almost 40% of the original game has been cut out from this remake. Which is a lost opportunity to reinvent the wheel, which they already did for the most part. I wouldn't have minded the cut, if they had only included the Clock Tower sequence from the original. But, no. Clock Tower is only teased and does not exist!

- The graphics in this game have been toned down compared to RE2: Remake. I do not understand this decision from Capcom at all! Why would you downgrade the graphics from last year? You will clearly notice this within the first 10 minutes of the game.

- Personally, I did not want to play as Carlos this game. Although, his gameplay sequences were fun, I only wanted to play as Jill.

- Little to no puzzles at all from the original. From the top of my head, there were like two super easy puzzles. That's about it.

- Whenever you are grabbed by any enemy, the quick time event seems to do nothing. I still get bitten or damaged.

- I managed to finish this game on Hardcore difficulty in about 5 hours game time max. This is with me trying to explore the game in its entirety. I wouldn't have minded this if they didn't cut 40% of the game!

I would still recommend this game at full price. Mainly because, Capcom did an amazing job with the gameplay, soundtrack, audio effects and action set pieces in this game. They cut out all the boring and frustrating parts from RE2: Remake and made this a game to enjoy! I can never judge a game with its price tag to its gameplay time as long as it has quality.

I had loads of fun playing through the story and having lots of fun on Resident Evil: Resistance multiplayer that comes along with the purchase of RE3. Which is similar to Dead by Daylight with Resident Evil flavor on top of it.

TL;dr: Decent game, terrible remake. 
If the original Nemesis was like The Terminator (aka, a ruthless killing machine), this one is like an incompetent cartoon villain, that's more interested in looking scary than actually killing you. It's absolutely dreadful what they did to the main antagonist.

As someone who liked both the original RE3, as well as the RE2 remake, this is a huge disappointment. While not being a bad game per se, it's an absolutely horrible "remake". They left out so much stuff from the original and the game feels a lot more linear, often railroading you into the only possible path to take. There is little to no exploration and Nemesis seems to just chase you in a few scripted sequences (absolutely dreadful chase sequences) and appears in very few areas otherwise.

[EDIT] To address some of the comments: 1) "hurdur, you only played 2 hours, how do you know stuff is missing?" - oh jeez, I dunno, maybe because I've played the original several times and know the general plot? Maybe because I remember Brad being killed by Nemesis, which btw is one of the most iconic scenes of the original. Now Nemesis is there from the very start of the game in a scripte chase sequence that feels like it's from one of the new Tomb Raider games and not Resident Evil and Brad dies off-screen. In fact, the entire first part of the game is way shorter and more linear than in the original and the areas Nemesis chases you through are way way smaller and there's no choices there either.
2) "Hurdur, it's a remake, not a remaster" - so what? RE2 remake was a remake too, but it managed to stay faithful to the original. If Nemesis was like Mr. X was in the RE2make, then I would be happy, but he isn't. He doesn't really chase you much in the open game like he did in the original, now most of his sections are corridor levels where you just  run away. Also, puzzles are almost completely gone, which were a big part of the original RE games. Damn, I wanted to like this game, I LOVED the RE2make and the original and I will still finish it, because might as well now that I own it, but I'm still vastly disappointed, because this game does not do the original justice AT ALL.

[EDIT2] Update after finishing the game: first off, it does get better in the 2nd half, there's a bit more Resident Evil like exploration and the level design feels a bit less railroading. However, the main point of RE3, the name-giving antagonist Nemesis, has been done awful. 90% of the time you encounter him in a) boss fights (which suck) or b) scripted chase sequences that have you running away from him in corridor-like sections. There's like 2 very short areas early on where he's after you in the normal game like he was in the original or like Mr. X was in the RE2 remake. In fact, that's what he should have been like. Like Mr. X in RE2 remake, NOT like he actually is, which made him more annoying than scary. In the original he was terrifying, because you felt he was constantly after you. He would burst through a window and then chase you through the normal areas. There's pretty much nothing like that in the remake. In fact, the Hunters are way more scary than he is. And that really shouldn't be the case in a remake of Resident Evil NEMESIS. 
So while I did get some enjoyment out of it and it's not a bad game per se, I will stick with saying as a remake, it does it's job terribly. It gets some things right, I like Jill's new look and Carlos is actually likeable this time around, it really does get a lot more wrong, most importantly the Nemesis...

[EDIT3 because why not] One thing I should mention, whoever was responsible for the soundtrack did a terrific job. Hearing the original outro theme during the credits gave me pure nostalgia chills. If only the rest of the remake had been even nearly this faithful, it would have been an amazing game...

RESIDENT EVIL 3 is a complete reimagining of the Raccoon City events. The changes are even more drastic than in RESIDENT EVIL 2 and that's where the main appeal is: the player gets to re-explore variety of familiar locations, but with an entirely different pace and experience. It's not a game made for those that wanted a carbon copy of the original, instead, it's for those that liked RE2 and wanted some more.

[h1][b]Fine Status[/b][/h1]
Boss battles are much more satisfying and far more enjoyable than they were in RE2. Instead of just running around in circles, kiting and hoping that the enemy won't hit you, you have a far more flexible dodge mechanic that can both save you and be used for offense. The original had mostly small, isolated battles that went on in a room or two, while the remake has whole segments and areas dedicated to building up suspense and fear.

One of my biggest complaints about RE2 was that fighting back against the tyrant was completely useless: it was a waste of ammo, health and time. Original RE3 (specifically on Hard Mode) had a reward system for those that could down Nemesis, providing you with unique gear and useful resources. The remake does not disappoint by rewarding the player for their ability to take down Nemesis. It's not possible to farm all items immediately, as the drops are tied to particular battles and time windows.

The dodge/counter mechanic is a mix between original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis and Resident Evil Revelations 2. While it's possible to dodge at any given time to gain some valuable distance between yourself and a creeping enemy, the real deal is the perfect dodge, which allows the player to do a powerful melee retaliation or a slow-motion aim follow-up. It's also possible to do classic dodges by just aiming shortly before being attacked and on top of that all perfect dodges give you invincibility frames. These mechanics change the odds in your favor and are your best friend if you can pull them off consistently.

Instead of ominous silence and just a bunch of suspense themes the game has a bigger focus on incorporating the soundtrack into the gameplay. You might notice familiar re-arranged themes playing in the background and it fits in well. I can't say I could pick any memorable themes from RE2 (DLC content had the best stuff), but here quite a couple of them caught my attention. The ending and credits tracks are much more impactful than anything RE2 had to offer.

Weapon audiovisual feedback has been improved as well. RE2 had fairly unappealing pea shooter sound effects, that were mere shadows of their original over the top selves. RE3 is somewhere in the middle with the handgun sounding far more adequately and the shotgun actually being a consistent, reliable weapon. General combat feel is satisfying, critical shots have extra visual oomph to them and exploding zombie flesh sounds are on point, as always.

The game has a good replay value thanks to its improved rewards system and additional difficulty levels, which offer an Arranged Mode kind of experience. I don't think that time and amount of saves should be the deciding factor for a rank and in RE2 the rank was what decided your rewards. RE3 fixes that and disconnects rewards from ranks, allowing the player to complete in-game challenges, milestones and get most of the desired rewards without being forced into speedrunning the game on highest difficulties. The rewards themselves are far more interesting and appealing than in RE2, where the scarce amount of them felt like a lost opportunity. 

[h1][b]Caution Status[/b][/h1]
The weapon selection is more or less similar to the original, except you don't get something as fancy as Western Custom M37 or EAGLE 6.0. The game goes the RE2 way of introducing your main weapons and offering upgrade parts, assuming you can find them. The lack of special weapons is a shame, but at least that can be compensated by the reward weapons.

There's a bit of a needless confusion regarding the difficulty naming schemes. In RE2 "Hardcore" was the highest difficulty, while in RE3 it isn't. My recommendation is that if you aced RE2's highest difficulty then consider doing your first RE3 play through on "Hardcore", as it's still slightly stricter Normal. In RE3's Normal the player will be swimming in ammo and it's not exactly challenging. For "Inferno", on the other hand, I would suggest investing into defense coins, because during one particular battle you will be One-Hit KO'd all the time until you master the quirky perfect dodge patterns. It's not for everyone and for an average player it would simply be better to use said coins instead of suffering through the same sequence for hours. Alternatively, rocket launcher will make things easier too.

[h1][b]Danger Status[/b][/h1]
It would seem that gore has suffered some downgrades in comparison to RE2, where shooting a limb enough times would disconnect it and drop it on the ground. Here whenever a limb gets destroyed it just vanishes, leaving a bit of goop on the ground. It's also not possible to destroy limbs of enemies that have already been downed, while RE2 gave complete freedom in that regard. Some have speculated that it's a hardware limitation due to more open world nature of the game, but I would probably bet that it was just an artistic decision, as a couple of limbs on the ground shouldn't kill your frame rate. On the other hand, there are a few scenes of "aftermath" environment, covered in blood, which looks really nice.

The checkpoint system is a bit weird, as some fall back points after the player's death are set before a string of cutscenes. It's a needless time waste to be forced to go through the same area and see the same things over and over again even if it's skippable. There's no real reason why the checkpoints couldn't been set after all the cinematics and dialogues. 

Quite a common complaint is that this game doesn't include all areas of the original. That is true, as the city progression has been altered significantly. That doesn't mean that there's less gameplay time, though. It might not include all areas, but it does offer some "new" ones and the already familiar ones are vastly different from the original. Both games rely on backtracking and that's a big bulk of the gameplay.

There's a severe lack of player outfits. Even though there are plenty of mods now, Capcom only provided 3 costumes, one of which is a pre-order bonus (now a purchasable DLC). The original had 5 costumes and Asian regions even got extra variations. Where's that Regina costume for some Dino Crisis hype?

If you wanted to fire up some Mercenaries after finishing the game then I have some bad news: by the looks of it the game doesn't have any mini-games at all and it is unknown if there's going to be any additional content in the near future, something like Ghost Survivors, perhaps?

[h1][b]PC Specifics[/b][/h1]
Same as RE2 this PC version has a very fancy graphics menu with well-described settings and tons of other submenus to tinker with. If other RE Engine games ran fine for you then this one will as well.

[h1][b]Conclusion:[/b][/h1]
The game's ending atmosphere created by the soundtrack and the audiovisually synchronized cinematic scenes left a long-lasting positive impression. It was a relief for me that Capcom didn't forget that soundtracks exist for a reason and that silence is not always the best way how to build suspense. I was also pleasantly surprised that there's actual rewards for downing Nemesis, unlike the situation with the RE2's tyrant, where downing the tyrant served almost no purpose. You could jump down the rabbit hole of "what this remake could've been" and I can agree that I would've liked to see more areas and more content, but on its own the remake's satisfying combat, dodging and the suspense did the trick for me.
